items.title: 2026 VA Disability Compensation Rate Tables (effective December 1, 2025)
items.who: Any veteran with a service-connected disability rated 0%-100% and a discharge other than dishonorable.
items.how: Rates apply automatically once rated. Payments arrive on the first business day of the month for the prior month. The next COLA (effective 12/01/2026) is announced by SSA in mid-October 2026 and applies automatically — no action needed.
items.hack: The dollar gaps are wildly uneven and that should drive your strategy. 40->50 is +$337/mo, 60->70 is +$373/mo, but 90->100 is +$1,576.28/mo ($18,915/year). Never stop at 90%. And because dependent allowances only exist at 30%+, a married veteran at 20% who gets to 30% gains $260.81/mo, not the $195.81 the veteran-alone table implies.
items.deadline: None. Rates update automatically each December 1.

items.title: 38 CFR 4.25 — The Combined Ratings Table (VA Math)
items.who: Every veteran with more than one service-connected condition.
items.value: Determines your entire paycheck. 30+20+10 = 50%, not 60% — a $302.12/month difference. A raw combined value of 64 pays $1,435.02 (60%); a raw 65 pays $1,808.45 (70%).
items.how: Order ratings high to low. Apply each rating to the remaining efficiency: 100 - 30 = 70 remaining; 70 x 0.20 = 14, running total 44; 56 remaining x 0.10 = 5.6, running total 49.6. Truncate to 49, round to nearest 10 = 50%. Round ONCE, at the end. Values ending in 5 round UP.
items.hack: Demand the RAW combined value from your rating code sheet — it is computed and printed there. If you are at a raw 62-64, one 10% secondary is worth $373/month. If you are at a raw 87-89, you are one small grant from 90%. If you are at a raw 90-94, a 10% or 20% grant is literally worth $0 — you need a single rating of 50%+ (or TDIU) to reach a raw 95 and round to 100%. Stop filing low-value claims and start filing high-value ones.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: 38 CFR 4.26 — The Bilateral Factor (free percentage points VA forgets)
items.who: Any veteran with partial disabilities of BOTH arms, BOTH legs, or paired skeletal muscles.
items.value: An extra 10% of the combined value of the paired disabilities, ADDED (not combined) before further combination. Two 10% knees combine to 19, plus 1.9 = 21 instead of 19 — and those 2 extra points are frequently what turns a raw 63 into a raw 65 and a 60% check into a 70% check ($373.43/month).
items.how: Combine the right- and left-side ratings normally, add 10% of that value, then continue combining in order of severity. VA's own example: 60, 20, 10, 10 (the two 10s bilateral) -> bilateral pair = 21 -> order 60, 21, 20 -> 60+21 = 68 -> 68+20 = 74 -> 70%.
items.hack: Read your code sheet. The bilateral factor should appear as a separate line. VA omits it constantly — bilateral knees, ankles, shoulders, plantar fasciitis, carpal tunnel, and especially bilateral lower-extremity radiculopathy secondary to a spine condition all trigger it. An omitted bilateral factor that changes the combined rating is textbook Clear and Unmistakable Error, which can be raised at ANY time with no deadline and pays back to the original effective date.
items.deadline: None — CUE has no time limit.

items.title: 38 CFR 4.14 — Pyramiding: what you can and cannot stack
items.who: Any veteran filing multiple claims from one underlying condition.
items.value: Knowing the line between prohibited pyramiding and permitted separate ratings is worth several rating tiers. Getting it wrong gets a claim denied; getting it right turns one back condition into four ratings.
items.how: The rule: 'The evaluation of the same disability under various diagnoses is to be avoided.' You cannot be paid twice for the SAME manifestation. But 38 CFR 4.25 expressly says disabilities arising from a single disease entity are to be rated separately when the manifestations are distinct.
items.hack: One service-connected lumbar spine condition properly yields: (1) an orthopedic rating for limitation of motion, (2) a separate rating for right lower extremity radiculopathy under DC 8520, (3) a separate rating for left lower extremity radiculopathy, (4) the bilateral factor on (2) and (3), (5) a secondary mental-health rating for depression due to chronic pain, and (6) a secondary GERD rating from long-term NSAID use. That is not pyramiding — those are six distinct manifestations. What IS pyramiding: two separate mental-health ratings (VA rates all psych conditions under one evaluation), or rating painful motion under both DC 5003 and a limitation-of-motion code.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: TDIU — Schedular Path, 38 CFR 4.16(a)
items.who: Veterans who cannot secure or follow substantially gainful employment because of service-connected disabilities and who meet the percentage gateway.
items.value: Paid at the full 100% rate: $3,938.58/month alone, $4,158.17 with spouse, $4,318.99 with spouse + one child. A veteran at 70% ($1,808.45) who wins TDIU gains $2,130.13/month — $25,562/year — without any change to the schedular rating.
items.how: The gateway: (1) ONE disability rated 60% or more, OR (2) TWO OR MORE disabilities with at least one rated 40% or more and a combined rating of 70% or more. Then you must show inability to secure or follow substantially gainful occupation due to SERVICE-CONNECTED disabilities only. File VA Form 21-8940 (Application for Increased Compensation Based on Unemployability); VA sends Form 21-4192 to your last employers.
items.hack: 4.16(a) lets you TREAT SEPARATE CONDITIONS AS ONE DISABILITY to clear the 60% bar: disabilities of one or both upper extremities or one or both lower extremities (including the bilateral factor), disabilities from a common etiology or a single accident, disabilities affecting a single body system, multiple injuries in one combat action, or multiple POW disabilities. Bilateral knees at 30% each + bilateral ankles at 10% each are not four small ratings — they are ONE 'lower extremity' disability that can exceed 60%. Argue this explicitly on the 21-8940; raters almost never apply it on their own.
items.deadline: No separate deadline, but TDIU is part of every increased-rating claim under Rice v. Shinseki (2009) whenever unemployability is raised by the record — so it reaches back to the date of the underlying claim, not the date you filed the 21-8940.

items.title: TDIU — Extraschedular Path, 38 CFR 4.16(b)
items.who: Veterans who are genuinely unemployable from service-connected disabilities but do NOT meet the 60%/70% percentage gateway.
items.value: Same 100% rate — $3,938.58 to $4,318.99+/month. A veteran at a combined 40% can be paid at 100% under this route.
items.how: 38 CFR 4.16(b) states it is VA POLICY that 'all veterans who are unable to secure and follow a substantially gainful occupation by reason of service-connected disabilities shall be rated totally disabled.' The rating board cannot grant it — it MUST refer the case to the Director, Compensation Service, with a full statement of the disabilities, employment history, educational and vocational attainment, and all other factors bearing on the issue.
items.hack: The regional office will simply not refer your case unless you force it. Put the words '38 CFR 4.16(b) extraschedular referral to the Director, Compensation Service' in writing in your submission, and build the record the regulation asks for: employment history, education level, vocational limitations. A private vocational expert report (typically $1,500-3,000) that ties your specific functional limitations to specific job requirements is the single highest-yield piece of evidence in an extraschedular case. If the RO decides the issue without referring, that is a procedural error you raise on Board appeal.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: TDIU Earnings Limit and Marginal Employment
items.who: Veterans receiving or applying for TDIU who work or want to work.
items.value: You may earn up to the Census poverty threshold for ONE person and still keep TDIU. The 2026 HHS poverty guideline for a household of one in the 48 contiguous states is $15,960 — the figure most commonly used as the working benchmark. Earning under that is 'marginal employment' and does not defeat TDIU.
items.how: 38 CFR 4.16(a): 'Marginal employment shall not be considered substantially gainful employment.' Marginal employment generally exists when earned annual income does not exceed the Census Bureau poverty threshold for one person. Critically, the regulation ALSO says marginal employment may be held to exist on a facts-found basis even when earnings EXCEED the poverty threshold — specifically where employment is in a protected environment such as a family business or sheltered workshop.
items.hack: Three things consultants charge for. (1) Only EARNED income counts — investment income, rental income, retirement pay, SSDI, and your VA compensation itself do NOT count against you. (2) The 'protected environment' clause is the loophole: a job where your brother-in-law tolerates you missing 10 days a month is not substantially gainful no matter what the W-2 says. Document the accommodations in writing from the employer. (3) VA no longer routinely mails the annual Form 21-4140 employment questionnaire but still cross-matches your earnings against Social Security wage data — an unreported job that crosses the threshold produces a retroactive overpayment demand plus a fraud referral. Report the work, then argue marginality.
items.deadline: Report any return to substantially gainful employment promptly. VA may terminate TDIU only after 12 continuous months of substantially gainful employment (38 CFR 3.343(c)).

items.title: TDIU vs 100% Schedular — the tradeoff nobody explains
items.who: Veterans choosing which route to pursue, or already on TDIU considering more claims.
items.value: Identical monthly money ($3,938.58 alone). Radically different rights.
items.how: TDIU pays AT the 100% rate but your schedular combined rating stays where it is (e.g., 70%). 100% schedular means the ratings themselves combine to 100%.
items.hack: Four practical differences worth real money. (1) EARNINGS: 100% schedular has NO income limit — earn a million dollars, keep every cent. TDIU caps you at marginal employment. If you can work, chase schedular. (2) PERMANENCE: both TDIU and schedular 100% can be P&T or not; CHAMPVA, Chapter 35 DEA and Space-A require P&T, not the raw 100%. (3) SMC-S: a 100% SCHEDULAR rating on one condition plus separate 60% gets you statutory housebound SMC-S at $4,408.53 — $469.95/month more than 100%. TDIU can also anchor SMC-S under Bradley v. Peake if the TDIU is based on a SINGLE disability, so always ask VA to specify which condition supports TDIU. (4) STATE BENEFITS: a minority of states require '100% schedular' for property tax exemption and will reject TDIU. Even after winning TDIU, KEEP FILING for increases until you reach 100% schedular.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: VA Form 21-8940 — Application for Increased Compensation Based on Unemployability
items.who: Any veteran claiming TDIU.
items.value: The form that converts a 70% check ($1,808.45) into a 100%-rate check ($3,938.58).
items.how: Lists your service-connected disabilities that prevent employment, your employment history for the last five years, your education and training, and the date you last worked full time. VA then sends VA Form 21-4192 (Request for Employment Information) to each employer listed.
items.hack: Three landmines. (1) The form asks the 'date you became too disabled to work' — put the EARLIEST defensible date, because that drives the effective date and the back pay, and VA will use whatever date you write. (2) It asks for education and training. Downplaying nothing is fine, but be aware VA uses high education to argue you are employable in sedentary work; pair the form with a vocational opinion. (3) If an employer never returns the 21-4192, VA will sit on the claim. Get the employer to complete it yourself and submit it with the 21-8940 — that alone routinely cuts months off the decision.
items.deadline: No filing deadline, but under Rice v. Shinseki TDIU is part of an increased-rating claim whenever the record raises unemployability — so file it WITH your increase claim to capture the earlier effective date.

items.title: SMC-K — $139.87/month for loss of use of a creative organ (the most-missed benefit in VA)
items.who: Any veteran, at ANY rating from 0% to 100%, with loss or loss of use of a creative organ, a hand, a foot, one eye, voice, or both ears.
items.value: $139.87/month added on top of everything else — $1,678/year, tax-free, for life. Stacks with 100%, with TDIU, and with other SMC levels. VA pays up to three K awards on top of the basic rate.
items.how: 'Creative organ' means reproductive function. Erectile dysfunction, testicular atrophy or removal, hysterectomy, removal of an ovary, or loss of a breast all qualify. The underlying diagnostic code (e.g., DC 7522 for ED) is usually rated 0% — the 0% rating does not matter. SMC-K is a separate statutory payment, not a percentage.
items.hack: This is the classic consultant play: erectile dysfunction is extraordinarily common as a SECONDARY to service-connected PTSD/depression (SSRIs cause ED), to diabetes, to hypertension medication, and to lumbar spine conditions with nerve involvement. File ED as secondary, get the 0% rating under DC 7522, and VA must then award SMC-K. Most veterans never file because '0%' sounds worthless. The rating is worthless; the SMC-K is $139.87/month forever. Same logic for a service-connected-condition-related hysterectomy or mastectomy.
items.deadline: None. Back pay runs from the date of the ED/creative-organ claim (or an Intent to File).

items.title: SMC-S (Housebound) — $4,408.53/month, $470 more than 100%
items.who: Veterans with one 100% disability plus separate 60%, OR who are substantially confined to their home by service-connected disability.
items.value: $4,408.53/month alone, $4,628.12 with a spouse. That is $469.95/month ($5,639/year) MORE than 100% schedular, and it is routinely never awarded because nobody asks.
items.how: Two paths. STATUTORY: a single disability rated 100% (schedular, or TDIU based on one condition per Bradley v. Peake) PLUS additional separate service-connected disabilities that independently combine to 60% or more, with no overlap with the 100% condition. FACTUAL: permanently and substantially confined to your dwelling and immediate premises by service-connected disability.
items.hack: The statutory path is pure arithmetic and VA is legally required to grant it on its own motion — and constantly does not. Pull your code sheet. If ONE condition is at 100% (say, a respiratory condition or a mental health condition at 100%), add up all your OTHER ratings using the combined table, ignoring the 100% condition. If they reach 60, write VA and demand SMC-S under 38 CFR 3.350(i). If you are on TDIU, first get VA to specify in writing WHICH single disability supports the TDIU — Bradley then lets that TDIU serve as the '100%.' This one letter is worth $5,639 a year.
items.deadline: None, and a failure to award SMC-S when the math was plainly on the face of the decision is a strong CUE claim reaching back to the original effective date.

items.title: SMC-L through SMC-O — the Aid & Attendance ladder ($4,900.83 to $6,877.12)
items.who: Veterans with anatomical loss or loss of use of extremities, blindness, or who need regular aid and attendance of another person.
items.how: SMC-L is the gateway: loss/loss of use of both feet, or one hand and one foot, or blindness both eyes at 5/200, or permanently bedridden, or in need of regular aid and attendance. Each higher letter reflects a more severe combination of anatomical losses. Half-steps (L-1/2, M-1/2, N-1/2) are intermediate rates under 38 CFR 3.350(f) for combinations that exceed one letter but do not reach the next.
items.hack: 'Loss of USE' does not require amputation. The legal test is whether any function remains beyond what an amputation stump with a prosthesis would provide. A foot with complete drop, no dorsiflexion, and no useful propulsion is loss of use of a foot even though the foot is attached. Get an examiner to answer that exact question in those exact words. Also: 'regular aid and attendance' for SMC-L does not require a paid caregiver or 24-hour care — needing help with bathing, dressing, feeding, toileting, or protection from the hazards of the daily environment is enough, and a spouse providing it counts.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: SMC-R.1 and R.2 — $9,826.88 and $11,271.67/month
items.who: Veterans entitled to SMC-O (or the maximum under L-N) who also require the regular aid and attendance of another person.
items.value: SMC-R.1: $9,826.88 alone / $10,046.47 with spouse. SMC-R.2: $11,271.67 — the statutory maximum, about $135,260/year tax-free.
items.how: R.1 requires regular aid and attendance from any person — a spouse, an adult child, a friend, unpaid. R.2 requires a HIGHER LEVEL of care: personal health-care services (physical therapy, wound care, catheter or ostomy care, medication administration) provided daily in the home by a person under the REGULAR SUPERVISION of a licensed health-care professional, and without which you would require hospitalization or nursing home placement.
items.hack: The gap between R.1 and R.2 is $1,444.79/month — $17,337/year — and the only difference is professional supervision of the caregiver. If your spouse already performs wound care, catheter care, or medication administration, get a VA or private home-health RN to establish a written plan of care and document periodic supervisory visits. That converts an unpaid spouse into a 'person under the regular supervision of a licensed health-care professional' and satisfies R.2. Most families provide R.2-level care and are paid at R.1 because no one documented the supervision.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: SMC-T — $11,271.67/month for TBI requiring in-home aid and attendance
items.who: Veterans with service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals needing regular aid and attendance, who would otherwise require institutional care.
items.value: $11,271.67/month — paid at the SMC-R.2 rate, the statutory maximum. About $135,260/year tax-free.
items.how: Created by the Caregivers and Veterans Omnibus Health Services Act of 2010. Requirements: (1) service-connected TBI residuals, (2) need for regular aid and attendance FOR THE TBI RESIDUALS, (3) not eligible for a higher level of SMC, and (4) in the absence of in-home aid and attendance you would require hospitalization, nursing home care, or other residential institutional care.
items.hack: SMC-T is the single easiest route to the maximum SMC rate, because unlike SMC-R.2 it does NOT require the caregiver to provide professional-level health-care services or be under professional supervision. A spouse providing supervision, cueing, and protection from environmental hazards for a TBI veteran satisfies SMC-T. If you have moderate-to-severe TBI residuals with cognitive impairment and a family caregiver, and you are being paid at 100% or R.1, you are potentially leaving $7,333/month on the table. Ask for an SMC-T-specific examination — the standard TBI DBQ does not capture the institutional-care element.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: 38 CFR 3.310 — Secondary Service Connection (including aggravation)
items.who: Any veteran with an established service-connected condition that causes or worsens another condition.
items.value: The highest-yield claim type in the entire system. Every secondary rating stacks into the combined rating and can move you across a rounding cliff worth $300-1,600/month.
items.how: 'Disability which is proximately due to or the result of a service-connected disease or injury shall be service connected.' You need three things: (1) the primary condition is already service-connected, (2) a current diagnosis of the secondary condition, and (3) a medical NEXUS linking them. You do NOT need to prove the secondary condition started in service.
items.hack: The aggravation clause in 3.310(b) is the sleeper. You can get service connection for the WORSENING of a completely non-service-connected condition if a service-connected condition made it worse. Example: pre-existing non-service-connected obesity aggravated by service-connected knee disability that prevents exercise. To win it you must establish a BASELINE level of severity before aggravation — get a medical opinion that states the baseline, the current level, and subtracts natural progression. VA almost never develops the baseline on its own, which is why aggravation claims get denied; supply the baseline yourself.
items.deadline: None. Effective date is the date of the secondary claim (or Intent to File), not the date of the primary grant.

items.title: Sleep apnea secondary to rhinitis, sinusitis, PTSD, or weight gain
items.who: Veterans with service-connected chronic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, deviated septum, PTSD/depression, asthma, or GERD who have a diagnosed sleep apnea requiring CPAP.
items.value: 50% under DC 6847 if a breathing assistance device (CPAP/BiPAP) is REQUIRED — $1,132.90/month standing alone, and a 50% rating is large enough to move a raw 90 to a raw 95 and produce a 100% combined rating. 30% for persistent daytime hypersomnolence; 0% if asymptomatic with documented sleep disorder breathing.
items.how: Two elements. First, a SLEEP STUDY with a diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnea and a prescription stating CPAP is required — VA will not grant 50% on a sleep study alone, the record must say the device is required. Second, a nexus opinion tying the OSA to the service-connected condition.
items.hack: Chronic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis are PACT Act burn-pit PRESUMPTIVES for anyone who served in the covered locations after 8/2/1990 or 9/11/2001. That means a Gulf War or post-9/11 veteran can get chronic rhinitis service-connected presumptively (often 10-30%), then claim sleep apnea SECONDARY to the rhinitis at 50%. That is the most valuable two-step in the modern system. The nexus theory the medical literature supports: nasal obstruction increases upper-airway resistance and negative inspiratory pressure, worsening pharyngeal collapse. For PTSD-secondary OSA, the supported theories are sleep fragmentation, medication-induced weight gain, and REM-sleep disruption. Have the opinion address the specific mechanism, not just 'as likely as not related.'
items.deadline: None — but file an Intent to File the day you get the sleep study to lock the effective date.

items.title: Radiculopathy secondary to a service-connected back or neck condition
items.who: Veterans with a service-connected lumbar or cervical spine condition who have numbness, tingling, shooting pain, or weakness in the legs or arms.
items.value: Each extremity is rated separately. Sciatic nerve (DC 8520): 10% mild, 20% moderate, 40% moderately severe with marked muscular atrophy, 60% severe with marked muscular atrophy, 80% complete paralysis. Two legs at 20% each plus the bilateral factor adds about 38 points of raw value on top of the spine rating.
items.how: You need (1) the spine condition service-connected, (2) objective findings — an EMG/nerve conduction study, or documented decreased sensation, diminished reflexes, or positive straight-leg raise, and (3) a nexus, which for radiculopathy is usually automatic because it is an expected neurological manifestation of the spine disability.
items.hack: This is NOT pyramiding and VA is required to rate it separately — the General Rating Formula for the spine expressly says to evaluate any associated objective neurologic abnormalities separately under an appropriate diagnostic code. Most veterans with a rated back condition have never claimed the radiculopathy. Then remember the bilateral factor applies to the two lower extremities, adding 10% of their combined value. A 40% back + 20% right leg + 20% left leg with bilateral factor lands around a raw 63-65 — which is the difference between a 60% and a 70% check.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Depression / anxiety secondary to chronic pain or physical disability
items.who: Veterans with any painful or limiting service-connected physical condition who have depressive or anxiety symptoms.
items.value: Rated under the General Rating Formula for Mental Disorders: 0%, 10%, 30%, 50%, 70%, 100%. A 50% or 70% mental health rating is usually the largest single rating a veteran can add, and is frequently the rating that pushes a raw 80s value past 95 to 100%.
items.how: Need (1) a current psychiatric DIAGNOSIS from a qualified provider (psychiatrist, psychologist, or in VA practice a licensed clinical social worker's diagnosis is generally accepted for the claim, though a doctoral-level opinion is stronger), and (2) a nexus opinion that the depression is proximately due to or aggravated by the chronic pain and functional limitation of the service-connected condition.
items.hack: Three things. (1) VA rates ALL mental health conditions under ONE evaluation — you cannot stack PTSD and MDD. So if you already have PTSD, a depression claim is an INCREASE claim, not a new claim; file it as 'increased rating for service-connected psychiatric disability including depression secondary to chronic pain.' (2) If you do not yet have any mental health rating, this is the highest-dollar secondary available. (3) The rating criteria are about OCCUPATIONAL AND SOCIAL IMPAIRMENT, not symptom count. The 70% criterion is 'deficiencies in most areas' — work, school, family relations, judgment, thinking, mood. Document with specific examples: missed workdays, terminated relationships, panic in public. A generic 'moderate depression' note gets 30%.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: GERD and IBS secondary to medication for a service-connected condition
items.who: Veterans taking long-term NSAIDs for musculoskeletal conditions, or SSRIs/SNRIs for service-connected mental health conditions.
items.value: GERD (rated by analogy, commonly DC 7206 or 7346 depending on the current criteria): typically 10-30%, up to 60% for severe symptoms with material weight loss and anemia. IBS / irritable colon syndrome (DC 7319): up to 30% for severe with diarrhea or alternating diarrhea and constipation with more or less constant abdominal distress.
items.how: The causal chain is straightforward and well supported in the literature: chronic NSAID use causes gastric mucosal injury and reflux; SSRIs cause GI motility disturbance. You need (1) the primary condition service-connected, (2) a documented prescription history showing long-term use, and (3) a nexus opinion naming the medication and the mechanism.
items.hack: Pull your full VA and private pharmacy records FIRST and attach them. The single most common denial reason on medication-secondary claims is that the examiner did not see a long enough prescription history. Also, for Gulf War veterans, IBS is separately available as a PRESUMPTIVE 'functional gastrointestinal disorder' under the undiagnosed illness rules — file it both ways in the same claim (presumptive AND secondary); VA must consider all theories of entitlement.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Migraine headaches — DC 8100, the 50% rating and the 'prostrating attack' magic words
items.who: Veterans with migraines directly from service, or secondary to TBI, neck condition, PTSD, or medication.
items.value: DC 8100: 0% (less frequent attacks), 10% (characteristic prostrating attacks averaging one in 2 months over the last several months), 30% (characteristic prostrating attacks occurring on average once a month over the last several months), 50% (very frequent completely prostrating and PROLONGED attacks productive of SEVERE ECONOMIC INADAPTABILITY). At 50% this is worth $1,132.90/month on its own.
items.how: Everything turns on two terms of art. 'Prostrating' means you must stop all activity and lie down in a dark, quiet room. 'Severe economic inadaptability' does not require unemployment — the Court has held it means the condition is capable of producing severe economic inadaptability, including missed work and reduced productivity.
items.hack: Keep a contemporaneous HEADACHE DIARY for at least 3-6 months before the exam: date, duration, whether you had to lie down, whether you missed work, what medication you took. Bring it to the C&P exam and ask the examiner to attach it. Then get a letter from your employer or supervisor documenting missed days. A veteran with a diary showing 8 prostrating attacks a month and an employer letter documenting 3 missed days a month wins 50%; a veteran who says 'I get bad headaches a lot' gets 10%. Migraines are also a top-tier SECONDARY to service-connected TBI (38 CFR 3.310(d) presumes certain TBI sequelae), cervical spine conditions, and PTSD.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Hypertension — presumptive under the PACT Act (Agent Orange) and secondary to PTSD, sleep apnea, or diabetes
items.who: Vietnam-era and herbicide-exposed veterans (presumptive), and any veteran with service-connected PTSD, OSA, diabetes, or kidney disease (secondary).
items.value: DC 7101: 10% (diastolic predominantly 100+, or systolic predominantly 160+, or a history of diastolic predominantly 100+ requiring continuous medication for control), 20% (diastolic 110+ or systolic 200+), 40% (diastolic 120+), 60% (diastolic 130+). Most awards are 10% — $180.42/month — but it stacks and often serves as the rating that tips a rounding cliff.
items.how: PRESUMPTIVE: the PACT Act added hypertension and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) to the Agent Orange presumptive list. If you have qualifying herbicide-exposure service (Vietnam, Korean DMZ, Thailand bases 1/9/1962-6/30/1976, Laos 12/1/1965-9/30/1969, Cambodia 4/16-30/1969, Guam/American Samoa 1/9/1962-7/31/1980, Johnston Atoll 1/1/1972-9/30/1977), no nexus is needed. SECONDARY: nexus opinion linking hypertension to PTSD (sympathetic nervous system hyperactivity), to OSA (nocturnal hypoxemia and sympathetic surge), or to diabetes/nephropathy.
items.hack: The 10% criterion includes 'a history of diastolic pressure predominantly 100 or more who requires continuous medication for control.' That means if your blood pressure is now NORMAL because the medication works, you still get 10% — provided the record shows the historical readings. Pull old service treatment records and early VA notes to establish the pre-medication baseline. Veterans routinely get denied because the C&P exam shows controlled BP and the examiner never looked at history.
items.deadline: None. PACT Act supplemental claims filed on a previously denied hypertension claim can reach back — see the PACT Act effective date item.

items.title: TBI residuals — DC 8045 and the separately-ratable sequelae
items.who: Veterans with a documented in-service head injury, blast exposure, or concussion.
items.value: TBI residuals are rated on 10 facets of cognitive impairment, each scored 0-3, with the HIGHEST facet level driving the rating: level 0 = 0%, level 1 = 10%, level 2 = 40%, level 3 = 70%, and 'total' = 100%. A single facet at level 2 produces a 40% rating.
items.how: 38 CFR 4.124a, DC 8045. The ten facets: memory/attention/concentration/executive functions, judgment, social interaction, orientation, motor activity, visual spatial orientation, subjective symptoms, neurobehavioral effects, communication, and consciousness. Separately, any residual with its OWN diagnosis (migraines, seizures, vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, depression, sleep disturbance) gets its own separate rating under its own code — that is not pyramiding because they are distinct manifestations.
items.hack: 38 CFR 3.310(d) creates PRESUMPTIONS for TBI sequelae with time limits keyed to TBI severity: parkinsonism, unprovoked seizures, certain dementias, depression, and diseases of hormone deficiency following moderate or severe TBI. If you have a documented moderate/severe TBI and later develop Parkinson's, dementia, or a pituitary hormone deficiency, the regulation presumes the connection — no nexus letter required. Most veterans and many raters do not know 3.310(d) exists. Also, the 'subjective symptoms' facet alone (headaches, insomnia, irritability, dizziness) can score level 2 and produce 40%.
items.deadline: None, but 3.310(d) presumptions carry specific time limits from the TBI depending on severity — read the regulation before filing.

items.title: The nexus letter — what it must actually say
items.who: Every veteran filing a direct (non-presumptive) or secondary service connection claim.
items.value: The difference between a grant and a denial. Private nexus opinions typically cost $500-2,000; a good one on a 50% secondary is worth $1,132.90/month for life.
items.how: The legal standard is 'at least as likely as not' — 50 percent probability or greater. Under 38 U.S.C. 5107(b) and 38 CFR 3.102, when the evidence is in equipoise, the benefit of the doubt goes to the veteran. A nexus letter must contain: (1) the author's credentials and specialty, (2) an express statement that the author REVIEWED the claims file / service treatment records / relevant medical records, (3) the current diagnosis, (4) the opinion in the magic words 'at least as likely as not (50 percent or greater probability),' and (5) a RATIONALE citing medical literature or clinical reasoning that explains the mechanism.
items.hack: Rationale is everything. The Board rejects conclusory opinions from both sides, but VA examiners' negative opinions survive when they have rationale and yours does not. Never accept a letter that says only 'it is at least as likely as not related.' Require your provider to name the MECHANISM — 'nasal obstruction from chronic rhinitis increases upper airway resistance and negative intrapharyngeal pressure during inspiration, promoting pharyngeal collapse and obstructive events' — and cite at least one peer-reviewed source. Also: your treating provider's opinion carries more weight than a paid one-time reviewer's, because they have longitudinal knowledge. Ask your VA primary care provider first; many will write it.
items.deadline: Submit before the C&P exam if possible, so the VA examiner must address it.

items.title: Disability Benefits Questionnaires (DBQs) — have your own doctor fill out VA's rating form
items.who: Any veteran with a private treating physician willing to complete VA's own examination form.
items.value: A completed DBQ from your own doctor can substitute for a C&P exam entirely, or contradict a bad one. It is the same form VA's contract examiners use, so it maps directly onto the rating criteria.
items.how: VA publishes public DBQs by condition. Download the DBQ for your condition, have your treating specialist complete it, and submit it with your claim. If the DBQ is complete and adequate, VA may decide the claim without scheduling an exam under the Acceptable Clinical Evidence (ACE) process.
items.hack: Know which DBQs are NOT public before you promise your doctor a form. VA restricts several — notably TRAUMATIC BRAIN INJURY, HEARING LOSS AND TINNITUS, and the General Medical examination — because of specialized training requirements. The mental disorders, PTSD review, sleep apnea, back, neck, joints, peripheral nerves, respiratory, GI and Gulf War DBQs ARE public. For a restricted condition, have your provider write a narrative that tracks the rating criteria verbatim instead. And for any musculoskeletal DBQ, make sure the provider addresses FLARE-UPS and functional loss during flares (Sharp v. Shulkin) and tests range of motion in both active and passive motion, weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing (Correia v. McDonald) — an exam that omits these is legally inadequate and is grounds for remand.
items.deadline: Submit with the claim or before the C&P exam.

items.title: VA Form 21-10210 — Lay/Witness Statement (buddy statement)
items.who: Any veteran; completed by the veteran, a fellow service member, a spouse, a coworker, or a family member.
items.value: Free. Often decisive where service treatment records are silent — which is most PTSD, tinnitus, back, and knee claims from an era when nobody went to sick call.
items.how: Anyone can complete VA Form 21-10210 to support a claim — their own or another veteran's. Submit online or by mail. Lay evidence is competent to establish facts observable by a layperson: what happened, what symptoms were visible, when they started, how they have continued.
items.hack: Lay evidence is COMPETENT for observable facts and for continuity of symptoms (Jandreau v. Nicholson; Buchanan v. Nicholson — VA cannot reject lay testimony merely because it is not corroborated by contemporaneous medical records). Write statements that describe SPECIFIC OBSERVED EVENTS with dates and places, not conclusions. 'He has PTSD' is worthless. 'On 14 March 2007 outside FOB Salerno our vehicle struck an IED; I was in the trail vehicle and pulled him out; he was dazed and could not answer questions for several minutes' is a stressor verification AND a TBI event. Get three statements from different people. Also use 21-10210 for a SPOUSE statement describing your nightmares, irritability, and social withdrawal — that is the exact evidence the mental-health rating criteria call for and no C&P examiner will elicit it.
items.deadline: Any time before the decision.

items.title: VA Form 21-4142 / 21-4142a — Authorization to Disclose Private Medical Records
items.who: Any veteran with treatment records held by non-VA providers.
items.value: Free. Triggers VA's duty to assist in obtaining private records — but it is also the single most common cause of claim delay.
items.how: 21-4142 is the authorization; 21-4142a is the list of providers, dates, and conditions treated. VA will make reasonable efforts (generally an initial request and one follow-up) to obtain the records.
items.hack: Do not rely on VA to get them. VA's 'reasonable efforts' regularly fail, and then VA decides the claim on an incomplete record and the burden falls on you. Request the records YOURSELF, pay the copying fee, and submit them directly. It converts a 6-month wait into a 2-week task and guarantees the decision-maker actually has the evidence. Also request your COMPLETE VA medical record and your C-file (claims file) via VA Form 20-10206 before filing anything contested — you cannot fight a decision you have not read.
items.deadline: Submit with the claim.

items.title: Intent to File (VA Form 21-0966) — the 1-year effective date lock
items.who: Every veteran about to file any claim for compensation, pension, or DIC.
items.value: Free, takes 5 minutes, and preserves up to 12 months of retroactive pay. At the 70% with-spouse rate ($1,961.45/month), a full year of preserved effective date is $23,537.
items.how: Submitting VA Form 21-0966 notifies VA you intend to file. You then have 365 days to submit the complete application (VA Form 21-526EZ), and VA treats the INTENT TO FILE date as your claim date. Filing the full claim online at VA.gov automatically sets an effective date when you start the form, so a separate ITF is unnecessary for online filers — but it is essential for paper filers and for anyone who needs time to gather evidence.
items.hack: This is the single highest return-on-effort action in the entire VA system. File an Intent to File the moment you think you might have a claim — before you find a doctor, before you get a nexus letter, before you know what to claim. It costs nothing and buys you a full year of back pay. An ITF covers compensation broadly, not one specific condition, so it protects every condition you later claim within that year. Set a calendar reminder for day 330. And file a NEW ITF every time you complete a claim, so the next one is already protected.
items.deadline: Complete application due within 365 days of the ITF or the effective date is lost.

items.title: VA Form 21-526EZ and the Fully Developed Claim program
items.who: Every veteran filing an initial or increased disability compensation claim.
items.value: Free. FDC processing is materially faster than a standard claim because VA does not have to chase evidence.
items.how: 21-526EZ is the Application for Disability Compensation and Related Compensation Benefits. Under the Fully Developed Claim route you certify that you have submitted all private evidence and identified all federal records, and you agree to report for any VA exam. VA then handles only federal records retrieval and the exam.
items.hack: FDC is a speed play, not an outcome play — and it has a trap. If you certify a fully developed claim and then submit additional evidence, VA moves the claim out of the FDC lane. Gather everything FIRST, then file once. Second trap: on the 21-526EZ, list EVERY condition you intend to claim, including 0%-likely ones like tinnitus, scars, and erectile dysfunction, because each listed condition gets its own effective date and its own appeal rights. Third: for each condition write the specific theory ('sleep apnea secondary to service-connected chronic rhinitis'), because VA adjudicates the claim as filed and will not develop a secondary theory you did not name.
items.deadline: None, but see Intent to File.

items.title: Supplemental Claim (VA Form 20-0995) — the 'new and relevant evidence' lane
items.who: Veterans with a prior VA decision who have new evidence, or whose claim is affected by a change in law such as the PACT Act.
items.value: Free. Preserves your original effective date if filed within one year of the decision. VA's stated goal is 125 days; actual average was 58.7 days as of August 2026 — by far the fastest lane.
items.how: Requires NEW evidence (not previously considered) that is RELEVANT (tends to prove or disprove a matter at issue). VA's duty to assist applies in this lane — VA must help develop the evidence, and will order a new exam if needed. There is no time limit to file a Supplemental Claim, but filing within ONE YEAR of the prior decision preserves continuous pursuit and therefore the original effective date.
items.hack: The Supplemental Claim is almost always the right first move after a denial, because it is the only lane where VA owes you a duty to assist and will order a new exam. The mistake veterans make is filing an HLR after a denial that was caused by inadequate evidence — HLR cannot consider new evidence, so it just re-denies you and burns a year. Rule of thumb: bad evidence -> Supplemental Claim. Bad decision on good evidence -> Higher-Level Review. Also, a Supplemental Claim is the correct vehicle for PACT Act reconsideration of a previously denied condition that is now presumptive.
items.deadline: File within 1 year of the decision to preserve the original effective date. No absolute deadline otherwise.

items.title: Higher-Level Review (VA Form 20-0996) — senior reviewer, no new evidence
items.who: Veterans who believe VA made an error or misapplied the rating criteria to evidence already in the file.
items.value: Free. VA goal: about 125 days (4-5 months).
items.how: A more senior rater reviews the SAME record de novo and can reverse based on an error OR a difference of opinion. You cannot submit new evidence. The reviewer can also find a DUTY-TO-ASSIST ERROR, which sends the claim back for correction. You may request an optional informal conference by phone with the reviewer (this lengthens the timeline).
items.hack: Always request the informal conference, and come to it with a written, numbered list of the specific errors: the diagnostic code misapplied, the rating criterion met but not credited, the evidence in the file the rater ignored, the bilateral factor omitted, the TDIU issue raised by the record but not adjudicated. HLR reviewers work from a checklist; handing them a clean list of identified errors is the difference between a reversal and a rubber stamp. Do NOT use HLR if your problem is missing evidence — you will lose, and you will have spent 4-5 months.
items.deadline: Within 1 year of the decision you are challenging.

items.title: Board Appeal (VA Form 10182) — three dockets, three very different timelines
items.who: Veterans appealing to the Board of Veterans' Appeals for review by a Veterans Law Judge.
items.value: Free. VA's target timelines by docket: Direct Review 365 days; Evidence Submission 550 days; Hearing 730 days.
items.how: Three docket choices. DIRECT REVIEW: judge decides on the existing record; no new evidence, no hearing; fastest. EVIDENCE SUBMISSION: you may submit new evidence within 90 days of filing the 10182. HEARING: a hearing with a Veterans Law Judge (virtual, videoconference, or in person in Washington DC), and you may submit evidence at the hearing or within 90 days after it.
items.hack: The docket choice is a pure time-versus-evidence trade. Choose Direct Review when the record is complete and the error is legal — it is a full year faster than a hearing. Choose Hearing when credibility matters (stressor testimony, symptom severity, unemployability) because a judge hearing you describe your day is worth more than any document, AND because the hearing docket gives you two bites at submitting evidence. One hard rule: you may NOT file two Board Appeals back to back on the same issue — after a Board denial your next move is a Supplemental Claim with new evidence, or an appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims within 120 days.
items.deadline: Within 1 year of the decision. CAVC appeal within 120 days of the Board decision.

items.title: Clear and Unmistakable Error (CUE) — 38 CFR 3.105(a), no deadline, full retroactive pay
items.who: Veterans with a FINAL prior decision containing an undebatable error of fact or law.
items.value: The only way to reach back past the normal effective date rules. A successful CUE pays from the ORIGINAL effective date — decades of back pay in some cases.
items.how: CUE is 'a very specific and rare kind of error' — the kind that, had it not been made, would have MANIFESTLY changed the outcome. The request must be in writing, signed, and must specifically identify the alleged error, the date of the decision, and the factual and legal basis. You can request it at any time after a decision becomes final. CUE does NOT include a later change in interpretation of a statute or regulation, and it does not include a mere disagreement about how evidence was weighed.
items.hack: Winnable CUE fact patterns are narrow and mechanical, not judgmental. The best ones: (1) the bilateral factor under 4.26 was not applied and applying it changes the combined rating; (2) the combined rating was computed wrong under 4.25; (3) a rating criterion was plainly met on the face of the exam report and not credited; (4) statutory SMC-S entitlement was mathematically apparent and not awarded; (5) the effective date was set later than the governing regulation permits. Do NOT file CUE arguing the examiner was wrong or the evidence should have been weighed differently — that is guaranteed to lose and you get only one CUE attack per issue per theory.
items.deadline: None — CUE can be raised at any time, including on decades-old decisions.

items.title: 38 CFR 3.400 — Effective dates and back pay
items.who: Every veteran. This regulation decides how much of your award is retroactive.
items.value: The difference between a $3,000 award and a $40,000 award on identical facts.
items.how: General rule: the later of (a) the date VA received the claim or (b) the date entitlement arose. Key exceptions: 3.400(b)(2) — for direct service connection, if you file within ONE YEAR of separation, the effective date is the DAY AFTER discharge. 3.400(o)(2) — for INCREASES, the effective date is the earliest date it is factually ascertainable that the increase occurred, up to one year before the date of claim, provided the claim (or Intent to File) is received within one year of that ascertainable date.
items.hack: Two plays. (1) The one-year-after-discharge rule is why BDD/pre-discharge filing is worth so much — file within a year of separation and your money starts the day after you take off the uniform. (2) The 3.400(o)(2) look-back is the increase-claim hack: when you file for an increase, submit medical records showing WHEN your condition worsened, not just that it is worse now. If a treatment note from 10 months ago documents the worse severity, you get 10 extra months of the higher rate. Veterans routinely leave this money behind by submitting only current records.
items.deadline: One year from separation for the day-after-discharge rule; one year look-back for increases.

items.title: C&P exam strategy — the 20 minutes that set your rating
items.who: Every veteran scheduled for a VA compensation and pension examination.
items.value: A single exam determines a rating worth $180 to $3,938/month for life.
items.how: VA or a contract examiner (QTC, LHI/Optum, VES, MSLA) performs the exam. They do not treat you, refer you, or prescribe. Exams run 15 minutes to over an hour. VA may skip the exam entirely under the Acceptable Clinical Evidence (ACE) process if the records already support a decision. Missing the exam without good cause means VA decides on the evidence of record — for an initial claim that usually means denial; for an increase claim, 38 CFR 3.655 requires denial.
items.hack: Six rules. (1) Describe your WORST day and your flare-ups, not the day you feel fine — Sharp v. Shulkin requires the examiner to estimate functional loss during flares, so state explicitly how you function during a flare. (2) Never minimize. 'I manage' becomes 'symptoms well controlled' in the report. (3) For musculoskeletal exams, Correia v. McDonald requires range of motion tested in active AND passive motion, in weight-bearing AND non-weight-bearing; if the examiner does not do it, note it and challenge the exam as inadequate. (4) Bring a written symptom list and ask that it be attached. (5) Bring someone who can describe what they observe. (6) IMMEDIATELY after the exam, write down who examined you, how long it took, and what was and was not done — then request the exam report through your VA.gov account or a records request and read it before the decision issues. If it misstates what you said, submit a rebuttal statement before VA rates the claim.
items.deadline: Attend or reschedule with good cause (death in family, hospitalization, homelessness are named examples).

items.title: Benefits Delivery at Discharge (BDD) — file 180 to 90 days before separation
items.who: Active duty, National Guard, Reserve and Coast Guard members on full-time active duty with a known separation date 180 to 90 days out.
items.value: Enormous. A BDD claim is typically decided by or near your separation date, so compensation starts the month after discharge instead of 6-18 months later. At the 50% with-spouse rate ($1,241.90/month), a 12-month head start is $14,903.
items.how: Requirements: (1) full-time active duty, (2) 180 to 90 days remaining, (3) available for VA exams within 45 days of submitting the claim, and (4) a completed Separation Health Assessment - Part A Self-Assessment. Exams are typically done at or near your installation while you are still in uniform.
items.hack: This is the highest-leverage window in a service member's entire life and most people miss it. Three things. (1) Claim EVERYTHING documented in your service treatment records, no matter how minor — tinnitus, knee pain, back pain, scars, GERD, sleep disturbance, skin conditions. In-service documentation plus in-service exam equals near-automatic service connection; the same condition claimed five years later requires a nexus letter and a fight. (2) Go to sick call NOW for anything that hurts — an undocumented condition is a future denial. (3) If you miss the 180-90 window, you can still file a standard pre-discharge claim at 89 days or fewer; and if you file within ONE YEAR of separation, 38 CFR 3.400(b)(2) makes your effective date the day after discharge anyway. Disqualifiers from BDD: needing case management for serious injury, terminal illness, active treatment during the separation window, pending character-of-discharge determination, or inability to attend exams within 45 days.
items.deadline: 180 to 90 days before separation for BDD. Within 1 year of separation for the day-after-discharge effective date.

items.title: Quick Start / standard pre-discharge claim (fewer than 90 days out)
items.who: Service members with 89 or fewer days until separation, or who are otherwise ineligible for BDD.
items.value: Still captures the day-after-discharge effective date under 38 CFR 3.400(b)(2) if the claim is filed within one year of separation.
items.how: File a standard disability claim (VA Form 21-526EZ) with whatever evidence you have; VA gathers the rest. Exams may occur after separation. Service members who cannot use BDD because of case management needs, terminal illness, active treatment at a VA or military facility, a pending character-of-discharge determination, or inability to attend exams within 45 days fall into this route.
items.hack: If you are inside 90 days and panicking, file an Intent to File TODAY. It costs nothing, takes five minutes, and locks your effective date for a year while you separate, move, find a doctor and get organized. The single worst outcome is separating, spending two years adjusting to civilian life, and then filing — losing two years of compensation that a five-minute form would have preserved.
items.deadline: File within 1 year of separation to get the day-after-discharge effective date.

items.title: PACT Act — burn pit and particulate matter presumptives
items.who: Veterans who served in the covered locations on or after 8/2/1990 (Gulf War) or 9/11/2001 (post-9/11).
items.value: No nexus required, no proof of exposure required. A presumptive grant is the cheapest service connection available.
items.how: Covered locations ON OR AFTER SEPTEMBER 11, 2001: Afghanistan, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Uzbekistan, Yemen, and the airspace above. ON OR AFTER AUGUST 2, 1990: Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, UAE, the airspace above, plus the Arabian Sea, Gulf of Aden, Gulf of Oman, Persian Gulf, Red Sea and the Iraq/Saudi neutral zone. CANCERS: brain, gastrointestinal (any type), glioblastoma, genitourinary (any type), head (any type), hematologic and lymphatic cancers, lymphoma (any type), melanoma, neck (any type), pancreatic, reproductive (any type), respiratory (any type). ILLNESSES: asthma diagnosed after service, chronic bronchitis, COPD, chronic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, constrictive/obliterative bronchiolitis, emphysema, granulomatous disease, interstitial lung disease, pleuritis, pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis.
items.hack: Chronic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis are the sleeper entries on that list. They are extremely common, easy to document, and they are the gateway condition for a 50% sleep apnea secondary claim. Also note VA has FOLDED the January 2025 interim final rules into this list — 'hematologic and lymphatic cancers' now captures acute and chronic leukemias, multiple myeloma (including MGUS), myelodysplastic syndromes and myelofibrosis, and 'genitourinary cancer' now captures bladder, ureter and urachal cancers. If you were denied any of those before January 2025, file a Supplemental Claim citing the change in law.
items.deadline: No filing deadline. The PACT Act's special retroactive effective date window (filing by August 9, 2023 for an August 10, 2022 effective date) has closed.

items.title: PACT Act — Agent Orange location and condition expansions
items.who: Veterans with herbicide exposure, including at newly covered locations.
items.value: Hypertension and MGUS added as presumptive conditions — hypertension alone affects an enormous share of the Vietnam-era population. Five new presumed-exposure locations added.
items.how: NEW CONDITIONS: high blood pressure (hypertension) and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), added to the existing Agent Orange presumptive list (which includes ischemic heart disease, type 2 diabetes, Parkinson's disease and parkinsonism, bladder cancer, hypothyroidism, several soft-tissue sarcomas, chronic B-cell leukemias, Hodgkin's and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, multiple myeloma, prostate cancer, respiratory cancers, AL amyloidosis, chloracne, porphyria cutanea tarda, and peripheral neuropathy). NEW LOCATIONS: Thailand military bases 1/9/1962-6/30/1976; Laos 12/1/1965-9/30/1969; Cambodia at Mimot or Krek, Kampong Cham Province 4/16/1969-4/30/1969; Guam, American Samoa and their territorial waters 1/9/1962-7/31/1980; Johnston Atoll or a ship that called there 1/1/1972-9/30/1977.
items.hack: The Thailand expansion is enormous and under-claimed. Previously VA required proof of perimeter duty at a Royal Thai Air Force Base; the PACT Act now presumes exposure for service at ANY U.S. or Royal Thai base in Thailand in the window, regardless of MOS or proximity to the perimeter. If you served in Thailand between 1/9/1962 and 6/30/1976 and were ever denied for lack of perimeter evidence, file a Supplemental Claim under the change in law. Note also: VA published a PROPOSED rule on February 9, 2024 that would further extend presumed herbicide exposure to U.S. testing and storage sites, Canada and India — verify its current status before relying on it.
items.deadline: No deadline. File a Supplemental Claim (20-0995) for previously denied conditions now presumptive.

items.title: PACT Act — radiation exposure expansions
items.who: Veterans who participated in three newly added radiation response efforts.
items.value: Presumed radiation exposure, opening the radiogenic disease presumptives (leukemia, thyroid cancer, breast, lung, bone, and other listed cancers).
items.how: Three response efforts added to the radiation-risk activity list: cleanup of Enewetak Atoll, 1/1/1977-12/31/1980; response to the Palomares, Spain B-52 nuclear accident, 1/17/1966-3/31/1967; response to the fire at the Thule Air Force Base, Greenland B-52 crash, 1/21/1968-9/25/1968. These join the existing radiation-risk activities (atmospheric nuclear test participation, Hiroshima/Nagasaki occupation, POW in Japan, service at gaseous diffusion plants at Paducah, Portsmouth, or K-25 at Oak Ridge).
items.hack: Radiation claims have two independent tracks and you should file BOTH. Track one: the 38 CFR 3.309(d) presumptive list of 21 radiogenic cancers for radiation-exposed veterans — no dose reconstruction needed. Track two: 38 CFR 3.311 for any other radiogenic disease, which requires a dose assessment but is not limited to the 21 listed cancers. Veterans file only track one, get denied because their cancer is not on the list, and stop. Cite 3.311 explicitly.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: 2025 interim final rules — leukemias, myeloma, MDS, myelofibrosis, bladder and ureter cancers
items.who: Veterans with covered Gulf War or post-9/11 service who have any of these cancers.
items.value: Presumptive service connection with no nexus requirement. Most of these cancers carry a 100% rating during active treatment under 38 CFR 4.115b/4.117 with a mandatory post-treatment re-evaluation.
items.how: Two interim final rules. (1) Effective January 2, 2025: urinary bladder cancer (including overlapping sites) and ureter cancer (including the ureteric orifice and urachus) presumed from fine particulate matter exposure. (2) Effective January 10, 2025: acute leukemias, chronic leukemias, multiple myelomas (including MGUS), myelodysplastic syndromes, and myelofibrosis. Both cover service in the Southwest Asia theater or Somalia on or after August 2, 1990, and in Afghanistan, Syria, Djibouti, Uzbekistan, Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon and Yemen on or after September 11, 2001.
items.hack: Because these were INTERIM FINAL rules effective immediately, they applied to pending claims on their effective dates. If you were denied any of these conditions BEFORE January 2025, file a Supplemental Claim (VA Form 20-0995) citing 'a change in law' — that is an express basis for a Supplemental Claim and does not require new medical evidence. A liberalizing law can also support a retroactive effective date up to one year before the date of the new claim under 38 CFR 3.114.
items.deadline: None, but file the Supplemental Claim promptly — 3.114 caps retroactivity at one year before the claim.

items.title: Camp Lejeune water contamination — 8 presumptive conditions plus the Justice Act lawsuit
items.who: Veterans, Reservists and National Guard members who served at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 cumulative days between August 1, 1953 and December 31, 1987 — plus family members who lived there.
items.value: Eight presumptive conditions for VA disability compensation, plus a separate federal LAWSUIT remedy under the Camp Lejeune Justice Act of 2022 that can pay money damages on top of VA benefits.
items.how: VA PRESUMPTIVE CONDITIONS (8): adult leukemia, aplastic anemia and other myelodysplastic syndromes, bladder cancer, kidney cancer, liver cancer, multiple myeloma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, Parkinson's disease. Requirement: 30 cumulative days at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River between 8/1/1953 and 12/31/1987, and a discharge other than dishonorable. FAMILY MEMBERS (spouses, children, legal dependents, including in utero) who lived there 30+ days qualify for VA reimbursement of out-of-pocket health care costs for 15 covered conditions. Separately, the Camp Lejeune Justice Act allows an administrative claim to the Department of the Navy and then suit in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina.
items.hack: Two independent pots of money and they do not offset each other for VA purposes — VA confirms that filing under the Justice Act does not affect eligibility for VA disability or health care. File the VA disability claim regardless of any lawsuit. Also note the VA presumptive list (8 conditions) is SHORTER than the health-care-reimbursement list (15 conditions) and shorter than the range of injuries litigated under the Justice Act — a condition not on the 8-item presumptive list can still be service connected on a direct basis with a nexus opinion citing the ATSDR water modeling.
items.deadline: No VA deadline. The Camp Lejeune Justice Act filing window is set by that statute — confirm the current status with counsel, as the statutory filing period has been the subject of litigation.

items.title: Gulf War undiagnosed illness and medically unexplained chronic multisymptom illness
items.who: Veterans who served in the Southwest Asia theater on or after August 2, 1990 (and Afghanistan under a companion rule).
items.value: Service connection WITHOUT a diagnosis and WITHOUT a nexus — the only place in the system where an undiagnosed symptom set is compensable.
items.how: Presumptive conditions: chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, functional gastrointestinal disorders (including IBS), medically unexplained chronic multisymptom illness, and undiagnosed illnesses manifesting as cardiovascular symptoms, muscle and joint pain, headaches, neurological signs, sleep disturbances, skin conditions, respiratory symptoms, or menstrual disorders. Qualifying locations: Afghanistan, Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, the Iraq/Saudi neutral zone, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Turkey, the UAE, and the waters of the Arabian Sea, Gulf of Aden, Gulf of Oman, Persian Gulf and Red Sea (airspace excluded for several countries). The condition must have lasted at least 6 months and may have arisen during service or at any time after separation.
items.hack: This is the correct route for the Gulf War veteran with a decade of 'everything came back normal' workups. Do NOT let a provider chase a diagnosis — an UNDIAGNOSED illness is what the regulation compensates, and a wrong diagnosis can actually take you out of the presumptive lane. File it as 'undiagnosed illness manifested by [chronic joint pain / chronic fatigue / chronic headaches]' and attach the normal lab and imaging results as PROOF the illness is medically unexplained. Fibromyalgia under DC 5025 rates at 10%, 20%, or 40% (40% for symptoms that are constant or nearly constant and refractory to therapy), and IBS under DC 7319 rates up to 30%.
items.deadline: The historic requirement that the illness manifest to a compensable degree by a set date has been extended repeatedly by rulemaking — verify the current manifestation deadline before relying on it.

items.title: Adding dependents — VA Form 21-686c and the 1-year retroactive rule
items.who: Veterans rated 30% or higher with a spouse, children, or dependent parents.
items.value: At 100%: a spouse adds $219.59/month, a spouse + 1 child adds $380.41, each additional child adds $109.11 (or $352.45 if in an approved school), and a spouse needing Aid & Attendance adds $201.41. At 30%: a spouse adds $65.00. Over 30 years at 100% with a spouse and two children that is well over $200,000.
items.how: File VA Form 21-686c (spouse or children under 18) online through VA.gov, or by mail to the Evidence Intake Center, PO Box 4444, Janesville WI 53547-4444. Add VA Form 21-674 for a child aged 18-23 in an approved school. Dependent parents use VA Form 21P-509 and require an income and net worth test. Benefits typically begin within 2 weeks of approval.
items.hack: THE ONE-YEAR RULE IS THE WHOLE GAME. If you file within one year of the marriage, birth, or adoption — OR within one year of the rating decision that first took you to 30% — VA pays retroactively to that event. File late and you get nothing before the filing date. Two specific traps: (1) When a rating decision takes you from 20% to 30%, VA does NOT automatically add your dependents; you have one year from that decision to file and capture the back pay. (2) A child drops off your award automatically at 18 — you must file the 21-674 to keep them on until 23, and that form must be filed within one year of the school term starting or you lose the back months.
items.deadline: Within 1 year of the qualifying event (marriage, birth, adoption, or the decision granting 30%) for retroactive payment.

items.title: CHAMPVA — health coverage for the family of a P&T veteran
items.who: Spouses and children of veterans rated PERMANENTLY AND TOTALLY disabled from a service-connected condition (or who were so rated at death), and survivors of veterans who died of a service-connected disability.
items.value: VA shares the cost of covered health care and supplies for your dependents. For a family of four with no employer coverage, this is commonly worth $12,000-20,000 a year in avoided premiums and cost-sharing.
items.how: Requires a PERMANENT and TOTAL service-connected rating — 100% disabling and not expected to improve. TDIU qualifies only if VA has also found it permanent. Children are covered to 18, or to 23 if enrolled in school, or for life if permanently incapable of self-support from a disability that occurred before age 18. A surviving spouse who remarries at 55 or older keeps CHAMPVA; remarriage before 55 ends it. You cannot use CHAMPVA if you are eligible for TRICARE.
items.hack: CHAMPVA is the single largest dollar benefit gated behind the word 'PERMANENT,' and thousands of 100% veterans never get it because their rating decision granted 100% without a P&T finding. Read your decision: look for 'Permanent and Total' or 'no future examinations are scheduled.' If it is not there, file a claim specifically requesting a permanency determination, citing your age, the static nature of the conditions, and 38 CFR 3.327(b)(2) (no re-exams where the disability is permanent, static, has persisted without material improvement for 5+ years, or the veteran is over 55). That one request unlocks CHAMPVA, Chapter 35 DEA and Space-A simultaneously.
items.deadline: None, but coverage generally starts from the application, so apply as soon as P&T is granted.

items.title: Chapter 35 DEA — Survivors' and Dependents' Educational Assistance
items.who: Spouses and children of veterans rated permanently and totally disabled from a service-connected condition, or who died of one.
items.value: $1,574.00/month full time, $1,244.00/month three-quarter time, $912.00/month half time for institutional training (effective October 1, 2025). 36 months of benefits for training beginning on or after August 1, 2018 (45 months if training began before that). Per dependent. Three children x 36 months x $1,574 is about $170,000.
items.how: Requires the veteran to be rated PERMANENTLY and TOTALLY disabled from a service-connected disability (or to have died from one, or to be MIA/captured/detained 90+ days, or hospitalized for a service-connected P&T condition with likely discharge). For children who became eligible ON OR AFTER AUGUST 1, 2023 there is NO AGE LIMIT. For children eligible before that date, benefits generally must be used by age 26 with limited exceptions.
items.hack: The August 1, 2023 removal of the age-26 cutoff for newly eligible children is the least-known change in VA education benefits. A child who becomes eligible today can use Chapter 35 at 40. Second point: Chapter 35 is paid DIRECTLY TO THE STUDENT as a monthly stipend — unlike Post-9/11 GI Bill, it is not paid to the school, so the student can use it at a cheap in-state school and pocket the difference. Third: a child eligible for both Chapter 35 and the Fry Scholarship must choose one, and combined benefits are capped at 81 months — run the math before electing.
items.deadline: Spouses generally have 10 years from the date VA establishes eligibility (20 years in some cases). Children eligible on/after 8/1/2023 have no age limit.

items.title: VA home loan funding fee waiver
items.who: Veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability (any rating, including 10%), those entitled to compensation but receiving retired or active-duty pay instead, surviving spouses receiving DIC, service members with a proposed or memorandum rating from a pre-discharge claim, and active-duty Purple Heart recipients.
items.value: The funding fee is 2.15% of the loan on a first-use purchase with less than 5% down, and 3.3% on subsequent use. On a $400,000 loan that is $8,600 on first use and $13,200 on every use after — waived entirely, every time, for life.
items.how: The exemption follows RECEIPT OF COMPENSATION, not a particular rating percentage. A 10% rating waives the fee exactly as completely as a 100% rating. The lender verifies through the Certificate of Eligibility.
items.hack: The refund rule is where money gets left behind. If you close a VA loan while a claim is pending and VA later grants compensation with an effective date BEFORE your loan closing date, you are entitled to a REFUND of the funding fee you paid. Nobody tells you, and no one initiates it for you — contact the VA Regional Loan Center in writing with your closing disclosure and your rating decision. Veterans have recovered five figures this way. Caveat: a proposed or memorandum rating received AFTER closing does not entitle you to a refund.
items.deadline: Request the refund as soon as the retroactive rating is granted.

items.title: VA health care Priority Group 1 at 50% — no copays, ever
items.who: Veterans rated 50% or more disabling, veterans determined unemployable (TDIU), and Medal of Honor recipients.
items.value: Zero copays for all VA inpatient and outpatient care and zero copays for VA prescriptions. For a veteran on five maintenance medications with several specialist visits a year, this is commonly $1,500-4,000/year.
items.how: Priority Group 1: 50%+ service-connected or unemployable. Group 2: 30% or 40%. Group 3: former POWs, Purple Heart recipients, veterans discharged for a service-connected disability, and 10%-20% ratings. Group 4: veterans receiving VA aid and attendance or housebound benefits, or designated catastrophically disabled. Groups 7 and 8 are income-based and agree to pay copays.
items.hack: Note that Priority Group 4 captures anyone receiving VA aid and attendance or housebound benefits OR designated CATASTROPHICALLY DISABLED — and catastrophic disability is a CLINICAL determination made by a VA physician, completely independent of your rating percentage. A veteran at 30% with a spinal cord injury, ALS, or severe functional dependency can be designated catastrophically disabled and move to Group 4, which also carries copay exemptions. Ask your VA provider for a catastrophic disability evaluation if your function is far worse than your rating suggests.
items.deadline: None. Enroll with VA Form 10-10EZ.

items.title: VA dental care — Class IV unlimited dental at 100% or TDIU
items.who: Veterans rated 100% service-connected, veterans paid at the 100% rate due to TDIU, former POWs (Class IIC), and veterans with a compensable service-connected dental disability (Class I).
items.value: ANY needed dental care, with no dollar limit and no copay. For a veteran needing implants, crowns, or full-mouth rehabilitation, this is routinely $10,000-40,000 of care.
items.how: Class I: service-connected compensable dental disability — any needed care. Class IV: rated 100% service-connected, OR unemployable and paid at the 100% rate — any needed care. Class IIC: former POWs — any needed care. Class II: one-time dental care for veterans with 90+ days of active duty who apply within 180 DAYS of discharge and whose separation paperwork does not certify prior comprehensive dental treatment.
items.hack: Two traps. (1) A TEMPORARY 100% rating (38 CFR 4.29 hospitalization or 4.30 convalescence) does NOT qualify for Class IV — VA states this expressly. (2) The one-time Class II benefit has a hard 180-DAY application deadline from discharge and is the most commonly forfeited benefit in the entire system. Every separating service member should apply on day one regardless of whether they think they need dental work; it costs nothing and it expires forever at 180 days. If you are not eligible for VA dental, VADIP offers reduced-cost dental insurance to anyone enrolled in VA health care or CHAMPVA.
items.deadline: 180 days from discharge for the one-time Class II benefit. No deadline for Class I or Class IV.

items.title: Specially Adapted Housing (SAH), Special Home Adaptation (SHA), and TRA grants — FY2026 amounts
items.who: Veterans with specific severe service-connected disabilities involving loss or loss of use of limbs, blindness, severe burns, or certain respiratory injuries.
items.value: SAH up to $126,526 (FY2026). SHA up to $25,350. Temporary Residence Adaptation: up to $50,961 for SAH-qualified veterans, up to $9,100 for SHA-qualified veterans.
items.how: SAH requires that you own or will own the home and have a qualifying disability: loss or loss of use of more than one limb; loss or loss of use of a lower leg plus lasting effects of a disease or injury; blindness in both eyes with 20/200 acuity or less; certain severe burns; or loss/loss of use of one lower extremity after September 11, 2001 (this last category is capped at 120 veterans per fiscal year by statute). SHA requires that you or a family member own or will own the home and that you have loss or loss of use of both hands, certain severe burns, or certain respiratory or breathing injuries.
items.hack: Three things. (1) TRA is the overlooked one — it adapts a home you do not own, including a family member's home you are temporarily living in, and it does NOT consume your full SAH entitlement. (2) The post-9/11 single-lower-extremity SAH category is capped at 120 veterans per fiscal year — apply at the START of the fiscal year (October), not in August. (3) 'Loss of use' does not require amputation; it means no more function remains than an amputation stump with a prosthesis would provide. Get an examiner to answer that specific question. Grant maximums are indexed and rise each fiscal year.
items.deadline: Apply with VA Form 26-4555. The post-9/11 lower-extremity SAH category is capped annually at 120 veterans.

items.title: Automobile allowance (VA Form 21-4502) and adaptive equipment (VA Form 10-1394)
items.who: Veterans with service-connected loss or permanent loss of use of one or both feet or hands, permanent vision impairment of 20/200 or worse in the better eye with correction, a severe burn injury, or ALS. Ankylosis of one or both knees or hips qualifies for adaptive equipment only.
items.value: One-time payment of up to $27,074.99 toward a specially equipped vehicle (effective October 1, 2025), PLUS separate, repeatable adaptive equipment grants for power steering, power brakes, power windows, lifts, and hand controls.
items.how: Automobile allowance: VA Form 21-4502, submitted online or by mail. Adaptive equipment: VA Form 10-1394, brought to the prosthetics representative at your VA medical center. VA pays the allowance directly to the seller.
items.hack: FILE AND GET APPROVAL BEFORE YOU BUY. VA states plainly that you must file the claim and get approval before purchasing the vehicle or the equipment, and the seller must agree to submit the completed form and itemized invoice to VA. Veterans buy the truck first and then discover the grant is unrecoverable. Also note the two benefits are separate: the automobile allowance is once in a lifetime, but the ADAPTIVE EQUIPMENT grant can be used again for a subsequent vehicle. And ALS is a qualifying condition on its own — ALS is also a 100% presumptive rating for any veteran with 90 days of continuous active service.
items.deadline: Approval must precede purchase.

items.title: Annual clothing allowance — $1,053.19/year, no minimum rating
items.who: Veterans whose clothing is damaged by a prosthetic or orthopedic device, OR by a prescribed medication for a service-connected skin condition.
items.value: $1,053.19 per year (effective December 1, 2025). Payable in multiples where more than one device or medication damages distinctly different types of clothing.
items.how: Apply with VA Form 10-8678 through your VA medical center's prosthetics service. There is no minimum disability rating — eligibility turns on the device or medication, not the percentage.
items.hack: The definition of 'prosthetic or orthopedic device' is far broader than veterans assume. It includes rigid and semi-rigid braces (knee, back, ankle), wheelchairs, and crutches — anything that wears on clothing. And the skin-medication route covers anyone using a topical corticosteroid or similar for a service-connected skin condition that stains or damages clothing. You can receive MULTIPLE allowances in the same year if separate devices damage separate types of clothing (e.g., a back brace damaging shirts and an ankle-foot orthosis damaging trousers) — you must claim each one separately and describe the distinct garment type. The application has an annual deadline (historically August 1) tied to the benefit year, so file early.
items.deadline: Annual application deadline tied to the benefit year — confirm the current date with VA prosthetics before assuming.

items.title: Beneficiary travel reimbursement at 30% — mileage for every VA appointment
items.who: Veterans rated 30% or higher (for ALL VA health care travel), veterans traveling for treatment of a service-connected condition at any rating, VA pension recipients, low-income veterans, and anyone attending a VA claim exam.
items.value: Mileage plus parking and tolls for every trip, both ways. A veteran driving 60 miles round trip to a VA medical center twice a month recovers hundreds of dollars a year. Travel to a C&P exam is reimbursable regardless of rating.
