items.how: File through the Beneficiary Travel Self-Service System (BTSSS) online, or VA Form 10-3542 by mail or in person, or at smartphone check-in (mileage from home only). Mileage and parking/tolls need no pre-approval; transportation (bus, taxi, rideshare, air, ambulance), meals and lodging require pre-approval.
items.hack: The 30-DAY DEADLINE is absolute and VA applies it strictly — claims filed after 30 days are usually denied outright. File from the parking lot on your phone before you drive home. Two more: (1) set up a SEPARATE direct deposit account for travel pay, because VA processes travel reimbursement on a different payment rail from compensation and a missing travel-specific deposit record is the most common cause of a paid-but-never-received claim. (2) Travel to a compensation and pension examination is reimbursable even for a veteran with no rating at all.
items.deadline: 30 days from the date of travel. Hard deadline.

items.title: Commissary, Exchange and MWR access for all service-connected veterans
items.who: All veterans with a VA-documented service-connected disability rating (0% through 100%), Purple Heart recipients, former POWs, and approved primary family caregivers under VA's Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers.
items.value: Commissary grocery prices average well below civilian retail, exchange purchases are exempt from sales tax, and MWR facilities (lodging, golf, outdoor recreation, ticket offices) are open at military rates. For a family that shops regularly, easily $1,500-3,000/year.
items.how: Granted by the Purple Heart and Disabled Veterans Equal Access Act, effective January 1, 2020. Access requires a Veteran Health Identification Card (VHIC) showing 'SERVICE CONNECTED,' 'PURPLE HEART,' or 'FORMER POW' on the front below the photo. Veterans rated 100% were already eligible under prior policy and hold a DoD/Uniformed Services ID with broader privileges.
items.hack: The card is the whole benefit and most eligible veterans do not have the right one. You must be ENROLLED IN VA HEALTH CARE to get a VHIC — file VA Form 10-10EZ even if you never intend to use VA medical care, purely to obtain the card. Then verify the front of the card actually prints 'SERVICE CONNECTED'; older VHICs do not, and gate guards will turn you away. Request a reissue at the VA medical center enrollment office. Online exchange shopping at ShopMyExchange, MyNavyExchange and ShopCGX is separately available to all honorably discharged veterans regardless of rating, via VetVerify.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Space-A military flights for 100% permanent and total veterans
items.who: Veterans with a PERMANENT AND TOTAL service-connected disability rating.
items.value: Free flights on military aircraft within the continental United States, Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam and American Samoa. A single CONUS-to-Hawaii trip is worth $800-1,500.
items.how: Eligible veterans travel in Category VI, the lowest priority, behind active duty on emergency leave and post-deployment respite. You must obtain a DD Form 2765 (Department of Defense/Uniformed Services Identification and Privilege Card), the 'TAN card,' from a military ID card office — a VA card will not work. Sign up through the AMC passenger terminals.
items.hack: Three hard limits people learn the expensive way. (1) DEPENDENTS ARE NOT ELIGIBLE on a disabled-veteran sponsor — your spouse cannot fly with you, unlike a retiree's family. (2) You must be able to board and deplane WITHOUT assistance. (3) Category VI means you can be bumped indefinitely, so never fly Space-A without a funded commercial backup plan for the return leg. Also note this requires P&T, not merely 100% — another reason to get 'Permanent and Total' printed on your rating decision.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VALife — guaranteed-acceptance whole life insurance starting at 0%
items.who: Veterans age 80 or younger with ANY service-connected disability rating, including 0%. Veterans 81 or older may qualify if they applied for compensation before turning 81 and apply within 2 years of the rating notification.
items.value: Up to $40,000 of whole life coverage in $10,000 increments, with NO health questions and NO medical exam. Premiums are locked at your application age and never increase. Monthly premiums range from $10.90 (age 18, $10,000) to $442.00 (age 95, $40,000). Cash value begins accruing after 2 years.
items.how: Guaranteed acceptance for anyone meeting the eligibility rules. There is a 2-YEAR WAITING PERIOD before the full death benefit is payable; if you die during the waiting period, beneficiaries receive all premiums paid plus interest (4.23% for 2026). No policy loans are available.
items.hack: This is the reason a 0% rating is worth having. A veteran with diabetes, heart disease, or any condition that makes commercial life insurance unaffordable or unobtainable can buy $40,000 of guaranteed-issue whole life at a locked rate with no underwriting. And because premiums are set by age at application and never rise, applying at 35 instead of 55 roughly halves the lifetime cost. There is no time limit to apply after getting your rating if you are 80 or younger — but the 2-year waiting period means applying today is always better than applying next year.
items.deadline: None if age 80 or younger. Age 81+ must apply within 2 years of the rating notification.

items.title: Social Security expedited processing for 100% P&T veterans and Wounded Warriors
items.who: Veterans with a 100% Permanent and Total VA rating, and service members who became disabled while on active duty on or after October 1, 2001 (Wounded Warriors), applying for SSDI or SSI.
items.value: Priority placement in the SSA queue. Standard SSDI initial decisions commonly take 6-8 months and reconsiderations longer; expedited cases move substantially faster.
items.how: Tell SSA at the time of application that you have a 100% P&T VA rating or were injured on active duty on or after 10/1/2001, and provide the VA rating decision letter. SSA flags the claim for expedited handling.
items.hack: The critical thing consultants charge to explain: EXPEDITED IS NOT AUTOMATIC APPROVAL. SSA applies its OWN definition of disability (inability to engage in any substantial gainful activity) which is stricter and all-or-nothing — there is no 70% in Social Security. A 100% P&T VA rating is strong evidence but is not binding on SSA. Two practical points: (1) SSDI and VA compensation do NOT offset each other — you can receive both in full, and VA compensation does not count as income for SSDI purposes. (2) If you are on TDIU, your VA file already contains the vocational evidence SSA wants; submit your 21-8940, your VA vocational opinion, and the TDIU grant letter with the SSA application.
items.deadline: None. Apply as soon as you stop working.

items.title: 30 Percent or More Disabled Veteran appointing authority — skip the competition
items.who: Veterans with a VA rating of 30% or more compensable service-connected disability, or retired from active military service with a 30%+ disability rating.
items.value: Noncompetitive appointment to federal positions with NO GRADE LIMIT — you can be hired directly at GS-13, GS-14 or GS-15 without ever competing through a USAJOBS announcement.
items.how: Authorized by 5 U.S.C. 3112 and 5 CFR 316.302. An agency may appoint you noncompetitively to a temporary appointment (60 days to 1 year) or a term appointment (1-4 years) in the competitive service, and may convert the appointment to permanent at its discretion. Documentation: DD-214 plus the VA rating decision letter, and SF-15 (Application for 10-Point Veterans' Preference) if claiming preference.
items.hack: Nobody hires you off USAJOBS with this authority — you use it by going around USAJOBS entirely. Identify the specific hiring manager for the job you want, email them your resume and a one-line note that you are eligible for noncompetitive appointment under the 30% or More Disabled Veteran authority (5 CFR 316.302) and they can hire you without a job announcement. You have just eliminated their entire hiring headache. Separately, at 30%+ you fall in the CPS category of 10-point preference, which places you at the TOP of the highest quality category on any competitive referral list — a functional guarantee of being referred. Both tools; use both.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Veteran Readiness and Employment (Chapter 31, VR&E) — better than the GI Bill for many
items.who: Veterans with a service-connected rating of at least 10% (with a serious employment handicap) or 20% (with any employment handicap).
items.value: Pays FULL tuition and fees with no cap, plus books, supplies, required equipment (including computers and tools), plus a monthly subsistence allowance — for up to 48 months. Unlike the Post-9/11 GI Bill, there is no per-credit or state-rate cap on tuition.
items.how: Apply with VA Form 28-1900. A Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor determines entitlement and you build a rehabilitation plan together. Five tracks: Reemployment, Rapid Access to Employment, Self-Employment, Long-Term Services, and Independent Living. The Independent Living track serves veterans whose disabilities make employment unfeasible, funding home modifications, assistive technology and services.
items.hack: Three plays. (1) VR&E pays tuition IN FULL at a private school where the Post-9/11 GI Bill would cap out — for an expensive private or graduate program that difference can exceed $100,000. (2) You can elect to receive the Post-9/11 GI Bill MONTHLY HOUSING ALLOWANCE rate instead of the lower Chapter 31 subsistence allowance while in a VR&E program, which usually pays far more. (3) The SELF-EMPLOYMENT track will fund a business plan, equipment, licenses, and startup inventory — this is the least-used and most valuable track for veterans who cannot tolerate a conventional workplace. Chapter 31 entitlement is separate from and in addition to your GI Bill entitlement.
items.deadline: Generally a 12-year basic period of eligibility from the later of separation or the date VA notifies you of a compensable rating, extendable for a serious employment handicap.

items.title: Protected ratings — the 5-year, 10-year and 20-year rules
items.who: Any veteran with an established rating, especially one facing a proposed reduction.
items.value: Permanent insulation from reduction. A 20-year-protected 70% rating ($1,808.45/month) can never be reduced absent proof of fraud.
items.how: THE 5-YEAR RULE (38 CFR 3.344(a)-(c)): a rating continued at the same level for 5 years or more is 'stabilized.' VA may not reduce it on the basis of one examination, and any reducing exam must be at least as full and complete as the exam that established the rating. Ratings for diseases subject to temporary or episodic improvement cannot be reduced on a single exam unless ALL the evidence clearly warrants a finding of SUSTAINED improvement. THE 10-YEAR RULE (38 CFR 3.957): service connection in effect for 10 or more years cannot be SEVERED except on a showing of fraud, or clear military records showing the person did not have the requisite service or character of discharge. THE 20-YEAR RULE (38 CFR 3.951(b)): a disability continuously rated at or above a given evaluation for 20 or more years cannot be reduced below that evaluation except on a showing of fraud.
items.hack: Know exactly which clock you are on and count from the EFFECTIVE DATE, not the decision date. Then understand the distinction the rules draw: the 10-year rule protects SERVICE CONNECTION (they can reduce you to 0% but can never take the service connection away, which preserves the funding fee waiver, VALife, commissary access and future increase claims); the 20-year rule protects the PERCENTAGE. Also 3.951(a): a change to the rating schedule itself is never grounds for reduction unless medical evidence shows the disability actually improved — so when VA modernizes a body-system's criteria, your existing rating is safe.
items.deadline: Count from the effective date of the rating.

items.title: The age-55 rule and other bars on routine re-examination (38 CFR 3.327(b)(2))
items.who: Veterans over 55, and veterans with static, permanent, or long-stable disabilities.
items.value: No routine future examinations means no reduction risk. This is the difference between keeping a 70% rating for life and defending it every three years.
items.how: 38 CFR 3.327(b)(2) bars scheduling periodic future examinations where: the disability is established as STATIC; findings have persisted WITHOUT MATERIAL IMPROVEMENT for 5 YEARS OR MORE; the disability from disease is PERMANENT in character with no likelihood of improvement; the veteran is OVER 55 YEARS OF AGE, except under unusual circumstances; the rating is a prescribed SCHEDULE MINIMUM rating; or the COMBINED evaluation would not be affected even if a future exam reduced one or more conditions.
items.hack: The last one is the most useful and the least known. If reducing any single condition would not change your COMBINED rating after rounding, VA is not supposed to re-examine you at all. Run the math yourself: if you are at 90% combined and dropping your 30% knee to 10% still leaves you at a raw 87 -> 90%, that exam is prohibited by regulation. Write to the RO citing 3.327(b)(2)(vi) and ask that the scheduled exam be cancelled. Similarly, if you are 56 and get a re-exam notice, cite 3.327(b)(2)(iv) and demand VA state the 'unusual circumstances' justifying it. Do NOT simply skip the exam — 38 CFR 3.655 lets VA reduce or discontinue benefits for failure to report.
items.deadline: Respond to any exam notice; never ignore it.

items.title: Fighting a proposed reduction — 38 CFR 3.105(e), the 60-day and 30-day clocks
items.who: Any veteran who receives a 'Proposed Reduction' letter.
items.value: Stopping a reduction from 70% to 30% preserves $1,255.98/month — $15,072/year — for the rest of your life.
items.how: When VA proposes a lower evaluation it must issue ADVANCE WRITTEN NOTICE and give you 60 DAYS to submit evidence showing the current evaluation should continue. You have 30 DAYS from the notice to REQUEST A PREDETERMINATION HEARING. If you request the hearing, payments CONTINUE AT THE CURRENT RATE pending the final determination, and the hearing must be conducted by personnel not involved in the proposed action. If you do nothing, the reduction takes effect the last day of the month following expiration of the 60-day period.
items.hack: ALWAYS request the predetermination hearing, within 30 days, in writing, even if you have no evidence yet. It is free, it freezes your payment at the current rate, and it buys you months to gather a medical opinion. Then attack on the law, not just the facts: VA must show ACTUAL IMPROVEMENT UNDER THE ORDINARY CONDITIONS OF LIFE AND WORK (Brown v. Brown; Faust v. West), the reducing examination must be at least as full and complete as the one that established the rating (3.344(a)), and for a rating in place 5+ years a single exam is not enough. Reductions get reversed on these procedural grounds constantly — VA loses these on the paperwork more often than on the medicine.
items.deadline: 30 days to request a predetermination hearing. 60 days to submit evidence. Both run from the date of the proposal letter.

items.title: Temporary 100% — convalescent ratings (38 CFR 4.30) and hospitalization (38 CFR 4.29)
items.who: Veterans who have surgery or are hospitalized for a service-connected condition.
items.value: Paid at the full 100% rate ($3,938.58 alone) for 1, 2, or 3 months, extendable up to 3 additional months, and up to 6 additional months in severe cases with Veterans Service Center Manager approval. A veteran at 30% who has a service-connected knee replacement can go from $552.47 to $3,938.58 for several months.
items.how: 38 CFR 4.30 assigns a temporary 100% rating when hospital discharge or outpatient release records show: surgery necessitating at least one month of convalescence; OR surgery with severe postoperative residuals (incompletely healed surgical wounds, recent amputation stumps, therapeutic immobilization of one or more major joints, a body cast, house confinement, or continued use of a wheelchair or crutches); OR immobilization by cast, without surgery, of one or more major joints. The rating runs from the first day of the month following discharge or release. 38 CFR 4.29 assigns a temporary 100% for hospitalization over 21 days for a service-connected disability.
items.hack: VA does not grant these automatically — you must claim them, and you must claim them with the DISCHARGE SUMMARY and the surgeon's note stating the required convalescent period. The magic language is 'at least one month of convalescence' or a listed severe residual; get the surgeon to write it before you leave. Two more: (1) a knee or hip replacement carries its own separate mandatory 100% period under the prosthetic-replacement diagnostic codes (DC 5051-5056), typically 1 year, which is BETTER than 4.30 — claim under the higher one. (2) Temporary 100% does NOT qualify you for Class IV dental or the other 100% benefits; VA states this expressly.
items.deadline: File after the surgery or discharge; the rating runs from the first day of the following month.

items.title: VA Form 20-10207 — Priority Processing request
items.who: Veterans with a qualifying hardship or status.
items.value: Free. Moves your claim to the front of the queue, often cutting many months off the wait. On a 100% claim at $3,938.58/month, six months saved is $23,631.
items.how: Submit VA Form 20-10207 to request priority processing based on a qualifying circumstance or status. Attach documentation of the qualifying circumstance (eviction notice, utility shutoff notice, physician's terminal prognosis, homelessness verification).
items.hack: Most veterans never learn this form exists. VA has long recognized priority categories including terminal illness, ALS, seriously or very seriously injured status, Medal of Honor recipients, former POWs, homelessness or imminent risk of homelessness, EXTREME FINANCIAL HARDSHIP, and advanced age. Extreme financial hardship is the broadly applicable one — an eviction notice, a foreclosure notice, or a utility shutoff notice is documentation, and it is a very low bar in practice. If you are in genuine financial distress waiting on a claim, file this form the same day. Confirm the currently qualifying circumstances on the form instructions before filing.
items.deadline: Any time while a claim is pending.

items.title: State property tax exemptions — the biggest benefit VA does not administer
items.who: Disabled veterans, with thresholds and amounts set entirely by each state (and sometimes county).
items.value: Ranges from a few hundred dollars to a COMPLETE exemption from property tax. In high-tax jurisdictions a full 100% homestead exemption is worth $6,000-15,000 per year, every year, and often passes to a surviving spouse.
items.how: Entirely state law. Common structures: full exemption at 100% or P&T (Texas, Florida, Virginia, Michigan, New Jersey, Oklahoma and others); banded partial exemptions starting at 10% or 30% and scaling up (Texas bands at 10-29%, 30-49%, 50-69%, 70%+); flat-dollar homestead reductions; and complete exemptions for SAH grant recipients. Administered by the county assessor or tax collector, not VA.
items.hack: Four things. (1) Nothing is automatic — you must apply to the county with your VA rating decision letter, and most states have an annual application deadline in the spring. (2) Many states allow RETROACTIVE refunds for prior years once you establish the rating had a retroactive effective date; ask specifically for a refund of prior-year taxes back to your effective date. (3) Many states extend the exemption to a SURVIVING SPOUSE for life or until remarriage — make sure your spouse knows the file location. (4) Whether TDIU counts varies: most states that key on '100% disabled' accept TDIU because VA pays at the 100% rate, but a minority require 100% SCHEDULAR. Verify with the STATE veterans affairs office, not the county clerk, who will usually guess.
items.deadline: Set by each state, commonly an annual spring filing deadline.

items.title: Use an accredited representative — and never pay for an initial claim
items.who: Every veteran filing or appealing a claim.
items.value: VSO representation is FREE. Accredited attorneys and agents may charge only after an initial decision, and fees are typically 20% of past-due benefits, paid by VA directly from the retroactive award.
items.how: Only VA-accredited attorneys, claims agents, and Veterans Service Organization representatives may legally represent you before VA. Appoint a representative with VA Form 21-22 (VSO) or 21-22a (attorney or agent). By law, NO ONE may charge a fee for preparing or presenting an INITIAL claim for benefits — representation on an initial claim must be free.
items.hack: This is the biggest consumer protection issue in the space. Unaccredited 'claim consultants' and 'coaches' who charge a percentage of your award, or a flat fee of several thousand dollars up front, for help with an INITIAL claim are operating outside 38 U.S.C. 5904 and 38 CFR 14.636. Use VA's accreditation search to verify anyone before you sign or pay. A free accredited VSO (DAV, VFW, American Legion, state Department of Veterans Affairs) can do everything on an initial claim; hire an accredited attorney only AFTER a denial, when a contingency fee against past-due benefits is legal and aligns incentives. Also: an appointed representative gets the decision letter at the same time you do and can flag deadlines you will otherwise miss.
items.deadline: Appoint a representative before filing, so they receive copies of all correspondence.

items.title: VA disability compensation is tax-free — and the retroactive military retirement play
items.who: All recipients of VA disability compensation, and especially medically retired service members.
items.value: Every dollar of VA compensation is excluded from federal gross income and is not counted as taxable income by essentially every state. At the 100% with-spouse rate of $4,158.17/month ($49,898/year), the pre-tax equivalent salary is roughly $65,000-70,000 depending on bracket and state.
items.how: VA compensation, SMC, DIC, grants for adapted housing and vehicles, and VR&E benefits are all excluded from gross income. VA does not issue a 1099 for compensation. Military retired pay, by contrast, IS taxable, which is why retirees waive retired pay dollar-for-dollar to receive VA compensation (or receive both under CRDP at 50%+, or CRSC for combat-related disabilities at any rating).
items.hack: The retroactive play for medical retirees: if you are awarded a VA rating with an effective date RETROACTIVE to a period during which you paid federal income tax on military retired pay, you can file amended returns (IRS Form 1040-X) to recover the tax on the portion now recharacterized as VA compensation. IRS Publication 525 addresses this, and the normal 3-year amendment limit is extended for retroactive VA determinations. Veterans have recovered five figures. Bring the VA rating decision showing the retroactive effective date and the DFAS corrected accounting to a tax preparer.
items.deadline: Amended returns generally within 3 years, with a special extension for retroactive VA disability determinations.

items.title: Never accept a low-ball rating — and the mistakes that cost the most
items.who: Every veteran who just received a rating decision.
items.value: The difference between a first-decision 30% and a correctly-litigated 70% on the same evidence is $1,255.98/month for life, plus every benefit gated at 50% and 70%.
items.how: Read the decision's REASONS AND BASES section and the CODE SHEET, not just the percentage. Compare what the examiner recorded against the literal text of the diagnostic criteria in 38 CFR Part 4. Then pick the right lane: missing evidence -> Supplemental Claim; correct evidence misapplied -> Higher-Level Review; undebatable error in a final decision -> CUE.
items.hack: The eight most expensive mistakes, in order. (1) Not filing an Intent to File — forfeits up to a year of back pay. (2) Not adding dependents within a year of hitting 30%. (3) Accepting the first decision because the check started arriving. (4) Missing the 180-day post-discharge dental window. (5) Never claiming secondaries — most veterans stop at the conditions documented in their STRs. (6) Never asking for SMC-K on erectile dysfunction or SMC-S when the math already supports it. (7) Choosing Higher-Level Review when the problem was missing evidence, burning 5 months for a guaranteed denial. (8) Filing 10% claims when already at 90% — where they are mathematically worth zero. Fix all eight and the average veteran's lifetime award moves by six figures.
items.deadline: 1 year from any decision to file HLR, Supplemental Claim, or Board Appeal in a way that preserves the effective date.

items.title: Post-9/11 GI Bill (Chapter 33)
items.who: Anyone with 90+ days of active duty on or after Sept 11, 2001; a post-9/11 Purple Heart; or 30+ continuous days ending in a service-connected-disability discharge. Also dependents using transferred entitlement.
items.value: 36 months. AY2026-27: net in-state tuition/fees at public schools with no cap; up to $30,908.34/yr at private or foreign schools; up to $1,000/yr books; BAH-based monthly housing allowance; plus tutoring, licensing exams and work-study.
items.how: Apply online with VA Form 22-1990 at va.gov/education/how-to-apply. VA issues a Certificate of Eligibility (COE) showing your tier percentage and remaining months; hand the COE to your school's certifying official (SCO), who submits the enrollment certification that triggers payment.
items.hack: Your COE tier is computed from what DFAS reported, and it is wrong often enough to be worth checking. Add up your qualifying active-duty days yourself from your DD-214(s) - including post-9/11 Title 10 mobilizations as a Guard/Reservist, which many COEs miss entirely - and if you cross 1,095 days, file a supplemental claim to get bumped to 100%. The jump from 90% to 100% is worth roughly $3,000/yr in tuition at a private school plus unlocking Yellow Ribbon, which is effectively unlimited money.
items.deadline: No expiration if your last discharge was on or after Jan 1, 2013 (Forever GI Bill). 15 years from separation if you separated before that date.

items.title: AY2026-27 Private/Foreign School Tuition Cap: $30,908.34
items.who: Ch 33 and Fry Scholarship students at private, foreign, or non-college-degree institutions.
items.value: $30,908.34 per academic year (Aug 1, 2026 - Jul 31, 2027) at 100% tier, prorated by tier. Flight training: $17,661.89/yr. Correspondence: $15,012.59/yr. Public schools: net in-state tuition and fees, NO cap.
items.how: VA pays the school directly after the SCO certifies. The cap resets each Aug 1, so a fall-spring academic year straddles only one cap - but a summer term that starts on or after Aug 1 draws from the NEXT year's cap.
items.hack: Schedule expensive coursework across the Aug 1 boundary. If you have a $50k/yr private program, taking a heavy summer term starting Aug 1 and a lighter fall gives you two separate $30,908.34 buckets inside twelve calendar months. Also: a 'public' school branch campus or a public university's contracted program can sometimes be certified as public (uncapped) rather than private - ask the SCO which approval code your specific program carries before you enroll.
items.deadline: Rate applies Aug 1, 2026 - Jul 31, 2027; new cap published each Aug 1.

items.title: Post-9/11 Monthly Housing Allowance - How It's Actually Computed
items.who: Ch 33 / Fry students enrolled at more than 50% rate of pursuit, not on active duty.
items.value: DoD BAH for E-5 WITH dependents at the campus ZIP code x your tier percentage x your rate of pursuit (rounded to nearest 10%). Ranges from roughly $1,300/mo in low-cost areas to over $4,800/mo in San Francisco, NYC and Honolulu.
items.how: VA uses the ZIP of the campus where you attend the majority of your classes - not your home address. Paid in arrears around the 1st of the following month, prorated by day, and it stops entirely during breaks between terms.
items.hack: Two levers most students never pull. (1) If your school has multiple campuses, enroll in sections physically located at the HIGHEST-BAH campus even if you take some classes elsewhere - the majority-of-classes rule determines the whole ZIP. A Manhattan campus versus an outer-borough campus of the same university can be a $900/mo difference. (2) Rate of pursuit rounds to the nearest 10%, so at a 12-credit full-time standard, 7 credits = 58.3% which rounds to 60%, and adding a single 1-credit course to hit 8 credits = 66.7% rounds to 70%. One cheap credit is worth ~10% of your MHA every month. (3) Take one in-person credit instead of going fully online - that flips you from the $1,261 flat online rate to the full local BAH rate.
items.deadline: Must complete VA's monthly enrollment verification (text or email); two consecutive missed verifications suspends MHA.

items.title: Online-Only MHA: $1,261/month (AY2026-27)
items.who: Ch 33 students taking 100% of coursework online, who started using benefits on or after Jan 1, 2018.
items.value: $1,261/month at 100% tier (half the national average BAH), prorated by tier and rate of pursuit. Foreign-school students get up to $2,522/month.
items.how: Automatic if every course you're certified for is online. Mixing in even one in-residence course moves you to the campus-ZIP BAH rate.
items.hack: This is the single highest-ROI schedule tweak in the GI Bill. If your local campus BAH is above $2,522/mo (most of CA, NY, DC, Seattle, Boston, Hawaii, Alaska), registering for one 1-credit in-person course - a PE class, a 1-credit seminar, a lab - can more than double your housing check for the whole term. Do the arithmetic before you register: (local E-5-w/deps BAH - $1,261) x months in term, versus the cost of one credit.
items.deadline: Applies for AY Aug 1, 2026 - Jul 31, 2027.

items.title: Books & Supplies Stipend: $1,000/year
items.who: All Ch 33 and Fry Scholarship students, including those in OJT/apprenticeship.
items.value: Up to $1,000 per academic year, paid at $41.67 per credit hour, capped at 24 credits per year, prorated by tier percentage.
items.how: Paid to you directly at the start of each term, based on certified credit hours. No receipts required - it is a stipend, not a reimbursement.
items.hack: It's paid per credit hour up to 24, so credits 25 and beyond in an academic year generate zero book money. If you're an overloader, you're leaving nothing on the table - but if you're a part-timer, front-loading credits into fall and spring (rather than spreading 24 credits across three terms including summer) gets you the same $1,000 sooner and avoids the risk of a summer term crossing the Aug 1 boundary into a new $1,000 bucket you won't fully use. Separately: this money is yours whether or not you buy books, so rent or buy used and pocket the difference tax-free.
items.deadline: Per academic year, Aug 1 - Jul 31.

items.title: Rural Relocation Benefit: $500 One-Time
items.who: Ch 33 students who resided in a county with 6 or fewer persons per square mile and physically relocated to attend school.
items.value: $500, one time, on top of all other benefits.
items.how: You must have relocated at least 500 miles to attend, or have traveled by air because no land-based travel was practicable. Claimed through your VA regional processing office / school certifying official.
items.hack: Almost nobody claims this because VA doesn't advertise it and SCOs at urban schools have never processed one. Check the Census population density of your pre-enrollment county (most of MT, WY, NV, ND, SD, AK and rural TX qualify). It is free money and it does not charge entitlement.
items.deadline: Claim for the term in which you relocated.

items.title: Forever GI Bill - No Expiration Date
items.who: Anyone whose last discharge from active duty was on or after Jan 1, 2013, and their transferees.
items.value: Unlimited time to use 36 months of Post-9/11 GI Bill. Pre-2013 separations still face a 15-year delimiting date.
items.how: Automatic under the Harry W. Colmery Veterans Educational Assistance Act of 2017. No application needed.
items.hack: If you separated slightly before Jan 1, 2013 and later did ANY qualifying active-duty period (a Guard/Reserve Title 10 mobilization, an IRR recall, even a short AGR tour) that ended on or after Jan 1, 2013, your delimiting date disappears entirely. Many veterans in this position have an expiring COE they believe is final. Submit the later DD-214 and ask VA to remove the delimiting date. Ch 35 DEA and Ch 30 did NOT get this protection - Ch 30 still expires 10 years after separation.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: Rudisill/Perkins: Up to 48 Months Across Ch 30 + Ch 33
items.who: Veterans with two qualifying periods of service (Rudisill), or a single obligated period long enough that different months qualify for different programs (Perkins).
items.value: Up to 48 months of combined entitlement instead of 36 - roughly 12 extra months, worth $30k-$70k depending on school and MHA.
items.how: After the Supreme Court's April 16, 2024 Rudisill decision and the subsequent Perkins ruling, you no longer must waive MGIB to use Post-9/11, and Post-9/11 entitlement is no longer limited to your remaining MGIB months. VA says it will automatically review files and issue new COEs; the prior Oct 1, 2030 claim deadline no longer applies.
items.hack: Do not wait for the automatic review. VA is prioritizing veterans currently enrolled or enrolled in the last six months, and files outside that window sit. If you previously signed the irrevocable MGIB waiver to get Post-9/11, that waiver can now be REVOKED - call the Education Call Center (888-442-4551) and ask for a Rudisill re-evaluation in writing. Sequence matters: burn Ch 30 first (it has a 10-year delimiting date and a lower value), then switch to Ch 33, which never expires.
items.deadline: No deadline; the Oct 1, 2030 cutoff was removed.

items.title: GI Bill for Apprenticeships & On-the-Job Training
items.who: Ch 33 users in a VA-approved apprenticeship or OJT program (union trades, police/fire academies, many employers).
items.value: Declining share of full local BAH on top of your paycheck: 100% months 1-6, 80% months 7-12, 60% months 13-18, 40% months 19-24, 20% at 2 years and beyond. Plus up to $1,000/yr books.
items.how: The employer or union must have a VA-approved OJT/apprenticeship program. Your employer's training supervisor certifies your hours monthly to VA.
items.hack: Two things almost no one exploits. (1) The declining schedule resets per PROGRAM, not per lifetime - finishing a 2-year apprenticeship and starting a different approved apprenticeship restarts you at 100% BAH. (2) The OJT MHA uses full BAH regardless of the 50%-rate-of-pursuit rule that constrains classroom students, and it stacks on top of a full-time union wage. A first-year electrical apprentice in a high-BAH metro can pull $3,500+/mo in MHA on top of scale for six months. (3) If your employer isn't approved, you can ask them to apply through the State Approving Agency - it costs them nothing and takes a few weeks.
items.deadline: None; entitlement charged month-for-month.

items.title: Yellow Ribbon Program
items.who: Ch 33 students at the 100% tier only; Fry Scholars; children using transferred entitlement; active-duty members with 36+ months (and, since Aug 2022, active-duty spouses at some schools). NOT available at 90% or below.
items.value: Covers tuition and fees above the $30,908.34 private-school cap. The school contributes an amount and VA MATCHES it dollar-for-dollar - so an 'unlimited' school effectively zeroes out tuition at any price.
items.how: School must have a Yellow Ribbon agreement with VA and must not have hit its enrollment cap for that program. Apply through your school's VA certifying official - it is a school-level, first-come-first-served process, not a VA application.
items.hack: The single most valuable move in veteran education planning: filter the GI Bill Comparison Tool for schools offering UNLIMITED Yellow Ribbon slots at UNLIMITED dollar amounts. Dozens of elite private and graduate programs - law schools, MBA programs, medical schools - do this, which means a $75,000/yr program costs you $0. Then apply EARLY in the cycle: caps are per-program per-year and first-come-first-served, so a January admit can get the slot a July admit is denied. Also confirm in writing which SCHOOL (undergrad vs. law vs. business) the agreement covers - they are often negotiated separately and a university-wide 'yes' does not mean your program participates.
items.deadline: Per school year; slots fill first-come, first-served, so ask before you accept an offer.

items.title: Find Yellow Ribbon Schools & Dollar Amounts
items.who: Prospective Ch 33/Fry students comparing private and graduate schools.
items.value: Searchable list showing each school's per-degree-level contribution amount and number of students covered.
items.how: Search by school name or state at the VA Yellow Ribbon participating schools tool, or use the GI Bill Comparison Tool's Yellow Ribbon filter.
items.hack: Read the 'number of students' column, not just the dollar column. A school offering $25,000 to only 5 students is worse for you than a school offering $10,000 to unlimited students if you're applying late. And schools update agreements each spring for the following academic year - a school that was capped last year may be unlimited this year, so re-check rather than relying on a forum post.
items.deadline: Agreements renew annually; new list posts each spring for the coming academic year.

items.title: Transfer of Entitlement (TEB) to Spouse or Children
items.who: Active-duty and Selected Reserve members with 6+ years of service who agree to serve 4 more. Purple Heart recipients are exempt from the service requirement but must still transfer while serving.
items.value: Up to 36 months of Post-9/11 GI Bill transferred to a spouse and/or children, in any split you choose (as little as 1 month each).
items.how: Request through milConnect (DMDC), NOT through VA. VA cannot process a TEB request. Dependents must be enrolled in DEERS. After DoD approves, the dependent applies to VA with Form 22-1990E.
items.hack: THE most important irreversible decision in the GI Bill: you can only transfer WHILE SERVING. The day you sign your DD-214, the door closes forever. So before you separate, transfer at least ONE MONTH to your spouse and to every child you have - including infants. One month costs you almost nothing and permanently locks in their eligibility. You can then log back into milConnect years later, as a civilian, and REALLOCATE months among people who already have a transfer on record. You cannot add a NEW person after separation, but you can move months between existing recipients freely. Every transitioning servicemember should do this on their out-processing checklist.
items.deadline: Must be requested and approved while still serving. The 4-year additional service obligation runs from the approval date.

items.title: TEB: Spouse vs. Child Rules (They're Very Different)
items.who: Dependents using transferred Post-9/11 entitlement.
items.value: Spouses: may use immediately, even while the sponsor is still serving, but get NO housing allowance while the sponsor is on active duty. Children: must wait until the sponsor completes 10 years of service, but DO receive MHA even while the sponsor is serving.
items.how: Children must have a high school diploma/equivalency or be 18+, and must use the benefit before turning 26. Spouses who received a transfer must use it within 15 years of the sponsor's separation IF the sponsor separated before Jan 1, 2013; for separations on or after that date there is no time limit.
items.hack: The age-26 wall for children is hard and unforgiving - a child who starts at 25 loses everything unused at 26. Plan the split around it: give months to the OLDER child first and reallocate to younger siblings later, since months sitting on a 24-year-old expire while months sitting on a 10-year-old don't. Conversely, if your sponsor is still on active duty, route entitlement to the CHILD (who gets MHA) rather than the spouse (who doesn't) - that's a $2,000-$4,000/mo difference for the exact same months of entitlement.
items.deadline: Children must use before age 26. Spouse 15-year rule applies only to pre-2013 separations.

items.title: Montgomery GI Bill - Active Duty (Chapter 30)
items.who: Service members who enrolled and paid the $1,200 buy-in ($100/month for 12 months) and served 2-3+ years of active duty.
items.value: FY2027 (from Oct 1, 2026): $2,601/month full time with 3+ years of service; $2,110/month with 2-3 years. 36 months maximum. Paid directly to you, not the school.
items.how: Apply with VA Form 22-1990. You certify enrollment monthly through WAVE (Web Automated Verification of Enrollment) or by calling 877-823-2378 - no monthly certification, no check.
items.hack: MGIB beats Post-9/11 in three specific cases: (1) you attend a cheap in-state public school or community college (tuition under ~$4,000/yr) and live rent-free - the $2,601 flat check exceeds tuition-plus-MHA math; (2) you're on ACTIVE DUTY using TA, where Ch 33 pays you $0 MHA but Ch 30 Top-Up still pays cash; (3) you're enrolled less than half time, where Ch 33 pays zero MHA but Ch 30 still prorates a check. Run both numbers on the Comparison Tool before electing - and post-Rudisill, you may not have to choose at all.
items.deadline: Expires 10 years after your last separation from active duty - this is NOT covered by the Forever GI Bill.

items.title: The $1,200 MGIB Buy-In Refund Quirk
items.who: Veterans who paid the $1,200 MGIB buy-in, switched to Post-9/11, and then fully exhausted their Post-9/11 entitlement.
items.value: Up to $1,200 back, prorated: (unused MGIB months / 36) x $1,200. Example: 20.5 unused months = $683.33.
items.how: Paid AUTOMATICALLY, bundled into your final monthly housing allowance payment. No form to file.
items.hack: Two traps. First, the refund only fires if you were RECEIVING MHA on the day your entitlement ran out - so if your last term ends and you stop enrollment before exhausting entitlement, you may never trigger it. Plan your final term so your last month of entitlement is consumed while enrolled and drawing MHA. Second, because it arrives folded into a housing payment, thousands of veterans have received it without noticing and thousands more never triggered it. Check your final MHA deposit against the expected amount. Note: the separate $600 Buy-Up program is NEVER refundable.
items.deadline: Triggered at exhaustion of Post-9/11 entitlement.

items.title: MGIB $600 Buy-Up Program
items.who: Active-duty members eligible for MGIB-AD (Ch 30), while still serving.
items.value: Contribute up to $600 extra (in $20 increments) and receive up to $150 more per month for 36 months - a maximum of $5,400 back on a $600 investment, a 9:1 return.
items.how: Enroll through your personnel/finance office while on active duty using DD Form 2366-1. Cannot be done after separation.
items.hack: A 9x return is the best math in the entire military benefits catalog - but ONLY if you actually use Chapter 30. The $600 is non-refundable and carries ZERO value if you end up using Post-9/11 instead, which most people do. So the buy-up is a good bet specifically for people who plan to use Ch 30 for a cheap in-state degree or Top-Up while on active duty. If you already paid it and are switching to Ch 33, that money is gone - don't let it anchor you into the worse benefit.
items.deadline: Must enroll before separating from active duty.

items.title: GI Bill Kickers (Army/Navy/MOS College Fund)
items.who: Service members who were contractually promised a 'kicker' or 'college fund' at enlistment or reenlistment, usually for hard-to-fill MOS/ratings or critical Reserve units.
items.value: Historically $100-$950+ per month added on top of your base GI Bill rate, for up to 36 months. Amount is set by the service contract, not by VA.
items.how: The service branch reports the kicker to VA; it is then paid with your monthly GI Bill payment. Under Ch 33, the kicker is paid to you monthly as a separate amount from MHA.
items.hack: Kickers are frequently lost in the transition from Ch 30 to Ch 33, or simply never reported by the branch to VA. Pull your enlistment/reenlistment contract and look for the kicker annex or DD Form 2384-1. If VA isn't paying it, contact your branch's education office to have it re-reported - it's a service-side data problem, not a VA claim, and veterans have recovered years of unpaid kicker retroactively. Also: kickers transfer with TEB, so a transferred benefit can carry the kicker to a dependent.
items.deadline: Tied to the underlying GI Bill program's delimiting date.

items.title: Montgomery GI Bill - Selected Reserve (Chapter 1606)
items.who: Guard and Reserve members with a 6-year Selected Reserve obligation who have completed IADT and hold a high school diploma/equivalency.
items.value: FY2027 (from Oct 1, 2026): $508/month full time; $408 three-quarter; $253 half; $127 less than half. 36 months maximum. Licensing/certification tests reimbursed up to $2,000 each; national tests reimbursed with no cap.
items.how: Your unit determines eligibility and issues a DD Form 2384-1 Notice of Basic Eligibility (NOBE); then apply to VA with Form 22-1990.
items.hack: Ch 1606 has no Forever GI Bill protection - eligibility generally ENDS when you leave the Selected Reserve, so use it while you're still drilling. The sleeper value isn't the $508/mo classroom rate, it's the test reimbursement: Ch 1606 will reimburse licensing and certification exams at up to $2,000 each and national tests with NO cap, and each $508 reimbursed only burns one month. A drilling reservist can stack CompTIA, PMP, CCNA and a state license through Ch 1606 while preserving every month of Post-9/11 for a degree.
items.deadline: Ends when you leave the Selected Reserve (with limited exceptions for disability separations).

items.title: VR&E / Veteran Readiness & Employment (Chapter 31)
items.who: Veterans with a service-connected disability rating of at least 10% and an employment handicap; active-duty members with a 20%+ pre-discharge memorandum rating. Not dishonorably discharged.
items.value: Tuition and fees paid IN FULL with no annual cap (public or private), ALL required books, supplies, tools, laptops, certification/licensing fees, plus a monthly subsistence allowance. Up to 48 months, extendable for serious employment handicap.
items.how: Apply with VA Form 28-1900 at va.gov/careers-employment/vocational-rehabilitation/apply. You are assigned a Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor (VRC) who conducts an evaluation and, if you're found entitled, co-writes an Individualized Rehabilitation Plan.
items.hack: For most disabled veterans, Ch 31 is strictly better than Ch 33 and they use Ch 33 anyway out of ignorance. Ch 31 has no tuition cap (so no Yellow Ribbon needed at a $90k/yr program), pays for a laptop and all tools, covers certification exams, runs to 48 months instead of 36, and - the decisive part - if you're ALSO Ch 33-eligible you can elect the Post-9/11 BAH-based housing rate instead of the flat Ch 31 subsistence rate, so you get Ch 33's housing money AND Ch 31's uncapped tuition. Using Ch 31 also does NOT consume Ch 33 entitlement unless you elect the Ch 33 subsistence rate. The correct default for a 10%+ rated veteran is: apply for Ch 31 first, and keep Ch 33 in reserve.
items.deadline: No time limit if you were discharged on or after Jan 1, 2013. 12-year basic eligibility period if discharged before that, extendable with a serious employment handicap finding.

items.title: The Five VR&E Tracks
items.who: Veterans found entitled to Ch 31.
items.value: Reemployment; Rapid Access to Employment; Self-Employment (including business plan development and startup capital for equipment/supplies); Long-Term Services (the track that funds degrees); Independent Living.
items.how: Your VRC assigns a track during the evaluation. The track determines what VA will fund - only Long-Term Services reliably funds a four-year or graduate degree.
items.hack: Counselors default to 'Rapid Access to Employment' because it closes cases fastest and it's cheapest. That track will NOT pay for a bachelor's or master's degree. If you want school funded, you must make the case at your very first meeting that your disability plus your labor-market reality require long-term training - bring labor market data, a specific occupational goal, and evidence that your prior occupation is now unsuitable. Ask explicitly for the Long-Term Services track and have the counselor document why the shorter track is inadequate. The self-employment track is separately underused: VA will fund equipment, licenses, and a business plan consultant for a viable venture.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: Ch 31 Subsistence Allowance Rates (FY2026)
items.who: Veterans in a VR&E training plan.
items.value: Institutional full time: $812.84/mo (no dependents), $1,008.24 (1 dependent), $1,188.15 (2 dependents), +$86.58 each additional. 3/4 time: $610.76 / $757.28 / $888.32. 1/2 time: $408.66 / $506.32 / $595.16. Apprenticeship/OJT full time: $710.67 / $859.43 / $990.47. Maximum possible: $3,439.23/mo.
items.how: Paid monthly during active training under your rehabilitation plan. Effective Oct 1, 2025 (2.5% increase); FY2027 rates were not yet published as of Sept 15, 2026.
items.hack: These flat rates are far below Ch 33 MHA in any metro area - which is exactly why you should elect the Post-9/11 subsistence option if you qualify for both. A veteran with no dependents attending school in Seattle gets $812.84 under standard Ch 31 versus roughly $3,300 under the Ch 33-rate election: a $30,000/year difference for identical training. Your VRC will not always volunteer this; ask in writing for the 'Post-9/11 GI Bill subsistence allowance rate' election and confirm it in your rehabilitation plan.
items.deadline: FY2026 rates run Oct 1, 2025 - Sep 30, 2026; a COLA increase is expected Oct 1, 2026.

items.title: VR&E Independent Living Track
items.who: Veterans with service-connected disabilities so severe that employment is not currently reasonably feasible.
items.value: Services and equipment to enable independent living: assistive technology, home modifications, adaptive equipment, independent living skills training, connection to community resources. Generally capped at 24 months, extendable to 30 months in limited cases.
items.how: Requested through the same Form 28-1900 and VRC evaluation process; the VRC must find that an employment goal is not currently feasible.
items.hack: This track is chronically under-referred because it doesn't generate an employment outcome statistic. Veterans with severe PTSD, TBI, or mobility limitations are frequently told they're 'not eligible for VR&E' when in fact they are the exact population Independent Living exists for. If a counselor says employment isn't feasible for you, that is not a denial - it is the trigger for the IL track. Ask for it by name and ask for the denial in writing if refused, because a written denial is appealable.
items.deadline: Typically 24 months of services, extendable to 30.

items.title: How to Apply for and Appeal VR&E (Form 28-1900)
items.who: Any veteran or servicemember seeking Ch 31.
items.value: Free application; a denial is fully appealable through the standard VA decision review process.
items.how: Apply online at va.gov or file VA Form 28-1900. If denied entitlement, you have three options under the Appeals Modernization Act: (1) Supplemental Claim with new and relevant evidence, (2) Higher-Level Review by a senior VRC/officer, or (3) appeal to the Board of Veterans' Appeals via VA Form 10182 - all with a 1-year window from the decision date.
items.hack: Most Ch 31 denials turn on 'no employment handicap,' not on your rating. Beat that by attacking it with evidence rather than argument: get a vocational expert or your treating clinician to write a short statement linking specific service-connected symptoms to specific functional limitations in your prior occupation, and pair it with Bureau of Labor Statistics data showing that occupation's physical/cognitive demands. Also request a Higher-Level Review with an informal conference - you get to talk to the reviewer by phone, which is the fastest route to an overturn. Separately, ask your VRC for a copy of the Counseling/Evaluation report; denials frequently rest on a factual error you can correct in one page.
items.deadline: One year from the date of the decision letter to file any of the three review options.

items.title: Chapter 35 DEA (Survivors' & Dependents' Educational Assistance)
items.who: Spouses and children of veterans who are permanently and totally disabled from a service-connected condition (100% P&T, including TDIU), who died of a service-connected condition, or who died while on active duty; plus dependents of servicemembers MIA/captured/detained.
items.value: 36 months. FY2027 (from Oct 1, 2026): $1,621/mo full time, $1,281 three-quarter, $939 half time. OJT: $1,029 / $774 / $508 / $259 by 6-month block. Flat cash to the student - no tuition paid to the school, no books stipend, no Yellow Ribbon.
items.how: Apply with VA Form 22-5490 (or 22-5495 to change programs/schools). Children apply in their own name once they're 18 or have a high school diploma.
items.hack: Ch 35 is a cash stipend, so it is at its most powerful at a very cheap school. A dependent at a community college paying $2,500/yr in tuition nets roughly $12,000+/yr in surplus cash from Ch 35 - then transfers to a four-year school. Also note Ch 35 is one of the few VA education benefits where the student can ALSO receive full federal Pell Grant and state aid without offset, because VA isn't paying the school. And since Aug 1, 2022, Ch 35 users are 'covered individuals' for in-state tuition under Section 702.
items.deadline: Spouses: 10 years from the date VA establishes eligibility (20 years in some cases, e.g., death on active duty). Children: generally between ages 18 and 26, extendable in limited circumstances.

items.title: Chapter 35 Age and Time Windows
items.who: Ch 35 children and spouses.
items.value: Children: eligibility normally runs from age 18 to age 26 (can begin at 17 if a high school graduate). Spouses: 10 years from VA's eligibility determination date, or 20 years if the servicemember died on active duty or the veteran was rated 100% P&T from the date of a qualifying determination.
items.how: Extensions beyond the child's 26th birthday are possible for periods of serious illness or active-duty service that prevented use.
items.hack: The spouse's 10-year clock starts on VA's ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION date, not the date of injury or death. If the veteran's 100% P&T rating was granted with a retroactive effective date, the clock may already be partly burned - but there's a corollary: for a spouse of a veteran rated 100% P&T, the 10-year window can be reset to start from the date of the P&T rating decision, and if the veteran's rating was later upgraded, ask VA to re-establish the beginning date. For children, if the child served on active duty between 18 and 26, those years are excluded from the window - so a dependent who enlists does not lose Ch 35.
items.deadline: Child: age 26. Spouse: 10 or 20 years from eligibility date.

items.title: Fry Scholarship (Post-9/11 GI Bill for Survivors)
items.who: Children and surviving spouses of service members who died in the line of duty on or after Sept 11, 2001, or who died of a service-connected disability within 120 days of discharge; and of Selected Reserve members who died from a service-connected disability.
items.value: Full Post-9/11 GI Bill at the 100% tier: tuition paid to the school (net in-state at public, up to $30,908.34/yr private), full BAH-based MHA, $1,000/yr books, Yellow Ribbon eligibility. 36 months.
items.how: Apply with VA Form 22-5490. Combined Fry + Ch 35 cap: 81 months if the death was before Aug 1, 2011; 48 months if on or after.
items.hack: Fry is dramatically better than Ch 35 and many survivors are steered into Ch 35 by habit. Run the comparison: at a private school, Fry is worth $30,908 tuition + ~$25,000 MHA + $1,000 books = roughly $57,000/year, versus about $19,000/year of flat cash under Ch 35. The one wrinkle: a CHILD must give up DIC payments to use Fry (a surviving SPOUSE does not). Do the math on the child's DIC amount versus the Fry delta before electing - in almost every case Fry wins by a wide margin, but the election is irrevocable. Also: unused expired Fry benefits may be restorable after Jan 2, 2025 for surviving spouses.
items.deadline: No time limit if the death occurred on or after Jan 1, 2013. Children of pre-2013 deaths: until age 33, unless they turned 18 or graduated high school after that date, which removes the limit.

items.title: Fry vs. Chapter 35: Which to Use and When
items.who: Survivors who are eligible for both Fry and DEA.
items.value: Fry ≈ $57,000/yr at a private school with Yellow Ribbon. Ch 35 ≈ $19,452/yr (FY2027 full-time rate x 12) in flat cash. Combined cap 48 months (deaths on/after Aug 1, 2011) or 81 months (before).
items.how: You may use both sequentially, but not simultaneously, and the combined months cap applies.
items.hack: Optimal sequence for a survivor eligible for both: use CHAPTER 35 first at a cheap community college (where the flat stipend exceeds costs and you pocket surplus cash), then switch to FRY for the expensive four-year or graduate portion where tuition coverage and full MHA dominate. That ordering can be worth $40,000+ versus using them in the reverse order. Also, Ch 35 has hard age deadlines while Fry (post-2013 deaths) has none - so burn the expiring benefit first.
items.deadline: Governed by each program's own deadlines; combined 48- or 81-month cap.

items.title: Edith Nourse Rogers STEM Scholarship
items.who: Ch 33 or Fry students with 6 months or less of entitlement remaining who are (a) enrolled in a qualifying STEM undergraduate program requiring 120+ semester hours with 60+ credits already completed, (b) hold a STEM degree and are in an approved post-graduate clinical training program, or (c) hold a STEM degree and are enrolled in a teaching certification program.
items.value: Up to 9 additional months of Post-9/11 benefits, or $30,000, whichever comes first - paid at your existing Ch 33/Fry rate including tuition and MHA.
items.how: Apply online (about 15 minutes) at va.gov. Decisions are made monthly, usually within 30 days.
items.hack: The teaching-certification and clinical-training pathways are far less competitive than the undergraduate STEM pathway and are almost invisible to applicants. If you already hold a STEM bachelor's and are pursuing a teaching credential or a post-grad clinical program (nursing residency, PA clinical year, clinical psych hours), you may qualify for 9 free months of GI Bill you didn't know existed. Apply at the moment you drop to 6 months remaining, not before - applying too early gets you denied - and you must START using the scholarship within 6 months of approval or lose it.
items.deadline: Must begin using within 6 months of approval notice. Funding is appropriated annually and applications are decided monthly.

items.title: VET TEC 2.0 (VA High-Tech Training Program)
items.who: Veterans with an honorable discharge (or active-duty members within 180 days of separation) who served at least 36 months on active duty and are under 62 at approval.
items.value: AY2026-27: tuition and fees paid to the provider - net cost at public providers, up to $30,908.34/yr at private providers; MHA at the BAH-based rate (or up to $1,261/mo online-only); up to $1,000/yr books. Program capped at 4,000 paid participants per year.
items.how: Apply with VA Form 22-10297 at va.gov/education/other-va-education-benefits/vet-tec-2. Charges 1 month of entitlement per month of full-time training IF you have remaining DEA/MGIB-AD/Post-9/11 entitlement - but you can participate even with zero remaining entitlement or no prior VA education benefits at all.
items.hack: This is the best deal in VA education for anyone who has already burned their GI Bill: VET TEC 2.0 will fund a full coding/cloud/cyber bootcamp for a veteran with ZERO remaining entitlement. Conversely, if you still have entitlement, understand you're spending it. Two operational notes: the program is capped at 4,000 paid participants annually and the counter was showing roughly 2,325 openings remaining as of September 2026, so apply early in the fiscal year; and you can only use VET TEC 2.0 ONCE in your lifetime, so pick the highest-value provider rather than the fastest one.
items.deadline: Rolling, but capped at 4,000 participants per year - openings run out. Rates apply Aug 1, 2026 - Jul 31, 2027.

items.title: VA Work-Study Allowance
items.who: Students enrolled at 75%+ in an approved program using Ch 33, MGIB, VET TEC 2.0, Rogers STEM, Ch 35 DEA, or Ch 31.
items.value: Hourly wage equal to the greater of federal or state minimum wage (some schools pay more), tax-free, for up to 25 hours x weeks in the enrollment period (about 375 hours for a 15-week semester).
items.how: Submit VA Form 22-8691. Work must be entirely veteran-related: VA facilities, VA offices, national cemeteries, the school's VA certifying office, state veterans agencies, VSOs, congressional offices, or veteran home-care settings.
items.hack: Two under-appreciated angles. First, VA work-study earnings are NOT taxable and do NOT count against Pell/FAFSA need calculations the way regular wages do - so it's worth more per hour than an equivalent campus job. Second, you can request your hours be paid in ADVANCE (up to 40% of the contract or 50 hours, whichever is less) at the start of the term - useful for covering the gap before your first MHA payment lands. Best placement: the school's own VA certifying office, where you learn the certification system from the inside and catch errors in your own file.
items.deadline: Apply each term; positions are limited and allocated by the regional processing office.

items.title: GI Bill Licensing & Certification Test Reimbursement
items.who: Ch 33, Ch 30, Ch 1606, and Ch 35 beneficiaries.
items.value: Up to $2,000 per test for VA-approved licensing and certification exams, including registration and administrative fees. Prep courses for approved tests are also covered, with prorated entitlement charges.
items.how: Pay for the test, then file VA Form 22-0803 for the test (or 22-10272 for a prep course) with your receipt, via QuickSubmit or mail to your regional processing office.
items.hack: Entitlement is charged based on the DOLLAR AMOUNT reimbursed, not a whole month. Under Ch 1606, $508 reimbursed = 1 month; under Ch 33 the charge is the reimbursement divided by your monthly rate. That means a $400 CompTIA Security+ exam costs you a fraction of a month, not a month. Veterans routinely stack five or six industry certifications for well under one month of total entitlement. Check the WEAMS approved-test list first, because an unapproved test gets you nothing - and if your target certification isn't listed, the certifying body can apply to have it approved.
items.deadline: Claim within one year of taking the test where possible; VA can pay retroactively in some cases.

items.title: GI Bill National Test Reimbursement (CLEP/DSST/GRE/LSAT/MCAT)
items.who: Ch 33, Ch 30, Ch 1606, Ch 35 beneficiaries.
items.value: Reimbursement for the cost of approved national tests including registration and administrative fees, with NO cap on the number of tests - SAT, ACT, TOEFL, AP, CLEP, DSST, GMAT, GRE, LSAT, MAT, DAT, MCAT, OAT.
items.how: File VA Form 22-0810 with your receipt and score report. Not covered: pretest fees, expedited scoring, optional add-ons.
items.hack: Stack this with DANTES. Active-duty members and spouses get CLEP/DSST free from DANTES once per subject; veterans don't get DANTES funding but CAN get GI Bill reimbursement for the same exams. So the optimal play for a veteran is: take CLEP/DSST exams to test out of 30-60 general-education credits, get reimbursed by VA for the exam fees at a tiny fractional entitlement charge, and save 1-2 full semesters of GI Bill entitlement (worth $30,000-$60,000) that you'd otherwise have burned on intro courses. This is the highest-leverage move available to any GI Bill user who hasn't started school yet.
items.deadline: No limit on number of tests while entitlement remains.

items.title: National Call to Service Program
items.who: Service members who enlisted under a specific National Call to Service contract (15 months active duty in a designated specialty plus additional obligated service).
items.value: Choice of incentives: a cash bonus, repayment of a qualifying student loan, 12 months of Ch 30-rate education benefits, or 36 months of education benefits at 50% of the Ch 30 rate.
items.how: Election is made through the service branch; VA administers the education incentive. Very few contracts remain in circulation.
items.hack: This program is effectively dormant - the enlistment option has not been actively offered for years - but a small number of veterans still hold unused NCS entitlement and don't know it, and it can stack with other benefits under the 48-month rule. If you enlisted between roughly 2003 and 2010 under an unusual short contract, check your enlistment documents. If you do have it, the 12-months-at-full-Ch-30-rate option almost always beats 36-months-at-half-rate because of the 48-month combined cap.
items.deadline: Tied to the individual enlistment contract; verify with VA at 888-442-4551.

items.title: GI Bill Tutorial Assistance
items.who: GI Bill students enrolled at half-time or more who have a deficiency in a required subject.
items.value: Up to $100 per month for tutoring, with a program maximum commonly cited at $1,200. Under Post-9/11, the first portion is paid without an entitlement charge.
items.how: Your instructor certifies the need and the tutor's qualifications; submit VA Form 22-1990t.
items.hack: Almost nobody uses this, and the eligibility bar is 'a deficiency in a subject,' not 'failing.' A B-minus in organic chemistry qualifies. You can also hire a qualified fellow student as your tutor (they can't be a relative), which effectively moves money to a classmate you'd study with anyway. File the 1990t the same week the term starts rather than after midterms, since VA pays prospectively for certified tutoring periods.
items.deadline: Per term, while enrolled at half time or more.

items.title: Monthly Enrollment Verification (Don't Lose Your MHA)
items.who: All Post-9/11 GI Bill students receiving MHA or a kicker.
items.value: Protects your entire monthly housing allowance - $1,261 to $4,800+ per month.
items.how: VA texts or emails you at the end of each month; reply 'YES' to confirm you're still enrolled, or verify through the Enrollment Verification tool on va.gov or by calling 888-442-4551.
items.hack: VA sends a text or email every month asking you to verify enrollment; VA policy suspends housing payments after consecutive missed verifications, and restoring them requires calling in and can take weeks while rent is still due. Opt in to TEXT verification (not email, which lands in spam) and set a recurring reminder for the last day of each month. If you are already suspended, calling the Education Call Center at 888-442-4551 is far faster than waiting for the online tool to sync.
items.deadline: Monthly, ongoing.

items.title: Military Tuition Assistance (TA)
items.who: Active duty, and in most branches drilling Guard/Reserve members.
items.value: $4,500 per fiscal year cap (all services), up to 18 semester hours per fiscal year in the Army. Lifetime limits: 130 undergraduate semester hours or a bachelor's degree; 39 graduate semester hours or a master's degree.
items.how: Army: ArmyIgnitED (first-time users must complete required training and use the decision support tool). Navy: MyNavy Education. Air/Space Force: AFVEC. Marines: MOL. Coast Guard: ETQC. Request must be approved BEFORE the course start date.
items.hack: TA is 'use it or lose it' every October 1, and it does not touch your GI Bill. The optimal sequence for anyone still serving: burn $4,500/yr of TA for your entire enlistment to finish an associate's or bachelor's for free, then separate with a completely untouched 36-month Post-9/11 GI Bill and use it on a master's or a professional degree - where Yellow Ribbon makes a $90k program free. Veterans who skip TA and use Ch 33 on their bachelor's typically leave $50,000-$100,000 of lifetime benefit on the table. Also: failing or withdrawing triggers recoupment, and in the Army two recoupments across TA and CA in one fiscal year now brings a 12-month suspension.
items.deadline: Annual cap resets each Oct 1; requests must be submitted before the course start date (typically 7-30 days depending on branch).

items.title: Tuition Assistance Top-Up
items.who: Active-duty members approved for DoD TA who are also eligible for MGIB-AD (Ch 30) or Post-9/11 (Ch 33).
items.value: Pays the difference between the full cost of a course and what TA covers, for up to 36 months.
items.how: Tell your school's certifying official you're using TA and want Top-Up; if you haven't already established GI Bill eligibility, file VA Form 22-1990 first.
items.hack: Top-Up is usually a BAD deal and the entitlement math is why: under Ch 30, VA charges you a FULL MONTH of entitlement for each payment equal to the full-time monthly MGIB rate ($2,601 in FY2027). So a $600 Top-Up payment can consume a disproportionate slice of a 36-month benefit that's worth far more later. Use Top-Up only when (a) the course is genuinely unavailable at a TA-covered price, and (b) you're confident you won't need the entitlement after separation. Otherwise pay the gap out of pocket or find a school whose per-credit rate fits under TA.
items.deadline: Must be on active duty and approved for TA.

items.title: Army Credentialing Assistance (CA) - Major FY2026 Cuts
items.who: Enlisted soldiers and warrant officers, active/Guard/Reserve. As of March 19, 2026, commissioned officers (O1-O10) are INELIGIBLE.
items.value: $2,000 per fiscal year (cut from $4,000). Aviation credentials capped at $1,000/yr. Limited to ONE credential per year and a maximum of THREE in 10 years.
items.how: Request through ArmyIgnitED with supervisor and commander approval. Covers exam fees, prep courses, books, and materials for credentials on the Army COOL list.
items.hack: The FY2026 rules changed sharply and a lot of published guidance is now wrong. Plan accordingly: with a one-credential-per-year and three-per-decade limit, do NOT spend CA on a cheap $300 certification you could pay for yourself - save it for the expensive, high-ROI credentials ($2,000 PMP prep packages, CISSP, journeyman licenses). Also note the new rule that you must actually TAKE the associated exam or the cost is recouped, so don't start a prep course you won't finish. Officers who were mid-credential before March 19, 2026 may complete what's pending, but cannot start new ones.
items.deadline: Fiscal-year cap resets Oct 1. Officer exclusion effective March 19, 2026.

items.title: COOL Programs (Army / Navy / Marine Corps / Air Force / Coast Guard)
items.who: Service members in all branches; each branch runs its own Credentialing Opportunities On-Line portal.
items.value: Maps your MOS/rating/AFSC to civilian certifications and licenses, and identifies which are funded. Funding levels differ by branch; Army CA is $2,000/FY in FY2026.
items.how: Search your occupational code at cool.osd.mil (the DoD hub links Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force and Coast Guard COOL). Each branch has its own request workflow.
items.hack: Use COOL as a research tool even if you're already a veteran and can't get branch funding - the credential-to-MOS mapping tells you exactly which certifications your military experience already qualifies you to sit for without additional coursework. Many certifications waive their experience prerequisite for documented military experience (documented via your JST), which can save you 2-4 years of qualifying work. Then pay for the exam with GI Bill licensing reimbursement (up to $2,000/test) rather than out of pocket.
items.deadline: Branch-specific fiscal-year funding cycles.

items.title: Free CLEP & DSST Exams via DANTES
items.who: Active duty, Reserves, National Guard, eligible military spouses, and Air Force civilian employees (on-base testing). Veterans are NOT DANTES-funded but can use GI Bill reimbursement.
items.value: Exam fee AND administration fee waived, once per exam subject. Each passed exam is typically worth 3-12 college credits - potentially 30-60 credits total, i.e. one to two years of college.
items.how: Register through the DANTES portal at a base or approved test center. Retakes require a 3-month wait and are self-pay.
items.hack: This is the highest dollar-per-hour activity available to anyone in uniform. Thirty credits of CLEP/DSST is roughly one full year of college - at a private school that's $30,908 of GI Bill entitlement preserved, for about 40 hours of studying free official practice material. Do it BEFORE you enroll anywhere: many schools cap the number of exam credits they'll accept AFTER matriculation, and some won't accept exam credit for courses you've already attempted. Confirm your target school's CLEP/DSST acceptance policy and score minimums in writing first, and prioritize subjects your school accepts for general-education requirements.
items.deadline: Must be eligible (in service or a covered spouse) at the time you test; one funded attempt per subject.

items.title: Joint Services Transcript & ACE Credit Recommendations
items.who: Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Coast Guard and Space Force members and veterans (Air Force uses the Community College of the Air Force transcript).
items.value: Free official transcript translating your MOS, schools, and courses into American Council on Education (ACE) college credit recommendations. Commonly worth 9-45 credits depending on career field.
items.how: Request free at jst.doded.mil and have it sent directly to schools. Air Force members request a CCAF transcript instead.
items.hack: Schools evaluate the JST only if you ASK them to, and only some evaluators know how to read it. Two moves: (1) before you commit to a school, send the JST during the admissions process and get a written transfer credit evaluation - the difference between schools can be 30 credits, which is a full year of GI Bill preserved; (2) if an evaluator rejects a recommendation, appeal with the ACE Military Guide entry printed out, since the ACE recommendation is the authoritative source and many registrar staff simply haven't looked it up. Also target schools that are 'military-friendly' in the specific sense of maximum ACE credit acceptance rather than the marketing sense.
items.deadline: None - request any time, free.

items.title: GI Bill Comparison Tool
items.who: Anyone choosing a school or program with VA education benefits.
items.value: Free. Estimates your exact tuition, MHA and book payments per school; shows Yellow Ribbon amounts and slot counts, veteran enrollment, graduation and retention rates, median salary, student complaint counts, and CAUTION FLAGS for schools under federal investigation or at risk of closure.
items.how: Search by school, location, or program type at va.gov/education/gi-bill-comparison-tool.
items.hack: The caution flags are the most valuable and least-read feature - a flag means the school is under Title IV heightened cash monitoring, facing an enforcement action, or at risk of losing accreditation, and enrolling anyway risks your entitlement. Also compare the 'veteran retention rate' against the overall retention rate: a large gap is the clearest signal that a school takes GI Bill money without supporting veterans. Finally, the tool's estimate assumes the campus ZIP - run the same program at each of a university's campuses to see the MHA difference before you pick a location.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: The 85/15 Rule
items.who: Any student about to enroll in a program using VA benefits.
items.value: Protects you from enrolling in a program VA can't pay for. At least 15% of students in a given program must be paying their own way; if more than 85% are VA- or school-funded, VA cannot certify NEWLY enrolling GI Bill students.
items.how: Ask your SCO for the program's current supported/non-supported ratio before you register. Exemptions exist for programs with fewer than 10 supported students, institutions charging no tuition, high school equivalency programs, farm co-op and flying clubs.
items.hack: The trap: returning from a break in enrollment makes you a 'new' student for 85/15 purposes. So a veteran who stops out for a semester - for a deployment, a medical issue, a family emergency - can come back to find VA will no longer pay for the same program they were enrolled in. Before taking any break, get written confirmation from the SCO of the program's 85/15 status and, if the break is for circumstances beyond your control, get that documented at the time, because that documentation is what exempts you from being reclassified as new.
items.deadline: Checked at each certification.

items.title: Principles of Excellence Schools
items.who: Veterans and dependents choosing a school.
items.value: Participating schools commit to: a written personalized cost summary before you enroll; an educational plan showing how you'll meet graduation requirements; a designated point of contact for academic and financial advising including disability services; accommodation of active-duty and Reserve service obligations; accreditation of new programs before enrollment; Title IV-compliant refund policies; and an end to fraudulent or aggressive recruiting.
items.how: Filter for Principles of Excellence participation in the GI Bill Comparison Tool. Established by Executive Order 13607 (2012).
items.hack: Use the written cost summary as a negotiating and verification document, not a formality. Demand it in writing BEFORE you accept an offer, then compare the number against the Comparison Tool's estimate - a mismatch usually means the school is quietly counting fees the GI Bill won't cover, which is exactly the surprise bill that ends veterans' enrollments. If a Principles school refuses to produce it, that refusal is itself reportable to the GI Bill Feedback System, which is a real enforcement channel.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: In-State Tuition Rights (Choice Act Section 702)
items.who: Veterans with 90+ days of active duty since Sept 10, 2001 who enroll after discharge; spouses and children using transferred entitlement; Fry Scholars; and since Aug 1, 2022, Ch 35 DEA users. Must be using Ch 33, MGIB-AD, or Ch 31, and must live in the school's state when classes begin.
items.value: In-state tuition rate at any public school regardless of state residency - frequently a $15,000-$30,000/year difference, which is also the difference between the GI Bill covering your tuition entirely and not.
