items.how: Automatic by law: a public school that charges you out-of-state rates loses its VA approval. Notify the registrar in writing, citing 38 U.S.C. 3679(c), and provide your DD-214 or COE. If refused, call the GI Bill hotline at 888-442-4551 and file through the GI Bill Feedback System.
items.hack: Registrars routinely apply a school's generic residency policy and never hear about Section 702 - this is the single most common avoidable overcharge for veteran students. Two details worth knowing: you must maintain CONTINUOUS enrollment to keep the rate (a gap can reset you to out-of-state, so use an approved leave of absence rather than withdrawing), and the requirement is that you LIVE in the state when classes begin - a lease signed before the term starts is sufficient, you do not need a year of domicile. Get the in-state determination in writing before you register, because unwinding a bill after the fact is far harder.
items.deadline: Must live in the state as of the term start date and maintain continuous enrollment.

items.title: Community College → University Transfer Pathway
items.who: Any GI Bill user, especially those at 50-70% tiers or with limited remaining entitlement.
items.value: Preserves 2 years (roughly $60,000+ at a private school) of Post-9/11 entitlement by completing lower-division coursework at community college rates.
items.how: Enroll at a community college with a guaranteed-transfer articulation agreement to your target university (California's ADT, Texas' Tuition Rebate/transfer compacts, Virginia's Guaranteed Admission Agreements, etc.), then transfer with junior standing.
items.hack: Three-part optimization most veterans miss. (1) You still receive FULL MHA at a community college - housing allowance is based on the campus ZIP, not the school's prestige or cost - so a community college in a high-BAH metro pays exactly the same housing as the expensive university next door. (2) Combine with CLEP/DSST and JST credit to enter the community college with 30 credits already banked, cutting the two years to one. (3) Because community college tuition is low, you burn entitlement at the same monthly rate but capture far more MHA-dollars-per-tuition-dollar - then arrive at the expensive university with 24+ months of entitlement left, which is exactly when Yellow Ribbon matters most.
items.deadline: Articulation agreements have their own application deadlines, often a year in advance.

items.title: Total & Permanent Disability (TPD) Student Loan Discharge
items.who: Veterans whose VA documentation shows a 100% service-connected disability that is Permanent and Total, OR individual unemployability (TDIU) based on a service-connected condition.
items.value: Complete discharge of Direct Loans, FFEL, Perkins Loans, and TEACH Grant service obligations. Average discharged balance for veterans has historically run in the tens of thousands of dollars.
items.how: Since 2019 the Department of Education runs an automatic quarterly data match with VA and discharges qualifying veterans' loans without an application; you receive a notice and a window to opt out (relevant only if you want to preserve PSLF progress or have state tax exposure). You can also apply directly at disabilitydischarge.com with VA documentation.
items.hack: Two things to check. First, the automatic match only works if the name and SSN VA has match what the Department of Education has - name changes after marriage/divorce are the most common reason a qualifying veteran never gets the automatic discharge. If you're 100% P&T and still have loans, apply manually rather than waiting. Second, the three-year post-discharge income monitoring period was eliminated for veterans discharged through the VA match, so a veteran who was discharged and later earned income should NOT have loans reinstated - if a servicer reinstates yours, dispute it. Federal tax exclusion on discharged amounts applies through the end of 2025 under ARPA; state tax treatment varies, so confirm your state before opting in if you're near a bracket edge.
items.deadline: Automatic quarterly matches; manual applications accepted any time.

items.title: Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF)
items.who: Veterans and service members employed full time by the federal government (including active-duty military and VA employment), state/local government, or a 501(c)(3) nonprofit.
items.value: Tax-free forgiveness of remaining Direct Loan balance after 120 qualifying monthly payments (10 years) on an income-driven repayment plan.
items.how: Certify employment annually with the PSLF form via the PSLF Help Tool at studentaid.gov. Consolidate FFEL/Perkins into a Direct Consolidation Loan first, or those payments won't count.
items.hack: Active-duty service counts as qualifying employment, and this is where servicemembers lose the most ground: months spent in deferment or forbearance generally do NOT count toward the 120. Instead, enroll in an income-driven plan where a deployed servicemember's calculated payment can be $0 - and a $0 IDR payment DOES count as a qualifying payment. Ten years of $0 payments equals full forgiveness. Also, if you're 100% P&T, compare PSLF against TPD discharge: TPD is immediate, but taking TPD wipes out PSLF progress, so if you're at month 100 of 120 in a VA job, finishing PSLF may be better.
items.deadline: Annual employment certification recommended; forgiveness at 120 qualifying payments.

items.title: SCRA 6% Interest Rate Cap
items.who: Active-duty service members with student loans (and other debts) taken out BEFORE entering active duty.
items.value: Interest rate capped at 6% for the duration of active-duty service; interest above 6% is forgiven outright, not deferred.
items.how: For federal student loans the cap is applied automatically using DoD service data. For PRIVATE loans you must send a written request with a copy of your active-duty orders. You may request any time during service or up to 180 days after.
items.hack: The automatic application only covers federal loans - private lenders almost never apply it on their own, and private student loans are where rates run 9-13%, making the cap worth the most. Send the written request with orders to every private servicer, and request it RETROACTIVELY to your activation date: the law entitles you to the cap from the first day of active duty, not from the date you ask, so lenders owe you a refund of over-6% interest already charged. Guard and Reserve members activated on Title 10 orders qualify and are the group most likely to miss it. Your JAG legal assistance office will send the demand letter for free.
items.deadline: Request during service or within 180 days after; relief is retroactive to the activation date.

items.title: Military Service Deferment & 0% Interest in Hostile Areas
items.who: Service members on active duty during a war, military operation, or national emergency, and those serving in areas qualifying for hostile fire / imminent danger pay.
items.value: Deferment of federal student loan payments during qualifying service plus 13 months after, and NO interest accrual on Direct Loans for up to 60 months while serving in a hostile fire or imminent danger pay area.
items.how: Request through your loan servicer with a copy of your orders, or have your commanding officer submit the certification. The 0% interest benefit applies to Direct Loans first disbursed on or after Oct 1, 2008.
items.hack: The 0% hostile-area interest benefit is the most under-claimed student loan provision in the military, because servicers won't apply it without documentation and nobody thinks about loan paperwork mid-deployment. Claim it retroactively: pull your travel vouchers, LES entries showing hostile fire pay/IDP, and deployment orders, and submit them to the servicer for every qualifying month up to 60. Important caveat for PSLF pursuers: deferment months do NOT count toward the 120 PSLF payments, so if you're chasing PSLF, choose a $0 income-driven payment instead of deferment - you get the same cash-flow result and the months still count.
items.deadline: Up to 60 cumulative months of the 0% interest benefit; deferment plus 13 months post-service.

items.title: DoD College Loan Repayment Programs (CLRP)
items.who: Enlistees who negotiated LRP into their enlistment contract, in qualifying MOS/ratings. Also service-specific programs: Army LRP, Navy LRP, Air Force JAG/medical LRP, National Guard LRP.
items.value: Historically up to $65,000 (Army active duty), $65,000 (Navy), and $50,000 (Army National Guard) of qualifying federal student loan principal repaid over the enlistment; health professions and JAG programs can exceed this.
items.how: Must be written into the enlistment/appointment contract at the time of enlistment - it cannot be added later. Payments are made annually after each year of service, directly to the lender.
items.hack: Two rules that trip people up: (1) LRP is generally INCOMPATIBLE with MGIB - accepting LRP in your contract often means declining the $1,200 MGIB buy-in, though Post-9/11 eligibility is unaffected, so read the annex carefully; (2) payments cover PRINCIPAL only on qualifying federal loans, and interest continues accruing, so keep making minimum payments during the service year or your balance can grow faster than LRP pays it down. Also: only certain loan types qualify (Direct/FFEL/Perkins - not private), so consolidate private loans before enlisting if you intend to use LRP.
items.deadline: Must be in the enlistment contract; annual payments after each completed year of service.

items.title: Pat Tillman Foundation - Tillman Scholars
items.who: Veterans, active-duty service members (all branches including National Guard), and current or surviving spouses pursuing full-time undergraduate, graduate, or professional degrees at accredited U.S. institutions. Dependent children and ROTC cadets are NOT eligible.
items.value: Average award approximately $10,000 per academic year, renewable, plus lifetime membership in a highly connected scholar network. Up to 60 scholars selected annually from thousands of applicants (under 3% acceptance).
items.how: Apply through pattillman.smapply.org. Requires a resume, two 500-word essays, a character recommendation, a 250-word bio, FAFSA and a financial worksheet, and DD-214 or equivalent.
items.hack: This is a leadership award, not a need award - the essays decide it, and the foundation is explicitly looking for a specific, articulated post-degree impact plan, not a story about your service. Write the essay about what you will DO with the degree, with a concrete plan and a measurable goal. Second: the 'character recommendation' is deliberately not a standard letter of recommendation - pick someone who can speak to how you behave under pressure, not a professor who can attest to your grades. Applications open December 1 each year; the network access is arguably worth more than the $10,000.
items.deadline: Applications open December 1 annually; window typically runs November-February. The 2026 class application is closed - watch for the 2027 cycle opening December 2026.

items.title: Folds of Honor Scholarships
items.who: Spouses and dependent children of service members killed or disabled in service (and, through a separate fund, first responders). Both K-12 (Children's Fund) and higher education tracks.
items.value: Up to $5,000 per academic year, disbursed at a maximum of $2,500 per term (minimum $100), paid directly to the institution. Award limited to demonstrated unmet need.
items.how: Apply only through the Folds of Honor online portal. Reapplication is required every year. Award notifications go out mid-July.
items.hack: Because awards are capped at your UNMET need after other aid, sequencing matters enormously: if your GI Bill or Yellow Ribbon already zeroes out tuition, Folds of Honor will pay you little or nothing. Apply in a year when you have genuine unmet need - a summer term outside your GI Bill coverage, a semester where Yellow Ribbon slots ran out, or a K-12 private school tuition year. Also, most applicants don't realize the K-12 Children's Fund exists and will pay private school tuition for a disabled veteran's child, which is often the larger lifetime value.
items.deadline: February 1 - March 31 annually (extended to the first business day after March 31 if it falls on a weekend). Awards announced mid-July.

items.title: Scholarships for Military Children (Fisher House / Commissaries)
items.who: Unmarried military dependents under age 23 with a valid Uniformed Services ID card, whose sponsor is active duty, Guard/Reserve, retired, or deceased. Must enroll full time in a bachelor's program or a transferable community college program.
items.value: $2,000 each; 500 scholarships awarded for the 2027-2028 academic year. Minimum 3.0 GPA for high school applicants, 2.5 for current college students.
items.how: Student must complete the application personally, including a 500-word essay, transcript, and validation of dependent status using the USID card benefits number. Administered through the commissary program.
items.hack: At least one scholarship is awarded per commissary location, so your odds depend heavily on WHICH commissary you designate. A remote or small installation's commissary receives a fraction of the applications a large base commissary does - designate the least-trafficked commissary you legitimately shop at and your probability of winning can multiply several times over for the identical application.
items.deadline: Applications open December 2026 for the 2027-2028 academic year; the 2026-2027 cycle has closed, with recipients notified around May 15.

items.title: MOAA Educational Assistance Program
items.who: Children of officers (any component) and children of ACTIVE DUTY or RETIRED enlisted personnel. Children of separated/discharged enlisted members are NOT eligible. Under age 24, minimum 3.0 GPA, full-time undergraduate only - no medical, law, or graduate programs.
items.value: Interest-free loans (repayment begins 6 months after graduation), Board of Directors grants, donor-designated scholarships, senior grants, and special-circumstance grants. Up to 5 disbursements over a 7-year period with a 2.0 GPA minimum for renewal.
items.how: Apply at charities.moaa.org during the November 1 - March 1 window. Officer parents must hold paid MOAA membership if their child is selected.
items.hack: MOAA's interest-free loan is structurally better than most 'scholarships' of similar size, because it's renewable for five disbursements and carries zero interest - effectively a large grant with a delayed, unindexed repayment. Most families apply only for the grant and ignore the loan. Apply for both. Also note the GPA and age requirements are waivable case by case, so a 2.9 GPA applicant should still apply with an explanatory statement rather than self-selecting out.
items.deadline: Application window November 1 - March 1 annually; finalists notified May 1. The 2026-27 cycle is closed - the 2027-28 window opens November 1, 2026.

items.title: Navy-Marine Corps Relief Society Education Assistance
items.who: Children under 23 (as of Sept 30) of active duty, retired, or deceased Sailors and Marines; spouses of active duty, retired or deceased Sailors/Marines; and active-duty members with written orders to MECEP/MECP enlisted-to-officer programs.
items.value: Scholarships of $500-$3,000, awarded once annually. Interest-free education loans up to $4,000, available on a ROLLING basis. Covers career/technical education, associate's, bachelor's, and master's degrees.
items.how: Apply at nmcrs.scholarshipapps.org. Awards are based on cost of attendance and your FAFSA Student Aid Index, and funds go directly to the institution.
items.hack: The rolling interest-free loan is the part almost nobody uses: unlike the scholarship, it has no annual application window, so a Sailor or Marine family facing an unexpected tuition bill in October can get up to $4,000 at 0% within days rather than waiting for a spring cycle. It also covers MASTER'S degrees and career/technical programs, which most military relief societies exclude. And spouses are eligible in their own right - not just as an add-on to the servicemember.
items.deadline: Scholarship window is annual (typically winter-spring); loans are rolling year-round.

items.title: Army Emergency Relief Scholarships
items.who: MG James Ursano Scholarship: dependent CHILDREN under 24 of active duty, retired, medically retired, or deceased Soldiers, listed in DEERS, pursuing a first undergraduate degree. Mrs. Patty Shinseki Spouse Scholarship: SPOUSES pursuing a first undergraduate degree or technical certification.
items.value: Award amounts vary annually with applicant volume and budget. Ursano supports children through the undergraduate degree; Shinseki supports spouses for up to 4 academic years full time or 8 years part time.
items.how: Apply at aerhq.academicworks.com. FAFSA Submission Summary is required. Annual reapplication is required for both programs.
items.hack: The Shinseki spouse scholarship accepts applications YEAR-ROUND, not in a fixed window - which means a spouse who discovers it in October can apply immediately rather than waiting until January. It also covers TECHNICAL CERTIFICATIONS, not just degrees, so a spouse pursuing a dental hygiene, HVAC, coding, or nursing-assistant credential qualifies. The part-time option (8 academic years) is specifically designed for spouses who PCS frequently, which is exactly the population that assumes they can't finish a degree.
items.deadline: Ursano (children): January 1 - April 1 annually. Shinseki (spouses): accepted year-round, reapply annually.

items.title: Marine Corps Scholarship Foundation
items.who: Children of U.S. Marines and Navy Corpsmen attending post-secondary, undergraduate, or career/technical education programs. Need-based.
items.value: For the 2026-2027 academic year MCSF awarded $12.635 million to 2,906 students - its largest investment in 64 years. 100% of applicants who met eligibility requirements received an award. Recipients graduate at a 91% rate and 63% finish with little or no debt.
items.how: Apply at mcsf.org; the application typically closes March 1. Requires FAFSA and proof of the parent's Marine Corps or Navy Corpsman service.
items.hack: The headline that matters: 100% of ELIGIBLE applicants received support. This is not a lottery - if your parent served as a Marine or a Navy Corpsman and you complete the application correctly and meet the need criteria, you get money. The failure mode is almost always an incomplete FAFSA or missing proof of the parent's service, not a competitive rejection. It also funds CAREER AND TECHNICAL education, not just four-year degrees, which most applicants don't realize.
items.deadline: Application typically closes March 1 for the following academic year.

items.title: VFW Sport Clips Help A Hero Scholarship
items.who: Service members and veterans, generally E-5 and below (with limited exceptions), enrolled in an accredited post-secondary institution. Must have a discharge other than dishonorable.
items.value: Up to $5,000 per award, paid directly to the school. Sport Clips has funded 3,500+ scholarships since 2013, contributing over $1 million annually; the VFW awarded nearly $550,000 in the most recent round.
items.how: Apply through the VFW Foundation at vfwfoundation.org. Multiple application windows per year tied to fall and spring terms.
items.hack: The enlisted-rank restriction is the whole advantage - by excluding officers and senior NCOs, this pool is far shallower than general veteran scholarships of the same size. It also runs MULTIPLE cycles per year rather than one, so a missed deadline costs you months, not a year. Apply in every cycle you're eligible for; there's no penalty for prior applications and the review committee changes.
items.deadline: Multiple cycles annually (commonly a late-April deadline for one round); check vfwfoundation.org for current windows.

items.title: Military Order of the Purple Heart Scholarship
items.who: Purple Heart recipients who are MOPH members, and their spouses, children, grandchildren, and (in some years) great-grandchildren. Full-time undergraduate or graduate enrollment with a minimum GPA (typically 2.75).
items.value: Awards historically in the $5,000-$6,000 range per year, renewable, with a modest application processing fee. Number of awards varies with annual fundraising.
items.how: Apply at purpleheart.org/ScholarshipProgram during the open window (typically winter through early spring). Requires proof of the Purple Heart award and MOPH membership.
items.hack: Eligibility extends to GRANDCHILDREN of Purple Heart recipients, which dramatically widens the eligible population while keeping the applicant pool small because almost nobody knows it. If a grandparent received a Purple Heart in Vietnam, Korea, or WWII, the grandchild is very likely eligible - you'll need a copy of the award citation or the DD-214 line entry, so request those from NARA well in advance of the deadline.
items.deadline: Applications were closed as of September 2026; the window typically opens in winter for the following academic year - verify current dates at purpleheart.org.

items.title: AMVETS National Scholarships
items.who: Veterans, active-duty members, Guard/Reserve, and their children and grandchildren, depending on the specific scholarship category. Several categories including a JROTC award.
items.value: Awards commonly in the $1,000-$4,000 range across categories; AMVETS also runs a Generations Scholarship and an entrepreneurship-focused award. Amounts and categories change annually with funding.
items.how: Apply at amvets.org/scholarships during the published window (historically closing in the spring, around April 30).
items.hack: AMVETS scholarships are among the least-applied-to national veteran awards because the organization has a much lower public profile than VFW or the American Legion, while the award sizes are comparable. If you're eligible, the expected value per hour of application effort is unusually high. Also check whether your AMVETS state department runs its own separate scholarship - state-level awards often have single-digit applicant counts.
items.deadline: Typically closes in spring (historically April 30); confirm the current cycle at amvets.org.

items.title: ThanksUSA Scholarships
items.who: Children (under 24) and spouses of active-duty, Guard/Reserve, and certain disabled or deceased U.S. military personnel, pursuing a first undergraduate degree or technical/vocational certification.
items.value: Awards historically $3,000 each, with several hundred awarded annually. Need-based, with essay and academic components.
items.how: Apply during the annual window (historically opening in spring) at thanksusa.org. Requires proof of the sponsor's service and financial information.
items.hack: ThanksUSA explicitly funds VOCATIONAL and technical certification programs, not just degrees - so a military spouse pursuing a CDL, cosmetology license, medical coding certificate, or IT certification qualifies. That category is dramatically less competitive than the four-year-degree pool applying for the same money. It also does not require a minimum GPA in the way most competitors do, which makes it a strong fit for a spouse returning to school after a gap.
items.deadline: Annual window, historically opening in spring; verify at thanksusa.org.

items.title: Student Veterans of America Scholarships & Chapter Resources
items.who: Student veterans enrolled at institutions with an SVA chapter (1,500+ chapters nationwide), and in some programs any student veteran.
items.value: SVA administers dozens of partner-funded scholarships annually (Google, Raytheon, Home Depot Foundation, Disabled American Veterans and others), typically $5,000-$20,000, plus fully funded travel to the annual National Convention (NatCon).
items.how: Apply through studentveterans.org/programs/scholarships. Individual scholarships have separate applications, criteria, and deadlines.
items.hack: The highest-value thing SVA offers isn't the scholarship money - it's the fully funded NatCon travel grant, where corporate recruiters hire directly out of the room. Apply for the travel grant through your campus chapter even if you don't win a scholarship. Second: many SVA partner scholarships are restricted to students at chapters in specific states or studying specific fields, which means the applicant pool for any single one is tiny. Read the full list rather than applying only to the flagship award.
items.deadline: Varies by individual scholarship; most cluster in spring and early summer.

items.title: Hope For The Warriors Spouse/Caregiver Scholarships
items.who: Spouses and caregivers of post-9/11 service members who were wounded, injured, or killed; and in some categories the service members themselves.
items.value: Awards typically $2,500-$5,000 across named funds (Restoring Family, Honoring Service, Spouse/Caregiver Scholarship). Renewable in some categories.
items.how: Apply at hopeforthewarriors.org during the published cycle. Requires documentation of the service member's injury, illness, or death.
items.hack: This is one of the very few scholarship programs that explicitly funds CAREGIVERS, not just spouses - so an adult child, parent, or sibling serving as a designated caregiver for a wounded post-9/11 veteran is eligible, and that category receives very few applications. If you're enrolled in VA's Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers, your PCAFC approval letter is exactly the documentation this application wants.
items.deadline: Annual cycle; verify current dates at hopeforthewarriors.org.

items.title: Warrior-Scholar Project - Free Academic Boot Camps
items.who: Enlisted veterans and transitioning service members (all branches) considering or preparing for college. Enlisted-only by design.
items.value: Completely free - tuition, housing, and meals covered, and in most cases travel. One- to two-week immersive academic boot camps at 20+ partner universities including Harvard, Yale, Princeton, Stanford, MIT, Caltech, Columbia, Cornell, Dartmouth, Brown, Chicago, Notre Dame, UVA and Michigan State. 88% of alumni have graduated or are on track for a bachelor's.
items.how: Apply at warrior-scholar.org. Programs run summer (in residence) plus virtual academic boot camps - College Readiness and STEM virtual camps were scheduled for December 6, 2026.
items.hack: The unadvertised value is admissions access, not the writing instruction. You spend a week living on an Ivy League campus, taught by that university's faculty, and you leave with faculty who know your name and can write a recommendation - at institutions where a veteran applicant with strong recommendations is an extraordinarily attractive candidate. Several partner schools admit WSP alumni at far above their general rate. It also costs zero GI Bill entitlement. Do this BEFORE you apply anywhere, not after you've enrolled.
items.deadline: Summer residential program applications typically open in winter; virtual boot camps run periodically (next scheduled December 6, 2026).

items.title: Service to School (VetLink) - Free Admissions Counseling
items.who: Enlisted veterans and transitioning service members applying to undergraduate, law, business, medical, or graduate school.
items.value: Free one-on-one admissions counseling from a veteran who attends the type of school you're targeting, plus VetLink partnerships with 50+ selective institutions that offer application fee waivers and direct admissions contact.
items.how: Sign up at service2school.org and get matched with an ambassador who reviews your essays, resume, and school list.
items.hack: The VetLink partnership is the leverage, not the essay help. Partner schools - including many top-25 universities and professional schools - have committed to reviewing S2S-referred veteran applications through a dedicated channel and frequently waive application fees. Applying through VetLink rather than the regular portal can mean a human at the admissions office is expecting your file. Combine it with Warrior-Scholar Project (for the academic prep and faculty relationships) and Yellow Ribbon (to make the tuition free once admitted) - those three together are the standard playbook for enlisted veterans who end up at elite schools.
items.deadline: Rolling; start 9-12 months before application deadlines.

items.title: Syracuse IVMF - Onward to Opportunity (O2O)
items.who: Transitioning service members (typically within 180 days of separation), veterans, and military spouses.
items.value: Completely free professional certification training - project management (PMP/CAPM), IT and cybersecurity (CompTIA, Cisco), customer service, HR (SHRM), sales, and more - plus career coaching, employer job matching, and lifetime alumni network access. Costs ZERO GI Bill entitlement.
items.how: Apply online at ivmf.syracuse.edu/programs/career-training. Delivered on 18+ military installations and fully online.
items.hack: The exam voucher is the piece people miss: O2O covers not just the training but the certification EXAM VOUCHER, which alone runs $300-$1,500 for credentials like PMP or CISSP. Because it costs no entitlement, the correct play is to stack O2O certifications BEFORE you touch the GI Bill - get certified and employed first, then use the GI Bill for a degree while already earning. IVMF also runs EBV (Entrepreneurship Bootcamp for Veterans with Disabilities) and V-WISE for women veterans, both free and both separately applied for.
items.deadline: Rolling cohorts year-round.

items.title: Microsoft Software & Systems Academy (MSSA)
items.who: Military veterans and retirees, Coast Guard, Guard and Reserve members, and U.S. or UK MoD service members within 6 months of separation. A separate MSSA-Military Spouse track exists.
items.value: Fully funded by Microsoft - '$0 and you keep your GI Bill.' 17-week full-time technical training in one of three tracks: Cybersecurity Operations, Cloud Application Development, or Server and Cloud Administration. Includes industry certification prep and a guaranteed interview with Microsoft or a hiring partner.
items.how: Apply at military.microsoft.com/mssa. Cohorts run several times per year, delivered live online (plus a Europe-based CET cohort).
items.hack: Microsoft has fully funded program costs since January 2021, so the explicit design goal is that you finish with a job AND an untouched GI Bill. That combination - a $100k+ tech job plus 36 unused months of Post-9/11 entitlement - is the single best outcome available in the transition space. Apply 6-9 months before separation, because cohorts fill and the application includes a technical aptitude screen you should prepare for. If you're rejected, the same three tracks are taught free through Onward to Opportunity and AWS Skills to Jobs.
items.deadline: Rolling cohorts; apply well before your separation date, ideally at the 6-9 month mark.

items.title: Free Tech Training: Vetforce, AWS, Google, Vets Who Code, Operation Code
items.who: Veterans, transitioning service members, and military spouses. Most programs include spouses; several include dependents.
items.value: All free, all preserve GI Bill entitlement. Salesforce Vetforce: free Trailhead training and certification vouchers. AWS Skills to Jobs / AWS Educate: free cloud training with certification discounts and a veteran hiring pipeline. Google Career Certificates: free scholarships for veterans and spouses via partner organizations (Certificates normally ~$49/month). Vets Who Code: free 100% remote software engineering fellowship. Operation Code: free mentorship, community, and scholarship connections for veterans entering software.
items.how: Vetforce: vetforce.org. AWS: aws.amazon.com/training/teams/aws-veteran-programs. Google: grow.google/certificates (veteran scholarships via partner orgs including Onward to Opportunity and Hiring Our Heroes). Vets Who Code: vetswhocode.io. Operation Code: operationcode.org.
items.hack: Do these in a deliberate order rather than picking one. Start with a free Google Career Certificate or AWS Cloud Practitioner to confirm you actually like the work (2-3 months, zero cost, zero entitlement). Then apply to a cohort-based program - Vets Who Code or MSSA - for depth and a hiring network. Only AFTER you have a job should you consider spending GI Bill or VET TEC 2.0 on anything. Veterans who do it the other way around routinely burn 9-12 months of entitlement on a bootcamp that a free program taught identically.
items.deadline: Mostly rolling; Vets Who Code and MSSA run fixed cohorts.

items.title: Tuition-Free and Deeply Discounted Schools for Veterans
items.who: Veterans, and in many states, dependents of disabled or deceased veterans.
items.value: Many states waive public university tuition entirely for qualifying veterans or their dependents - Texas Hazlewood Act (150 credit hours, transferable to a child via Hazlewood Legacy), Illinois Veteran Grant, Florida's out-of-state fee waiver plus Scholarships for Children and Spouses of Deceased or Disabled Veterans, New York VTA, California College Fee Waiver (Cal Vet), Minnesota GI Bill, and others. Several private institutions also offer full veteran tuition waivers.
items.how: Apply through your STATE department of veterans affairs (find yours via the NASDVA directory or your state's .gov veterans agency) or the school's veterans certifying office. These are STATE benefits, entirely separate from and stackable with the federal GI Bill. The GI Bill Comparison Tool does NOT show state waivers, so you must research your state separately.
items.hack: The sequencing move that saves an entire GI Bill: use the STATE tuition waiver for your bachelor's degree (many states cover 100% of public tuition), while still drawing full Post-9/11 MHA and the books stipend - because the GI Bill pays housing based on enrollment regardless of who paid the tuition. Then arrive at graduate school with your entire 36 months of Post-9/11 tuition coverage unused, where Yellow Ribbon can make a $90,000 program free. California's Cal Vet waiver and the Texas Hazlewood Act are the two largest; Hazlewood's Legacy provision also lets you transfer unused hours to a child, which is a second GI Bill most Texas veterans never claim.
items.deadline: Varies by state; most require annual reapplication and many have residency-at-enlistment requirements.

items.title: Get your VA funding fee back years after closing
items.who: Any veteran who paid a VA funding fee and later received a service-connected compensation award with an effective date before the loan closed.
items.value: Full refund of the funding fee — 2.15% to 3.3% of the loan. On a $400,000 loan that is $8,600–$13,200.
items.how: Once the rating decision issues, send the rating letter plus the closing disclosure to the VA Regional Loan Center that serves the property (or ask your servicer to submit it). VA refunds through the lender or by direct payment.
items.hack: The trigger is the EFFECTIVE DATE of the rating, not the decision date. A claim filed before closing that takes 18 months to decide still produces a refund, because the effective date relates back to the filing date. There is no deadline — veterans have recovered fees from loans closed a decade earlier. If you financed the fee into the loan, VA applies the refund to principal rather than cutting a check.
items.deadline: None

items.title: The 5% down payment that saves 1.8 points on a second VA loan
items.who: Veterans using their VA entitlement a second or later time who are not fee-exempt.
items.value: Funding fee drops from 3.3% to 1.5% — $7,200 saved on a $400,000 loan.
items.how: Bring 5% to closing instead of zero. The fee tier changes at exactly 5.00% down.
items.hack: Run the math before assuming zero-down is optimal. At 3.3%, financing the fee on a $400,000 zero-down loan adds $13,200 to principal. Putting $20,000 down instead drops the fee to $5,700 and the loan to $385,700 — you are $27,500 better off on the balance sheet for $20,000 of cash. Anyone exempt from the fee should ignore this entirely and put nothing down.
items.deadline: At closing

items.title: No VA loan limit with full entitlement
items.who: Veterans with full entitlement — never used it, or used it and had it fully restored, or repaid a prior VA loan in full and sold the property.
items.value: Zero down payment on any loan amount a lender will approve and an appraisal will support. No PMI ever.
items.how: Pull a Certificate of Eligibility at VA.gov. If it says full entitlement, the county conforming limit is irrelevant to VA.
items.hack: The county limit still shows up in lender software and loan officers routinely quote it as a cap. It is not. Since January 1, 2020 the FHFA limit only constrains veterans with PARTIAL entitlement. If a lender tells you the ceiling is $832,750 with full entitlement, they are running the wrong worksheet — escalate or change lenders. Lenders may still impose their own overlays on jumbo VA loans (often 10% down above ~$1.5M), but that is a lender policy, not a VA rule.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Second-tier entitlement: keep the old house, buy the new one
items.who: Veterans with an active VA loan who are PCSing, relocating, or converting the current home to a rental.
items.value: A second simultaneous VA loan with zero or minimal down payment.
items.how: Remaining bonus entitlement = (county one-unit conforming limit × 25%) − entitlement already charged. In 2026 the baseline conforming limit is $832,750, so baseline max guaranty is $208,187.50. Multiply remaining entitlement by 4 for the approximate zero-down second loan.
items.hack: Entitlement charged is what VA guaranteed on the first loan, NOT the loan balance and not what you still owe. Paying the first loan down does not free up entitlement. But moving to a higher-cost county does: the calculation uses the limit for the county of the NEW property, so a veteran who used $100,000 of entitlement in a baseline county and then buys in a $1,209,750-limit county has ($1,209,750 × 0.25) − $100,000 = $202,437 of remaining entitlement, roughly an $809,000 zero-down second loan.
items.deadline: None

items.title: One-time entitlement restoration without selling
items.who: Veterans who paid off a VA loan in full but still own the property.
items.value: Full entitlement restored while keeping the paid-off house — enables a full zero-down VA purchase elsewhere.
items.how: Submit VA Form 26-1880 with evidence the prior loan is paid in full and request one-time restoration. Normally VA requires both payoff AND disposal of the property; this waives the disposal requirement.
items.hack: It is literally once per lifetime, so spend it on the largest purchase you will ever make, not the first. Veterans commonly burn it on a modest second home and then have nothing left when they want the retirement house. Also note: assumption of your VA loan by another ELIGIBLE veteran who substitutes their entitlement restores yours without consuming the one-time restoration.
items.deadline: Once per lifetime

items.title: Assume a 2.x% VA loan in a high-rate market
items.who: Any buyer — veteran or not — willing to assume an existing VA-backed mortgage, and any veteran seller holding a low-rate VA loan.
items.value: Inheriting a 2.5%–3.5% rate instead of financing at market. On a $400,000 balance, roughly $1,000+/month in payment difference.
items.how: Buyer applies to the SERVICER (not VA) for assumption approval, meets credit/income standards, and pays a 0.5% funding fee plus a processing charge. Servicer must approve; VA loans originated after March 1, 1988 require it.
items.hack: The trap is entitlement. If the buyer is a non-veteran or a veteran who does NOT substitute their own entitlement, the seller's entitlement stays tied up in that house for the life of the loan — potentially 25 more years — and the seller cannot get it back. Sellers should insist on a veteran buyer who executes a substitution of entitlement. The second trap is the equity gap: the buyer must cover the difference between price and loan balance in cash or a second lien, which in an appreciated market can be enormous.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Buy a 4-plex with zero down and let tenants pay the mortgage
items.who: Veterans with VA entitlement willing to live in one unit.
items.value: Up to 4 units financed with $0 down and no PMI. In some cases projected rental income from the other units can be used to qualify.
items.how: VA allows 1–4 unit properties as long as the veteran occupies one unit as a primary residence. Occupancy must begin within a reasonable time, generally 60 days of closing.
items.hack: VA will count rental income from the non-occupied units toward qualifying, but generally requires either documented prior landlord experience or six months of PITI in reserves — plan for the reserve requirement before you shop. Also: two eligible veterans can COMBINE entitlement on one property, which stacks guaranty and makes larger multi-unit deals work. And there is a rarely-used provision allowing more than 4 units when multiple eligible veterans purchase jointly.
items.deadline: Occupy within ~60 days of closing

items.title: VA occupancy rules bend for deployment and PCS
items.who: Active duty members deploying, PCSing, or unable to move in within 60 days.
items.value: Keeps the VA loan compliant without refinancing or selling.
items.how: A spouse's occupancy satisfies the requirement for a deployed service member. A dependent child's occupancy can satisfy it with an attorney-in-fact certification. Occupancy can be delayed beyond 60 days up to 12 months with a documented reason plus a date certain when occupancy will occur.
items.hack: Spousal occupancy is the workhorse here, and it survives deployment to a combat zone indefinitely. There is no VA rule requiring you to keep living there after you have satisfied the initial occupancy — once you legitimately occupy and circumstances change, converting to a rental is permitted, which is the entire legal foundation of the serial house-hacking strategy.
items.deadline: 60 days standard; up to 12 months with certification

items.title: IRRRL streamline refinance at a 0.5% funding fee
items.who: Anyone with an existing VA-backed loan, including a non-veteran who assumed one.
items.value: 0.5% funding fee (vs 2.15%–3.3%), typically no appraisal, no new Certificate of Eligibility, and often no income or credit re-underwriting.
items.how: Apply through any VA lender — it does not have to be your current servicer. All closing costs including the funding fee can be rolled into the new loan.
items.hack: The occupancy certification is PRIOR occupancy, not current. You can IRRRL a home you moved out of and now rent, which is the only VA refinance product that permits it. Watch the recoupment rule: VA requires all fees and costs to be recouped through payment savings within 36 months, and requires a minimum 0.5% rate reduction on fixed-to-fixed. Seasoning: 210 days from the first payment due date on the existing loan AND six consecutive monthly payments made.
items.deadline: 210 days / 6 payments of seasoning on the existing loan

items.title: VA cash-out refinance to 90% LTV
items.who: Veterans with equity who need cash, or who want to refinance a conventional/FHA loan into a VA loan.
items.value: Up to 90% loan-to-value cash-out — higher than most conventional cash-out programs — with no mortgage insurance.
items.how: Full underwriting, new appraisal, funding fee 2.15% first use or 3.3% subsequent (waived if exempt).
items.hack: A VA cash-out is the only way to move a conventional or FHA loan INTO the VA program. If you are FHA and paying lifetime mortgage insurance premiums, a VA cash-out (even at 0% cash out) eliminates MIP permanently — and if you are funding-fee exempt, the conversion costs you almost nothing beyond normal closing costs. VA also requires a net tangible benefit test and a 36-month recoupment on certain refinances, so document the MIP savings as the benefit.
items.deadline: None

items.title: VA residual income — why VA loans approve where conventional loans fail
items.who: Veterans with high debt-to-income ratios.
items.value: Approval at DTI well above 41% when residual income exceeds the regional guideline.
items.how: VA underwriting uses 'balance available for family support' — actual monthly dollars left after housing, debts, taxes, and estimated maintenance/utilities — calculated by family size and by region (Northeast, Midwest, South, West) and by loan amount bracket.
items.hack: When the DTI exceeds 41%, VA lets the loan pass anyway if residual income exceeds the table figure by at least 20%. Underwriters must document the justification but VA explicitly authorizes it. This is why VA is often the only path for a large family with a pension plus disability compensation: tax-free VA compensation can also be GROSSED UP (commonly 1.25×) for qualifying, because it is not taxed. Combining the gross-up with the 20% residual cushion moves a lot of marginal files into approval.
items.deadline: None

items.title: 4% seller concessions on top of normal closing costs
items.who: VA purchase buyers negotiating with a seller.
items.value: Up to 4% of the loan amount in seller concessions — $16,000 on a $400,000 loan — plus unlimited seller payment of ordinary closing costs.
items.how: Negotiate concessions into the purchase contract. VA defines a 'concession' as anything of value beyond normal closing costs.
items.hack: The 4% cap applies only to concessions, and normal closing costs paid by the seller do NOT count against it. That means the seller can pay all your closing costs AND give 4% more toward prepaid taxes and insurance, paying off your car loan or credit cards, or a rate buydown. Paying off buyer debt with seller concessions is explicitly permitted by VA and simultaneously improves your DTI — a two-for-one that most agents never raise.
items.deadline: Negotiated at contract

items.title: VA construction loan — zero down on a build
items.who: Veterans who want to build rather than buy.
items.value: Zero-down construction-to-permanent financing with no PMI and no payments during construction in many programs.
items.how: Find a lender that actually offers VA construction financing (many do not), use a VA-registered builder, and the loan converts to a permanent VA loan at completion. Funding fee is the standard purchase table.
items.hack: Because the funding fee and entitlement are based on the final loan amount and the appraisal is a 'subject to completion' valuation, veterans building in an appreciating market frequently end up with instant equity at conversion while still having paid nothing down. The scarcity of lenders is the real constraint — start with the VA Regional Loan Center list rather than a retail bank.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Native American Direct Loan at a below-market fixed rate
items.who: Native American veterans (or a veteran married to a Native American) buying, building, or improving a home on federal trust land where the tribe has a signed MOU with VA.
items.value: VA lends directly at a rate starting around 2.5% — far below market — with no down payment, no PMI, and limited closing costs. Funding fee is 1.25%, waived for the usual exemptions.
items.how: Confirm your tribe has a current MOU with VA, obtain a COE, then apply through the VA Regional Loan Center. VA is the lender, not a bank.
items.hack: This is the single most underused benefit in the VA housing portfolio — utilization is in the low hundreds of loans per year nationwide. It can also be used to REFINANCE an existing NADL to a lower rate, and to make improvements, not just to purchase. If your tribe has no MOU, VA will work with tribal leadership to execute one; a single veteran's inquiry has repeatedly been the trigger for a new MOU.
items.deadline: None

items.title: SAH grant — $126,526 to adapt or build an accessible home
items.who: Veterans/service members with a qualifying permanent and total service-connected disability: loss or loss of use of both legs; loss of use of both arms; blindness in both eyes plus loss of use of one extremity; severe burns; certain ALS and respiratory conditions.
items.value: Up to $126,526 in FY2026, usable across up to 6 separate grants in a lifetime.
items.how: VA Form 26-4555, submitted online or through a VA Regional Loan Center SAH agent.
items.hack: The lifetime cap is re-indexed every October 1 and UNUSED entitlement is revalued at the new rate. A veteran who used $60,000 in FY2019 does not have '$126,526 minus $60,000' in original dollars — VA recalculates the remaining balance against the current maximum, so waiting can literally increase the dollars available. The grant can be used on a home owned by a family member the veteran lives with, and it can be combined with a VA purchase loan on the same transaction.
items.deadline: FY2026 amount expires September 30, 2026

items.title: SHA and TRA — the smaller adaptive housing grants
items.who: SHA: veterans with blindness (20/200 or less), loss of use of both hands, certain severe burns, or specified respiratory conditions. TRA: SAH/SHA-eligible veterans temporarily living in a family member's home.
items.value: SHA up to $25,350 (FY2026). TRA up to $50,961 for SAH-eligible or $9,100 for SHA-eligible (FY2026).
items.how: Same VA Form 26-4555.
items.hack: TRA is the sleeper. A veteran recovering at a parent's or sibling's house can get up to $50,961 of adaptations done on a home they do not own — and using TRA does not count against the 6-use lifetime limit on SAH/SHA usages, only against the dollar cap. Veterans routinely leave this on the table because they assume grants require ownership.
items.deadline: FY2026 amounts expire September 30, 2026

items.title: HISA grant — the medical-center housing grant nobody mentions
items.who: Enrolled VA health care patients needing medically necessary home modifications. $6,800 lifetime if service-connected (or non-service-connected with a 50%+ SC rating); $2,000 otherwise.
items.value: Up to $6,800 lifetime for ramps, roll-in showers, widened doorways, accessible sinks, driveway/entry path improvements, and plumbing/electrical for medical equipment.
items.how: Apply through Prosthetic & Sensory Aids Service at your VA medical center with a prescription from your VA provider. VA Form 10-0103.
items.hack: HISA is administered by VHA (the hospital), not VBA (the benefits side), so SAH/SHA claims processors will not tell you about it and it does not appear on the disability housing grants page most veterans find. It STACKS with SAH/SHA — you can receive both for the same house. It also covers rented homes with the landlord's written consent, and it is available to veterans with NO service-connected rating at the $2,000 level.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Certificate of Eligibility — get it before you shop
items.who: Any veteran, service member, Guard/Reserve member, or eligible surviving spouse.
items.value: The document that proves entitlement and reveals exactly how much you have left.
items.how: Request online at VA.gov (fastest), through a lender's WebLGY portal (often instant), or by VA Form 26-1880. Surviving spouses receiving DIC use VA Form 26-1817.
items.hack: Have your lender pull it through WebLGY — it returns in seconds versus days for the online consumer path, and it shows the exact entitlement CHARGED figure you need for second-tier math. Also check the funding fee status code on the COE: if it says 'EXEMPT' you should never pay a fee, and if it says 'NON-EXEMPT' but you have a pending claim, flag it to the lender before closing so the fee can be held in escrow pending the rating rather than paid outright.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Surviving spouses get the VA loan benefit — fee-free
items.who: Un-remarried surviving spouses of veterans who died in service or from a service-connected disability; surviving spouses of veterans who were rated totally disabled for the required period; surviving spouses who remarried on or after age 57 and on or after December 16, 2003.
items.value: Full zero-down VA home loan entitlement with the funding fee WAIVED entirely.
items.how: VA Form 26-1817 plus VA Form 21P-534EZ if DIC is not already established.
items.hack: Surviving spouses receiving DIC are automatically funding-fee exempt — that is a 2.15% saving on top of zero down, roughly $8,600 on a $400,000 purchase. The remarriage-after-57 rule is widely unknown and restores both DIC and home loan eligibility to spouses who assumed they had forfeited everything by remarrying.
items.deadline: None

items.title: CRDP — stop the VA offset if you have 20 years and 50%+
items.who: Military retirees with 20+ qualifying years (or TERA retirees) and a VA rating of 50% or higher. Reserve/Guard retirees qualify once they are receiving retired pay, normally at 60 or at a reduced age.
items.value: Restores the retired pay that was dollar-for-dollar waived to receive VA compensation. For a retiree with $3,000 retired pay and $2,000 VA compensation, that is $2,000/month recovered.
items.how: Automatic. DFAS enrolls you when VA notifies them of a qualifying rating. No application.
items.hack: CRDP is fully phased in — the old 10-year phase-in ended in 2014, so there is no partial restoration anymore at 50%+. The number to watch is the rating cliff at 50%: going from 40% to 50% not only raises compensation, it flips on CRDP and can be worth thousands per month. If you are at 40% with 20 years, a successful increase claim is the highest-leverage financial move available to you. CRDP is TAXABLE because it is retired pay.
items.deadline: None — but retroactive payment is generally limited

items.title: CRSC — tax-free concurrent receipt at any rating from 10%
items.who: Military retirees (including Chapter 61 medical retirees with fewer than 20 years, and TERA retirees) with a VA-rated disability of at least 10% that is combat-related: combat, instrumentality of war, hazardous service, or simulated war/training.
items.value: Tax-free monthly payment replacing the waived retired pay attributable to combat-related conditions.
items.how: Apply to your BRANCH OF SERVICE — not DFAS and not VA — using DD Form 2860, with documentation tying each condition to a combat-related cause.
items.hack: Three things almost everyone misses. First, CRSC has NO 20-year requirement — Chapter 61 medical retirees at 30% with 8 years of service can get it, and CRDP will never be available to them. Second, 'instrumentality of war' is far broader than combat: a training accident with a Humvee, an injury from a weapons system, or Agent Orange exposure all qualify, and Purple Heart conditions are automatically combat-related. Third, there is no filing deadline and awards can be retroactive as far back as June 1, 2003 (January 1, 2008 for disability retirees with under 20 years), so a claim filed today can produce a very large lump sum — this is not a six-year cap like most federal claims.
items.deadline: No filing deadline; retroactivity to June 1, 2003 (Jan 1, 2008 for sub-20-year disability retirees)

items.title: The annual CRDP/CRSC open season — pick the bigger check
items.who: Retirees who qualify for both CRDP and CRSC. You may receive only one.
items.value: Potentially hundreds to thousands per month, plus a large difference in after-tax value.
items.how: DFAS mails an election form when you first qualify for both (45 days to respond). After that, changes are made during Open Season, which normally runs in January.
items.hack: Do not compare the gross amounts — compare AFTER TAX. CRSC is tax-free; CRDP is taxable as retired pay. A $1,700 CRSC payment beats a $2,000 CRDP payment for anyone in a 22%+ marginal bracket. DFAS automatically pays whichever is greater in gross terms unless you affirmatively elect otherwise, which means the default can quietly cost you money. Also: CRSC is not counted as income for many needs-based programs and is not divisible as marital property in most jurisdictions, while CRDP retired pay is.
items.deadline: Open Season, typically January each year; 45 days on the initial election letter

items.title: How the VA waiver and offset actually works
items.who: Every military retiree who also receives VA disability compensation.
items.value: Understanding this prevents a surprise DFAS debt of thousands of dollars.
items.how: By law you cannot receive both retired pay and VA compensation for the same period. You waive retired pay dollar-for-dollar to receive the (tax-free, usually larger) VA payment. CRDP or CRSC then restores some or all of the waived amount.
items.hack: The most common financial disaster in military retirement is a retroactive VA award creating a retroactive retired-pay overpayment. VA pays you a lump sum back to the effective date; DFAS then discovers you were overpaid retired pay for that same period and recoups it, sometimes by taking 100% of your monthly retired pay. Before you spend a VA retro check, call DFAS at 800-321-1080 and ask what the waiver recoupment will be — and if it creates hardship, request a repayment plan or waiver from DFAS in writing before the recoupment begins, not after.
items.deadline: Act before spending any VA retroactive award

items.title: Chapter 61 medical retirees — the CRSC-only lane
items.who: Service members medically retired under 10 U.S.C. Chapter 61 with fewer than 20 years of service.
items.value: CRSC is the only concurrent-receipt option available, and it is tax-free.
items.how: Apply via DD Form 2860 to your branch. Payment is capped at the retired pay you would have received based on YEARS OF SERVICE (not the disability percentage multiplier).
items.hack: Chapter 61 retirees with under 20 years are permanently locked out of CRDP no matter how high their VA rating goes — CRDP requires 20 years. So the only path is CRSC, and it turns on proving combat-relatedness, not on the rating percentage. Even a 10% combat-related condition opens the door. The years-of-service cap means a 6-year medical retiree gets less than a 19-year one, but it is still tax-free money that is otherwise entirely waived away.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Disability severance pay recoupment from VA compensation
items.who: Service members separated with disability severance pay who later receive VA compensation for the same condition.
items.value: Knowing the rules prevents assuming your VA compensation was miscalculated.
items.how: VA withholds monthly compensation until the gross severance amount is recouped — but only for the SAME disability that generated the severance.
items.hack: Two protections most veterans never assert. First, if the disability was combat-related (or incurred in a combat zone), the National Defense Authorization Act prohibits recoupment entirely — VA should not withhold at all. Second, VA recoups only the AFTER-TAX amount for severance paid after January 28, 2008, so if taxes were withheld, the recoupable figure is lower than the gross. If VA is withholding the gross on a post-2008 severance, file a written dispute with evidence of the withholding.
items.deadline: None

items.title: St. Clair / Combat-Injured Veterans Tax Fairness Act refund
items.who: Veterans who received a lump-sum disability severance payment after January 17, 1991 that had federal income tax improperly withheld.
items.value: A standard refund of $1,750 (tax years 1991–2005), $2,400 (2006–2010), or $3,200 (2011–2016) — or the actual tax withheld, if higher.
items.how: File Form 1040-X for the year the severance was received. Write 'Veteran Disability Severance' or 'St. Clair Claim' across the top, put the standard amount on line 15 column B and line 22, attach the DoD notice letter, and mail to IRS, 333 W. Pershing Street, Stop 6503, P5, Kansas City, MO 64108.
items.hack: The simplified method requires no records at all — you claim the flat amount without proving what was actually withheld, and for most veterans the flat amount is close to or above the real figure. The filing window is the LATER of one year from the DoD notice date, three years from the original return due date, or two years from when the tax was paid — which means the one-year-from-DoD-notice clock can revive a claim from 1995. If you never received a DoD notice, attach records from the National Archives or VA instead.
items.deadline: 1 year from the DoD notice letter, or the normal 3-year/2-year window, whichever is later

items.title: BRS vs High-3 — the 2.0% vs 2.5% multiplier
items.who: Everyone who entered service on or after January 1, 2018 is in BRS. Those who entered before and opted in during 2018 are in BRS. Everyone else is legacy High-3.
items.value: High-3 pays 2.5% × years × high-3 average basic pay. BRS pays 2.0% × years × high-3, plus TSP matching and continuation pay.
items.how: At 20 years: High-3 = 50% of high-3 pay. BRS = 40% of high-3 pay plus a TSP balance built from up to 5% government contributions over the career.
items.hack: BRS is better for the roughly 81% who do NOT reach 20 years, because the TSP match vests and travels with you while a High-3 pension worth $0 does not. But BRS only beats High-3 for a 20-year retiree if you actually contribute 5% every month from day one to capture the full match — leaving the match on the table converts BRS into a strictly worse deal. If you are BRS and contributing less than 5%, you are declining free money that is worth more than the 0.5% multiplier difference.
items.deadline: Opt-in window closed December 31, 2018

items.title: TSP matching — 5% in, 5% back, and the timing trap
items.who: BRS participants.
items.value: 1% automatic service contribution plus up to 4% matching — dollar-for-dollar on the first 3% and 50 cents on the dollar for the next 2%. Contributing 5% yields a 10% total.
items.how: Set your contribution to at least 5% of basic pay in myPay. Automatic 1% starts after 60 days of service; matching begins at the start of the 25th month of service and continues through 26 years.
items.hack: The timing trap: TSP matching is calculated PER PAY PERIOD, not annually. If you front-load and hit the $24,500 elective deferral limit in September, your contributions stop and so does the match for the rest of the year — you forfeit several months of free money. Spread contributions across all 12 months. The exception is a combat-zone year where you are deliberately maxing tax-exempt contributions toward the $72,000 annual additions limit.
items.deadline: Per pay period, continuously

items.title: 2026 TSP limits: $24,500 / $8,000 / $11,250 / $72,000
items.who: All TSP participants.
items.value: $24,500 elective deferral; $8,000 catch-up at 50+; $11,250 enhanced catch-up for those turning 60, 61, 62 or 63 in 2026; $72,000 total annual additions (section 415(c)).
items.how: Elect in myPay. Catch-up contributions are now made through the same election — there is no separate catch-up form; the system 'spillover' handles it automatically once you hit the elective deferral limit.
items.hack: The SECURE 2.0 Roth catch-up rule now bites: if your prior-year FICA wages exceeded $150,000, your catch-up contributions MUST be Roth. Also, the $11,250 enhanced catch-up applies only in the years you turn 60 through 63 — at 64 you drop back to $8,000, so those four years are a narrow, large window to accelerate. Uniformed services members should note that the $72,000 annual additions ceiling is what makes the combat-zone strategy possible.
items.deadline: Calendar year 2026

items.title: Combat-zone TSP: contribute up to $72,000 of tax-exempt pay
items.who: Service members receiving pay excluded under the Combat Zone Tax Exclusion.
items.value: The ability to push far past the $24,500 elective deferral limit — up to the $72,000 annual additions limit for 2026 — using tax-exempt dollars.
items.how: While in a designated combat zone, increase your TSP election. Tax-exempt contributions to the TRADITIONAL balance are not counted against the $24,500 elective deferral limit; they count only against the $72,000 annual additions limit.
items.hack: This is the highest-value financial move available in the military, and it is used by almost no one. Contribute tax-exempt combat pay to the ROTH TSP and the money goes in tax-free AND comes out tax-free — a permanently untaxed dollar, which is not achievable through any other US retirement vehicle. If you instead route tax-exempt pay to the traditional balance, the contributions are tax-free going in but EARNINGS are taxable coming out, and TSP must track two separate bases. For a deployed member, Roth is almost always the right answer.
items.deadline: While serving in a designated combat zone

items.title: TSP age-55 rule (age 50 for uniformed services) beats the IRA at 59½
items.who: Anyone separating from federal or uniformed service in or after the year they turn 55 — or age 50 for public safety employees and certain uniformed services members.
items.value: Penalty-free TSP withdrawals years before the normal 59½ threshold. Ordinary income tax still applies.
items.how: Separate from service in or after the qualifying year and take withdrawals directly from TSP.
items.hack: This exception is destroyed the moment you roll the TSP into an IRA — an IRA has no age-55 rule and you are back to 59½ plus a 10% penalty. Retirees are routinely talked into rolling everything to a brokerage IRA by advisors who never mention it, costing early retirees 10% of every dollar they touch between 50/55 and 59½. If you retire in your early fifties, keep enough in TSP to cover the bridge years and roll the rest later. TSP's expense ratios are also among the lowest available anywhere, which is a second reason to stay.
items.deadline: Must separate in or after the qualifying birthday year

items.title: BRS continuation pay — 2.5x to 13x monthly basic pay
items.who: BRS participants between completion of 8 and before completion of 12 years of service (measured from Pay Entry Base Date).
items.value: Active component: 2.5 to 13 times monthly basic pay. Reserve component: 0.5 to 6 times monthly basic pay (computed as if on active duty).
items.how: Each service publishes its own multipliers annually and its own application window. Requires an additional service obligation, typically 3 to 4 years.
items.hack: Continuation pay can be rolled straight into TSP, and doing so in a year you are ALSO in a combat zone lets you shelter a very large lump sum against the $72,000 annual additions limit rather than the $24,500 deferral limit. Separately, the multiplier varies dramatically by service and specialty and is re-set each year — if your service raised your career field's multiplier this year, taking it at 8 years versus waiting to 11 can be a five-figure decision. Check your service's current-year message, not last year's.
items.deadline: Between 8 and 12 years of service; service-specific windows

items.title: SBP costs 6.5% of the base amount for 55% coverage
items.who: Military retirees electing spouse coverage.
items.value: The annuity pays 55% of the elected base amount to the surviving spouse for life, with COLA. Premium is 6.5% of the base amount, deducted pre-tax from retired pay.
items.how: Elect at retirement. You can elect full retired pay as the base, or any lower base amount down to a statutory floor.
items.hack: Premiums are paid with PRE-TAX dollars out of retired pay, so the effective cost is roughly 6.5% × (1 − your marginal rate) — closer to 5% for most retirees. And SBP becomes PAID UP after 360 months of premiums AND age 70, both conditions met: after that the annuity continues for free for life. A retiree who retires at 42 stops paying at 72 and the spouse is covered for decades at zero cost. No commercial annuity with full COLA protection comes close. The main counter-argument is a spouse who is older or in poor health, or a retiree whose estate already funds the survivor.
items.deadline: Elect before retirement date

items.title: SBP-DIC offset is fully repealed — survivors get both in full
items.who: Surviving spouses receiving both SBP from DFAS and DIC from VA.
items.value: Full SBP plus full DIC with no reduction. Previously SBP was reduced dollar-for-dollar by DIC — the 'widow's tax.'
items.how: Automatic. The phase-out ran 2021–2022 and the offset was fully eliminated effective January 1, 2023, first full payment February 1, 2023.
items.hack: Because the offset is gone, the Special Survivor Indemnity Allowance (SSIA) also ended — survivors who see SSIA disappear from their statement are NOT losing money, they are receiving more. The bigger consequence: the 'optional child annuity' workaround, where retirees redirected SBP to a child to dodge the offset, is now usually the WRONG answer, since a child annuity ends when the child ages out while a spouse annuity is lifetime. Families who made that election during the offset era should revisit it — DFAS opened a reversion window and many never acted.
items.deadline: Offset fully eliminated January 1, 2023

items.title: SBP election windows: 1 year to change, 30 days to revoke
items.who: Retirees and their spouses.
items.value: Preserving or correcting an SBP election worth hundreds of thousands over a survivor's lifetime.
items.how: Key windows: spousal concurrence is required to elect less than full coverage or decline. A retiree who marries AFTER retirement has 1 year from the marriage to elect spouse coverage. A retiree may withdraw from SBP between the 25th and 36th month of receiving retired pay, with spousal concurrence — but premiums paid are NOT refunded.
items.hack: The most valuable and least-known window is the disability withdrawal: a retiree rated 100% by VA for a continuous period (generally 10 years, or 5 years from date of discharge) may withdraw from SBP entirely, and DFAS will REFUND premiums paid — but only if the spouse concurs, and only because the surviving spouse would then be entitled to DIC. Do the math first: post-repeal, the spouse can receive both SBP and DIC, so withdrawing often destroys more value than it recovers.
items.deadline: 1 year after post-retirement marriage; 25th–36th month for withdrawal

items.title: SBP vs. term life insurance — running the real comparison
items.who: Retirees deciding whether to decline SBP and 'buy term and invest the difference.'
items.value: Correctly valuing a COLA-adjusted lifetime annuity against a level death benefit.
items.how: Compare the 6.5% pre-tax premium against the cost of a policy large enough to generate 55% of retired pay, inflation-adjusted, for the spouse's full remaining life expectancy.
items.hack: The honest comparison usually favors SBP for three reasons civilian advisors miss: (1) SBP has full annual COLA, so a 30-year survivor's payment roughly doubles while a level term benefit does not; (2) SBP goes paid-up at 360 payments and age 70, while term premiums explode at exactly the age the spouse most needs coverage; (3) SBP premiums are pre-tax. Term life wins in a narrow band — a much younger and healthier retiree with a much older spouse, or a retiree whose survivor already has independent income. If you decline SBP, the decision is irrevocable except in the 25th–36th month window and requires notarized spousal concurrence for a reason.
items.deadline: Elect before retirement

items.title: Reserve/Guard retirement at 60 — and the early-credit reduction
items.who: Reserve and National Guard members with 20 qualifying years.
items.value: Retired pay normally begins at 60. Post-2008 mobilizations reduce the start age by 3 months per qualifying 90-day period, with a hard floor of age 50.
items.how: Qualifying active duty under 10 U.S.C. 12301(a), 12302, 12304, 12304a, 12305, 12406, 688, or 502(f) full-time NG duty for a designated emergency. Credit accrues in 90-day aggregate increments; since FY2015 the days may be aggregated across two consecutive fiscal years. Years of service for the multiplier = total retirement points ÷ 360; the multiplier is 2.5% per year (2.0% under BRS).
items.hack: Two traps. First, the 90-day periods must be within a single fiscal year (or, for service after 30 September 2014, across two consecutive fiscal years) — a 100-day mobilization that straddles September 30 in the wrong years can yield zero credit, so mobilization DATES matter enormously. Second, and larger: reduced-age retirement does NOT accelerate TRICARE. TRICARE Prime/Select eligibility for a gray-area retiree still begins at 60 regardless of how early the retired pay starts, so a member drawing pay at 55 must bridge five years of health coverage (TRICARE Retired Reserve is the usual answer at $645.90/month member-only in 2026).
items.deadline: Verify mobilization orders against qualifying authorities before separation

items.title: VA disability compensation is entirely tax-free
items.who: All recipients of VA disability compensation, VA pension, DIC, grants for home/vehicle adaptation, and VA education benefits.
items.value: Zero federal income tax, zero state income tax in every state, and no reporting on Form 1040.
items.how: Do not report it. VA does not issue a 1099 for compensation because it is not income.
items.hack: Because it is untaxed, a mortgage underwriter may GROSS IT UP — commonly by 25% — when calculating qualifying income. $2,000/month of VA compensation can count as $2,500/month for loan qualification. Many lenders do not apply the gross-up unless you ask. The same logic applies to child support calculations and some state benefit formulas, where untaxed status can work for or against you depending on the statute.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Retroactive rating opens a special window to amend old returns
items.who: Retirees who paid tax on retired pay that a later VA rating decision converted into tax-free VA compensation, or who received CRSC retroactively.
items.value: Refund of federal tax paid on retired pay for the retroactive period — often several thousand dollars per year affected.
items.how: File Form 1040-X for each affected year, attaching the VA rating decision showing the retroactive effective date and the DFAS documentation of the waiver.
items.hack: The normal 3-year statute of limitations is not the only clock. Under the special rule for retroactive VA determinations, you generally have ONE YEAR from the date of the VA determination to file amended returns, even for years otherwise closed. A veteran who in 2026 receives a rating retroactive to 2014 can amend 2014 forward — but only if they act within a year of the decision letter. Veterans routinely discover this after the window closes. Open the letter, calendar the date, file immediately.
items.deadline: Generally 1 year from the VA determination date

items.title: Combat Zone Tax Exclusion — all enlisted pay, capped for officers
items.who: Service members serving in a designated combat zone, a direct support area, or a qualified hazardous duty area for any part of a month.
items.value: Enlisted members and warrant officers: ALL military pay for that month is excluded from gross income, including reenlistment bonuses. Commissioned officers: excluded up to the highest enlisted rate of basic pay plus hostile fire/imminent danger pay per month.
items.how: Automatic through DFAS once your unit is coded. Current zones include the Afghanistan area, the Arabian Peninsula area, the Kosovo area, and the Sinai Peninsula.
items.hack: Serving even ONE DAY in a combat zone excludes the ENTIRE month's pay. Time a reenlistment bonus, a PCS, or a large lump payment to land in a month you set foot in the zone and the whole payment is tax-free. Officers should note the cap is per month, not per year. Also, filing deadlines are extended by 180 days after the last day in the zone, plus the days remaining in the filing season when you deployed — and that extension suspends interest and penalties, including on collection actions.
items.deadline: Filing deadline extended 180 days after leaving the zone

items.title: The EITC nontaxable combat pay election
items.who: Lower- and moderate-income service members with combat pay excluded from income.
items.value: Can swing the Earned Income Tax Credit by thousands of dollars — in either direction.
items.how: You may ELECT to include nontaxable combat pay in earned income for EITC purposes. It is an all-or-nothing election for the full amount, made on the return.
items.hack: This is one of the rare places where adding income raises a credit. If your taxable earned income is below the EITC plateau, including combat pay pushes you up the phase-in ramp and increases the credit. If you are already past the plateau, including it phases you OUT and costs you money. The only way to know is to compute the return both ways — MilTax and most software will do this automatically if you tell them to test it, but they will not test it unless prompted. Married couples elect separately, so one spouse can include and the other not.
items.deadline: Made on the return for the year

items.title: Pick your state of residence: the 2023 three-way residency election
items.who: Active duty service members and their spouses.
items.value: Potentially eliminating state income tax entirely by electing a no-income-tax state of residence.
items.how: Under SCRA as amended by the Veterans Auto and Education Improvement Act of 2022 (effective for tax year 2023 forward), the service member and spouse may EACH elect, for state tax and voting purposes: the service member's state of legal residence, the spouse's state of legal residence, or the state of the member's current permanent duty station.
items.hack: The 2023 change is transformative and badly under-publicized. Before it, the spouse had to share the member's domicile. Now a couple stationed in Texas, Florida, Tennessee, Washington, Nevada, South Dakota, Wyoming or Alaska can BOTH elect that duty-station state and pay zero state income tax on all wages — including the civilian spouse's civilian salary — regardless of where either grew up. The election is made on the state return and by updating DD Form 2058 / state withholding. Note SCRA protects military and spouse WAGES; rental income and business income sourced to another state usually remain taxable there.
items.deadline: Elect on each year's state return

items.title: Property tax exemptions are a state benefit, not a federal one
items.who: Disabled veterans and, in many states, their surviving spouses.
items.value: In several states a 100% service-connected rating eliminates primary-residence property tax entirely — frequently worth $4,000–$12,000 per year.
items.how: Apply through the COUNTY assessor, not VA and not the state. Requires a VA rating decision letter and usually proof of ownership and occupancy.
items.hack: There is no federal property tax exemption — VA does not administer this and will not tell you about it. The rules, thresholds and surviving-spouse continuation vary enormously by state, and many states require annual re-filing or a one-time filing by a specific date (often before the tax year begins). Two structural points: most states key off the VA rating letter's PERMANENT AND TOTAL language rather than the 100% figure alone, and many states allow the exemption to transfer to an un-remarried surviving spouse — a benefit that survives the veteran and that families frequently fail to claim after a death.
items.deadline: State- and county-specific; often an annual filing deadline

items.title: Free tax prep: MilTax, VITA, and IRS Free File
