items.who: Service members, veterans and families.
items.value: $0 federal and state preparation, plus free consultation with tax professionals trained in military issues.
items.how: MilTax through Military OneSource: free federal and up to three state returns, available to service members and to veterans for up to 365 days after separation or retirement. VITA: free in-person preparation, including on-base sites. IRS Free File: free guided software for AGI at or below $89,000; Free File Fillable Forms at any income.
items.hack: MilTax has no income limit at all — a retiring O-6 with rental properties uses it free. And the 365-day post-separation window is the hidden value: your separation year is your most complicated return ever (partial-year income, final leave sell-back, moving expenses, severance, state residency change) and MilTax's consultants specialize in exactly that. Most veterans discover MilTax exists after the window closes. Set a calendar reminder at separation.
items.deadline: MilTax: 365 days after separation/retirement

items.title: Priority Group 1 pays absolutely nothing
items.who: Veterans rated 50% or higher, veterans rated TDIU (unemployable), and Medal of Honor recipients.
items.value: No copay for any VA care: primary, specialty, inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, urgent care. Zero.
items.how: Enroll in VA health care. Placement is automatic based on rating.
items.hack: The 40%-to-50% rating jump is the largest single copay cliff in the system. At 40% (Priority Group 2) you still owe medication copays up to $700/year; at 50% everything drops to zero. If you are at 40% with multiple conditions, a supplemental claim or increase that reaches 50% is worth the compensation increase PLUS the copay elimination PLUS CRDP eligibility if you are a 20-year retiree. Also note TDIU puts you in Group 1 even at a 60% or 70% schedular rating.
items.deadline: None

items.title: PACT Act opened VA health care to every toxic-exposed veteran
items.who: Veterans who served in a toxic exposure location or were exposed to burn pits, Agent Orange, radiation, Camp Lejeune water, particulates, or chemical/warfare agents.
items.value: Direct enrollment in VA health care — generally Priority Group 6 — without needing a service-connected rating first, and $0 copays for care related to the exposure.
items.how: Apply at VA.gov/health-care/apply. Since March 5, 2024, VA has enrolled all eligible toxic-exposed veterans regardless of the previous phase-in schedule.
items.hack: You do NOT need an approved disability claim to enroll under this pathway — enrollment and compensation are separate tracks, and enrolling first gets you into the system, gets you the mandatory toxic exposure screening, and builds the VA treatment record that later supports the compensation claim. Veterans commonly wait for a rating decision before enrolling, which is exactly backwards. Every enrolled veteran also gets a toxic exposure screening at least once every 5 years.
items.deadline: No deadline — enrollment is open

items.title: The 10-year post-discharge combat veteran enrollment window
items.who: Veterans who served in a theater of combat operations after November 11, 1998, or who were discharged/released from active duty on or after September 11, 2001.
items.value: Enhanced enrollment in Priority Group 6 with $0 copays for care related to combat service, without any means test and without a service-connected rating.
items.how: Enroll within 10 years of discharge (extended from 5 years by the PACT Act for post-9/11 combat veterans). Present your DD-214.
items.hack: The window controls ENROLLMENT, not eligibility forever — once you enroll during the window, you stay enrolled for life, even if your income later rises above the limits. Enroll on the way out the door even if you feel fine and have employer insurance; it costs nothing and locks in access permanently. Veterans who miss the window and later develop a condition must qualify through income or a rating instead, which is far harder. The PACT Act also created a special one-year enrollment period for those who previously missed it.
items.deadline: 10 years from discharge for post-9/11 combat veterans

items.title: Community Care: 30/60 minutes drive, 20/28 days wait
items.who: Enrolled VA health care patients.
items.value: VA pays for care from a community provider near you instead of making you travel or wait.
items.how: You qualify if VA cannot meet: a 30-minute average drive time for primary or mental health care, a 60-minute average drive time for specialty care, a 20-day wait for primary/mental health, or a 28-day wait for specialty care. Also if VA does not offer the service, if your state has no full-service VA facility, if VA cannot meet its quality standards, or if you and your provider agree it is in your best medical interest.
items.hack: 'Average drive time' is calculated by VA's geospatial tool, not by your odometer, and the 'best medical interest' criterion is a genuine discretionary standard — a VA provider can authorize community care on that basis alone when the drive-time and wait-time clocks technically fail. Ask your provider to document the best-medical-interest rationale rather than fighting the mileage calculation. Also: the wait-time clock runs from the date you REQUEST the appointment, not the date VA offers one, so document your request date.
items.deadline: Prior authorization required except for urgent/emergency care

items.title: VA urgent care: first 3 visits free for Priority Groups 1–5
items.who: Veterans enrolled in VA health care who have received VA care within the past 24 months.
items.value: $0 for the first three urgent care visits each calendar year (Priority Groups 1–5), then $30. No referral or prior authorization needed.
items.how: Go to any in-network urgent care or retail clinic. Find one at VA.gov's facility locator under 'in-network community urgent care.'
items.hack: The 24-month rule is the gate most veterans trip over — if you have not used VA care in two years, you are not eligible for the urgent care benefit at all. A single primary care visit resets the clock. Also, a flu shot alone at an in-network urgent care or pharmacy is always free and does NOT burn one of your three visits. Prescriptions written at an urgent care for 14 days or less can be filled at an in-network pharmacy; longer prescriptions must go through VA.
items.deadline: Must have used VA care within the past 24 months

items.title: VA dental care: who actually gets it
items.who: Only specific classes — dental is NOT part of standard VA health care enrollment.
items.value: Free comprehensive dental care for Class I (service-connected compensable dental condition), Class IIC (former POWs), and Class IV (rated 100% or TDIU).
items.how: Classes: I — compensable SC dental condition, any needed care. IIA — noncompensable SC dental condition from combat wounds/trauma, care to restore function. IIB — homeless veterans in the Homeless Veterans Dental Program, one-time course. IIC — former POWs, any needed care. II — 90+ days active duty in the qualifying era, one-time care if applied within 180 days of discharge. III — dental condition worsening a service-connected medical condition. IV — 100% P&T or TDIU, any needed care. V — active Veteran Readiness & Employment participants. VI — inpatients needing dental care for their treatment.
items.hack: Class III is the underused door: if your dental condition is aggravating a service-connected condition — the classic case is dental disease worsening service-connected diabetes, or an oral condition interfering with treatment for a service-connected illness — you qualify for treatment of that condition even without a dental rating. Ask your VA primary care provider to document the linkage. Also note TDIU puts you in Class IV with FULL dental, same as a schedular 100%, which many unemployability recipients never realize.
items.deadline: Class II: apply within 180 days of discharge

items.title: VADIP — buy discounted dental insurance through VA
items.who: Any veteran enrolled in VA health care, and any CHAMPVA beneficiary — no rating required.
items.value: Group-rate dental insurance covering diagnostic, preventive, restorative, endodontic, surgical and emergency dental care at below-market premiums.
items.how: Choose Delta Dental (855-370-3303) or MetLife (888-310-1681) and enroll directly with the carrier. VA does not enroll you.
items.hack: This is the answer for the roughly 90% of enrolled veterans who do not qualify for any VA dental class. Premiums are paid entirely by the veteran, but the rates are negotiated group rates well below individual-market dental. CHAMPVA beneficiaries — spouses and children of 100% P&T veterans — are eligible too, which is often the cheapest family dental available to them. Enrollment is done at the carrier's site, so nothing on VA.gov will confirm your coverage.
items.deadline: Carrier enrollment periods

items.title: Hearing aids, eyeglasses and prosthetics at no cost
items.who: Enrolled veterans meeting specific criteria — notably any compensable service-connected rating, former POWs, Purple Heart recipients, VA pension recipients, and those whose vision/hearing loss results from a service-connected condition or from VA treatment.
items.value: Hearing aids and batteries, eyeglasses, prosthetic limbs, wheelchairs, adaptive equipment, home oxygen, and repairs — furnished at no cost with no copay.
items.how: Referral from a VA audiologist, optometrist, or Prosthetic & Sensory Aids Service. Detailed eligibility criteria are set out in VHA Directive 1034 (Prescribing and Providing Eyeglasses, Contact Lenses, and Hearing Aids).
items.hack: The eligibility gate for hearing aids is far wider than veterans assume: ANY compensable service-connected rating — including a 10% rating for an unrelated knee — qualifies you for VA hearing aids, which retail for $3,000–$7,000 a pair. VA also supplies batteries and repairs for life and replaces them on a schedule. Same logic applies to eyeglasses. Veterans with a 10% rating for anything should book an audiology consult.
items.deadline: None

items.title: COMPACT Act: free emergent suicide care at ANY facility
items.who: Any veteran in acute suicidal crisis — including veterans NOT enrolled in VA health care, and including many with other-than-honorable discharges.
items.value: Up to 30 days of inpatient/crisis residential care and up to 90 days of outpatient follow-up at NO cost, at a VA facility or any non-VA emergency department. Ambulance transport is covered.
items.how: Go to the nearest emergency department — VA or not. Notify VA within 72 hours by calling 844-724-7842 or through the Emergency Care Reporting portal (the facility can do this).
items.hack: This is the single most important thing to know in VA health care and almost nobody knows it. You do not need to be enrolled, you do not need a rating, you do not need to go to a VA hospital, and the community ED does not need a prior agreement with VA to be reimbursed. Veterans with OTH discharges who served 100+ days in a combat/contingency deployment, or who experienced sexual assault or harassment in service, are covered. If you are billed anyway, call 877-881-7618 — improper billing is common and VA will fix it.
items.deadline: Notify VA within 72 hours of arrival

items.title: Vet Centers — counseling with no rating, no enrollment, no record
items.who: Combat veterans, veterans who experienced military sexual trauma, those who provided mortuary services or drone crew duty, Guard/Reserve members, and their FAMILIES. Bereavement counseling for families of those who died on active duty.
items.value: Free individual, group, marriage, family and bereavement counseling, plus MST and PTSD counseling.
items.how: Walk into any of the ~300 Vet Centers or call 877-927-8387. No enrollment, no referral, no rating, no copay.
items.hack: Vet Center records are kept SEPARATE from VA medical records and from DoD — this is the one place a still-serving member or someone worried about a security clearance can get counseling without it entering the VA/DoD medical record. That confidentiality is the entire design purpose. Family members are eligible in their own right for counseling related to the veteran's service, and bereavement counseling is available to parents, spouses and children of service members who died on active duty regardless of the veteran's own eligibility.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Veterans Crisis Line: 988, press 1
items.who: Any veteran, service member, Guard/Reserve member, or family member — no enrollment or eligibility requirement.
items.value: 24/7 confidential crisis support from responders, many of whom are veterans themselves.
items.how: Dial 988 then press 1. Text 838255. Chat at VeteransCrisisLine.net.
items.hack: The line is not only for imminent crisis — responders handle sleep problems, relationship stress, financial crisis, homelessness risk and substance use, and can connect you directly to a Suicide Prevention Coordinator at your local VA who has authority to expedite appointments. Family members can call ON BEHALF of a veteran who will not call themselves. Calling does not create a VA medical record entry unless you request services.
items.deadline: None

items.title: PCAFC caregiver stipend — up to 100% of a GS-4 salary
items.who: Family caregivers of veterans with a single or combined 70%+ service-connected rating who need in-person personal care services for at least 6 continuous months due to a serious injury.
items.value: Level 1 = 62.5% and Level 2 = 100% of the monthly OPM GS-4 step 1 rate for the veteran's locality. Depending on locality, Level 2 commonly runs from roughly $2,700 to over $3,600 per month.
items.how: VA Form 10-10CG, submitted online or at the local Caregiver Support Program office. A clinical assessment follows.
items.hack: Three things. First, the stipend is paid to the CAREGIVER and VA has treated it as non-taxable — do not let a tax preparer report it as wages. Second, because it is locality-based on the veteran's address, the same care is worth substantially more in a high-locality metro; this matters for families weighing a move. Third, approved primary caregivers also get CHAMPVA health coverage if not otherwise insured, mental health services, respite care and travel reimbursement — the stipend is often the smaller half of the package. Caregivers who do not qualify should still enroll in PGCSS, which requires no rating and provides coaching, peer support, respite and skills training.
items.deadline: None

items.title: CHAMPVA — health coverage for the family of a 100% P&T veteran
items.who: Spouse/children of a veteran rated permanently and totally disabled from a service-connected condition; surviving spouse/children of a veteran who died from a service-connected condition or who was rated P&T at death; certain surviving spouses of members who died in the line of duty. Not eligible if eligible for TRICARE.
items.value: No premium. $50 per person / $100 per family annual deductible, 25% cost share, and a $3,000 annual catastrophic cap — after which CHAMPVA pays 100%.
items.how: VA Form 10-10d plus supporting documents, submitted online, by mail or fax to the VHA Office of Community Care in Denver.
items.hack: There is no premium at all, which makes the total worst-case annual cost $3,000 for an entire family — cheaper than almost any marketplace plan's deductible alone. Two catches: at 65 you must have Medicare Parts A AND B to keep CHAMPVA (CHAMPVA then wraps around Medicare and often eliminates nearly all cost sharing), and an un-remarried surviving spouse keeps CHAMPVA for life while remarriage before 55 ends it. Also use CITI — the CHAMPVA In-House Treatment Initiative — where participating VA medical centers treat CHAMPVA beneficiaries at zero cost, no deductible and no cost share.
items.deadline: None, but apply promptly — retroactive coverage is limited

items.title: CHAMPVA vs TRICARE — you cannot have both
items.who: Families who are potentially eligible for both — typically a military retiree who is also rated 100% P&T.
items.value: Choosing correctly can be worth thousands per year.
items.how: By statute, eligibility for TRICARE disqualifies you from CHAMPVA. If the sponsor is a military retiree, the family is TRICARE-eligible and CHAMPVA is unavailable.
items.hack: Run the real comparison for a 100% P&T retiree's family: TRICARE Select for a Group A retiree family costs $375/year in enrollment fees plus a $300 deductible with a $3,000 cat cap; CHAMPVA costs $0 in premiums, $100 deductible, $3,000 cat cap. CHAMPVA is cheaper on paper — but it has a much narrower provider network in practice, no guaranteed acceptance by providers, and reimbursement rates that lead some doctors to decline it. The decision usually turns on whether your existing physicians accept CHAMPVA. Note also that a surviving spouse of a retiree who dies of a service-connected condition may gain a choice they did not previously have.
items.deadline: None

items.title: TRICARE 2026 retiree costs: Prime and Select, Group A vs B
items.who: Military retirees and their families. Group A = sponsor entered service before January 1, 2018; Group B = on or after.
items.value: Prime Group A: $381.96 individual / $765 family per year. Prime Group B: $462.96 / $927. Select Group A: $186.96 / $375. Select Group B: $594.96 / $1,191. Catastrophic cap: $3,000 Group A, $4,635 Group B.
items.how: Enroll or change during TRICARE Open Season (typically November–December) or within 90 days of a Qualifying Life Event.
items.hack: The Group A/Group B split flips the usual logic. For Group A retirees, Select is dramatically cheaper than Prime ($186.96 vs $381.96 individual) and gives you freedom of provider — Prime is only worth it if you live near an MTF and want $0 copays. For Group B retirees the relationship inverts: Select ($594.96) costs MORE than Prime ($462.96). Many Group B retirees default to Select out of habit and overpay. Check which group you are in before Open Season.
items.deadline: TRICARE Open Season, typically November–December

items.title: TRICARE For Life — the Medicare wraparound
items.who: Medicare-eligible TRICARE beneficiaries (retirees, family members, survivors) who have Medicare Part A and Part B.
items.value: No enrollment fee. TFL pays as second payer after Medicare, typically leaving $0 out of pocket for Medicare-covered services.
items.how: Automatic once you have Part A and Part B. You must PAY the Medicare Part B premium — that is the real cost of TFL.
items.hack: Declining Part B to save the premium terminates TRICARE For Life entirely and leaves you with essentially nothing — this is the most expensive mistake in military retirement health care, and it is irreversible without late-enrollment penalties. Separately, for a claim Medicare covers but TRICARE does not, you pay Medicare's share; for a claim TRICARE covers but Medicare does not (overseas care, for example), TFL pays first. Keep both cards.
items.deadline: Enroll in Medicare Part B during your Initial Enrollment Period

items.title: CHCBP — the 18-to-36 month TRICARE bridge
items.who: Anyone losing TRICARE eligibility: separating service members (18 months), certain former spouses (36 months or longer), and children aging out.
items.value: TRICARE Select-equivalent coverage. 2026 premiums: $2,103 per quarter individual, $5,339 per quarter family.
items.how: Enroll within 60 DAYS of losing TRICARE eligibility using the CHCBP enrollment form and paying the first quarterly premium.
items.hack: It is expensive — $8,412/year individual — but it is guaranteed-issue with no medical underwriting and no pre-existing condition exclusion, which makes it the right answer for someone mid-treatment or uninsurable. The 60-day deadline is absolute and there is no grace period. Critically, for certain un-remarried former spouses CHCBP can be purchased INDEFINITELY, not just 36 months — a fact that divorce attorneys routinely miss in settlement negotiations. Compare against an ACA marketplace plan with subsidies before enrolling; for many separating members the marketplace is cheaper.
items.deadline: 60 days from loss of TRICARE eligibility

items.title: TRICARE Young Adult for dependents 21–26
items.who: Unmarried adult children of TRICARE-eligible sponsors, ages 21 through 25, not eligible for their own employer-sponsored coverage.
items.value: 2026 monthly premiums: TYA Prime $794, TYA Select $363.
items.how: Purchase directly; coverage ends at 26.
items.hack: At $4,356/year, TYA Select is often more expensive than putting the young adult on an ACA marketplace plan with a subsidy, or on their own employer plan — and TYA is explicitly unavailable if an employer plan is offered. Check the marketplace first. Where TYA wins is for a young adult who travels, lives overseas, or attends school abroad, since TRICARE's overseas coverage is unmatched by marketplace plans.
items.deadline: Coverage ends at age 26

items.title: TRICARE Reserve Select — the cheapest family health plan in America
items.who: Selected Reserve members not eligible for or enrolled in the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.
items.value: 2026: $57.88/month member-only, $286.66/month member and family.
items.how: Purchase through milConnect. Available while in the Selected Reserve.
items.hack: At $3,440 per year for a whole family, TRS is almost certainly the least expensive comprehensive family coverage available to anyone in the United States — a comparable employer plan costs three to six times that. This alone is a legitimate financial reason to stay in the Selected Reserve. The disqualifier is FEHB eligibility: a federal civilian employee in the Reserves cannot buy TRS, which is a meaningful hidden cost of taking a federal job. When you retire from the Reserves into gray-area status, TRS ends and TRICARE Retired Reserve ($645.90/$1,548.30 monthly) is the far pricier successor until age 60.
items.deadline: While in the Selected Reserve

items.title: VA Pension 2026: $17,441 base, $29,093 with Aid & Attendance
items.who: Wartime veterans age 65+ or permanently and totally disabled (non-service-connected), with countable income below the MAPR and net worth below $163,699.
items.value: VA pays the DIFFERENCE between your countable income and the MAPR. Veteran alone $17,441/year; with one dependent $22,839; Housebound $21,313; Aid & Attendance $29,093 (or $34,488 with one dependent).
items.how: VA Form 21P-527EZ. Requires 90 days active service with at least one day during a wartime period (24 months for post-1980 entrants).
items.hack: Pension is an income-DIFFERENCE benefit, so unreimbursed medical expenses exceeding 5% of the MAPR are deducted from countable income — and that includes Medicare Part B premiums, prescriptions, insurance premiums, and the full cost of assisted living or in-home care. A veteran with $40,000 of income and $30,000 of assisted living costs can have countable income low enough to qualify for the full A&A rate. Aid & Attendance is where the money is: $29,093 vs $17,441 is an $11,652 difference, and the qualifying criteria (needing help with bathing, dressing, eating, or being bedridden, or a nursing home resident, or corrected vision 5/200 or worse) are met by most assisted living residents.
items.deadline: None; benefits generally effective from date of claim

items.title: The $163,699 net worth limit and the 3-year lookback
items.who: Applicants for VA Pension, Survivors Pension, and Aid & Attendance.
items.value: Net worth (assets plus annualized income) must be at or below $163,699 for December 1, 2025 – November 30, 2026.
items.how: The limit is indexed to the Social Security COLA each December 1. Assets transferred for less than fair market value during the 3 years before the claim can trigger a penalty period of up to 5 years.
items.hack: Two exclusions people miss. The primary residence is EXCLUDED from net worth regardless of value, along with up to 2 acres of the lot — a veteran in a fully-paid $900,000 house can still qualify. And a vehicle and personal effects are excluded. The lookback only applies to transfers made on or after October 18, 2018, and only to assets that would have exceeded the limit. The penalty is calculated on the covered amount divided by the monthly pension rate, capped at 5 years — so 'spending down' on legitimate expenses (home repairs, medical care, paying off debt) is fine, while gifting to children is not.
items.deadline: Limit resets each December 1

items.title: Survivors Pension for low-income surviving spouses
items.who: Un-remarried surviving spouses and unmarried dependent children of wartime veterans, with income and net worth below the limits.
items.value: Needs-based monthly payment bringing income up to the survivor MAPR, with Housebound and Aid & Attendance increases available.
items.how: VA Form 21P-534EZ. Same $163,699 net worth limit and 3-year lookback as veteran pension.
items.hack: File Form 21P-534EZ even when you are applying for DIC — it is the combined application and VA will consider you for DIC, Survivors Pension, and accrued benefits from the single form, paying whichever is greater. Many surviving spouses file a DIC-only claim, get denied for lack of service connection, and never learn they qualified for Survivors Pension instead. The same form also captures accrued benefits — money VA owed the veteran but had not paid at death — which must be claimed within one year of death.
items.deadline: Accrued benefits must be claimed within 1 year of death

items.title: DIC 2026: $1,699.36 base, tax-free, for life
items.who: Surviving spouses, children and parents of service members who died in the line of duty, or of veterans who died from a service-connected condition.
items.value: $1,699.36/month base for a surviving spouse (effective December 1, 2025). Add $360.85 for the 8-year provision, $421.00 per child under 18, $421.00 for Aid & Attendance, $197.22 for Housebound, and $359.00/month for 2 years if there are children under 18.
items.how: VA Form 21P-534EZ.
items.hack: DIC is entirely tax-free and continues for life, and since the SBP-DIC offset repeal in 2023 a survivor can receive DIC AND full SBP simultaneously — a combination worth over $4,000/month for many families. Remarriage: DIC terminates on remarriage UNLESS the remarriage occurs at or after age 55 (and on or after December 16, 2003), in which case DIC continues for life. Surviving spouses who remarried after 55 and stopped receiving DIC should reapply — VA has restored benefits retroactively in these cases.
items.deadline: None; file promptly for full retroactivity

items.title: The DIC 10-year rule — death from ANY cause
items.who: Surviving spouses of veterans who were rated totally disabled (100% schedular or TDIU) for a qualifying period before death.
items.value: Full DIC even when the veteran died of something completely unrelated to service — cancer, a car accident, anything.
items.how: The veteran must have been continuously rated totally disabled for: 10 or more years immediately preceding death; OR at least 5 years from the date of discharge; OR at least 1 year if the veteran was a former POW who died after September 30, 1999.
items.hack: This is the most valuable and least-known survivor provision in the system. A veteran rated 100% at age 55 who dies at 66 of a heart attack entirely unrelated to service leaves a spouse entitled to $1,699.36/month tax-free for life. Families routinely never file because the death certificate says something non-service-connected. The 8-YEAR PROVISION stacks on top: if the veteran was rated totally disabled for the 8 years immediately before death and the spouse was married to them that whole time, add $360.85/month. Check the rating history, not the death certificate.
items.deadline: None

items.title: DIC for parents — the forgotten survivor benefit
items.who: Low-income parents (including adoptive and, in some cases, foster parents) of a service member or veteran who died from a service-connected cause.
items.value: Income-based monthly payment on a separate sliding-scale rate table, reduced as parental income rises.
items.how: VA Form 21P-535.
items.hack: Parents' DIC is income-tested on a sliding scale, and unreimbursed MEDICAL EXPENSES are deducted from countable income — for elderly parents with significant medical costs, that deduction frequently brings them under the threshold even when gross income looks too high. The rate table also provides an Aid & Attendance increase for a parent who needs regular aid. Almost no one files this claim; VA's own data shows parent DIC recipients numbering in the low thousands nationally.
items.deadline: None

items.title: VA disability does not reduce SSDI — and vice versa
items.who: Veterans receiving or applying for Social Security Disability Insurance.
items.value: Both benefits paid in full, concurrently. VA compensation is not counted against SSDI at all.
items.how: Apply for SSDI separately at SSA.gov. The two agencies use entirely different disability standards — SSA requires inability to engage in substantial gainful activity, VA uses a percentage schedule.
items.hack: SSI is a different story: it IS needs-based, and VA compensation counts as unearned income that reduces SSI dollar for dollar (after a $20 general exclusion). So a veteran on SSI who wins a VA claim can lose most of the SSI — but should still file, since VA compensation is tax-free and SSI is not, and VA compensation does not have SSI's asset limits. Also note a VA 100% P&T rating does NOT bind SSA; a substantial share of 100% P&T veterans are denied SSDI because they are still working above the SGA threshold.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Expedited SSDI processing for 100% P&T veterans
items.who: Veterans with a VA rating of 100% Permanent and Total, and separately, Wounded Warriors who became disabled while on active duty on or after October 1, 2001.
items.value: Claims moved to the front of the queue — months faster than standard processing.
items.how: When applying, state you are a 'Veteran rated 100% P&T' to the representative, or type 'Veteran 100% P&T' in the Remarks field of the online application, and submit the VA rating notification letter.
items.hack: The expedite is not automatic — SSA does not cross-check VA ratings. If you do not say the magic phrase and attach the letter, your claim sits in the normal queue. Two more points: the Wounded Warrior expedite applies regardless of where the injury occurred, not just in combat, and applies even if you are still on active duty receiving military pay (military pay is not automatically substantial gainful activity if you are not performing substantial work). Expedited processing is not expedited APPROVAL — SSA still applies its own standard.
items.deadline: State it at the time of application

items.title: Special extra Social Security wage credits for military service
items.who: Veterans with active duty service between 1940 and 2001.
items.value: Additional deemed earnings added to your Social Security record, which can increase your monthly retirement or disability benefit.
items.how: Service from 1957–1977: $300 in additional earnings credited per quarter of active duty. Service from 1978–2001: $100 in additional earnings for each $300 of active duty basic pay, up to $1,200 per year. Service from 1940–1956 was not covered by Social Security but may be credited at $160 per month of active duty. No credits for service after 2001.
items.hack: For 1968 and later these credits are usually already on your record automatically — but for earlier service, and especially for 1940–1956 service, you may need to PROVE it with a DD-214 at the time you file. Check your Social Security Statement at ssa.gov/myaccount against your service dates before you file for retirement; correcting the record after benefits start is possible but slower. The credits are modest individually but compound through the benefit formula over a lifetime.
items.deadline: Verify before filing for Social Security

items.title: HUD-VASH — permanent housing voucher plus VA case management
items.who: Veterans experiencing homelessness who need ongoing intensive case management, typically due to chronic health, mental health or substance use conditions.
items.value: A HUD Housing Choice Voucher paying the majority of rent (veteran generally contributes about 30% of adjusted income) plus wraparound VA clinical case management. Over 116,000 vouchers awarded since 2008.
items.how: Call the National Call Center for Homeless Veterans at 877-424-3838, available 24/7, or ask at any VA medical center. VA refers eligible veterans to the local public housing authority.
items.hack: HUD-VASH does not require a service-connected rating, does not require VA health care enrollment beforehand (VA will enroll you), and notably accepts many veterans with other-than-honorable discharges, who are often eligible for VA homeless program services even when barred from other benefits. The voucher is tenant-based and portable — it can move with the veteran to another jurisdiction. Case management is mandatory, which is the trade-off.
items.deadline: None

items.title: SSVF and Grant and Per Diem — rapid rehousing and prevention
items.who: SSVF: very low-income veteran families who are homeless or at imminent risk. GPD: veterans needing transitional housing with supportive services.
items.value: SSVF provides temporary financial assistance — rent arrears, security deposits, utility payments, moving costs, emergency housing — plus case management, through community nonprofit grantees. GPD funds transitional housing beds.
items.how: Call 877-424-3838 or find a local SSVF grantee through VA's directory.
items.hack: SSVF is the prevention program — it is designed to intervene BEFORE eviction, and it can pay back rent to stop a pending eviction outright. Veterans consistently wait until after they lose housing, when the far harder rapid-rehousing track is the only remaining option. If you have an eviction notice, call today. SSVF also does not require a service-connected rating and covers the veteran's whole family, including non-veteran spouses and children.
items.deadline: Call before eviction, not after

items.title: VALife — guaranteed-acceptance whole life for any rated veteran
items.who: Any veteran with a service-connected disability rating, INCLUDING 0%, who is age 80 or younger. Limited eligibility past 81 in specific circumstances.
items.value: Up to $40,000 of whole life coverage in $10,000 increments, with guaranteed acceptance regardless of health and a premium that never increases.
items.how: Apply online at VA.gov. There is a 2-year waiting period before the full death benefit is payable; death during the waiting period returns all premiums paid plus interest (4.23% for 2026).
items.hack: VALife replaced S-DVI and removed the old program's crippling limitations: there is NO time limit to apply after receiving a rating (S-DVI had a 2-year window that stranded thousands of veterans), and a 0% rating qualifies. A veteran rated 0% for tinnitus in 1998 can apply today at 70 and be accepted with no medical questions. The trade-off is the 2-year wait, so apply as early as possible — the waiting period is the whole cost of the guarantee. VALife builds cash value after year 2 but does not offer policy loans.
items.deadline: No deadline to apply if under 81

items.title: VGLI: 240 days with no health questions, then it gets hard
items.who: Service members separating with SGLI coverage.
items.value: Up to $500,000 of term life insurance with no medical underwriting if you apply within 240 days of separation.
items.how: Apply within 240 days for guaranteed acceptance. Between 240 days and 1 year + 120 days you can still apply but must prove good health. After 1 year and 120 days, you are permanently ineligible.
items.hack: The 240-day window is the single most time-sensitive benefit in the separation process, and it is buried in out-processing paperwork. Apply on day one if you have ANY health condition that would complicate commercial underwriting — VGLI premiums rise steeply with age and are worse than commercial term for a healthy 30-year-old, but for anyone uninsurable it is irreplaceable. If you are healthy, price commercial term first and use the 240 days to shop. Separately: you can INCREASE VGLI by $25,000 one year after enrolling and every 5 years thereafter until age 60 — no health review — so enrolling at a low amount preserves an escalator.
items.deadline: 240 days for no health review; 1 year and 120 days absolute

items.title: SGLI continues free for 120 days after separation — or 2 years if disabled
items.who: Separating service members.
items.value: $500,000 of coverage at $0 for 120 days after discharge. Up to 2 years free if totally disabled at separation.
items.how: Automatic. The 2-year extension requires application and applies to members who are totally disabled at discharge, or who have total hearing loss in both ears, permanent loss of use of both hands/feet/eyes, or loss of speech requiring an artificial device.
items.hack: The 2-year free extension for the totally disabled is essentially unknown and is free $500,000 of coverage during the exact period a severely injured veteran is least insurable and most financially fragile. Critically, the VGLI application clock is measured from the end of the SGLI extension, not from separation — so a disabled veteran on the extension has far more time than 240 days. SGLI premiums in 2026 are $0.05 per $1,000 of coverage (so $25/month for the full $500,000) plus $1/month for TSGLI.
items.deadline: 120 days standard; apply for the 2-year disability extension

items.title: TSGLI — $25,000 to $100,000 for a traumatic injury, including retroactive claims
items.who: Service members with SGLI who suffer a qualifying traumatic injury, on duty or off duty.
items.value: $25,000 to $100,000 depending on the loss. Paid as a lump sum.
items.how: SGLV Form 8600 (or 8600A for retroactive) submitted to your branch's TSGLI office. The scheduled loss must occur within 730 days of the traumatic injury.
items.hack: TSGLI covers OFF-DUTY injuries — a motorcycle accident on leave, a fall at home — and this catches almost everyone by surprise. It also pays for things people do not think of as 'traumatic loss': inability to perform at least two activities of daily living for 15+ consecutive days, hospitalization in intensive care for 15+ days, and (since April 2023) limb reconstruction surgery and transitional home care. RETROACTIVE claims are available for injuries between October 7, 2001 and November 30, 2005 regardless of duty status and regardless of whether SGLI was in force at the time — and the old requirement that the injury occur in OEF/OIF has been removed. Denials are appealable and frequently reversed.
items.deadline: Scheduled loss must occur within 730 days of injury

items.title: FSGLI — spouse and child coverage under SGLI
items.who: Spouses and dependent children of service members insured under SGLI.
items.value: Up to $100,000 for a spouse (not exceeding the member's own SGLI amount) and $10,000 per dependent child at no cost.
items.how: Automatic for children. Spouse coverage is automatic at the maximum unless declined or reduced; premiums are age-based and deducted from the member's pay.
items.hack: Child coverage is completely FREE — there is no premium at all — and it continues automatically. Spouse coverage can be CONVERTED to an individual commercial policy within 120 days of the member's separation or of the spouse losing coverage, with no medical underwriting, through a participating company. That conversion right is the valuable part for an uninsurable spouse and it is almost never exercised because nobody is told about it at out-processing.
items.deadline: 120 days to convert spouse coverage after eligibility ends

items.title: Burial allowance 2026: $2,000 service-connected, $1,002 + $1,002 otherwise
items.who: The person who paid the burial/funeral costs — surviving spouse, family member, estate executor, or in some cases the funeral home.
items.value: Service-connected death: $2,000. Non-service-connected death (on or after October 1, 2025): $1,002 burial allowance plus $1,002 plot/interment allowance.
items.how: VA Form 21P-530EZ. For a surviving spouse of record, VA now often pays automatically without an application.
items.hack: The plot allowance is payable IN ADDITION to the burial allowance and is frequently missed — that is $1,002 left on the table on most non-service-connected claims. But note the plot allowance is generally not payable if burial is in a national cemetery (since the plot is already free). Transportation of remains is separately reimbursable if the veteran died in a VA facility, while traveling under VA authorization, or while receiving VA-authorized care — and that reimbursement has no dollar cap, which for a cross-country transport can dwarf the burial allowance itself.
items.deadline: Generally 2 years from burial for non-service-connected claims; no limit for service-connected

items.title: National cemetery burial — free, including the spouse
items.who: Veterans discharged under conditions other than dishonorable, service members who die on active duty, and their spouses, surviving spouses and dependent children.
items.value: Gravesite, opening and closing of the grave, a grave liner, a government headstone or marker, perpetual care, and a burial flag — all at no cost to the family.
items.how: The funeral director contacts the National Cemetery Scheduling Office at 800-535-1117. Pre-need eligibility determination is available via VA Form 40-10007.
items.hack: Get a PRE-NEED eligibility determination while the veteran is alive. It takes weeks or months at time of death to establish eligibility from scratch, during which the family is making expensive decisions under pressure; a pre-need determination letter turns it into a phone call. Also: a spouse can be buried in a national cemetery even if they predecease the veteran, and even if they later remarried (if the subsequent marriage ended). And a surviving spouse who remarries does NOT lose national cemetery eligibility with the veteran. State veterans cemeteries, built with VA grants, often have residency-based eligibility and may accept a veteran when the nearest national cemetery is full.
items.deadline: None — pre-need determination recommended

items.title: Free headstone, marker, or bronze medallion for a private grave
items.who: Eligible veterans buried in ANY cemetery, including private ones.
items.value: A government headstone or marker at no cost, or — if the grave already has a privately purchased headstone — a bronze medallion affixed to it identifying the decedent as a veteran.
items.how: VA Form 40-1330 for a headstone/marker; VA Form 40-1330M for a medallion. Delivered free; the family pays only any cemetery setting fee.
items.hack: The medallion exists precisely for the family that already bought a private headstone and thought they had forfeited the benefit — you have not. Medallions come in three sizes and there is no time limit, so a family can obtain one for a veteran buried in 1975. Note the limit: spouses and dependent children buried in a PRIVATE cemetery are not eligible for their own government headstone or marker, but they can receive an inscription added to the veteran's marker at no cost — a cheaper and faster path most families never ask about. Emblems of belief include over 80 approved options.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Burial flag and Presidential Memorial Certificate
items.who: Families of eligible veterans.
items.value: A United States burial flag to drape the casket and be presented to the next of kin, and an engraved Presidential Memorial Certificate signed by the President.
items.how: Burial flag: VA Form 27-2008, available at any VA regional office, most funeral homes, and many US Post Offices. PMC: VA Form 40-0247.
items.hack: You can request MULTIPLE Presidential Memorial Certificates — VA will issue one for each close family member who wants one, and there is no time limit, so families can obtain certificates for veterans who died decades ago. The burial flag is limited to one per veteran, but if it is lost, destroyed or stolen, VA cannot replace it — so order the PMCs and consider a flag case. Any veteran buried with military funeral honors is also entitled to a flag folding and presentation plus Taps, provided by the veteran's service branch on request through the funeral director (call 877-MIL-HONR).
items.deadline: None

items.title: Medal of Honor pension: $5,780/month
items.who: Living Medal of Honor recipients.
items.value: $5,780.00 per month effective December 1, 2025, adjusted annually for COLA. Paid in addition to any other VA or military compensation.
items.how: Administered by VA upon verification of the award.
items.hack: The MOH pension is paid on top of retired pay, VA compensation, and Social Security with no offset of any kind, and it is retroactive to the date of the act for which the Medal was awarded when the award comes late. MOH recipients also receive Priority Group 1 VA health care, space-available military air travel, commissary and exchange privileges for life, and a supplemental uniform allowance.
items.deadline: None

items.title: $27,074.99 automobile allowance plus unlimited adaptive equipment
items.who: Veterans/service members with service-connected loss or permanent loss of use of one or both feet or hands, permanent impaired vision in both eyes (20/200 or worse), or severe burn injury. Ankylosis of a knee or hip qualifies for adaptive equipment only.
items.value: One-time $27,074.99 payment toward a vehicle (effective October 1, 2025), plus adaptive equipment with NO dollar cap.
items.how: VA Form 21-4502 for the allowance; VA Form 10-1394 for adaptive equipment.
items.hack: The two benefits are separate and the adaptive equipment benefit is the more valuable one over a lifetime: it has no dollar limit, it is repeatable (VA will re-equip a replacement vehicle, generally every two vehicles or when medically necessary), and it covers power lifts, hand controls, wheelchair ramps, raised roofs and custom seating that can exceed the cost of the car. Veterans with ankylosis of a knee or hip qualify for adaptive equipment even though they do not qualify for the auto allowance itself — a distinction that is almost never explained.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Clothing allowance: $1,053.19/year — and it can be paid more than once
items.who: Veterans whose service-connected condition requires a prosthetic or orthopedic appliance that wears out or tears clothing, or who use a prescribed skin medication that stains clothing.
items.value: $1,053.19 annually (effective December 1, 2025), tax-free.
items.how: VA Form 10-8678, submitted to the prosthetics office at your VA medical center. Deadline for the 2026 payment is August 1, 2026.
items.hack: You can receive MULTIPLE clothing allowances in the same year. If a knee brace damages your trousers and a shoulder brace damages your shirts, those are separate garment types affected by separate appliances and VA will pay two allowances. The same applies to multiple prescribed skin medications staining different garments. Veterans routinely receive one and never learn they qualified for two or three. Also: wheelchair use qualifies (the chair wears clothing), as do rigid braces, artificial limbs, and even certain shoe inserts.
items.deadline: August 1, 2026 for the 2026 payment

items.title: Aid & Attendance exists in two entirely different programs
items.who: Both pension recipients and service-connected compensation recipients — but through different mechanisms.
items.value: Pension A&A raises the MAPR from $17,441 to $29,093/year. Compensation-side A&A is Special Monthly Compensation (SMC), a separate and far larger set of rates paid above the 100% schedular rate — SMC-L alone pays $4,900.83/month for a veteran with no dependents (effective December 1, 2025), rising to $11,843.74/month at SMC-R.2/T with a spouse and two parents.
items.how: Pension A&A: VA Form 21-2680 (Examination for Housebound Status or Permanent Need for Regular Aid and Attendance) with the pension claim. SMC: claimed as part of a compensation claim.
items.hack: These get conflated constantly, including by claims agents. If you have a service-connected rating, do not file for 'pension Aid & Attendance' — you want Special Monthly Compensation, which pays far more and has no income or asset test at all. SMC-L through SMC-R cover loss of use, aid and attendance, and housebound status, with SMC-R/2 exceeding $10,000/month. A veteran at 100% schedular who needs help with daily activities should be screened for SMC-L at minimum.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Catastrophically disabled status wipes out copays without a rating change
items.who: Veterans determined by a VA clinician to be catastrophically disabled — a clinical determination based on functional impairment, independent of any service-connected rating.
items.value: Placement in Priority Group 4, eliminating inpatient and outpatient copays.
items.how: A VA provider makes the determination based on specified diagnostic and functional criteria (quadriplegia, persistent vegetative state, certain amputations, severe functional dependency scores).
items.hack: This is a purely CLINICAL pathway that bypasses the rating system entirely — a veteran with a 0% rating or no rating at all who is catastrophically disabled from a non-service-connected cause can land in Priority Group 4 and stop paying copays. It requires a clinician to make and document the determination, which they will not do unless asked. If you or a family member meet the functional criteria, ask your VA primary care provider directly to evaluate for catastrophic disability status.
items.deadline: None

items.title: The $700 medication copay cap resets every January 1
items.who: Veterans in Priority Groups 2–8 paying medication copays.
items.value: Once you have paid $700 in medication copays in a calendar year, all further medication copays for that year are $0.
items.how: Automatic — VA tracks the total and stops billing.
items.hack: Because the cap is per CALENDAR year, a veteran on expensive maintenance medications who hits the cap in August gets free medications from August through December, and the counter resets January 1. Where possible, ask your provider for 90-day fills (which cost 3× a 30-day fill but count 3× toward the cap) and time a large refill in December versus January deliberately. Also, Tier 0 medications — certain preventive drugs and OTC-equivalents — are always $0 and do not consume the cap; ask whether a therapeutic equivalent on Tier 0 or Tier 1 exists before accepting a Tier 3 copay.
items.deadline: Resets each January 1

items.title: VA copay debt can be waived, compromised, or repaid over time
items.who: Veterans who owe VA copay or benefit overpayment debt.
items.value: Full waiver, a reduced compromise settlement, or an extended repayment plan with no interest.
items.how: Request a waiver within 1 YEAR of the date you received your first debt letter or copay bill — VA extended this from the old 180-day window. Submit VA Form 5655 (Financial Status Report) online through the VA Debt Management Center or call 800-827-0648.
items.hack: The waiver window is now a full year, up from 180 days, and it runs from the FIRST notice letter, not the most recent one — anyone told they missed a 180-day deadline should re-check, because the longer window may still be open. Waivers are granted where collection would be against equity and good conscience — financial hardship is the usual ground, and VA's grant rate on well-documented hardship requests is substantial. Separately, a veteran whose income later falls below the VA national income threshold can request retroactive copay exemption for past years by filing an updated means test (VA Form 10-10EZR), which can eliminate old copay debt at its source rather than waiving it.
items.deadline: 1 year from the date you received the first debt letter or copay bill

items.title: Add dependents at 30% and your compensation goes up immediately
items.who: Veterans rated 30% or higher.
items.value: Additional monthly compensation for a spouse, children under 18 (or under 23 in school), and dependent parents. At 100%, a spouse and two children add several hundred dollars per month.
items.how: VA Form 21-686c for dependents, VA Form 21-674 for a school-age child 18–23. File through VA.gov.
items.hack: Retroactivity is the trap. If you add a dependent within ONE YEAR of the qualifying event (marriage, birth, adoption) VA pays retroactive to the event date. File later and you generally get paid only from the date of claim, forfeiting the interim months. Veterans who marry and file two years later lose a year of additional compensation permanently. The same one-year rule applies when a child turns 18 and enrolls in school — file Form 21-674 within a year of the school start. Conversely, REPORT divorces and children aging out promptly, because failing to do so creates an overpayment debt VA will recoup.
items.deadline: 1 year from the qualifying event for full retroactivity

items.title: Intent to File locks your effective date for a year
items.who: Anyone about to file a VA compensation or pension claim.
items.value: Preserves an effective date up to a year earlier than the eventual claim, which at 70% with a spouse is worth over $20,000 in retroactive pay.
items.how: File VA Form 21-0966 (Intent to File) online, by phone at 800-827-1000, or in person. You then have ONE YEAR to submit the complete claim, and benefits are paid retroactive to the Intent to File date.
items.hack: This is free, takes five minutes, and is the highest dollar-per-minute action in the entire VA system. File an Intent to File the moment you think you might have a claim — before you gather a single record, before you see a doctor, before you talk to a VSO. The date is what matters. The same mechanism applies to pension and to survivor benefits (DIC and Survivors Pension). Separating service members should instead use the Benefits Delivery at Discharge program, filing 180 to 90 days before separation, which can produce a rating effective the day after discharge.
items.deadline: Complete the claim within 1 year of the Intent to File

items.title: Beneficiary travel pay for VA appointments
items.who: Veterans traveling for VA care who have a 30%+ service-connected rating, are traveling for treatment of a service-connected condition, receive VA pension, have income below the maximum annual VA pension rate, or meet other specified criteria.
items.value: Mileage reimbursement at the current federal rate, plus meals and lodging for long trips, with a per-trip deductible that is capped monthly.
items.how: File within 30 days of the appointment through the Beneficiary Travel Self-Service System (BTSSS) at AccessVA, or at the travel office in the facility.
items.hack: VA accepts late claims but states they are 'usually denied,' so treat the 30 days as hard — set a recurring reminder and file from the parking lot. For veterans who travel long distances for specialty care, VA will also authorize and pay for a special mode of transportation (ambulance, wheelchair van) and for an attendant's travel and meals when medically necessary. And if you are traveling more than 30 or 60 minutes for care, that same drive time may make you eligible for Community Care instead, which eliminates the trip entirely.
items.deadline: 30 days from the appointment

items.title: Stack SAH, HISA, a VA loan and the funding fee exemption on one house
items.who: A severely disabled veteran buying or adapting a home.
items.value: Up to $126,526 (SAH) + $6,800 (HISA) in grants, plus a zero-down VA loan with the funding fee waived, plus potentially a full state property tax exemption.
items.how: Apply for SAH (VA Form 26-4555) and the VA loan concurrently; VA's SAH agents coordinate grant disbursement with the loan closing. HISA is applied for separately through the medical center's prosthetics office.
items.hack: These programs live in three different VA organizations — Loan Guaranty for SAH and the loan, VHA Prosthetics for HISA, and the county assessor for property tax — and none of them will tell you about the others. Stacking them is entirely permitted and routinely done by informed veterans: SAH funds the structural build-out, HISA funds the medically prescribed fixtures SAH will not cover, the loan finances the purchase at 0% down with no funding fee, and the state exemption eliminates the recurring tax. A 100% P&T veteran who runs all four can acquire and adapt a home for a near-zero lifetime cost of ownership.
items.deadline: Coordinate SAH before closing where possible

items.title: DoD SkillBridge — up to 180 days of civilian work on military pay
items.who: Active-duty service members within their last 180 days of service who have at least 180 days of continuous active duty and unit commander approval. Available to all branches; Guard/Reserve on Title 10 in some cases.
items.value: You keep full active-duty pay, BAH, BAS, TRICARE and benefits while working a full-time civilian internship for up to 180 days. The employer pays you nothing — DoD keeps paying you — so the internship is free labor for them and a free paid job audition for you. Effective value is 6 months of salary (median E-6 total comp ~$65-85k/yr, O-3 ~$110k+) while you interview from inside a company.
items.how: Start 12-18 months out. Find an authorized partner at skillbridge.osd.mil (Partner Program Locator, 2,000+ organizations). Get a written offer/training plan from the partner, then route a SkillBridge application with the training plan through your chain of command — approval authority is typically your first O-5/O-6 commander, and some branches require higher. Submit 6+ months before your desired start. You must have your separation/retirement date approved first.
items.hack: The partner list is not the constraint — command approval is. Two under-used moves: (1) a company not on the list can be added via a simple MOU with DoD, so you can create your own SkillBridge with a company that wants to hire you; (2) stack SkillBridge back-to-back with terminal leave — do the 180-day SkillBridge, then take terminal leave after, effectively getting 7-8 months of paid civilian work and job search.
items.deadline: Must begin with no more than 180 days remaining on your service obligation; apply 6+ months in advance.

items.title: SkillBridge approval has tightened — plan for a harder 'no'
items.who: Anyone planning a SkillBridge in 2026.
items.value: Knowing the current restrictions is what gets your packet approved instead of denied. Since 2024 the services have layered on their own limits on top of DoDI 1322.29.
items.how: Verify three things before you build your plan: (1) your branch's current SkillBridge instruction (Air Force AFI 36-2671; Navy NAVADMIN; Army and USMC MARADMIN equivalents) — these set approval level and unit-readiness caps; (2) whether your MOS/AFSC/rating is on a critical-skills or manning-shortfall exclusion list, which is the most common denial reason; (3) DoD now requires partners to submit detailed training plans and report completion and hire-rate outcomes, and periodically re-reviews approved providers — so confirm your partner is still active on the locator, not just listed in an old blog post.
items.hack: Denials are usually 'unit readiness' calls made by one commander, not policy bars. Build the packet so the commander's risk is near zero: propose a gaining-unit backfill plan, offer to remain on-call/recallable, get the partner to write the training plan in DoD's own format, and time the request so your departure lands after a major exercise or deployment cycle. If denied, you can usually reapply for a shorter window (60 or 90 days instead of 180) and get a yes.
items.deadline: Ongoing; re-verify branch guidance within 60 days of applying.

items.title: Hiring Our Heroes Corporate Fellowship — structured 12-week SkillBridge with a hiring pipeline
items.org: U.S. Chamber of Commerce Foundation — Hiring Our Heroes
items.who: Active-duty service members on terminal/transition leave who will be within 180 days of separation when the 12-week cohort begins, and who meet education and leadership requirements. Free to both the fellow and the host company.
items.value: 12-week paid-by-DoD fellowship placing you inside a major employer (Microsoft, Deloitte, Amazon, USAA and dozens more), five days a week with a two-hour professional development session each Friday. Zero cost. Operates through 12 regional hubs covering all U.S. states and territories.
items.how: Apply at hiringourheroes.org. Cohorts run roughly quarterly: 2026 Cohort 3 applications closed June 11, 2026 and run Aug 31–Nov 19, 2026; 2027 Cohort 1 deadline Oct 8, 2026 (runs Jan 11–Apr 1, 2027); 2027 Cohort 2 deadline Feb 11, 2027 (runs May 3–Jul 22, 2027). You still need your command's SkillBridge approval under DoDI 1322.29.
items.hack: This is the highest-conversion SkillBridge path because the host companies join specifically to hire — unlike ad-hoc SkillBridges where the company may have no headcount. Apply to the cohort roughly 8 months before separation so the application deadline, command approval and your 180-day window all line up. Missing a cohort deadline costs you an entire quarter.
items.deadline: Cohort application deadlines run ~4-5 months before cohort start; next deadline Oct 8, 2026 for Jan 2027 start.

items.title: Terminal leave vs. selling leave back — the math almost always favors taking the leave
items.who: Any separating or retiring service member with accrued leave.
items.value: Terminal leave pays you full base pay PLUS BAH, BAS and any special pays, and you stay on TRICARE — and you can legally work a civilian job at the same time, so you double-dip salary. Sold-back leave pays ONLY base pay (no BAH, no BAS), and is taxed as supplemental wages at a 22% federal flat withholding. For a typical E-6 with BAH, a day of terminal leave is worth roughly 1.6-2.0x a day of sold-back leave.
items.how: Decide at your final out-processing/separation counseling. You elect sell-back on your separation paperwork; terminal leave is requested as ordinary leave that runs up to your separation date. Confirm your leave balance on your LES well before you out-process.
items.hack: The double-dip is the whole game: start your civilian job (or SkillBridge) while on terminal leave and you collect two paychecks for the same weeks. Sell back only the leave you physically cannot burn before your separation date. Note the career cap: you may sell back a maximum of 60 days of leave over an entire career, so days you sold back at an earlier reenlistment are already gone from that pool.
items.deadline: Elected at separation; leave must be used by your separation date or it is lost (above the carryover cap).

items.title: The 60-day career leave sell-back cap (and the tax bite)
items.who: All service members. The cap is cumulative across an entire career, not per separation.
items.value: Up to 60 days of leave may be sold back over a career, at base pay only. Sold leave is taxed as supplemental wages — 22% federal withholding plus FICA — and does not carry BAH or BAS.
items.how: Verify how many sell-back days you have already used (prior reenlistments count against the 60). Check your LES and ask your finance office for your career sell-back history before you plan your terminal leave.
items.hack: People discover mid-separation that they burned 30 of their 60 days at a reenlistment a decade ago. Pull that number early, because it changes whether you should schedule 90 days of terminal leave or 45. Also: leave sold at separation is paid in your final settlement, which routinely takes 30-60 days after separation — do not budget as if it arrives on your last day.
items.deadline: Check before you submit separation paperwork.

items.title: Permissive TDY (PTDY) — up to 20 extra non-chargeable days for job/house hunting
items.who: Separating and retiring service members. Amounts vary by branch: commonly up to 20 days permissive TDY for retirees and up to 10 days for those separating, with longer authorizations for overseas returnees.
items.value: Non-chargeable leave — it does not come out of your accrued leave balance — specifically for job hunting and house hunting. Stack it with terminal leave to extend your paid runway by up to three weeks without spending a single leave day.
items.how: Request through your command with your separation orders; it is granted on your DD-214-generating orders. Branch-specific regulations control the number of days, so ask your career counselor or transition office for the exact authorization in writing.
items.hack: PTDY is the most-forgotten free time in the entire transition. Sequence it as: SkillBridge (180 days) → PTDY (10-20 days) → terminal leave (however much you have) → separation date. Done right, that is close to nine months of full pay and benefits while you are already working or interviewing in the civilian world.
items.deadline: Must be used before your separation date.

items.title: Transition Assistance Program (TAP) — mandatory, and the tiered tracks are where the value is
items.who: Required for service members with 180+ days of continuous active duty who are separating, retiring, or being released. You must begin no later than 365 days before separation.
items.value: Free: pre-separation counseling, a mandatory DoL Employment Fundamentals of Career Transition course, a VA Benefits and Services brief, and then a two-day elective track. Tracks: Employment, Education, Vocational (trades/credentials), and Entrepreneurship (Boots to Business).
items.how: Your command schedules you through your installation's transition office / Military and Family Readiness Center. Start at 365 days out; the capstone is a commander-verified review confirming you met Career Readiness Standards and have a viable plan (resume, budget, job offers or acceptance letters) — you cannot out-process without it.
items.hack: Most people treat TAP as a box to check and take whichever two-day track has open seats. You can request a specific track, and you can often attend more than one if you start early enough. The Entrepreneurship track (Boots to Business) is the only one that continues after you separate, into a free SBA-funded follow-on course — sign up for it even if you have no business idea, because it is the on-ramp to VBOC counseling and SBA lending relationships later.
items.deadline: Begin no later than 365 days before separation; capstone completed no later than 90 days before separation.

items.title: The TAP Capstone — use it as leverage, not a formality
items.who: All TAP participants, no later than 90 days before separation.
items.value: A commander-level verification that you have met Career Readiness Standards. If you have NOT met them, you get a warm handover to DoL or VA for continued support after separation — which is a benefit, not a punishment.
items.how: Bring your resume, 12-month post-separation budget, job application log or acceptance letter, and your individual transition plan. If you cannot meet a standard, say so — the warm handover triggers follow-on assistance.
items.hack: Deliberately declaring an unmet standard at the capstone is an underused move: it forces a documented referral to a DoL American Job Center or VA benefits advisor who will keep working your case after you are a civilian, when nobody in uniform is obligated to help you anymore.
items.deadline: No later than 90 days before separation.

items.title: Pick your separation date deliberately — it moves real money
items.who: Anyone with any flexibility on their separation or retirement date.
items.value: Separating on the 1st vs. the 30th changes your final month's pay, your BAH end date, when TAMP starts, and which tax year your leave sell-back and final settlement land in. Shifting a date by a few days can be worth thousands.
items.how: Model three scenarios with your finance office: end of month, start of month, and end of calendar year. Check: (1) BAH stops on your separation date, not the end of the month; (2) leave sell-back is taxed in the year it is PAID, and final settlements often pay 30-60 days late, so a December separation can push a large lump sum into the next tax year; (3) a separation date that starts a month means you draw a fuller final month of pay.
items.hack: If you expect a big leave sell-back and you are moving from a high-tax state to a no-income-tax state, controlling which tax year and which state of residence the payment lands in is worth more than most re-enlistment bonuses. Also confirm your state of legal residence is updated on your DD Form 2058 BEFORE the final settlement is cut.
items.deadline: Set when you submit separation/retirement paperwork — typically 6-12 months out.

items.title: TAMP — 180 days of free TRICARE after separation
items.who: Members involuntarily separated from active duty, separating after being called to active duty for more than 30 consecutive days in support of a contingency, receiving a sole-survivorship discharge, separating from active duty following a Reserve involuntary retention, or separating after voluntary agreement to stay on active duty for less than a year in support of a contingency. NOT everyone who separates qualifies.
items.value: 180 days of premium-free TRICARE coverage for you and your family beginning the day after separation. You can enroll in TRICARE Prime (if you live in a Prime Service Area) or use TRICARE Select. This is full family medical coverage worth roughly $1,200-$2,000+/month on the civilian market.
items.how: Eligibility is determined automatically from DEERS based on your separation code — verify your DEERS record shows TAMP eligibility BEFORE you separate, at a RAPIDS/ID card office. If you want Prime, you must actively enroll; you are not auto-enrolled.
items.hack: The single biggest transition healthcare mistake is assuming you have TAMP when you do not — a routine voluntary ETS at end of contract generally does NOT qualify. Check the code in DEERS while you still have someone obligated to fix it. If you are not TAMP-eligible, your coverage ends the day you separate and CHCBP is your only bridge.
items.deadline: Runs 180 days from the day after separation; verify DEERS eligibility before your separation date.

items.title: CHCBP — the 60-day-window TRICARE bridge nobody tells you about
items.who: Service members losing TRICARE eligibility, including after TAMP ends. Also available to certain former spouses and dependent children.
items.value: Coverage identical to TRICARE Select, including prescriptions. Up to 18 months for the separating member (up to 36 months for unremarried former spouses and dependent children). It is a premium program — you pay the full quarterly premium — but it is generally cheaper than an unsubsidized ACA plan and has no network gap for military families.
items.how: Enroll with Humana Military using DD Form 2837. Call 800-444-5445 or enroll via the Humana Military CHCBP site.
items.hack: The window is 60 days from loss of TRICARE eligibility — and only 30 days if you are coming off TRICARE Reserve Select. Miss it and there is no appeal and no exception. Critically, if you have TAMP, your 60-day CHCBP clock starts when TAMP ENDS (day 180), not at separation — put a calendar reminder at day 150. CHCBP also counts as creditable coverage, which matters for pre-existing-condition continuity.
items.deadline: 60 days from loss of TRICARE eligibility (30 days if losing TRICARE Reserve Select).

items.title: Your final PCS move — use it or lose it (and the clock is shorter than you think)
items.who: Separating and retiring service members entitled to a final move to a home of selection.
items.value: Government-funded shipment of household goods, plus travel allowances, to your home of selection. For a mid-career family this is commonly $8,000-$25,000+ of moving cost the government absorbs. Retirees may also store household goods at government expense for up to one year.
items.how: Arrange through your installation transportation office / MilitaryOneSource Move.mil before you separate. You must have your orders in hand.
items.hack: The default entitlement window is one year from your separation or retirement date, and it can be extended in specific circumstances — but extensions must be REQUESTED AND APPROVED IN WRITING before the deadline expires, not after. Veterans lose this benefit constantly by assuming they can move 'whenever.' Verify the current JTR deadline and extension procedure with your transportation office and get any extension in writing. Retirees generally get more favorable terms than those separating — know which one you are.
items.deadline: Generally one year from separation/retirement date; extensions must be approved before expiration. Verify current JTR rule with your transportation office.

items.title: DITY / Personally Procured Move (PPM) — keep the difference as taxable income
items.who: Any service member authorized a government-funded move, including the final move.
items.value: The government pays you 100% of what it would have cost the government to move you (the GCC). If you move yourself for less — rental truck, friends, a cheap freight service — you keep the difference. Profits of $2,000-$8,000+ on a mid-size CONUS move are common.
items.how: Get a PPM authorized through your transportation office before you move. Weigh the vehicle empty and full at a certified scale (keep both tickets — this is the single most common reason claims get denied), keep every receipt, and file the claim with DD Form 2278 and your weight tickets.
items.hack: Two levers: (1) do a partial PPM — let the government move the heavy furniture and PPM only the high-weight-per-dollar items you can move cheaply; (2) the profit is taxable income, but your legitimate moving expenses offset it, so keep receipts for fuel, tolls, boxes, truck rental, and hired labor. Also, on your FINAL move, storage entitlements run separately from the move itself, so you can PPM the move and still use government storage.
items.deadline: Weight tickets and claim must be filed per your transportation office's deadline, typically within 45 days of the move.

items.title: Benefits Delivery at Discharge (BDD) — file 180 to 90 days before you get out
items.who: Service members on full-time active duty (including Guard/Reserve on Title 10) with 180 to 90 days remaining before separation, who can attend VA exams before separation and provide a copy of their service treatment records.
items.value: Your VA disability claim is adjudicated BEFORE you separate, so compensation can begin the month after your discharge date instead of 4-12 months later. For a veteran who ends up at 50% ($1,200+/month in 2026 for a single vet, more with dependents), avoiding a 9-month backlog is roughly $10,000+ of cash you would otherwise wait for.
items.how: File at va.gov (or through a VSO) in the 180-90 day window, upload your STRs, and complete all VA exams before you separate. Between 89 and 1 days out you can still file a 'Pre-Discharge' / Quick Start claim — it just will not be decided before separation.
items.hack: The hard floor is 90 days: at 89 days out you lose BDD and drop into the slower queue. Work backward — you want your claim FILED at about day 175, which means you need your STRs assembled and your conditions documented at day 210+. Also, file for everything documented, including things that seem minor (tinnitus, mild sleep apnea symptoms, knee/back pain, migraines, GERD, skin conditions) — you cannot easily add a condition later without a nexus opinion, and an in-service record is the strongest nexus evidence that exists.
items.deadline: Must file between 180 and 90 days before separation. Hard cutoff at 90 days.

items.title: Separation Health Assessment — your single most valuable transition document
items.who: All separating service members. Required as part of separation processing.
items.value: A documented, dated medical record of every condition you have on the day you leave. It is the evidence base for every VA claim you will ever file, including ones you file 20 years from now.
items.how: Schedule it during separation processing. Bring a written list of every symptom and complaint you have ever had — joints, back, hearing, sleep, mood, skin, stomach, headaches, breathing. If you have a BDD claim in, the VA exam and the SHA can often be combined into one integrated exam.
items.hack: Be exhaustive and specific, and insist that every complaint is written into the record even if the provider thinks it is minor. 'Occasional knee pain' documented at separation is worth far more than a perfect memory ten years later. Then request a COMPLETE copy of your service treatment records — paper and electronic — before your last day, because getting them from the National Personnel Records Center afterward can take months. Scan everything to cloud storage the day you get it.
items.deadline: Completed during separation processing, typically within 90 days of separation.

items.title: DD-214 errors and how to fix them (DD Form 149)
items.org: Board for Correction of Military Records (BCMR), each service
items.who: Any veteran whose DD-214 contains an error — wrong dates, missing awards, wrong character of service, missing combat service, incorrect separation code or reenlistment code.
items.value: Your DD-214 gates almost every benefit you will ever claim: VA compensation, GI Bill, veterans' preference in federal hiring, state benefits, home loan eligibility, burial benefits. A missing campaign medal can cost you a hiring preference; a wrong separation code can cost you everything.
items.how: File DD Form 149 (Application for Correction of Military Record) with your service's Board for Correction of Military Records. Attach every supporting document — orders, award citations, performance reports, medical records. There is no fee.
items.hack: Check your DD-214 line by line on the day you receive it, while you are still on active duty and your admin shop is obligated to fix it — an on-the-spot correction takes days, while a BCMR case takes 12-18 months. The most commonly missed items are campaign/expeditionary medals (which drive veterans' preference eligibility) and combat service dates (which drive PACT Act presumptives and enhanced VA healthcare enrollment). There is a nominal 3-year filing statute of limitations but boards routinely waive it in the interest of justice, so file even if you are late.
items.deadline: Nominally 3 years from discovery of the error; waivers routinely granted.

items.title: Discharge upgrades (DD Form 293) — especially for PTSD, TBI, MST and LGBTQ separations
items.org: Discharge Review Boards / BCMRs, each service
items.who: Veterans with an Other Than Honorable, General, Bad Conduct or (via BCMR) Dishonorable discharge. Use DD Form 293 for a Discharge Review Board within 15 years of discharge; use DD Form 149 to a BCMR after 15 years or for a court-martial discharge.
items.value: An upgrade can unlock VA healthcare, disability compensation, the GI Bill, home loan eligibility and federal hiring preference — often retroactively. For a veteran who has been denied for a decade, this is frequently a six-figure lifetime swing.
