items.hack: Blue Star Museums is a genuinely large free benefit that runs every summer and almost nobody tracks — free admission for the service member and up to five family members at thousands of museums nationwide, which for a family on a summer PCS road trip is worth hundreds of dollars. It is limited to active duty (including Guard and Reserve) and their families, not all veterans. Check the participating list before you plan summer travel.
items.deadline: Blue Star Museums runs annually from Armed Forces Day through Labor Day.

items.title: Code Platoon, VetsinTech and veteran coding bootcamps
items.who: Veterans, transitioning service members and military spouses seeking software engineering and technical careers.
items.value: Code Platoon runs full-stack software engineering bootcamps for veterans and spouses, historically with living stipends for full-time students and GI Bill acceptance, and is a SkillBridge partner. VetsinTech provides free technical training, certification pathways and employer connections in software, cybersecurity and cloud. Operation Code advocates for GI Bill coverage of coding bootcamps and runs a free developer community and mentorship network.
items.how: Code Platoon: codeplatoon.org. VetsinTech: vetsintech.co. Operation Code: operationcode.org (free to join).
items.hack: The funding stack is the point: many veteran-focused bootcamps accept the GI Bill, several are SkillBridge-approved (so you attend on active-duty pay), and Code Platoon has historically layered a living stipend on top. That combination means you can complete an intensive software engineering program while still being paid — versus a civilian paying $18,000 out of pocket. Sequence it as a SkillBridge in your final 180 days and you keep your GI Bill entirely intact for later.
items.deadline: Cohort-based; align SkillBridge application with cohort start 9-12 months out.

items.title: VR&E (Chapter 31 / Veteran Readiness and Employment) — better than the GI Bill for many veterans
items.who: Veterans and service members with a service-connected disability rating of at least 10% (20% in some circumstances) and an employment handicap. Service members can apply before discharge with a memorandum rating of 20% or more.
items.value: Pays full tuition and fees with NO annual cap (unlike the Post-9/11 GI Bill's private school cap), plus books, supplies, required equipment including computers, and a monthly subsistence allowance. Also funds apprenticeships, on-the-job training, self-employment start-up (equipment, licenses, inventory) and independent living services. Entitlement is typically 48 months and does not consume your GI Bill.
items.how: Apply at va.gov using VA Form 28-1900. You are assigned a Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor who must find you entitled and develop a rehabilitation plan with you.
items.hack: This is the most valuable and most misunderstood education benefit in the system. Three things: (1) it does NOT use up your Post-9/11 GI Bill, so you can do a bachelor's on Chapter 31 and a master's on the GI Bill; (2) tuition is uncapped, so for an expensive private university or a graduate program it dramatically outperforms the GI Bill; (3) the self-employment track will actually buy equipment and fund a business plan for a veteran whose disability makes conventional employment unsuitable, which is a direct business-funding path almost nobody knows exists. Apply even at 10% — entitlement turns on employment handicap, not rating percentage.
items.deadline: Generally must apply within 12 years of separation or notification of service-connected rating, though extensions are available for serious employment handicaps.

items.title: State veteran benefits — the second system nobody reads
items.org: State departments of veterans affairs (all 50 states plus territories)
items.who: Veterans who are legal residents of the state. Requirements vary enormously — some states require wartime service, a minimum disability rating, or residency at the time of enlistment.
items.value: Varies dramatically but frequently includes: property tax exemptions (in several states a 100% disabled veteran pays ZERO property tax for life, worth $3,000-$12,000+ per year); free or reduced state college tuition for veterans and often their dependents; free hunting and fishing licenses; free or discounted state park access; state income tax exclusions on military retired pay and VA compensation; veteran-designated driver's licenses; state veterans homes; and county-level emergency relief funds.
items.how: Start at your state department of veterans affairs website and your COUNTY Veterans Service Officer, who is a paid government employee whose job is to know exactly these benefits for your county.
items.hack: The property tax exemption is the single largest dollar benefit available to disabled veterans in the United States and it is administered at the county level, is never automatic, and is frequently missed. In states like Texas, Florida and Virginia a 100% service-connected veteran can have their entire primary-residence property tax eliminated permanently — that is often worth more annually than the state's entire remaining benefit package combined. File it with your county appraisal district or assessor the moment your rating is granted, and ask whether it can be applied retroactively to the effective date of your rating. Also: where you establish residency at separation can be worth tens of thousands over a lifetime.
items.deadline: Property tax exemptions typically have annual filing deadlines set by county; file immediately upon receiving a rating.

items.title: Veterans Expeditions and veteran outdoor adventure organizations
items.org: Veterans Expeditions and similar outdoor nonprofits
items.who: Veterans and service members of all eras, typically with no disability requirement.
items.value: Free or low-cost mountaineering, climbing, backcountry skiing and wilderness trips designed around veteran peer cohorts, with gear and instruction typically provided.
items.how: Check the organization's current site for scheduled trips and application process. Because the veteran outdoor nonprofit space is fragmented and organizations come and go, also check Sierra Club Military Outdoors, Outward Bound for Veterans, Higher Ground, and the VA Adaptive Sports Grant recipient list for currently funded programs in your area.
items.hack: Treat this whole category as a portfolio rather than betting on one organization — small veteran outdoor nonprofits are chronically underfunded and several have quietly folded or merged in recent years. The durable, verified anchors are Outward Bound for Veterans, Sierra Club Military Outdoors, Project Healing Waters and the VA-funded adaptive sports grantees. Verify any smaller organization is currently running trips before you plan around it.
items.deadline: Trip-dependent; verify organization status before planning.

items.title: AMVETS, MOAA and choosing the right VSO for your situation
items.org: AMVETS; Military Officers Association of America; Military Order of the Purple Heart; Vietnam Veterans of America
items.who: Veterans seeking free accredited claims representation. Each organization's service officers will represent any veteran, member or not.
items.value: All maintain VA-accredited National Service Officers who file and appeal claims for free. AMVETS runs HEAL (Healthcare Evaluation and Legislative) teams providing free claims help and a focus on toxic exposure. MOAA provides members with career transition services, financial counseling and strong legislative advocacy, and is the primary advocate behind the GUARD Act claim-shark fight. Military Order of the Purple Heart serves combat-wounded veterans. Vietnam Veterans of America has deep expertise in Agent Orange and toxic exposure claims.
items.how: Find accredited representatives through the VA OGC accreditation search at va.gov, or contact each organization directly. Appoint one with VA Form 21-22.
items.hack: Match the organization to your claim type rather than picking the nearest office. Toxic exposure and PACT Act claims: VVA or AMVETS. Catastrophic disability, SMC and TDIU: PVA. Combat-wounded and Purple Heart issues: MOPH. General claims with the densest office network: DAV, VFW or American Legion. And you can CHANGE your representative at any time by filing a new 21-22 — veterans routinely stay with a representative who is not serving them well because they think the appointment is permanent. It is not.
items.deadline: Rolling; representation can be changed at any time with a new VA Form 21-22.

items.title: VA entitlement math: $36,000 basic + bonus entitlement and the 25% guaranty rule
items.who: Any veteran, service member or eligible surviving spouse using a VA-backed purchase loan.
items.value: Basic entitlement is $36,000 (statutory). For loans over $144,000 VA guarantees up to 25% of the loan amount via 'bonus' (Tier 2) entitlement, which is pegged to the FHFA one-unit conforming loan limit for the county. With full entitlement there is no loan cap at all — the 25% guaranty follows the loan.
items.how: Lenders want guaranty + down payment to equal at least 25% of the loan. With full entitlement, VA's 25% guaranty satisfies that by itself, so $0 down. VA states: 'For a loan that's more than $144,000, we guarantee to your lender that we'll pay up to 25% of the loan amount.'
items.hack: The $36,000 figure is nearly meaningless on its own in 2026 — it only binds on loans of $144,000 or less. What actually constrains you is 25% of the county one-unit limit MINUS entitlement already charged. Loan officers who quote '$36,000 of entitlement' to a borrower buying a $600,000 house are reading a 1980s script.
items.deadline: None. Entitlement does not expire.

items.title: Computing remaining entitlement when you already have a VA loan outstanding (VA's own worked example)
items.who: Veterans who already have one VA loan outstanding and want a second, or who had a VA loan foreclose/short-sell without restoration.
items.value: VA's published example: $50,000 of entitlement already used, county One-Unit Limit $900,000. $900,000 x 25% = $225,000. $225,000 - $50,000 = $175,000 remaining bonus entitlement. $175,000 x 4 = $700,000 maximum zero-down loan.
items.how: Pull the county One-Unit Limit from FHFA's conforming loan limit table (use the One-Unit column even for a duplex/triplex/fourplex). Multiply by 0.25, subtract entitlement already charged as shown on the COE, then multiply the remainder by 4.
items.hack: Above that ceiling you are NOT shut out — you put down 25% of the excess only. On a $780,000 purchase in the example above, the down payment is 25% x ($780,000 - $700,000) = $20,000, not 25% of $780,000. Most veterans (and many LOs) think partial entitlement means a full conventional down payment. It does not.
items.deadline: County limits reset each January 1 with the FHFA announcement.

items.title: 2026 conforming loan limit: $832,750 — and why it still matters on a VA loan
items.who: Veterans with partial (used) entitlement; anyone computing second-tier entitlement in 2026.
items.value: 2026 baseline one-unit conforming loan limit is $832,750 (up $26,250, +3.26% over 2025). High-cost-area ceiling is $1,249,125. Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands: baseline $1,249,125, ceiling $1,873,675.
items.how: VA adopts the FHFA one-unit limit for the county as the base for bonus entitlement (VA Circular 26-25-10 announced the 2026 figures). $832,750 x 25% = $208,187.50 of bonus entitlement in a baseline county.
items.hack: Full-entitlement VA loans have no cap — but the moment you have a second loan, a prior foreclosure, or an unrestored entitlement, the county limit becomes the binding constraint. In a high-cost county the same veteran has $312,281 of bonus entitlement instead of $208,188 — a $416,000 difference in zero-down buying power purely from geography.
items.deadline: Effective for loans closed on or after January 1, 2026.

items.title: How to read the entitlement codes on your Certificate of Eligibility (codes 01–11)
items.who: Every VA borrower. The COE is the single document that determines your cap and your funding fee.
items.value: The COE shows an entitlement code (01 = WWII, 02 = Korean, 03 = post-Korean, 04 = Vietnam, 05 = entitlement previously used and RESTORED, 06 = surviving spouse, 07 = Public Health Service, 08 = pre-WWII, 09 = post-WWII, 10 = Persian Gulf and later, 11 = selected reserve), plus 'Entitlement Code', 'Entitlement Charged to Previous VA Loans', and funding-fee exemption status.
items.how: Order the COE through the eBenefits/VA.gov portal, through your lender via the Web LGY system (usually instant), or by mailing VA Form 26-1880.
items.hack: Code 05 is the tell. It means you have already burned your one-time restoration-without-sale. If you see 05 on a COE, that veteran can never again restore entitlement while keeping a VA-financed home — they must sell and pay off. Read it before you write the offer, not after. Also check the 'Entitlement Charged to Previous VA Loans' dollar figure — that is the number you subtract in the partial-entitlement formula, and it is frequently stale after a payoff.
items.deadline: None, but a stale COE (pre-payoff) will underquote your buying power.

items.title: VA Form 26-1880 — the paper COE request, and the payoff evidence VA actually wants
items.who: Veterans whose COE cannot be auto-issued: prior VA loans, prior foreclosure, restoration requests, reserve/guard service, or discharge-record problems.
items.value: Free. Form 26-1880 (Request for a Certificate of Eligibility). Items 13A ('Have you used the VA home loan program before?') and 13B ('Do you still own any of the homes you used the VA home loan program for?') drive everything downstream.
items.how: Attach proof the prior VA loan is paid in full: a paid-in-full letter from the former servicer, a recorded satisfaction/release of mortgage from the county clerk, or the HUD-1 / Closing Disclosure from the sale or refinance. VA's instructions explicitly note many counties post the satisfaction of mortgage online for free.
items.hack: Do not wait for the servicer. Pull the recorded satisfaction of mortgage yourself off the county recorder's website, attach it to the 26-1880, and you can cut weeks off restoration. Veterans have sold, restored entitlement and closed on a new home the same day when the payoff evidence was already in hand.
items.deadline: No deadline, but process it before you go under contract.

items.title: One-time restoration of entitlement without selling the house (Items 14D/15D/16D on Form 26-1880)
items.who: A veteran who paid off a VA loan in full but still owns that home and wants to use VA financing again.
items.value: Full restoration of the entitlement charged to that loan — once per lifetime. Turns a paid-off rental into a free-and-clear asset while you buy the next home with $0 down.
items.how: On VA Form 26-1880, answer 13A yes and 13B yes, then check 'ONE-TIME RESTORATION' at item 14D, 15D or 16D for the specific prior loan, and attach the payoff evidence. VA's instruction text: 'If you have paid off your VA loan, but still own the home purchased with that loan, you may apply for a one-time only restoration of your entitlement in order to purchase another home.' You must have satisfied the original occupancy requirement at closing — continued occupancy through payoff is not required.
items.hack: This is the single highest-leverage move in the VA program for a veteran with a low-balance older loan. Pay off the small remaining balance (cash, HELOC, 401k loan, family loan), restore full entitlement, buy the new primary residence at $0 down, and keep the first house as a rental. Once used, your COE is permanently flagged (entitlement code 05) and you can never do it again — so spend it on the biggest purchase, not the first one.
items.deadline: None, but it is one use, ever.

items.title: Restoration after sale and payoff — including same-day sell-and-buy
items.who: Any veteran selling a VA-financed home and buying another.
items.value: 100% of entitlement charged to the prior loan comes back once ownership transfers AND the loan is paid in full. Both conditions must be met — a sale where the buyer assumes the loan does NOT restore entitlement.
items.how: Submit VA Form 26-1880 (or have the lender request restoration through Web LGY) with the settlement statement showing the payoff. Experienced VA lenders routinely run restoration and the new COE in the same business day when a sale and purchase close back to back.
items.hack: The two failure modes: (1) the buyer assumes your VA loan instead of paying it off — your entitlement stays tied up until they pay it off or a veteran substitutes entitlement; (2) a short sale or deed-in-lieu where VA pays a claim — entitlement stays charged until you reimburse VA the claim amount. Ask the listing agent, in writing, whether the buyer is assuming or paying off. It changes your next purchase by six figures.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Two VA loans at the same time — when it is allowed and exactly how much you can borrow
items.who: Veterans PCSing, relocating for work, or converting a current home to a rental while buying a new primary residence.
items.value: Legal and routine. Remaining bonus entitlement = (county One-Unit Limit x 25%) - entitlement charged to the outstanding loan. Multiply by 4 for the zero-down ceiling; above that, put down 25% of the excess.
items.how: Keep loan #1 outstanding, order a fresh COE showing the charged entitlement, and document occupancy intent on the new property. Lenders will also want the old property's rental income (usually a signed lease plus proof of a security deposit) or enough income to carry both.
items.hack: The order of operations matters. If you refinance loan #1 into a conventional loan BEFORE closing loan #2, you free up 100% of entitlement and get no-limit, $0-down buying power on the new house. If rates make that a bad trade, keep the VA loan and eat the partial-entitlement math. Run both scenarios before you list.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Occupancy: the statute lets your SPOUSE or DEPENDENT CHILD satisfy it for you (38 U.S.C. 3704(c))
items.who: Active-duty service members who cannot personally occupy — deployed, at a school house, on an unaccompanied tour, or hospitalized.
items.value: Statutory occupancy relief. 38 U.S.C. 3704(c) is satisfied if 'the spouse of the veteran occupies or intends to occupy the property as a home and the spouse makes the certification required,' or if 'a dependent child of the veteran occupies or will occupy the property as a home and the veteran's attorney-in-fact or legal guardian of the dependent child makes the certification.'
items.how: The occupying spouse signs the occupancy certification at application and at closing. For a dependent child, the veteran's attorney-in-fact or the child's legal guardian signs. The statute's standard is that the veteran intends to move in 'within a reasonable time' — lenders treat that as 60 days, but the 60 days is lender/VA policy, not the statute.
items.hack: Deployed service members are told constantly that they cannot buy. Wrong. A spouse-occupancy certification plus a power of attorney (get a VA-specific POA, not a general one — many lenders reject general POAs on VA files) closes the loan. Do the POA at the base legal office before you deploy; it costs nothing and expires with your orders.
items.deadline: Certification signed at application and again at closing.

items.title: The 60-day occupancy rule, what an extension requires, and the PCS exception
items.who: Every VA purchase borrower; especially those with a pending PCS, retirement, or a home under construction.
items.value: VA's working standard is occupancy within 60 days of closing as a 'reasonable time.' Extensions beyond 60 days (up to 12 months in practice) are available when the veteran certifies a specific future date and the delay is documented — new construction, major repairs, or a known separation/retirement date.
items.how: The borrower signs an occupancy certification. For an extension, the file documents the reason and the veteran certifies the specific date occupancy will begin. Veterans separating or retiring may certify intent to occupy after their release date.
items.hack: Two things blow up occupancy files: (1) using a VA loan on a home you never intend to live in — that is loan fraud, not a gray area; (2) signing a 12-month lease on the new property before closing. VA has no minimum stay after you move in; the requirement is honest intent at closing, not a sentence. Move in, live there, and if life changes in a year you are clean.
items.deadline: 60 days from closing absent a documented extension.

items.title: VA loan assumption mechanics — 0.5% funding fee, $300 processing cap, 45-day clock (Circular 26-23-10)
items.who: Anyone buying a home with an existing VA loan — including non-veterans. Every VA loan closed after March 1, 1988 is assumable with lender/VA approval.
items.value: Assume the seller's note rate. Funding fee on an assumption is 0.5% of the loan balance, collected at closing and NOT financeable. Servicer processing fee is capped at $300 with automatic authority, $250 where VA prior approval is required, and $50 for unrestricted transfers (record update only). A $50 refund is required if the request is disapproved after 60 days.
items.how: Buyer applies to the current servicer, who underwrites to VA credit standards. Servicers with automatic authority have 45 days to decide; prior-approval cases must be submitted to VA within 35 days. Documents are uploaded to VALERI as 'Release of Liability' type.
items.hack: This is the most valuable and least understood play in residential real estate right now. A 2020-2021 vintage VA loan at 2.25%-3.0% assumed in a 6%+ market is worth hundreds of thousands in lifetime interest — and the 0.5% assumption fee replaces a full 2.15%-3.3% funding fee. The catch is the equity gap: the buyer must bring cash or a second lien for the difference between price and loan balance. Non-veterans CAN assume. Market the assumability in the MLS remarks; most listing agents don't.
items.deadline: Servicer must decide within 45 days (automatic authority) or submit to VA within 35 days (prior approval).

items.title: The assumption entitlement trap — the seller's benefit stays hostage unless a veteran substitutes entitlement
items.who: Any veteran letting someone assume their VA loan.
items.value: Avoids a six-figure mistake. Without substitution of entitlement, the selling veteran's entitlement remains encumbered for the life of that loan — even after release of personal liability, even after the veteran no longer owns the house.
items.how: Two different things must happen, and they are separate: (1) release of liability (protects your credit if the assumer defaults); (2) substitution of entitlement (frees your VA benefit). Substitution requires the assumer to be an eligible veteran who has and is willing to pledge their own entitlement, using VA Form 26-8106.
items.hack: Price it. If you let a non-veteran assume your 2.5% loan, you have effectively sold your VA entitlement along with the house — and you will be doing 25%-down math on your next purchase for the next 25 years. Either (a) demand a premium for the assumption, (b) market specifically to veteran buyers who will substitute entitlement, or (c) sell conventionally and restore. A listing agent who understands this earns their commission twice.
items.deadline: Must be arranged at assumption closing; cannot be fixed afterward.

items.title: The three assumption forms nobody names correctly: 26-8106, 26-6382 and 26-6381
items.who: Sellers, buyers, agents and servicers processing a VA assumption.
items.value: Getting the right form on the right party is the difference between a released, restored seller and a seller still on the hook.
items.how: VA Form 26-8106 — Statement of Veteran Assuming GI Loan: signed by a VETERAN assumer who is substituting their entitlement. VA Form 26-6382 — Statement of Purchaser or Owner Assuming Seller's Loan: signed by a NON-veteran assumer. VA Form 26-6381 — Application for Assumption Approval and/or Release From Personal Liability to the Government on a Home Loan: the release-of-liability application itself (OMB 2900-0110). VA Form 26-6807 is the credit statement used in the package.
items.hack: Ask the servicer to confirm in writing which forms went into the VALERI upload. Servicers routinely process the assumption (26-6382) and never process the release (26-6381), leaving the veteran personally liable on a loan they don't own. Get the executed release of liability in your closing file before you hand over the keys.
items.deadline: Submit with the assumption package; release cannot be granted retroactively without VA action.

items.title: Divorce and the VA loan: spousal transfers don't require a full assumption
items.who: Divorcing couples where one spouse keeps a VA-financed home.
items.value: Avoids an unnecessary assumption underwrite and fee when a decree awards the property to the veteran whose entitlement is already on the loan.
items.how: VA Circular 26-23-10: 'spousal releases don't require full assumptions when dissolving marriage/legal separation awards property to the encumbered veteran.' The servicer processes a release of the non-obligated spouse rather than a full assumption package.
items.hack: The reverse case is the dangerous one. If the decree awards the home to the NON-veteran ex-spouse and they simply keep paying, the veteran's entitlement stays charged and the veteran stays liable. The fix is a real assumption with release of liability (26-6381 + 26-6382), or a refinance out of the VA loan. Put that obligation, with a deadline, in the decree.
items.deadline: Address it in the divorce decree; retroactive fixes require the ex-spouse's cooperation.

items.title: Using projected rental income on a 2–4 unit VA purchase: reserves and landlord experience
items.who: Veterans buying a duplex, triplex or fourplex and occupying one unit.
items.value: Projected rent from the non-occupied units can be counted as qualifying income — but only if you clear two gates.
items.how: VA's own credit-standards guidance states the principle plainly: 'if the Veteran can support the mortgage payment without using rental income then landlord experience and cash reserves are not required.' Where rental income IS needed to qualify, VA Lender's Handbook Chapter 4 requires (a) documented prior experience managing rental units and (b) cash reserves — commonly applied by lenders as six months of PITI. Income is typically taken at 75% of market rent from the appraiser's rent schedule (Form 1007/216).
items.hack: The reserve and experience tests only bite if you NEED the rent to qualify. Structure the file so you qualify on W-2 income alone with the rents excluded, and the landlord-experience requirement disappears entirely — which is how a first-time landlord buys a fourplex with zero down. If you do need the rent, get a signed lease and a copy of the deposited security deposit before underwriting, not after.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: On a 2–4 unit VA purchase, entitlement is computed off the ONE-UNIT county limit
items.who: Veterans with partial entitlement buying multi-unit property.
items.value: Prevents a nasty surprise at underwriting. VA instructs borrowers to 'use the One-Unit Limit, even if your property has more than one unit.'
items.how: Fourplex in a baseline 2026 county: bonus entitlement base is $832,750 (not the 4-unit conforming limit of ~$1.6M). With full entitlement there is no cap and this is moot; with partial entitlement, the one-unit limit sets the zero-down ceiling.
items.hack: Full entitlement + fourplex is the single most powerful zero-down play in American real estate, because VA imposes no loan cap on a full-entitlement borrower even though the entitlement math would have used the one-unit number. Burn your entitlement on a fourplex FIRST, while it is full, not on a starter condo.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA construction loans: one-time close vs two-time close, formal escrows, and the 2% construction fee (Circular 26-18-7)
items.who: Veterans building a new home on land they own or are buying.
items.value: Zero-down construction-to-permanent financing. Maximum loan = lesser of VA reasonable value or acquisition cost, PLUS energy-efficiency improvements up to $6,000, PLUS the funding fee.
items.how: VA recognizes both one-time (single) close and two-time close structures. 'VA requires the use of formal escrows.' Lenders may charge a construction fee of up to 2% only if they disburse at least 51% of proceeds during actual construction. Funding fee is due within 15 days of closing; the lender must report to VA within 60 days of a clear final compliance inspection, and VA does not issue the guaranty until that clear final inspection is received.
items.hack: Builder registration was the historic bottleneck; VA Circular 26-25-1 (March 31, 2025) rescinded the builder VA identification number requirement for certain guaranteed loans, which widened the builder pool considerably. If a lender tells you 'your builder isn't VA-approved,' ask them specifically about 26-25-1 — many shops are still running 2018 checklists.
items.deadline: Funding fee due within 15 days of closing; lender report within 60 days of clear final inspection.

items.title: VA Energy Efficient Mortgage: roll up to $6,000 of upgrades into the loan with no extra down payment
items.who: Any VA purchase or IRRRL borrower. Works on refinances too.
items.value: Up to $6,000 added to the loan amount for energy improvements. VA does not permit EEMs above $6,000.
items.how: Up to $3,000: documentation of cost alone is sufficient. $3,000–$6,000: itemized bids or contracts, plus lender certification that projected monthly energy savings exceed the increased monthly cost. Eligible: solar, insulation, weather stripping, storm windows, vapor barriers, heat pumps — permanent fixtures that cut energy use. Not eligible: hot tubs, spas, appliances, new construction, non-permanent fixtures. Work must generally be completed within six months of closing, with funds held in escrow until the lender verifies completion.
items.hack: On an IRRRL this is free money with no appraisal and no income documentation in most cases — but note: if the new EEM payment exceeds the old payment by 20% or more, the lender must verify the borrower qualifies for the higher payment. Stay under 20% and the streamline stays streamlined. Also: EEM dollars sit on top of the appraised value, so a home that appraised exactly at contract price can still absorb $6,000 of solar.
items.deadline: Improvements generally completed within 6 months of closing.

items.title: Circular 26-25-7 — home energy efficiency ratings can now help you qualify
items.who: Veterans buying homes with a HERS rating, ENERGY STAR certification or similar documented efficiency rating.
items.value: VA issued Circular 26-25-7 (September 22, 2025), 'The Effect of Certain Home Energy Efficiency Ratings on VA Underwriting Decisions,' clarifying how an energy rating may be used in the underwriting decision.
items.how: Ask the seller or builder for the HERS/ENERGY STAR documentation and give it to the underwriter at submission, alongside any EEM request.
items.hack: This matters most on residual-income-tight files. Documented low utility costs are exactly the kind of evidence that supports an exception when the file is over 41% DTI. Pair a HERS report with a $6,000 EEM and you can move a marginal file to an approval.
items.deadline: Effective for loans underwritten after September 22, 2025.

items.title: VA renovation (Alteration & Repair) loans — real, but only a handful of lenders offer them
items.who: Veterans buying a home that needs work, or who want to finance repairs into a purchase.
items.value: Repair costs are financed into the purchase loan and the appraisal is made subject to completion (as-improved value), so you are not limited to the as-is value. Zero down still applies.
items.how: Same guaranty rules as a purchase loan; VA requires formal escrows for the repair funds and a clear final compliance inspection before the guaranty issues. Repairs must be to the existing structure and completed by an approved contractor within the lender's timeline.
items.hack: The binding constraint is lender appetite, not VA policy. A very small number of VA lenders actually run A&R files, and they often cap repairs well below what VA allows. Call three VA renovation lenders before you write the offer, and get the repair cap in writing — a dead A&R file at day 25 costs you the house. If nobody will do it, the fallback is a conventional 203(k)-style product for the purchase plus a VA cash-out refinance later.
items.deadline: None; escrowed repairs typically must finish within 6 months.

items.title: IRRRL seasoning: 210 days AND six consecutive monthly payments (38 U.S.C. 3709)
items.who: Any veteran refinancing an existing VA loan with a streamline IRRRL.
items.value: Statutory anti-churning protection. VA will not guarantee the IRRRL until the LATER of: the date the borrower has made at least six consecutive monthly payments, and 210 days after the FIRST PAYMENT DUE DATE of the loan being refinanced.
items.how: Count from the first payment due date, not the closing date. VA Circular 26-19-22 states the first payment due date must be 210 days or more prior to the IRRRL closing date and six consecutive monthly payments must have been made.
items.hack: The number people get wrong is which date starts the 210-day clock. Closing on June 1 means the first payment is due August 1 — so the earliest IRRRL closing is roughly late February, not late December. If a loan officer calls you at month five offering a streamline, they are either wrong or planning to close late; get the projected closing date in writing.
items.deadline: Earliest eligible IRRRL closing = later of 6 payments made or first-payment-due-date + 210 days.

items.title: The IRRRL fee recoupment rule: all fees must be recouped within 36 months
items.who: Any IRRRL borrower.
items.value: Statutory consumer protection: 'all of the fees and incurred costs are scheduled to be recouped on or before the date that is 36 months after the date of loan issuance' through the reduction in monthly payments.
items.how: Recoupment = total fees and incurred costs divided by the monthly payment reduction. If the quotient exceeds 36, the loan cannot be guaranteed. VA Circular 26-19-22 measures the recoupment period from the date of loan closing. Where the new payment is the same or higher (e.g., ARM-to-fixed or a term reduction), the veteran must incur NO fees, closing costs or expenses other than taxes and escrow.
items.hack: Ask for the recoupment worksheet, not the 'monthly savings' flyer. Lenders pad the loan amount with financed costs and still pass at 34-35 months. If your recoupment is 33+ months you are being sold a rate that barely clears the statutory floor — shop it. And if the payment isn't dropping, you should be paying literally nothing.
items.deadline: 36 months from loan issuance/closing.

items.title: IRRRL net tangible benefit: 50 bps fixed-to-fixed, 200 bps fixed-to-ARM — plus the discount point/LTV trap
items.who: IRRRL borrowers and their lenders.
items.value: Statutory minimum rate reductions: fixed-to-fixed must drop at least 50 basis points; fixed-to-adjustable must drop at least 200 basis points.
items.how: Discount points may be added to principal only if: (a) points of 1.0 or less and the resulting LTV stays at or below 100%; or (b) points greater than 1.0 and the resulting LTV stays at or below 90%.
items.hack: The 200-basis-point fixed-to-ARM rule is the one that catches people. A lender offering to move you from a 6.5% fixed to a 5.0% ARM cannot do it as an IRRRL — that is only 150 bps. And if they want to finance more than one discount point, your loan must come in at 90% LTV or less, which on a streamline means an appraisal you weren't expecting. Ask 'are you financing more than one point?' before you lock.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA cash-out refinance: Type I vs Type II, the eight net tangible benefit tests, and the double disclosure
items.who: Veterans refinancing into a VA cash-out loan, including refinancing a non-VA loan into VA.
items.value: Type I: new loan amount (including the VA funding fee) does NOT exceed the payoff. Type II: new loan amount (including funding fee) EXCEEDS the payoff. Type II carries the stricter cost tests.
items.how: The refinance must pass at least one of eight net tangible benefit tests: (1) eliminates monthly mortgage insurance; (2) shorter loan term; (3) lower interest rate; (4) lower monthly P&I; (5) increases the veteran's monthly residual income; (6) pays off an interim construction loan; (7) LTV of 90% or less; (8) converts an ARM to a fixed rate. Seasoning: the first payment must have been made 210+ days before closing AND six monthly payments completed. Lenders must deliver a loan comparison disclosure TWICE — within 3 business days of application and again at closing — with the borrower certifying receipt.
items.hack: Two things. First, financing the funding fee can push you over the value ceiling — VA will not guarantee above 100% LTV and the financed funding fee 'cannot cause the loan to exceed the reasonable value of the property.' Second, if you didn't get the loan comparison disclosure at BOTH application and closing, the file is out of compliance; that is real leverage in a dispute with a lender who churned you.
items.deadline: Disclosure within 3 business days of application and again at closing.

items.title: VA residual income: the actual dollar tables by region and family size (38 CFR 36.4340)
items.who: Every VA borrower. This is the test that makes VA loans approve where conventional loans die.
items.value: For loan amounts of $80,000 and above — Family of 1: Northeast $450, Midwest $441, South $441, West $491. Family of 2: $755 / $738 / $738 / $823. Family of 3: $909 / $889 / $889 / $990. Family of 4: $1,025 / $1,003 / $1,003 / $1,117. Family of 5: $1,062 / $1,039 / $1,039 / $1,158. Add $80 per additional member up to a 7-person household. For loans of $79,999 and below the figures are lower (family of 4: $888 NE / $868 MW / $868 S / $967 W; add $75 per additional member).
items.how: Residual income = gross monthly income minus taxes, minus the proposed PITI, minus all recurring debts, minus job-related childcare, minus a maintenance-and-utilities figure computed from the home's square footage. The remainder must meet or exceed the table amount for your region and family size.
items.hack: These tables have not been indexed in decades, which is exactly why they are so easy to clear on paper — and why VA loans have historically had strong performance. Know your number before you shop: if your household of four in the West needs $1,117 of residual and you're clearing $2,400, you have room for a materially larger payment than a conventional underwriter would allow at the same DTI.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: The 41% DTI guideline is not a cap — the 20% residual income override
items.who: Veterans whose debt-to-income ratio exceeds 41%.
items.value: 'The standard is 41 percent or less.' But when DTI exceeds 41% AND residual income exceeds the applicable table figure by at least 20%, 'the second level review and statement of justification are not required.'
items.how: Compute residual income first. If you are at 120% or more of your table number, the over-41% DTI does not require a supervisory write-up. If you are between 100% and 120%, the file needs a supervisor's statement of justification documenting compensating factors.
items.hack: This is the single most misapplied rule in VA lending. Loan officers deny at 42% DTI because their internal overlay stops there — but VA's own regulation blesses a 55%+ DTI file with 120% residual income and no extra paperwork. If you are told 'VA caps at 41%,' that is a lender overlay, not a VA rule. Take the file to a true VA shop and ask them to run the residual income test.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Grossing up tax-free income (VA disability, DIC, some retirement) — real buying power, routinely missed
items.org: Lender practice under VA underwriting guidelines
items.who: Veterans receiving VA disability compensation, surviving spouses receiving DIC, and anyone with documented non-taxable income.
items.value: Non-taxable income can be grossed up for the DTI calculation — commonly 25%, though the percentage varies by lender. $2,000/month of tax-free VA compensation becomes $2,500 of qualifying income, which in a worked example drops DTI from 45% to 36%.
items.how: Provide the VA benefit summary/award letter showing the monthly compensation amount and that it will continue for at least three years. The lender documents the non-taxable status and applies its gross-up factor in the DTI calculation only.
items.hack: Two things every veteran should know. (1) Ask the loan officer directly: 'Are you grossing up my VA compensation, and at what percentage?' Many automated systems do not do it unless the income is coded correctly, and a 25% gross-up on a $3,500/month 100% rating is $875/month of phantom qualifying income. (2) The gross-up applies to DTI ONLY — it is NOT used in the residual income calculation, where VA wants the actual cash. A lender who grosses up in the residual calc has made an error that can kill the file at audit. CONFIDENCE NOTE: the specific 25% factor is lender practice; VA's Lender's Handbook Chapter 4 is served through a JavaScript portal and the exact current handbook language could not be machine-verified for 2026.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: The childcare statement — a required VA document that quietly shrinks your residual income
items.who: Every VA borrower with dependent children; both working and non-working households.
items.value: VA requires a signed statement about job-related childcare expenses, because childcare is a direct deduction from residual income.
items.how: Borrowers with children typically sign a statement either itemizing the monthly cost of job-related childcare or certifying that no childcare expense is incurred (e.g., a stay-at-home spouse, school-age children with no after-care, or family providing care at no cost).
items.hack: If nobody pays for childcare, say so explicitly and in writing at the start of underwriting. Underwriters who don't have the statement will sometimes impute an estimated childcare figure, and on a tight residual-income file that imputation is the difference between an approval and a denial. This is a one-page document that moves real dollars. CONFIDENCE NOTE: described from VA underwriting practice; exact handbook wording not machine-verified for 2026.
items.deadline: Provide at underwriting.

items.title: VA sets no minimum credit score — every score floor you hear is a lender overlay
items.who: Veterans with thin, damaged or nonexistent credit.
items.value: VA's regulation and handbook evaluate credit through satisfactory payment history and residual income, not a FICO cut-off. Lender floors of 580, 620 or 640 are overlays that individual lenders impose to sell loans into Ginnie Mae pools.
items.how: Shop at least three VA-focused lenders and ask each, explicitly: 'What is your minimum FICO overlay on a VA purchase, and do you do manual underwrites?' Manual underwriting (with alternative trade lines — rent, utilities, insurance, phone) is how thin-file veterans get approved.
items.hack: The tell that you are talking to an overlay shop: they quote a score minimum before they ask about residual income. A lender that does true manual underwriting will ask about your rent history and your residual income first. CalVet, for instance, publicly states no minimum credit score and uses manual underwriting. CONFIDENCE NOTE: the absence of a VA score minimum is well established; the precise handbook language could not be machine-verified because VA's Lender's Handbook is served through a JavaScript portal.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Bankruptcy, foreclosure and short sale seasoning on a VA loan
items.who: Veterans rebuilding after a Chapter 7, Chapter 13, foreclosure, short sale or deed in lieu.
items.value: VA's seasoning periods are materially shorter than conventional. General standards: Chapter 7 — 2 years from discharge (1 year with strong re-established credit and documented extenuating circumstances); Chapter 13 — as little as 12 months of satisfactory plan payments with trustee/court approval, without waiting for discharge; foreclosure, short sale or deed in lieu — generally 2 years.
items.how: Provide the discharge order or trustee payment history, a letter of explanation, and evidence of re-established credit. A foreclosure on a prior VA loan additionally requires dealing with the entitlement charged to that loan.
items.hack: The entitlement consequence is the part people miss. If VA paid a claim on your foreclosed VA loan, that entitlement stays charged until you repay VA the claim amount — but you can still buy again using REMAINING bonus entitlement with a partial down payment, well before you have paid the debt. Many veterans wait seven years thinking they're locked out. Order the COE and find out what's actually left. CONFIDENCE NOTE: seasoning periods stated from VA underwriting practice; exact 2026 handbook language not machine-verified.
items.deadline: Seasoning runs from discharge/sale date.

items.title: Collections and judgments on a VA file: what actually has to be paid
items.who: Veterans with medical collections, charge-offs or outstanding judgments.
items.value: VA does not automatically require every collection to be paid. Isolated or medical collections generally do not require payoff if the overall payment history is satisfactory. Outstanding JUDGMENTS, however, must generally be paid or under a documented, seasoned repayment plan — and any federal debt (including a VA overpayment or defaulted student loan) must be resolved because it triggers CAIVRS.
items.how: Run CAIVRS early. Federal debt delinquency will hard-stop the file regardless of FICO. Judgments need either a satisfaction of judgment or a payment plan with proof of on-time payments, with the plan payment counted in DTI.
items.hack: Get a CAIVRS check before you shop, not at underwriting. An old VA copay debt or a defaulted federal student loan will kill a VA file 48 hours before closing — and resolving it (a repayment agreement with VA's Debt Management Center, or student loan rehabilitation) takes weeks. This single check saves more deals than any credit repair service. CONFIDENCE NOTE: general standards; exact 2026 handbook wording not machine-verified.
items.deadline: Resolve federal debt before application.

items.title: VA Form 26-6393 (Loan Analysis) — ask to see it, it shows exactly why you were approved or denied
items.who: Every VA borrower, especially anyone who got a denial or a smaller approval than expected.
items.value: The 26-6393 is the underwriter's worksheet: income, debts, the estimated maintenance-and-utility figure, taxes, the computed residual income, the DTI ratio, and the underwriter's written justification when the file exceeds 41% DTI.
items.how: Request a copy of the completed VA Form 26-6393 from your lender. On a denial, it will show which line failed.
items.hack: Nine times out of ten a surprise VA denial is an input error on the 26-6393 — a paid-off debt still counted, a non-taxable income line not grossed up, a childcare figure imputed, or the maintenance-and-utilities number computed off the wrong square footage. Ask for the form, audit the lines, and resubmit. Borrowers almost never ask for this document, and lenders almost never volunteer it.
items.deadline: Request at or immediately after underwriting decision.

items.title: Tidewater Initiative: you get exactly 2 working days to save a low appraisal (Circular 26-17-18)
items.who: Any VA purchase where the appraiser's opinion of value is coming in below the contract price.
items.value: A pre-report rescue window. The appraiser must notify a designated Point of Contact BEFORE finalizing a low value, and that POC has '2 working days' to submit additional comparable sales.
items.how: The POC is whoever the loan requestor designates on the appraisal request — the real estate agent, the loan officer/originator, or the borrower. Comps must be presented in a format matching the URAR grid. If pending sales are submitted they must include all contract addenda plus a short narrative on similarities and differences, and written verification that sales actually closed is mandatory. The appraiser attaches a 'Tidewater' addendum documenting what was received.
items.hack: Name the LISTING AGENT as the Point of Contact, not the loan officer. The listing agent has the local comps, the pending-sale contracts, and the motivation — and they can respond in hours. A loan officer who gets the Tidewater call on a Friday afternoon may not reach anyone before the two working days expire, and then the low value is locked in and you are fighting a much harder ROV. Set the POC at the time the appraisal is ordered.
items.deadline: 2 working days from the appraiser's notification.

items.title: Reconsideration of Value (ROV) — the appeal after the appraisal report is already issued
items.who: Buyers and sellers stuck with a completed VA appraisal below contract price.
items.value: A formal second look. Where Tidewater happens before the report is written, the ROV happens after — the lender submits additional comparable sales and factual corrections back through the appraiser, and unresolved disputes can be escalated to the VA Regional Loan Center's Staff Appraisal Reviewer for a Notice of Value adjustment.
items.how: Submit through the lender, not directly to the appraiser (VA appraisers are independent and lender contact is regulated). Provide closed comps the appraiser did not use, with an explanation of why each is more comparable, plus factual errors (wrong square footage, missed bedroom, unrecorded addition, wrong lot size).
items.hack: ROVs win on FACTS, not on opinion. 'The market is hot' loses. 'The appraiser reported 1,850 sq ft; the county assessor and the builder plan both show 2,140 sq ft' wins. Pull the assessor card and the original plat before you write the ROV. And remember the escape clause: if the ROV fails, you get your earnest money back regardless.
items.deadline: Submit promptly — most lenders want the ROV within days of the report, and your financing contingency is running.

items.title: The VA escape clause — the exact sentence that gets your earnest money back
items.who: Every VA purchase buyer. It is mandatory in the contract.
items.value: Full refund of earnest money if the VA appraised value comes in below the contract price — regardless of any other contract language.
items.how: The required text: 'Notwithstanding any other provisions of this contract, the purchaser shall not incur any penalty by forfeiture of earnest money or otherwise or be obligated to complete the purchase of the property described herein, if the contract purchase price or cost exceeds the reasonable value of the property established by the Department of Veterans Affairs.' The purchaser retains the option to proceed anyway and pay the difference in cash. Statutory authority: 38 U.S.C. 501, 3703(c)(1).
items.hack: Note the words 'notwithstanding any other provisions of this contract.' This overrides a waived appraisal contingency. Veterans in competitive markets are told to waive the appraisal contingency to win the bid — but the VA escape clause cannot be waived out of a VA-financed contract. You can compete on that term and still keep your deposit protected. Make sure the signed addendum is in the file; some agents in non-military markets have never seen it.
items.deadline: Signed at contract; applies through closing.

items.title: VA Minimum Property Requirements — the 44 topics that kill appraisals
items.who: VA buyers, listing agents, and anyone selling a rural, older or deferred-maintenance property to a VA buyer.
items.value: VA maintains 44 MPR topics in Pamphlet 26-7 covering safety, sanitation and structural soundness: defective conditions, geological stability, structural integrity, water supply and individual wells, sewage disposal and septic, drainage, heating and mechanical systems, roof covering, attics, crawl spaces, basements, lead-based paint, radon, wood-destroying insects, environmental hazards, swimming pools, burglar bars, energy conservation, and manufactured homes.
items.how: VA has an open rulemaking (ANPRM published December 11, 2023; comment period closed February 9, 2024; 152 comments received) exploring replacing the 44-item list with the Fannie/Freddie Uniform Appraisal Dataset C1–C4 condition ratings. As of this writing the 44-topic framework still governs.
items.hack: The four that most often kill a VA deal: (1) peeling paint on a pre-1978 home (lead-based paint — must be scraped and repainted before closing); (2) a roof with less than a few years of remaining life; (3) a well or septic that is too close to the other, or lacks a potability test; (4) active wood-destroying insect evidence with no treatment certificate. All four are cheap to cure and catastrophic to discover at day 20. Walk the property with this list before you write the offer.
items.deadline: Cure before the compliance inspection; VA will not issue the guaranty otherwise.

items.title: The 1% flat charge and the non-allowable fee list (38 CFR 36.4313)
items.who: Every VA borrower reviewing a Loan Estimate or Closing Disclosure.
items.value: 'A lender may charge and the veteran may pay a flat charge not exceeding 1 percent of the amount of the loan, provided that such flat charge shall be in lieu of all other charges relating to costs of origination not expressly specified and allowed in this schedule.'
items.how: Fees the veteran MAY be charged, itemized in the regulation: VA appraiser and compliance inspector fees; recording fees and taxes; credit report; current-year taxes and initial tax/insurance escrow deposits; hazard insurance; survey if required; title examination and title insurance; flood zone determination (third-party guaranteed); items authorized by the Under Secretary for Benefits; and an assumption processing fee of up to $300 or actual cost, whichever is less. Expressly prohibited: 'brokerage or service charges,' premiums for life insurance on the borrower, and appraisal fees for predetermination requests made by a party other than the veteran or lender. The catch-all: 'No charge shall be made against, or paid by, the borrower incident to the making of a guaranteed or insured loan other than those expressly permitted.'
items.hack: Read your Closing Disclosure against this list. Underwriting fees, processing fees, document prep fees, application fees, tax service fees, attorney fees for the lender, and escrow/settlement fees to the lender's affiliate are classic non-allowables that must either fit inside the 1% flat charge or be paid by the seller or lender. On a $500,000 loan that 1% cap is $5,000 total for all origination-side charges — I have seen disclosures with $7,800 of them. Challenge it in writing before closing; lenders fix it rather than take the VA audit finding.
items.deadline: Review before signing the Closing Disclosure.

items.title: Circular 26-24-19 (Change 1) — VA now requires invoices for itemized fees charged to veterans
items.who: VA borrowers and lenders, for loans closing in 2026.
items.value: VA issued 'Invoice Requirements for Itemized Fees and Charges,' Change 1 dated June 4, 2026, clarifying lender invoicing procedures for itemized fees charged to veterans obtaining VA-guaranteed loans.
items.how: Lenders must be able to document the actual third-party invoice supporting each itemized charge passed to the veteran.
items.hack: This is your enforcement hook on the non-allowable fee list. Ask the lender for the underlying invoices on every itemized third-party charge. A marked-up credit report fee or a padded title charge has no supporting invoice, and under this circular the lender has to either produce it or remove it. Very few borrowers ask.
items.deadline: Applies to loans closing after June 4, 2026.

items.title: 2026 VA funding fee table — every rate, including the 0.5% assumption and IRRRL fee
items.who: Every VA borrower not exempt from the fee.
items.value: Purchase, first use: 2.15% (<5% down), 1.5% (5%+ down), 1.25% (10%+ down). Purchase, after first use: 3.3% (<5% down), 1.5% (5%+ down), 1.25% (10%+ down). Cash-out refinance: 2.15% first use, 3.3% after first use. IRRRL: 0.5%. Loan assumption: 0.5%. NADL: 1.25% purchase, 0.5% refinance.
items.how: Exempt if you receive VA compensation for a service-connected disability; are eligible for compensation but receive retirement or active-duty pay instead; receive DIC as a surviving spouse; received a proposed or memorandum rating before closing; or are active duty with a Purple Heart awarded on or before closing.
items.hack: The 5%-down cliff on a subsequent-use purchase is the biggest single arbitrage in the table: going from 4.99% down to 5.00% down cuts the fee from 3.3% to 1.5%. On a $500,000 loan that is $9,000 saved for roughly $50 of extra down payment. And note the memorandum-rating line — if you have a proposed rating in hand before closing, you are exempt, even if the final decision hasn't issued.
items.deadline: Fee is due at closing; refunds available if a retroactive exemption is later established.

items.title: The new VA Partial Claim Program — live since June 15, 2026
items.who: Veterans with a VA-guaranteed loan who are behind on payments and can resume the regular payment but cannot repay the arrearage.
items.value: VA advances the delinquent amount as a subordinate, non-interest-bearing lien so the loan is brought current and the original note rate is preserved. Policy published June 1, 2026; servicers could begin submitting partial claims June 15, 2026. The claim amount is capped at a percentage of the unpaid principal balance (VA's servicer FAQ references 25% or 30% of UPB depending on circumstances).
items.how: Restrictions in VA's servicer FAQ: borrowers who received a partial claim under the prior COVID-era program are excluded; no more than one modification per 3-year period; a veteran cannot receive another partial claim on the same guaranteed loan if a previous one was paid; pre-approval for a subsequent modification is allowed if the most recent one was more than 24 months ago. VA states the Loss Mitigation Waterfall and the Partial Claim program 'must be implemented together, as neither can operate independently.' Servicers have 180 days from June 1, 2026 (i.e., through approximately November 28, 2026) to implement.
items.hack: Between June 15 and late November 2026 your servicer may not have implemented yet — that is not the same as you being ineligible. Call VA at 1-877-827-3702, ask for a loan technician, and ask them specifically whether your servicer has stood up partial claims. VA can escalate. Do not let a servicer's implementation lag turn into a foreclosure referral. Also relevant: Circular 26-26-2 (August 11, 2026) covers terminating VA-guaranteed loans where VA holds a partial claim interest.
items.deadline: Servicer implementation deadline approximately November 28, 2026.

items.title: VA loan technicians: 1-877-827-3702 — free intervention with your servicer
items.who: Any veteran with a VA-guaranteed loan who is delinquent, in forbearance, facing foreclosure, or getting stonewalled by a servicer. You do NOT have to be the original borrower — VA will help a surviving spouse or a veteran whose loan was assumed.
items.value: Free financial counseling from VA Regional Loan Center technicians, 'designed to help you avoid foreclosure.' VA technicians can contact your servicer directly and advocate on your behalf.
items.how: Call 1-877-827-3702. Have your loan number, servicer name, and a short written timeline of what you've been told. VA's guidance: contact your servicer BEFORE you miss a payment, be forthright about your finances, and do not take on additional debt to cover the mortgage.
items.hack: The single most underused phone number in veteran housing. Servicer loss-mitigation departments behave differently the moment a VA technician is on the file, because VA is the guarantor and reviews servicer performance. Call VA the week you realize you'll be short — not after the referral to foreclosure, when the options narrow to a compromise sale or deed in lieu.
items.deadline: Call before the foreclosure referral; options shrink sharply afterward.

items.title: Homeowner Assistance Fund — state money that can pay off a VA partial claim lien
items.org: U.S. Treasury / state housing finance agencies, via VA
items.who: Homeowners with a COVID-era financial hardship, including VA-guaranteed borrowers. Availability varies by state and several state programs have exhausted funds.
items.value: HAF pays mortgage reinstatement, loan payments, utilities, insurance and other housing costs. VA explicitly confirms VA borrowers may use HAF to bring a delinquent loan current, in combination with a VA modification or partial claim, and to pay off existing partial claim or refund modification liens.
items.how: Applications are run by individual states. Find your state's program through NCSHA's HAF directory or the CFPB's homeowner assistance page, and talk to your servicer about coordinating HAF funds with a VA loss-mitigation option.
items.hack: The lien-payoff use is the sleeper. If you took a COVID-era VA partial claim, that lien sits behind your mortgage and has to be satisfied when you sell or refinance. HAF dollars can retire it — which can be the difference between a clean refinance and being stuck. Check your state's program status first; many have closed, and VA's page was last updated September 12, 2025.
items.deadline: Varies by state; many state HAF programs have closed to new applications.

items.title: Texas Veterans Land Board home loan — up to $832,750, with a rate discount at 30% disability
items.org: Texas General Land Office / Veterans Land Board
items.who: Texas residents age 18+, honorable/general/medical discharge, who are: active duty; Texas National Guard; reserve with 20+ qualifying years; veterans with 90+ days active duty (or fewer if medically discharged); or the surviving spouse of a veteran who died in service or is MIA.
items.value: Fixed-rate 15, 20, 25 or 30-year loans up to $832,750. Veterans with a VA service-connected disability rating of 30% or more receive a DISCOUNTED interest rate. Rates adjust weekly.
items.how: Get a VLB Certification of Eligibility, then work through a VLB-approved lender. Home must be the veteran's primary residence in Texas and must remain so for at least 3 years. No refinancing offered; cannot be used for a down payment on an existing mortgage. Call 800-252-8387.
items.hack: The VLB home loan works WITH the federal VA guaranty rather than instead of it — so a Texas veteran can stack the VLB below-market rate on top of the VA zero-down guaranty and the funding fee exemption. Also note: you may have one active VLB land loan AND one VLB home loan at the same time, though not two of the same type. Texas veterans who only shop national VA lenders leave the rate discount on the table.
items.deadline: Rates change weekly; no application deadline.

items.title: Texas VLB land loan — $150,000 at 5% down ($275,000 for two veteran spouses)
items.org: Texas General Land Office / Veterans Land Board
items.who: Same eligibility as the VLB home loan; must be a Texas resident age 18+.
items.value: Up to $150,000 per eligible veteran, or up to $275,000 when two eligible veteran spouses purchase the same tract together. Minimum 5% down. 30-year fixed. Rate quoted at 7.25% as of this research (subject to change). Minimum one acre of usable land in Texas. No prepayment penalty.
items.how: Five steps: review credit and gather income documents, complete the online prequalification, locate qualifying land, submit documentation, close. A $325 appraisal and contract service fee applies after the application is submitted. Apply at glo.texas.gov or call 800-252-8387.
items.hack: This is the only true consumer land loan in America at these terms — raw land normally requires 20-35% down at 2-4 points above mortgage rates. Two eligible veteran spouses buying together get $275,000, nearly double the individual cap, on the same tract. Buy the land with the VLB loan, then build on it with a VA construction loan: that sequence gets a veteran from nothing to a finished custom home with roughly 5% total cash in.
items.deadline: None; rates change.

items.title: Texas VLB home improvement loan — up to $50,000 at 6.35%, or 5.85% with a 30% rating
items.org: Texas General Land Office / Veterans Land Board
items.who: Texas resident veterans and military members age 18+ meeting VLB service criteria, on their existing Texas primary residence.
items.value: Up to $50,000 for 2-20 years, or $7,500-$10,000 for 2-10 years. Base rate 6.35%; discounted rate 5.85% for veterans with a VA service-connected disability rating of 30% or more. No down payment required. Rates adjust weekly.
items.how: Eligible properties: single-family homes, condos, duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes at least 5 years old, and manufactured homes on a permanent foundation. Secure contractors and obtain bids before the loan is processed. Fees: $10 flood certification, $125 title search, plus closing costs. Loans over $25,000 require VLB to hold first lien position.
items.hack: At 5.85% unsecured-feeling money for a disabled Texas veteran, this beats every home equity loan, HELOC and contractor financing product in the market by several points — and there is no down payment. The first-lien requirement above $25,000 is the constraint: if you have an existing mortgage, keep the improvement loan at $25,000 or below to stay in second position and avoid a refinance.
items.deadline: Rates adjust weekly.

items.title: CalVet Home Loans — California's own veteran mortgage, no minimum credit score
items.who: Veterans and active-duty members buying an owner-occupied home in California. Generally requires at least 90 days of active duty (wartime or peacetime, excluding training) and an honorable discharge; National Guard and Reserve members federally activated also qualify.
items.value: CalVet offers standard financing, construction loans, rehabilitation-purchase options and home improvement loans. CalVet often uses the federal VA guaranty to offer up to 100% financing with no monthly private mortgage insurance. Notably, CalVet states NO minimum credit score and uses manual underwriting rather than automated approval engines.
items.how: Apply through CalVet directly (calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) or through a CalVet-participating lender. CalVet historically holds title under a contract-of-sale structure and bundles property/hazard coverage and a disaster indemnity into the loan — verify the current structure and coverage with CalVet before closing.
items.hack: The no-minimum-score, manual-underwriting policy is the real benefit and almost nobody markets it. A California veteran declined by three national lenders on a FICO overlay should call CalVet directly — the file gets read by a human who looks at residual income and payment history. CONFIDENCE NOTE: calvet.ca.gov blocks automated fetching, so 2026 maximum loan amounts, current rates, and the exact insurance/indemnity package could not be independently verified. Confirm all figures with CalVet at 866-653-2510.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Oregon ODVA Home Loan — four loans per lifetime, and you don't have to live in Oregon to apply
items.who: Veterans who establish eligibility with ODVA. The property must be in Oregon, but 'veteran borrowers are not required to be an Oregon resident upon application.'
items.value: Financing up to the Fannie Mae limit with up to 95% LTV. Four-loan maximum lifetime benefit, with only one loan open at a time. Owner-occupied primary residences only. Eligible properties: site-built single family, condos, townhomes, and manufactured homes affixed to land and taxed as real estate.
items.how: Start at oregon.gov/odva/Home-Loans. Rates are published on ODVA's rate sheet flyer; call (800) 633-6826 or (503) 373-2373 for current pricing.
items.hack: Two things distinguish this from every other state program. First, the four-loans-per-lifetime structure means an Oregon veteran can use it repeatedly across a career — sell, pay off, use it again, four times. Second, the non-residency rule means a veteran living in Washington or California who buys an Oregon property qualifies. ODVA is funded by a separate constitutional program independent of the federal VA benefit, so this stacks with — it does not consume — your federal entitlement.
items.deadline: None; four uses per lifetime.

items.title: Alaska AHFC State Veterans Interest Rate Preference — 1% off the first $50,000
items.who: Honorably discharged veterans with at least 90 days active duty; Alaska Army or Air National Guard members; reservists with five years of service; and widows/widowers of qualified veterans. Family income must not exceed the State Veteran income limits.
items.value: 'A 1% interest rate reduction applies to the first $50,000 of the loan amount.' Above $50,000 the borrower gets a blended rate rounded up to the next 0.125%.
items.how: Provide a DD-214 and a VA Certificate of Eligibility or discharge paperwork to an AHFC-participating lender. The preference is an add-on option that layers onto AHFC's underlying loan programs.
items.hack: Because it blends, the effective benefit shrinks as the loan grows — on a $250,000 loan the 1% on $50,000 works out to roughly 0.20% off the whole note. Worth having, but do not let a lender sell it as '1% off your rate.' Ask them to quote the blended rate in writing and compare it against a straight VA loan from a national lender before choosing.
items.deadline: Income limits are set annually; verify current State Veteran income limits with AHFC.

items.title: Montana Veterans Home Loan Program — 1% below the Board of Housing bond rate, no income or asset limits
items.org: Montana Board of Housing / Montana Department of Commerce
items.who: Montana residents with honorable service or discharge from the Montana National Guard or the U.S. armed forces and reserves, who are first-time homebuyers (never previously owned a primary residence) and complete a first-time homebuyer class.
items.value: Fixed-rate 30-year mortgage at 1% BELOW the Montana Board of Housing Regular Bond Loan Program rate. NO income or asset limits apply — unusual for an HFA program. Maximum loan amount $538,036 (as of July 24, 2026). Minimum $2,500 out-of-pocket borrower investment.
items.how: Originate through a Montana Board of Housing participating lender; MBOH purchases and services the loan. Funds are limited and revolving — check availability through Lender Online before writing an offer. Condominiums are NOT allowed under the program.
items.hack: The 'no income or asset limits' line is the unlock. Most state HFA below-market programs cut off at 80-140% of area median income; Montana's veteran program does not, so a high-earning veteran buying their first home gets a full percentage point off a 30-year fixed with no means test. That is worth roughly $100,000+ of interest on a $400,000 loan. The constraint is fund availability — House Bill 924 (2025) moved the funding source from the Coal Tax Trust Fund to the new Montana Housing Trust, so confirm the pipeline is open.
items.deadline: Revolving funds; availability varies.

items.title: NIFA Military Home Program (Nebraska) — veterans skip the first-time buyer rule entirely
items.who: Two groups: active military members (who must meet NIFA's first-time homebuyer requirements) and qualified veterans discharged under conditions other than dishonorable — and 'Qualified Veterans do not have to meet the first-time homebuyer eligibility requirements.'
items.value: Below-market government loan rate — 6.125% as of the program page's September 24, 2026 update (no conventional option currently offered). Works with VA, FHA or USDA Rural Development financing.
items.how: Contact NIFA at (402) 434-3900 or 1-800-204-NIFA (6432), or go through a NIFA-participating lender. Income and purchase price limits apply under NIFA's general program rules.
items.hack: The first-time-buyer waiver for veterans is a FEDERAL rule (mortgage revenue bond statute), not a Nebraska quirk — which means the same waiver exists in most state HFA bond programs even when the state doesn't advertise it. If you are a veteran who has owned a home before and a state HFA tells you you're ineligible as a repeat buyer, ask them specifically about the qualified-veteran exception to the first-time homebuyer requirement. Many front-line lenders do not know it exists.
items.deadline: Rates change; verify current pricing with NIFA.

items.title: Mortgage Credit Certificate: veterans are exempt from the first-time buyer rule — up to $2,000/yr for the life of the loan
items.org: State housing finance agencies under the federal mortgage revenue bond rules
items.who: Veterans in states with an active MCC program. The qualified-veteran exception means you do NOT have to be a first-time homebuyer.
items.value: A dollar-for-dollar FEDERAL INCOME TAX CREDIT equal to a percentage of the mortgage interest paid each year, for the life of the loan. The credit rate is set by the issuing HFA between 10% and 50%; when the rate exceeds 20% the annual credit is capped at $2,000. The remaining interest stays deductible. Texas's program, for example, uses a 20% credit rate and illustrates roughly $2,000/year of savings on a $200,000 loan at 6%.
items.how: The MCC must be issued AT or BEFORE closing — it cannot be added later. Apply through an HFA-participating lender at the same time as the mortgage. The Texas Homebuyer Program's materials state it 'waives the first time homebuyer requirement for qualified veterans,' requiring active duty service, an honorable discharge (DD-214), and that you have not previously financed through a mortgage revenue bond program. Income and purchase price limits still apply, and a recapture tax may apply if you sell within 9 years at a gain with rising income.
items.hack: This is the most valuable benefit in this entire domain that almost no veteran claims, because it must be requested before closing and loan officers get paid nothing for it. Over a 30-year loan a $2,000/year credit is up to $60,000 of tax savings — and the qualified-veteran exception means even a veteran on their fourth house qualifies. Ask every lender, in writing: 'Does my state HFA offer an MCC, and am I eligible under the qualified veteran exception?' Then get it issued at closing.
items.deadline: MUST be issued at or before loan closing. Cannot be obtained retroactively.

items.title: SONYMA Homes for Veterans (New York) — 0.40% rate cut and up to $15,000 down payment assistance
items.org: State of New York Mortgage Agency (SONYMA) / NYS Homes and Community Renewal
items.who: Active service members, veterans, and their spouses or co-borrowers. National Guard and reservists qualify if active or honorably discharged. 'US Military veterans with an other than dishonorable discharge do not need to be first time homebuyers.'
items.value: Interest rates 0.40% lower than standard SONYMA rates when used with down payment assistance. Down payment assistance of the greater of $3,000 or 3% of purchase price, up to a $15,000 maximum. The borrower needs only 1% of their own funds — the remaining 2% may come from gifts or other acceptable sources.
items.how: Apply through a SONYMA participating lender. Documentation: DD214 or NGB Form 22; Leave and Earnings Statements for active duty; military ID for active service members. A Military Veteran's Eligibility Affidavit is required only if you are NOT a first-time homebuyer.
items.hack: Note the 'other than dishonorable' language — New York's waiver covers general and OTH discharges, which are excluded from many benefits. And the 1% own-funds rule means a veteran with $4,000 saved can close on a $400,000 home with the DPA covering the rest. Combine with the SONYMA rate cut and this beats a market-rate VA loan for many NY buyers.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Ohio Heroes (OHFA) — discounted rate for veterans, active duty, reservists and surviving spouses
items.who: Veterans and active-duty military including reserve components AND surviving spouses; also first responders, healthcare professionals and educators.
items.value: A discounted mortgage interest rate, with optional down payment assistance that can be added to the loan.
items.how: Credit score minimums: 640+ for conventional, USDA and VA; 650+ for FHA. Income and purchase price limits vary by county. Free HUD-approved homebuyer education is required after the loan application is submitted. Find an OHFA-approved lender or call 888-362-6432.
items.hack: Surviving spouses are explicitly named as eligible — that is rare in state HFA hero programs and is worth checking in every state. Stack Ohio Heroes' rate discount with a VA loan's zero down and funding fee exemption, and add OHFA's DPA to cover closing costs; an Ohio disabled veteran can realistically close with almost nothing out of pocket.
items.deadline: None; income/purchase limits update annually.

items.title: How to find YOUR state's veteran housing program (and the two questions to ask)
items.org: National Council of State Housing Agencies / state HFAs
items.who: Every veteran buying a home, in every state.
items.value: Most states run at least one of: a veteran-specific below-market first mortgage (Montana, Nebraska, Ohio, New York, Wisconsin's WHEDA VALOR, Alaska's rate preference), veteran down payment assistance, or an MCC with the qualified-veteran first-time-buyer waiver. A handful run their own direct lending (Texas VLB, CalVet, Oregon ODVA). Massachusetts runs Operation Welcome Home with a closing cost credit; Florida has run Salute Our Soldiers.
items.how: Go to ncsha.org/housing-help, find your state HFA, and search its site for 'veteran' or 'military.' Then call the HFA directly rather than relying on a lender.
items.hack: Ask exactly two questions: (1) 'Do you have a veteran or military rate product, and what is the rate differential versus your standard program?' (2) 'Do you issue Mortgage Credit Certificates, and does the qualified-veteran exception to the first-time homebuyer rule apply?' Those two questions surface nearly every state benefit that exists. Note also that a few states have NO veteran home loan program at all — Idaho, for example, offers a disabled-veteran property tax reduction but no state veteran mortgage, so don't waste time hunting for one.
items.deadline: Program funds are often limited and revolving; ask about availability before writing an offer.

items.title: Wisconsin WHEDA VALOR — Veterans Affordable Loan Opportunity Rate
items.org: Wisconsin Housing and Economic Development Authority
items.who: Qualified Wisconsin veterans and military service members.
items.value: A below-market first mortgage rate reserved for veterans, layered on WHEDA's standard loan programs (which also offer down payment assistance).
