items.hack: This creates a real and rarely-discussed cost to a promotion or a dependency change in a falling market: the event breaks your rate protection and re-rates you at the current, lower table. It is almost never a reason to decline a promotion, but it is a reason to check the new number before you plan around it.
items.deadline: Applies at each January rate change.

items.title: BAH-Diff and partial BAH — the two small housing allowances almost nobody claims
items.who: BAH-Diff: a member living in single-type government quarters who pays child support. Partial BAH: a member without dependents who is living in government quarters and therefore not entitled to full BAH.
items.value: BAH-Diff is a housing differential paid to a member in government quarters who is paying child support — it exists so that a barracks-dwelling member supporting a child is not left with nothing. Partial BAH is a small flat allowance for members without dependents housed in government quarters. Neither is large, but both are commonly missed because neither starts automatically.
items.how: Both require you to notify finance of your circumstances. For BAH-Diff, provide proof of the child-support obligation and the amount; the entitlement generally requires that your support payment be at least equal to the BAH-Diff amount. Ask your S-1/MPF/PSD to start it and verify it appears on the LES.
items.hack: Members in the barracks paying child support are the most common group missing money here. If that is you, ask finance about BAH-Diff by name — a general 'am I getting all my allowances' question usually does not surface it. Look up the current BAH-Diff and partial BAH tables at travel.dod.mil rather than relying on a quoted amount.
items.deadline: Starts when you claim it; retroactivity is limited, so claim immediately.

items.title: OHA overseas — the reimbursement allowance that works nothing like BAH
items.who: Members stationed OCONUS (outside the 50 states and U.S. territories covered by BAH) who live in private-sector housing.
items.value: OHA is a REIMBURSEMENT up to a ceiling, not a flat allowance. It has three separate components: (1) a rental allowance reimbursing your actual rent up to a grade-based ceiling, (2) a utility/recurring maintenance allowance, and (3) a Move-In Housing Allowance (MIHA) covering one-time move-in costs, security enhancements in designated areas, and rent-related fees. Rates are recomputed frequently to track currency fluctuations.
items.how: Submit DD Form 2367 (Individual Overseas Housing Allowance Report) with your lease. Rent is reimbursed at actual cost up to the ceiling — if your rent is below the ceiling you receive only what you pay, and the excess is NOT yours to keep. Look up current OHA rates and MIHA amounts on the DTMO site.
items.hack: The BAH instinct — rent cheap and bank the difference — backfires completely overseas. Under OHA you keep nothing by renting below the ceiling. The optimization is instead to use the full rental ceiling on better housing, and to claim MIHA aggressively: agent fees, deposits that are non-refundable, and required security modifications are frequently left unclaimed.
items.deadline: File DD 2367 as soon as you sign the lease; MIHA claims have submission windows — ask the housing office.

items.title: BAS — the food allowance, the enlisted/officer split, and Essential Station Messing
items.who: Officers receive BAS at a single rate. Enlisted members receive a different (higher) standard rate, with variations for members on field duty or assigned to Essential Station Messing.
items.value: BAS is a non-taxable allowance intended to offset the cost of the member's own meals — not the family's. Rates are adjusted each January based on the USDA food cost index, not on the military pay raise percentage, so BAS can move by a very different amount than basic pay in the same year.
items.how: Look up the current-year enlisted and officer BAS rates on the DoD military compensation site. Check your LES: if you are assigned to Essential Station Messing (required to eat in a government dining facility), a meal deduction or collection will appear, and members frequently find they are being charged for meals they are not eating.
items.hack: The single most common BAS error is continuing meal collections after a member moves out of the barracks or is released from ESM status. Audit the meal-deduction line on your LES after every move, every deployment return and every change of quarters. Current BAS rates: look them up at militarypay.defense.gov.
items.deadline: Rates change January 1; audit meal deductions after every status change.

items.title: CONUS COLA vs. OCONUS COLA — two different allowances with the same nickname
items.who: CONUS COLA: members at high-cost duty locations inside the continental U.S. that exceed a national average threshold. OCONUS COLA: members stationed overseas, to offset higher non-housing goods and services costs.
items.value: CONUS COLA is TAXABLE and relatively small; it covers non-housing costs in expensive domestic areas and only a limited number of locations qualify in any given year. OCONUS COLA is NON-taxable, is based on a periodic living pattern survey plus local currency exchange rates, and varies with grade, years of service and dependents. OCONUS COLA can change mid-year — sometimes sharply — when the exchange rate moves.
items.how: Look up current COLA rates and qualifying locations on the DTMO site. Verify your entitlement is coded correctly on the LES after every PCS.
items.hack: Overseas members should treat OCONUS COLA as variable income, not base income. When the dollar strengthens against the local currency, COLA drops and household budgets built around it break. Budget to the low end of the past year's range, not to today's rate. Look up current rates at travel.dod.mil.
items.deadline: OCONUS COLA can be adjusted throughout the year; CONUS COLA locations are re-evaluated annually.

items.title: Family Separation Allowance — the 30-day trigger people miss by a week
items.who: Members with dependents who are involuntarily separated from those dependents for more than 30 continuous days due to military orders — deployment, TDY, unaccompanied tour, or a ship deployed away from homeport.
items.value: A flat monthly allowance (FSA) paid in addition to all other pay and allowances, payable in monthly increments once the 30-day threshold is crossed, and retroactive to day one of the separation. There are three statutory variants: FSA-R (restricted/unaccompanied tour), FSA-S (ship away from homeport over 30 days) and FSA-T (TDY away from permanent station over 30 days). Only one may be paid at a time.
items.how: Submit DD Form 1561 (Statement to Substantiate Payment of Family Separation Allowance) through your unit. It is NOT automatic — many members return from a long TDY without ever filing. Once the 30-day mark is passed, payment reaches back to the first day.
items.hack: Because payment is retroactive to day one once you cross 30 days, a 31-day TDY is worth substantially more than a 29-day TDY. If your TDY is running 27 or 28 days and the mission supports it, an extension request is worth making. Look up the current FSA monthly rate at militarypay.defense.gov.
items.deadline: File DD 1561 promptly; claims are subject to the general six-year pay claim limitation.

items.title: Hostile Fire / Imminent Danger Pay and Hardship Duty Pay — how they are triggered and prorated
items.who: Members serving in designated imminent danger areas, exposed to hostile fire or a hostile mine explosion, or assigned to designated hardship locations or missions.
items.value: Hostile Fire Pay (HFP) is payable for any month in which you are exposed to a hostile fire or mine event, at the full monthly rate. Imminent Danger Pay (IDP) is payable for service in a designated IDP area and is PRORATED by day. Hardship Duty Pay comes in variants — location (HDP-L), mission (HDP-M) and tempo (HDP-T) — at tiered monthly rates based on the severity of the conditions.
items.how: Entitlements flow from your orders and the designated-area lists, which the Under Secretary of Defense (Personnel & Readiness) updates. Verify the entitlement codes appear on your LES in the first full month downrange — a missing IDP line is a frequent and easily-fixed error.
items.hack: IDP and HFP matter far beyond the cash: for an officer, imminent danger pay is what raises the combat zone tax exclusion cap, and any month with qualifying service can make the entire month's pay CZTE-eligible. Getting the code right on the LES protects both. Look up current HFP/IDP and HDP rates at militarypay.defense.gov.
items.deadline: Verify on the first LES after arriving in the designated area.

items.title: Hazardous duty and incentive pays — jump, dive, flight, demolition, and the ones you can stack
items.who: Members performing qualifying duties under competent orders: parachute duty (with a higher rate for HALO/military free fall), flight crew and non-crew flying duty, aviation career incentive pay for rated officers, diving duty (rates vary by qualification), demolition and explosive ordnance disposal duty, toxic fuels and pesticides handling, experimental stress duty, and others.
items.value: Monthly special pays on top of basic pay. Several hazardous duty incentive pays may be paid concurrently up to a statutory limit, so a member with multiple qualifications (say, jump plus demolition) can draw more than one — a fact that surprises members who assume they must pick.
items.how: Each requires (a) competent orders assigning you to the duty and (b) meeting the performance requirement for the period — for parachute duty, the required number of qualifying jumps in the period; for flight pay, the required flight hours or an approved waiver. Missing the requirement stops the pay and can trigger recoupment.
items.hack: Track your own jump/flight currency independently of the unit's tracker. Recoupment for a period where the unit failed to document your qualifying jumps is a painful and common pay problem, and the burden of producing the record falls on you. Look up current hazardous duty incentive pay rates at militarypay.defense.gov.
items.deadline: Qualification requirements are periodic — usually per month or per stated period; keep your own records.

items.title: Career Sea Pay and the sea pay premium — rewarded by cumulative sea duty, not by deployment
items.who: Members assigned to a ship, ship-based staff or aviation unit, or other designated sea duty — Navy, Coast Guard, Marine Corps, and Army watercraft crews.
items.value: Career Sea Pay is a monthly special pay whose rate rises with pay grade AND with cumulative years of sea duty, so it compounds over a career at sea. A Career Sea Pay Premium is payable after a defined period of consecutive sea duty beyond the normal tour length — designed specifically to reward members who stay at sea past the usual rotation.
items.how: Entitlement follows the unit's sea-duty designation and your cumulative sea-duty record. Verify your cumulative sea duty time in your service record before a reenlistment or assignment decision — the counter determines your rate.
items.hack: The premium is the underused piece: if you are already past a normal sea tour, check whether an extension crosses the consecutive-duty threshold. Sailors have extended a few months and picked up the premium for the whole remaining period. Look up current sea pay tables at militarypay.defense.gov.
items.deadline: Premium requires a specified period of consecutive sea duty — check the threshold before extending or rotating.

items.title: Special Duty Assignment Pay (SDAP) — the tiered pay for hard-to-fill jobs
items.who: Enlisted members assigned to duties designated by their service as extremely difficult or requiring an unusual degree of responsibility — recruiter, drill instructor/military training instructor, career counselor, certain instructor billets, special operations support, and service-specific lists that change regularly.
items.value: A monthly special pay in tiered levels (commonly SD-1 through SD-6, with higher tiers for the most demanding billets). Services adjust which billets qualify and at what tier, sometimes annually, as retention needs change.
items.how: Entitlement comes from the billet, not from you — check your service's current SDAP billet list before volunteering for or accepting an assignment, and verify the SDAP line appears on your LES once you report.
items.hack: Because the tier attaches to the billet, two apparently identical jobs at different commands can pay different SDAP. Ask the detailer/assignment manager for the SDAP tier of a specific billet number in writing before you accept — it is a legitimate factor in assignment negotiation and it is rarely volunteered. Look up current SDAP tier rates at militarypay.defense.gov.
items.deadline: Verify on the LES within the first full month in the billet.

items.title: Foreign Language Proficiency Bonus — paid for a test score, not a job
items.who: Members who demonstrate proficiency in a language on the service's payment list, generally by testing on the Defense Language Proficiency Test (DLPT) or an Oral Proficiency Interview. In most services you do NOT need to hold a linguist job to be paid — you need a qualifying score in a language the service currently pays for.
items.value: A monthly bonus whose amount depends on your proficiency level in listening, reading and speaking, on whether the language is on the service's immediate-need list, and on whether you hold multiple qualifying languages (multiple payments are possible up to a statutory monthly ceiling).
items.how: Request a DLPT through your unit training or education office — testing is free. Scores are valid for a defined period (commonly one year) and must be retested to keep the pay. Each service publishes its own current payable language list and rate schedule; the lists change as strategic needs change.
items.hack: Heritage speakers routinely leave this on the table for an entire career because they assume it only applies to linguists. If you grew up speaking a language on your service's list, take the DLPT — the test costs nothing, the downside is a bad score nobody sees, and the upside is a monthly payment for the rest of your career as long as you retest. Look up your service's current payable languages and rate table before relying on any amount.
items.deadline: Scores expire — normally annually. Calendar the retest.

items.title: Enlistment and reenlistment bonuses — the tax move that is worth more than the bonus negotiation
items.who: Members receiving an enlistment, reenlistment, or critical skills retention bonus.
items.value: Bonuses are generally taxable income and are typically withheld at a supplemental flat rate. But a reenlistment bonus earned while serving in a designated combat zone is excluded from income under the Combat Zone Tax Exclusion — the whole bonus, subject to the officer cap. Re-enlisting downrange rather than two weeks after you get home can be the difference between a taxed and an untaxed bonus.
items.how: The exclusion attaches when you become ELIGIBLE for and execute the reenlistment while serving in the combat zone (a single day of qualifying service in the month can make that month's pay excludable). Coordinate the timing with your career counselor and confirm with a MilTax consultant before you plan around it.
items.hack: Two additional mechanics: (1) bonuses paid in installments are taxed as received, so timing later installments matters too; (2) if you fail to complete the obligated service, the unearned portion is recouped — and recoupment of a bonus taxed in an earlier year creates a messy claim-of-right situation. Get the recoupment terms in writing before signing.
items.deadline: Timing-sensitive — coordinate before executing the reenlistment.

items.title: The CZTE officer cap — it is pegged to the top enlisted pay rate, and it moves every January
items.who: Commissioned officers serving in a designated combat zone or qualified hazardous duty area. Enlisted members and warrant officers have no cap.
items.value: For enlisted members and warrant officers, ALL military pay earned in a month of qualifying combat zone service is excluded from gross income. For commissioned officers, the exclusion is capped at the highest rate of ENLISTED basic pay (the top E-9 rate) plus any hostile fire or imminent danger pay actually received for that month. Because the cap is defined as a formula against the pay table, it rises automatically with every January pay raise — you never need to memorize a number, you need to look at the current top enlisted rate.
items.how: The exclusion is applied by DFAS on your LES and reflected on your W-2 in the non-taxable combat pay reporting. Verify the excluded amount matches your expectation for each qualifying month.
items.hack: Two consequences officers miss: (1) since the cap includes IDP/HFP, making sure your imminent danger pay is coded correctly literally raises your tax-free ceiling; (2) excluded combat pay still counts as compensation for Roth IRA contribution purposes and can be elected into the Earned Income Tax Credit calculation. Compute your own cap from the current-year top enlisted basic pay rate at militarypay.defense.gov rather than using a figure from an article.
items.deadline: Applies month by month; verify each qualifying month's LES.

items.title: How to read your LES — the ten lines where money actually goes missing
items.who: Every member; check monthly.
items.value: The Leave and Earnings Statement is the only document that shows entitlements, deductions, allotments, leave balance, tax withholding, TSP contributions and the remarks section where finance explains what it just did to you. Most pay problems are visible on the LES months before they become a debt letter.
items.how: Pull the LES from myPay each month. Check, in order: (1) pay grade and PEBD; (2) BAH rate against the current table and your duty ZIP; (3) BAS and any meal deduction; (4) every special and incentive pay you are entitled to; (5) state tax code against your DD 2058 state of legal residence; (6) TSP percentages for both traditional and Roth, and the agency/service match line; (7) SGLI coverage and premium; (8) leave balance and use-or-lose; (9) every allotment, including ones you forgot; (10) the REMARKS section, which is where debts, collections and retroactive adjustments are announced.
items.hack: The remarks block is the single most ignored and most important field. Overpayment recoupments, meal collection restarts and BAH re-rates are almost always announced there first, in plain language, one to two months before the money disappears. Read it every month and you will never be blindsided by a DFAS debt.
items.deadline: Monthly. Pay claims generally must be brought within six years.

items.title: The pay errors that cost the most — and how to open a claim before they become a debt
items.who: Anyone who has PCS'd, deployed, promoted, married, divorced, had a child, gone to school, mobilized or demobilized — in other words, everyone.
items.value: The recurring expensive errors: wrong PEBD holding you at a lower longevity step; BAH continuing at an old duty station's rate after PCS (which creates an overpayment debt); BAH stopping when dependents move but entitlement continues; meal deductions restarting after you leave the barracks; dependency changes not filed so BAH-with-dependents never starts; special pays not started on arrival in a billet; a mobilized Guard/Reserve member paid at the wrong rate; and overpayments discovered years later and recouped in a lump sum.
items.how: Audit the LES monthly. When something is wrong, open a case through your servicing finance office / S-1 first, in writing, and keep the ticket number. If DFAS asserts a debt you dispute, you can request a waiver or remission of the indebtedness and request a hearing/suspension of collection while it is reviewed — ask finance for the specific waiver application route for your service and debt type.
items.hack: Never let a disputed debt go to involuntary collection without filing the waiver request in writing first. A waiver request filed promptly can suspend collection; one filed after the money is gone becomes a refund request, which is far harder. And remember the six-year limitations period runs both ways — it limits what you can claim, and it limits nothing about your obligation to document what you were paid.
items.deadline: File waiver/remission requests as soon as a debt notice appears; military pay claims generally subject to a six-year limitation.

items.title: Allotments — what you can still start, what DoD banned, and why they are a predatory-lending magnet
items.who: Active duty members (and, with limits, retirees) using myPay to route pay automatically.
items.value: Allotments split your pay before it reaches you. Non-discretionary allotments (things like government indebtedness, SGLI, certain insurance and charitable deductions) are distinct from discretionary allotments, which are limited in number. DoD restricted NEW discretionary allotments for the purchase, lease or rental of personal property — the change was made specifically because off-base retailers were using allotments to lock in high-cost purchases. Separately, the Military Lending Act prohibits a covered creditor from requiring repayment by allotment.
items.how: Start, change and stop allotments in myPay. Review the allotment list on every LES — old allotments to closed accounts, former spouses and defunct memberships run for years unnoticed.
items.hack: If a merchant near the gate offers financing 'through allotment,' that is the tell. It is very likely a covered MLA transaction where requiring allotment repayment is prohibited, and it is almost always priced far above what a credit union would charge. Walk out and call your on-base credit union or the relief society instead.
items.deadline: n/a — but audit allotments on every LES.

items.title: High-3 legacy retirement — the exact formula, and which 36 months count
items.org: DoD / DFAS Retired and Annuitant Pay
items.who: Members who entered service before January 1, 2018 and did not opt into the Blended Retirement System, and members who entered between September 8, 1980 and July 31, 1986 (High-3 applies to all of them).
items.value: Retired pay = 2.5% x years of creditable service x the average of your highest 36 months of BASIC pay. Twenty years yields 50%; thirty years yields 75%. 'High-36' means the highest 36 months, which for almost everyone is the last three years — but not always, and it is basic pay only: BAH, BAS and special pays are excluded entirely.
items.how: Partial years count toward the multiplier (active duty retirement credits months). Confirm your creditable service computation and your high-36 window with your service's retirement services office before you set a retirement date.
items.hack: Because the multiplier is 2.5% per year, each additional YEAR served is worth 2.5% of your high-3 for life — and each additional month past a promotion pulls a higher basic pay figure into the high-36 average. Retiring a few months after a promotion rather than a few months before it can raise the annuity permanently. Run the exact numbers against the current basic pay table at militarypay.defense.gov.
items.deadline: Set the retirement date deliberately — the high-36 window and the multiplier both depend on it.

items.title: BRS vs. legacy — who was grandfathered, who had to choose, and who had no choice
items.who: Three groups. (1) Members with a Date of Initial Entry into Military Service on or after January 1, 2018: automatically enrolled in the Blended Retirement System, no election. (2) Members who entered before January 1, 2018 with fewer than 12 years of service (active) or fewer than 4,320 retirement points (Reserve/Guard) as of December 31, 2017: had a one-year opt-in window during calendar year 2018. (3) Everyone else: grandfathered into the legacy High-3 system permanently.
items.value: The opt-in window closed at the end of 2018 and cannot be reopened. Knowing which system you are in determines your multiplier (2.0% vs 2.5%), whether you get TSP matching, and whether continuation pay and the lump-sum option exist for you at all.
items.how: Your system is recorded in your personnel record and reflected in whether you receive service TSP matching contributions on your LES. If your LES shows agency/service matching contributions, you are in BRS.
items.hack: If you are unsure, look at your LES TSP block. Legacy High-3 members receive no service matching; BRS members receive the automatic 1% plus matching. It is the fastest reliable check and it takes ten seconds.
items.deadline: The opt-in window closed December 31, 2018 — this is historical and cannot be changed.

items.title: The BRS lump-sum option — 25% or 50% of your retired pay, and why the discount rate makes it a bad deal
items.who: BRS retirees, at the time they apply for retired pay.
items.value: A BRS retiree may elect to receive either 25% or 50% of the discounted present value of their retired pay as a lump sum, in exchange for receiving only the remaining 75% or 50% of the monthly annuity until full Social Security retirement age, at which point the full annuity is restored. The lump sum can be taken as a single payment or in up to four annual installments.
items.how: The election is made when you apply for retired pay. The present value is computed using a personal discount rate published annually by DoD — and that rate has historically been set well above prevailing market interest rates, which mathematically means the lump sum is worth substantially less than the stream of payments you give up.
items.hack: Run the arithmetic before you are dazzled by a six-figure number: you are selling an inflation-adjusted, government-backed lifetime annuity at a discount rate you do not set. For the lump sum to win, you would need to reliably beat that discount rate after tax for decades. It also reduces your income during the exact years you are raising a family and paying a mortgage. The lump sum makes sense for a narrow set of cases (terminal illness, a genuinely higher-return opportunity, immediate debt crisis) and is a losing trade for most retirees. Look up the current-year DoD discount rate before deciding.
items.deadline: Elected at the time you apply for retired pay — irrevocable.

items.title: REDUX and the Career Status Bonus — historical, terminated, and still worth understanding
items.who: Members who entered service on or after August 1, 1986 and elected the Career Status Bonus at 15 years of service. The CSB/REDUX election was TERMINATED for new elections — it is no longer available, and members in service today generally cannot choose it.
items.value: Historical mechanics, for anyone already in it or advising someone who is: REDUX pays a reduced multiplier — 40% at 20 years instead of 50%, increasing by 3.5% per year to reach 75% at 30 years — in exchange for a $30,000 Career Status Bonus taken at 15 years. It also imposes a reduced COLA (CPI minus one percentage point) with a one-time catch-up recomputation at age 62, after which the reduced COLA resumes.
items.how: If you are already under REDUX, nothing to elect — but understand that the COLA penalty compounds for life and is the largest cost, larger than the multiplier reduction. Plan retirement income assuming your purchasing power erodes relative to a High-3 or BRS retiree.
items.hack: The practical lesson for today's force is the structure, not the program: REDUX is the textbook example of a lump sum offered in exchange for lifetime annuity value, and the BRS lump-sum option is the same trade in modern clothing. The $30,000 CSB was overwhelmingly a bad deal for people who served 20+ years. Treat the BRS lump sum with the same suspicion.
items.deadline: Closed to new elections — historical only.

items.title: Retired pay COLA — how the adjustment is set and why your first one is prorated
items.who: All military retirees and SBP annuitants.
items.value: Military retired pay is adjusted annually for inflation based on the change in the Consumer Price Index (CPI-W), the same index used for Social Security, effective with the December payment (received in January). High-3 and BRS retirees receive full CPI; REDUX retirees receive CPI minus one percentage point until the age-62 recomputation.
items.how: No action required. Your first COLA after retiring is typically PRORATED based on how many months you have been retired during the measurement period, so a member who retires late in the year should not expect the full published percentage in their first adjustment.
items.hack: This inflation protection is the feature that makes military retired pay hard to replicate with private savings — an inflation-indexed lifetime annuity is extremely expensive to buy. It is the strongest single argument against the BRS lump sum, and the strongest argument for weighing SBP (which is also COLA-adjusted) more seriously than a term life comparison suggests.
items.deadline: Effective with the December payment each year.

items.title: SBP base amount election and the paid-up rule — 360 payments and age 70
items.who: Retiring members electing the Survivor Benefit Plan, and current SBP participants.
items.value: SBP is elected on a 'base amount' — you may elect full retired pay as the base, or any lesser amount down to a statutory minimum. The premium is a percentage of the base amount you choose, and the annuity is 55% of that base amount, adjusted by the same COLA as retired pay. Separately, SBP coverage becomes PAID UP — premiums stop while coverage continues for life — once you have made 360 months of premium payments AND reached age 70. Both conditions must be met.
items.how: Elect at retirement with spousal concurrence required to elect less than full coverage or to decline. Track your premium months; DFAS should stop collecting automatically when you hit the paid-up threshold, but verify on your retiree account statement.
items.hack: Electing a reduced base amount is the least-discussed lever: it lets a retiree buy partial coverage at a proportionally reduced premium instead of the all-or-nothing choice most briefings present. For a couple with substantial other assets but some survivor gap, a partial base amount can be the right answer where full SBP feels too expensive and no SBP feels too risky. Look up current premium percentages and the statutory minimum base amount at DFAS before running your numbers.
items.deadline: Election made at retirement; paid-up status requires 360 premium months AND age 70.

items.title: Reserve and Guard retirement points — exactly how each type accrues
items.who: National Guard and Reserve members in a retirement-point-earning status.
items.value: Points come from four streams. (1) Membership points: 15 points per anniversary year simply for being in a qualifying status. (2) Inactive duty training (drills): 1 point per drill period, with the standard drill weekend generating 4 points. (3) Active duty and active duty for training: 1 point per day. (4) Correspondence/distance learning courses and funeral honors duty: points as authorized. There is an annual ceiling on the number of inactive-duty points that may be credited in a retirement year, and the ceiling has changed over time by statute.
items.how: Review your annual retirement point statement (the form name varies by service — ARPC Form 249-E for Air Force, the Chronological Statement of Retirement Points for Army, etc.) EVERY year when it is issued. Errors are far easier to fix in the year they occur than at age 58.
items.hack: Correspondence course points are the most under-claimed. They are free, can be earned from home, and count toward both the 50-point good year and the total-points divisor that sets your retired pay. A member who is short on drills in a bad year can often save the good year with coursework — but only if it is completed and recorded inside the anniversary year.
items.deadline: Points are credited by anniversary year; audit the statement annually.

items.title: The 50-point good year and the 20-good-years requirement
items.who: Guard and Reserve members working toward a non-regular (Reserve) retirement.
items.value: A 'satisfactory year' — a good year — requires at least 50 retirement points earned in your anniversary year. Twenty good years qualifies you for non-regular retired pay. A year with 49 points counts for nothing toward the 20, regardless of how much you actually served, which makes the 50-point line one of the hardest cliffs in military compensation.
items.how: Know your anniversary year dates — they run from your pay-entry or retirement-year beginning date, NOT the calendar or fiscal year, and this trips up members constantly. Track points against that window. Membership points (15) plus a full drill schedule normally clears 50 comfortably; the risk years are ones with medical non-availability, a transfer between units, or a gap between components.
items.hack: In a year running short, the fastest recovery levers are correspondence courses, additional drill periods (with approval), funeral honors duty, and short active duty for training periods. Check the point count at the 9-month mark of your anniversary year, not at the end — by the last month there may be no way to close a 20-point gap. Once you have 20 good years, request your Notice of Eligibility (the '20-year letter') and store it permanently; reconstructing eligibility without it is miserable.
items.deadline: 50 points per anniversary year; check your count no later than month nine of each year.

items.title: Converting points to a retired pay check: points divided by 360
items.who: Guard and Reserve retirees.
items.value: Non-regular retired pay = (total creditable retirement points / 360) x multiplier x high-3 average basic pay. The multiplier is 2.5% per equivalent year under the legacy system and 2.0% under BRS. Dividing by 360 converts points into 'equivalent years' — 360 points equals one year of active-duty-equivalent credit. The high-3 used is the average of the highest 36 months of basic pay for your grade and longevity, computed from the pay table in effect, not from what you were actually paid on drill weekends.
items.how: Request your official point total from your component before retirement and reconcile it against your own annual statements. DFAS computes the annuity from the point total the service certifies — an error in the service's record becomes an error in your check for life.
items.hack: This formula explains why extra points matter permanently: 360 additional points over a career is a full additional 2.5% (or 2.0%) of your high-3, every month, for life, plus COLA. Correspondence courses, extra drill periods and short active duty tours are not just good-year insurance — each point is a permanent, compounding piece of the annuity.
items.deadline: Reconcile the point total BEFORE you submit retirement paperwork.

items.title: Reserve retired pay before 60 — the 90-day active duty reduction rule
items.who: Guard and Reserve members with qualifying active duty service performed on or after January 28, 2008.
items.value: The standard age to begin non-regular retired pay is 60. Qualifying active duty service under specified authorities reduces that age by three months for each aggregate 90 days of such service performed within a fiscal year — but the age may not be reduced below 60 for service before the statutory start date, and not below age 50 in any case.
items.how: The 90 days must aggregate within a single FISCAL year, and the qualifying authorities are specific (certain mobilization and contingency-support authorities), so not every set of active duty orders counts. Your component tracks this; request a written statement of your reduced retirement age well before you approach 60 and challenge it if orders you believe qualify are missing.
items.hack: The fiscal-year aggregation is the planning lever nobody mentions: two 60-day mobilizations split across a fiscal year boundary produce NO reduction, while the same 120 days inside one fiscal year produces a three-month reduction. If you have any say in when a set of orders starts, the fiscal year it lands in can be worth months of earlier retired pay.
items.deadline: Applies to qualifying service on or after January 28, 2008; verify your computed age before age 58.

items.title: Armed Forces Recreation Centers — five DoD resorts, rank-based rates, and eligibility that differs at each one
items.who: Eligibility VARIES BY PROPERTY and is stricter at some than others. Broadly: active duty, Guard and Reserve, military retirees, DoD civilians (varies), and in many cases 100% service-connected disabled veterans and other categories of veterans with Commissary/MWR privileges. Some properties — particularly the overseas ones — have narrower eligibility and additional sponsorship requirements.
items.value: Five DoD-operated resort hotels where room rates are set on a sliding scale BY PAY GRADE — a junior enlisted family pays dramatically less than an O-6 for the same room, and every category pays well under comparable commercial rates in the same location. Hale Koa (Waikiki, Hawaii), Shades of Green (Walt Disney World, Florida), Edelweiss Lodge and Resort (Garmisch-Partenkirchen, Germany), Dragon Hill Lodge (Seoul, South Korea) and the New Sanno (Tokyo, Japan).
items.how: Book directly with each property. Booking windows open far in advance — the popular properties and dates (Hale Koa in summer, Shades of Green over holidays) fill essentially the day the window opens, often 12 months out.
items.hack: CONFIRM YOUR ELIGIBILITY WITH THE SPECIFIC PROPERTY BEFORE BOOKING FLIGHTS. Eligibility rules differ property by property and have changed over time, particularly for veterans and DoD civilians. A booking confirmation is not an eligibility determination — some properties verify ID at check-in and will turn away an ineligible guest who has already flown to Honolulu or Tokyo. One phone call to the reservations line settles it.
items.deadline: Booking windows typically open around 12 months ahead; peak dates sell out immediately.

items.title: Hale Koa Resort, Waikiki — a beachfront hotel on Fort DeRussy at military rates
items.who: Active duty, Guard and Reserve, retirees, and other authorized patrons — with categories that have expanded over time to include certain veterans with MWR privileges. Confirm your specific category with the resort.
items.value: A full-service beachfront resort on the Fort DeRussy Armed Forces Recreation Center in the middle of Waikiki, with rates set by pay grade rather than by market. The location is the point: it sits on the same beach as commercial hotels charging several times as much, with no resort fee structure resembling the commercial properties around it.
items.how: Book direct at halekoa.com. Rates vary by room category (garden view through oceanfront) and by pay grade band. The property also runs luau shows, a fitness center, restaurants and an ITT-style tour desk open to guests.
items.hack: Book the moment the window opens — roughly a year out for summer and holiday weeks. Also check the resort's own tour and activity desk before booking Oahu activities elsewhere; it functions as an Information, Tickets and Tours office and frequently beats retail pricing on the same excursions and attraction tickets.
items.deadline: Reservations open approximately 12 months in advance for most categories.

items.title: Shades of Green — the DoD resort inside Walt Disney World
items.who: Active duty, Guard and Reserve, retirees, Medal of Honor recipients, 100% service-connected disabled veterans and other authorized categories, plus certain DoD civilians. Categories and their rate tiers differ — confirm yours with the resort.
items.value: A DoD-owned resort located on Walt Disney World property, between the Polynesian and the Grand Floridian, with room rates set by pay grade. It is the only way to stay inside Disney World at military pricing, and the on-site ticket office sells the Disney military ticket offerings to eligible patrons.
items.how: Book direct at shadesofgreen.org. Rooms are released on a rolling window and peak periods (holidays, spring break, marathon weekend) go instantly. The resort operates its own ticket sales office and provides transportation to the Disney parks.
items.hack: The ticket office is often worth more than the room. Disney's military ticket offerings are limited-quantity, have specific eligibility rules that many veterans do NOT meet, and have blackout and expiration terms that change year to year — buy through the resort's ticket office where the staff verify eligibility on the spot, rather than assuming you qualify. Confirm current ticket eligibility and terms before planning the trip around them.
items.deadline: Book as early as the window allows; ticket program terms change annually.

items.title: Edelweiss Lodge and Resort, Garmisch — the Alps at military rates
items.who: Active duty, Guard and Reserve, retirees, DoD civilians and other authorized categories; eligibility for Europe-based AFRC properties has specific rules and some categories require a sponsor. Confirm before booking.
items.value: A modern resort in Garmisch-Partenkirchen at the foot of the Zugspitze, Germany's highest peak, with pay-grade-based rates. It functions as the base camp for the Army's Europe outdoor recreation program: skiing, hiking, guided tours to Neuschwanstein and Munich, and an adventure/outdoor center that rents equipment.
items.how: Book direct at the resort. It is reachable by train from Munich, which matters because a rental car in Europe often costs more than the train. The resort's tour office sells guided trips across Bavaria, Austria and northern Italy at rates well below commercial tour operators.
items.hack: Stateside travelers routinely overlook this because they assume it is only for Europe-stationed personnel. If you can get to Germany — including on a Space-A Patriot Express rotator — the lodging and the guided tours are among the best values in the entire military recreation system. Check eligibility and current rates with the resort directly.
items.deadline: Ski season and Oktoberfest periods book far ahead.

items.title: Dragon Hill Lodge, Seoul — the AFRC property in Korea
items.who: Active duty, Guard and Reserve, retirees, DoD civilians and other authorized categories. Access to the installation itself is a separate question from hotel eligibility — confirm both with the property before traveling.
items.value: A DoD-run hotel on U.S. Army Garrison Yongsan in central Seoul with pay-grade-based rates, restaurants, a fitness center, and a tour office running trips including the DMZ, which is otherwise expensive and logistically fussy to arrange.
items.how: Book direct with the property. Because it sits on an installation, plan for base access requirements and bring your military ID plus any required documentation for accompanying guests.
items.hack: The tour office is the underrated part — DMZ and Panmunjom tours through the lodge are typically cheaper than commercial equivalents and handle the clearance paperwork for you. Verify installation access rules for your category and for any non-ID-card guests well before you fly.
items.deadline: n/a — but arrange base access questions in advance.

items.title: The New Sanno, Tokyo — the most restricted AFRC property, and worth checking anyway
items.who: ELIGIBILITY IS NARROWER HERE THAN AT THE OTHER AFRC PROPERTIES and is governed by the U.S.-Japan Status of Forces Agreement. Access is generally limited to SOFA-status personnel and specified categories, and retiree and veteran access has historically been more restricted than at Hale Koa or Shades of Green. You MUST verify your specific eligibility with the hotel before making any travel plans.
items.value: A U.S. military hotel in the Hiroo district of central Tokyo, with rates set by pay grade in one of the most expensive hotel markets in the world. It includes restaurants, a Navy Exchange outlet and a tour desk.
items.how: Contact the hotel directly to confirm eligibility for your exact status category BEFORE booking flights, then reserve through its reservation system. Sponsorship requirements may apply to guests.
items.hack: Because eligibility is tied to SOFA status rather than simply to a military ID, this is the one AFRC property where 'I have a retiree ID, so I'm fine' is a genuinely risky assumption. Get the eligibility answer in writing (email confirmation) and carry it with you. If you do not qualify, the on-base lodging at Yokosuka, Yokota or Atsugi may be an alternative — ask about those in the same call.
items.deadline: Verify eligibility before booking any travel.

items.title: On-base lodging — Navy Gateway Inns, IHG Army Hotels and Air Force Inns as a travel strategy
items.org: Navy Gateway Inns & Suites / IHG Army Hotels / Air Force Inns
items.who: Official travelers have priority; Space-Available (leisure) room reservations are open to active duty, Guard and Reserve, retirees, and in many cases DoD civilians and other ID cardholders. Availability for leisure travel depends entirely on the installation's official-travel load.
items.value: Government lodging at government rates — typically a fraction of comparable commercial hotels, often with kitchenettes, free parking, free laundry and no resort fees. Booking 'Space-A' here means space-available ROOMS, which is unrelated to Space-A air travel. Combined with base access, it makes trips to expensive cities (San Diego, Honolulu, Washington DC, Monterey, Key West) dramatically cheaper.
items.how: Navy: navygatewayinns.com. Army: ihg.com/armyhotels (which also earns IHG loyalty points on eligible stays). Air Force: through the Air Force Inns reservation system. The DoD Lodging portal at dodlodging.net indexes properties across the services. Call the front desk directly if the online system shows nothing — leisure inventory is often released by phone.
items.hack: Two moves. (1) Army lodging booked through IHG earns hotel loyalty points and status nights on a government-rate stay, which is unusual and valuable. (2) For any leisure trip near an installation, check base lodging FIRST and use the commercial hotel as the fallback, not the other way round. Look up current nightly rates on each property's site — they vary by installation and are adjusted periodically.
items.deadline: Leisure reservations are subject to displacement by official travelers — confirm the cancellation/displacement policy when booking.

items.title: Space-A air travel — the six-category priority system decoded
items.who: Eligibility and category depend on your status and your purpose of travel.
items.value: Space-A seats are allocated by CATEGORY, and your category determines everything about whether you actually fly. Broadly: Category I is emergency leave; Category II is sponsored environmental and morale leave (EML); Category III is ordinary leave for active duty and their accompanying dependents; Category IV is unaccompanied dependents on EML; Category V is permissive TDY, students and certain others; Category VI is retirees, Reserve/Guard members in specified statuses, and — since eligibility was expanded — 100% service-connected permanently disabled veterans, traveling in the lowest priority. Within a category, seats go by date and time of sign-up, so an early registration in Cat VI beats a late one.
items.how: Register at the passenger terminal or via the terminal's published sign-up method (email or online) as early as your eligibility window allows. Sign up at MULTIPLE terminals simultaneously — your sign-up date/time carries at each one.
items.hack: The whole game is sign-up timestamp within your category. Active duty on leave should sign up the moment leave is approved, not the day of travel, because Cat III competition is decided by minutes. Retirees and disabled veterans in Cat VI should register at every terminal within driving distance and treat any single flight as unlikely — Space-A rewards flexibility and redundancy, not planning.
items.deadline: Sign-up windows are tied to leave dates; register as early as your status permits.

items.title: Space-A mechanics that decide whether you actually get on the plane
items.who: Anyone in any Space-A category.
items.value: Practical rules that matter more than eligibility: sign-up is free and remains active for 60 days or the duration of your leave, whichever is shorter; you must be present at roll call to be selected; you may sign up at multiple terminals; and you are responsible for your own onward travel if you get stranded — Space-A carries no obligation to bring you home.
items.how: Each terminal publishes its 72-hour flight schedule and roll call times on its own official page or social media. Show up for roll call with your ID, passport (required for most overseas destinations regardless of the aircraft), and any country-specific entry documents. Carry-on and baggage rules follow AMC policy, not commercial airline policy.
items.hack: Four hard-won rules. (1) Never Space-A somewhere you must return from by a fixed date — always hold a refundable commercial ticket home or the cash to buy one. (2) Bring a passport even for flights you think are domestic; diversions happen. (3) Terminals publish the seat releases from the previous days — read them to learn which routes actually move. (4) Sign up for your destination AND for any terminal near it; a flight to a base 200 miles away that actually departs beats a perfect route that never flies.
items.deadline: Sign-up remains valid 60 days or the length of your leave, whichever is shorter.

items.title: The Patriot Express — the DoD 'rotator' that is the most reliable Space-A route
items.who: Space-A eligible travelers in all categories, plus duty passengers on orders.
items.value: The Patriot Express is a DoD-contracted commercial-style passenger flight on scheduled routes serving major overseas destinations (Europe, the Pacific, and other locations). Because it is a passenger aircraft on a published schedule with seats routinely released to Space-A, it is far more predictable than catching a cargo aircraft — and it is the backbone of realistic Space-A planning for families.
items.how: Find the schedule through the departure terminal's published information. Unlike cargo missions, Patriot Express flights charge a small head tax and, on some routes, a meal fee for Space-A passengers — so it is not strictly free. Baggage allowances are generous compared to commercial carriers.
items.hack: Plan any family Space-A trip around Patriot Express routes and treat cargo aircraft as a bonus. Also note the pet policy: Patriot Express flights accept a limited number of pets, reserved separately and far in advance, which makes them the preferred routing for PCS travelers moving animals overseas. Confirm current fees, pet slots and baggage rules with the terminal — they change.
items.deadline: Pet reservations in particular must be made well in advance and are capacity-limited.

items.title: USO airport centers — free lounges open to far more people than most realize
items.who: Active duty, Guard and Reserve, military retirees, and their families — and at most locations, this includes travelers in civilian clothes with a valid military ID. Eligibility is broader than the 'uniformed service member only' assumption, though individual centers set their own rules and some have capacity limits.
items.value: A network of centers in major airports and at overseas hubs offering free snacks and drinks, Wi-Fi, quiet space, showers at some locations, family and nursing rooms, luggage storage at some, and a place to sleep during a long connection. Completely free — no membership, no card, no annual fee.
items.how: Find locations at uso.org/locations. Bring your military ID (DoD ID card, retiree ID, or dependent ID). Check the individual center's hours, which vary and are not always the airport's hours.
items.hack: This is the free alternative to a paid airport lounge and it beats many of them on the things that matter during a long layover — free food, showers, and somewhere to actually sleep. Retirees and dependents frequently do not realize they qualify. Before buying a lounge day pass at an airport with a USO, check the USO first.
items.deadline: n/a

items.title: Airport lounge access via premium cards — the mechanism, and why it pairs with the fee waiver
items.who: Cardholders of premium travel cards that include lounge membership as a benefit.
items.value: Premium travel cards typically bundle airport lounge access — a membership in a third-party lounge network, access to the issuer's own lounges, or airline-club membership — as a benefit that would otherwise cost a substantial annual membership fee on its own. Stacked with the SCRA/MLA annual fee waiver, an active-duty member can hold the lounge benefit at no annual cost.
items.how: Lounge benefits normally require enrolling separately after you get the card — the membership is not automatic, and a large share of cardholders never activate it. Log into the card's benefits portal and enroll, then add the digital membership card to your phone wallet. Guest policies, network coverage and enrollment steps differ by card and change frequently.
items.hack: Enroll the moment the card arrives, and check whether authorized users get their own lounge membership — on some products they do, which can cover a spouse traveling separately. Do NOT choose a card based on a lounge benefit described in an article; benefit terms are revised often, so confirm current lounge network, guest rules and enrollment requirements directly with the issuer before you count on it.
items.deadline: Enrollment is usually required before first use — do it when the card arrives.

items.title: Airline baggage waivers — the difference between traveling on orders and traveling on leave
items.who: Military travelers. The rules split sharply between orders-based travel and personal/leisure travel.
items.value: Most major U.S. airlines waive or substantially increase checked baggage allowances for military travelers, but the two tiers are different: travelers ON ORDERS (PCS, deployment, TDY) typically get the most generous allowance, often several free checked bags plus oversize/overweight relief; travelers on personal leisure trips typically get a smaller allowance, sometimes only one or two free bags, and some carriers require uniform or ID presentation at the counter.
items.how: Carry a copy of your orders in paper or on your phone plus your military ID. Baggage waivers usually cannot be applied online — check in at the counter, not at a kiosk, and state that you are traveling on military orders. If a fee is charged in error, keep the receipt and request a refund through the airline's customer service with the orders attached.
items.hack: Book the ticket in the traveler's exact name as it appears on the orders and the ID, and check in at the counter every time — the single most common cause of a denied military baggage waiver is a kiosk check-in that has already assessed the fees. For PCS moves, also compare the airline excess-baggage route against shipping through the Personally Procured Move process; sometimes the baggage waiver is the cheaper path for the same weight. Confirm each airline's current military baggage policy directly — these change without notice.
items.deadline: n/a — present orders at the counter at each check-in.

items.title: VA facility locator — find every VA medical center, clinic, Vet Center and benefits office near you
items.who: All veterans, family members and caregivers.
items.value: One official search that covers VA medical centers, community-based outpatient clinics (CBOCs), Vet Centers, VA regional benefit offices, national cemeteries, and in-network community care providers. Filterable by service type — mental health, dental, prosthetics, women's health, urgent care — so you can find which specific facility actually provides the service you need rather than driving to the nearest one and finding out it does not.
items.how: Use va.gov/find-locations. Search by ZIP or city, choose the facility type, then filter by service. Each result shows the address, phone, hours and the services offered.
items.hack: Use the service filter BEFORE you call. VA facilities differ enormously in what they offer — a large CBOC may have no audiology, no prosthetics and no mental health intake — and the locator's service filter is the fastest way to find the right facility the first time. It is also the authoritative source for whether a location is a full medical center or a clinic, which affects eligibility for beneficiary travel and for emergency care rules.
items.deadline: n/a

items.title: Vet Center locator — the separate, confidential network that is not a VA hospital
items.who: Combat veterans, veterans who experienced military sexual trauma, veterans who provided mortuary services or emergency medical care, certain drone crew members, Vietnam-era veterans, and family members for bereavement and family counseling. No VA disability rating, no VA health care enrollment and no discharge-status hurdle for most services.
items.value: Roughly 300 community-based Vet Centers plus mobile Vet Centers and community access points, offering free readjustment counseling, group therapy, marriage and family counseling, and referral. Records are kept separately from the VA medical record — a genuine confidentiality distinction that matters to servicemembers worried about clearances and career effects.
items.how: Find locations at vetcenter.va.gov, or call the Vet Center Call Center, which is staffed around the clock by combat veterans. Walk-ins are accepted at most centers.
items.hack: Mobile Vet Centers and community access points reach rural areas where there is no brick-and-mortar center at all, and they are not always visible in the main VA facility locator. Search the Vet Center site specifically, and ask the Call Center about mobile unit schedules in your county — rural veterans regularly conclude there is nothing near them when a mobile unit visits their town monthly.
items.deadline: n/a

items.title: National cemetery and gravesite locators — find burial space, and find where someone is buried
items.who: Veterans and families planning burial; anyone searching for the grave of a veteran.
items.value: Two separate official tools. The National Cemetery Administration site lists every VA national cemetery, state veterans cemetery grant-funded cemetery, and the Department of the Army cemeteries, with which ones are open to new interments (many are closed to first interments and accept only subsequent family interments). The Nationwide Gravesite Locator searches burial records for veterans and eligible family members in VA national cemeteries, state veterans cemeteries, and many private cemeteries where a government headstone or marker was provided.
items.how: Cemetery directory and eligibility information at cem.va.gov; gravesite search at gravelocator.cem.va.gov. For pre-need eligibility determination, VA accepts an application in advance so the family is not establishing eligibility during a funeral.
items.hack: Apply for PRE-NEED eligibility determination while the veteran is living. It costs nothing, it does not reserve a specific plot, and it converts the worst 48 hours of a family's life from a documents scramble into a phone call. Pair it with locating the DD-214 now — the two together are the entire burial process.
items.deadline: Pre-need determination can be requested at any time — do it early.

items.title: The Access Pass — a separate free lifetime federal lands pass for people with permanent disabilities
items.org: National Park Service / Interagency pass program
items.who: U.S. citizens or permanent residents of ANY age with a permanent disability. This is DISTINCT from the free veteran/Gold Star pass — a veteran who does not qualify for one may qualify for the other, and 'permanent disability' here is the interagency program's own standard, not a VA rating percentage.
items.value: A free lifetime interagency pass covering entrance fees at national parks and other federal recreation sites, plus a 50% discount on many EXPANDED AMENITY fees — most importantly camping fees at federal campgrounds, including many U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and Forest Service sites. The camping discount is where the real recurring money is.
items.how: Obtain in person at a federal recreation site with documentation of permanent disability (a statement from a licensed physician, a document from a federal agency such as a VA disability determination, or a document from a state agency), or apply by mail/online through the USGS pass store with the required documentation and processing fee.
items.hack: If you hold BOTH the veteran pass and qualify for the Access Pass, get the Access Pass too — the veteran pass covers entrance, while the Access Pass adds the 50% camping-fee discount that the veteran pass does not provide. For anyone who camps on federal land more than a few nights a year, that discount is worth more than the entrance waiver. Confirm current pass rules and fees at nps.gov/planyourvisit/passes.htm.
items.deadline: Lifetime pass, no renewal.

items.title: Army Corps of Engineers campgrounds — the most overlooked federal camping system
items.who: Everyone; pass holders (Access Pass and Senior Pass) receive a discount on camping fees at Corps-operated sites.
items.value: The Corps of Engineers is one of the largest providers of outdoor recreation in the country — hundreds of lakes and thousands of campgrounds, almost all on water, and generally cheaper and far less crowded than national park campgrounds. Access Pass and Senior Pass holders receive a 50% discount on the camping fee at Corps-managed sites (the discount applies to the site fee; some fees such as certain utility or day-use charges are treated differently).
items.how: Search and reserve through recreation.gov, which handles Corps campgrounds alongside National Park Service, Forest Service and other federal sites. Apply your Interagency pass number during booking to get the discount applied at reservation time.
items.hack: Enter your pass number in your recreation.gov profile so the discount applies automatically to every booking — a large share of pass holders pay full price for years because they never linked the pass to the account. Also search by 'Army Corps of Engineers' as the managing agency on recreation.gov to surface lakeside sites that never appear in national-park-focused searches.
items.deadline: Popular Corps sites book months ahead for summer weekends.

items.title: Base MWR — Outdoor Recreation rentals and Information, Tickets and Tours (ITT), the discount channel nobody uses
items.who: Anyone with installation access and MWR privileges — active duty, Guard and Reserve, retirees, and (since access was expanded) service-connected disabled veterans, Purple Heart recipients, former POWs and eligible caregivers.
items.value: Two programs on almost every installation. (1) Outdoor Recreation / Equipment Rental: campers, boats, kayaks, trailers, canopies, tools, party equipment, ski gear, camping kits — rented by the day at a fraction of commercial rates, plus cabins and campgrounds at many installations. (2) ITT (also called Leisure Travel Services or Tickets & Travel): discounted tickets to theme parks, concerts, sporting events, ski resorts and local attractions, plus discounted hotel and vacation packages, sold only to eligible patrons.
items.how: Find your installation's MWR program through the service portals (armymwr.com, navymwr.org, and the Air Force and Marine Corps equivalents) or look up the installation on MilitaryINSTALLATIONS. Walk into the ITT office or call — most do not publish their ticket prices online because the contracts prohibit it.
items.hack: The fact that ITT prices are usually NOT published online is exactly why this is underused: you have to call or walk in, so almost nobody comparison-shops it, and the theme park and ski ticket pricing is frequently the best available anywhere. Before buying any attraction ticket, call the nearest installation's ITT office. Veterans with expanded access since 2020 often do not know they can use ITT at all.
items.deadline: n/a — but call ITT before buying any attraction tickets.

items.title: The Veterans Online Shopping Benefit — lifetime, tax-free online exchange access for every honorably discharged veteran
items.org: Army & Air Force Exchange Service, Navy Exchange, Marine Corps Exchange, Coast Guard Exchange
items.who: ALL honorably discharged veterans of any era — no disability rating required, no commissary privileges required, no installation access required. This is a much broader group than the in-person access benefit. Discharge must be honorable (or general under honorable conditions, per the program's verification standard).
items.value: Lifetime online shopping privileges at the military exchanges' websites — ShopMyExchange, MyNavyExchange, ShopCGX and the Marine Corps exchange site. Purchases are exempt from sales tax, which by itself is a permanent percentage discount on every purchase, and exchange pricing is generally competitive before that. Military Star card and exchange promotions apply.
items.how: Verify your eligibility once at VetVerify.org, which checks your discharge status against DoD records. Once verified you create an account on the exchange sites and shop indefinitely. If automated verification fails (common for older records, name changes, or Guard/Reserve service), the site provides a manual upload path for your DD-214.
items.hack: This is distinct from the in-person commissary/exchange access granted to service-connected disabled veterans, Purple Heart recipients, former POWs and caregivers — the ONLINE benefit is open to every honorably discharged veteran regardless of rating. Millions of eligible veterans have never verified. It takes about ten minutes once and lasts for life. If verification fails, do not give up: upload the DD-214 through the manual review path.
items.deadline: No deadline — verify once, use for life.

items.title: The four exchange systems — and why the Military Star card matters
items.who: Eligible in-person patrons (active duty, retirees, service-connected disabled veterans, Purple Heart recipients, former POWs, eligible caregivers and others) and, online, all honorably discharged veterans.
items.value: Four separate systems, all honoring the same eligibility rules and all selling sales-tax-free: the Army & Air Force Exchange Service (ShopMyExchange), the Navy Exchange (MyNavyExchange), the Marine Corps Exchange, and the Coast Guard Exchange (ShopCGX). Exchange earnings fund MWR programs, so spending there returns money to quality-of-life programs. The Military Star card is accepted across all four and typically carries a lower interest rate than general-purpose cards plus purchase discounts and a fuel discount at exchange stations.
items.how: Shop online at the respective sites after VetVerify eligibility, or in person with your ID card. Compare the Military Star card's current APR and benefits against your existing cards before applying — it is issued by the Exchange Credit Program, not a commercial bank.
items.hack: Price-match policies are the sleeper: the exchanges generally price-match major retailers, and when you combine a price match with no sales tax, the exchange frequently wins on large purchases — appliances, electronics, furniture — by the full sales tax percentage of your state. Bring the competitor's listing to customer service. Confirm the current price-match terms with the specific exchange before relying on it.
items.deadline: n/a

items.title: In-person commissary, exchange and MWR access — the Purple Heart and Disabled Veterans Equal Access Act
items.who: Since January 1, 2020, in-person commissary, exchange and MWR retail privileges extended to: veterans with ANY service-connected disability rating (not just 100%), Purple Heart recipients, former prisoners of war, and individuals approved and designated as the primary family caregiver of an eligible veteran under VA's caregiver program.
items.value: Physical access to commissaries (groceries at cost plus a surcharge), exchanges, and MWR retail facilities. For a family near an installation, commissary savings on routine grocery shopping are the largest recurring dollar value in the whole military discount landscape.
items.how: Eligible veterans use a Veteran Health Identification Card (VHIC) for installation access and privileges; Purple Heart recipients, former POWs and caregivers use the credential their category requires. Installation ACCESS is a separate step from commissary ELIGIBILITY — you may also need to be vetted at the visitor center for a base access credential.
items.hack: The two-step nature is what stops people. Being eligible for the commissary does not automatically get you through the gate. Call the installation's visitor control center first and ask exactly which credential they require for your category — requirements differ between installations and have changed since 2020. Bring the VHIC, a REAL ID-compliant driver's license and your DD-214 to the first visit.
items.deadline: Effective since January 1, 2020 — no application deadline.

items.title: ID.me, SheerID, VerifyPass and GovX — set up military verification once and stop proving it every time
items.who: Veterans, active duty, Guard and Reserve, military spouses and dependents, and in many programs Gold Star family members.
items.value: Retailers do not verify military status themselves; they outsource it to a handful of providers. ID.me, SheerID and VerifyPass each verify your status once and then confirm it instantly to any participating merchant at checkout. GovX operates both as a verification provider and as its own storefront for military and first-responder pricing on gear, apparel and outdoor equipment. Setting up an account with each takes minutes and unlocks discounts at hundreds of merchants that you would otherwise have to prove eligibility for individually, often by emailing a DD-214 to a stranger.
items.how: Create an account with each provider and complete verification using your DD-214, VA letter, military ID or by connecting your DoD/VA record. ID.me is also the sign-in provider for VA.gov and many federal services, so most veterans already have one — link the military affiliation to it if you have not.
items.hack: Do all three (ID.me, SheerID, VerifyPass) plus GovX in one sitting. Merchants use different providers and there is no way to know which one a given retailer uses until checkout. Having all of them already verified converts a 'do I bother proving it for 10% off?' decision into a single click, which is the difference between capturing these discounts and ignoring them. Never email a DD-214 to a merchant that asks for one directly — use the verification provider instead.
items.deadline: Verification may require periodic re-confirmation; keep the accounts active.

items.title: How to find military discounts systematically instead of one at a time
items.who: Veterans, servicemembers and families.
items.value: A repeatable method beats a list, because published discount lists go stale within months. The method: (1) verify once with ID.me, SheerID, VerifyPass and GovX so eligibility is never the obstacle; (2) call the nearest installation's ITT office before buying any attraction, theme park or event ticket; (3) check your state's veterans affairs department for state-level benefits, which change annually and are where the largest non-federal dollars are (property tax, hunting and fishing licenses, park passes, tuition); (4) ask at the point of sale every time, because many merchants offer a discount that is not advertised anywhere; (5) check your bank or credit union — military-affiliated institutions run their own merchant discount networks.
items.how: Build it as a habit rather than a research project. The single highest-yield recurring action is simply asking, in person, at local businesses — restaurants, auto shops, barbers, hardware stores — where unadvertised military discounts are extremely common and no online list will ever capture them.
items.hack: Never plan a purchase around a discount you read about in an article, including this one. Military discount programs are voluntary, they are revised constantly, and eligibility definitions (veteran vs. active duty vs. retiree vs. dependent) differ from program to program. Verify the current terms with the merchant before you make the buying decision, and treat every published amount as a starting point for a phone call.
items.deadline: n/a

items.title: Women Veterans Call Center — 855-829-6636, call or text
items.org: VA Center for Women Veterans / VHA
items.who: Any woman veteran, plus family, caregivers and survivors. No enrollment, no rating, no eligibility screen to call.
items.value: A staffed line — all the responders are women veterans themselves — that will tell you what you are eligible for, get you enrolled in VA health care over the phone, and warm-transfer you to your local Women Veterans Program Manager. It also takes text messages, which matters if you are in a house where a phone call is not safe.
items.how: Call or text 855-829-6636. You can also email 00w@va.gov or use ask.va.gov and pick the Women Veterans category.
items.hack: Use it as an enrollment shortcut. Most women veterans who never enrolled assume they do not qualify because they were not in combat, were not injured, or served before 1990. The call center will run your eligibility while you are on the line instead of leaving you to guess at the 10-10EZ.
items.deadline: None. Ongoing.

items.title: Women Veterans Program Manager — one at every VA medical center
items.who: Women veterans enrolled in or trying to enroll in VA health care.
items.value: A named, assigned advocate inside the facility whose entire job is women veterans. They fix scheduling failures, get you assigned to a designated women's health primary care provider, arrange community care when the facility cannot provide a service, and escalate when the front desk has told you no. This is a statutory position, not a collateral duty someone invented.
items.how: Ask for the WVPM by title at the facility switchboard, or use the locator through va.gov/womenvet, or have the Women Veterans Call Center (855-829-6636) connect you.
items.hack: Go to the WVPM before you file a patient advocate complaint, not after. The WVPM can usually move a women's-health problem faster than the general patient advocate because they own the outcome and they sit on the facility's leadership reports.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Center for Women Veterans — the policy office, and what it can actually do for you
items.who: Women veterans, servicewomen, family members, caregivers, advocates.
items.value: CWV is the Secretary's advisor on women veterans. It does not adjudicate your claim, but it runs national outreach, publishes the trend data that drives VA budget decisions, and takes systemic complaints — which is the right channel when a problem is not one facility failing you but a policy that is wrong everywhere.
items.how: Email 00w@va.gov, or use ask.va.gov and select Women Veterans. Individual clinical or claim problems go to the WVPM or Women Veterans Call Center first.
items.hack: If you hit the same wall at three different VA facilities, that is a policy problem, not a local one. Write CWV with dates, facilities and names. Systemic patterns are what they exist to escalate.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA maternity care — full pregnancy coverage plus 7 days of newborn care
items.who: Women veterans enrolled in VA health care who become pregnant. No service connection required for the maternity benefit itself; standard enrollment and copay rules apply.
items.value: VA covers prenatal care, full physical exams and labs, obstetric ultrasound, genetic testing, labor and delivery (purchased in the community, because VA facilities do not deliver babies), postpartum care, lactation support including breast pumps and nursing bras, social work and mental health through pregnancy and postpartum, and support after miscarriage or stillbirth. VA pays for the newborn's care on the date of birth plus the 7 days immediately after.
items.how: Tell your VA primary care provider or the Women Veterans Call Center you are pregnant immediately. Every VA facility has a Maternity Care Coordinator who arranges the community obstetrician and handles the authorization. Do not self-refer and expect reimbursement.
items.hack: The 7-day newborn window is a hard cliff, and it catches people. The baby is not a VA beneficiary on day 8. Before you deliver, have the newborn's own coverage lined up — the other parent's plan, Medicaid, or CHIP — because a NICU admission that runs past day 7 becomes your bill. Also: VA does not cover home birth or doulas, so if that is your plan, you are paying for it.
items.deadline: Notify VA as early in the pregnancy as possible; newborn coverage ends 7 days after birth.

items.title: VA fertility evaluation and treatment — for all enrolled veterans, service connection not required
items.who: Any veteran enrolled in VA health care, regardless of service connection, gender or marital status.
items.value: VA covers the full infertility workup and a broad set of treatments with no service-connection requirement: history and physical, lab testing, imaging including ultrasound and HSG, genetic counseling and testing, hormonal therapy, surgical treatment, intrauterine insemination (IUI), and fertility counseling. This is separate from and much broader than the IVF benefit.
items.how: Ask your VA primary care provider or women's health provider for a fertility evaluation referral. The Women Veterans Call Center (855-829-6636) can find the nearest facility that provides it.
items.hack: Most veterans think fertility care at VA means IVF and stop when they learn IVF requires service connection. IUI, the surgical treatments and the entire workup do not. Get the workup done at VA on VA's dime even if you will pursue IVF privately — the diagnostic record is worth thousands and it also builds the evidence file if the infertility turns out to be service-connected.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA IVF benefit (38 CFR 17.380) — 6 embryo-creation attempts, 3 transfer cycles, lifetime
items.who: A veteran with a VBA-adjudicated service-connected disability — or treatment for one — that is causally related to their infertility. The veteran's lawful spouse is also covered. Marital status is not a bar to the veteran's own eligibility; single and unmarried veterans qualify.
items.value: Lifetime benefit of up to 6 attempts to create embryos and up to 3 completed embryo transfer cycles, plus ART counseling and evaluation, plus cryopreservation of sperm, eggs and embryos with storage until the veteran's death. On the private market the same course runs $60,000 to $120,000 or more.
items.how: Start with a VA fertility evaluation. The service-connection link has to be documented — the disability, or the treatment for it, has to be causally related to the infertility. VA handles the eligibility determination; ART is usually delivered through a contracted community clinic.
