items.hack: The causal link is where these get denied, and it is winnable. Medication side effects count: if you are infertile because of a drug VA prescribed for a service-connected condition, that is 'treatment of a service-connected disability causally related to infertility.' Get that in writing from the prescribing physician before you apply. Note what VA will not pay for: donor eggs, donor sperm and donor embryos are on you even if you are otherwise eligible.
items.deadline: No application deadline. Lifetime caps of 6 embryo-creation attempts and 3 transfers.

items.title: VA adoption expense reimbursement — $2,000 per child, $5,000 per year (VA Form 10-10152)
items.who: Veterans who meet the same service-connected-infertility eligibility as the IVF benefit, who adopt a child under 18.
items.value: Up to $2,000 per adopted child and up to $5,000 in any calendar year, reimbursing qualifying adoption expenses — agency fees, legal and court costs, and other expenses recognized under the federal adoption tax credit rules.
items.how: File VA Form 10-10152, Reimbursement Request for Qualifying Adoption Expenses, with receipts and the adoption decree, through your VA facility.
items.hack: Almost nobody files this because it is not on any benefits checklist. If you qualified for the IVF benefit and IVF did not work, you are very likely eligible for this too — the same service-connected-infertility predicate covers both. Claim in the calendar year the expense hit, and if you adopt siblings, each child carries its own $2,000 up to the $5,000 annual ceiling.
items.deadline: Annual $5,000 cap resets each calendar year; file in the year the expense was incurred.

items.title: Designated Women's Health Primary Care Provider — ask for one by name
items.who: Any woman veteran enrolled in VA health care.
items.value: VA trains and designates specific primary care providers in women's health so you can get your primary care and your gender-specific care — cervical screening, breast exams, contraception, menopause management, gynecologic referral — from one clinician in one visit rather than being bounced between a PCP and a separate women's clinic. Comprehensive covered services include Pap tests, mammography, contraception, PCOS management, osteoporosis screening, thyroid and diabetes screening, and cardiovascular care.
items.how: Tell your facility you want to be assigned to a designated Women's Health Primary Care Provider. If they say there isn't one, that goes to the Women Veterans Program Manager, who can arrange community care if the facility cannot staff it.
items.hack: Mammography is a known VA weak point — many facilities have no mammography unit and must buy it in the community. If you are told to 'wait for the mobile unit,' ask for a community care referral instead, citing the access standards. A screening interval you miss is a diagnosis you get later and worse.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Menopause care at VA — covered, and worth claiming as secondary
items.who: Women veterans in perimenopause, menopause, or surgical/treatment-induced menopause.
items.value: VA covers menopause evaluation and management including hormone therapy, non-hormonal treatment of vasomotor symptoms, bone density screening and osteoporosis treatment, genitourinary symptom management, and the sleep and mood consequences.
items.how: Raise it with your women's health primary care provider. VA has menopause-specific clinical resources and some facilities run dedicated menopause clinics or e-consults.
items.hack: Surgical menopause caused by a service-connected condition or its treatment is a compensable chain, not just a health problem. If a service-connected condition drove a hysterectomy or oophorectomy, the resulting premature menopause, osteoporosis and associated depression can each be claimed as secondary under 38 CFR 3.310. Most women are never told this and file nothing.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: 38 CFR 4.116 — the gynecological rating schedule, code by code
items.who: Women veterans with service-connected gynecological or breast conditions.
items.value: The general formula for disease, injury or adhesions of the female reproductive organs (DC 7610-7615) is blunt: 0% if symptoms need no continuous treatment, 10% if they require continuous treatment, 30% if they are not controlled by continuous treatment. Specific codes pay far more: DC 7617 (uterus and both ovaries removed) 100% for 3 months then 50%; DC 7618 (uterus removed) 100% for 3 months then 30%; DC 7619 (both ovaries removed) 100% for 3 months then 30%, one ovary 0%; DC 7620 (atrophy of both ovaries) 20%; DC 7629 (endometriosis) 10 / 30 / 50% with the 50% requiring bowel or bladder involvement plus uncontrolled symptoms; DC 7626 (breast surgery) up to 80% for bilateral radical mastectomy.
items.how: File on 21-526EZ with the diagnosis, the surgical records, and — critically — evidence of whether continuous treatment controls your symptoms.
items.hack: The words 'not controlled by continuous treatment' are the entire difference between 10% and 30%. Your treatment records have to show you are on continuous treatment AND still symptomatic. If your gynecologist writes 'stable on therapy,' you get 10%. Bring a symptom log to the exam. Separately: DC 7632, female sexual arousal disorder, is rated 0% — but a 0% rating is the gateway to SMC-K, which is real money.
items.deadline: None; effective date rules under 38 CFR 3.400 apply.

items.title: Hysterectomy, oophorectomy and SMC-K — the women's version almost nobody files
items.who: Women veterans with service-connected loss or loss of use of a creative organ — removal of the uterus, removal of both ovaries, or service-connected anatomical loss of one or both breasts.
items.value: Special Monthly Compensation under 38 USC 1114(k) is paid on top of your combined rating and does not go through VA math — it is added to the check. Several codes in 38 CFR 4.116 are flagged for SMC entitlement, and the SMC determination is made under 38 CFR 3.350.
items.how: It is supposed to be awarded automatically when the rating is granted. It frequently is not. Check your rating decision for an SMC-K line. If it is missing, file a supplemental claim or, if the error is on the face of the decision, raise clear and unmistakable error — CUE has no deadline and pays the full retroactive amount.
items.hack: This is the single most-missed award for women veterans. SMC-K for male veterans gets written about constantly; the identical entitlement for service-connected hysterectomy or bilateral oophorectomy gets skipped by raters because the gynecological codes are rated less often. Pull every rating decision you have ever received and look for it. Years of retroactive SMC-K are recoverable through CUE.
items.deadline: No deadline on CUE.

items.title: Homeless women veterans — the VA programs, and the gap that makes them fail
items.who: Women veterans who are homeless or at imminent risk, including those with dependent children.
items.value: The same four programs serve women: SSVF served 91,005 veterans in FY2025 of whom 14,264 (16%) were women; HUD-VASH served 93,560 of whom 12,195 (13%) were women; Grant and Per Diem served 24,968 of whom 1,667 (7%) were women; HCHV contracted residential served 11,382 of whom 749 (7%) were women. HUD-VASH has designated special services for women veterans.
items.how: National Call Center for Homeless Veterans, 877-424-3838, free, confidential, 24/7. Or walk into any VA medical center and ask for the homeless program coordinator.
items.hack: Read those percentages: women are roughly 16% of SSVF but only 7% of transitional housing beds. That is the mechanism of the problem — transitional housing frequently cannot take children, and a mother will not separate from her kids to take a bed. If you have children, say so on the first call and ask specifically for SSVF rapid re-housing or HUD-VASH rather than a GPD bed, because those put you in a unit, not a congregate facility. If VA has nothing that takes children, that is exactly what Final Salute Inc exists for.
items.deadline: None; call before eviction, not after.

items.title: Final Salute Inc — housing for homeless women veterans and their children
items.who: Homeless women veterans and their children.
items.value: Transitional and permanent housing through its H.O.M.E. program, plus S.A.F.E. (financial assistance for rent, utilities and deposits) and Next Uniform (professional clothing). It exists because more than 60% of surveyed VA Grant and Per Diem programs serving homeless women veterans did not house children — a woman with kids had nowhere to go.
items.how: Apply through finalsaluteinc.org. Intake is through the organization directly, not through VA.
items.hack: Apply to Final Salute at the same time you apply for SSVF, not after SSVF denies you. They are different money and can stack — SSVF pays the landlord, Final Salute can cover the deposit, the gap month, and the furniture that SSVF will not. Waiting for one to fail before starting the other is how families end up in a car.
items.deadline: Rolling; capacity-limited.

items.title: Service Women's Action Network (SWAN) — advocacy, mentoring and MST policy work
items.who: Servicewomen, women veterans and their families.
items.value: SWAN runs peer mentoring and networking, a help line for benefits and claims navigation, and the national policy advocacy that produced much of the legal change around MST reporting, combat-exclusion repeal and women's health access at VA. It is the organization that pushed the data on MST claim denials into the public record.
items.how: servicewomensactionnetwork.org. Mentoring and member programs are free.
items.hack: If your MST claim was denied and you believe the denial reflects a pattern rather than your individual file, SWAN is the organization that collects and escalates those patterns. Individual representation still needs an accredited VSO or an attorney — but SWAN will point you at one who actually handles MST.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Grace After Fire and Women Veterans Alliance — peer support built by women veterans
items.org: Grace After Fire; Women Veterans Alliance
items.who: Women veterans of any era, any discharge, any rating.
items.value: Grace After Fire runs peer-led groups and the Table Talk program focused on self-knowledge, trauma recovery and substance use, originating in Texas with online reach. Women Veterans Alliance runs national and regional unconferences, a member directory of women-veteran-serving organizations, and connection programming. Neither requires VA enrollment or a rating.
items.how: graceafterfire.org and womenveteransalliance.com. Programs are generally free or low-cost to women veterans.
items.hack: These fill the gap VA structurally cannot: a room where you are not the only woman. Women veterans consistently report they do not use VA mental health because the waiting room and the group are 90% men, which is intolerable after MST. Peer programs are not a substitute for treatment, but they are often what gets someone to treatment.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Women's Health Transition Training — VA/DoD course before you separate
items.who: Servicewomen transitioning out, and recently separated women veterans.
items.value: A VA/DoD course that walks through what VA women's health actually covers, how to enroll, what to expect from a VA women's clinic, and how to move your care from military to VA without a gap. It exists because women separate at higher rates without ever enrolling.
items.how: Offered through the Transition Assistance Program and separately online; the Women Veterans Call Center (855-829-6636) can point you to the current delivery.
items.hack: Take it even if you already separated. The single biggest cost of not enrolling is not the health care — it is that you never get a VA treatment record, and without treatment records your disability claim five years from now has nothing to hang on. Enrollment is the evidence pipeline.
items.deadline: Best before separation; still useful after.

items.title: MST-related care is free, with no rating, no service connection, and no time limit
items.who: Any veteran or former service member who experienced sexual assault or repeated threatening sexual harassment during military service — any gender, any era.
items.value: Free treatment for any physical or mental health condition related to MST. No copay. No VA disability rating needed. No service connection needed. You do not have to have reported it at the time, and you do not have to have any proof that it happened. The standard length-of-service requirements do not apply — you are eligible even if you served under two years. Veterans with an Other Than Honorable discharge are eligible. National Guard and Reserve members with federal active duty or a service-connected disability are eligible.
items.how: Contact the MST Coordinator at any VA medical center, call 800-827-1000, or walk into a Vet Center. Tell them it is MST-related; that triggers the fee waiver.
items.hack: The two things people get wrong: first, they assume they need a filed report or an investigation, and there is no such requirement — VA does not ask you to prove it to get care. Second, they file a disability claim first, get denied, and conclude they are not entitled to anything. Health care and compensation are completely separate determinations. A denied MST compensation claim has no effect on your right to free MST care. Get the care, then fight the claim.
items.deadline: None. There is no time limit — a 1971 assault qualifies you today.

items.title: MST Coordinator — every VA medical center has one, and they are the door in
items.who: Any veteran seeking MST-related care.
items.value: A designated point of contact at every VA health care system whose job is to get MST survivors into care without making them retell the story to five people. They arrange the fee waiver, find MST-trained clinicians, and can request a clinician of your preferred sex — which VA is required to accommodate on request.
items.how: Ask the facility operator for the MST Coordinator. You do not need a referral and you do not need to be enrolled yet.
items.hack: Ask for the clinician-sex preference in the first contact, in writing if possible, not at the appointment. If you wait until you are in the room with a provider you cannot talk to, you lose the appointment and often you never come back. VA policy allows the request; the failure is usually scheduling, not policy.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: 38 CFR 3.304(f)(5) — the relaxed evidence rule for MST-based PTSD claims
items.who: Veterans claiming PTSD or another mental health condition caused by in-service personal assault, including MST.
items.value: For personal-assault stressors, VA is required to accept evidence from sources other than the service records to corroborate that the assault occurred. That is the whole point of the rule — most assaults were never reported, so requiring an official record would deny every claim. VA must also tell you it will consider this alternative evidence, and must give you the chance to furnish it.
items.how: File on VA Form 21-526EZ and submit markers.
items.hack: Markers are the mechanism. Build the list deliberately: a sudden unexplained request for transfer; a drop in performance evaluations or a demotion; disciplinary action or AWOL episodes that start abruptly; a sudden onset of substance use; requests for STI or pregnancy testing in the service treatment records with no other explanation; unexplained weight change; a documented mental health or chaplain visit; a divorce or breakup in that window; anxiety or panic symptoms appearing in the record; statements from family, roommates, fellow service members or clergy who remember you changing. Buddy statements go on VA Form 21-10210. Any DoD sexual assault or harassment reporting form, and any investigative report, is direct evidence if it exists — but the whole design of 3.304(f)(5) is that it does not have to.
items.deadline: None, but effective date runs from the claim or intent-to-file date.

items.title: MST Outreach Coordinator at the regional office — different person from the clinical MST Coordinator
items.who: Veterans filing an MST-related disability compensation claim.
items.value: Every VBA regional office has an MST Outreach Coordinator dedicated to MST claims — a benefits-side specialist, not a clinician. Both male and female coordinators are available. They help you assemble markers, understand what the rater is looking for, and track the claim.
items.how: Call 800-827-1000 and ask for the MST Outreach Coordinator at your regional office.
items.hack: People confuse this with the VHA MST Coordinator and get bounced. The clinical MST Coordinator arranges treatment; the VBA MST Outreach Coordinator works your claim. You want both, and they do not talk to each other automatically. Also: MST claims are supposed to be routed to specially trained raters. If your denial letter reads like the rater had no idea 3.304(f)(5) exists, that is grounds for a Higher-Level Review on a duty-to-assist or misapplication-of-law theory.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: MST claims are denied more than combat claims — know the number before you file
items.who: Anyone filing an MST-related PTSD claim.
items.value: Peer-reviewed analysis of VA claims from October 2017 through May 2022 found MST-related PTSD claims denied at 27.6% versus 18.2% for combat-related PTSD. The disparity was worse for male MST claimants and worse still for Black veterans. An earlier ACLU analysis of 2008-2012 data found MST-related PTSD granted at rates 16 to 30 percentage points below other PTSD claims annually.
items.how: Use the number as a planning input, not a reason to skip filing.
items.hack: Three practical consequences. One: do not file a bare claim and hope — MST claims are the ones where a thin file gets denied, so front-load markers and a private nexus opinion. Two: assume you may need the appeal, and preserve your effective date with an Intent to File (21-0966) the day you start. Three: get an accredited representative before the first decision, not after — an MST-experienced VSO or attorney changes outcomes on exactly these claims. Denial is not the end; supplemental claims and Board appeals overturn a substantial share of them.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: MST residential and inpatient treatment — including single-gender programs
items.who: Veterans whose MST-related symptoms are not manageable in outpatient care.
items.value: VA operates residential and inpatient MST programs, some of them single-gender, as part of the free MST-related care benefit. Covered at no cost like the rest of MST care. VA also funds travel to these programs, which are frequently not in your state.
items.how: Referral comes through your MST Coordinator or mental health provider. Ask specifically about single-gender residential options and about programs outside your VISN.
items.hack: Do not accept 'we don't have that here.' These are national programs and VA routinely sends veterans across the country for them, with travel covered. The limiting factor is usually that nobody at your facility mentioned they exist. Ask the MST Coordinator for the national MST residential program list by name.
items.deadline: None; waitlists are real, so ask early.

items.title: MST survivors with bad paper get VA mental health care by statute (38 USC 1720I)
items.who: Former service members with an Other Than Honorable discharge who were the victim of a physical assault of a sexual nature, a battery of a sexual nature, or sexual harassment while serving.
items.value: 38 USC 1720I requires VA to furnish an initial mental health assessment and the mental and behavioral health care needed to treat conditions arising from that trauma. The sexual-trauma pathway has no deployment requirement and no minimum-days requirement — unlike the combat pathway in the same statute, which requires more than 100 cumulative days and a deployment. Dishonorable discharges and discharges by court-martial are excluded.
items.how: Present at any VA medical center or Vet Center and state that you experienced MST and have an OTH discharge. Ask for care under 38 USC 1720I. Care can be delivered at non-VA facilities where clinically appropriate or geographically necessary.
items.hack: This is the most misunderstood eligibility rule in the system. An enormous number of MST survivors were pushed out with bad paper precisely because of the behavioral fallout from the assault — and then told they are not veterans and get nothing. That is wrong as a matter of law. You do not need an upgrade, you do not need a favorable character-of-discharge determination, and you do not need to wait. Ask for it by statute number if the clerk says no.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Sexual harassment — not just assault — is MST for VA purposes
items.who: Veterans who experienced repeated, threatening sexual harassment in service without a physical assault.
items.value: VA's statutory definition of MST covers psychological trauma resulting from a physical assault of a sexual nature, battery of a sexual nature, or sexual harassment which occurred while the veteran was serving on active duty, active duty for training, or inactive duty training. Harassment alone qualifies you for free MST-related care and can support a compensation claim.
items.how: Same doors: MST Coordinator for care, 21-526EZ plus markers for compensation.
items.hack: Survivors of harassment routinely disqualify themselves — 'nothing actually happened to me.' Under the statute, repeated threatening harassment is MST. The marker evidence is the same: transfer requests, performance drops, the abrupt AWOL, the sudden drinking. If a hostile command climate ended your career, that is the claim.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Don't Ask Don't Tell discharge upgrades — and the DoD proactive review
items.org: Department of Defense service review boards
items.who: Veterans separated because of sexual orientation under DADT (1994-2011) or the earlier outright bans that preceded it, going back decades.
items.value: An upgrade restores access to the full benefit set — VA health care, GI Bill, VA home loan, burial in a national cemetery — and corrects a DD-214 that has followed people through 30 years of job applications. DoD has moved to proactively review DADT-era discharges and correct narrative reasons, separation codes and characterizations, following litigation and a settlement covering LGBTQ+ veterans discharged under those policies.
items.how: Discharged within the last 15 years: apply to your service's Discharge Review Board on DD Form 293. More than 15 years ago — which covers most DADT and all pre-DADT separations: apply to the Board for Correction of Military/Naval Records on DD Form 149. Most services now take these online through their review boards agency portal.
items.hack: Do not wait for the proactive review to find you. It corrects records in batches and it is not a substitute for an individual application, especially if you want the narrative reason and separation code changed and not just the characterization. Ask for all three: characterization of service, narrative reason for separation, and the RE code. A DD-214 that still says 'homosexual conduct' under narrative reason is a document you hand to employers for the rest of your life. Also ask for the corrected DD-214 to be issued, not just a board decision letter.
items.deadline: BCMR has a 3-year statute of limitations from discovery of the error — but boards routinely waive it in the interest of justice for these cases, so file regardless and ask for the waiver explicitly.

items.title: VA gender-affirming care as of 2026 — what the official policy actually says
items.who: Transgender and gender-diverse veterans enrolled in VA health care.
items.value: Per VHA Notice 2025-01(1), effective March 17, 2025, which rescinded VHA Directive 1341: VA continues to provide health care to all veterans with gender dysphoria, including preventive and mental health care. Cross-sex hormone therapy is available only to veterans who were already receiving it from VA as of March 17, 2025, or who received it during military service and separated while eligible for VA care. For everyone else, VA does not provide cross-sex hormone therapy. VA does not provide any other medical or surgical therapy for gender dysphoria. The notice cites Executive Order 14168 and is scheduled for recertification by March 31, 2030.
items.how: If you were receiving hormone therapy from VA before March 17, 2025, or received it in service, document that and raise it with your provider — that is the grandfather clause and it is in writing. Otherwise VA will not initiate it.
items.hack: Get your grandfather status documented in your VA record now, in writing, rather than relying on a future clinician to reconstruct it. If you received hormone therapy in service, pull the service treatment records showing it and get them into the VA record — that is an independent eligibility path and it is easy to lose. Mental health care for gender dysphoria remains covered regardless. For care VA will not provide, community options and state Medicaid rules vary enormously; a VA social worker can sometimes help map them even when VA cannot deliver the care.
items.deadline: Grandfather status keys to March 17, 2025.

items.title: LGBTQ+ Veteran Care Coordinators — redesignated in June 2026, but the people are still there
items.who: LGBTQ+ veterans seeking a navigator inside a VA facility.
items.value: VA had an LGBTQ+ Veteran Care Coordinator at every health care system. A June 12, 2026 memorandum from the Under Secretary for Health redesignated those positions as general 'Care Coordinators' serving all veterans, and directed that VHA funds, official time, facilities and resources not be used for activities promoting gender ideology or gender identity. National supports — monthly coordinator calls, regional leadership meetings, new-coordinator orientation and dedicated channels — were discontinued. Members of Congress have publicly pressed VA to restore the role. In practice, many facilities still list an LGBTQ+ care coordinator and continue to provide mental health care, hormone therapy for grandfathered patients, gender-affirming prosthetics, and HIV and STI testing and treatment.
items.how: Call your VA facility and ask for the Care Coordinator, or search your facility's page — some still publish the LGBTQ+ title. If your facility has no one, ask the patient advocate for a named navigator.
items.hack: This is in flux and facility-by-facility. Do not conclude from a headline that VA will not treat you. Call the specific facility and ask what they currently provide. Document what you are told and by whom — if services you were receiving are withdrawn, that record is what a congressional caseworker or a VSO needs. Vet Centers are a separate system with their own counselors and remain a low-friction option for counseling.
items.deadline: Policy environment is actively changing; verify before relying.

items.title: Changing your name or gender marker in VA records
items.who: Veterans who have legally changed their name, or who want their VA record to reflect their gender identity.
items.value: A legal name change is straightforward and unaffected by the 2025-2026 policy shifts: VA updates your name in both health and benefits records on presentation of the court order or corrected identity documents. Gender marker handling in VA records has changed following Executive Order 14168 and the rescission of VHA Directive 1341, and current practice varies — verify with your facility rather than relying on older guidance describing self-identified gender identity fields.
items.how: For a legal name change, bring the court order or updated Social Security record to enrollment/eligibility at your VA facility and submit VA Form 10-10EZR to update health record information; VBA updates benefits records separately, so do both. For gender marker, ask the facility's enrollment office what the current process is.
items.hack: Do the name change in both systems on the same day. Veterans routinely update VHA and not VBA and then find their compensation deposits, letters and CHAMPVA cards carry the old name for years, which creates identity-verification failures at banks and lenders. Keep a copy of the court order in your own file — VA loses documents and you will be asked for it again.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: After an LGBTQ-related discharge upgrade — what you get back, and the retroactive question
items.who: Veterans whose discharge was upgraded because the separation was based on sexual orientation.
items.value: An upgrade to honorable restores the full benefit set: VA health care enrollment, disability compensation eligibility, GI Bill (subject to its own delimiting rules), VA home loan entitlement, burial in a national cemetery, and the veteran's preference in federal hiring. VA then re-examines eligibility from the corrected record.
items.how: Send the corrected DD-214 and the board decision to VA and file or re-file. If you previously had a claim denied solely on character of discharge, file a supplemental claim (VA Form 20-0995) attaching the upgrade.
items.hack: The effective date is where the money is. When a service department corrects a record, VA may be able to award benefits back to an earlier date than the date you re-filed — this is exactly the situation where you want an accredited representative arguing the effective date rather than accepting the date on the new decision letter. Also file an Intent to File (21-0966) the moment the board grants, before you assemble the claim, so you lock a date while you gather evidence.
items.deadline: File the supplemental claim promptly after the upgrade; effective-date rules under 38 CFR 3.400 apply.

items.title: PRIDE in All Who Served — the VA health education group, status uncertain in 2026
items.who: LGBTQ+ veterans.
items.value: A 10-week VA group health education program for LGBTQ+ veterans covering identity, minority stress, health engagement and suicide prevention. It ran at facilities across the country and had measurable effects on care engagement.
items.how: Ask your facility's mental health service or care coordinator whether the group is currently offered.
items.hack: Its status became uncertain after the June 2026 memorandum restricting VHA resources for gender-identity-related activities. Ask locally — some facilities have continued group programming under different framing. If it is gone at your facility, Vet Center groups and community organizations are the fallback, and Vet Centers operate under separate authority.
items.deadline: Verify current availability.

items.title: Character of Discharge determination — how OTH veterans get VA benefits with no upgrade at all
items.who: Veterans with an Other Than Honorable, bad conduct (special court-martial), or uncharacterized discharge.
items.value: This is the single most important thing bad-paper veterans do not know. VA makes its own decision about whether your service was 'under conditions other than dishonorable' for VA purposes. That decision is completely separate from a DoD discharge upgrade. A favorable Character of Discharge determination makes you eligible for VA benefits — health care, compensation, and more — with the same OTH discharge paper you have right now. You do not need the military to change anything.
items.how: File a claim (VA Form 21-526EZ) or apply for health care (10-10EZ). VA will open a character-of-discharge determination. Submit evidence going to 38 CFR 3.12(e): your service record, awards, deployments, the reasons for the misconduct, and any mental health condition. Get an accredited representative — this is a legal determination and it is winnable with argument.
items.hack: Run both tracks at once. File for the VA Character of Discharge determination AND apply to the DoD board for an upgrade, because they are independent, use different standards, and the COD determination is usually faster. Veterans lose years assuming they must be upgraded first. They must not.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: 38 CFR 3.12 — the statutory bars, the regulatory bars, and the compelling circumstances escape hatch
items.who: Anyone going through a Character of Discharge determination.
items.value: Six statutory bars are absolute: conscientious-objector refusal of duty or orders; discharge by sentence of general court-martial; officer resignation for the good of the service; being characterized as a deserter; release as an alien during hostilities on affirmative request; and AWOL for a continuous period of at least 180 days. Two regulatory bars have no compelling-circumstances exception: discharge in lieu of trial by general court-martial, and mutiny or espionage. But the two most common regulatory bars — offenses involving moral turpitude, and willful and persistent misconduct — DO have a compelling circumstances exception under 3.12(e).
items.how: Argue 3.12(e) explicitly. VA weighs three things: (1) whether the quality and length of your service was otherwise honest, faithful and meritorious; (2) the reasons for the AWOL or misconduct — and the regulation names mental health conditions including PTSD, depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and ADHD, plus physical health, combat hardship, sexual abuse, duress, family obligations, age and education; (3) whether you had a valid legal defense that would have precluded a UCMJ conviction.
items.hack: The 180-day AWOL statutory bar is the one that ends cases, and it is measured as a continuous period. Multiple short AWOLs that add to more than 180 days are willful and persistent misconduct — a regulatory bar, which means compelling circumstances is available. Get the exact AWOL dates from the service record before you concede anything. Separately, 38 CFR 3.12(b): insanity at the time of the offense removes all bars, and VA's definition of insanity is broader than the criminal-law one.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Discharge Review Board vs Board for Correction of Military Records — pick the right one
items.who: Any veteran seeking a discharge upgrade or record correction.
items.value: Two different boards, two different forms, two different windows. The Discharge Review Board (DD Form 293) handles discharges within the last 15 years and can change characterization, narrative reason and RE code — but it cannot touch a discharge by general court-martial. The Board for Correction of Military/Naval Records (DD Form 149) handles anything older than 15 years and anything the DRB cannot do, including general court-martial discharges, and can correct any error or injustice in a military record. BCMR carries a 3-year statute of limitations from discovery of the error, which boards may waive in the interest of justice.
items.how: Under 15 years: DD Form 293 to the service DRB, and you can request a personal appearance hearing, which materially improves outcomes. Over 15 years: DD Form 149 to the BCMR, which is normally decided on the written record.
items.hack: If you are inside 15 years, go to the DRB first and request a personal appearance. Two reasons: a DRB denial does not bar a later BCMR application, and the hearing is the only place a human hears you describe what happened. If you are outside 15 years, do not skip the statute-of-limitations issue — state in the application that you request waiver in the interest of justice and explain why the delay was reasonable (you did not know the mental health condition was the cause; you only recently obtained the diagnosis).
items.deadline: DRB: 15 years from discharge. BCMR: 3 years from discovery of the error, waivable.

items.title: Hagel, Kurta and Wilkie — the three memos that changed discharge upgrades
items.who: Veterans seeking an upgrade where PTSD, TBI, MST or another mental health condition contributed to the misconduct.
items.value: Hagel (September 2014) requires liberal consideration for veterans with PTSD or related conditions, and accepts VA determinations, civilian medical records and service treatment records as evidence. Kurta (August 2017) extends the framework to TBI, MST and other invisible wounds, applies it to both DRBs and BCM/NRs, and supplies four questions boards must work through — including whether the condition existed even if undiagnosed at the time, and whether it excuses or mitigates the misconduct. Wilkie (July 2018) adds clemency and rehabilitation as independent grounds: candor, acceptance of responsibility, character references and post-discharge conduct. Together they mean a board must ask whether the condition outweighs the misconduct, not whether you proved you were diagnosed in service.
items.how: Cite them by name in the application. Attach a mental health opinion linking the condition to the misconduct — a VA diagnosis, a civilian provider letter, or a psychological evaluation. State explicitly that you are requesting liberal consideration under Kurta and clemency under Wilkie.
items.hack: Answer Kurta's four questions in your own application, in order, as headings. Did the condition exist during service? Did it excuse or mitigate the discharge? Does it outweigh the discharge? If upgraded, would the veteran have been discharged anyway? Boards work through those questions; handing them the answers already organized is the difference between a grant and a form denial. Add the Wilkie clemency argument even if your Kurta case is strong — it is a separate, independent path to relief and it costs nothing to include.
items.deadline: Same board deadlines apply.

items.title: Discharge Appeal Review Board (DARB) — the final DoD appeal, and its hard limits
items.who: Veterans discharged on or after December 20, 2019 with a less-than-honorable characterization, whose upgrade request was denied or only partially granted by a service BCM/NR after exhausting the DRB.
items.value: An independent DoD-level review of the case record that applies DoD policy without deference to the prior board's decision, and can recommend a full upgrade, a partial upgrade, or denial. A surviving spouse, next of kin or legal representative can petition on behalf of a deceased or legally incompetent former member.
items.how: No form is required — an email or letter requesting final review is sufficient; sample templates are on the Air Force Review Boards Agency portal. You must submit within 365 calendar days of receiving the BCM/NR decision; DARB may deny an untimely request.
items.hack: Two traps. First, the December 20, 2019 discharge-date floor excludes most bad-paper veterans entirely — if you were discharged before that date, DARB is not available to you and your path is BCMR reconsideration. Second, DARB cannot consider new evidence. If you have anything new — a fresh diagnosis, a new nexus letter, records you just obtained — do NOT send it to DARB. Take it back to the BCM/NR as a reconsideration request first, because new evidence is what reopens a board and DARB will simply refuse to look at it.
items.deadline: 365 calendar days after receiving the BCM/NR decision.

items.title: Bad paper does not block emergency mental health care
items.who: Former service members with OTH discharges in crisis.
items.value: Two independent authorities. Under the COMPACT Act and 38 CFR 17.1200-17.1230, individuals described in 38 USC 1720I — which includes OTH veterans — get emergent suicide care at any VA or non-VA facility at no cost. Under 38 USC 1720I itself, OTH former members who deployed for more than 100 cumulative days, or who experienced sexual trauma in service, get an initial mental health assessment and ongoing mental and behavioral health care. Dishonorable and court-martial discharges are excluded from 1720I.
items.how: In crisis: call 988 and press 1, or go to the nearest emergency department, VA or not. For non-emergency care: present at a VA medical center and ask for care under 38 USC 1720I, or walk into a Vet Center, which does not check discharge status for counseling.
items.hack: The words that work at an intake desk are 'I am requesting emergent suicide care under the COMPACT Act' or 'I am requesting care under 38 USC 1720I.' Clerks are trained on enrollment, not on these authorities, and an OTH will trip the enrollment screen. Naming the authority moves it to someone who knows. And do not let a facility bill you — the regulation says VA will not charge eligible individuals for emergent suicide care at VA or non-VA facilities.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: What an OTH veteran can already get today, with no upgrade and no COD determination
items.who: Veterans with less-than-honorable discharges.
items.value: Without any change to your paper: free MST-related care regardless of discharge; mental and behavioral health care under 38 USC 1720I if you deployed 100+ days or experienced MST; emergent suicide care at any facility under the COMPACT Act; Vet Center readjustment counseling, which does not screen on characterization; homeless program services and the National Call Center for Homeless Veterans (877-424-3838); Veterans Justice Outreach and HCRV services; and, at many nonprofits — Cohen Veterans Network among them — full clinical mental health care with any discharge status.
items.how: Each door is separate. Do not ask one intake desk about all of them.
items.hack: The thing that costs bad-paper veterans the most is the belief that the OTH ended everything, so they never walk in anywhere. It did not. Start with a Vet Center, because they are the least bureaucratic front door in the entire system and they will tell you which of the other doors you can walk through.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Veterans Treatment Courts — roughly 745 of them, and how to get into one
items.org: State and local courts; VA Veterans Justice Outreach
items.who: Veterans facing criminal charges, typically where a service-connected condition — substance use, PTSD, TBI — drove the offense.
items.value: As of VA's December 2025 inventory, approximately 745 Veterans Treatment Courts and other veteran-focused court programs operate nationally, served by VJO specialists. A VTC substitutes structured treatment, judicial supervision and a veteran mentor for incarceration. Successful completion typically means dismissal or reduction of charges — which means no felony conviction, which means the 61st-day compensation reduction never happens and your employability survives.
items.how: Raise veteran status at the first possible moment — arrest, booking, arraignment, first meeting with counsel. Tell your defense attorney you are a veteran and ask for a VTC referral. Ask the jail for the VJO specialist. Do not wait for anyone to notice your DD-214.
items.hack: Eligibility criteria vary enormously court to court — VA's own fact sheet says there is considerable variation in participant eligibility and process — and VA does not decide who gets admitted. The decision belongs to the prosecutor and the judge. That means the advocacy matters: a VJO specialist's treatment assessment, delivered to the court early, is often what converts a prosecutor's 'no' into a 'yes.' Timing is everything: once a plea is entered, the diversion window usually closes.
items.deadline: Effectively, before plea. Move at arrest.

items.title: Veterans Justice Outreach specialists — VA staff assigned to jails and courts
items.org: VA Homeless Programs / Veterans Justice Programs
items.who: Justice-involved veterans in jails, in diversionary treatment courts, or in contact with law enforcement.
items.value: VJO specialists conduct outreach and assessment in jails and courts nationwide, link veterans to VA health care, housing, treatment and recovery services, and report treatment progress to the court with the veteran's permission. They are the connective tissue between a courtroom and the VA system, and they operate at every intercept from pre-arrest through court.
items.how: Ask the jail, the public defender or the court for the VJO specialist. Contacts are published by region on VA's Veterans Justice Programs page. The National Call Center for Homeless Veterans, 877-424-3838, can also route you.
items.hack: The VJO's assessment is evidence a judge can act on. A defense attorney who submits a VJO treatment plan at sentencing is offering the court a concrete alternative to jail — courts take that far more seriously than a defendant's own promise to get help. Have your attorney request it in writing and attach it. Note the consent point: VJO reports progress to the court only with your permission, so understand what you are authorizing.
items.deadline: None; earlier is better.

items.title: Health Care for Re-entry Veterans (HCRV) — start it before the release date
items.who: Veterans incarcerated in state or federal prison who will be returning to the community.
items.value: HCRV specialists conduct outreach and pre-release assessment inside the prison, build referrals to medical, mental health, social and employment services timed to the release date, and provide short-term case management after release. The program exists specifically to prevent post-incarceration homelessness, which is the dominant failure mode for released veterans.
items.how: Request an HCRV specialist through the prison's classification, medical or re-entry staff, or have a family member call the National Call Center for Homeless Veterans at 877-424-3838. Regional HCRV specialist contacts are published on VA's site.
items.hack: Start 6 to 12 months before release, not at the gate. The things that take time — restarting compensation, a HUD-VASH voucher, a housing placement, a primary care appointment — all have queues, and a veteran released with nothing queued sleeps outside. VA does not duplicate medical care the institution already provides, so HCRV's real value is the handoff, and a handoff has to be arranged in advance.
items.deadline: Begin 6-12 months pre-release.

items.title: VA compensation during incarceration — the 61st day rule, exactly
items.who: Veterans imprisoned for a felony conviction in a federal, state or local penal institution for more than 60 days.
items.value: Reduction starts on the 61st day of incarceration, not day one, and not at conviction. If you are rated 20% or more, payment drops to the rate payable at 10% under 38 USC 1114(a). If you are rated less than 20%, payment drops to one-half of that 10% rate. Surviving spouses, children and parents incarcerated for a felony are likewise reduced to one-half the 10% rate. Misdemeanor convictions do not trigger the reduction. Work release and halfway house placements do not trigger it. VA pension stops entirely on the 61st day, for felony or misdemeanor.
items.how: Notify VA of the incarceration. Failure to report creates an overpayment debt that VA will recoup from your benefits for years after release.
items.hack: Report it. Veterans hide the incarceration hoping the check keeps coming, and VA finds out through data matching with corrections agencies — then assesses an overpayment with interest against a man who just got out with nothing. Reporting also starts the apportionment clock for your family, which is money your dependents can actually receive while you cannot. Note the other trap: this is a reduction in payment, not a reduction in rating. Your rating is untouched, and it resumes in full on release.
items.deadline: Reduction effective the 61st day of incarceration.

items.title: Apportionment — the money your family can collect while you are inside
items.who: Spouses, children and dependent parents of an incarcerated veteran whose compensation has been reduced.
items.value: The compensation not paid to the incarcerated veteran may be apportioned to the spouse, to the children in equal shares, or to dependent parents in equal shares. This is not automatic — the dependent must file their own claim. Dependents who are themselves incarcerated for a felony conviction are not eligible, and no apportionment is made if the veteran or the dependent is a fugitive felon.
items.how: The dependent files an apportionment claim with VA on their own behalf. The claim must be filed within 1 year after notice to the incarcerated person, and supporting evidence within 1 year of VA's request for it.
items.hack: Nobody tells the family. The veteran is reduced to the 10% rate, the household loses the income, and the spouse never learns that the withheld amount is claimable by her. File it the same week you report the incarceration. Watch the one-year clocks — they are real and they run from VA's notice, not from your awareness of the program. On release, the veteran's award resumes at the full rate from the date of last payment to the apportionee, so the money is not double-counted but it is also not lost.
items.deadline: 1 year after notice to file; 1 year to furnish requested evidence.

items.title: Restarting VA compensation on release — request it 30 days before the gate
items.who: Veterans being released from incarceration whose benefits were reduced.
items.value: The award resumes at the full rate effective the date of release, provided VA receives notice of the release within 1 year. If VA does not get notice within that year, resumption runs only from the date notice is received — and you permanently lose the months in between.
items.how: VA accepts a resumption request up to 30 days before the anticipated release date, using official documentation from the parole board or the institution. Send it in advance with the projected release date.
items.hack: This is the most expensive deadline in the justice-involved benefits world and the least known. A veteran released in March who tells VA the following June is fine. A veteran who spends 18 months re-establishing himself and then files loses roughly a year and a half of full-rate compensation with no recourse. File the 30-day advance request from inside, and have a family member confirm VA received it. If you are already past the year, file anyway and get a representative — the record of when VA had constructive notice sometimes exists in the file.
items.deadline: Notify VA within 1 year of release. Request can be filed 30 days before release.

items.title: VA Office of Tribal Government Relations — the tribal-side entry point
items.org: VA Office of Tribal Government Relations (OTGR)
items.who: American Indian and Alaska Native veterans, tribal governments, tribal veterans service organizations.
items.value: OTGR runs VA's government-to-government relationship with tribes under VA's Tribal Consultation Policy, works to increase access to health care in Indian Country, and supports tribal access to VA housing, education and benefits programs. It has regional program specialists assigned to state groupings, which is how a tribe or an individual gets a named VA contact rather than a call center.
items.how: Email tribalgovernmentconsultation@va.gov or call 202-227-7935, and ask for the regional specialist covering your state.
items.hack: Use OTGR when the problem is structural — the nearest VA facility is four hours away, the tribal clinic cannot get reimbursed, the tribe wants to stand up a veterans cemetery or a VSO program. For an individual claim, go to a Tribal Veterans Service Officer or an accredited VSO instead. OTGR's leverage is on the institutional side, and that is where it is worth a great deal.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA/IHS and VA/Tribal Health Program reimbursement agreements — get VA care at your tribal clinic
items.org: VA, Indian Health Service, tribal health programs
items.who: Native veterans who are enrolled in VA health care and who use an IHS facility, a Tribal Health Program, or an Urban Indian Organization.
items.value: Under authority from the Indian Health Care Improvement Act, VA reimburses IHS and tribal health programs for direct care services provided to eligible American Indian and Alaska Native veterans. The practical effect: you can receive covered care at the clinic in your community and VA pays the clinic, rather than you driving hours to a VA medical center. There is no charge to the veteran for services covered under the agreement.
items.how: Enroll in VA health care (10-10EZ) — enrollment is the predicate, and many eligible Native veterans have never enrolled. Then ask your tribal health program or IHS facility whether they hold a reimbursement agreement with VA, and tell them you are a VA-enrolled veteran.
items.hack: Enrollment is the whole game and it is free. Native veterans often use IHS exclusively and never enroll with VA because they already have a clinic — but without VA enrollment, the tribal clinic cannot bill VA, and you also have no VA treatment record, which is what a future disability claim runs on. Enroll even if you never intend to set foot in a VA hospital. Note that agreements are held facility by facility, so a 'yes' at one clinic does not mean 'yes' at the next.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Tribal Veterans Service Officers and Tribal Veterans Representatives
items.org: Tribal governments; VA OTGR; state departments of veterans affairs
items.who: Veterans living on or near tribal lands.
items.value: Many tribes maintain their own veterans service officers, trained and in some cases VA-accredited, who file claims, obtain records and navigate both the VA and tribal benefit systems. Tribal Veterans Representative training has been delivered through VA and partner organizations to put trained advocates in communities where the nearest VA regional office is hundreds of miles away.
items.how: Ask your tribal government's veterans office. Your state department of veterans affairs and OTGR's regional specialist can identify who serves your area.
items.hack: Verify accreditation before handing over your file. A tribal veterans representative who is not VA-accredited can help you gather documents but cannot formally represent you before VA, and you want an accredited representative of record on the claim. Search the veteran's representative in VA's accreditation database. If your tribal officer is not accredited, keep them for the local knowledge and add an accredited VSO as representative of record — the two roles coexist fine.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Veterans Cemetery Grants Program — tribal organizations can build and run their own cemetery
items.who: Federally recognized tribal governments and tribal organizations; and Native veterans and families who want burial in their own community.
items.value: NCA's grant program funds up to 100% of the development cost of establishing, expanding or improving a veterans cemetery operated by a state or a tribal organization, including initial operating equipment. VA cannot pay for land acquisition, and administration, operation and maintenance are solely the recipient government's responsibility. Tribal veterans cemeteries now exist on tribal lands across the country. For a family, this is the difference between burying a veteran hundreds of miles away in a national cemetery and burying them at home with full honors and a VA headstone.
items.how: Tribes apply through the NCA grants program. Families should check cem.va.gov's list of grant-funded cemeteries for one near them — eligibility and residency rules are set by the operating tribe or state, not by VA.
items.hack: Grant-funded cemeteries are not national cemeteries, and the eligibility rules differ — many have a residency requirement and some have different spouse rules. Check with the specific cemetery before you assume. The federal headstone or marker and the burial flag are available either way, and so is the Presidential Memorial Certificate.
items.deadline: Grant cycles are announced periodically on grants.gov.

items.title: Center for Minority Veterans and the Minority Veterans Program Coordinator at your facility
items.who: American Indian and Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, Black, Hispanic and Asian American veterans.
items.value: CMV is the Secretary's principal advisor on minority veterans and runs the Minority Veterans Program, which places coordinators at VA regional offices, health care facilities and cemeteries. Those coordinators are a named local contact for access problems, and CMV runs the Advisory Committee on Minority Veterans, which reports to the Secretary and to Congress.
items.how: Phone 202-461-6191, email vacocmv@va.gov, or use ask.va.gov and select Center for Minority Veterans. For a local problem, ask your facility for the Minority Veterans Program Coordinator.
items.hack: Native Hawaiian and Alaska Native veterans in particular fall between programs — OTGR's authority runs to federally recognized tribes, which leaves Native Hawaiian veterans outside it. CMV is the office that covers them, and it is the right channel when the tribal-specific programs do not apply to you.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VHA Office of Rural Health — 2.99 million rural veterans and the programs built for them
items.who: Veterans in rural and highly rural counties.
items.value: 2.99 million rural veterans are enrolled in VA health care. Rural veterans enroll at 66% versus 47% for urban veterans — they depend on VA far more heavily. ORH funded 34 Enterprise-Wide Initiatives in FY2025 spanning primary care, specialty care, mental health, geriatrics, transportation and workforce, which is the mechanism that pushes services into places that cannot support a full medical center.
items.how: ruralhealth.va.gov lists the current Enterprise-Wide Initiatives. Ask your VA facility which ORH-funded programs it hosts — most veterans have never heard the term and the programs are not advertised locally.
items.hack: The EWI list is the useful artifact. When your facility says a service is unavailable, check whether an ORH initiative funds that exact service somewhere in your VISN — tele-specialty care, rural mental health, geriatric outreach — and ask to be referred into it. These are funded programs looking for patients, and the mismatch is almost always that nobody at the local clinic knows they exist.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: ATLAS telehealth sites — a private VA appointment room at the VFW post or Walmart
items.org: VA Office of Connected Care, with VFW, American Legion, Philips and Walmart
items.who: Rural veterans who lack broadband at home or cannot drive to a VA facility.
items.value: Accessing Telehealth through Local Area Stations puts a private, equipped room with a high-quality connection and peripheral devices in a community building — VFW posts, American Legion posts, Walmart locations, county veterans service offices — so a veteran can attend a VA telehealth appointment without a two-hour drive and without home internet. Free to the veteran.
items.how: Ask your VA care team to schedule your telehealth appointment at an ATLAS site and ask which sites serve your area. Local VFW and American Legion posts often know before VA schedulers do.
items.hack: This solves the specific rural failure that telehealth otherwise creates: VA moves your appointment to video, you have no broadband, and you simply miss care. Before you accept a video appointment, ask where the nearest ATLAS site is. If there is none, that is also a concrete fact to give your VA care team when you request an in-person or community care referral instead.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Veterans Transportation Service — VA drives you, free
items.who: Enrolled veterans who need transportation to VA health care, particularly those who cannot drive or have no vehicle.
items.value: VTS operates VA-owned and VA-contracted vehicles, including wheelchair-accessible vans, that take veterans to and from VA appointments at no cost. It is separate from mileage reimbursement — this is an actual ride, not money back after you find your own way there. Mobility managers at facilities coordinate it alongside DAV volunteer drivers and community transit.
items.how: Call your VA facility and ask for the VTS office or the mobility manager. Book in advance; same-day is rarely possible.
items.hack: Veterans get told about travel reimbursement and never about VTS, which is the wrong benefit for someone who cannot drive at all. Ask specifically for the mobility manager, who can combine VTS, DAV volunteer drivers, highly rural transportation grantees and local transit into one solution. If you need a wheelchair-accessible vehicle or a ride to a distant specialty appointment, say that at booking — those require specific vehicles and lead time.
items.deadline: None; book ahead.

items.title: Beneficiary travel — 41.5 cents a mile, and the deductible that eats short trips
items.who: Veterans eligible for travel reimbursement — 30% or higher rating, travel for treatment of a service-connected condition, pension recipients, income below the threshold, or inability to afford travel. Caregivers and required attendants also qualify.
items.value: VA pays 41.5 cents ($0.415) per mile for approved health-related travel. The deductible is $3 per one-way trip, $6 per round trip, capped at $18 per calendar month — after $18 in a month, everything is covered. VA also pays tolls and parking, preapproved public transit and taxi or plane fare, ambulance and wheelchair-van transport, and meals and lodging up to 50% of the local government employee rate with receipts and preapproval.
items.how: File in the Beneficiary Travel Self-Service System (BTSSS), or on VA Form 10-3542 at the facility, or at smartphone check-in for mileage-only claims. File within 30 days — later claims are usually denied.
items.hack: Three things people leave on the table. One: the deductible can be waived if you receive VA pension, are attending a VA claim exam, or meet the income threshold — ask for the waiver rather than assuming. Two: the special-mode transport benefit (ambulance, wheelchair van) requires preauthorization except in an emergency, so get it arranged in advance rather than paying for a van and fighting about it later. Three: meals and lodging exist and almost nobody claims them, but they need preapproval and receipts — if VA is sending you 200 miles for a specialty appointment, ask about lodging before you go.
items.deadline: File within 30 days of the appointment.

items.title: VA Community Living Centers — VA's own nursing homes
items.who: Enrolled veterans who need short-stay rehabilitation or long-term nursing care.
items.value: VA-operated nursing centers designed to feel residential, with 24/7 nursing and medical care and assistance with daily activities. Used for post-hospital rehabilitation, skilled nursing, dementia care, respite and hospice. Copays may apply depending on service connection and income.
items.how: Referral comes through your VA primary care team or a VA social worker. Ask for a geriatric or long-term care assessment.
items.hack: Ask for a Geriatric Evaluation before any placement decision. It is a comprehensive interdisciplinary assessment that produces a written care plan, and it frequently concludes that home and community-based services — home health aide, adult day health care, Veteran-Directed Care — will work, which is both better for the veteran and far cheaper. Families default to 'nursing home' because it is the only option they can name. VA has eleven others.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: State Veterans Homes — and the rule that makes them free for 70%+ veterans
items.org: VA Geriatrics and Extended Care; state governments
items.who: Veterans, and in many states spouses and Gold Star parents. 172 State Veterans Homes operate across all 50 states and Puerto Rico, serving roughly 20,000 veterans.
items.value: Here is the part almost nobody knows. Under 38 USC 1745 and 38 CFR 51.41, for a veteran who needs nursing home care for a VA-adjudicated service-connected disability, or who is rated 70% or higher (including TDIU) and needs nursing home care, VA pays the State Home the full prevailing rate for the geographic area — and the regulation states the State Home shall not charge any individual, insurer or entity other than VA for that care. For everyone else, VA pays basic per diem at the lesser of half the daily cost of care or the published basic rate, and the resident pays the balance — still typically far below private nursing home pricing, which runs well over $100,000 a year in most of the country.
items.how: Apply directly to the state home; each state runs its own admission process and residency rules. Have VA confirm your rating and whether the nursing care is for a service-connected condition — that determination is what unlocks 38 USC 1745.
items.hack: Before admission, get in writing whether you are being admitted under 38 USC 1745 prevailing-rate payment or under basic per diem. The financial difference for a family is total: one path costs the veteran nothing, the other has the family paying a monthly balance for years. If the veteran is at 60% and the nursing need is arguably tied to a service-connected condition, that is worth an increase claim or a TDIU claim before admission, not after.
items.deadline: None; admission waitlists in many states are long.

items.title: Medical Foster Home — a private home instead of a nursing home, $1,500-$3,000/month
items.who: Veterans who need nursing-home-level care but want a small residential setting, and who are enrolled in VA Home Based Primary Care.
items.value: A private residence where a trained caregiver provides 24/7 care to a small number of residents — typically three or fewer. The veteran pays $1,500 to $3,000 per month depending on income and care needs. VA inspects and approves the homes and provides the clinical care through the Home Based Primary Care team, but VA does not pay the room-and-board cost.
items.how: Ask your VA social worker or case manager. Enrollment in Home Based Primary Care is mandatory, and availability is by facility — not every VA medical center runs the program.
items.hack: The math is the point: a private nursing home in most markets is $8,000 to $12,000 a month. A Medical Foster Home is $1,500 to $3,000, and VA's clinical team comes to the house. And this is the ideal use of VA Aid and Attendance pension — the A&A rate can cover most or all of the monthly cost, which means a low-income wartime veteran can receive 24-hour care at effectively no net cost. Almost no family is told these two benefits fit together.
items.deadline: None; limited by local availability.

items.title: Veteran-Directed Care — VA hands you a budget and you hire your own caregiver, including family
items.org: VA and the Administration for Community Living (ACL), delivered through Area Agencies on Aging and ADRCs
items.who: Veterans of any age at risk of nursing home placement who need help with daily activities.
items.value: The veteran receives a flexible, VA-funded budget and directs their own care: they decide who to hire, what services to buy, and how to spend it, with fiscal management services handling payroll and paperwork. In practice this is the program that lets a veteran pay a family member to be the caregiver — which is what most families are already doing for free. Operating across all 50 states and territories; as of ACL's reporting, 95 VA medical centers had referred at least one veteran and 48 had referred none.
items.how: Ask your VA social worker or primary care team for a Veteran-Directed Care referral. The program is administered locally by an Area Agency on Aging or Aging and Disability Resource Center, which does the assessment and counseling.
items.hack: This is the most underused program in VA geriatrics, and the reason is on the referral side: 48 VA medical centers have referred nobody. If your facility says they do not have it, that usually means nobody there has made a referral, not that it is unavailable — it runs in all 50 states. Escalate to the Geriatrics and Extended Care chief or the patient advocate. And understand the distinction from PCAFC: VDC has no 70% rating requirement and no line-of-duty injury requirement, so it reaches veterans PCAFC excludes, including Vietnam and Korea-era veterans with age-related needs.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Homemaker and Home Health Aide services — a VA-paid aide in your home
items.who: Enrolled veterans who need help with activities of daily living and want to stay at home.
items.value: A trained home health aide, supervised by a registered nurse, comes to the home to help with bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting and other personal care. It is a clinical VA service, covered under standard VA health benefits with possible copays — not a cash benefit and not the same as Veteran-Directed Care.
items.how: Ask your VA primary care team or social worker for a referral and an assessment of activities-of-daily-living needs.
items.hack: The number of hours is set by the assessment, so how the assessment is documented determines what you get. Before the assessment, write down what actually happens on the worst days, not an average day — families consistently understate need out of pride and then get four hours a week. If the award is inadequate, ask for a reassessment, and ask about combining it with Adult Day Health Care and Respite, which are separate authorizations and stack.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Adult Day Health Care — daytime care that keeps a caregiver employed
items.who: Veterans with chronic conditions who want to remain at home, and their caregivers.
items.value: A daytime program providing social activities, companionship, recreation, and clinical care and supervision, at a VA facility or a VA-contracted community site. Covered under standard VA health benefits with possible copays.
items.how: Referral through your VA primary care team or social worker.
items.hack: This is the program that determines whether the family caregiver can keep a job. A spouse caring for a veteran with dementia cannot work; a spouse whose veteran is in ADHC five days a week can. Frame the request that way in the referral conversation — the clinical need and the caregiver's employment are both legitimate factors, and the second one is what makes the placement durable.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Respite Care — the caregiver's benefit, and it is a distinct authorization
items.who: Enrolled veterans with a family caregiver.
items.value: VA pays for someone to come into the home, or for the veteran to attend a program outside the home or have a short inpatient stay, so the family caregiver can take a break. Primary Family Caregivers approved in PCAFC receive at least 30 days of respite care per year; respite is also available as a general VA health benefit outside PCAFC.
items.how: Ask your VA social worker or the Caregiver Support Coordinator. If you are in PCAFC, ask the Caregiver Support Line at 1-855-260-3274.
items.hack: Respite goes unused because caregivers feel guilty taking it, and because it is authorized separately from everything else — nobody offers it, you have to ask. Use it before you are in crisis. Caregiver collapse is the most common reason a veteran who could have stayed home ends up in a nursing home permanently, and that outcome costs everyone, including VA, far more than the respite would have.
items.deadline: PCAFC respite: at least 30 days per year, use-it-or-lose-it by year.

items.title: Home Based Primary Care — a VA physician-led team that comes to the house
items.who: Enrolled veterans with complex chronic conditions for whom clinic visits are difficult or unsafe.
items.value: A VA interdisciplinary team led by a VA physician — nursing, therapy, pharmacy, social work, dietetics, mental health — delivers primary care in the veteran's home. Covered under standard VA benefits. It is also the gateway requirement for the Medical Foster Home program.
items.how: Ask your VA primary care provider for an HBPC referral, or ask a VA social worker.
items.hack: HBPC is the highest-value geriatric program VA runs and it is capacity-limited, so referrals are rationed by whoever asks. Ask by name. Two specific triggers that strengthen a referral: repeat emergency department visits, and a documented pattern of missed clinic appointments because of transportation or frailty. And if a Medical Foster Home is your eventual goal, HBPC enrollment is mandatory — start it early.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA hospice and palliative care — and what it does to copays
items.who: Veterans with serious illness (palliative) or a terminal condition with a prognosis under 6 months who are no longer pursuing curative treatment (hospice).
items.value: VA provides hospice at home, in a Community Living Center, in a contracted community hospice, or in an inpatient setting, and palliative care for symptom and pain management alongside ongoing treatment. Hospice care furnished by VA is provided without copayment, and VA can purchase community hospice when that is where the veteran wants to be.
items.how: Ask the VA care team for a palliative care consult. You do not have to be dying to get palliative care — that is the most common misunderstanding, and palliative consults improve both symptoms and survival in serious illness.
items.hack: Two things families miss. First, ask for the palliative consult early, at diagnosis of a serious illness, not at the end — it is symptom management, not a decision to stop treatment. Second, check burial and survivor benefits before the death, not after: burial allowance, headstone, flag, Presidential Memorial Certificate, and critically, whether there is a pending claim that a survivor should substitute into. A pending claim that dies with the veteran can be worth tens of thousands of dollars to the family, and the window to act is one year.
items.deadline: None for hospice; see accrued benefits and substitution for the 1-year survivor deadline.

items.title: Aid and Attendance, VA pension and Medicaid — how they actually interact for long-term care
items.who: Low-income wartime veterans and surviving spouses needing long-term care.
items.value: VA pension with Aid and Attendance is cash that can be used for any care arrangement, including paying a family member or a Medical Foster Home. Medicaid pays for institutional nursing home care and, through waivers, home and community-based services. They are different programs with different rules, and both matter: A&A is not counted the way earned income is for many purposes, and the combination is what makes home-based care affordable.
items.how: Apply for VA pension and A&A through VA. Apply for Medicaid through the state. Do both — eligibility is determined separately.
items.hack: Watch three collisions. One: when a veteran on VA pension enters a Medicaid-funded nursing home, VA pension is typically reduced to $90/month — that is by design and the $90 is protected as a personal needs allowance, but families are blindsided. Two: VA's 3-year net worth lookback and Medicaid's 5-year lookback are different rules with different penalties, and a transfer that is fine for one can disqualify you for the other. Three: never pay a 'pension poacher' who offers to restructure your assets to qualify you — charging for initial claim assistance is illegal, and the annuity products they sell usually destroy Medicaid eligibility. Use an accredited VSO and, for the asset planning, an elder law attorney who is not selling a financial product.
items.deadline: VA: 3-year lookback. Medicaid: typically 5-year lookback.

items.title: Geriatric Evaluation — ask for it before any placement decision
items.org: Veterans Health Administration, Geriatrics and Extended Care
items.who: Aging veterans and their families facing a care decision.
items.value: A comprehensive interdisciplinary assessment of health, functional status, cognition, medications, home safety and caregiver capacity, producing a written care plan that drives what VA will authorize. Available in outpatient, inpatient and home settings.
items.how: Ask your VA primary care provider for a geriatric evaluation or a Geriatrics and Extended Care consult.
items.hack: The evaluation is the document that unlocks everything else — home health aide hours, adult day health care, respite, HBPC, Veteran-Directed Care, Medical Foster Home. Families who skip it get whatever the primary care clinic thinks of first. Get the evaluation, get the written care plan, and then ask for each service in the plan by name. If a service in the plan is denied, the plan itself is your evidence on appeal.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: PCAFC eligibility — the 70% wall and the three qualifying need criteria
items.who: Family caregivers of veterans who sustained or aggravated a serious injury or illness in the line of duty, any service era.
items.value: The veteran must have a combined VA service-connected rating of 70% or higher, and must need in-person personal care services for at least six continuous months based on one of: inability to perform activities of daily living; need for supervision, protection or instruction because of a neurological or other impairment; or need for regular instruction or supervision. The caregiver must be 18 or older and either related to the veteran or living with them full time.
items.how: Apply on VA Form 10-10CG online, or mail it to the 10-10CG Evidence Intake Center, PO Box 5154, Janesville WI 53547-5154, or hand it to your local Caregiver Support Program team. Caregiver Support Line: 1-855-260-3274, Monday-Friday 8am-8pm ET.
items.hack: The 70% rating is a hard wall and it is also a fixable one. If the veteran is at 50% or 60% and clearly needs daily personal care, the right move is an increase claim or a TDIU claim first — TDIU counts as total for many purposes and a successful increase can open PCAFC. Do not apply, get denied on the rating, and stop. Also: if the veteran does not and will not meet 70%, go to Veteran-Directed Care instead, which has no rating requirement at all and can also pay a family caregiver.
items.deadline: Six-month continuous need requirement; no application deadline.

items.title: PCAFC stipend — exactly how the number is calculated
items.who: Approved Primary Family Caregivers.
items.value: The monthly stipend is the OPM General Schedule annual rate for grade 4, step 1, for the locality pay area where the veteran lives, divided by 12, then multiplied by the level: Level 1 pays 62.5% of that monthly amount; Level 2 pays 100%, and Level 2 applies when the veteran is determined unable to self-sustain in the community. VA's published example: with a GS-4 step 1 annual rate of $34,916 in Dallas, Level 1 was about $1,818.54/month and Level 2 about $2,909.67/month. Rates update when OPM updates the GS tables.
items.how: The level is set by VA's clinical assessment. Stipend questions go to the VHA Caregiver Stipend Team at 1-833-930-0816, Monday-Friday 8am-8pm ET. VA no longer issues PCAFC paper checks — enroll in direct deposit through the Customer Engagement Portal at cep.fsc.va.gov.
items.hack: Two levers. First, locality: the stipend follows the veteran's locality pay area, and the spread between a low-cost locality and a high-cost one is thousands of dollars a year. If a move is already contemplated, the locality is a real financial factor. Second, 'unable to self-sustain in the community' is the phrase that separates 62.5% from 100%, and it is a clinical finding — if the veteran cannot be left alone safely, that must be documented in the assessment in those terms, with specifics, not implied.
