Homegrown By Heroes is the official national farmer-veteran branding program, administered by FVC, and the label measurably lifts retail price and placement. FVC also runs the H.I.V.E. cohort program.
items.how: Apply during the open Fellowship Fund cycle at farmvetco.org. Phone (855) 382-3276. The 2026 Fellowship cycle has closed and recipients were announced; watch for the next cycle.
items.hack: Fellowship awards are made as equipment or goods purchased on your behalf rather than as cash, so have specific vendor quotes ready when the cycle opens - applications with concrete line items beat applications with a narrative. The Homegrown By Heroes label is free to qualifying members and is separate from the grant, so get the label regardless of whether you win the Fellowship. Marked medium confidence because current award amounts and the next deadline were not published.
items.deadline: 2026 cycle closed; next cycle date not published - monitor the site

items.title: TAPS - the survivor organization, and it does not matter how your person died
items.who: Anyone grieving the death of a military service member or veteran - spouses, parents, children, siblings, fiances, battle buddies. TAPS does not screen by manner of death, which matters enormously for suicide and illness losses that DIC and some other programs treat differently.
items.value: A 24/7 national helpline, one-on-one peer mentorship matched by relationship and manner of death, regional and national survivor seminars, Good Grief Camps for children, casework and benefits assistance, and grief counseling referrals. Services to survivors are free.
items.how: Call the TAPS 24/7 helpline at 800-959-TAPS (8277) or go to taps.org. A survivor care team member will connect you to a peer mentor.
items.hack: The peer mentor match is the thing. TAPS pairs you with someone who lost the same relationship the same way - a widow of a suicide is matched with a widow of a suicide - and that is something no VA program, no chaplain and no general grief group provides. Marked high confidence on the organization; specific 2026 seminar dates and program details were not confirmed on the page fetched, so check taps.org for the current calendar.
items.deadline: Helpline is 24/7; seminars and Good Grief Camps run on a published annual calendar

items.title: Children of Fallen Patriots - college paid for children of those who died in the line of duty
items.who: Children who lost a parent in the line of duty - combat casualties, training accidents, service-related illness, suicide, and other duty-related deaths, across all branches.
items.value: College and trade school scholarships, educational counseling, pre-college support, career guidance through the Fallen Patriots Career Center, mentorship, internship placement and employment connections. $82 million in scholarships to 4,000+ children since 2002; 91% graduation rate versus a 64% national average.
items.how: Enroll at fallenpatriots.org/enroll-a-student/. Contact 866-917-CFPF or contact@fallenpatriots.org.
items.hack: Two things. First: they explicitly include suicide and service-related illness, not only combat deaths - many families wrongly assume they do not qualify. Second, and important in 2026: Fallen Patriots is transitioning to the Tunnel to Towers Foundation; their site states no updates are necessary for current scholars, but if you are a new applicant, confirm the current intake path by phone. Fallen Patriots fills the gap AFTER Chapter 35 DEA and the Fry Scholarship run out - enroll early, they identify and track children for years before college.
items.deadline: Rolling enrollment; enroll years before college if possible

items.title: Special Operations Warrior Foundation - cradle-to-career funding for SOF families and wounded operators
items.who: Children of fallen Special Operations personnel; children of active-duty Special Operators whose spouse has died; children of all Medal of Honor recipients; and severely wounded, ill and injured active-duty Special Operations personnel.
items.value: 'Cradle to career' educational funding from early childhood through professional development, full scholarships, mentorship programs (Operation EPIC, C2CT), family outreach and advocacy, and immediate financial assistance for wounded SOF personnel during hospitalization and recovery.
items.how: Contact specialops.org/contact/, email alexg@specialops.org, or call (813) 805-9400. Site verified current for 2026.
items.hack: 'Cradle to career' is literal - SOWF enrolls children as infants and funds tutoring, test prep and counseling for fifteen years before the scholarship ever gets spent. If you are an eligible family, enrolling the child now costs nothing and turns on a decade of support. The immediate financial assistance track for wounded operators during hospitalization is separate and moves fast.
items.deadline: Rolling; enroll children as early as possible

items.title: Hope For The Warriors - critical needs assistance, Warrior's Wish, peer support and a Cohen clinic
items.who: The post-9/11 military community - service members, veterans and their families. Celebrating its 20th year in 2026.
items.value: Critical Needs Assistance (emergency financial aid), clinical support services including a Steven A. Cohen Military Family Clinic, Warrior's Compass transition support, military veteran peer support, Warrior's Wish (grants a significant wish to a catastrophically wounded or ill service member), Team Hope For The Warriors endurance program, and a military airport lounge. 48,800 military lives served in 2025; 203,900+ since 2006; 90 cents of every dollar to programs.
items.how: Use the Connect to Services page at hopeforthewarriors.org/programs-and-services/connect-to-services/.
items.hack: Warrior's Wish is the one nobody asks for because it sounds like a children's charity - it is not. It funds significant, life-changing requests for catastrophically wounded or ill post-9/11 service members, and demand is far below what you would expect. Critical Needs Assistance is the fast lane for a rent or utility emergency and is separate from the wish program.
items.deadline: Rolling

items.title: Shades of Green at Walt Disney World - an on-property Disney resort at military rates
items.org: Armed Forces Recreation Center - Shades of Green
items.who: Active duty, retirees, and - under the Purple Heart and Disabled Veterans Equal Access Act - Purple Heart recipients, former POWs, veterans with any VA-documented service-connected disability rating, and VA-approved primary family caregivers. DoD civilians also qualify.
items.value: A DoD-owned resort sitting inside Walt Disney World between the Polynesian and the Magic Kingdom, with rooms priced on a sliding scale by pay grade rather than by season. Rates run dramatically below comparable on-property Disney resorts. The resort also sells discounted Disney attraction tickets and helps sort out which military ticket offer applies.
items.how: Book at bookings.shadesofgreen.org or call +1 (888) 593-2242 for same-day. Check the eligibility page at shadesofgreen.org/about-shades-green/eligibility before booking, and bring the ID that matches your eligibility category.
items.hack: This is probably the single largest unclaimed dollar benefit for disabled veterans in the country and almost nobody outside the military knows it exists. The eligibility expansion under the Disabled Veterans Equal Access Act means a veteran at 10% service-connected can book it. Rates are set by pay grade, which for retirees means your retired grade. Book 11 months out - it sells out, particularly around school holidays.
items.deadline: Books up to about 11 months ahead; reserve as early as possible

items.title: Hale Koa Hotel, Waikiki - 72 beachfront acres on Fort DeRussy at military rates
items.org: Armed Forces Recreation Center - Hale Koa Hotel
items.who: Active duty, Reserve and National Guard across Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Space Force and Coast Guard; military retirees; current and retired DoD civilians; and under the Disabled Veterans Equal Access Act - Purple Heart recipients, former POWs, veterans with a VA-documented service-connected disability rating, and VA-approved primary family caregivers.
items.value: A full-service beachfront hotel on Waikiki at rates based on military status rather than the Waikiki market, with on-site dining, a luau, and MWR-priced tours and rentals. Eligible guests may sponsor up to two additional rooms for non-eligible friends and family, remaining on-site and financially responsible.
items.how: Book at bookings.halekoa.com or call 1-800-367-6027 / 1-808-955-0555. Waitlist requests at halekoa.com/your-stay/waitlist. Address: 2055 Kalia Road, Honolulu HI 96815.
items.hack: Bring a Veteran Health Identification Card (VHIC) PLUS a REAL ID-compliant driver's license or U.S. passport - the VHIC alone is explicitly insufficient under the stated credentialing rules, and this trips people up at check-in. The sponsorship rule is the other hidden feature: you can bring two rooms of civilian family onto the property with you. Book far out; Hale Koa is routinely full.
items.deadline: Books far in advance; join the waitlist if your dates are full

items.title: Edelweiss Lodge and Resort, Garmisch, Germany - an Alpine resort at AFRC rates
items.org: Armed Forces Recreation Center - Edelweiss Lodge and Resort
items.who: Guests must hold a valid DoD common access card or be accompanied by an authorized sponsor. Check the resort's eligibility page and, critically, confirm your installation access before traveling.
items.value: A full Alpine resort in Garmisch-Partenkirchen at military rates - junior and deluxe suites, cabins and alpine-view rooms, plus MWR-run ski, hiking and tour programs across Bavaria and Austria. Children 17 and under stay free on available bed space.
items.how: Book at bookings.edelweisslodgeandresort.com. Phone from the U.S.: (011-49) 8821-9440; from Europe: (49) 8821-9440. Address: St. Martinstrasse 120, 82467 Garmisch, Germany.
items.hack: Marked medium confidence for veterans specifically: the site's stated requirement is a valid DoD CAC or an authorized sponsor, which is a narrower gate than Hale Koa's and Shades of Green's published veteran categories. Verify YOUR eligibility with the resort before booking international flights. The children-stay-free rule and the on-site tour desk are what make this cheaper than any comparable Bavarian resort.
items.deadline: Seasonal demand - ski season books earliest

items.title: Dragon Hill Lodge, Seoul - AFRC hotel inside USAG Yongsan with tour packages
items.org: Armed Forces Recreation Center - Dragon Hill Lodge
items.who: Military members and families of the Total Defense Force. Gate access to USAG Yongsan is required - verify your eligibility and installation access before booking.
items.value: An American-style hotel in Seoul's Yongsan district just inside USAG Yongsan Gate #1, with multiple dining venues, a wellness club with pool and fitness center, and packaged tours. Published 2026 offers include a 20-night extended stay at $1,899 and 6-day/5-night Seoul packages; a Seoul Escapes 2027 package bundles 11 nights with tours, daily breakfast and receptions.
items.how: Book at bookings.dragonhilllodge.com. Call the lodge for changes to reservations made in the prior booking system.
items.hack: A $1,899 20-night extended stay works out to roughly $95 a night in central Seoul, which is far below the market. The catch is gate access - if you cannot get onto USAG Yongsan, the reservation is worthless. Confirm access in writing before you book flights.
items.deadline: Package-specific; Seoul Escapes runs in 2027

items.title: The New Sanno, Tokyo - a 149-room military hotel in one of Tokyo's best neighborhoods
items.org: U.S. Navy - The New Sanno Hotel
items.who: Eligible ID card holders and their guests. Check the hotel's eligibility page - this is a narrower gate than the AFRC resorts.
items.value: 149 rooms in Minami-Azabu, roughly a 7-minute walk from Hiroo Station on the Hibiya Line, with multiple restaurants, a Navy Exchange, and rates far below Tokyo market for the location. Address: 4-12-20 Minamiazabu, Minato City, Tokyo 106-0047.
items.how: Book online at thenewsanno.com or call DSN 229-8002, Japan 03-6868-2322, U.S. 1-702-951-8002 or toll-free 1-833-937-1841.
items.hack: Operational note verified for 2026: the hotel is replacing its kitchen floor September 20-30, 2026, with several dining outlets on reduced menus and Pacific Standard closed for dinner - if you are traveling in that window, plan to eat out. Marked medium confidence on eligibility because the hotel does not publish its category list on the homepage; call before booking international flights.
items.deadline: Books far ahead; cherry blossom season is the hardest

items.title: ID.me - the identity credential VA itself uses, and the key to most online military discounts
items.who: Veterans, service members, military family members.
items.value: A single free login that both proves your identity to VA.gov and other federal services AND verifies military status for retailer discounts. Once verified, partner retailers surface military offers (commonly around 20% at participating brands) without you re-proving status each time.
items.how: Create a free account at id.me, verify identity (government ID plus, for military status, DD214 or an existing military affiliation record), then link it at checkout on participating sites.
items.hack: Do the military affiliation verification once, thoroughly, with your DD214 uploaded - after that it is one click at every partner. VA.gov now steers most users to ID.me or Login.gov anyway, so you are likely going to have the account regardless; adding the military affiliation is a five-minute extra step that pays for years. Marked high confidence on the mechanism; specific retailer discount percentages change constantly and should be checked at checkout.
items.deadline: None

items.title: GovX and GovX ID - a military-exclusive storefront and the verification layer behind many brands
items.who: Military, veterans, law enforcement, firefighters, EMS and government employees.
items.value: GovX describes itself as the largest military and government exclusive ecommerce site, with discounts up to 50% off current-season goods from 1,000+ lifestyle and tactical brands. GovX ID is the separate verification service that many outside brands use on their own checkout pages.
items.how: Create a free GovX account and verify service status, then shop govx.com or use GovX ID at checkout on partner brand sites.
items.hack: The tactical and outdoor categories (boots, optics, packs, eyewear) are where GovX genuinely beats retail; general lifestyle goods often do not. Compare against the exchange sites, which are tax-free - a 30% GovX discount and a tax-free exchange price are often within a few dollars of each other, and the exchange has an easier return process. Marked medium confidence: the specific brand list and discount depths were not verifiable for 2026 from the site content.
items.deadline: None

items.title: SheerID - the verification service behind military offers at 200+ brands
items.who: Military members and veterans, alongside students, educators and healthcare workers.
items.value: Instant eligibility verification at checkout for brands that run military offers. SheerID's own shopper directory lists military-specific deals across 200+ brands (examples seen in 2026 include MUD\WTR up to 43% off a first starter kit and Allen Edmonds at 15% for students and military).
items.how: When a brand's checkout asks you to verify military status, SheerID is often the widget doing it - enter your name, service branch and dates and it verifies instantly against authoritative records. Browse offers at shop.sheerid.com.
items.hack: If SheerID cannot verify you instantly it will ask for a document upload - use your DD214 member copy 4. Keep a clean PDF of it on your phone, because ID.me, SheerID, VerifyPass and GovX will each ask for it at some point and a bad phone photo is the most common reason a verification fails. Marked medium confidence: individual brand offers change constantly.
items.deadline: Offer-specific

items.title: VerifyPass - a free directory of 1,400+ companies with military offers
items.who: Military and veterans (also first responders, healthcare workers, teachers, government employees).
items.value: A free browsable directory: pick a company, see its offers, verify once, get the discount code. 1,400+ participating companies across apparel, tactical gear, services and more. Free to consumers.
items.how: Browse verifypass.com/offers/mil, pick a company, complete verification.
items.hack: Use it as a lookup tool rather than a shopping destination: before any large purchase, search the brand name on VerifyPass, GovX ID and SheerID - brands typically pick exactly one verification vendor, so if you only check one you will miss offers. Marked medium confidence: the brand roster and terms change without notice.
items.deadline: Offer-specific

items.title: Luke's Wings - emergency airfare so family can reach a hospitalized service member or veteran
items.who: Families and loved ones of wounded, ill and injured service members, veterans, and fallen officers, during hospital recovery and rehabilitation.
items.value: Emergency travel planning and paid airline tickets, at no cost to the family, to get loved ones to the bedside and keep them there through recovery and rehab.
items.how: Request at lukeswings.org/request-a-flight/. Emergency line: 512-971-9848. Address: 1054 31st Street NW Suite 540, Washington DC 20007.
items.hack: Call the emergency number rather than using the web form if the situation is acute - this organization is built for speed. Luke's Wings covers VETERANS in VA hospitals, not just active duty at military treatment facilities, which is a distinction most people miss. It complements Fisher House (which covers the lodging once they arrive) and Hero Miles - use all three together.
items.deadline: Rolling / emergency

items.title: Veterans Airlift Command - free private aircraft flights for combat-injured veterans and their families
items.who: Combat-injured veterans and their families, and in some cases close friends visiting a hospitalized service member.
items.value: Free air transportation on a volunteer network of private aircraft owners and pilots, in three categories: medical travel for service-connected medical needs; family support travel to visit service members and veterans at medical facilities; and healing and compassion travel to therapeutic events and unit reunions. Zero cost to the veteran.
items.how: Submit at veteransairlift.org/request-flight/. Phone (952) 582-2911. Address: 5775 Wayzata Blvd Suite 700, St. Louis Park MN 55416.
items.hack: Private aircraft means no TSA line, no connections, and a plane that can land at a small field near a rural home - which matters enormously for someone traveling with a prosthesis, a wheelchair, a service dog or severe PTSD. Because it depends on volunteer pilots, request as far ahead as you can and give flexible dates. The 'healing and compassion' category covers unit reunions, which almost nothing else funds.
items.deadline: Rolling; volunteer-pilot dependent, so give lead time

items.title: Mercy Medical Angels - free transport to medical care by air, ground or gas card, 54 years running
items.who: Patients traveling for medical care who cannot afford the trip, nationwide. Runs a dedicated 'Angel Wings for Veterans' program and has served 49,689+ veterans.
items.value: Commercial airline tickets, volunteer pilot flights in the Mid-Atlantic, rideshare and ground transportation, and gas cards nationwide - all free to the patient. Serving since 1972.
items.how: Start a request at travel.mercymedical.org with your appointment details, origin and provider. Mercy Medical Angels coordinates the travel.
items.hack: Gas cards are the underrated piece. VA beneficiary travel reimburses you AFTER the trip, which does not help if you cannot afford the tank of gas today. Mercy Medical Angels can put fuel in the car before the appointment, then you still claim VA beneficiary travel reimbursement for the same trip. That is a legitimate stack, not double-dipping - one is a charitable gift, the other is a VA reimbursement of your mileage.
items.deadline: Rolling; request ahead of the appointment

items.title: Homes for Heroes - an average $3,000 rebate when a veteran buys or sells a home
items.who: Military and veterans, plus firefighters, law enforcement, healthcare professionals and teachers.
items.value: A rebate paid at closing through affiliated real estate agents and lenders. The company states heroes save an average of $3,000 buying or selling, and about $6,000 if they do both. Over 81,000 heroes served and $166 million returned; 2,700+ participating agents and lenders. Free to join.
items.how: Sign up at homesforheroes.com and get matched to a participating agent in your area BEFORE you engage any other agent.
items.hack: Timing is everything and this is where people lose the money: the rebate comes out of the participating agent's commission, so you must be registered and matched BEFORE you sign a buyer representation agreement or listing agreement with someone else. Once you have an agent, it is gone. Availability is restricted in Alaska, Kansas and Mississippi. This stacks cleanly on top of a VA loan and the funding fee exemption - it is a commission rebate, not a loan product.
items.deadline: Must register before engaging an agent

items.title: Minnesota Assistance Council for Veterans (MACV) - statewide housing, employment and VetLaw
items.who: Minnesota veterans who are homeless or at risk of homelessness, and their families. Also serves justice-involved veterans.
items.value: Three integrated service lines - housing (including MACV-owned properties), employment services, and VetLaw free legal aid. 2025: 3,281+ veterans served, 1,022+ prevented from becoming homeless, 83+ housed in MACV properties. Operating since 1990.
items.how: Call (833) 222-MACV (6228) or submit at mac-v.org/request-for-service/. Offices statewide including 1000 University Avenue West Suite 10, St. Paul.
items.hack: MACV is one of the few state-level organizations that owns its own housing stock, which means it can place a veteran without waiting on a HUD-VASH voucher or a landlord's approval. If you are in Minnesota and the VASH waitlist is the obstacle, call MACV directly rather than waiting. New President and CEO as of September 2026.
items.deadline: Rolling

items.title: Operation Stand Down Tennessee - 31 counties, four service centers, 83 cents on the dollar
items.who: Veterans across a 31-county region of middle and west Tennessee.
items.value: SSVF housing assistance, transitional housing, Career Recon employment services, legal services, Operation Commissary food support (5,500+ bags delivered in 2025), and walk-in service centers. Served over 10,000 veterans in 2025; 83 cents of every dollar goes to veterans.
items.how: Call (615) 248-1981, email info@osdtn.org, or walk into a service center - Nashville (1125 12th Ave South), Clarksville, Columbia or Brownsville.
items.hack: OSDTN is an SSVF grantee, which means it controls actual rental assistance and deposit money, not just referrals. If you are facing eviction in middle or west Tennessee, this is a faster door than the VA medical center because the caseworker has the checkbook.
items.deadline: Rolling

items.title: Combined Arms - one intake that fires referrals to 300+ vetted organizations, free
items.who: Military-connected individuals and families. Texas is the core focus through the Texas Veterans Network, with 300+ member organizations across all 50 states and a South Carolina coalition.
items.value: A single intake that routes you to vetted organizations for housing, employment, benefits, food assistance, wellness and financial support, with referral tracking so nothing disappears into a void. 100,000+ Texas veterans connected; 10 years operating. Free to the veteran.
items.how: Sign up at veteranportal.combinedarms.us/sign-up or call (844) 489-8387. Houston office: 2929 McKinney St.
items.hack: The tracking is the feature. Most 'referral' organizations hand you three phone numbers and wish you luck; the CAX platform records whether the organization actually contacted you and escalates when they do not. If you are in Texas and have been bounced between five agencies, start here and let the platform do the chasing.
items.deadline: Rolling

items.title: Veterans Village of San Diego - residential substance treatment plus housing, since 1981
items.who: All veterans in San Diego County and their families. 3,000+ veterans served annually.
items.value: Residential substance use treatment, housing programs at five locations, workforce development, Cohen Veterans Network mental health clinic services, Homeless Court legal support, and SSVF supportive services.
items.how: Call (619) 393-2000 or visit 4141 Pacific Highway, San Diego CA 92110, Monday-Friday 7am-4pm.
items.hack: VVSD's residential treatment program is one of the very few veteran-specific inpatient substance programs that is not run by VA, which matters if you have a discharge status that limits VA care or if the VA program has a months-long wait. The Homeless Court program can clear the accumulated citations and warrants that block housing and employment - ask for it by name.
items.deadline: Rolling

items.title: Nation's Finest - 15 locations plus mobile service units across California, Arizona and Nevada
items.who: Veterans and their families in California, Arizona and Nevada.
items.value: Housing assistance, mental health navigation and support services delivered through 15 brick-and-mortar locations (including Santa Rosa, Sacramento, Flagstaff, Reno and Carson City) plus Mobile Service Units that bring services directly to rural veterans.
items.how: Call 1-833-468-9676, email welcome@nationsfinest.org or go to nationsfinest.org/get-help/.
items.hack: The Mobile Service Units are the differentiator - if you are a rural veteran in northern California, northern Arizona or rural Nevada and the nearest VA is three hours away, ask specifically when the MSU is next in your county. Site content verified current as of July 2026.
items.deadline: Rolling; MSU visits are scheduled by county

items.title: Soldier On - permanent supportive housing communities for at-risk veterans, since 1994
items.who: Veterans experiencing homelessness or housing instability.
items.value: Permanent housing communities designed as a pathway to stability for at-risk veterans, plus supportive services. Operating since 1994.
items.how: Call the Soldier On toll-free line listed at wesoldieron.org for immediate assistance.
items.hack: Marked medium confidence: the organization is clearly operating, but its current geographic service area was not published on the page reviewed - it has historically been concentrated in Massachusetts and the Northeast with locations in several other states. Call before you travel. Soldier On is known for veteran-owned limited equity cooperative housing, a model where residents hold an ownership stake rather than renting, which is rare and worth asking about specifically.
items.deadline: Rolling

items.title: Veterans Outreach Center, Rochester NY - no appointment necessary, six counties, everything free
items.who: All veterans regardless of branch, rank or length of service, in Genesee, Livingston, Monroe, Ontario, Orleans and Wayne counties, New York.
items.value: Workforce development, transitional housing (Richards House, Otto's Phoenix House, Liberty Landing), mental health services, a fitness center, peer support groups, the Quartermaster program for free food, clothing and hygiene items, free legal consultations, and care management. All services free.
items.how: Walk in Monday-Friday 8:30am-4:30pm at 447 South Ave, Rochester NY 14620 - NO APPOINTMENT NECESSARY. Or call 585-546-1081.
items.hack: The no-appointment walk-in policy is genuinely rare and is the whole point: a veteran in crisis at 10am on a Tuesday can be seen at 10:15. The Quartermaster program hands out work clothes and boots, which is the unglamorous thing that decides whether someone can take a job offer this week.
items.deadline: None - walk in

items.title: Illinois Joining Forces - one statewide number that routes Illinois veterans to local help
items.who: Service members, veterans and families in Illinois.
items.value: A statewide public-private network of veteran-serving organizations with a Care Coordination Center providing holistic resource navigation, Veteran Support Communities at the local level, and the Illinois Warrior Assistance Program. Founded 2012.
items.how: Call 833-INFO IJF (833-463-6453) or go to illinoisjoiningforces.org.
items.hack: One number instead of thirty. IJF's Care Coordination Center does the navigation work so you are not calling agencies one at a time and re-telling your story. Cost is not published, but IJF operates as a nonprofit network and services to veterans are not fee-based - confirm when you call.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Veterans Guest House, Reno - free lodging so northern Nevada veterans do not sleep in the car for care
items.who: Veterans and their families traveling to Reno/Sparks for medical care.
items.value: Free temporary lodging for up to 33 guests a night while a veteran or family member receives medical treatment. The organization exists specifically because northern Nevada veterans were sleeping in cars or skipping care.
items.how: Reserve at veteransguesthouse.org, call (775) 324-6958 or email info@veteransguesthouse.org. Located at 880 Locust St, Reno NV 89502.
items.hack: This is the Fisher House equivalent for a region that does not have a Fisher House - and it is open to family members, not only the patient. If you are driving in from rural Nevada or northeastern California for VA or civilian care in Reno, reserve before you drive; 33 beds goes fast.
items.deadline: Reserve in advance

items.title: Michigan Veterans Trust Fund - state emergency grants through county committees
items.who: Michigan wartime-era veterans and their families facing a temporary financial emergency. County-level committees make the decisions.
items.value: Emergency grant assistance for a short-term financial crisis - typically housing, utilities, and other urgent needs. This is a state trust fund, not a charity, and it is grant money rather than a loan.
items.how: Call 1-800-MICH-VET (1-800-642-4838), Monday-Friday 8am-4:50pm, or email MVAAResourceCenter@michigan.gov. Applications go through your county's Trust Fund committee, usually via the county Veterans Service Officer.
items.hack: Marked medium confidence on current eligibility and award amounts, which are set by MVAA and the county committees and were not published on the page reviewed. Go through your county VSO rather than applying cold - the VSO sits with the committee and knows what documentation gets approved. The Trust Fund is emergency-only, so present it as a one-time crisis with a plan, not an ongoing shortfall.
items.deadline: Rolling; committee meeting schedules vary by county

items.title: Veterans Multi-Service Center, Philadelphia - comprehensive regional services since 1980
items.who: Veterans of the U.S. military and their families in the greater Philadelphia region.
items.value: A nationally recognized nonprofit providing comprehensive services - historically housing, employment, benefits assistance and supportive services - operating since 1980.
items.how: Contact through vmcenter.org.
items.hack: Marked medium confidence: the organization is clearly operating as a 501(c)(3) (EIN 23-2764079) but current service lines, service area boundaries and eligibility were not published on the page reviewed. Call before making the trip. Listed here because the Philadelphia/Delaware Valley region is otherwise thinly covered by national organizations.
items.deadline: Rolling

items.title: Agent Orange — Vietnam service, January 9, 1962 to May 7, 1975 (the core presumption)
items.who: Any veteran who set foot in the Republic of Vietnam, or served aboard a vessel operating on its inland waterways ('brown water'), at any time from 9 Jan 1962 through 7 May 1975. Even one day counts; there is no minimum duration.
items.value: Herbicide exposure is conceded — you never have to prove you were sprayed. Any condition on the 38 CFR 3.309(e) list is then presumptively service-connected, which turns a hard nexus case into a paperwork case.
items.how: File VA Form 21-526EZ. Attach the DD-214 showing Vietnam service (a Vietnam Service Medal, Vietnam Campaign Medal, or RVN-based unit assignment is normally enough) plus a diagnosis of a listed condition. No nexus letter is required for a listed condition.
items.hack: The dates are the outer envelope of the whole herbicide system: every other location presumption (Korea, Thailand, Laos, Guam) is written as an exception to this one. If your service falls a day outside a window, do not give up — file on a direct/actual-exposure theory under 38 CFR 3.303(d) with unit records, which VA must consider separately from the presumption.
items.deadline: No deadline. File an Intent to File (21-0966) first to lock the effective date for a year.

items.title: Blue Water Navy — the 12-nautical-mile offshore zone (Blue Water Navy Vietnam Veterans Act of 2019)
items.who: Veterans who served aboard a ship operating not more than 12 nautical miles seaward from the demarcation line of the waters of Vietnam and Cambodia, between 9 Jan 1962 and 7 May 1975. You do not need to have gone ashore or entered inland waterways.
items.value: Full herbicide presumption for blue-water sailors who were denied for decades under VA's old 'boots on ground' rule. Awards can carry very large retroactive payments.
items.how: File VA Form 21-526EZ. VA checks ship deck logs and its own Navy/Coast Guard ship list; you can strengthen the claim by naming the ship, hull number, and dates, and citing deck-log coordinates. If your ship is not on VA's list, submit deck-log extracts obtained from the National Archives.
items.hack: If you were denied before 1 Jan 2020 on blue-water grounds, the 2019 Act plus Procopio v. Wilkie means you can re-file as a Supplemental Claim (VA Form 20-0995) and VA must assign the effective date of the ORIGINAL denied claim, not the new one. This is where the money is — decades of back pay. Also check Nehmer class status.
items.deadline: No deadline to file, but re-file the old denial rather than starting fresh, or you forfeit the retroactive date.

items.title: Agent Orange — Korean DMZ, September 1, 1967 to August 31, 1971
items.who: Veterans who served in or near the Korean Demilitarized Zone for any length of time between 1 Sep 1967 and 31 Aug 1971. Originally limited to a short list of units; the window was later broadened and the unit-list requirement relaxed.
items.value: Same full 3.309(e) presumptive list as Vietnam service.
items.how: File 21-526EZ citing DMZ service. Provide unit designation and duty location; VA cross-checks DoD herbicide-use records for the DMZ.
items.hack: 'In or near' is doing a lot of work — service at a camp south of the DMZ with duties that took you to the fence line can qualify. A buddy statement (VA Form 21-10210) describing patrols, wire details, or convoy runs to the DMZ is often what tips a marginal case.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Agent Orange — Thailand, January 9, 1962 to June 30, 1976 (PACT Act killed the perimeter requirement)
items.who: Veterans who served at ANY U.S. or Royal Thai military base in Thailand from 9 Jan 1962 through 30 Jun 1976. This includes U-Tapao, Ubon, Nakhon Phanom, Udorn, Takhli, Korat, and Don Muang — and, since the PACT Act, it no longer matters whether you worked near the base perimeter.
items.value: The single biggest quiet change of the PACT Act for Vietnam-era veterans. Before August 2022, VA required proof you were a security policeman, dog handler, or had duties at the perimeter. Now, base presence alone during the window is enough.
items.how: File 21-526EZ; a DD-214 or orders showing a Thailand base assignment in the window plus a listed diagnosis. No perimeter evidence needed.
items.hack: If VA denied your Thailand claim before 10 Aug 2022 because you could not prove perimeter duty, that denial is now legally wrong on its face. File a Supplemental Claim (20-0995) citing the PACT Act liberalizing-law provision — a liberalizing law can give up to one year of retroactive benefits before the claim date under 38 CFR 3.114, and PACT Act claims filed in the first year had a special retroactive rule.
items.deadline: None, but the PACT Act's special one-year retroactive filing window (through 9 Aug 2023) has closed.

items.title: Agent Orange — Laos (Dec 1, 1965 – Sep 30, 1969) and Cambodia at Mimot or Krek (Apr 16–30, 1969)
items.who: Laos: any service 1 Dec 1965 through 30 Sep 1969. Cambodia: service at Mimot or Krek, Kampong Cham Province, only from 16 Apr 1969 through 30 Apr 1969 — a two-week window.
items.value: Full herbicide presumption. These are PACT Act additions that cover special operations, Air America-adjacent, and MACV-SOG personnel whose service was classified for decades.
items.how: File 21-526EZ. Because much of this service was covert, VA will accept alternate evidence: unit histories, declassified records, buddy statements, and personal narratives.
items.hack: The Cambodia window is punishingly narrow — 16 to 30 April 1969 at two named locations. If you were in Cambodia outside that window, the presumption does not apply, but direct service connection still does. Build the claim on actual-exposure evidence instead, and do not let a rater treat 'no presumption' as 'no claim.'
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Agent Orange — Guam and American Samoa (Jan 9, 1962 – Jul 31, 1980) and Johnston Atoll (Jan 1, 1972 – Sep 30, 1977)
items.who: Guam or American Samoa, or the territorial waters off either, 9 Jan 1962 through 31 Jul 1980. Johnston Atoll, or aboard a ship that called at Johnston Atoll, 1 Jan 1972 through 30 Sep 1977 (where surplus Agent Orange was stored and later incinerated).
items.value: Full 3.309(e) presumption for a population — Andersen AFB and Naval Station Guam personnel, and Johnston Atoll storage crews — that had no path at all before the PACT Act.
items.how: File 21-526EZ with orders or a DD-214 showing the assignment. 'Territorial waters off Guam or American Samoa' means shipboard service counts; name the ship and dates.
items.hack: The Guam window runs to 31 July 1980 — far later than most veterans assume. Post-Vietnam Guam assignments in the mid-to-late 1970s qualify, which catches a lot of people who never connected their service to Agent Orange at all.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: The complete Agent Orange presumptive condition list as of 2026 (38 CFR 3.309(e))
items.who: Any veteran with a qualifying herbicide-exposure location and date range, who is diagnosed with a listed condition.
items.value: Cancers: bladder cancer, chronic B-cell leukemias (including hairy cell leukemia), Hodgkin's disease, multiple myeloma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, prostate cancer, respiratory cancers (lung, bronchus, larynx, trachea), soft tissue sarcomas (excluding osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, Kaposi's sarcoma, mesothelioma). Other conditions: AL amyloidosis, chloracne or similar acneiform disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, high blood pressure (hypertension), hypothyroidism, ischemic heart disease, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), Parkinson's disease, parkinsonism, early-onset peripheral neuropathy, porphyria cutanea tarda.
items.how: Diagnosis + qualifying service = grant. File 21-526EZ; a Disability Benefits Questionnaire from your own physician speeds the rating.
items.hack: Three entries on this list are chronically under-claimed: hypertension (added by the PACT Act and extremely common), MGUS (a blood finding many veterans have and ignore — ask your doctor to check your SPEP results), and 'parkinsonism' as distinct from Parkinson's disease, which captures drug-induced and atypical presentations that a rater may otherwise reject. Chloracne, porphyria cutanea tarda, and early-onset peripheral neuropathy carry a manifestation deadline; the rest do not.
items.deadline: Chloracne, porphyria cutanea tarda, and early-onset peripheral neuropathy must have appeared to 10% within one year of the last herbicide exposure. All other listed conditions may appear at any time.

items.title: Hypertension and MGUS — the two PACT Act herbicide additions almost nobody files for
items.who: Any veteran with qualifying herbicide exposure who has a hypertension diagnosis or a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance finding.
items.value: Hypertension is rated under DC 7101 and, on its own, is usually a 10% or 20% award — but it is also a gateway: once service-connected, it supports secondary claims and feeds the combined rating. MGUS can be rated and, critically, converts to multiple myeloma in a subset of patients, which is already presumptive.
items.how: File 21-526EZ. For hypertension, provide blood-pressure readings and any prescription history; VA wants predominant diastolic readings or a history of diastolic 100+ requiring continuous medication. For MGUS, provide the serum protein electrophoresis / immunofixation report.
items.hack: MGUS is usually an incidental lab finding a civilian doctor mentions once and never revisits. If you are a herbicide-exposed veteran, specifically ask for an SPEP with immunofixation — a positive result is a presumptive service connection you are currently carrying around unclaimed. And if you were denied hypertension before the PACT Act, file a Supplemental Claim; the old denial rested on a rule that no longer exists.
items.deadline: None. The PACT Act's one-year special retroactive window closed 9 Aug 2023; ordinary effective-date rules now apply.

items.title: C-123 aircrew and maintainers, 1969–1986 — herbicide exposure long after Vietnam
items.who: Air Force and Air Force Reserve personnel who flew, maintained, or performed medical duties aboard contaminated C-123 Provider aircraft (the former Operation Ranch Hand spray planes) between 1969 and 1986, at units including Westover ARB MA, Pittsburgh IAP PA, and Rickenbacker ANGB OH.
items.value: Full herbicide presumption — for service that occurred up to eleven years after the last U.S. troops left Vietnam. This cohort is overwhelmingly unaware it qualifies.
items.how: File 21-526EZ identifying the unit, aircraft tail numbers if known, and the duty (flight crew, aerial port, maintenance, aeromedical evacuation). VA maintains an internal list of affected units and tail numbers and checks it.
items.hack: The eligible AFSCs are broader than aircrew — maintenance and aeromedical evacuation personnel who spent repeated duty time inside the airframe qualify. If you served in an Air Force Reserve C-123 unit in the 1970s or early 1980s and have any condition on the 3.309(e) list, file. This is also an Agent Orange Registry exam category.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Herbicide testing and storage sites inside the United States — no presumption, but a real claim path
items.who: Veterans who served at DoD-acknowledged herbicide test or storage locations, including: Port of Mobile AL (Aug 1965–Dec 1968); Fort Chaffee AR (May–Aug 1967); Davis-Monthan AFB AZ (1973–1977); Eglin AFB, Avon Park, and Apalachicola National Forest FL (1951–1969); Fort Gordon GA (1964–1968); Vigo Plant, Terre Haute IN (1945); Aberdeen Proving Ground, Fort Detrick, Fort Meade, Fort Ritchie MD (1946–1970); Naval Construction Battalion Center Gulfport MS (1968–1977); Gallatin Valley MT (1953); Fort Drum NY (1959); Kelly AFB TX (1970+); Dugway Proving Ground UT (1963–1964).
items.value: These sites are NOT presumptive locations. But DoD's own acknowledgment of herbicide use there is powerful direct evidence of exposure under 38 CFR 3.303(d) — which means you can win without a presumption.
items.how: File 21-526EZ on a direct service-connection theory: (1) DoD's site list as proof herbicide was present, (2) orders or a DD-214 placing you there in the window, (3) a nexus opinion linking your diagnosis to herbicide exposure. The nexus letter is required here — that is the difference from a presumptive claim.
items.hack: Print the DoD site list page and attach it to the claim as evidence. Raters routinely deny these claims by writing 'not a presumptive location,' which is true but irrelevant to a direct claim. Say the words 'direct service connection under 38 CFR 3.303(d), not a presumption' in your statement so the denial cannot rest on the wrong legal test.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Nehmer class retroactive payments (38 CFR 3.816) — back pay to your first claim, not your latest one
items.who: Vietnam-era herbicide-exposed veterans (and their survivors) who filed a claim for a condition BEFORE that condition was added to the presumptive list, and were denied. The Nehmer court order class.
items.value: Instead of an effective date tied to your new claim, VA must pay back to the date of the earlier denied claim — or to the date of death for a survivor's DIC claim. Awards routinely run into six figures.
items.how: When a condition is newly added (as hypertension and MGUS were in 2022), VA is supposed to review its records and pay Nehmer retroactively without being asked. It often does not. Write to your regional office citing 38 CFR 3.816 and Nehmer v. U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, listing every prior claim date and denial for the condition.
items.hack: Survivors are the most-missed Nehmer group. If a Vietnam veteran filed and was denied for, say, ischemic heart disease or hypertension, and later died, the surviving spouse can claim DIC with a Nehmer effective date going back to the veteran's original claim. Pull the veteran's full C-file (FOIA request to the regional office) to find every prior claim date — that document is where the retroactive money is proven.
items.deadline: No deadline, but you must be able to document the earlier claim, so order the C-file early.

items.title: PACT Act burn pit locations — the exact two-tier list and its two start dates
items.who: Tier 1 (on or after 2 Aug 1990): Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, United Arab Emirates, and the airspace above. Tier 2 (on or after 11 Sep 2001): Afghanistan, Djibouti, Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Uzbekistan, Yemen, and the airspace above.
items.value: Service in ANY of these places on or after the applicable date concedes toxic exposure. No proof you stood next to a burn pit is required.
items.how: File 21-526EZ. Deployment orders, a DD-214 with a campaign medal, or DoD deployment records establish the location.
items.hack: Note the two different start dates, and note that Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, and Yemen only count from 11 Sep 2001 — while Somalia counts from 2 Aug 1990, which reaches back to pre-Black Hawk Down deployments. Also note 'airspace above': aircrew who flew over these countries without landing qualify, which catches a great many tanker, airlift, and bomber crews who assume they do not.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: The burn pit presumptive condition list — 23+ conditions, cancers and respiratory illness
items.who: Veterans with qualifying burn pit / particulate matter locations and dates.
items.value: Cancers: head cancer of any type, neck cancer of any type, respiratory cancer of any type, gastrointestinal cancer of any type, reproductive cancer of any type, lymphoma of any type, lymphomatic cancer of any type, kidney cancer, brain cancer, melanoma, pancreatic cancer, glioblastoma. Respiratory illnesses: asthma diagnosed after service, chronic bronchitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), chronic rhinitis, chronic sinusitis, constrictive bronchiolitis or obliterative bronchiolitis, emphysema, granulomatous disease, interstitial lung disease, pleuritis, pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis.
items.how: Diagnosis + qualifying deployment = presumptive grant. File 21-526EZ.
items.hack: The phrase 'of any type' is the leverage. 'Head cancer of any type' and 'neck cancer of any type' sweep in oral, tongue, thyroid, salivary, and sinus cancers that a rater might otherwise try to exclude. 'Gastrointestinal cancer of any type' covers colon, stomach, esophageal, rectal, and liver. If a rater denies on the ground that your specific histology is not named, quote the regulation's 'any type' language back.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: 38 CFR 3.320 — fine particulate matter: asthma, rhinitis and sinusitis at ANY time after separation
items.who: Veterans with a qualifying period of service in the Southwest Asia theater during the Persian Gulf War, or in Afghanistan, Syria, Djibouti or Uzbekistan on or after 19 Sep 2001.
items.value: Asthma, rhinitis, and sinusitis (including rhinosinusitis) are service-connected if manifested to ANY degree — including non-compensable — at any time following separation. There is no manifestation deadline and no minimum severity to establish the connection. Nine rare respiratory cancers are also covered: squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx; squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and salivary-gland-type tumors of the trachea; adenosquamous carcinoma, large cell carcinoma, salivary-gland-type tumors, sarcomatoid carcinoma, and typical/atypical carcinoid of the lung.
items.how: File 21-526EZ with the diagnosis and deployment evidence, citing 38 CFR 3.320 by name.
items.hack: 'Manifested to any degree, including non-compensable, at any time' is the most generous standard in the presumptive system, and most veterans do not know it exists. A 0% service connection for rhinitis still opens the door to secondary claims (obstructive sleep apnea secondary to rhinitis is the classic), to Priority Group placement, and to future increases. File even if your asthma is mild and controlled.
items.deadline: None — there is no manifestation window.

items.title: Airborne Hazards and Open Burn Pit Registry — you are probably already enrolled and do not know it
items.who: Veterans and service members who deployed to Iraq, Afghanistan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman, UAE, Yemen, Syria, Jordan, Lebanon, Djibouti or Uzbekistan (or the associated airspace and waters) between 2 Aug 1990 and 31 Aug 2021, or who served in Desert Shield/Storm, OIF, OEF, or New Dawn.
items.value: Since VA's 2024 relaunch, eligible veterans are enrolled AUTOMATICALLY from DoD deployment records — the old self-questionnaire is gone. Registry participation supports a free, no-copay in-person environmental health evaluation and feeds the research that creates future presumptives.
items.how: Check your status through the VA registry inquiry portal or your local VA Environmental Health Coordinator. To get the evaluation, ask the Environmental Health Coordinator at your VA medical center or contact VET-HOME.
items.hack: Registry participation neither helps nor hurts a disability claim — it is not a compensation exam and VA does not use it to decide claims. But the free in-person evaluation generates medical documentation of your exposure history and symptoms in your VA record, and that documentation is useful in a claim. Get the exam; do not expect the registry itself to do anything for your rating. You can opt out and later rejoin at any time.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: The toxic exposure screening every enrolled veteran is entitled to — every five years, by law
items.who: Every veteran enrolled in VA health care, regardless of rating or era.
items.value: An initial screening plus a repeat screening at least once every five years, at no cost. The screening asks about burn pits and airborne hazards, Gulf War exposures, Agent Orange, radiation, Camp Lejeune water, and other hazards, and routes positive answers to a VA Environmental Health Coordinator.
items.how: Ask for it at any primary care appointment — it is a short set of questions a nurse or clinician can run. If you are not enrolled, enroll first (VA Form 10-10EZ); PACT Act eligibility opened enrollment to most toxic-exposed veterans.
items.hack: The screening's real value is documentary. Answering 'yes' to an exposure puts a dated, clinician-recorded exposure history into your VA medical record, which later serves as evidence in a claim and as the trigger for a registry exam referral. Ask for it explicitly by name — many clinics do not offer it unprompted, and there is no penalty for asking again if it has been more than a year.
items.deadline: None; repeat entitlement every 5 years.

items.title: K2 / Karshi-Khanabad, Uzbekistan (2001–2005) — the worst exposure profile of the post-9/11 war
items.who: Approximately 15,000 service members who occupied the former Soviet air base at Karshi-Khanabad, Uzbekistan, between 2001 and 2005, supporting early Operation Enduring Freedom.
items.value: Uzbekistan is now a PACT Act presumptive location (on or after 11 Sep 2001), so K2 veterans get the full burn pit presumptive list PLUS the 38 CFR 3.320 particulate matter presumption for asthma, rhinitis, and sinusitis. VA also offers free depleted uranium bioassay testing.
items.how: File 21-526EZ citing K2/Uzbekistan service. For DU testing, contact a VA Environmental Health Coordinator and request a 24-hour urine bioassay at no cost.
items.hack: K2's exposure profile is uniquely stackable and most K2 veterans only file on one theory. The documented hazards were: a leaking Soviet-era underground jet fuel distribution system (JP-8/benzene), volatile organic compounds, particulate matter, low-level depleted uranium in surface soil from destroyed Soviet missiles, asbestos in roof tiles and dirt, lead-based paint in the in-processing center, and burn pit smoke. Claim the presumptives first, then file separately on direct exposure for anything the presumptive list misses — the DoD's own K2 site characterization documents are your evidence.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Camp Lejeune — the 8 VA presumptive conditions and the 30-day rule (Aug 1, 1953 – Dec 31, 1987)
items.who: Veterans, Reservists, and National Guard members who served at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River, North Carolina, for at least 30 days (cumulative, not necessarily consecutive) between 1 Aug 1953 and 31 Dec 1987, and were not dishonorably discharged.
items.value: Eight presumptive conditions for VA disability compensation: adult leukemia; aplastic anemia and other myelodysplastic syndromes; bladder cancer; kidney cancer; liver cancer; multiple myeloma; non-Hodgkin's lymphoma; Parkinson's disease. Codified at 38 CFR 3.309(f).
items.how: File 21-526EZ with orders, a DD-214, or any record placing you at Lejeune/New River for 30 days in the window, plus the diagnosis.
items.hack: The 30 days are cumulative. Two separate two-week TDYs add up. School attendance, temporary duty, and unit rotations all count, and so do dependents-of-record periods for the health care side. If your records burned or are thin, a buddy statement plus unit records can establish presence — VA does not require a specific duty document.
items.deadline: None for VA disability. (The separate Camp Lejeune Justice Act lawsuit deadline has passed — see that entry.)

items.title: Camp Lejeune family member health care — 15 covered conditions, reimbursed for spouses and children
items.org: VHA / Camp Lejeune Family Member Program
items.who: Spouses, dependents, children (including those exposed in utero), and other family members who lived at Camp Lejeune or MCAS New River for at least 30 days between 1 Aug 1953 and 31 Dec 1987.
items.value: VA reimburses out-of-pocket medical costs for 15 specified conditions, with no copay. The list covers esophageal cancer, breast cancer, kidney cancer, multiple myeloma, renal toxicity, female infertility, scleroderma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, lung cancer, bladder cancer, leukemia, myelodysplastic syndromes, hepatic steatosis, miscarriage, and neurobehavioral effects.
items.how: Apply using VA Form 10-10068 (Camp Lejeune Family Member Program Application) plus VA Form 10-10068b for each claim. You must show proof of residence (base housing records, school records, tax records, utility bills, birth certificate showing birth at the base hospital) and proof of the relationship.
items.hack: This is the most-missed benefit in the whole Camp Lejeune file, because it is not a veterans' benefit — it goes to family members, and most families never hear of it. A birth certificate showing birth at Camp Lejeune Naval Hospital during the window is, by itself, strong residence proof. VA pays only after other health insurance, so keep every explanation of benefits.
items.deadline: None, but bills must be submitted for reimbursement within two years of the date of service.

items.title: Camp Lejeune Justice Act tort claims — a different system entirely, and the filing window has closed
items.org: Department of the Navy (JAG) / U.S. District Court, Eastern District of North Carolina
items.who: Anyone (veteran, family member, civilian worker, or the legal representative of someone who died or was exposed in utero) who was at Camp Lejeune for at least 30 days between 1 Aug 1953 and 31 Dec 1987.
items.value: Money damages in tort — pain and suffering, lost wages, medical costs, wrongful death — which VA disability compensation does not pay. This is a lawsuit against the United States, not a benefits claim.
items.how: The CLJA required an administrative claim to the Department of the Navy first, then suit in the Eastern District of North Carolina. The Act was signed 10 Aug 2022 with a two-year filing window; that window closed 10 Aug 2024. Claims already filed continue to be litigated and settled.
items.hack: The critical distinction: the CLJA is a TORT claim and VA disability is a BENEFITS claim. They are separate systems, filed with different agencies, on different evidence, and one does not bar the other. But they are not fully independent — the statute requires any CLJA award to be REDUCED by the amount of VA disability compensation, VA health care, and Medicare/Medicaid payments already received for the same injury. So filing for VA disability does not disqualify you, but it does shrink a later tort award dollar-for-dollar. Never let anyone tell you to skip the VA claim to protect a lawsuit; VA compensation is tax-free, lifelong, and carries dependent and survivor benefits a settlement does not.
items.deadline: CLOSED. Administrative claims had to be filed by 10 Aug 2024. VA disability claims remain open with no deadline.

items.title: 38 CFR 3.317 — undiagnosed illness and the Southwest Asia theater definition
items.who: Veterans with a qualifying period of active service in the Southwest Asia theater of operations during the Persian Gulf War. The theater is defined exactly as: Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, the neutral zone between Iraq and Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, the Gulf of Aden, the Gulf of Oman, the Persian Gulf, the Arabian Sea, the Red Sea, and the airspace above these locations.
items.value: A chronic disability from an undiagnosed illness — objective signs and symptoms with no diagnosis at all — can be service-connected and rated. This is the only corner of VA law where the ABSENCE of a diagnosis helps you.
items.how: File 21-526EZ describing the symptoms (fatigue, headache, joint pain, neurological signs, sleep disturbance, GI symptoms, cardiovascular signs, skin abnormalities, menstrual disorders). The disability must have become manifest during qualifying service or to a degree of 10 percent or more by the presumptive period deadline, and must have existed for six months or more.
items.hack: Afghanistan is NOT in the Southwest Asia theater for 3.317 purposes — the theater list above is exhaustive and Afghanistan appears in 3.317 only for the separate presumptive infectious-disease provision (on or after 19 Sep 2001). Afghanistan veterans should file under the PACT Act burn pit presumptives and 38 CFR 3.320 instead. Getting this wrong is the single most common reason a Gulf War claim is denied on the wrong theory.
items.deadline: The presumptive period currently runs through December 31, 2026 — VA has repeatedly extended it by rulemaking, but as the regulation reads, a qualifying disability must manifest to 10% by that date. Verify the current extension before relying on the deadline.

items.title: Gulf War illness — the three named MUCMIs: chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, functional GI disorders
items.who: Southwest Asia theater veterans with a medically unexplained chronic multisymptom illness (MUCMI).
items.value: 38 CFR 3.317 names three MUCMIs outright: chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, and functional gastrointestinal disorders (which excludes structural GI disease). These are presumptive — you do not need a nexus opinion. Functional GI disorders include irritable bowel syndrome, functional dyspepsia, functional constipation, functional bloating, and functional abdominal pain syndrome.
items.how: File 21-526EZ with the diagnosis. Fibromyalgia is rated under DC 5025 (10/20/40%); chronic fatigue syndrome under DC 6354 (10 to 100%); functional GI disorders under the digestive schedule.
items.hack: IBS is the quiet winner here. An enormous number of Gulf War veterans carry an IBS diagnosis from a civilian gastroenterologist and never connect it to service — it is a named functional GI disorder and therefore presumptive. Also note that the regulation says 'a diagnosed illness without conclusive pathophysiology or etiology' — so a MUCMI does NOT have to be one of the three named ones; the list is illustrative, not exhaustive. Argue that explicitly if your condition is unexplained but unnamed.
items.deadline: Same 3.317 presumptive-period deadline (currently 31 Dec 2026 as written).

items.title: Gulf War and Afghanistan presumptive infectious diseases (38 CFR 3.317(c))
items.who: Southwest Asia theater veterans (Gulf War onward) and veterans who served in Afghanistan on or after 19 Sep 2001.
items.value: Presumptive service connection for brucellosis, Campylobacter jejuni, Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), malaria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, nontyphoid Salmonella, Shigella, visceral leishmaniasis, and West Nile virus — plus their long-term health effects, which is where the real disability usually lives.
items.how: File 21-526EZ with the diagnosis and deployment evidence.
items.hack: Most of these have a one-year manifestation window after separation — EXCEPT visceral leishmaniasis and tuberculosis, which have no time limit. Q fever's chronic sequelae (endocarditis, vascular infection, chronic fatigue) can appear years later; if you had an undiagnosed acute febrile illness downrange, ask for Q fever serology now. The 'long-term health effects' language means the residuals are claimable even when the acute infection resolved decades ago.
items.deadline: Generally must manifest to 10% within one year of separation; no limit for visceral leishmaniasis or tuberculosis.

items.title: Gulf War Registry health exam — free, no enrollment required, and it does not touch your claim
items.who: Any veteran who served in the Gulf War theater (Operations Desert Shield/Desert Storm, Iraqi Freedom, New Dawn, Enduring Freedom, Inherent Resolve) — VA enrollment is NOT required.
items.value: A free, no-copay exposure history, medical history, physical examination, and any indicated laboratory tests, followed by a clinician consultation and a written summary letter.
items.how: Contact the Environmental Health Coordinator at your nearest VA medical center, or call 1-877-222-8387.
items.hack: This is a documentation play, not a benefits play. The exam explicitly is not a compensation and pension exam and will not confirm exposure — but the written summary letter it produces is a dated medical document describing your exposure history and findings, and that is evidence you can attach to a 21-526EZ. Ask for a copy of the summary letter; do not assume it will reach your claims file on its own.
items.deadline: None. You can have the exam more than once if new symptoms appear.

items.title: The complete list of VA 'radiation-risk activities' with exact dates (38 CFR 3.309(d)(3)(ii))
items.who: Atomic Veterans and related cohorts. The qualifying activities are: onsite participation in a test involving the atmospheric detonation of a nuclear device; service in the occupation of Hiroshima or Nagasaki from 6 Aug 1945 through 1 Jul 1946; internment as a POW in Japan during WWII (or active duty in Japan immediately following such internment) with comparable exposure opportunity; service at the gaseous diffusion plants at Paducah KY, Portsmouth OH, or Area K-25 at Oak Ridge TN for at least 250 days before 1 Feb 1992 with dosimetry monitoring or comparable job exposure; service before 1 Jan 1974 on Amchitka Island, Alaska, with exposure during the Long Shot, Milrow, or Cannikin underground tests; cleanup of Enewetak Atoll from 1 Jan 1977 through 31 Dec 1980; response to the Palomares, Spain B-52 accident from 17 Jan 1966 through 31 Mar 1967; response to the Thule, Greenland B-52 fire from 21 Jan 1968 through 25 Sep 1968.
items.value: Qualifying under any one of these makes you a 'radiation-exposed veteran' and unlocks the 21 presumptive cancers of 3.309(d)(2) with no dose reconstruction required.
items.how: File 21-526EZ. VA verifies participation through DTRA (Defense Threat Reduction Agency) records for nuclear test participation and through DoD/DOE records for the plants and cleanups.
items.hack: Three of these — Enewetak, Palomares, and Thule — were added by the PACT Act and are still unknown to most of the affected veterans and to a lot of VSO representatives. The gaseous diffusion plant entry is the strangest: it requires 250 days of service BEFORE 1 Feb 1992, which reaches deep into the 1970s and 80s and covers Army and Air Force personnel assigned to those DOE sites. Ask DTRA directly for your participation record before filing.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: The 21 presumptive cancers for radiation-exposed veterans (38 CFR 3.309(d)(2))
items.who: Anyone who meets a radiation-risk activity definition.
items.value: Leukemia other than chronic lymphocytic leukemia; cancer of the thyroid; cancer of the breast; cancer of the pharynx; cancer of the esophagus; cancer of the stomach; cancer of the small intestine; cancer of the pancreas; multiple myeloma; lymphomas except Hodgkin's disease; cancer of the bile ducts; cancer of the gall bladder; primary liver cancer (except if cirrhosis or hepatitis B is indicated); cancer of the salivary gland; cancer of the urinary tract; bronchiolo-alveolar carcinoma; cancer of the bone; cancer of the brain; cancer of the colon; cancer of the lung; cancer of the ovary.
items.how: Diagnosis plus verified radiation-risk activity equals a grant, with no dose estimate and no nexus opinion.
items.hack: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia is deliberately excluded here — but it IS on the Agent Orange list as a chronic B-cell leukemia. Veterans with both exposures should file on the herbicide theory for CLL. Note also that 'cancer of the urinary tract' includes kidney, renal pelvis, ureter, bladder and urethra, which is broader than most raters treat it.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: 38 CFR 3.311 — the radiogenic disease path when you do not qualify as a 'radiation-exposed veteran'
items.who: Any veteran with any documented in-service ionizing radiation exposure — nuclear weapons technicians, dental and medical X-ray technicians, nuclear propulsion sailors, radar and radioisotope handlers, LORAN station personnel, McMurdo Station Antarctica nuclear plant personnel, nasopharyngeal radium irradiation recipients, Fukushima responders — who does NOT meet a 3.309(d) radiation-risk activity.
items.value: A completely separate, non-presumptive route. VA must obtain a radiation dose estimate and then refer the case to the Under Secretary for Benefits for an opinion on whether the disease is related. Twenty-four radiogenic diseases are named, including all forms of leukemia except CLL; thyroid, breast, lung, bone, liver, skin, esophageal, stomach, colon, pancreatic, kidney, bladder, rectal, salivary gland, prostate and ovarian cancers; multiple myeloma; lymphomas except Hodgkin's; brain and CNS tumors; posterior subcapsular cataracts; non-malignant thyroid nodular disease; parathyroid adenoma; tumors of the brain and central nervous system; and 'any other cancer' supported by competent scientific or medical evidence.
items.how: File 21-526EZ and explicitly request development under 38 CFR 3.311. VA must request dose data from DoD (for testing and Hiroshima/Nagasaki) or from the Under Secretary for Health (for all other exposures). Submit your DD Form 1141 (Record of Occupational Exposure to Ionizing Radiation) if you have one — request it from NPRC if not.
items.hack: Two rules in 3.311 are worth knowing. First, where a dose RANGE is reported, VA must presume the HIGHEST dose in the range. Second, if your own credible dose estimate differs materially from the military's — the regulation contemplates roughly double or more — VA must refer the case to an independent expert. Latency thresholds: leukemia any time after exposure; posterior subcapsular cataracts 6 months or more; bone cancer within 30 years; all other diseases 5 years or more. And the catch-all 'any other cancer' clause means this path is never closed just because your cancer is not on the list.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Enewetak Atoll cleanup, January 1, 1977 – December 31, 1980 — the 'atomic cleanup' veterans
items.who: The roughly 4,000 service members — mostly Army engineers, Navy Seabees, and Air Force personnel — who conducted the radiological cleanup of Enewetak Atoll in the Marshall Islands, site of 43 nuclear tests between 1948 and 1958, during the window 1 Jan 1977 through 31 Dec 1980.
items.value: PACT Act made this a radiation-risk activity, which means full presumptive service connection for the 21 cancers of 3.309(d)(2). These veterans were denied for forty years on the ground that the cleanup was not a 'test.'
items.how: File 21-526EZ citing Enewetak cleanup service. Orders, a DD-214 showing the Marshall Islands or Enewetak, or unit assignment to Task Group 8-2 / the Enewetak Radiological Support Project establish participation.
items.hack: Every pre-2022 Enewetak denial rests on a rule Congress has since overturned. File a Supplemental Claim (VA Form 20-0995) rather than a new claim, and cite the PACT Act as a liberalizing law under 38 CFR 3.114 — that is the argument that reaches back for retroactive benefits. Survivors of Enewetak veterans who died of a listed cancer should file for DIC on the same theory.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Palomares, Spain (1966–67) and Thule, Greenland (1968) — the Broken Arrow cleanup crews
items.who: Palomares: personnel who participated in the response to the 17 Jan 1966 B-52/KC-135 collision that scattered plutonium from four hydrogen bombs over Palomares, Spain — qualifying window 17 Jan 1966 through 31 Mar 1967. Thule: personnel who responded to the 21 Jan 1968 crash and fire of a B-52 carrying nuclear weapons near Thule Air Base, Greenland — qualifying window 21 Jan 1968 through 25 Sep 1968.
items.value: Both are PACT Act radiation-risk activities, giving full presumptive service connection for the 21 cancers under 3.309(d)(2).
items.how: File 21-526EZ. Service records showing assignment to the recovery operations, or to the supporting units at Torrejón AB (Spain) or Thule AB during the windows, establish participation.
items.hack: These windows are longer than the accidents. Palomares runs 14 months past the crash and Thule runs 8 months — because the cleanup and monitoring continued. Airmen who arrived weeks or months after the incident and worked contaminated soil, aircraft, or ice recovery still fall inside. If your DD-214 places you at Torrejón or Thule in those months, pull your unit's history and check whether it supported the recovery.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Paducah, Portsmouth and K-25 gaseous diffusion plants — 250 days before February 1, 1992
items.who: Veterans who performed duty at the DOE gaseous diffusion plants at Paducah Kentucky, Portsmouth Ohio, or Area K-25 at Oak Ridge Tennessee, for at least 250 days before 1 Feb 1992, AND who either were monitored by a dosimetry badge or whose job had exposures comparable to a monitored worker.
items.value: Radiation-risk activity status, so the 21 presumptive cancers of 3.309(d)(2) apply. It also parallels the DOE Special Exposure Cohort, and 3.309(d)(3)(ii) separately recognizes veterans who performed tasks equivalent to Special Exposure Cohort membership.
items.how: File 21-526EZ. Request your DD Form 1141 dosimetry record from NPRC and, separately, request exposure records from DOE for the site. The 250-day threshold is cumulative.
items.hack: Most veterans in this category do not think of themselves as radiation veterans at all — they were assigned to support a uranium enrichment plant, not to a weapons test. The 'comparable job exposure' alternative matters: you do NOT need a dosimetry badge record if your duties were equivalent to those of a monitored worker, which a supervisor's or coworker's statement can establish. Also check whether you qualify separately under the DOE Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program (EEOICPA), which is a different agency and a different, additional payment.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Fort McClellan, Alabama (1935–1999) — recognized exposure, no presumption, case-by-case claims
items.who: Veterans who trained or served at Fort McClellan, Alabama, from 1 Jan 1935 to 20 May 1999 — particularly the U.S. Army Chemical Corps School, the Army Combat Developments Command Chemical/Biological/Radiological Agency, the Army Military Police School, and the Women's Army Corps.
items.value: VA acknowledges three documented hazards at the post: radioactive compounds (cesium-137 and cobalt-60) from decontamination training; chemical warfare agents including mustard and nerve agents from testing; and airborne PCBs from the adjacent Monsanto plant in Anniston.
items.how: There is NO presumptive condition list and NO Fort McClellan registry. Claims are decided case by case. File 21-526EZ on a direct service-connection theory with (1) proof of assignment, (2) VA's own public health page as evidence the hazards existed, and (3) a nexus opinion from a physician.
items.hack: Because there is no presumption, the nexus letter is everything — and the strongest version cites VA's own acknowledgment of the specific agent and your specific MOS's contact with it. Chemical Corps School graduates and Women's Army Corps members who did decontamination training have the most direct evidentiary path. Also check whether a separate exposure theory applies: if you later served in a presumptive location, file on that instead, because a presumption always beats a direct claim.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Red Hill, Hawaii jet fuel spill (November 2021) — 93,000 people, no presumption yet
items.who: Service members, dependents, and civilians on the Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam water system when JP-5 jet fuel from the Red Hill Bulk Fuel Storage Facility contaminated the drinking water on Oahu beginning in November 2021. Roughly 93,000 people were affected.
items.value: No presumptive conditions exist. VA decides claims case by case. What does exist: VA health care and disability claims on a direct-exposure theory, the University of Hawai'i Red Hill Independent Health Registry for long-term monitoring, and a DoD Red Hill roster maintained in the Defense Occupational and Environmental Health Readiness System (DOEHRS).
items.how: Enroll in the University of Hawai'i Red Hill Independent Health Registry. Ask DoD to confirm you are on the DOEHRS Red Hill roster — that roster is the cleanest proof of exposure. Then file 21-526EZ with a nexus opinion.
items.hack: Get on both rosters NOW even if you are healthy. Presumptions get written years after the event, and when they are, VA will look for a contemporaneous record placing you in the affected population. The DOEHRS roster and the UH registry are that record. Nearly 90% of registry participants reported at least one new or worsening symptom — neurological, gastrointestinal, dermatologic, or mental health — so document symptoms with a clinician now, dated.
items.deadline: None, but registry enrollment is time-sensitive in practical terms — enroll before memory and records degrade.

items.title: NAF Atsugi, Japan waste incinerator, 1985–2001 — the Shinkampo Incinerator Complex
items.who: Navy and Marine Corps personnel and their families stationed at Naval Air Facility Atsugi, Japan, from 1985 to 2001, downwind of the off-base Shinkampo Incinerator Complex, which burned industrial and medical waste.
items.value: No presumptive conditions. VA decides claims individually. A 2009 Navy study found no increased cancer risk but did find higher rates of skin complaints among exposed personnel.
items.how: File 21-526EZ on a direct theory with assignment records, VA's public health acknowledgment of the incinerator, and a nexus opinion. Contact a VA Environmental Health Coordinator for an exposure evaluation.
items.hack: The Atsugi cohort includes dependents who lived in base housing for years, and their exposure is undocumented in any military record. If you were an Atsugi dependent and later served, your own DD-214 will not show the childhood exposure — you need housing records, school records, or your sponsor's orders. This one is genuinely hard; set expectations accordingly and use the environmental health evaluation to build a record.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: 38 CFR 3.316 — mustard gas and Lewisite testing: full-body exposure and what it presumes
items.who: Veterans who underwent full-body exposure to nitrogen or sulfur mustard or Lewisite during active service — including the WWII chamber and field test subjects at Edgewood Arsenal, Bushnell FL, Camp Sibert AL, Dugway Proving Ground, Naval Research Laboratory, and San Jose Island Panama, and the troops trained in gas chambers.
items.value: Full-body exposure to nitrogen or sulfur mustard presumes: chronic conjunctivitis, keratitis, corneal opacities, scar formation, nasopharyngeal cancer, laryngeal cancer, lung cancer (except mesothelioma), and squamous cell carcinoma of the skin. Full-body exposure to nitrogen or sulfur mustard OR Lewisite presumes: chronic laryngitis, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Full-body exposure to nitrogen mustard alone presumes acute nonlymphocytic leukemia.
items.how: File 21-526EZ. DoD declassified the WWII test-subject rosters; VA can query the DoD Chemical Biological Warfare exposure database. If you were sworn to secrecy, say so in your statement — VA is on notice that participants were ordered not to disclose.
items.hack: The legal trigger is 'full-body exposure,' which is broader than being a formal test subject — gas chamber training with a breached mask, or work handling contaminated munitions, can qualify. Service connection is denied only where the condition is due to willful misconduct or an intervening supervening cause.
