For a WWII-era veteran or a survivor, this is one of the few presumptive paths still meaningfully open, and DIC follows if death was from a listed cancer.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Project 112 / Project SHAD (1962–1973) — chemical and biological testing on U.S. ships and troops
items.who: Service members who participated in Project 112 (land-based) and Project SHAD (Shipboard Hazard and Defense) tests conducted by DoD from 1962 to 1973, which exposed personnel to chemical and biological warfare agents and simulants to test shipboard vulnerability.
items.value: VA provides health care and considers claims for Project 112/SHAD participants and their survivors. VA's position remains that there is no clear evidence of specific long-term health problems from SHAD participation, so there is no presumptive list — claims are individual.
items.how: Call VA health care at 1-877-222-8387 or VA benefits at 1-800-827-1000 to determine whether you appear on the DoD participant roster. DoD declassified and published the test rosters; being on one is the single strongest piece of evidence. Then file 21-526EZ with a nexus opinion.
items.hack: Many participants never knew what they were exposed to, because the tests were classified and often used code names. Ask VA specifically to query the DoD Project 112/SHAD roster by your name and service number rather than describing the test — most veterans cannot name the test they were in. If you are on the roster, the agents used in your specific test are published, which lets a physician write a targeted nexus opinion instead of a generic one.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Depleted uranium — VA's free bioassay testing and the Depleted Uranium Follow-Up Program
items.org: VHA / Baltimore VA Depleted Uranium Follow-Up Program
items.who: Veterans with potential DU exposure: those in or on a vehicle struck by DU munitions, those who entered or worked on burning DU-armored vehicles, those near DU fires, those who salvaged damaged vehicles, and K2 veterans exposed to DU-contaminated soil from destroyed Soviet missiles.
items.value: A free 24-hour urine bioassay for uranium isotopes, and for the highest-exposure group, enrollment in the Baltimore VA's Depleted Uranium Follow-Up Program with periodic comprehensive evaluation.
items.how: Contact the Environmental Health Coordinator at your VA medical center and request DU screening at no cost. Embedded DU fragments are handled through the Toxic Embedded Fragment Surveillance Center.
items.hack: A negative bioassay does not defeat a claim and a positive one does not win it — but a documented DU exposure history in your VA record supports a direct service-connection theory for renal and other conditions. The more valuable step for anyone with retained metal fragments is enrollment in the Toxic Embedded Fragment Surveillance Center, which tracks fragment composition over time; that surveillance record is durable evidence that outlives your memory of the incident.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Asbestos — no presumption, but a MOS-based exposure concession VA actually applies
items.who: Veterans in high-exposure occupations: Navy shipboard personnel (especially boiler tenders, machinist's mates, hull technicians, pipefitters, enginemen, and anyone berthed below decks on pre-1980 ships), shipyard workers, construction and demolition trades, Seabees, carpenters, insulators, vehicle mechanics doing brake and clutch work, and personnel in pre-1980 barracks and hangars.
items.value: VA's adjudication manual (M21-1) directs raters to concede asbestos exposure based on military occupational specialty when the MOS carries a high probability of exposure. Claimable conditions include asbestosis, pleural plaques and thickening, mesothelioma, lung cancer, and gastrointestinal cancers.
items.how: File 21-526EZ naming your rating/MOS and ship or installation, and ask VA to apply the M21-1 asbestos exposure probability determination. Include a chest CT or pulmonary function test showing pleural disease, and a nexus opinion where the diagnosis is a cancer.
items.hack: Pleural plaques on a chest CT are frequently reported as an incidental finding and ignored — they are, for a Navy veteran, near-diagnostic evidence of asbestos exposure and support service connection even when asymptomatic. Ask your doctor to re-read any prior chest imaging specifically for pleural changes. Separately: mesothelioma has a decades-long latency and an asbestos trust fund system outside VA entirely; pursue both, they do not conflict.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Toxic Embedded Fragment Surveillance Center — for anyone still carrying shrapnel
items.org: VHA / Toxic Embedded Fragment Surveillance Center (Baltimore)
items.who: Any veteran with retained metal fragments from a blast injury — IED, RPG, mortar, mine, or gunshot — regardless of era.
items.value: Long-term surveillance of fragment composition and systemic metal levels, periodic urine metal testing, and a clinical record tying retained fragments to later systemic disease.
items.how: Ask your VA provider for a referral to the Toxic Embedded Fragment Surveillance Center, or contact your VA Environmental Health Coordinator. Bring imaging showing the fragments.
items.hack: Retained fragments are almost always rated once, at the time of the original injury, for the wound itself — and then forgotten. But fragments leach metals (lead, tungsten alloys, depleted uranium, cobalt) for decades, and the systemic effects are separately claimable as secondary conditions under 38 CFR 3.310. Surveillance testing is what turns 'I have shrapnel' into documented, dated, rising metal levels.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Former Prisoners of War — the two presumptive lists (any internment vs. 30 days or more), 38 CFR 3.309(c)
items.who: Any veteran who was a prisoner of war, any era.
items.value: For ANY period of internment: psychosis; any of the anxiety states (including PTSD); dysthymic disorder / depressive neurosis; organic residuals of frostbite (where the POW experienced localized cold injury); post-traumatic osteoarthritis; atherosclerotic heart disease or hypertensive vascular disease and their complications; stroke and its residuals; and osteoporosis where PTSD is also diagnosed. For internment of 30 DAYS OR MORE, additionally: avitaminosis; beriberi (including beriberi heart disease); chronic dysentery; helminthiasis; malnutrition (including optic atrophy associated with malnutrition); pellagra and other nutritional deficiencies; irritable bowel syndrome; peptic ulcer disease; peripheral neuropathy except where directly related to infectious causes; cirrhosis of the liver; and osteoporosis (claims filed on or after 28 Sep 2009, with no PTSD requirement).
items.how: File 21-526EZ; VA verifies POW status from service records or the DoD POW database. A diagnosis of a listed condition at any degree of 10% or more at any time after service is enough.
items.hack: There is no manifestation deadline for POW presumptives — a condition appearing fifty years later still qualifies. The 30-day list is where the money usually is, because it captures the chronic GI and neuropathic sequelae of captivity that families attribute to aging. And note 'any of the anxiety states' includes PTSD: a former POW with PTSD has a presumptive grant and does not need to prove a stressor at all.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Former POW status beyond compensation — Priority Group 3, no copays, and a dedicated coordinator
items.who: Any veteran with verified former POW status.
items.value: Automatic enrollment in VA health care at Priority Group 3 (or higher if the rating warrants), exemption from copayments for care and medications related to POW status, a designated Former POW Coordinator at every VA medical center, a dedicated POW protocol examination, and eligibility for the POW medal. Former POWs also have in-person commissary, exchange and MWR access.
items.how: Ask your VA medical center for the Former POW Coordinator by name. Request the POW protocol examination — it is a structured, comprehensive evaluation specifically designed to surface the presumptive conditions.
items.hack: The POW protocol exam is the leverage point and almost nobody asks for it. It is a specialized, head-to-toe evaluation that explicitly screens for every condition on the 3.309(c) lists — which means it generates the diagnoses that then feed a presumptive claim. Request the exam BEFORE filing the claim, not after.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Filipino Veterans Equity Compensation Fund — closed to new claims, but survivor and recognition paths remain
items.who: Filipino veterans of World War II who served in the Philippine Commonwealth Army, recognized guerrilla units, or the New Philippine Scouts.
items.value: The FVEC Fund, created by the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, paid a one-time lump sum of $15,000 to eligible U.S. citizens and $9,000 to non-citizens. The filing deadline was 16 Feb 2010 and the fund is closed to new applications.
items.how: Claims already adjudicated can still be appealed through the standard VA appeals system, and errors in the National Archives' Missouri List determinations remain contestable. Separately, the Filipino Veterans of World War II Congressional Gold Medal remains available: surviving veterans and next of kin may request a bronze replica through the Filipino Veterans Recognition and Education Project.
items.hack: The practical living benefit for this cohort is not FVEC — it is the ordinary VA benefits system. Recognized guerrilla and New Philippine Scout service can support VA disability compensation, and surviving spouses can claim Survivors Pension and DIC. Because the National Archives' service verification is the usual point of failure, appeal a negative service determination rather than accepting it; the Missouri List is known to be incomplete.
items.deadline: FVEC claims deadline was 16 Feb 2010 — CLOSED. No deadline for appeals of decided claims or for Congressional Gold Medal replicas.

items.title: WWII, Korea and Cold War veterans — what is still claimable in 2026
items.who: Surviving WWII, Korean War, and Cold War era veterans and their surviving spouses.
items.value: Still open: radiation presumptives (atmospheric testing, Hiroshima/Nagasaki occupation, POW in Japan); mustard gas and Lewisite testing under 3.316; former POW presumptives; cold injury residuals (a distinct VA claim category for Korea, rated for peripheral neuropathy, arthritis, skin and nail changes); tropical disease presumptives; VA Pension with Aid & Attendance for low-income wartime veterans; Survivors Pension and DIC for spouses; and burial and memorial benefits.
items.how: File 21-526EZ for the veteran; VA Form 21P-534EZ for a surviving spouse claiming DIC, Survivors Pension, and accrued benefits together.
items.hack: Cold injury is the most-missed Korea-era claim. VA has a specific cold injury protocol examination and rates the residuals — Raynaud's phenomenon, peripheral neuropathy, arthritis in the affected joints, nail and skin changes, and amputations — separately for each affected extremity, which stacks fast under the bilateral factor. Ask for the cold injury protocol exam by name. For surviving spouses, note that 21P-534EZ is a single form that VA must treat as a claim for every survivor benefit at once — never file for just one.
items.deadline: None. Surviving spouses should file within one year of death to maximize the effective date for accrued benefits.

items.title: 38 CFR 3.310(d) — the five conditions presumed secondary to TBI, with exact severity and time thresholds
items.who: Any veteran with a service-connected traumatic brain injury.
items.value: Five conditions are presumed to be proximately due to service-connected TBI: (1) Parkinsonism, including Parkinson's disease, following moderate or severe TBI — no time limit; (2) unprovoked seizures following moderate or severe TBI — no time limit; (3) dementias of the specific types presenile dementia of the Alzheimer type, frontotemporal dementia, and dementia with Lewy bodies, if manifest within 15 years following moderate or severe TBI; (4) depression, if manifest within 3 years of moderate or severe TBI, or within 12 months of mild TBI; (5) diseases of hormone deficiency that result from hypothalamo-pituitary changes, if manifest within 12 months of moderate or severe TBI.
items.how: File 21-526EZ for the secondary condition, citing 38 CFR 3.310(d) explicitly. VA must classify the TBI severity using the regulation's own table, which weighs loss of consciousness, alteration of consciousness/mental state, post-traumatic amnesia, and Glasgow Coma Scale score.
items.hack: Two things. First, depression is the one with a mild-TBI pathway — 12 months after a mild TBI — and mild TBI is by far the most common. Second, and this is the sentence that wins cases: the regulation expressly states that these severity levels and time limits do NOT preclude a finding of service connection based on other evidence. So if your dementia appears at year 17, you have lost the presumption but not the claim — you switch to an ordinary secondary claim under 3.310(a) with a nexus opinion. Raters conflate the two constantly.
items.deadline: The time windows above are for the PRESUMPTION only, not for filing.

items.title: Proving 'moderate or severe' TBI when nobody wrote it down
items.who: Veterans whose TBI happened in a combat zone, a training accident, or a vehicle rollover where no one performed a Glasgow Coma Scale assessment.
items.value: The 3.310(d) presumptions all turn on the moderate-or-severe threshold (except the 12-month depression window for mild TBI). Getting reclassified from mild to moderate is worth five presumptive conditions.
items.how: VA's severity table looks at: structural imaging findings, duration of loss of consciousness, duration of alteration of consciousness or mental state, duration of post-traumatic amnesia, and Glasgow Coma Scale within 24 hours. Moderate generally means LOC of 30 minutes to 24 hours, alteration of mental state over 24 hours, or post-traumatic amnesia of 1 to 7 days.
items.hack: Post-traumatic amnesia is the most winnable criterion because it is measured in DAYS and can be established by lay evidence. If you cannot remember the day of the blast and the day after, that is post-traumatic amnesia of more than 24 hours, which pushes you into moderate. Get buddy statements (VA Form 21-10210) from people who saw you confused, repeating questions, or unable to account for time. A medic's or squadmate's account of your behavior in the hours after the event is worth more than a CT scan that was never ordered.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Requesting your records from NPRC — eVetRecs, ID.me, and what to expect
items.org: National Archives / National Personnel Records Center, St. Louis
items.who: Veterans themselves, and the next of kin of a deceased veteran (an un-remarried surviving spouse, parent, child, or sibling). Anyone may request records that are more than 62 years past the date of separation.
items.value: Your DD-214, your full Official Military Personnel File, and your service treatment records — free to the veteran and to next of kin.
items.how: Use eVetRecs at vetrecs.archives.gov, which now requires identity verification through ID.me. Or mail/fax Standard Form 180 to: National Personnel Records Center, Military Personnel Records, 1 Archives Drive, St. Louis, MO 63138; fax 314-801-9195. Include full name, service number, Social Security number, branch, dates of service, and date and place of birth.
items.hack: NPRC processes roughly 4,000–5,000 requests a day and routine turnaround runs 90 days or more. Two ways to move faster: (1) if you separated after 1997, try milConnect (milconnect.dmdc.osd.mil) first — DoD holds those records electronically and can deliver a DD-214 in days, not months; (2) state veterans affairs offices and county veterans service officers often hold a filed copy of your DD-214 and will give you one the same day, because discharge papers are commonly recorded with the county at separation. Call the county recorder in the county where you separated before you write to St. Louis.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: The 1973 St. Louis fire — whose records burned, and what to do if yours did
items.who: Army personnel discharged 1 Nov 1912 through 1 Jan 1960 (approximately 80% loss) and Air Force personnel discharged 25 Sep 1947 through 1 Jan 1964 with surnames alphabetically after Hubbard, James E. (approximately 75% loss). Between 16 and 18 million Official Military Personnel Files were destroyed on 12 July 1973. There were no duplicates and no microfilm.
items.value: NPRC reconstructs burned files from alternate sources: VA claims files, state adjutant general records, Adjutant General's Office Multiple Name Pay Vouchers, Selective Service registration records, GAO pay records, military hospital records, entrance and separation X-rays, and organizational (unit) records. Roughly 6.5 million burned and water-damaged records were salvaged and are indexed in separate 'B' (Burned) and 'R' (Reconstructed) registries.
items.how: When requesting, state that the record may be fire-related and include everything you can: place of entry into service, last unit of assignment, place of discharge, and exact dates. NPRC will search the B and R files. NPRC will typically send NA Form 13055 (Request for Information Needed to Reconstruct Medical Data) asking you to list units, dates, and places of treatment.
items.hack: Fill out NA Form 13055 with obsessive specificity — three-month date ranges, exact unit designations down to company and battalion, and the names of the installations and hospitals. NPRC searches unit morning reports and Surgeon General records by date range; a vague answer produces a vague search and a 'no records found.' Also: your VA claims file, if you ever filed anything, frequently contains a copy of records that burned. Request your C-file by FOIA from the VA regional office in parallel — it is a completely separate holding from NPRC and is the single best workaround for a burned file.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Emergency and expedited records requests — the priority lanes NPRC does not advertise
items.who: Anyone needing records urgently for a burial in a national cemetery, a medical emergency, a homeless veteran's benefits application, or a hardship.
items.value: NPRC operates priority handling for burial-related requests and for documented emergencies, which can compress a 90-day wait to days.
items.how: Write 'URGENT — BURIAL' or 'EMERGENCY' prominently on the SF-180 and in the eVetRecs comments field, state the specific emergency, and give the funeral home's name and the date and time of the service. Fax rather than mail: 314-801-9195. For burials, the funeral director should also contact the VA National Cemetery Scheduling Office at 1-800-535-1117, which can often verify eligibility without the DD-214 in hand.
items.hack: For a burial, do not wait on NPRC at all if you can avoid it. The National Cemetery Scheduling Office has its own access to DoD records and routinely establishes eligibility from a name, date of birth, and service number. The DD-214 is the convenient path, not the required one. Meanwhile, homeless veterans should go through a VA Homeless Program coordinator, who has an expedited records channel most veterans never learn about.
items.deadline: None, but the burial lane is time-critical by nature.

items.title: Request the FULL Official Military Personnel File, not just the DD-214
items.who: Any veteran or next of kin.
items.value: The complete OMPF — enlistment documents, assignment orders, performance evaluations, awards and decorations records, training records, disciplinary actions, and the service treatment record — rather than the single-page separation summary.
items.how: On SF-180 block 2 or in eVetRecs, check or write 'Complete Official Military Personnel File (OMPF) — ALL pages' and separately request 'Service Treatment Records / Health Record' and 'Dental Record.' These are held separately and are NOT included by default.
items.hack: This is the highest-leverage sentence in this entire category: most veterans request 'my DD-214' and receive exactly that, then spend years fighting a disability claim without the in-service medical evidence that would have won it in a month. Ask for the OMPF, the service treatment records, AND the dental record in the same request. The dental record matters because it contains dated entries placing you at specific installations, which is how you prove presence at an exposure site when your personnel file is thin. Service treatment records for post-1992 separations may be held by VA rather than NPRC — request from both.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: The DD-214 paywall scam — every one of these records is free
items.who: Every veteran and next of kin.
items.value: Your DD-214, your OMPF, your service treatment records, your medals, and your headstone are all free from the government. Commercial sites charging $40 to $200 to 'expedite' or 'retrieve' a DD-214 are simply filling out the same free SF-180 you can file yourself, and they do not have a faster lane.
items.how: Use only these: vetrecs.archives.gov (eVetRecs), archives.gov (SF-180), milconnect.dmdc.osd.mil (post-1997 separations), va.gov, and your county recorder or state veterans affairs office. Anything with a .com that asks for a card number to get your DD-214 is a middleman.
items.hack: Three tells that you are on a paid middleman site: it asks for payment before showing you the SF-180; it claims a 'priority' or 'rush' channel with the National Archives; or it appears as a sponsored search result above archives.gov. NPRC has no paid expedite tier. The only legitimate fees anywhere in this space are the $25–$70 copying fees the National Archives charges the GENERAL PUBLIC for archival records more than 62 years old — never the veteran, never next of kin. Accredited VSO representatives (DAV, VFW, American Legion, county service officers) will do the whole thing for free and are the correct answer if you want help.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Boards for Correction of Military Records (DD Form 149) — the 3-year clock and how it gets waived
items.org: Army Review Boards Agency / BCNR / AFBCMR / Coast Guard BCMR
items.who: Any veteran seeking to correct an error or remove an injustice in a military record — a wrong discharge characterization beyond the 15-year DRB limit, a missing award, an incorrect narrative reason or separation code, a denied medical retirement, or an incorrect date of service.
items.value: The BCMRs are the highest administrative authority over military records and can change almost anything, including retroactive promotion, retroactive medical retirement, and back pay.
items.how: File DD Form 149 with the correct service's board: Army Review Boards Agency (ARBA, with the ACTSOnline portal); Board for Correction of Naval Records for Navy and Marine Corps; Air Force Board for Correction of Military Records for Air Force and Space Force; Coast Guard BCMR for Coast Guard. Do NOT send it to the National Archives.
items.hack: The statute says file within three years of discovering the error, but the boards waive the deadline 'in the interest of justice' routinely — so file anyway, and include a short paragraph explaining why the delay is excusable (you did not know, records were unavailable, a condition prevented it). Never leave the timeliness section blank; an unexplained late filing is the easiest procedural denial a board can write. Also: exhaust the Discharge Review Board first where it has jurisdiction, because the BCMR will often decline to act until you have.
items.deadline: 3 years from discovery of the error, waivable in the interest of justice.

items.title: DD Form 215 — the correction document that amends your DD-214 without reissuing it
items.who: Any veteran whose DD-214 omits an award, a deployment, a campaign, education, or a correct separation code.
items.value: A DD Form 215 is an official addendum that corrects or adds to a DD-214. It travels with the DD-214 and has the same legal force. It is how a retroactively awarded medal, a corrected narrative reason, or a missed campaign star gets onto your discharge record.
items.how: Request it from your service branch's personnel command — NOT from the National Archives, which no longer issues DD-215s. For administrative corrections (a misspelling, a missing award you can prove you earned), the branch can issue a DD-215 directly. For substantive changes (discharge characterization, narrative reason, separation code), you need the DRB (DD Form 293) or BCMR (DD Form 149) first, and the board's decision then triggers the DD-215.
items.hack: The distinction that saves months: an ADMINISTRATIVE correction needs no board. If the underlying record already shows you earned the Combat Action Ribbon, or that you deployed, and the DD-214 simply omits it, that is a clerical fix your branch can make on request. Only file a DD-149 when you are asking someone to change a decision, not to fix a typo. Adding a retroactively awarded medal is the most common legitimate DD-215 request.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Using a Congressional office to unstick a records or claims request
items.org: U.S. House and Senate constituent services
items.who: Any veteran whose NPRC request, medal request, records correction, or VA claim has stalled beyond normal timelines.
items.value: Every House and Senate office runs a casework operation with dedicated liaisons at NPRC, the service personnel commands, and VA. A Congressional inquiry gets logged in a separate queue with a response requirement, and it is free.
items.how: Find your Representative's and Senators' websites, look for 'Help with a Federal Agency' or 'Casework,' and submit the privacy release form they require (each office has its own; it authorizes them to access your records). Include your request's tracking number, the date you filed, and what you have already tried.
items.hack: Three things make an inquiry effective. First, go to BOTH Senators and your Representative — they are separate offices with separate liaisons and there is no penalty for parallel inquiries. Second, be specific and unemotional: 'SF-180 submitted 14 March, no response in 190 days, request number X' works; a long narrative does not. Third, ask your caseworker to request a STATUS AND ESTIMATED COMPLETION DATE rather than asking them to 'approve' anything — casework offices cannot change a decision, but they can force a file to the top of a stack, and that is usually all you need. This is also the standard path for a stalled retroactive medal request, which can otherwise sit for years.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Replacing lost or stolen medals — free from your branch, and the branch-by-branch routing
items.who: Veterans and, in most branches, authorized next of kin of a deceased veteran. Replacements are free.
items.value: A full replacement set of every medal, decoration, and award you earned, issued by your branch at no cost.
items.how: Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Air Force requests start at the National Personnel Records Center, 1 Archives Drive, St. Louis, MO 63138 (or online at archives.gov) — NPRC verifies the entitlement from your record and forwards to the issuing command. Coast Guard requests go directly to Coast Guard Personnel Service Center, 4200 Wilson Blvd, Suite 900, Arlington, VA 20598-7200. Issuing commands: U.S. Army TACOM in Philadelphia; HQ AFPC at Randolph AFB (or the Air Reserve Personnel Center at Buckley for reserve and guard); Navy Personnel Command at Millington TN for Navy and Marine Corps.
items.hack: Next-of-kin eligibility differs by branch and the order matters. Army: surviving spouse, then eldest child, then parents, then eldest sibling. Other branches: un-remarried widow or widower, then children, then parents, then siblings. If you are not the highest-priority next of kin, get a short letter from whoever is. Turnaround commonly runs six to twelve months — this is the classic case for a Congressional inquiry after the six-month mark.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Claiming medals you earned but were never issued
items.who: Any veteran whose record shows qualifying service for an award that was never presented — extremely common for campaign and service medals created or amended after the veteran separated.
items.value: Medals created retroactively (the Global War on Terrorism Expeditionary and Service Medals, the Korea Defense Service Medal, the Kosovo Campaign Medal, the Armed Forces Service Medal, and campaign stars added later) plus unit awards earned while you were assigned but conferred after you left.
items.how: Submit the same request as for replacements (SF-180 or archives.gov, marked as a request for award determination and issuance), but include the EVIDENCE of entitlement: orders, a DD-214 showing the qualifying deployment dates, or the unit award general order number.
items.hack: NPRC will verify entitlement from your file, but if the file is thin it will simply say 'not shown in record' — so do the entitlement research yourself before filing. The Korea Defense Service Medal (for service in Korea after 28 July 1954) and the Global War on Terrorism Service Medal are the two most widely unclaimed. Once the medal is approved, ask in the same letter for a DD Form 215 adding it to your DD-214, or you will have the medal and no document proving it.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Retroactive Purple Heart — including for TBI from blast exposure
items.who: Any service member wounded or killed by enemy action, in any conflict, whose award was never processed. Since 2011 DoD policy has expressly recognized mild traumatic brain injury and concussion from enemy blast as a qualifying wound.
items.value: The Purple Heart carries far more than the medal: permanent commissary, exchange and MWR access; VA health care Priority Group 3; exemption from VA health care copayments; preference in federal hiring; and eligibility in many state benefit programs.
items.how: If the injury is documented in your service treatment records, request the award through your branch's awards branch with the medical documentation and a statement of the circumstances. If the record is incomplete or the request is denied, file DD Form 149 with your service's BCMR.
items.hack: The blast-TBI pathway is the live one. Thousands of Iraq and Afghanistan veterans were concussed by IEDs, treated by a medic, returned to duty, and never had it written up. What the boards look for is: (1) the injury was caused by enemy action, (2) it required treatment by a medical officer, and (3) it is documented in the record. Reconstruct all three with buddy statements (VA Form 21-10210), the unit's significant-activity reports, the medic's own statement if you can find them, and any later VA TBI diagnosis. Being 'returned to duty' does not disqualify you — that misconception defeats more of these than anything else.
items.deadline: None. BCMR's 3-year rule is routinely waived for Purple Heart cases.

items.title: Retroactive Combat Action Badge, Combat Infantryman Badge, and Combat Action Ribbon
items.org: Army HRC / Navy and Marine Corps awards branches / Air Force AFPC
items.who: Army: the Combat Action Badge is awardable retroactively to 18 September 2001 for soldiers who were personally present and actively engaged by or engaging the enemy. Navy and Marine Corps: the Combat Action Ribbon. Air Force: the Combat Action Medal, retroactive to 11 September 2001.
items.value: Formal documentation of combat service — which is the evidentiary key to combat-related presumptions, the relaxed PTSD stressor standard under 38 CFR 3.304(f)(2), Combat-Related Special Compensation, and combat veteran health care enrollment.
items.how: Army: submit a retroactive CAB request through Army Human Resources Command using their published packet requirements — a memorandum from the first O-5 or above in your chain, two eyewitness sworn statements, supporting documents (SIGACT reports, storyboards, AARs), and a narrative. Navy/Marine Corps and Air Force: through the respective awards branch, or the BCMR if the chain of command no longer exists.
items.hack: The value here is usually not the badge — it is what the badge proves. A CAB or CAR on your record means VA must accept your lay statement of an in-service stressor for PTSD without further corroboration under 38 CFR 3.304(f)(2), and it supports CRSC at DFAS. If your chain of command has dissolved and you cannot get an O-5 memorandum, go straight to the BCMR with DD Form 149 and the eyewitness statements — the board can award it where HRC cannot.
items.deadline: None; CAB retroactive to 18 Sep 2001, Air Force Combat Action Medal to 11 Sep 2001.

items.title: Veteran Health Identification Card (VHIC) — the card that is also your base access credential
items.who: Any veteran enrolled in VA health care.
items.value: Free photo ID for checking in at VA facilities, accepted for veteran discounts — and, critically, the VHIC is the credential that establishes eligibility for in-person commissary, exchange and MWR access when it is annotated SERVICE CONNECTED, PURPLE HEART, or FORMER POW.
items.how: Enroll in VA health care (VA Form 10-10EZ), then request the VHIC online through VA.gov or in person at the enrollment or eligibility office of any VA medical center. Bring a government photo ID.
items.hack: The annotation is the whole point and it is not automatic. A VHIC issued before your service-connection rating came through will NOT carry the SERVICE CONNECTED eligibility line — and without it, the commissary gate will turn you away. If your rating changed, or you received a Purple Heart determination, or your POW status was confirmed, go back and request a REPLACEMENT VHIC so the new status prints on the card. Check the expiration date too; an expired VHIC is not an accepted credential.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Veteran ID Card (VIC) — free proof of service for discounts, no health enrollment needed
items.who: Veterans who served on active duty, in the Reserves, or in the National Guard (including Coast Guard) and received an honorable or general (under honorable conditions) discharge. Other than honorable, bad conduct, and dishonorable discharges are ineligible; uncharacterized or unknown statuses require verification.
items.value: A free digital photo ID proving veteran status, so you do not have to carry a DD-214 (which contains your Social Security number and should never be in your wallet) to claim a retail or restaurant discount.
items.how: Apply online at VA.gov. You need a copy of your DD-214 or equivalent, a digital photo of yourself (passport-style, no hat or sunglasses), and a government-issued photo ID.
items.hack: The VIC is NOT a military ID and does not get you on a base or into a commissary — that is the VHIC's job, and only with the right annotation. Know which card does what before you drive to a gate. What the VIC does well is exactly one thing: it ends the practice of photocopying a DD-214 and handing it to a cashier, which is how veterans' Social Security numbers end up in strangers' hands. If you were denied for an uncharacterized discharge, VA will verify with DoD — resubmit rather than assuming you are ineligible.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Veteran designation on your state driver's license — available in all 50 states and Puerto Rico
items.who: Veterans in every state and Puerto Rico. Specific eligibility (honorable discharge, minimum service, residency) varies by state.
items.value: A permanent 'VETERAN' marking on the license or state ID you already carry — the most practical proof of service in existence, because it is in your wallet, it is free or nearly free in most states, and it never needs to be renewed separately.
items.how: Bring your DD-214 (member copy 4) to a DMV office at your next license renewal or replacement, and ask for the veteran designation. Most states will image the DD-214 and return it. Some states require verification through the state department of veterans affairs first; a few charge a small duplicate-license fee.
items.hack: Do this at your normal renewal and it usually costs nothing extra. Two things to know: some states use a distinct designation for DISABLED veterans that unlocks additional state benefits (property tax, park passes, hunting and fishing licenses), so ask which designations your state offers rather than accepting the default; and a handful of states will accept a VA benefit summary letter in place of a DD-214 if your records burned in 1973. Several states also add a Purple Heart or combat-veteran designation on request.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA benefit summary and proof-of-service letters — instant, free, printable
items.who: Any veteran with a VA.gov account.
items.value: Downloadable official letters: the Benefit Summary and Service Verification Letter (proves service dates, character of discharge, disability rating, and monthly award amount), the Civil Service Preference Letter, the Service Verification Letter, and the Proof of Creditable Prescription Drug Coverage Letter. Generated on demand, in seconds.
items.how: Sign in at VA.gov and go to 'Download VA letters.' You can customize the Benefit Summary Letter to include or exclude your disability rating and your award amount before printing.
items.hack: Use the customization. When you need to prove veteran status to a landlord, a lender, or a discount program, generate the version WITHOUT the disability rating and award amount — the recipient gets what they need and nothing else. When you need to prove eligibility for a property tax exemption or a state disabled-veteran benefit, generate the version WITH the rating and the permanent-and-total indicator. This is faster and safer than sending a DD-214, and the letter is accepted almost everywhere the DD-214 is.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Getting through the gate — installation enrollment for veteran patrons
items.who: Veterans and caregivers eligible under the Purple Heart and Disabled Veterans Equal Access Act who do not hold a DoD-issued credential.
items.value: A recurring installation access credential, typically valid one to three years, or one year after your last installation visit.
items.how: Go to the installation's visitor control center (not the main gate) with your annotated VHIC or alternate VA letter and a REAL ID-compliant identity document. You will be run through a criminal record and terrorism background check and an electronic verification of your on-installation benefits eligibility. Once enrolled, you present the credential at the gate.
items.hack: Do the enrollment on a weekday morning at the visitor center, never at 5pm at the gate — the gate guard cannot run the enrollment and will simply turn you away, which is the experience that convinces most veterans the benefit does not exist. Call the visitor center first and ask what they require; implementation varies by installation. Bring the physical VHIC, not a photo of it. And if you were denied before, try again: DoD has repeatedly streamlined this process since 2020 and gate procedures that failed in the first year often work now.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Online exchange shopping — open to ALL honorably discharged veterans, tax-free, no rating required
items.who: EVERY veteran with an honorable discharge. No disability rating, no VA enrollment, no base access, no Purple Heart required. This is a separate and much broader benefit than in-person access.
items.value: Lifetime online shopping at shopmyexchange.com, mynavyexchange.com, shopcgx.com and the Marine Corps exchange — with no sales tax charged, plus access to exchange price-matching and the Military Star card.
items.how: Verify your status once at VetVerify.org, which checks DoD records. If automatic verification fails, you upload a DD-214. Once verified, you create an account at the exchange site and shop indefinitely.
items.hack: No sales tax is the whole benefit, and on large purchases it is substantial — on a $2,000 appliance or electronics order in a 9% sales tax state, that is $180 saved before any price comparison. Exchanges also price-match major retailers, so the tax exemption stacks on top of a matched price. Verify now even if you have nothing to buy; verification can take days if DoD records do not match and you do not want to discover that mid-purchase. Note that this online benefit does NOT get you into a physical store or a commissary — those require the Equal Access Act criteria.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Space-Available travel — the six priority categories and who is in each
items.who: Category I: emergency leave unfunded travel. Category II: accompanied environmental and morale leave (EML). Category III: ordinary leave, house-hunting permissive TDY, Medal of Honor recipients, and foreign military. Category IV: unaccompanied EML. Category V: permissive TDY other than house hunting, students, dependents, and post-deployment/mobilization respite absence. Category VI: retirees, their dependents, Reserve members, ROTC and related programs, veterans with a permanent service-connected disability rated as total, and surviving spouses of members who died on active duty, inactive duty training, or annual training.
items.value: Free or nearly free air travel on military aircraft, on a space-available basis after mission requirements and higher categories are filled.
items.how: Sign up through the AMC Space-A automated form, or download AMC Form 140 and email it to the passenger terminals you want to depart from. You list up to five destinations, your category, your travel dates, and the number of seats needed. Sign-up is free and you may be signed up at multiple terminals at once.
items.hack: Category is everything, because seats fill from Category I down. Category VI travelers — which includes retirees and 100% P&T veterans — are last in line, and on popular routes that means genuinely long waits. Sign up as early as your window allows (typically 60 days ahead), register at several terminals simultaneously, travel midweek and off-season, and always have the money for a commercial ticket home. Space-A is a way to travel cheaply if you are flexible, not a way to be somewhere on a date.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Space-A for 100% permanently disabled veterans — the FY2019 NDAA expansion and its limits
items.who: Veterans with a permanent service-connected disability rated as total (100% permanent and total). Authorized by the John S. McCain National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2019 and implemented in 2019.
items.value: Category VI Space-A travel, the same priority as military retirees. In practice this has been implemented primarily as travel within the continental United States and to and from Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands, rather than full overseas access — verify the current geographic scope with the AMC passenger terminal before planning.
items.how: Present a Veteran Health Identification Card annotated SERVICE CONNECTED along with a VA letter confirming a permanent and total rating. Sign up at the passenger terminal via the AMC automated form or AMC Form 140.
items.hack: Two practical points. First, a 100% rating that is not PERMANENT does not qualify — the letter has to say permanent and total, so pull the Benefit Summary Letter from VA.gov and confirm the P&T indicator before you drive to a terminal. Second, dependents do not travel on this authority; unlike a retiree, a 100% P&T veteran travels alone. Call the specific passenger terminal before your first trip — terminal-level interpretation of the geographic scope has varied, and a five-minute phone call prevents a wasted drive.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Pre-need burial eligibility determination (VA Form 40-10007) — do this now, for your family
items.who: Veterans, eligible spouses and surviving spouses, dependent children including adult children who are permanently disabled, and authorized representatives acting for them.
items.value: A written determination, issued while you are alive, that you are eligible for burial in a VA national cemetery. It does not reserve a specific plot and it does not guarantee a particular cemetery will still have space, but it settles the eligibility question permanently.
items.how: Submit VA Form 40-10007 online at VA.gov, by mail to the NCA Evidence Intake Center in Janesville WI, or by fax. Include the DD-214 or separation documents, Social Security number, and your preferred cemetery. Pre-need does not apply to Arlington National Cemetery or to state and tribal veterans cemeteries, which run their own processes.
items.hack: This is the single kindest piece of paperwork a veteran can do for their family, and it takes twenty minutes. Without it, your family spends the 48 hours after your death hunting for a DD-214 that may have burned in 1973, while a funeral director waits. With it, they call the National Cemetery Scheduling Office at 1-800-535-1117 and read them a determination number. Do it, then put the determination letter with your will — not in a safe deposit box, which may be sealed at death. Tell at least two people where it is.
items.deadline: None, but the entire point is to do it in advance.

items.title: Who else can be buried with you — spouses, remarried surviving spouses, and dependent children
items.who: Spouses and surviving spouses of eligible veterans (including a surviving spouse who has REMARRIED — remarriage no longer bars burial with the veteran), minor children, and unmarried adult children who became permanently physically or mentally disabled and incapable of self-support before reaching age 21 (or age 23 if a full-time student).
items.value: Burial in the same gravesite as the veteran, at no cost: the grave, opening and closing, perpetual care, and inclusion on the government headstone. VA typically provides one gravesite and one headstone for the veteran and all eligible family members — though two married veterans may each request their own gravesite.
items.how: At time of need, the funeral director calls the National Cemetery Scheduling Office at 1-800-535-1117. For pre-need determination, include the family members on VA Form 40-10007.
items.hack: The remarriage rule is the one people get wrong. A surviving spouse who remarried after the veteran's death is STILL eligible for burial with the veteran — the old bar was removed. Families routinely assume otherwise and bury a parent elsewhere. The other trap is the disabled adult child rule: the disability must have begun before 21 (or 23 if a student), not later, so document the onset date while the records still exist. Note also the disqualifications: dishonorable discharge, a final conviction for a capital crime, a Tier III sex offense with a life sentence, and subversive activities convictions after 1 Sep 1959.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: State and tribal veterans cemeteries — closer to home, and they have their own residency rules
items.org: VA NCA Veterans Cemetery Grants Program / state and tribal governments
items.who: Veterans and eligible family members meeting the operating state's or tribe's eligibility rules — which almost always include a state RESIDENCY requirement that VA national cemeteries do not have.
items.value: More than 100 VA-grant-funded state, territorial, and tribal veterans cemeteries, built with NCA construction grants and operated locally. Burial benefits closely mirror national cemeteries — free gravesite, opening and closing, perpetual care, and a government headstone — but residency and sometimes a modest fee for spouses apply.
items.how: Apply directly to the state or tribal cemetery, not to NCA. Pre-need determination through VA Form 40-10007 does NOT cover these cemeteries; each has its own pre-need process.
items.hack: For most families the grant-funded cemetery is the better practical choice, because it is far closer to home than the nearest national cemetery — VA built the program specifically to reach veterans more than 75 miles from a national cemetery. Two things to check before deciding: the residency rule (some states require residency at time of death, some accept residency at time of entry into service, some accept either) and whether the state charges a spouse interment fee, which several do and national cemeteries do not. Ask both questions in one phone call to the cemetery.
items.deadline: None, but do the state's pre-need process separately from VA's.

items.title: Arlington National Cemetery — stricter than every other national cemetery
items.org: Department of the Army / Arlington National Cemetery
items.who: Arlington is administered by the Army, not by VA's National Cemetery Administration, and its eligibility criteria are substantially narrower. In-ground casket interment is generally limited to service members who died on active duty, military retirees (20+ years and retired pay), recipients of the nation's highest decorations (Medal of Honor, Distinguished Service Cross and service equivalents, Silver Star, Purple Heart), former prisoners of war, certain senior government officials, and close family members of those eligible. Above-ground inurnment in the Columbarium is available to a broader group of honorably discharged veterans.
items.value: Interment at Arlington, with full military honors available.
items.how: Contact Arlington National Cemetery directly at 1-877-907-8585. VA's pre-need determination (Form 40-10007) does NOT apply to Arlington.
items.hack: The distinction families most need to hear in advance: many honorably discharged veterans who do not qualify for in-ground burial at Arlington DO qualify for inurnment in the Columbarium. If Arlington matters to your family, ask about the Columbarium rather than accepting a flat 'not eligible.' Also understand that Arlington's capacity constraints have driven repeated eligibility tightening, and the rules in effect at your death are the ones that govern — which is a strong argument for also completing a VA pre-need determination for a national cemetery as a fallback.
items.deadline: None, but no pre-need reservations are available at Arlington.

items.title: Government headstone or marker for a grave in a PRIVATE cemetery (VA Form 40-1330)
items.who: Veterans not dishonorably discharged. For a privately purchased headstone already in place, the death must have occurred on or after 1 Nov 1990. For an UNMARKED grave anywhere in the world, there is no date-of-death restriction. Veterans who enlisted after 7 Sep 1980, or entered as officers after 16 Oct 1981, generally need 24 months of continuous active duty or death in service.
items.value: A free government headstone, flat marker (granite, marble, or bronze), or niche marker — delivered at no charge to the cemetery. The government does not pay the cemetery's setting fee.
items.how: Submit VA Form 40-1330 online through QuickSubmit on AccessVA, by mail to NCA FP Evidence Intake Center, PO Box 5237, Janesville WI 53547, or by fax. The cemetery or funeral home must sign to confirm they will accept and set it. Help line: 1-800-697-6947.
items.hack: The most overlooked case is the UNMARKED grave with no date restriction — which means a Civil War, Spanish-American War, or WWI ancestor lying in an unmarked family plot is eligible for a free government headstone today, and a descendant can request it. Genealogical societies do this routinely. Also: the applicant does not have to be next of kin; a personal representative, a VSO representative, or a government employee serving veterans may apply. Budget for the cemetery's setting fee, which is the only real cost and is typically $150–$500.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Bronze medallion for a privately purchased headstone (VA Form 40-1330M)
items.who: Veterans who died on or after 1 Nov 1990, whose grave in a private cemetery is already marked with a privately purchased headstone — where the family wants to keep that headstone.
items.value: A free bronze medallion, affixed to the existing private headstone, identifying the deceased as a veteran. Available in multiple sizes (large, medium, small) plus a Medal of Honor medallion.
items.how: Submit VA Form 40-1330M with proof of service and proof that the grave is marked with a privately purchased headstone. Mail or fax to the NCA FP Evidence Intake Center in Janesville WI, or use QuickSubmit.
items.hack: This exists precisely for the family that already bought and set a beautiful private headstone and does not want a government marker beside it. You choose the medallion OR the government headstone, not both — so decide before ordering. The medallion is also the right answer for a shared family monument where a separate government marker would be unwelcome. It comes with mounting hardware; a monument company can affix it in under an hour.
items.deadline: None; requires death on or after 1 Nov 1990.

items.title: Headstone inscription rules — emblems of belief, nicknames, and what VA will and will not engrave
items.who: Anyone ordering a government headstone or marker.
items.value: Mandatory inscription items (name, branch, years of birth and death) are provided at no cost. VA also permits at government expense: rank, war service, month and day of birth and death, awards, an emblem of belief, and a limited additional personal inscription. VA maintains a published list of more than 100 approved emblems of belief, and families may request approval of an emblem not on the list.
items.how: Specify all inscription elements on VA Form 40-1330 before submission. Review the NCA emblems of belief list and cite the emblem by its assigned number.
items.hack: Two things families discover too late. First, the additional inscription space is limited and VA will not engrave anything it deems inappropriate — plan the wording carefully and keep it short, because a rejected inscription restarts the order. Second, if your faith's emblem is not among the approved emblems, you can PETITION to have a new one added; VA has approved many this way, including humanist and atheist emblems, but the process takes months, so start it early rather than at time of need. Replacement headstones are provided free if the original is damaged, illegible, or contains a government error — but a family-requested change of wording is generally at the family's expense.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: United States burial flag (VA Form 27-2008) — and the flag case nobody tells you about
items.who: Generally: veterans who served in wartime, died on active duty, or served after 31 Jan 1955; peacetime veterans discharged or released before 27 Jun 1950; certain Reserve and ROTC members; and some Selective Service members. One flag per eligible veteran.
items.value: A free 5-by-9.5-foot cotton U.S. flag to drape the casket or accompany the urn, which is then presented to the next of kin. Also available: a free flag for the grave of a veteran whose remains are unavailable.
items.how: Submit VA Form 27-2008 (Application for United States Flag for Burial Purposes). A funeral director will normally handle it. You can obtain the flag at most Post Offices and at VA regional offices — bring the completed form and a copy of the DD-214.
items.hack: Two practical notes. VA issues only ONE flag per veteran, so if multiple family members want one, the others must be purchased. And VA does not provide the display case — the Department of Veterans Affairs does not, but many VSO posts (American Legion, VFW, AMVETS) and woodworking volunteer groups will donate one, and the Veterans of Foreign Wars and some funeral homes keep them on hand. Ask; do not buy one at a funeral home markup. Finally, get the flag BEFORE the service; a Post Office can hand it over the same day if you bring the form and DD-214, while a mailed application will not arrive in time.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Presidential Memorial Certificate (VA Form 40-0247) — and you can request more than one
items.who: The next of kin, any family member, or a close friend of a deceased veteran or Reservist who was eligible for burial in a national cemetery.
items.value: An engraved paper certificate bearing the current President's signature, honoring the deceased's military service. VA explicitly accepts MULTIPLE requests, so every child and grandchild can have one.
items.how: Submit VA Form 40-0247 online, by mail to the NCA FP Evidence Intake Center in Janesville WI, through QuickSubmit, in person at any VA regional office, or by fax. Include a copy of the death certificate and the discharge documents. If you have not received it in four months, contact VA for status.
items.hack: The 'multiple requests' policy is the part nobody uses. Families order one, frame it, and the other children get nothing. Order one per household in the same submission. Also note that there is no deadline — a certificate can be requested for a veteran who died decades ago, which makes this a meaningful gesture for a grandchild researching a grandparent's service. There is also no requirement that the veteran actually be buried in a national cemetery, only that they were ELIGIBLE.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Military funeral honors — the two-person minimum, and how to get more than the minimum
items.org: DoD / service branch funeral honors programs
items.who: Every eligible veteran who was not dishonorably discharged is entitled by law to military funeral honors upon request.
items.value: The statutory minimum detail is TWO uniformed service members, at least one from the deceased's own branch. The core ceremony is the folding and presentation of the United States flag to the next of kin and the sounding of Taps. Larger details — a firing party for a three-volley salute, a color guard, a casket team, a live bugler — are provided where personnel are available but are not guaranteed.
items.how: The funeral director requests honors on the family's behalf by calling the appropriate branch's funeral honors coordinator; Military OneSource maintains a Military Funeral Honors Directory and can be reached at 1-800-342-9647. You must provide a copy of the DD-214 to establish eligibility.
items.hack: Two things. First, 'Taps' is frequently played by a ceremonial bugle with an electronic insert rather than a live bugler, because live buglers are scarce — if a live bugler matters to your family, ask the funeral director to contact Bugles Across America, a volunteer organization that provides live buglers at no cost nationwide, and to request them well in advance. Second, VSO honor guards (American Legion, VFW, AMVETS, Marine Corps League) will frequently supplement the military detail with a firing party and color guard at no charge — the military two-person minimum plus a VSO honor guard produces the full ceremony most families are picturing. Ask for both.
items.deadline: None, but request as early as possible — details are scheduled against limited personnel.

items.title: Missing in America Project — burying the unclaimed cremated remains of veterans
items.org: Missing in America Project (MIAP), a nonprofit, working with funeral homes, coroners, and VA national cemeteries
items.who: Unclaimed and abandoned cremated remains sitting in funeral homes, coroners' offices, and storage facilities — MIAP identifies which of them belonged to veterans and arranges interment with full military honors in a national or state veterans cemetery.
items.value: Thousands of veterans have been located, identified, and interred with honors since 2007. For families, MIAP can also reunite them with a relative's remains they did not know existed.
items.how: Volunteers work with funeral homes to inventory unclaimed remains, research service records, and coordinate interment. Contact MIAP at miap.us. Many American Legion posts, Patriot Guard Riders chapters, and Sons of the American Legion detachments run local MIAP efforts.
items.hack: Two ways in. If you are a funeral home owner or work in one, MIAP will do the research for you at no cost — most unclaimed-remains inventories have veterans in them and nobody has the time to find out. If you are looking for a relative who disappeared from the family record, MIAP's identification work has reunited families with remains held for decades. And if you simply want to serve, attending a MIAP dignified transfer is one of the few volunteer commitments that costs nothing and matters visibly; a veteran who would have been shelved forever gets a flag, a bugler, and witnesses.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Veterans Legacy Memorial — a free online memorial page for nearly every American veteran
items.who: Veterans interred in VA national cemeteries, VA grant-funded state and tribal cemeteries, Department of the Army cemeteries including Arlington, overseas American Battle Monuments Commission cemeteries, and — since NCA's private-cemetery expansion — millions of veterans buried in private cemeteries.
items.value: A permanent, free, digital memorial page for each veteran, where family and friends can post tributes, photographs, biographies, documents, and historical records. More than ten million veterans are represented.
items.how: Search for the veteran at vlm.cem.va.gov. Family members can register, verify their relationship, and become the page's designated custodian, which allows them to add and moderate content. Living veterans can now also register to chronicle their own life story.
items.hack: The under-used feature is custodianship. Anyone can post a tribute, but a verified family member can curate the page — upload the discharge papers, the unit photographs, the letters home, the oral history — and it stays there permanently at no cost, maintained by the federal government rather than by a commercial genealogy site that may put it behind a paywall or disappear. If you are the person in your family who holds the box of photographs, this is where they should live. Start with the veteran's name and date of death; the search is free and requires no account.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Quilts of Valor — a hand-made quilt for any veteran touched by war
items.who: Any service member or veteran who has been touched by war — any era, any branch, any discharge status. There is no rating requirement, no combat requirement, and no cost.
items.value: A hand-made, hand-quilted quilt, awarded in a presentation ceremony, plus a signed presentation case and a record in the Foundation's registry. More than 400,000 quilts have been awarded.
items.how: Nominate a veteran (or yourself) through the nomination form at qovf.org. Nominations go to a local group, which makes the quilt and arranges a presentation — often at a VFW or American Legion post, a reunion, a church, or a family gathering.
items.hack: Two notes. You CAN nominate yourself and it is not considered unseemly — the Foundation says so explicitly, and many veterans wait years for a family member to do it. And the wait can be long (months to over a year) because each quilt is made by hand, so nominate an aging veteran now rather than when they are in hospice. If time is short, say so in the nomination; local groups keep finished quilts on hand for exactly that case.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Honor Flight — a free trip to see your memorials in Washington, D.C.
items.org: Honor Flight Network and its ~130 regional hubs
items.who: Priority goes to World War II, Korean War, and Vietnam War veterans, and to veterans of any era with a terminal illness. Many hubs have expanded to later eras as the WWII generation has passed; eligibility and era priority are set by each local hub, not nationally.
items.value: An all-expenses-paid day trip to Washington, D.C. to visit the war memorials — airfare, ground transport, meals, and a volunteer guardian who accompanies the veteran throughout. The veteran pays nothing. Guardians typically pay their own way.
items.how: Find your regional hub at honorflight.org and apply directly to it. Applications go through the hub, not through the national office. Wheelchairs and medical support are provided; each hub flies with medical staff aboard.
items.hack: Apply to your hub even if the wait list is long, and mark any terminal diagnosis or serious illness on the application — every hub moves those applicants to the front, immediately. The other thing families should know: a guardian slot is how an adult child or grandchild goes along, and guardian applications are separate and usually shorter. If you want to accompany your parent, apply as a guardian at the same time you submit their veteran application, and note on both that you are traveling together.
items.deadline: None, but hub wait lists run long and priority is age- and illness-driven.

items.title: Vietnam War 50th Commemoration lapel pin — the federal program has ended, but pins are still being presented
items.org: Congressional offices, state veterans affairs departments, VSOs, and Commemorative Partner organizations
items.who: U.S. veterans who served on active duty at any time from 1 November 1955 through 15 May 1975, regardless of where they served. Surviving spouses are recognized in many local programs.
items.value: The Vietnam Veteran Lapel Pin — a bronze pin bearing the eagle, laurel wreath and six stars, inscribed 'A Grateful Nation Thanks and Honors You' — presented with a certificate at a public ceremony or by mail.
items.how: The federal United States of America Vietnam War Commemoration concluded in late 2025 and its original pin supply is exhausted. Pins and ceremonies continue through Commemorative Partner organizations, state departments of veterans affairs, VSO posts, and Congressional offices, many of which maintain their own stock. Contact your Representative's or Senators' constituent-services office, your state veterans affairs department, or a local American Legion or VFW post.
items.hack: The eligibility window is broader than almost anyone believes: 1 Nov 1955 to 15 May 1975, ANY location. You did not have to go to Vietnam. A veteran who spent 1969 at a base in Germany is eligible and almost certainly does not know it. Congressional offices are the most reliable remaining source and will usually mail a pin with a certificate after a short phone call; several have expanded their programs to Persian Gulf War veterans as well. Verify current availability before promising a pin to someone.
items.deadline: The federal Commemoration has ended; remaining distribution is by local organizations while supplies last.

items.title: State veteran registries and recognition programs — the second recognition system
items.who: Veterans residing in (or in some cases originating from) a given state.
items.value: Varies widely by state but commonly includes: a state veterans registry that pushes benefit notifications to you; state-issued veteran recognition medals (many states award their own Vietnam, Korea, WWII, Gulf War, and Global War on Terrorism medals); a Veterans Hall of Fame; free or discounted state park passes and hunting and fishing licenses; special license plates including Purple Heart, Combat Wounded, and Gold Star plates; and property tax relief.
items.how: Find your state department of veterans affairs and search for 'veteran registry,' 'state veteran medal,' or 'veteran recognition.' Most require a DD-214 and proof of residency. County veterans service officers can enroll you in one appointment.
items.hack: State-issued campaign medals are the most-missed recognition item in the country, because they are issued by states rather than by DoD and therefore appear nowhere in your military record and are never mentioned at separation. Many states will mail one for the cost of a phone call and a DD-214 copy. Registering with the state registry is also how you find out about state benefits before the deadlines — several states have time-limited bonus payments for recent-conflict veterans that expire, and the registry is the only thing that will tell you.
items.deadline: Varies by state; some state bonus programs have hard deadlines.

items.title: 5-Point Preference (TP) — 5 U.S.C. 2108(1), and the service windows that actually qualify
items.who: Veterans discharged under honorable conditions who served in a declared war; during 4/28/1952–7/1/1955; more than 180 consecutive days between 1/31/1955 and 10/14/1976; during the Gulf War period 8/2/1990–1/2/1992; or 180+ consecutive days after 9/11/2001 ending before 8/31/2010; OR in any campaign/expedition for which a campaign badge was authorized.
items.value: 5 points added to a passing examination score, and preference-eligible status inside category rating. Worth more than the 5 points: it makes you un-passable-over without OPM-level process.
items.how: Claim 'TP' in the USAJOBS profile AND upload a DD-214 Member Copy 4 (it is the only copy that shows the character-of-service and narrative reason for separation). If you separated after 10/1/1990 you generally also need to meet the 24-month continuous-service rule of 38 U.S.C. 5303A(d) unless discharged for disability or hardship.
items.hack: Campaign-badge service is the back door. Many people who served a short post-9/11 tour do not meet the 180-day rule but DO hold a GWOT-Expeditionary, Iraq Campaign, Afghanistan Campaign, Kosovo Campaign or Armed Forces Expeditionary Medal — which grants preference regardless of length of service. Read block 13 of your DD-214 line by line before concluding you have no preference.
items.deadline: None — claim at time of application, every application

items.title: 10-Point Preference — CP vs CPS vs XP, and why the letters matter more than the points
items.who: CP = service-connected disability rated 10% or 20% (5 U.S.C. 2108(3)(C)). CPS = rated 30% or more (2108(3)(D)). XP = service-connected disability at 0%, Purple Heart recipient, or receipt of a VA pension (2108(3)(E)).
items.value: 10 points on a rated examination. In category rating, CP and CPS float to the TOP of the highest quality category for positions other than professional/scientific at GS-9 and above — this is the single most powerful preference mechanic in federal hiring.
items.how: File Standard Form 15 (SF-15, 'Application for 10-Point Veteran Preference') plus the proof it asks for: a VA benefit summary letter (download from VA.gov under 'Download VA Benefit Letters') dated within the last year showing the combined rating, or your DD-214 plus DD-215/orders for a Purple Heart.
items.hack: A 0% service-connected rating is still XP 10-point preference. Veterans routinely leave 10 points on the table because they assume 0% is worthless. It is not — it converts you from non-preference to preference eligible, which is the difference between being on the certificate and not.
items.deadline: SF-15 and the VA letter must be attached to each application; VA letters older than 12 months are commonly rejected by HR

items.title: Derived Preference (XP) — spouses, widows/widowers and mothers of veterans can claim 10 points
items.who: Under 5 U.S.C. 2108(3)(F)–(H): the spouse of a veteran who is 100% disabled and unable to work; the unremarried widow/widower of a veteran who died in service or of a service-connected cause; the mother of a servicemember who died in service, or the mother of a permanently and totally disabled veteran (with specific marital-status conditions).
items.value: Full 10-point XP preference in the family member's own name for federal jobs.
items.how: Complete SF-15 in the family member's name, attach the veteran's DD-214, the VA letter establishing the qualifying disability or the cause of death, and the marriage or birth documentation. The rule that kills most claims: 'neither may receive preference if the veteran is living and is qualified for Federal employment.'
items.hack: This is the most-missed benefit in the entire federal hiring system, and it belongs to the family, not the veteran. A spouse of a 100% P&T veteran who cannot work has the same 10 points as a Purple Heart recipient — and almost no spouse knows it. It stacks with, and is separate from, the military-spouse noncompetitive appointing authority.
items.deadline: None; must be re-claimed on each application

items.title: Sole Survivorship Preference — 0 points, but full preference-eligible status
items.who: Servicemembers discharged or released from active duty after 8/29/2008 because of a sole survivorship discharge under 10 U.S.C. 1174(i).
items.value: Preference-eligible status with 0 added points. You get the floating and pass-over protections of preference without a points bump.
items.how: Select 'Sole Survivorship Preference' in the USAJOBS preference question and upload the DD-214 showing the sole survivorship separation reason.
items.hack: Because it carries 0 points, applicants assume it is worthless and skip the box. In category rating, points are irrelevant — preference-eligible status is what moves you above non-preference applicants in the same quality category. Always claim it.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Where veterans' preference does NOT apply — the list nobody gives you
items.who: Every veteran applying to federal jobs
items.value: Knowing this saves months of wasted applications.
items.how: Preference does not apply to: the Senior Executive Service; executive branch positions requiring Senate confirmation; internal agency merit-promotion actions (promotion, reassignment, transfer, reinstatement of current employees) — preference is an ENTRY mechanism, not a promotion mechanism; most excepted-service positions outside the competitive service (though 5 CFR Part 302 applies preference to many excepted-service hires); and the legislative and judicial branches except where positions are in the competitive service.
items.hack: The practical consequence: once you are inside the government, your preference stops helping you and you compete like everyone else. That is why the entry authority you use (VRA, 30% disabled, Schedule A) matters far more than the preference points — use the strongest door on the way in, because the door only opens once.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: The Rule of Three and the pass-over process — 5 U.S.C. 3318
items.who: Applicants referred on a competitive certificate built under numerical ranking (not category rating)
items.value: Selection must be made from the highest three available eligibles on the certificate. An agency may not select a non-preference eligible over a preference eligible on that certificate without a sustained pass-over objection.
items.how: If the agency wants to pass over a preference eligible, it must file written reasons with OPM (for a 30%-or-more disabled veteran, OPM alone decides and cannot delegate it). The agency must notify the veteran and give at least 15 days to respond. If OPM finds the veteran physically able to perform the duties, the agency may not pass over the veteran.
items.hack: If you are CPS (30%+) and you are told you were 'not selected' after being referred, ask in writing whether a pass-over request was filed with OPM and request a copy of the agency's stated reasons. Most agencies would rather select you than build the pass-over file.
items.deadline: 15 days to respond to a pass-over notice

items.title: Category Rating under 5 U.S.C. 3319 — how preference actually works in the modern system
items.who: Anyone applying to a competitive-service job posted since the Chief Human Capital Officers Act of 2002 made category rating permanent
items.value: Most federal jobs no longer use numeric scores. Applicants who meet basic qualifications are sorted into two or more predefined quality categories (commonly 'Best Qualified / Well Qualified / Qualified'). Within EACH category, preference eligibles are listed ahead of all non-preference eligibles.
items.how: Read the announcement's 'How You Will Be Evaluated' section to find the category names. Your answers to the occupational questionnaire — not your resume alone — determine the category. The resume must substantiate every questionnaire answer or HR will downgrade you.
items.hack: The 5 or 10 points are meaningless here; category placement is everything. Being a 10-point veteran in the 'Qualified' category loses to a non-veteran in 'Best Qualified.' Spend your effort on the questionnaire and on mirroring the announcement's specialized-experience language verbatim in the resume, not on your preference paperwork.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: The CP/CPS float-to-top rule — 30% disabled veterans go to the top of the highest category
items.who: CP (10–20% compensable) and CPS (30%+ compensable) preference eligibles
items.value: For positions OTHER than professional or scientific positions at GS-9 and above, CP and CPS eligibles are placed at the TOP of the highest quality category — ahead of other 10-point veterans, ahead of 5-point veterans, and ahead of every non-veteran. Under the older numeric-register rules the same effect applied at GS-8 and below.
items.how: Nothing extra to do beyond documenting CP/CPS correctly with the SF-15 and a current VA rating letter — but you must be rated in the highest quality category first. Float-to-top does not rescue a weak questionnaire.
items.hack: This is why a 30% rating is worth targeting a GS-7/GS-8/GS-9 administrative or technical series rather than a GS-9 professional series: in the non-professional lane the float applies, and you are effectively first in line. Many disabled veterans enter one grade lower than their ceiling on purpose, then promote internally — where preference no longer matters but competition is far thinner.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: VRA — Veterans Recruitment Appointment, 5 CFR Part 307: the easiest door into federal service
items.who: Disabled veterans; veterans who served on active duty during a war or in a campaign/expedition for which a campaign badge was authorized; veterans who received an Armed Forces Service Medal (including GWOT-SM); and veterans separated from active duty within the last 3 years. Separation must be under honorable conditions.
items.value: A non-competitive excepted-service appointment at GS-11 or equivalent and below. No competition, no certificate, no rating panel. After 2 years of satisfactory substantially continuous service the agency MUST convert you to a career or career-conditional appointment in the competitive service.
items.how: Apply to announcements open to 'Veterans' hiring path, or — far more effective — email a hiring manager directly with a one-page note: 'I am VRA-eligible under 5 CFR 307. You can appoint me non-competitively at GS-11 or below without a job announcement.' Attach DD-214 Member 4 and, if disabled, the VA letter.
items.hack: VRA is the single easiest path into federal service because an agency can hire you without ever posting the job. Most hiring managers do not know they have this authority. Recently separated veterans have a hard 3-year clock — if you are inside it and not using VRA, you are wasting the most valuable window of your career. Veterans' preference still applies among competing VRA candidates.
items.deadline: Recently-separated category expires 3 years from date of discharge; other categories do not expire

items.title: VEOA — the authority that lets an outsider apply to internal-only federal jobs
