items.who: Preference eligibles, OR veterans separated after 3 or more years of continuous active service performed under honorable conditions (you do NOT need preference or a disability for the second route).
items.value: Lets you compete for merit-promotion announcements that are otherwise restricted to current federal employees ('status candidates'). Appointment is to the competitive service at any grade for which you qualify — there is no GS-11 ceiling like VRA.
items.how: Look for 'Veterans Employment Opportunities Act' or 'VEOA eligibles' in the 'This job is open to' block. Apply under the Veterans hiring path, attach DD-214 Member 4 showing 3+ years continuous active service or your preference documentation. Note: veterans' preference points do NOT apply in a VEOA selection — you compete head-to-head on merit.
items.hack: This is the authority most veterans never use, and it is the one that gets you in at GS-12/13/14. Merit-promotion announcements typically draw a fraction of the applicants that public announcements draw — often 20 applicants instead of 800. Filter USAJOBS to the Veterans hiring path and read only the announcements whose 'Who May Apply' says status candidates; those are your VEOA jobs.
items.deadline: None — VEOA eligibility does not expire

items.title: 30% or More Disabled Veteran appointing authority — exactly what to send, and to whom
items.who: Veterans retired from active military service with a disability rating of 30% or more, OR veterans rated by the VA as having a compensable service-connected disability of 30% or more.
items.value: Non-competitive appointment at ANY grade level, in any occupation. The agency makes an initial time-limited appointment of more than 60 days and may convert you to permanent competitive-service status non-competitively at any time during it, with no break in service.
items.how: Send a single email to (1) the agency's Veterans Employment Program Manager, (2) the Selective Placement Program Coordinator, and (3) the hiring manager for the specific vacancy. Attach: DD-214 Member Copy 4; a VA benefit summary letter dated within 12 months showing combined rating of 30% or more; and a federal-format resume. Say plainly: 'I am eligible under the 30 Percent or More Disabled Veteran appointing authority, 5 CFR 316.302(b)(4). You may appoint me non-competitively at any grade without a vacancy announcement.'
items.hack: There is no grade cap. A 30% disabled veteran with a GS-14-level private-sector resume can be appointed directly at GS-14 if a manager wants them — no certificate, no competition, no float-to-top math. The bottleneck is entirely that managers do not know the authority exists. Put the regulation citation in the subject line of the email.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Schedule A (5 CFR 213.3102(u)) — and when it beats veterans' preference
items.who: People with an intellectual disability, a severe physical disability, or a psychiatric disability — including veterans. Eligibility is proven by a 'proof of disability' letter, not by a VA rating.
items.value: Non-competitive appointment at any grade level, to any position, permanent or time-limited. After 2 years of satisfactory service, conversion to the competitive service without competition.
items.how: Obtain a Schedule A letter from a licensed medical professional, a licensed vocational rehabilitation specialist, or any federal/state agency that issues disability benefits (a VA VR&E counselor or a VA physician can write one). The letter must state that you have an intellectual, severe physical, or psychiatric disability and are able to perform the duties of the position — it does NOT need to name the diagnosis or a percentage.
items.hack: Schedule A beats veterans' preference when your VA rating is under 30% but your condition is genuinely severe — PTSD, major depression and TBI commonly qualify as psychiatric or severe physical disabilities for Schedule A even at a 10% or 20% VA rating. You are allowed to claim Schedule A AND veterans' preference on the same application; the agency will use whichever authority is more favorable. Never choose one over the other — claim both.
items.deadline: Schedule A letters have no statutory expiration, but many agencies want one dated within 12 months

items.title: Find your agency's Selective Placement Program Coordinator (SPPC) — the person who can actually hire you
items.who: Veterans using Schedule A or the 30% disabled authority, and applicants with disabilities generally
items.value: Every federal agency is required to have an SPPC. They hold the non-competitive hiring authorities, maintain resume banks of Schedule A and 30%-disabled candidates, and can route your resume to hiring managers directly.
items.how: Use OPM's searchable SPPC Directory (search by agency or by state) and email the coordinator for every agency with a presence in your commuting area — not just one. Send the federal resume, Schedule A letter and/or VA rating letter, and a two-sentence statement of the series and grades you are targeting.
items.hack: Contacting 25 SPPCs in one afternoon is a higher-yield hour than 25 USAJOBS applications, because SPPCs are measured on placements and are actively looking for qualified candidates to hand to managers. Most veterans have never heard the job title.
items.deadline: None

items.title: DVAAP — the affirmative action program every agency must run for disabled veterans
items.org: OPM / all federal agencies (5 U.S.C. 3112, 5 CFR Part 720 Subpart C)
items.who: Disabled veterans, with emphasis on 30%-or-more disabled veterans
items.value: Each agency must maintain a written DVAAP plan for recruiting, hiring, placing and advancing disabled veterans, and must report accomplishments to OPM annually. The plan names the officials responsible — which is a directory of people whose performance is measured on hiring you.
items.how: Search '[agency name] DVAAP plan' — most agencies publish the current plan and accomplishment report as a PDF. The plan lists the Veterans Employment Program Manager and the disabled-veteran hiring points of contact by name and email.
items.hack: Use the DVAAP accomplishment report as a targeting tool: agencies that report missing their disabled-veteran hiring goals are the ones most motivated to use non-competitive authorities this fiscal year. Cite their own plan back to them in your email.
items.deadline: Agency plans and reports are annual (fiscal year)

items.title: Feds Hire Vets (fedshirevets.gov) — OPM's official veteran hiring portal
items.who: Veterans, transitioning servicemembers, military spouses and family members, and federal hiring officials
items.value: The authoritative, non-commercial source for every federal veteran hiring authority, the Vet Guide, agency Veterans Employment Program Manager contacts, and the federal resume and interview guidance HR actually uses.
items.how: Start at fedshirevets.gov (redirects into opm.gov/fedshirevets). Read the 'Veteran Job Seekers' section end to end before applying anywhere, then use the 'Hiring Officials' section — it tells you exactly what a manager must do to hire you non-competitively, which is the script you paste into your outreach email.
items.hack: Read the hiring-official pages, not the job-seeker pages. The job-seeker pages tell you what you are entitled to; the hiring-official pages tell you what to ask a manager to do. That asymmetry is worth more than any resume service.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: The USAJOBS document set that gets you referred — and the versions HR rejects
items.who: Every veteran applying to a federal job
items.value: Getting the documents right is the difference between 'Referred' and 'Not referred — preference not verified.'
items.how: Upload, in the USAJOBS Documents locker: (1) DD-214 MEMBER COPY 4 — Copy 1 does not show character of service and is routinely rejected; (2) SF-15 for any 10-point claim, signed; (3) a VA benefit summary letter dated within the last 12 months, downloaded from VA.gov under 'Download VA Benefit Letters,' showing the combined evaluation; (4) for active-duty applicants within 120 days of separation, a certification/statement of service on command letterhead with the expected separation date and character of service; (5) SF-50 (Notification of Personnel Action) if you are or were a federal employee.
items.hack: Re-download your VA letter every January. A letter dated more than a year ago is the single most common reason a valid 10-point claim is disallowed — and HR is not required to tell you before they drop you from the certificate. Also: name the files literally ('DD214-Member4.pdf', 'SF15-signed.pdf'); HR specialists screening 400 applications do not open ambiguous filenames.
items.deadline: All documents must be in the locker before the announcement closes — no late uploads

items.title: The self-certification trap — how veterans disqualify themselves on the questionnaire
items.who: Every federal applicant
items.value: Avoiding an automatic 'ineligible' rating, or worse, a fraud referral.
items.how: The occupational questionnaire asks you to self-rate your experience ('I am considered an expert…'). HR then verifies every high self-rating against your resume. Two failure modes: rating yourself 'expert' on something your resume does not document — HR lowers your entire score or rates you ineligible; and rating yourself conservatively — the automated system screens you out before a human ever reads the resume.
items.hack: Rate yourself at the highest level you can PROVE in the resume, then go back and add a bullet to the resume that proves it, with the same nouns the questionnaire used. The questionnaire is the scoring key; the resume is the evidence file. Write the resume after you read the questionnaire, never before. And never claim preference you cannot document — a false preference claim is a federal false-statement issue, not a clerical error.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: The federal resume format HR actually scores
items.who: Every federal applicant
items.value: Federal resumes are scored against a written 'specialized experience' standard, not skimmed. A 2-page private-sector resume will be rated ineligible for lacking required data, not for lacking merit.
items.how: For every position, include: employer name and full address; job title; series and grade if federal; start and end dates as MM/YYYY; HOURS PER WEEK (omitting this lets HR credit the job at zero, or pro-rate it); supervisor name and phone with a release statement; and dense accomplishment bullets. Expect 4–8 pages. Mirror the announcement's 'Specialized Experience' paragraph phrase-for-phrase in your most recent position.
items.hack: Translate military duty titles into the occupational series language of the announcement and put the civilian equivalent first: 'Logistics Management (equivalent to 25 direct reports, $14M property book)' beats 'Platoon Sergeant.' Then paste the announcement's specialized-experience sentence into your resume as a section header and answer it directly underneath. HR specialists are looking for that sentence; make it impossible to miss.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: How to read 'Who May Apply' / 'This job is open to' — the single most important block in the announcement
items.who: Every federal applicant
items.value: Applying to an announcement you are not eligible for is the number one reason veterans get 'not referred.'
items.how: Decode the icons: 'The public' = open to everyone, preference applies, and you are competing against thousands. 'Federal employees — Competitive service' / 'Internal to an agency' = merit promotion, closed to outsiders UNLESS 'Veterans' also appears, which is your VEOA lane. 'Veterans' = VEOA and/or VRA and/or 30% disabled. 'Individuals with disabilities' = Schedule A. 'Military spouses' = the EO 13473 noncompetitive authority. 'Career transition (CTAP, ICTAP)' = displaced federal employees.
items.hack: Many agencies post the SAME job twice on the same day — once to the public (delegated examining) and once to status candidates (merit promotion). Apply to both. The merit-promotion version usually has one-tenth the applicants, and your VEOA eligibility gets you in the door on it. Searching only the public announcements means you never see half the openings.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: USAJOBS saved searches — set up ten, not one
items.who: Every federal applicant
items.value: Merit-promotion and direct-hire announcements are frequently open for 3–5 days. If you check the site weekly you will miss most of them.
items.how: In your USAJOBS profile, build separate saved searches for: each target occupational series (e.g., 0343, 0201, 2210, 1102); each hiring path (Veterans, Individuals with disabilities, Military spouses); each duty location; and each agency. Set notification frequency to DAILY on each one. Also complete the profile's 'Eligibility' section — checking the Veterans, disability, and military-spouse boxes changes which announcements you are shown.
items.hack: Add a saved search on the keyword 'Direct Hire Authority' in your geography. DHA announcements skip category rating entirely and are often filled within a week of posting; they are the fastest hires in government and almost nobody is watching for them.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: The FERS military deposit — buying back your time at 3% of military basic pay
items.who: Federal employees under FERS with post-1956 active military service
items.value: Your military years count toward BOTH your FERS annuity computation and your years-of-service eligibility. Cost is 3% of the military basic pay you earned during that service (CSRS: 7%). For a typical 4-year enlistment the deposit is often $2,000–$5,000, and it commonly adds 4% of high-3 to a lifetime annuity — the payback period is measured in months, not years.
items.how: (1) Request estimated earnings from your service's finance center using form RI 20-97 (Request for Estimated Earnings During Military Service) with a copy of your DD-214; (2) take the earnings statement plus RI 20-97 to your agency HR/payroll, which computes the deposit; (3) file SF 3108 (FERS) or SF 2803 (CSRS) and pay by payroll deduction or lump sum before you separate for retirement.
items.hack: Start it in your first week of federal employment. There is a 2-year interest-free grace period from the date you become subject to FERS; after that an Interest Accrual Date is set and interest compounds annually on the unpaid balance for the rest of your career. Waiting ten years can double or triple the cost of the exact same service. The deposit must be paid in full to your agency before you separate — OPM cannot accept it after you retire.
items.deadline: Interest-free for 2 years after entering FERS-covered service; must be paid in full before separation for retirement

items.title: Military retirees: you must usually WAIVE retired pay to credit military time — with two exceptions
items.who: Military retirees who become federal civilian employees
items.value: Knowing this before you pay a deposit you cannot use.
items.how: General rule: a military retiree cannot credit military service toward a FERS/CSRS annuity while also drawing military retired pay — you must waive the retired pay, effective the day before the civilian annuity begins, by written request to DFAS at least 60 days before retiring, and the deposit must already be paid. TWO EXCEPTIONS where you keep both: (1) retired pay awarded for a service-connected disability incurred in combat with an enemy or caused by an instrumentality of war in wartime; (2) retired pay under 10 U.S.C. Chapter 1223 — that is, Reserve/Guard non-regular retirement at age 60.
items.hack: Exception (2) is enormous and almost unknown: Guard and Reserve retirees keep their reserve retired pay AND get full civilian credit for the active-duty portions of that service after paying the 3% deposit. If you are a drilling reservist heading into federal service, buy back every day of Title 10 active duty — you are one of the few people who genuinely gets paid twice for the same years. Active-duty regular retirees should run the math before waiving; often the deposit is not worth it.
items.deadline: Waiver request to DFAS at least 60 days before civilian retirement; deposit paid before separation

items.title: CSRS 'Catch-62' — the trap that deletes your military service at age 62
items.who: CSRS and CSRS Offset employees with post-1956 military service who did not pay the deposit
items.value: If you are CSRS, first employed before 10/1/1982, and you did not pay the 7% post-1956 deposit, your military service is credited in your annuity until the month before you turn 62 — then, if you are eligible for Social Security at 62, it is REMOVED and your annuity is permanently recomputed downward.
items.how: Pay the 7% CSRS deposit (SF 2803) before you retire. Employees first hired on or after 10/1/1982 get no credit at all without the deposit, at any age.
items.hack: People discover Catch-62 in the month it hits them, when the annuity drops by hundreds of dollars a month with no warning letter. If you are CSRS or CSRS Offset with unpaid military service, request the deposit computation this year — the fix is only available while you are still an employee.
items.deadline: Deposit must be paid before separation for retirement

items.title: Unused sick leave converts to annuity service — 2,087 hours = one full year
items.who: FERS and CSRS retirees
items.value: Since 1/1/2014, FERS employees receive 100% credit for unused sick leave in the annuity computation (CSRS always did). 2,087 hours is one year of service credit; at a 1% FERS multiplier that is another 1% of high-3 for life, and it is counted in addition to actual service.
items.how: Do not burn sick leave in your final years. Sick leave credit is added after the annuity is computed — it cannot make you ELIGIBLE to retire, but it does increase the payment permanently.
items.hack: Veterans with service-connected conditions accrue heavy VA appointment schedules. Use the separate 'disabled veteran leave' entitlement under the Wounded Warriors Federal Leave Act of 2015 (P.L. 114-75, 5 U.S.C. 6329) — 104 hours (full-time; prorated for part-time/seasonal) for a veteran with a service-connected disability rating of 30% or more who was HIRED ON OR AFTER NOVEMBER 5, 2016, usable only for medical treatment of that disability. It is a single continuous 12-month use-or-lose bucket beginning on your first day of employment, and using it protects your sick leave balance from the start of your career.
items.deadline: Disabled veteran leave: 104 hours, usable only during the single continuous 12-month period beginning on the first day of employment; forfeited thereafter, no carryover

items.title: Veterans' preference in reduction in force — 5 U.S.C. 3501–3502
items.who: Federal employees who are preference eligibles
items.value: In a RIF, employees are ranked within competitive levels by tenure group, then by veterans' preference subgroup. Preference eligibles go in subgroup AD (retention preference for 30%-or-more disabled veterans), then A (other preference eligibles), then B (non-preference). Subgroup AD is retained ahead of everyone in the same tenure group.
items.how: Make sure your official personnel folder reflects your preference and disability rating — RIF retention registers are built from the SF-50 and the eOPF, not from what you told the hiring manager years ago. Submit an updated VA rating letter to HR whenever your rating changes.
items.hack: A rating increase from 20% to 30% moves you from subgroup A to subgroup AD, which in a RIF is the difference between keeping your job and being separated. If your rating crossed 30% at any point, file the letter with your servicing HR office in writing and keep the confirmation. Note: retired members of the armed forces have restricted RIF preference unless disability-retired or the retirement is based on reserve service.
items.deadline: Update the eOPF before any RIF notice is issued

items.title: Maximum-entry-age rules and preference eligibles — the Isabella rule
items.who: Preference-eligible applicants for positions that carry a maximum entry age (notably federal law enforcement and firefighter positions under 5 U.S.C. 3307)
items.value: Following the MSPB's Isabella v. Department of State line of decisions, qualified preference eligibles may apply and be considered for vacancies regardless of whether they meet a maximum entry-age requirement, unless the agency analyzes the position and demonstrates that age is essential to performance of the duties.
items.how: If you are rejected solely on maximum entry age and you are a preference eligible, put the agency on notice in writing and file a VEOA complaint with DOL VETS within 60 days of the rejection, then appeal to MSPB.
items.hack: This is a live, winnable claim, and the 60-day DOL VETS clock is short. Agencies still auto-reject over-age preference-eligible applicants routinely. Do not accept the rejection email as final — the burden is on the agency to prove age is essential.
items.deadline: VEOA complaint to DOL VETS within 60 days of the alleged violation

items.title: Military spouse noncompetitive appointment — 5 CFR 315.612 / EO 13473
items.who: Three categories: (1) the spouse of an active-duty member of the armed forces; (2) the spouse of a servicemember or veteran who has a 100% disability rating from active service; (3) the unremarried widow/widower of a servicemember killed on active duty.
items.value: Non-competitive appointment to a competitive-service position — career or career-conditional — without competing on a certificate. The FY2019 NDAA and EO 13832 broadened category (1) so the appointment is no longer confined to a narrow post-PCS window in the way the original 2009 rule required.
items.how: Apply to announcements whose 'This job is open to' block includes 'Military spouses.' Attach: the sponsor's active-duty orders (or PCS orders), the marriage certificate, and for category (2) the VA/DoD documentation of the 100% disability, or for category (3) the DD-1300 / casualty report.
items.hack: This is separate from — and stackable with — derived 10-point preference under SF-15 and with DoD's Program S. A spouse of a 100% disabled veteran can hold noncompetitive appointment eligibility AND 10-point derived preference simultaneously, and should claim both on every application. Agencies will apply whichever helps most.
items.deadline: Verify current time limits with the agency; documentation must show the qualifying relationship at time of appointment

items.title: Program S — DoD Military Spouse Preference in the Priority Placement Program
items.who: Spouses of active-duty members relocating on PCS orders to the sponsor's new duty location, applying for DoD appropriated-fund positions
items.value: Where the spouse is among the best qualified for a DoD appropriated-fund vacancy (generally GS-15 equivalent and below) in the commuting area of the sponsor's new duty station, Program S requires the spouse to be selected over other candidates, subject to the program's rules.
items.how: Register through the DoD Priority Placement Program with the servicing civilian personnel office at the gaining installation. Bring the PCS orders and the marriage certificate. Registration is location-specific and time-bounded to the PCS.
items.hack: Program S is a DoD internal placement program, not a USAJOBS hiring path — registering on USAJOBS alone does not enroll you. You must walk into (or email) the gaining installation's CPAC/HRO. Spouses lose this benefit constantly by assuming the USAJOBS 'Military spouses' checkbox covers it. It does not; they are two different systems and you should use both.
items.deadline: Register at the gaining location in connection with the PCS; time limits are set by DoD policy — confirm with the servicing HRO

items.title: VA for Vets — VA hires more veterans than any other federal agency
items.who: Veterans, transitioning servicemembers, Guard/Reserve members and military spouses seeking VA employment
items.value: Roughly a third of VA's workforce are veterans. VA for Vets provides military-skills translation into VA occupational series, career coaching, and direct connections to VA's Veterans Employment Program Managers at every facility.
items.how: Start at vaforvets.va.gov for the skills translator and hiring-authority brochure; apply through USAJOBS filtered to Department of Veterans Affairs; and separately email the Veterans Employment Program Manager and Selective Placement Program Coordinator at each VA medical center in your area.
items.hack: VA facilities are chronically short-staffed in non-clinical support roles — Medical Support Assistant (GS-0679), Program Support (0303), Health Technician (0640), Supply Technician (2005) — and these are exactly the series where VRA (GS-11 and below) and the float-to-top rule for CP/CPS work best. Get in at a support grade, then use internal merit promotion where the competition is a handful of coworkers rather than a national applicant pool.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: Title 38 and Hybrid Title 38 — VHA's clinical hiring lane that bypasses GS competition
items.who: Veterans with clinical credentials or clinical training: nurses, physician assistants, pharmacists, psychologists, social workers, physical/occupational therapists, respiratory therapists, medical technologists, and physicians
items.value: Pure Title 38 occupations (physician, dentist, podiatrist, optometrist, chiropractor, nurse, PA, expanded-function dental auxiliary) are appointed under 38 U.S.C. 7401(1) — outside the competitive service, outside category rating, with pay set by VA's own schedules rather than the GS table. Hybrid Title 38 occupations (psychologist, social worker, pharmacist, PT/OT, and many others) use Title 38 qualification standards with Title 5 procedures.
items.how: Apply directly to VA announcements in these series; appointment runs through a professional standards board rather than a rating panel. Credentialing and licensure — not a questionnaire score — is the gate.
items.hack: If you are using Post-9/11 GI Bill or VR&E for a clinical credential, pick one on VA's Hybrid Title 38 list and you convert a degree into a hiring authority, not just a diploma. VA's own list of Title 38 and Hybrid Title 38 occupations (linked) is the definitive roster — read it before you pick a program of study.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: VA disability, military retired pay and a federal salary — what does and does not offset
items.who: Veterans working in federal civilian jobs
items.value: VA disability compensation is not reduced by federal civilian employment, and a federal civilian salary is not reduced by VA compensation. Since the repeal of the dual-compensation reduction in 1999, military retired pay is likewise not reduced by federal civilian salary — a military retiree may draw full retired pay and a full federal salary at the same time.
items.how: No action required for the salary side. The only place a waiver comes in is crediting military service toward a FERS/CSRS ANNUITY (see the retired-pay waiver item) — that is a retirement-computation question, not a paycheck question.
items.hack: Veterans turn down federal jobs every year because they wrongly believe the salary will offset their VA compensation or their retired pay. It will not. The only genuine offset questions in this space are VA-vs-retired-pay (CRDP/CRSC) and the annuity-credit waiver — neither of which touches your biweekly civilian paycheck.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: State veterans' preference — absolute-preference states vs points states
items.who: Veterans applying for state government jobs
items.value: State preference schemes are structurally different from the federal one, and in a handful of states they are far stronger. 'Absolute preference' states place qualifying veterans ahead of ALL non-veterans on the eligible list regardless of exam score — a veteran who passes outranks a non-veteran who scored higher. Points states (the majority) add a fixed number of points to a passing exam score, commonly 5 for wartime/veteran status and 10 for service-connected disability.
items.how: Find your state's civil service commission or department of administrative services and read the veterans preference statute itself, not the summary page. Preference is usually claimed at the time of exam application and requires a DD-214 and, for disabled preference, a current VA rating letter.
items.hack: In absolute-preference states, the exam score barely matters — passing does. Veterans in those states should sit for every exam they minimally qualify for, because passing places them at the head of the list. In points states, the opposite is true: spend the effort on the exam, because 5 points does not rescue a mediocre score. Know which system you are in before you decide how to spend your preparation time.
items.deadline: State exam cycles — check the commission's exam calendar

items.title: New Jersey — absolute veterans preference in state and local civil service
items.org: NJ Department of Military and Veterans Affairs / NJ Civil Service Commission
items.who: New Jersey residents with qualifying wartime service who obtain a Veterans Preference determination from NJ DMAVA
items.value: New Jersey grants absolute preference: veterans who pass an open competitive examination are placed at the top of the eligible list ahead of all non-veterans, and disabled veterans are placed ahead of other veterans. In promotional examinations, veterans status can break ties.
items.how: Apply to NJ DMAVA for a Veterans Preference determination BEFORE the civil service exam closing date; DMAVA certifies your status to the Civil Service Commission. Submit the DD-214 and, for disabled veterans preference, the VA rating letter.
items.hack: The determination is the whole game and it takes time — veterans lose absolute preference every year by taking the exam first and applying for the determination afterward. Get the DMAVA determination on file before you ever sit for an NJ exam, and it carries forward to every future exam.
items.deadline: Veterans preference determination must be on file with the Civil Service Commission by the exam's closing date

items.title: Pennsylvania — mandatory veterans' preference in state and municipal hiring
items.who: Pennsylvania veterans (soldiers as defined by the Military and Veterans Code, 51 Pa.C.S. Ch. 71) and, in some circumstances, spouses of disabled veterans and unmarried surviving spouses
items.value: Pennsylvania adds 10 points to a passing civil service examination score, and Pennsylvania case law treats preference in appointment as mandatory rather than discretionary where the veteran is qualified — a stronger posture than a pure points state.
items.how: Claim preference on the PA civil service application and submit the DD-214. Municipal police and fire hiring in Pennsylvania is also covered by the veterans preference provisions of the Military and Veterans Code.
items.hack: Pennsylvania's preference reaches municipal and county appointing authorities, not just the state. Veterans applying to a borough police department or a county agency in PA should cite 51 Pa.C.S. Ch. 71 explicitly in the application — local HR offices frequently do not apply it unless prompted.
items.deadline: Claim at time of application

items.title: Buying military service credit in a STATE retirement system
items.who: Veterans employed by state or local government, including teachers, police, fire and municipal employees
items.value: Most state and municipal retirement systems permit a member to purchase service credit for active military service — commonly up to 4 or 5 years — and some grant a limited amount of free credit for wartime service or for service interrupting public employment. The effect on a defined-benefit pension is usually larger than the federal FERS buyback because state multipliers are higher (2.0%–2.5% per year is common versus FERS's 1.0%).
items.how: Request the military service purchase packet from your state retirement system, submit the DD-214, and get a written cost quote. Costs are typically actuarial (a percentage of current salary per year purchased) rather than a percentage of old military pay.
items.hack: Two rules decide whether this is a great deal or a bad one: (1) many systems price the purchase at your CURRENT salary, so buying early in your career is dramatically cheaper; (2) USERRA requires that service credit for military duty that INTERRUPTED your public employment be made available at the employee-contribution rate you would have paid, with the employer funding its share — that is a statutory right, not a purchase, and is often free. Ask which bucket your service falls in before you write a check.
items.deadline: Many systems impose purchase windows (e.g., within 3–5 years of hire or before retirement); USERRA repayment window is up to 3x the period of service, not to exceed 5 years

items.title: Municipal police and fire hiring — where veterans' preference is strongest
items.who: Veterans applying to city and county police and fire departments
items.value: Police and fire entrance exams in civil-service jurisdictions are among the few remaining ranked-list hiring systems in America, and veterans preference on a ranked list is worth far more than in a category-rating system. Many jurisdictions add points to the written exam, extend the maximum hiring age for veterans by the length of military service, and give disabled-veteran preference on top.
items.how: Ask the municipal civil service commission (not the department's recruiter) for the written preference rule and the age-extension rule. Register for preference before the exam. Bring the DD-214 to the application, not to the interview.
items.hack: The age extension is the sleeper benefit. Many departments set a maximum hiring age of 35 but extend it by the number of years of active military service — which puts a 39-year-old veteran back in the applicant pool. This is almost never advertised on the recruiting page; it lives in the civil service rules.
items.deadline: Exam cycles, typically annual or biennial

items.title: JVSG — the DVOP and LVER staff sitting in your American Job Center, free
items.who: All veterans; DVOP services are targeted to veterans with significant barriers to employment (including 'special disabled' veterans, homeless veterans, veterans aged 18–24, and recently separated veterans who are long-term unemployed)
items.value: The Jobs for Veterans State Grants program funds Disabled Veterans' Outreach Program (DVOP) specialists — who provide intensive one-on-one case management — and Local Veterans' Employment Representatives (LVER), who work the employer side to open jobs for veterans. Both are free, and by law veterans receive priority of service in every DOL-funded employment program.
items.how: Find your nearest American Job Center at careeronestop.org/localhelp and ask specifically for the DVOP specialist, by title. Ask about priority of service when you register — it moves you ahead of non-veterans for training slots funded under WIOA.
items.hack: Walking in and asking for 'job help' gets you a computer terminal. Walking in and saying 'I need to see the DVOP specialist, I am a veteran with a service-connected disability, and I am requesting priority of service' gets you a case manager with a caseload cap and a placement metric. The words matter.
items.deadline: None

items.title: SBA VetCert — SDVOSB and VOSB certification after the January 2023 move from VA CVE
items.who: Small businesses at least 51% unconditionally and directly owned and controlled by one or more veterans (VOSB) or service-disabled veterans (SDVOSB)
items.value: Certification is now MANDATORY, not optional. Since the self-certification sunset, a firm must hold SBA VetCert certification to receive SDVOSB/VOSB sole-source or set-aside awards, and (as of December 22, 2024) for subcontracting and agency goaling credit. Self-certified status no longer buys anything.
items.how: Apply free at certifications.sba.gov. You will need: SAM.gov registration active with a UEI; the VA rating letter establishing service-connected disability (any compensable rating, including 0% where the disability is documented); operating agreement/bylaws/stock ledger proving 51%+ unconditional direct ownership; evidence the service-disabled veteran holds the highest officer position and controls day-to-day management and long-term decisions; and tax returns. SBA support: 866-SBA-HELP (866-722-4357), certifications@sba.gov.
items.hack: The application dies on CONTROL, not ownership. The most common rejections: a non-veteran holds a higher salary or title; the operating agreement gives a minority owner veto rights over ordinary business decisions (that is 'negative control' and defeats unconditional control); the veteran has outside full-time employment inconsistent with running the firm; or a franchise/licensing agreement restricts the veteran's control. Rewrite the operating agreement BEFORE applying — a denial carries a wait period before you can reapply.
items.deadline: Certification is generally valid 3 years, then recertify; SAM registration must be renewed annually

items.title: The SDVOSB ownership and control tests — the specific traps
items.who: Applicants and certified SDVOSBs
items.value: Understanding the test before you apply, and surviving a size/status protest after award.
items.how: Ownership: at least 51% unconditional and direct ownership by one or more service-disabled veterans; ownership through a trust is permitted only in narrow circumstances; ownership must not be subject to conditions, options or agreements that could cause it to lapse. Control: a service-disabled veteran must hold the highest officer position, must manage day-to-day operations AND long-term strategy, must work full-time during normal business hours, and generally must be the highest-compensated individual (or justify why not in writing). Exception: where the veteran is permanently and totally disabled and cannot manage daily operations, a spouse or permanent caregiver may direct daily management.
items.hack: Three quiet killers: (1) a non-veteran investor with a supermajority-consent clause — remove veto rights over ordinary-course decisions; (2) the veteran holding a full-time W-2 job elsewhere; (3) the veteran not being the highest-paid person in the company. Fix all three on paper before you file, and keep board minutes showing the veteran making the decisions. In a post-award status protest, SBA reads the documents, not your intentions.
items.deadline: Protests are decided on the documents as of the date of the offer

items.title: The SDVOSB government-wide contracting goal — raised from 3% to 5%
items.who: Certified SDVOSBs
items.value: The statutory government-wide prime contracting goal for service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses was the long-standing 3%; Congress increased the SDVOSB prime contracting goal to 5%. SBA's current guidance to contractors states the government aims to award at least 5% of federal contracting dollars to SDVOSBs each year. Agencies are scored on this in SBA's annual Small Business Procurement Scorecard.
items.how: Use the goal as a sales argument, not a legal entitlement: agency small business specialists are personally measured on it. Identify agencies missing their SDVOSB goal in the current Scorecard and approach their Office of Small and Disadvantaged Business Utilization (OSDBU) directly.
items.hack: The fiscal-year-end run (July–September) is when contracting officers with an unmet SDVOSB goal will move fast on a sole-source award. A certified SDVOSB with a clean capability statement and a GSA Schedule or an existing contract vehicle in hand is who gets that call. Be in the OSDBU's inbox in June, not September.
items.deadline: Federal fiscal year ends September 30

items.title: FAR Subpart 19.14 — SDVOSB set-asides and sole-source thresholds (current dollar figures)
items.who: Certified SDVOSBs competing government-wide
items.value: Set-aside: a contracting officer SHALL set aside an acquisition for SDVOSB competition when there is a reasonable expectation that two or more certified SDVOSBs will submit offers and award can be made at a fair market price. Sole source under FAR 19.1406: a contracting officer may award directly to a single SDVOSB when only one is reasonably expected to offer, the firm is responsible, price is fair and reasonable, and the anticipated award price including options will not exceed $8.5 million for a requirement in a manufacturing NAICS code, or $5 million for any other NAICS code.
items.how: Register the correct NAICS codes in SAM.gov, hold active SBA VetCert certification and the SDVOSB designation in SAM, and make sure your capability statement maps to the exact NAICS and PSC codes the agency buys under.
items.hack: Sole source is the whole ballgame for a small SDVOSB. Your job is not to win competitions — it is to be the only certified SDVOSB the contracting officer can find in that NAICS code in their market research. Answer every Sources Sought notice and RFI in your NAICS, even ones you would not bid: the market-research record is what creates (or destroys) the set-aside decision, and appearing in it is how a CO concludes only one qualified SDVOSB exists.
items.deadline: Thresholds are adjusted periodically for inflation — reverify before relying on a specific figure

items.title: VA's 'Vets First' Rule of Two — 38 U.S.C. 8127(d) and Kingdomware
items.who: Certified SDVOSBs and VOSBs selling to VA
items.value: VA's Rule of Two is materially stronger than the government-wide rule. Under 38 U.S.C. 8127(d), a VA contracting officer SHALL award to a veteran-owned small business using restricted competition whenever the CO has a reasonable expectation that two or more VOSBs/SDVOSBs will submit offers and award can be made at a fair and reasonable price. The Supreme Court held unanimously in Kingdomware Technologies v. United States (2016) that 'shall' is mandatory and applies even when VA has already met its contracting goals, and even to orders placed under the Federal Supply Schedule.
items.how: Order of priority at VA: SDVOSB first, then VOSB, before other small business set-asides and before open competition. Watch VA solicitations for improper failures to apply the rule and protest at GAO or the Court of Federal Claims.
items.hack: This is the strongest procurement preference any demographic has in the federal government, and the leverage point is the pre-solicitation phase. When VA issues a Sources Sought for a requirement in your NAICS, respond with a capability statement that demonstrates you can do the whole scope — because two credible SDVOSB responses legally force the set-aside. Coordinate with one other SDVOSB to both respond and the requirement must be set aside. That is not collusion; it is exactly what the statute contemplates.
items.deadline: Sources Sought response windows are typically 5–10 business days

items.title: VA sole-source to a veteran-owned firm — VAAR 806.302-570, up to $5 million
items.who: Certified SDVOSBs and VOSBs
items.value: A VA contracting officer may award a noncompetitive contract to an SDVOSB first (then a VOSB if no SDVOSB can meet the need) for amounts below the simplified acquisition threshold, and above the SAT up to $5 million where the firm is a responsible source, the price is fair and reasonable, and the award offers best value.
items.how: Build the sole-source justification FOR the contracting officer: a capability statement mapped to the requirement, past performance with dollar values and CPARS references, pricing that is demonstrably at or below market, and your SBA VetCert certification number. Deliver it to the VA program office and the VA OSDBU before a solicitation exists.
items.hack: The $5 million ceiling means a single VA sole-source award can be larger than most small businesses' entire annual revenue, and it does not require you to beat anyone. Every hour spent on relationship-building with VA program offices before a requirement is written is worth more than ten hours writing proposals after it is posted.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: Finding SDVOSB set-aside opportunities on SAM.gov — the search that actually works
items.who: Certified SDVOSBs and VOSBs
items.value: SAM.gov is the only official source for federal contract opportunities. Used correctly it becomes a daily pipeline instead of a haystack.
items.how: At sam.gov/search/?index=opp, filter by: Set Aside = 'Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business Set-Aside (FAR 19.14)' and 'SDVOSB Sole Source (FAR 19.14)' and 'Veteran-Owned Small Business Set-Aside'; Notice Type = include 'Sources Sought' and 'Presolicitation' (not just 'Solicitation'); your NAICS codes; and place of performance. Save the search and turn on email notifications.
items.hack: Filter for Sources Sought and Presolicitation notices, not Solicitations. By the time a solicitation posts, the acquisition strategy is locked and the incumbent has been shaping it for six months. Sources Sought is the only stage where your response changes whether the work is set aside for you at all — and the response is one page, not a proposal.
items.deadline: Set daily email alerts; Sources Sought windows are short

items.title: California DVBE — 3% participation goal on every state contract
items.org: California Department of General Services, Office of Small Business and DVBE Services
items.who: Disabled Veteran Business Enterprises: at least 51% owned by one or more disabled veterans with a service-connected disability of at least 10%, with daily business operations managed and controlled by one or more disabled veterans, and the home office in the United States (not a branch or subsidiary of a foreign corporation)
items.value: California law sets a 3% DVBE participation goal for state contracting dollars, and many state solicitations require bidders to meet the DVBE goal or document a good-faith effort. DVBE certification also opens DVBE-only small business option and incentive provisions on state bids.
items.how: Certify through the California DGS Cal eProcure portal. California requires its own certification — federal SBA VetCert does NOT substitute.
items.hack: The real money in DVBE is not direct state contracts — it is subcontracting. Prime bidders on California state contracts must hit the 3% DVBE participation or justify a good-faith effort, so every large prime in the state is actively hunting for certified DVBEs to put on their team sheet. Market to the primes, not to the state.
items.deadline: Certification renewal required; check current DGS renewal cycle

items.title: New York SDVOB — a 6% statewide goal, the highest state target in the country
items.org: NYS Office of General Services, Division of Service-Disabled Veterans' Business Development
items.who: Businesses at least 51% owned by one or more veterans with a service-connected disability rating of at least 10%, independently controlled by those veterans, qualifying as a small business under New York standards, with a significant business presence in New York State
items.value: New York sets a 6% participation goal for SDVOBs on state contracts — double the federal 3% baseline and the most aggressive state goal in the country. Certification is required to count.
items.how: Apply through the NYS Division of Service-Disabled Veterans' Business Development. Start at ny.gov/services/become-certified-service-disabled-veteran-owned-small-business or call 518-474-2015.
items.hack: The 'significant business presence in New York State' test is the gate, and it is more flexible than out-of-state firms assume — a real New York office with real New York employees and revenue can qualify a firm headquartered elsewhere. If you already hold federal SBA VetCert and do any work in New York, the incremental cost of NY SDVOB certification is a few hours of paperwork against a 6% statewide goal.
items.deadline: Recertification required; check current OGS cycle

items.title: State veteran business certifications beyond California and New York — where to look
items.who: Veteran-owned businesses selling to state government
items.value: Most states now operate some form of veteran or service-disabled veteran business preference: a certification program, a bid preference percentage, a participation goal, or a tie-breaker. The mechanisms vary enormously — a bid-price preference (your bid is evaluated as if it were X% lower), a set-aside, a subcontracting goal, or a simple registry.
items.how: For any state you sell into, search '[state] service-disabled veteran owned business certification' on the state's official procurement or administrative services domain (.gov only), and read the statute the page cites. Confirm three things: whether the state accepts SBA VetCert in lieu of its own certification; whether the preference is a goal (soft) or a bid preference/set-aside (hard); and whether there is a residency or in-state presence requirement.
items.hack: Never rely on a third-party list of 'states with veteran business programs' — they are stale and frequently wrong, and several list programs that were repealed. Go to the state procurement office's own page and check the statute citation. Also check whether your state accepts SBA VetCert reciprocally: a growing number do, which turns one federal certification into several state registrations at zero extra cost.
items.deadline: Varies by state

items.title: SBA Express loans to veterans — $0 upfront guaranty fee, confirmed for FY2026
items.who: Small businesses owned and controlled (51% or more) by a veteran, or by the spouse of a veteran; the authority also reaches service-disabled veterans, active-duty members eligible for TAP, reservists and National Guard members
items.value: The upfront SBA guaranty fee on SBA Express loans to veteran-owned businesses is $0 under SBA's FY2026 fee schedule. On a $350,000 Express loan at the standard 3% fee on the guaranteed portion, that is roughly $5,250 saved at closing — real cash, not a rate discount.
items.how: Ask the lender specifically for an SBA EXPRESS loan (not a standard 7(a)) and to apply the veteran fee waiver. Provide the DD-214 and ownership documentation. Find participating lenders through SBA's Lender Match tool or your local VBOC.
items.hack: The waiver applies to SBA Express specifically — not to standard 7(a). Lenders frequently default customers into standard 7(a) because they process more of them, and the veteran pays a fee they did not owe. Ask in writing: 'Is this an SBA Express loan, and are you applying the $0 veteran upfront guaranty fee?' Get the answer in the term sheet. Separately confirm whether the FY2026 manufacturer fee relief (0% for loans under $950,000 in NAICS 31-33) gives you a better result.
items.deadline: SBA fee schedules are set each fiscal year (October 1); reverify annually

items.title: SBA 7(a) fees for FY2026 — what the loan actually costs
items.who: Any small business borrower, veteran or not
items.value: FY2026 upfront guaranty fees on 7(a) loans with maturities over 12 months: 2% of the guaranteed portion for loans of $150,000 or less; 3% for $150,001–$700,000; 3.5% for $700,001–$5,000,000 (plus an additional 0.25% on the guaranteed portion above $1,000,000). Loans with maturities of 12 months or less: 0.25%. Lender annual service fee: 0.55% of the guaranteed portion of the outstanding balance. Maximum 7(a) loan: $5 million.
items.how: The fee is charged on the GUARANTEED portion, not the loan amount — on a $500,000 7(a) with a 75% guaranty, the 3% fee applies to $375,000, or $11,250. Lenders may pass it through to the borrower and usually do.
items.hack: Because the fee is tiered at $150,000, a $155,000 loan carries a materially higher fee rate than a $150,000 loan. If you are borrowing near a break point, ask the lender to model both. And always ask whether SBA Express with the veteran $0 fee gets you to the same capital for free — Express caps lower but costs nothing upfront.
items.deadline: Fee schedule set annually effective October 1

items.title: SBA microloans and 504 loans — the two programs veterans actually get approved for
items.org: SBA and its intermediary lenders / Certified Development Companies
items.who: Veteran-owned small businesses, especially startups and firms without three years of tax returns
items.value: MICROLOAN: up to $50,000, made through nonprofit community-based intermediaries, with mandatory business training attached; these are the loans startups and thin-credit borrowers actually receive, because the intermediary underwrites character and the training, not just the financials. 504: long-term fixed-rate financing for owner-occupied real estate and heavy equipment through a Certified Development Company, typically 50% bank / 40% CDC-debenture / 10% borrower equity.
items.how: Microloan: find your local SBA microloan intermediary through sba.gov or your VBOC. 504: find a CDC through SBA's CDC locator. Both are listed at sba.gov/funding-programs/loans.
items.hack: Veterans keep applying for $250,000 7(a) loans and getting declined for lack of operating history, when a $35,000 microloan from a community intermediary would fund the same first step and build the SBA payment history that makes the 7(a) approvable two years later. Also: 504 is the right tool if you are buying the building — as a veteran with a VA home loan you already know the power of long-term fixed-rate debt; 504 is that for commercial property, and the 10% down structure is close to unmatched.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: MREIDL — the Military Reservist Economic Injury Disaster Loan
items.who: Small businesses that sustain economic injury because an essential employee — including the owner — is called to active duty as a military reservist or Guard member
items.value: A working-capital loan of up to $2 million (waivable for businesses that are a major source of employment) to cover operating expenses the business cannot meet because a key person was mobilized. It is not a grant, but it is priced and termed as disaster assistance rather than commercial credit. SBA must first find that credit is not available elsewhere without undue hardship, and businesses with the capacity to fund their own recovery are not eligible.
items.how: Apply at SBA's disaster lending portal or call the Disaster Assistance Customer Service Center at 800-659-2955. You will need the activation orders, evidence that the mobilized person is essential to the business, and financial statements showing the economic injury. The filing window runs from the date the essential employee receives the notice of expected call-up through one year after their discharge or release from active duty.
items.hack: This is the single most underused SBA program for Guard and Reserve business owners, because the owner is deployed and nobody at home knows it exists. If you are a drilling reservist who owns a business, brief your spouse or business partner on MREIDL BEFORE you get mobilized, and put the SBA disaster assistance number in the continuity folder alongside the power of attorney. The clock starts at the notice of call-up, not at return.
items.deadline: Filing window: from the date of the notice of expected call-up through one year after the essential employee's discharge or release from active duty

items.title: Boots to Business — the free SBA entrepreneurship course inside TAP
items.who: Transitioning servicemembers (all branches) and their spouses, delivered on military installations worldwide as the TAP entrepreneurship track
items.value: A free two-day introduction to business ownership and business model development, taught by SBA resource partners, with no obligation and no cost. It is the on-ramp to the rest of the SBA veteran ecosystem.
items.how: Register through your installation's TAP office as part of the entrepreneurship track, or at sbavets.force.com. Spouses can attend.
items.hack: Take it even if you have no intention of starting a business. It is the only TAP track that hands you a live relationship with a VBOC counselor you can call for free for the rest of your life, and it is the prerequisite for Revenue Readiness. Bring your spouse — spouse attendance is permitted and spouse-owned businesses qualify for VetFran and most state programs too.
items.deadline: Offered continuously on installations; register through TAP

items.title: Boots to Business Reboot and Revenue Readiness — for veterans who already separated
items.who: REBOOT: veterans of all eras, National Guard and Reserve members, and military spouses — in their communities, not on an installation. REVENUE READINESS: graduates of B2B or B2B Reboot.
items.value: Reboot delivers the same Boots to Business curriculum to veterans who are already out — it is the fix for everyone who skipped the TAP track years ago. Revenue Readiness is a six-week online course that converts a business idea into a workable revenue model.
items.how: Find scheduled Reboot classes through your regional VBOC or at sbavets.force.com. Both are free.
items.hack: Most veterans assume Boots to Business is closed to them because they separated in 2009. Reboot exists precisely for that person, it is free, and it is the credential that gets you into Revenue Readiness and into the VBOC counseling relationship. There is no era cutoff and no discharge-character requirement published as a bar to attending.
items.deadline: Rolling class schedules

items.title: Veterans Business Outreach Centers — 31 of them, free for life, and how to find yours
items.who: Veterans, service-disabled veterans, transitioning servicemembers, National Guard and Reserve members, and military spouses
items.value: SBA funds 31 organizations as VBOCs across the United States and territories. Services: one-on-one business counseling with no time limit and no fee, business plan development, concept assessment, mentorship including on-site visits and financial statement review, specialized training in franchising, international trade, manufacturing and accounting, and referrals to lenders and to SBA capital programs. VBOCs also deliver Boots to Business and B2B Reboot.
items.how: Find your VBOC by ZIP code at sba.gov's VBOC locator; centers are organized into geographic regions (New England, Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, Southeast, Great Lakes, South Central, Great Plains, Rocky Mountain, Pacific). Call the center directly and ask for an intake appointment with a business advisor.
items.hack: VBOC counseling is free, unlimited and permanent — there is no graduation. The highest-value use is not the business plan; it is having a counselor review your SBA loan package BEFORE the lender sees it, and having them warm-introduce you to the lenders in their region who actually close veteran loans. Ask the counselor directly: 'Which three lenders in this district have closed the most SBA loans to veteran-owned firms in the last year?' They know.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Veteran Institute for Procurement (VIP) — free executive training for government contractors
items.org: National Veteran Institute for Procurement (nonprofit, DoD/corporate supported)
items.who: Veteran-owned small businesses already holding or pursuing federal contracts
items.value: Three programs delivered at no cost to accepted companies: VIP START (entry into the federal marketplace — certification, SAM registration, capture basics), VIP GROW (three-day executive program on scaling an existing government contracting business: accounting systems, contract vehicles, teaming, M&A readiness), and VIP INTERNATIONAL (exporting and international contracting). Alumni companies form one of the densest teaming networks in veteran contracting.
items.how: Apply at nationalvip.org. Programs are competitive and cohort-based; tuition is underwritten by sponsors, so the company pays nothing but travel in most cases.
items.hack: The curriculum is good; the alumni network is the actual product. VIP GROW graduates subcontract to each other constantly, and a large share of SDVOSB joint ventures in the DC market trace back to a VIP cohort. Apply to GROW as soon as you have your first prime contract — not after you have ten.
items.deadline: Cohort application deadlines — check nationalvip.org

items.title: National Veteran Small Business Coalition (NVSBC) — the trade association for veteran federal contractors
items.who: Veteran-owned and service-disabled veteran-owned businesses in the federal marketplace
items.value: The largest nonprofit trade association exclusively representing veteran-owned small businesses in federal contracting. Provides advocacy on SDVOSB policy, matchmaking with agency OSDBUs and large primes, and runs the annual VETS conference — the principal national matchmaking event for veteran federal contractors.
items.how: Membership at nvsbc.org/membership (paid, tiered by company size). Events and matchmaking sessions at nvsbc.org/events.
items.hack: If you can only afford one industry event a year, the VETS conference is the one where contracting officers and OSDBU directors actually take one-on-one matchmaking meetings with SDVOSBs, rather than standing behind a booth. Book the matchmaking slots the day registration opens — they fill before the conference agenda is even published.
items.deadline: Annual VETS conference; membership is annual

items.title: VetFran — franchise fee discounts tiered by brand commitment
items.who: U.S. military veterans and military-connected families, including spouses
items.value: Free educational program. Participating brands commit to minimum initial franchise fee discounts by tier: VetFran 1-Star partners a minimum 10% discount, 3-Star a minimum 15%, and 5-Star a minimum 20%. Many brands exceed their tier minimum or add financing, training or royalty concessions.
items.how: Use the IFA franchise directory at franchise.org with the veteran filter to see participating brands and their specific incentives. There is no membership fee and no application to join VetFran as a veteran.
items.hack: The franchise fee is the smallest number in a franchise deal — a 20% discount on a $45,000 fee is $9,000 against a total investment that may be $400,000. Negotiate the things VetFran does not publish: reduced or deferred royalties in year one, waived marketing fund contributions, territory size, and the transfer fee. Ask the franchise development officer 'what else do you do for veterans beyond the VetFran fee discount' — most brands have unpublished concessions and will not volunteer them. And check whether SBA Express with the $0 veteran guaranty fee covers your franchise fee.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Warrior Rising — free training and a genuine non-dilutive grant up to $20,000
items.who: Veterans, active duty servicemembers, Guard and Reserve members, military spouses, and immediate family members
items.value: Free Warrior Academy / Warrior University training, then eligibility to pitch at a 'Business Shower' for up to $20,000 in non-dilutive funding — a grant, not an investment and not a loan. Also provides coaches, masterclasses, office hours and an active founder community. VA's own news service has covered the program, which is a meaningful legitimacy signal.
items.how: Apply at warriorrising.org; complete or enroll in Warrior Academy/University first; selected founders are invited to pitch at a Business Shower.
items.hack: This is one of the very few verifiable cash grant programs for veteran businesses in the United States — treat the training requirement as the price of admission rather than an obstacle. The pitch is the filter: bring a specific use of funds with a number attached ('$18,400 for a CNC machine that removes my largest outsourcing cost'), not a vision statement.
items.deadline: Cohort-based with application deadlines; check warriorrising.org for the current cycle

items.title: PenFed Foundation Veteran Entrepreneur Program — mentorship and network, NOT money
items.who: Veterans and military spouses who are the majority owner of a business
items.value: Three tracks — Incubator (idea stage, no MVP or customers yet), Accelerator (existing customers, scalable high-growth), and a forthcoming Bootcamp for transitioning servicemembers. The program covers participant travel, hotel and meals for the Accelerator and meals for the Incubator. Since 2018 it has supported more than 120 veteran and military-spouse founders.
items.how: Apply at penfedfoundation.org/our-programs/vep/. Applications are reviewed monthly; selected applicants are interviewed before a selection committee decides.
items.hack: IMPORTANT CORRECTION to what most veteran benefit guides still say: the current PenFed Foundation Veteran Entrepreneur Program provides NO financial investment and NO grants. The earlier 'Veteran Entrepreneur Investment Program (VEIP)' branding led many lists to describe it as an equity or cash program; it is now mentorship, education and network only. Apply for the network and the introductions — not for a check.
items.deadline: Rolling monthly application review

items.title: Hivers & Strivers — angel capital for service-academy and veteran founders
items.who: Early-stage startups founded by U.S. military academy graduates and veterans
items.value: An angel investment group that invests specifically in veteran-founded early-stage companies, with typical angel-round check sizes. The investor base is heavily service-academy alumni, which means the diligence conversation starts with a shared vocabulary.
items.how: Approach through hiversandstrivers.com. This is equity investment — you are selling a piece of the company, not receiving a grant.
items.hack: Veteran-focused angel and venture money is real but small, and it is not a substitute for revenue or for SBA debt. Its actual value is the second conversation: a warm introduction from a veteran angel to a defense-adjacent customer is often worth more than the check. Only pursue this if you have a venture-scale business; a profitable services firm should take the SBA Express loan and keep 100% of the equity.
items.deadline: Rolling

items.title: TFX Capital (Task Force X) and Veteran Ventures Capital — institutional funds backing veteran founders
items.who: Veteran-founded and veteran-led companies, generally seed through growth stage
items.value: Two of the largest institutional venture funds with an explicit veteran-founder thesis. TFX Capital (formerly Task Force X Capital) invests in veteran- and military-connected-led B2B and government-adjacent technology companies. Veteran Ventures Capital, based in Knoxville, invests in veteran-led companies with a defense and dual-use emphasis and has operated an SBIC-style structure.
items.how: TFX at tfxcap.com; Veteran Ventures Capital at veteranventures.us. Both take inbound but strongly prefer warm introductions — VIP, IVMF and NVSBC alumni networks are the usual route in.
items.hack: Both funds are heavily weighted toward defense, dual-use and govtech. If your company sells to DoD or a federal agency and you are a veteran founder, you are exactly their thesis and you should be in front of them. If you run a restaurant, a construction firm or a staffing agency, you are not — go to SBA debt instead, and stop wasting quarters pitching venture funds that structurally cannot invest in you.
items.deadline: Rolling

items.title: Veteran business 'grants' — what is real, and how to spot the fake lists
items.who: Any veteran searching for business funding
items.value: Avoiding weeks of wasted effort and the fee-harvesting sites that monetize the search.
items.how: Start from the truth: SBA does not make grants to start or grow a for-profit small business. Federal grants at grants.gov are overwhelmingly for research (SBIR/STTR), nonprofits and government entities. The verifiable cash-grant programs for veteran-owned for-profit businesses are a short list — Warrior Rising (up to $20,000, non-dilutive) and the Second Service Foundation Military Entrepreneur Challenge are among the few with documented, repeated awards. SBIR/STTR at sbir.gov is real federal money and is genuinely open to veteran-owned firms, but it funds R&D, not operations.
items.hack: Four red flags that identify an affiliate-marketing grant list: (1) it asks you to pay anything, including a 'grant application fee' or a 'database access fee' — no legitimate grant charges to apply; (2) it lists StreetShares Foundation awards as current (that program is no longer operating as previously described and should not be relied upon); (3) it describes PenFed Foundation's veteran entrepreneur program as providing investment or grants (it currently provides neither); (4) the page's outbound links go to lead-generation lenders rather than to .gov or to the sponsoring foundation's own domain. Verify every grant on the sponsoring organization's own website before you spend an hour on it.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: USERRA — the five conditions for reemployment, 38 U.S.C. 4312
items.who: Anyone absent from a civilian job because of service in the uniformed services — active duty, active duty for training, initial active duty, inactive duty training, full-time National Guard duty, funeral honors duty, and certain National Disaster Medical System service. USERRA applies to virtually every employer regardless of size, public or private.
items.value: The statutory right to be reemployed, with seniority and benefits as if you had never left.
items.how: Five conditions must all be met: (1) you gave the employer advance written or verbal notice; (2) your cumulative period of service with that employer does not exceed five years (with exceptions); (3) you returned to work or applied for reemployment within the statutory deadline; (4) you were not separated from service with a disqualifying discharge (dishonorable, bad conduct, or dismissal); and (5) the employer has no statutory defense (impossibility, undue hardship, or a genuinely brief non-recurrent position).
items.hack: Notice does not have to be in writing and does not have to be on a form — but PROVE it anyway. Send the orders to your supervisor and to HR by email and keep the sent copy. Nine out of ten USERRA disputes turn on whether notice was given, and email timestamps win those arguments. Notice is excused only where military necessity prevents it or it is otherwise impossible or unreasonable.
items.deadline: See the reporting deadlines item

items.title: The USERRA five-year cumulative limit — and the eight exceptions that swallow it
items.who: Guard and Reserve members with repeated mobilizations
items.value: The five-year cap applies to cumulative service with a single employer — but the exceptions are so broad that most modern mobilizations do not count against it at all.
items.how: Service EXEMPT from the five-year limit includes: service required beyond five years to complete an initial period of obligated service; service from which a person could not obtain release through no fault of their own; required training for Reservists and National Guard members (drills, annual training); involuntary active duty during domestic emergency or national security situations; service ordered under a war or national emergency declared by the President or Congress; volunteer active duty in support of an operational mission for which Selected Reservists were ordered to active duty without their consent; service designated by the Service Secretary as a critical mission or requirement; and National Guard federal service called by the President to suppress an insurrection.
items.hack: Drill weekends and annual training NEVER count toward the five years. Neither do the overwhelming majority of post-9/11 mobilizations, which were ordered under declared national emergencies. If an employer tells you that you have 'used up your USERRA,' ask them in writing to identify which of your periods of service they believe counted, and under which exception each one does not fall. That letter usually ends the dispute.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: USERRA reporting and application deadlines — the three tiers by length of service
items.who: Servicemembers returning from duty to a civilian job
items.value: Missing the deadline does not automatically forfeit reemployment, but it does subject you to the employer's ordinary rules for unexcused absence — which is how people lose jobs they had a right to keep.
items.how: Service of 1–30 days: report at the beginning of the first regularly scheduled work period after completion of service, allowing safe travel home plus an 8-hour rest period. Service of 31–180 days: submit an application for reemployment within 14 days after completion of service. Service of 181 days or more: submit an application within 90 days after completion of service. A person hospitalized for or convalescing from a service-connected injury gets the reporting/application period extended for up to two years, plus any additional time made necessary by circumstances beyond their control.
items.hack: Apply in writing even when the statute permits an oral application, and apply on day one rather than day 89. The 90-day window is not a vacation allowance — employers fill positions in the interim and 'I had 90 days' is a far weaker position than a written application submitted the week you demobilized. Put your intended return date in the application.
items.deadline: 1–30 days: next work period. 31–180 days: 14 days. 181+ days: 90 days. Disability: up to 2 years.

items.title: The escalator principle — 38 U.S.C. 4313, the most valuable and least understood USERRA rule
items.who: Returning servicemembers
items.value: You are not entitled to the job you left. You are entitled to the 'escalator position' — the position you would have attained with reasonable certainty had you remained continuously employed, with full seniority. That may mean a PROMOTION, a higher pay grade, accrued leave, a step increase, or a different job entirely.
items.how: Identify what happened to your peers while you were gone: automatic step increases, scheduled promotions, seniority-based bidding rights, pension accrual, accrued vacation. If your cohort advanced, you advance with them. The escalator can also move down — if your position was eliminated in a legitimate reduction that would have reached you, the escalator reflects that too.
items.hack: Returning servicemembers routinely accept their old job at their old pay and think USERRA was satisfied. It was not. Before you report back, write down the names of three peers hired around the same time as you, find out their current title and pay band, and bring that to the reemployment conversation. 'What would have happened to me' is the legal standard, and the evidence is sitting one cubicle over.
items.deadline: Raise it at reemployment; do not wait

items.title: USERRA health coverage continuation — 24 months at no more than 102% of premium
items.who: Servicemembers on military leave from a civilian employer with a health plan
items.value: You may elect to continue employer-sponsored health coverage for yourself and your dependents for up to 24 months from the start of the absence, or for the period of service plus the time allowed to apply for reemployment, whichever is SHORTER. For service of 30 days or fewer, you pay only the normal employee share. For longer service, the employer may charge no more than 102% of the full premium.
items.how: Elect in writing before or at the start of the leave. On reemployment, there is no waiting period and no exclusion for pre-existing conditions (other than for VA-determined service-connected conditions) that would not have applied had you never left.
items.hack: For most mobilizations this is a trap door in your favor: you and your family get TRICARE while you are activated, so paying 102% for the civilian plan is usually wasted money — EXCEPT where a family member is mid-treatment with a provider who does not take TRICARE, or where dropping the plan would break continuity for a specialist. Run that one question before you decline. And the no-waiting-period reinstatement right on return is absolute; do not let HR impose a new-hire waiting period.
items.deadline: Elect at the start of the leave; 24-month maximum

items.title: USERRA pension accrual — your military leave counts as service for the civilian plan
items.who: Servicemembers with employer retirement plans, defined benefit or defined contribution
items.value: Military service must not be treated as a break in service for pension purposes. The period counts toward vesting and toward benefit accrual. The employer is liable for funding any resulting obligation, and you may make up your own employee contributions (including 401(k) elective deferrals and the matching that goes with them) over a period of up to three times the length of the service, not exceeding five years.
items.how: On reemployment, give HR the exact dates of service in writing and ask for a written schedule of: (1) the employer contributions being credited retroactively, and (2) the make-up contribution window and the maximum you may contribute. Then actually make the contributions — the employer match usually follows the make-up deferral.
items.hack: This is the single largest dollar item in USERRA and nearly everyone forfeits it. A 12-month deployment can represent five figures of missed 401(k) match, and you have up to 36 months (3x a 12-month deployment) to put the money in and claim the match. Set a calendar reminder the month you return. HR will not initiate this conversation.
items.deadline: Make-up contributions allowed over 3x the period of service, capped at 5 years

items.title: USERRA now covers certain STATE active duty — the January 5, 2021 amendment
items.who: National Guard members performing State Active Duty under the authority of a Governor
items.value: USERRA section 4303 was amended effective January 5, 2021 to extend employment and reemployment protections to National Guard members on State Active Duty when the duty (1) lasts 14 days or more, OR (2) supports a national emergency declared by the President under the National Emergencies Act, OR (3) supports a major disaster declared under the Stafford Act. State Active Duty of 13 days or fewer is not covered, nor is duty supporting a Stafford Act emergency declaration under Section 501.
items.how: If your employer disciplines or fires you for a Governor-ordered activation meeting one of those three tests, you have a federal USERRA claim — file with DOL VETS on Form 1010 or request ESGR mediation.
items.hack: This is the newest and least-known protection in the whole USERRA scheme, and it matters enormously for Guard members who spend more days on state hurricane, wildfire, flood and civil-disturbance missions than on federal orders. Before 2021 those days had no federal protection at all. Many employers — and many employment lawyers — still believe State Active Duty is unprotected. Print the DOL fact sheet and hand it to HR.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: USERRA discrimination and retaliation — and the burden-shifting rule that favors you
items.who: Applicants and employees with past, current or future military obligations
items.value: Employers may not discriminate in hiring, promotion, retention, termination or any benefit of employment because of past, present or future military service or obligation, and may not retaliate against anyone who asserts USERRA rights or testifies in a USERRA proceeding.
