The evidentiary standard is unusually favorable: once you show that military service was a MOTIVATING FACTOR, the burden shifts to the employer to prove it would have taken the same action anyway.
items.how: Document the timeline: the date you disclosed the obligation, the date of the adverse action, and any statements about your availability, deployments or drill schedule. 'Motivating factor' — not sole cause — is the test.
items.hack: The most common and most provable USERRA violation is in HIRING: an interviewer asks whether you will deploy, or how often you drill, and then passes. That question is itself evidence of a motivating factor. Write down the question and the interviewer's name the day it happens. Note also that USERRA protects FUTURE obligations — an employer cannot decline to hire you because you intend to join the Guard.
items.deadline: No statute of limitations for USERRA claims (38 U.S.C. 4327(b)); file promptly regardless

items.title: Filing a USERRA complaint with DOL VETS — Form 1010
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Any servicemember or veteran with a USERRA, veterans' preference or VEOA complaint
items.value: A free federal investigation of your claim. If VETS cannot resolve it, the case can be referred to the Attorney General (for private and state employers) or to the Office of Special Counsel (for federal executive agencies), either of whom may represent you in court at no cost to you.
items.how: File VETS Form 1010 (VETS USERRA/VP/VEOA Claim Form), available at dol.gov/agencies/vets, or file online through the DOL VETS electronic filing system. There is no filing fee, no lawyer required, and no statute of limitations for USERRA claims under 38 U.S.C. 4327(b).
items.hack: Filing with DOL VETS is OPTIONAL for USERRA — you may go straight to federal court (private employer) or straight to MSPB (federal employer). But filing is free and it produces an investigative record that a private attorney can later use. The one thing to know: if you file with DOL VETS, ESGR will NOT open a mediation case on the same matter. Try ESGR mediation FIRST if the relationship with the employer is salvageable; file Form 1010 when it is not.
items.deadline: No USERRA statute of limitations; VEOA complaints must be filed within 60 days of the violation

items.title: ESGR Ombudsman Services — free neutral mediation, and why to use it first
items.org: Employer Support of the Guard and Reserve (DoD)
items.who: Guard and Reserve members with a civilian employment problem related to military service, and their employers
items.value: Free, neutral, informal mediation by trained volunteer ombudsmen located throughout the United States and territories. ESGR educates both sides on USERRA and brokers a resolution. Most cases close in days or weeks, not the months an investigation or lawsuit takes.
items.how: Call the ESGR Customer Service Center at 800-336-4590, Option 1, Monday–Friday 8:00 a.m.–4:30 p.m. ET, or submit a USERRA Support Request online at esgr.mil/USERRA/USERRA-Contact.
items.hack: Use ESGR BEFORE DOL VETS and long before a lawyer, for one structural reason: ESGR does not enforce USERRA and takes no side, which means your employer will talk to them. The moment a DOL investigator or an attorney appears, the employer's counsel takes over and the informal fix becomes impossible. Also note the mutual exclusivity — once you file with DOL VETS, ESGR will not open a mediation case. Sequence matters: ESGR first, Form 1010 second, litigation last.
items.deadline: None, but mediate early while the employment relationship is intact

items.title: MSPB appeals — USERRA has NO deadline, VEOA has a 60-day and a 15-day clock
items.org: Merit Systems Protection Board (5 CFR Part 1208)
items.who: Federal employees and applicants
items.value: Two different routes with two very different rules, and confusing them is fatal to a VEOA claim.
items.how: USERRA: there is NO time limit for filing a USERRA appeal with MSPB. Exhausting DOL is optional — you may file directly with the Board, or file with the Secretary of Labor first and then proceed to MSPB once the Secretary notifies you the complaint was not resolved. VEOA: you MUST first file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor within 60 DAYS after the date of the alleged violation. Then, after the Secretary notifies you that efforts to resolve were unsuccessful, you have only 15 DAYS from receipt of that notice to file with MSPB. Alternatively, if 60 days pass with no resolution, you may give the Secretary written notice of intent to file and proceed.
items.hack: The 60-day VEOA clock starts on the date of the violation — which is the date you were not selected or not considered, not the date you figured out why. If you believe your preference or VEOA rights were violated in a federal hiring action, file the DOL VETS Form 1010 immediately and sort out the details later. That one filing preserves everything. The 15-day window after DOL's notice is brutally short; watch your mail.
items.deadline: USERRA: none. VEOA: 60 days to DOL VETS, then 15 days to MSPB after DOL's notice.

items.title: The Office of Special Counsel route for federal-employee USERRA claims
items.who: Federal executive branch employees and applicants with USERRA claims
items.value: OSC has authority to investigate and prosecute USERRA claims against federal executive agencies before the MSPB — free representation by a federal prosecutor rather than a private attorney.
items.how: If you file a USERRA complaint with DOL VETS against a federal executive agency and VETS cannot resolve it, you may ask VETS to refer the case to OSC. OSC then decides whether to represent you before MSPB. You may also file directly with MSPB yourself without OSC.
items.hack: Federal employees have THREE doors (DOL VETS → OSC → MSPB, or straight to MSPB) and no deadline on any of them for USERRA. That combination is nearly unique in employment law. Use it: file with DOL VETS and request OSC referral, and file your own MSPB appeal in parallel to preserve the record — there is no penalty for doing both, and OSC declining to represent you does not end your case.
items.deadline: No USERRA statute of limitations

items.title: Reserve retirement — what a 'good year' actually is, and the 50-point floor
items.who: Guard and Reserve members
items.value: Non-regular (reserve) retirement under 10 U.S.C. Chapter 1223 requires 20 qualifying years of service. A year 'qualifies' (a 'good year') when you earn at least 50 retirement points in your anniversary/retirement year.
items.how: Points are earned as: 1 point per drill period (a standard drill weekend is 4 periods = 4 points); 1 point per day of active duty or active duty for training; 15 membership points per year automatically; plus points for correspondence/distance-learning courses and funeral honors duty, subject to annual caps on non-active-duty points. Track them on your annual Retirement Points Accounting Statement (ARPC Form 249-E for Air Force/Space Force, NGB Form 23 for Army Guard, or the service equivalent).
items.hack: Audit the points statement EVERY year, not at year 19. The two most common defects — a drill weekend never posted, or a short active-duty tour never credited — take ten minutes to fix in the same year and become nearly impossible to reconstruct a decade later. A single year that lands at 49 points instead of 50 is a bad year, and one bad year can mean an extra year of drilling to reach 20.
items.deadline: Review the points statement annually within the retirement/anniversary year

items.title: How retirement points convert to retired pay — the actual formula
items.who: Guard and Reserve retirees
items.value: Reserve retired pay = (total career retirement points ÷ 360) × multiplier × high-36 average basic pay. The multiplier is 2.5% per equivalent year under the legacy High-3 system and 2.0% per equivalent year under the Blended Retirement System. The 'high-36' is the average of your highest 36 months of basic pay at the pay grade and longevity you would have held — not what you were actually paid on drill status.
items.how: Divide lifetime points by 360 to get 'equivalent years of active service.' A 20-year reservist with 3,600 points has 10 equivalent years; at 2.5% that is a 25% multiplier applied to high-36 basic pay.
items.hack: Every additional point is money for life. 360 extra points over a career is one extra equivalent year — worth 2.5% of high-36 basic pay every month from age 60 (or your reduced age) until death, plus survivor benefit implications. Volunteer for the extra school, the extra ADT, the correspondence courses, the funeral honors — within the annual caps. And take the promotion late in your career even if it means more years: the high-36 is set by the highest 36 months, so a final promotion can lift the whole annuity.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: Reduced-age reserve retirement — 10 U.S.C. 12731(f), three months off for every 90 days
items.who: Ready Reserve members who performed qualifying active duty after January 28, 2008
items.value: For every 90 AGGREGATE days of qualifying active service performed in a single fiscal year, the age at which reserve retired pay begins is reduced by three months. The eligibility age cannot be reduced below age 50, and the 20-year service requirement still applies.
items.how: Qualifying service includes active duty under 10 U.S.C. 12301(d) and 12304b, and full-time National Guard duty under 32 U.S.C. 502(f) performed in response to a national emergency declared by the President or supported by federal funds, plus certain Coast Guard emergency augmentation duty. Service performed after January 28, 2008 counts; days are aggregated within a fiscal year (for fiscal years after September 30, 2014, aggregation may span consecutive fiscal years under the current rule).
items.hack: The aggregation is by FISCAL YEAR (October 1–September 30), which means a 180-day mobilization that straddles September 30 can split into two chunks of under 90 days and earn you nothing — while the same 180 days timed inside one fiscal year earns six months off your retirement age. If you have any influence over report dates, look at the calendar. Then: pull your own orders, count the days by fiscal year yourself, and submit the credit request. The services do not reliably compute this for you, and members routinely reach age 60 without ever claiming years of earned reduction.
items.deadline: Claim before age 60; keep every set of orders

items.title: Gray Area Retiree — what you have between 20 years and age 60
items.who: Reserve and Guard members who have completed 20 qualifying years and transferred to the Retired Reserve but are not yet drawing retired pay
items.value: You are retirement-eligible but unpaid. What you DO have: a DD Form 2 (Reserve Retired) identification card; eligibility to purchase TRICARE Retired Reserve; commissary, exchange and MWR privileges; Space-A travel (Category VI); SBP election rights; and continued access to milConnect/DEERS for you and your dependents. What you do NOT have: retired pay, TRICARE Prime/Select, or TRICARE For Life, until you reach age 60 or your reduced age.
items.how: Request your Notice of Eligibility (the '20-year letter') and keep the original forever — it is the document that proves entitlement at 60. Apply for retired pay through your service's reserve personnel center roughly 6–9 months before your pay-eligibility date; pay does NOT start automatically.
items.hack: Two failures dominate gray-area retirements. First, people forget to apply and lose months of retired pay — there is no automatic start. Second, the SBP election at the 20-year letter stage is a decision with a 90-day window and lifelong consequences; declining requires spousal concurrence and cannot simply be undone later. Calendar both. And keep DEERS addresses current for 20 years, because that is how the service finds you at 60.
items.deadline: SBP election window at receipt of the 20-year letter; apply for retired pay ~6–9 months before your pay-eligibility age

items.title: TRICARE Reserve Select 2026 premiums — $57.88 member-only, $286.66 member-and-family
items.who: Selected Reserve members not on active duty orders for more than 30 days and not eligible for (or enrolled in) the Federal Employees Health Benefits program
items.value: For January 1 – December 31, 2026, TRICARE Reserve Select monthly premiums are $57.88 for member-only coverage and $286.66 for member-and-family. This remains, by a wide margin, the least expensive comprehensive family health plan available to a working American family.
items.how: Purchase through milConnect (Beneficiary Web Enrollment) or by submitting DD Form 2896-1. Coverage operates like TRICARE Select — you may see any TRICARE-authorized provider, with cost-shares.
items.hack: The FEHB disqualifier is the trap: a Guard/Reserve member who takes a federal civilian job and enrolls in FEHB loses TRS eligibility — and FEHB family premiums routinely run 8–15 times the TRS family premium. If you are a drilling reservist entering federal service, price TRS against FEHB before you elect anything during your new-hire window. Also, a technician position may force FEHB; ask before you accept.
items.deadline: Premiums set annually on a calendar-year basis; qualifying life events open enrollment windows

items.title: TRICARE Retired Reserve 2026 premiums — $645.90 member-only, $1,548.30 member-and-family
items.who: Gray area retirees — members of the Retired Reserve under age 60 who are not eligible for FEHB
items.value: For January 1 – December 31, 2026, TRICARE Retired Reserve monthly premiums are $645.90 member-only and $1,548.30 member-and-family. Coverage ends when you become eligible for retired pay at age 60 (or your reduced age), at which point you move to TRICARE Prime or Select.
items.how: Purchase through milConnect or DD Form 2896-1 after transferring to the Retired Reserve.
items.hack: TRR is expensive because it is unsubsidized — the member pays the full cost. Do the comparison honestly: a gray-area retiree with employer coverage or an ACA marketplace plan with a subsidy often does better than TRR, and a gray-area retiree with a chronic condition or a large family often does much better with TRR. The one thing not to do is default into TRR without pricing the alternatives, or let coverage lapse and then find TRR unavailable. Note the enormous jump from TRS ($286.66 family) to TRR ($1,548.30 family) — plan for it in the year you leave the Selected Reserve.
items.deadline: Calendar-year premiums; coverage ends at retired-pay eligibility

items.title: Pre-activation TRICARE — coverage starting up to 180 days BEFORE you report
items.who: Guard and Reserve members who receive delayed-effective-date active duty orders for more than 30 days or in support of a contingency operation, and their family members
items.value: Active-duty TRICARE benefits begin on the LATER of the date the orders are issued or 180 days before you report to active duty — not on the day you report. Family members become eligible at the same time.
items.how: Ensure your unit updates DEERS with the delayed-effective-date orders as soon as they are cut. Within 50 miles/one hour of a military hospital or clinic you can enroll in TRICARE Prime with a military PCM; remote members cannot enroll in Prime Remote during pre-activation but can see any TRICARE-authorized provider with regional-contractor pre-authorization for specialty care.
items.hack: This is up to six months of free family health coverage that members throw away because nobody tells them the orders themselves trigger it. The moment you have delayed-effective-date orders in hand, check milConnect to confirm DEERS reflects them and drop your civilian plan if TRICARE is better. Caveat: if the orders are cancelled before you report, eligibility ends the same day the orders are cancelled — so do not cancel a civilian plan you cannot re-enter.
items.deadline: Up to 180 days before the report date; ends immediately if orders are cancelled

items.title: TAMP — 180 days of premium-free TRICARE after deactivation
items.who: Guard and Reserve members separating from active duty of more than 30 consecutive days in support of a contingency operation, and their families
items.value: The Transitional Assistance Management Program provides 180 days of premium-free TRICARE coverage beginning the day after active duty ends. During TAMP you and your family may use TRICARE Prime (where available) or TRICARE Select.
items.how: TAMP eligibility is established by your separation orders in DEERS. Verify in milConnect on the day you demobilize, and re-enroll in a plan during TAMP — coverage is not automatic in every plan option.
items.hack: Sequence TRS to start on day 181, not day 1. Members routinely buy TRICARE Reserve Select the month they demobilize and pay six months of premiums for coverage they already had for free. Set a calendar reminder for day 150 to purchase TRS so there is no gap and no overlap. If you are leaving the Selected Reserve entirely, day 181 is also when CHCBP becomes the fallback.
items.deadline: 180 days from the day after active duty ends

items.title: Line of Duty determinations and Incapacitation Pay — the paperwork that makes or breaks a Guard/Reserve VA claim
items.who: Guard and Reserve members injured or who become ill during active duty for training (ACDUTRA) or inactive duty training (INACDUTRA)
items.value: An approved Line of Duty (LOD) determination is the document that establishes the injury or illness was incurred or aggravated in the line of duty. Without it, VA service connection for an injury sustained on a drill weekend is extraordinarily difficult. Incapacitation Pay (INCAP) separately compensates a member who cannot perform military duties, or who loses civilian earned income, because of an in-line-of-duty injury or illness.
items.how: Report the injury to your chain of command IMMEDIATELY and in writing — before you leave the drill floor if possible. Insist that an LOD investigation be opened. Get seen and get the treatment documented, even at a civilian ER, and get the records into the LOD packet. Apply for INCAP through your unit's personnel/medical section with the LOD, medical documentation of the inability to perform, and — for the lost-civilian-income component — proof of civilian earnings.
items.hack: This is the single biggest structural disadvantage Guard and Reserve members face in the VA system. An active-duty soldier's injury is documented automatically in the service medical record; a drilling reservist's is documented only if someone opens an LOD. Members go home, treat it as a civilian injury on their own insurance, and twenty years later have no way to service-connect it. Rule: any injury on any military status gets reported in writing the same day, every time, no exceptions — even a minor one. And if an LOD was denied or never opened, LOD determinations can be appealed and corrected years later through the service's Board for Correction of Military Records.
items.deadline: Report immediately; LOD corrections via BCMR generally within 3 years of discovery, with waiver available

items.title: VA eligibility for Guard members who never federalized — the rule, precisely
items.who: National Guard and Reserve members whose entire career was drills, annual training and state duty, with no Title 10 active duty
items.value: The precise answer, because this is the most confused topic in veterans benefits.
items.how: The general rule: 'active military, naval, air, or space service' under 38 U.S.C. 101(24) means (a) active duty; (b) any period of ACTIVE DUTY FOR TRAINING during which the individual was disabled or died from a disease or injury incurred or aggravated in line of duty; and (c) any period of INACTIVE DUTY TRAINING during which the individual was disabled or died from an injury (or from an acute MI, cardiac arrest, or cerebrovascular accident) incurred or aggravated in line of duty. So: a Guard member with no Title 10 time is NOT a 'veteran' for most VA purposes — no VA health care enrollment on service alone, no VA pension, no Post-9/11 GI Bill on that service. BUT if you were injured on a drill weekend or at annual training and it is documented in an approved LOD, that specific period becomes qualifying service and you can be service-connected for that disability — which then brings VA health care for the condition and, at a compensable rating, the rest of the compensation system.
items.hack: Two exceptions Guard members constantly miss. (1) VA HOME LOAN: under Public Law 116-315 (effective January 5, 2021, and RETROACTIVE regardless of service dates), a National Guard member qualifies with at least 90 cumulative days of full-time National Guard duty under 32 U.S.C. 316, 502, 503, 504 or 505, of which at least 30 were consecutive — excluding inactive duty and initial training. Guard members previously denied a COE should reapply. (2) POST-9/11 GI BILL: Title 32 502(f) full-time National Guard duty performed in response to a Presidentially declared national emergency and supported by federal funds DOES count toward Chapter 33 eligibility. COVID-19 mobilizations under 502(f) are the common case, and many Guard members never applied.
items.deadline: Home loan COE change is retroactive — reapply at any time

items.title: Title 10 vs Title 32 vs State Active Duty — what each status actually buys you
items.who: National Guard members
items.value: Your duty status determines your pay source, your legal command, your federal benefits, your GI Bill tier and your employment protections. Three statuses, three different answers.
items.how: TITLE 10 (federal active duty, federal pay, federal command): counts as active duty for VA purposes; builds Post-9/11 GI Bill entitlement at standard rates; counts toward the 20-year federal retirement and toward reduced-age retirement; full USERRA protection; active-duty TRICARE; may build 'veteran' status. TITLE 32 (full-time National Guard duty, FEDERAL pay, STATE command under the Governor): counts for the VA home loan under the 90/30 rule; counts for Post-9/11 GI Bill when performed under 32 U.S.C. 502(f) in response to a Presidentially declared national emergency supported by federal funds; counts for reduced-age retirement under 12731(f) for 502(f) national-emergency service; full USERRA protection. STATE ACTIVE DUTY (state pay, state command, Governor's order): generally builds NO federal benefit entitlement; USERRA protection only where the 2021 amendment applies (14+ days, or supporting a Presidential national emergency, or a Stafford Act major disaster).
items.hack: When you are offered a mission, ask ONE question before you volunteer: 'Is this Title 10, Title 32, or State Active Duty?' The same 90 days of hurricane response can be worth federal retirement credit, GI Bill entitlement and a VA home loan — or worth nothing but the paycheck — depending entirely on which statute the orders cite. Read the authority line on the orders and keep a copy of every set for your entire career.
items.deadline: N/A — but keep every set of orders permanently

items.title: MGIB-Selected Reserve (Chapter 1606) — current rates and the six-year obligation
items.who: Selected Reserve members with a six-year service obligation who completed initial active duty for training and remain in good standing in a drilling unit
items.value: Effective October 1, 2025 through September 30, 2026: $493.00 per month full-time; $369.00 three-quarter time; $246.00 half time; $123.25 less than half time, for institutions of higher learning and non-college degree programs.
items.how: Apply through VA (VA Form 22-1990) and have your unit certify the six-year obligation via a DD Form 2384-1 Notice of Basic Eligibility (NOBE). Benefits stop if you leave the Selected Reserve.
items.hack: Chapter 1606 is use-it-while-you-drill money — entitlement generally ends when you leave the Selected Reserve, so an unused balance at separation is usually lost. Reservists who also qualify for Post-9/11 GI Bill through Title 10 mobilization should burn Chapter 1606 FIRST while drilling and preserve Chapter 33, which never expires under the Forever GI Bill. Getting this order backwards costs thousands.
items.deadline: Entitlement generally ends on separation from the Selected Reserve; rates set each October 1

items.title: Chapter 1607 REAP — dead since 2015, and what replaced it
items.who: Guard and Reserve members who were mobilized post-9/11
items.value: Closing out a benefit that still appears on many guides. The FY2016 National Defense Authorization Act ENDED the Reserve Educational Assistance Program on November 25, 2015. Members already attending school on or before November 24, 2015 could continue to receive benefits only through November 25, 2019. No new eligibility has been available since November 25, 2015, and no entitlement remains.
items.how: If you were REAP-eligible, your mobilization almost certainly makes you Post-9/11 GI Bill (Chapter 33) eligible instead, usually at a higher benefit level. Apply for Chapter 33 with VA Form 22-1990 and provide the mobilization orders.
items.hack: Do not let a school certifying official or an outdated benefits guide send you looking for REAP. The practical question for a mobilized reservist today is always Chapter 33 versus Chapter 1606 versus Chapter 30, and the Rudisill decision may let you use more than one in sequence. REAP is not on the menu and has not been for a decade.
items.deadline: Program ended November 25, 2015; final use deadline was November 25, 2019

items.title: State tuition assistance for National Guard members — the benefit that beats the GI Bill
items.who: Drilling National Guard members, in the state where they drill
items.value: Most states fund a tuition waiver, tuition assistance or scholarship program for their Guard members at state institutions. Structures vary enormously: full tuition waivers at state schools (Texas, Colorado, New Jersey and several others operate waiver or free-tuition programs), fixed dollar caps per semester, or percentage-of-tuition assistance. Because it is state money, it does NOT consume federal GI Bill entitlement.
items.how: Apply through your state's National Guard Education Services Office — not through VA and not through the school's VA certifying official. Most programs require a service obligation, continued satisfactory participation, and application before the term begins.
items.hack: This is the highest-leverage move in the entire Guard benefit stack: use STATE tuition assistance plus federal military Tuition Assistance for your undergraduate degree, and preserve 36 months of Post-9/11 GI Bill entirely untouched for graduate school — or transfer it to a child. Guard members who burn Chapter 33 on an in-state bachelor's degree that the state would have paid for are giving away a benefit worth six figures. Ask the state education office for the stacking rules in writing; many states allow state TA to pay what federal TA does not.
items.deadline: Per-term application deadlines set by the state education office, usually well before the term starts

items.title: Space-A travel for Guard, Reserve and gray-area retirees — Category VI and the DD Form 1853
items.who: Selected Reserve and Ready Reserve members in good standing; gray-area retirees (Retired Reserve members not yet drawing retired pay)
items.value: Free travel on military aircraft on a space-available basis. Drilling Guard and Reserve members travel in Category VI, generally limited to travel within the continental United States and to, from and between Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands and American Samoa. Gray-area retirees also travel in Category VI.
items.how: Drilling members need a DD Form 1853 (Verification of Reserve Status for Travel) signed by the unit, plus the military ID. Gray-area retirees travel on the DD Form 2 (Reserve Retired). Sign up (register) for flights through the AMC passenger terminal Facebook pages or the AMC travel page, up to 60 days out; there is no reservation and no guarantee.
items.hack: Get the DD Form 1853 signed at your next drill and keep a current one in your travel bag — terminals will not take an expired one, and you cannot get one signed at 0400 at Baltimore-Washington on a Saturday. Also: gray-area retirees at Category VI do far better flying out of smaller terminals than the big ones, and mid-week beats weekends. Category VI is the bottom of the priority list; treat every Space-A trip as a bonus, never as the way home.
items.deadline: Register up to 60 days before travel; DD Form 1853 validity is limited — renew at drill

items.title: Commissary, exchange and MWR for Guard, Reserve and retirees — who gets in
items.who: Selected Reserve and Ready Reserve members, Retired Reserve (gray area) members, and — since January 1, 2020 — a much broader group of veterans
items.value: Drilling Guard and Reserve members and their dependents have unlimited commissary, exchange and MWR privileges on the military ID. Gray-area retirees retain those privileges on the DD Form 2 (Reserve Retired). Separately, since January 1, 2020, commissary, exchange and MWR access was extended to all veterans with a VA-documented service-connected disability rating (0%–100%), Purple Heart recipients, former prisoners of war, and primary family caregivers approved under VA's Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers.
items.how: Drilling and gray-area members: military ID. Veterans under the 2020 expansion: a Veteran Health Identification Card (VHIC) displaying 'PURPLE HEART,' 'FORMER POW' or 'SERVICE CONNECTED.' Veterans rated 0% who are ineligible for a VHIC because of income may use VA Form H623A together with a REAL ID-compliant driver's license or passport. Caregivers use a VA Office of Community Care eligibility letter plus an acceptable credential.
items.hack: The VHIC is the key and most eligible veterans do not have one, or have an old one that does not show the eligibility line. Request a new VHIC through your VA medical center's enrollment office and specifically confirm it will print the 'SERVICE CONNECTED' legend — a card without that legend will be turned away at the gate even if your rating is 70%. Gray-area retirees should also confirm their DD Form 2 is current; expired cards are refused.
items.deadline: N/A

items.title: ASVAB line scores decide which jobs you are even allowed to want
items.who: Anyone considering enlistment; anyone planning to retest
items.value: The AFQT percentile only decides whether you can enlist. The composite line scores (VE, AR, MK, GS, EI, AS, MC, AO, and the service-specific composites built from them) decide which rate, MOS or AFSC you qualify for. A 20-point swing in one subtest is the difference between a nuclear or cryptologic pipeline and a general-detail job.
items.how: Take the full ASVAB, not just a practice AFQT. Pull the qualification standards for the two or three jobs you actually want and work backward to the subtests those composites use. Study those subtests specifically: Arithmetic Reasoning and Mathematics Knowledge for technical rates, General Science and Electronics Information for electronics and nuclear, Mechanical Comprehension and Auto & Shop for engineering and maintenance ratings.
items.hack: Do not let the recruiter tell you what you qualify for and then pick from that list. Walk in with the job you want already chosen, ask what line score it needs, and if you are short, retest before you sign anything. Once you sign a contract for a rate you settled for, you have bought your next six years and, functionally, your civilian resume for the twenty years after that. Retesting is free. A wrong rate is not.
items.deadline: Before signing an enlistment contract. Retest rules vary; a one-month wait after a first retest is typical.

items.title: How to actually prepare for the ASVAB (and what the PiCAT is)
items.who: Pre-enlistment candidates and DEP members
items.value: Six to eight weeks of focused arithmetic and vocabulary work routinely moves an AFQT by 15-25 percentile points and opens technical pipelines with enlistment bonuses and civilian-portable credentials attached.
items.how: Work the math sections by hand with no calculator, because the test does not allow one. Drill word problems, fractions, ratios, percentages and basic algebra daily. Read anything dense for the Word Knowledge and Paragraph Comprehension sections. Ask your recruiter about the PiCAT, an unproctored full-length version taken at home with a short in-person verification test; if your verification confirms the score, you are done.
items.hack: The technical subtests are the ones almost nobody studies, and they are the ones that gate the good jobs. Everybody grinds the AFQT math. Spend two of your eight weeks on Electronics Information, Mechanical Comprehension and Auto & Shop, from a library book if you have to, and you will outscore people who are smarter than you on exactly the composites that matter.
items.deadline: Before your scheduled MEPS test date

items.title: Delayed Entry Program: the free head start almost everyone wastes
items.org: All services (Navy DEP; Army Future Soldier Program; Air Force/Space Force DEP; Marine Corps Delayed Entry/Poolee program; Coast Guard DEP)
items.who: Anyone who has signed a contract but not yet shipped
items.value: Weeks to a full year of paid-nothing, risk-nothing time in which you can arrive at boot camp physically ahead, academically ahead, and already known to your recruiting chain as someone who shows up.
items.how: Attend every DEP or poolee function, not the minimum. Show up to the physical training sessions. Learn the rank structure, the chain of command, the general orders, the creed and the customs and courtesies cold. Get your paperwork, dependency documentation, and any waivers cleaned up now, not at the gate.
items.hack: Show up to boot camp already able to max the initial physical fitness assessment and already able to recite the rank structure and the creed, and you will get picked as a recruit division leader or equivalent in the first week. That is the first line in your record and the first performance evaluation of your career, and it was decided before you got off the bus. The people who cruise DEP arrive as the guy getting corrected in front of the division.
items.deadline: Your ship date

items.title: Arrive at boot camp fit, not planning to get fit at boot camp
items.who: DEP members and poolees
items.value: Injury is the single largest cause of boot camp attrition and of the medical holds that push a ship date back by months. Arriving fit also protects your knees, back and shoulders, which are the joints you will be filing VA claims about in twenty years.
items.how: Build a base of running volume in actual running shoes over at least eight weeks before you ship, not two. Train the events your branch tests: push-ups, plank or curl-ups, the 1.5-mile or 2-mile run, and swim qualification for Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard. Learn to swim before you show up if you cannot.
items.hack: Do not go to boot camp with an untreated injury and do not hide one. Get it documented and treated on the civilian side before you ship, because anything already in your record at entry becomes a pre-existing condition argument the VA can use against you later, while anything that first appears on active duty is service-connected by default. Ten minutes at a civilian clinic before you ship is worth more than a year of appeals at the end.
items.deadline: Ongoing until ship date

items.title: Choose the rate, MOS or AFSC for who you will be at 38, not who you are at 18
items.who: Anyone selecting a job at enlistment, converting, or reenlisting into a new field
items.value: Your occupational specialty is the single highest-leverage decision of your military career. It determines your advancement odds, your sea or deployment rotation, your clearance, whether you can pick up a nationally recognized civilian credential on the government's dime, and what a hiring manager sees on your resume two decades later.
items.how: For each rate you are considering, look up three things: the current advancement opportunity for that community, the civilian occupations and licenses it maps to, and whether it has a formal apprenticeship or credentialing path. Run every candidate rate through the COOL portal for your branch and look at the credential list attached to it.
items.hack: There are two kinds of military jobs: the ones where the civilian world already has a licensing board that recognizes what you did, and the ones where you have to explain yourself for the rest of your life. Electronics, IT and cyber, nuclear, aviation maintenance, HM and corpsman-adjacent medical, electrician, welding, machinist, logistics with a certification behind it, and anything that hands you a clearance are all the first kind. If a recruiter is pushing you toward an undesignated or general-detail path because it ships fastest, that is a quota problem, not your career plan.
items.deadline: At contract signing; again at conversion or reenlistment windows

items.title: Read the contract, and get every promise in the annex
items.who: Anyone about to sign at MEPS
items.value: Guaranteed A-School or guaranteed MOS, enlistment bonuses, advanced paygrade for prior credits or JROTC or Eagle Scout, and duty-station or program guarantees are only real if they are written into the enlistment document and annexes.
items.how: Read the DD Form 4 and every annex before signing. Ask specifically which of your guarantees are contractual and which are conditional on training pipeline performance. Get your own copy of every page before you leave the building and keep it forever.
items.hack: If it is not in the annex, it did not happen. Recruiters rotate, get promoted, and get orders. In three years the person who promised you a school verbally will not be reachable and will not remember. Ask for the annex, photograph every page on your phone before you leave MEPS, and email it to yourself. That five-minute habit is the same habit that wins VA claims twenty years later.
items.deadline: Before signing

items.title: Treat a security clearance as compensation
items.who: Anyone choosing a rate or a follow-on billet
items.value: An active Secret or Top Secret with SCI eligibility is worth a substantial salary premium in the civilian market and is the entry ticket to the entire cleared contracting world. Clearances lapse, typically becoming reinstatable within roughly 24 months of separation depending on the level and current policy.
items.how: Choose a rate that requires a clearance, keep your financial and legal record clean because finances are the most common disqualifier, complete the investigation and any periodic reinvestigation on time, and know your clearance level, investigation date and adjudication date well enough to put them on a resume.
items.hack: Debt and unreported foreign contacts kill more clearances than anything dramatic. Do not co-sign for anybody in your barracks, do not let a collection go to judgment, and self-report before someone else reports for you. And time your separation: leaving with a current investigation and a clean adjudication means a contractor can hire you immediately, while letting it go cold for two years means you are competing with people who did not.
items.deadline: Ongoing; clearance currency matters most in the 24 months around separation

items.title: Boot camp: the goal is not to survive it, it is to be noticed in it
items.org: Navy Recruit Training Command Great Lakes; Army BCT; Marine Corps Recruit Depot; Air Force BMT; Coast Guard Cape May
items.who: All new enlistees
items.value: Recruit training produces your first documented performance record, your first leadership billet if you earn one, honor graduate or equivalent recognition, and in several branches an early meritorious advancement.
items.how: Volunteer for the recruit leadership billets. Be the one who knows the material, helps the person who is failing, and never has to be told twice. Pass every academic and practical test on the first attempt. Qualify at swim, weapons and firefighting or the branch equivalents without remediation.
items.hack: Be the person who quietly makes the whole division better and you will be the honor graduate. Be the person who makes themselves look good and the recruit division commanders will see it in a week and so will your shipmates. One of those two people shows up to a first command with a meritorious advancement and a reputation. The other shows up with stories.
items.deadline: 7-13 weeks depending on branch

items.title: A-School: class standing is an asset you spend later
items.org: Navy Training Commands / NETC; equivalents: Army AIT, Air Force Technical Training, Marine Corps MOS School
items.who: First-term enlisted in the initial technical pipeline
items.value: Class standing frequently drives follow-on C-School selection, first-duty-station choice within the available billets, and eligibility for meritorious advancement. It is also the last time in your career that a straightforward academic ranking directly buys you geography.
items.how: Treat it like a job with graded outputs. Study before you are behind, not after. Get the tech manuals and the practical checkouts done early. Ask instructors which follow-on C-Schools exist for your rate and what standing it took last cycle to get one.
items.hack: Ask your instructors on day three which billets and C-Schools the top three in class have gotten in the last several classes, then decide whether you are willing to study for them. Most of your class will figure this out in the last week, when the list comes out and it is already decided. The distance between first and fifteenth in class is usually about forty minutes a night for two months.
items.deadline: Duration of A-School

items.title: C-School: chase the specialty training, do not wait to be sent
items.org: Navy NETC; equivalents: Army advanced/functional courses and ASI producing schools, Air Force advanced technical training and special experience identifiers
items.who: First-term and mid-career enlisted
items.value: C-School produces a Navy Enlisted Classification code, the Army's additional skill identifier, or the Air Force's special experience identifier. These codes make you the person the detailer has to place in specific billets, drive advancement in tight communities, and are the difference on a resume between a generic maintainer and a named system specialist.
items.how: Find out which NECs or skill identifiers exist in your rate and which are in short supply. Ask your chief and your career counselor what it takes to get quota. Keep your quals, PRT, and eval marks clean, because those are the screens for school quotas.
items.hack: Go find out which NEC in your rate the detailers are short on, then ask for that school by name in writing. Nobody is going to knock on your door and offer you a school. Quotas go to the person the chief thinks of first and the person whose name is already on a list, and you can put yourself on the list with one email. Chase the short-supply code, not the popular one, because short supply is what buys you orders later.
items.deadline: Quota cycles vary by rate and community

items.title: Reporting to your first command: the check-in sheet is your first test
items.who: Anyone reporting to a new unit
items.value: How you check in sets the reputation you will spend the next three years either enjoying or fighting. It also protects you administratively: pay, dependency data, medical and dental readiness, records, and your service record entries all get built or broken in week one.
items.how: Report in the correct uniform, early, with your orders, records, and a copy of everything. Work the check-in sheet aggressively and finish it in days, not weeks. Walk into admin, medical, dental, personnel, the training office and the command career counselor yourself. Verify your pay, your dependency data, your record of emergency data and your beneficiary designations.
items.hack: Finish your check-in sheet in three days when the command expects three weeks, and hand it to the chief signed. You will have done one thing before you have done anything, and every chief in that command will have heard about it by Friday. Then verify your own pay and record entries, because the admin error that costs you six thousand dollars is always found by the person who checked, never by the person who assumed.
items.deadline: First week at a new command

items.title: Use the sponsor program before you arrive
items.who: Anyone with orders in hand
items.value: A sponsor gets you housing intelligence, division-level politics, uniform and gear requirements, and school and family logistics before you land, which prevents the first-month mistakes that define new arrivals.
items.how: Email the command sponsor coordinator as soon as you have orders and ask to be assigned someone in your rate and division. Ask specifically: what does the division actually do, who are the key players, which quals should I start studying now, what gear will I need, and what is the housing situation.
items.hack: Ask your sponsor for the qualification card or PQS for the watch station you will stand, and start studying it before you report. Showing up already knowing the plant, the system or the aircraft well enough to ask an intelligent question puts you six months ahead of your peers on the day you walk in, and getting qualified first is the whole game in your first year.
items.deadline: As soon as orders are received

items.title: A mentor and a champion are different people, and you need both
items.who: Everyone, from day one
items.value: A mentor teaches you. A champion spends their own credibility on you in rooms you are not in. Mentorship improves your performance; a champion is what converts performance into selection, quota, and orders.
items.how: For mentors, ask people one to three paygrades above you specific questions and come back with what you did about the answer. For champions, do visible, hard, well-documented work for a senior leader who has a vote, then keep them informed without being asked. Have several of each, in different chains, and keep them for the rest of your career.
items.hack: Your mentor can be anybody who will talk to you. Your champion has to be somebody who sits on boards and whose name carries in the community, and you cannot ask for one, you can only earn one. The test is simple: when your name comes up for a school quota or a meritorious board and you are not in the room, who argues for you? If the answer is nobody, you have mentors and no champion, and you will watch less capable people get selected.
items.deadline: Ongoing; start in your first year

items.title: Get qualified faster than anyone expects you to
items.org: Your command; PQS, warfare qualification and watch station programs
items.who: First-term enlisted, and anyone at a new command
items.value: Quals are the objective currency of a command. They gate watchbill standing, collateral duties, eval ranking, warfare devices, meritorious advancement boards, and the trust that gets you the good jobs. Being first to qualify in your check-in group is a permanent label.
items.how: Get the PQS or qualification card on day one. Schedule your own signatures, chase the qualified watchstanders, and get your board scheduled instead of waiting for it. Then immediately start on the next station up and on the warfare device, whether that is ESWS, EAWS, the submarine or expeditionary equivalents, or your branch's readiness badge.
items.hack: Nobody is going to schedule your qualification board for you. Walk up to the qualified petty officer during the watch, have the card out, and ask for the line item you already know cold. Get it signed on the spot. Do that for six weeks and you will be qualified while your check-in group is still asking who signs their cards, and you will be on the watchbill in a paid, trusted seat while they are still standing messenger.
items.deadline: As fast as the program allows; typically within the first 6-12 months

items.title: Become the subject-matter expert on something the command needs
items.who: Enlisted at any paygrade
items.value: Being the only person who can fix, run or explain a specific system makes you indispensable, which converts directly to eval marks, awards, school quotas and the ability to ask for things and get them.
items.how: Pick the system, program or process in your division that is important, technically annoying, and currently owned by nobody. Read the actual technical manual and the governing instruction, not the turnover notes. Build the reference the next person will use. Then teach it.
items.hack: Pick the thing everybody complains about and nobody owns, and own it completely. In six months the wardroom will know your name because you are the answer to a question they keep asking. That is worth more than five collateral duties. But write down everything you learn while you learn it, because expertise you cannot hand off makes you unpromotable, not indispensable.
items.deadline: Ongoing

items.title: Collateral duties: which ones actually move a record
items.org: Your command; command-wide programs assigned by instruction
items.who: Enlisted building toward boards and advancement
items.value: Command-wide collateral duties that are formally assigned by the command's organizational instruction, are inspected by an outside body, and have a measurable output are the ones that score on boards and read well on an eval. Everything else is time.
items.how: Ask to be formally assigned in writing, with your name in the command's organization and regulations manual or equivalent appointment letter. Favor programs that get inspected or assessed: safety, training and records, 3-M or maintenance management, hazardous material, urinalysis, command fitness leader, career development team, damage control training team, command assessment or climate teams, security and key control, financial specialist and voting assistance with a real audit behind them.
items.hack: Two well-run, formally appointed, inspected collateral duties beat seven side jobs you got volunteered for at quarters. Boards score verified command-wide appointments, so if your name is not in the instruction and there is no appointment letter in your record, on paper you did not do it. Get the letter, put a copy in your binder, and get a measurable result you can put a number on: a zero-discrepancy inspection, a percentage improvement, a dollar figure, a number of people trained.
items.deadline: Ongoing; establish before the board cycle you are targeting

items.title: The collateral duties to say no to, carefully
items.who: Anyone already carrying a full load
items.value: An overloaded person who does eight collateral duties at 60 percent gets a mediocre eval. A person who does two at 100 percent and can prove it gets ranked.
items.how: When handed a new collateral, ask what the deliverable is, who inspects it, and what you should stop doing to make room. If there is no inspection, no deliverable and no appointment letter, it is labor, not career development. Negotiate rather than refuse: offer to take it after the current inspection closes, or trade one you already have.
items.hack: The honest answer is that you cannot refuse a tasking, but you can ask one question that changes the conversation: which of my current programs do you want me to hand off to make room for this one? That is not insubordination, it is workload management, and a good chief will respect it. A chief who cannot answer it was just filling a square on a spreadsheet, and now they know you know.
items.deadline: Ongoing

items.title: Balancing work, self and family without losing any of the three
items.org: Military OneSource; Fleet and Family Support Centers and branch equivalents
items.who: Everyone, especially first-term and first-deployment
items.value: The people who burn out or lose a marriage in their first enlistment do not get to have the twenty-year career they planned. Sustainability is a career strategy, not a soft topic.
items.how: Protect a fixed, non-negotiable block of family and personal time each week and defend it like a watch. Use the free counseling available through Military OneSource, which is confidential and non-medical. Take your leave; do not carry a balance you will lose. Get your family enrolled, informed and connected to the ombudsman or family readiness group before the first deployment, not during it.
items.hack: Take your leave. Sailors sit on 60 days of leave to prove something, then lose it, then wonder why they are exhausted at year eight. Nobody at your retirement ceremony is going to mention your leave balance. And use the non-medical counseling early, because it is confidential and it is not a mental health record; the time to learn that distinction is before you need it, not after.
items.deadline: Ongoing; use-or-lose leave typically resets at the end of the fiscal year

items.title: The 33% rule: peers, seniors, juniors, in thirds
items.who: Everyone, at every paygrade
items.value: A deliberate structure for the time you spend on other people. One third with peers who are better than you and will push you, one third with people senior to you who will teach and sponsor you, and one third teaching people junior to you. Iron sharpens iron. The third you teach is the one that actually proves you understand the material and the one leadership notices.
items.how: Audit a normal week honestly and see where the time actually goes; almost everybody finds they spend 90 percent of it with peers at the same level and no structure. Then build the other two thirds in on purpose: a standing question to a mentor, a study group with peers who outperform you, and a junior you are personally getting qualified.
items.hack: The uncomfortable part is the peer third. If you are the most capable person in your circle, you are not the standout, you are stuck. Go find the peers who make you feel a step behind and attach yourself to them, even when it stings. And take the teaching third seriously, because the fastest way to get a reputation as a leader before you have the rank is to have three juniors who got qualified because of you and who say so.
items.deadline: Ongoing

items.title: Pareto's 80/20 applied to a military career
items.who: Everyone, especially people who feel busy and unrewarded
items.value: Roughly 20 percent of what you do produces 80 percent of your record. Identifying that 20 percent and protecting it is the difference between being busy and being promoted.
items.how: Look at the last three evaluations in your division that were ranked at the top and identify what those people actually did. It is usually a very short list: qualified early and completely, ran one or two inspected command-wide programs with measurable results, finished a warfare device, held a high physical readiness score, completed visible professional military education or a degree, and won a board. Then map your week against that list.
items.hack: Read the eval bullets of the person who got ranked number one in your division last cycle. Those bullets are the answer key. Almost none of them describe the things that ate your week. If your week is full of work that will never generate a bullet, you are working hard in a direction nobody scores. Fix the ratio before the cycle closes, not after you read your eval.
items.deadline: Review each evaluation cycle

items.title: The rolling brag sheet, updated weekly from day one
items.who: Everyone, starting the week you report aboard
items.value: Evaluations, award recommendations, board packages, commissioning applications, resumes and VA claims all draw on the same raw material: a dated, quantified list of what you did. People who keep one write their own evals. People who do not get whatever their supervisor can remember from the last six weeks.
items.how: Keep one running file, in a format you will actually open, with one dated line per accomplishment. Write each line with a number in it: quantity, dollar value, percentage, hours saved, people trained, discrepancies closed, inspection result. Add to it weekly, not monthly. Include the names of the people who witnessed or benefited, because those are your future endorsers.
items.hack: Reconstructing five years of accomplishments the week before an eval is how people lose promotions. Your chief has eleven people and a deadline; the one who hands over twelve quantified bullets on a clean page gets those bullets in the eval, and the one who says just put whatever you think gets three vague lines and a middle ranking. Fifteen minutes every Friday for four years will outperform talent. Put a recurring calendar reminder on Friday afternoon and treat it like a watch turnover.
items.deadline: Weekly, forever

items.title: Build the I-love-me binder, in paper and in the cloud
items.who: Everyone
items.value: One place holding every document that proves your career happened: every evaluation, every award and citation, every letter of appreciation and commendation, every certificate of completion and school graduation, appointment letters, qualification letters, PRT and physical fitness results, transcripts, JST, clearance data, orders, contracts, medical documentation and page-13 entries. Personnel systems lose things. Commands disestablish. Records get purged.
items.how: Keep a physical binder with tabbed sections and a scanned copy in at least two places, one of which is not a government system and not a single laptop. Scan everything the day you receive it. Organize chronologically within categories. Bring the relevant tabs to boards, interviews and detailer calls.
items.hack: Assume the official record will be wrong when you need it most, because it will be, and the day you find out is the day a board is looking at it. The person who can produce a signed copy of the award, the appointment letter or the qual letter within an hour wins the argument. The person who says it should be in my record loses it. Scan it the day you get it; do not put it in a pile for later, because later is a moving truck and a deployment.
items.deadline: Continuously; audit annually

items.title: Document everything medically: the highest-value habit in this entire section
items.who: Every service member, from the first week of service
items.value: VA disability compensation, and everything that flows from it including health care priority, dependent education benefits, property tax relief in many states and vocational rehabilitation, is built on evidence of in-service occurrence. Every documented sick call visit, every diagnosis, every complaint entered in the record is future evidence. It costs nothing and it is worth, over a lifetime, hundreds of thousands of dollars.
items.how: Go to sick call and make sure a note is entered every single time something hurts, rings, itches, keeps you awake or does not work right, even when you do not need treatment and do not want a profile. Say out loud that you want it documented. Get copies of your records at every PCS and at least annually, and keep them in your binder. Document the exposures too: noise, jet and engine noise, fuels and solvents, asbestos, burn pits, hazardous material, welding fumes, ionizing radiation, repetitive lifting. At separation, complete the separation physical exhaustively and list every condition, including the ones that seem minor.
items.hack: Every sick call visit you skip because you do not want to look weak is evidence you are handing away. Twenty years from now you will be trying to prove your back, your knees, your hearing, your sleep and your tinnitus started on active duty, and the only thing that will do it is a note somebody typed while you were twenty-two. Tinnitus alone, one sentence in a record, is a lifetime payment. Go to medical, say the words I want this documented, and get a copy for your own file before you leave the building. Nothing else in this section returns as much for as little.
items.deadline: Every occurrence, for your entire career; separation physical is the last chance

items.title: Get your own copies of your medical and dental records, repeatedly
items.who: Everyone; critical at every PCS and before separation
items.value: Records get split between systems, paper and electronic, and between commands, deployed platforms and clinics. Missing in-service records are the most common reason an otherwise valid VA claim fails or takes years.
items.how: Request a complete copy of your health record at each PCS, after every deployment, after any injury or surgery, and at separation. Include dental, hearing conservation audiograms, immunization records, any behavioral health notes you are willing to include, and any line-of-duty determinations. Store them digitally in two places plus paper.
items.hack: Pull your audiograms specifically and keep every one of them. Hearing conservation testing creates a dated, objective trend line, and a shift documented across your career is close to unarguable. Most people never look at them, then argue about their hearing for three years with nothing in hand. Ask for the audiogram history by name; the hearing conservation program has it even when your chart does not.
items.deadline: At every PCS, deployment return, and separation

items.title: Write your own award recommendation and keep it staged
items.org: Your command awards process; branch awards manuals
items.who: Everyone, at every paygrade
items.value: Personal awards score on boards, appear on evaluations, and are permanent. In practice, awards go to the people whose write-up exists, is well written, and can be routed today. Awards that require a busy supervisor to start from a blank page frequently never get written.
items.how: Learn your branch's award format, the summary of action, the citation, and the recommendation form. Draft your own in that exact format, with quantified impact and correct language, then keep it current and ready. When a qualifying event closes, a deployment ends, an inspection is passed, a tour ends or you detach, hand your chief a finished package that needs a signature and a routing sheet, not a writing session.
items.hack: Write your own citation, keep it staged, and hand it to your chief the day the qualifying event closes, because the person who writes it controls how it reads. This feels arrogant the first time and then you watch someone else get the Achievement Medal for the project you ran, because their chief had a draft in hand on Monday and yours was going to get to it. Also write them for your people, unasked, and route them early; that is the same play run for someone else, and it is the fastest way to build the reputation that makes chiefs argue for you.
items.deadline: The day any qualifying period closes; end-of-tour awards route 60-90 days before detaching

items.title: Awards timing: route early, endorse widely, never let one lapse
items.who: Anyone detaching, deploying, or closing a major project
items.value: Awards have submission windows and approval chains. A late package is a downgraded or dead package, and an unwritten end-of-tour award is the most commonly lost career asset in the service.
items.how: Know your command's awards board schedule and the routing timeline. Submit end-of-tour recommendations well before your detachment date, typically two to three months out. Get endorsements from outside your division or department when the work crossed boundaries. Track your submissions and follow up in writing.
items.hack: Nobody is going to chase your end-of-tour award after you detach, because the person who would have signed it now has your relief to worry about. Put your own package in ninety days out and ask your chief every two weeks where it is, politely, in email so there is a trail. Half of all uncollected awards die in the two weeks after somebody leaves.
items.deadline: 60-90 days before detachment; per command awards board cycle

items.title: Read deliberately, and turn dead time into study time
items.org: Chief of Naval Operations Professional Reading Program and branch equivalents; Navy General Library Program
items.who: Everyone; highest return for people standing watch or driving long distances
items.value: A structured reading habit is what separates the senior enlisted leaders who can write, brief and think from the ones who cannot. It is also free, and it is the input that makes your eval bullets, board answers and award write-ups sound like a professional wrote them.
items.how: Build a list from your branch's professional reading program, your community's technical publications, and leadership and communication titles. Use the free library services available to service members and the free audiobook and periodical access those programs carry. Use text-to-speech on your phone for instructions, technical manuals and rate training material.
items.hack: A watch rotation is roughly a thousand hours a year of time you cannot use for anything else. Load the audiobook and the text-to-speech version of your rate training manual and your advancement bibliography onto your phone and you have converted the worst part of your schedule into a degree's worth of study time. The people who advance first are not smarter; they were listening to the bibliography on the mid-watch while everybody else listened to music.
items.deadline: Ongoing

items.title: Work yourself out of a job on purpose
items.who: Anyone who owns a program, watch station or process
items.value: Documenting, simplifying and training your own job away is the single most reliable way to be given a bigger one. The alternative, being the only person who can do it, gets you kept in place while other people get developed.
items.how: For each thing you own, build a turnover binder, a one-page process sheet, and a trained relief. Automate or simplify what is manual. Then tell your leadership the program can be run by someone junior and ask for the next hard problem.
items.hack: Being irreplaceable is a trap, not a compliment. The guy nobody can replace does not get the C-School, does not get the shore billet and does not get the meritorious board, because the command cannot afford to move him. Train your relief to a standard higher than you were trained to, hand your chief a binder and a name, and then ask for the job nobody else wants. That is how you get moved up instead of held in place.
items.deadline: Ongoing; complete before you want your next opportunity

items.title: Take ownership: it is your career and nobody else will chart it
items.who: Everyone
items.value: The services provide programs, counselors, boards and quotas. They do not provide a plan for you specifically. Every person who ends up at fourteen years with no degree, no credential, no warfare device and no path was waiting for somebody to bring them one.
items.how: Write a one-page career plan with dates: target paygrade by year, quals and warfare device by date, degree or credential milestones, NEC or specialty codes, sea and shore rotation, commissioning or conversion decision points, and reenlistment and High Year Tenure gates. Take it to your career development board and your chief. Update it annually and every time you get orders.
items.hack: Show up to your career development board with your own written plan instead of waiting to be asked questions, and the entire dynamic changes; you stop being a record being processed and become a person with a plan that people start helping. Do the same with your detailer. And put the ugly dates on the plan too, the High Year Tenure gate and the reenlistment window, because those are the dates the Navy will enforce whether or not you were paying attention.
items.deadline: Write it now; review annually and at every career development board

items.title: Deployment and geographic separation are the main threat to your marriage
items.org: Fleet and Family Support Centers; Military OneSource; ombudsman and family readiness programs
items.who: Anyone married, partnered, or with children; anyone facing sea duty or unaccompanied orders
items.value: Geographic bachelorhood, back-to-back deployments and duty station churn end more military marriages than anything else, and a divorce at year twelve costs you money, stability, and often the career itself. Managing it is a career skill.
items.how: Before deployment, get the practical things done: powers of attorney, wills, Servicemembers Group Life Insurance beneficiaries, dependency data, access to accounts, a plan for how bills and emergencies get handled, and the ombudsman or family readiness contact in your spouse's phone. Agree in advance on a communication rhythm and what happens when it breaks. Use pre-deployment and return and reunion briefs, and use the free confidential counseling before you are in crisis.
items.hack: Your spouse has a career and a life too, and unaccompanied orders that solve your career problem can end their career and your marriage. Have that conversation before you accept the orders, not after you sign them. And the reintegration month after homecoming is harder than the deployment; plan leave and counseling for that month specifically, because that is where the damage actually happens.
items.deadline: Before each deployment and each set of orders

items.title: Go home. Do not take your family for granted.
items.who: Everyone
items.value: Leave is earned compensation. Relationships with parents, grandparents, siblings and old friends are the support system you will need at the bad points of a twenty-year career and after it, and they do not survive a decade of not showing up.
items.how: Plan and take leave to go home on a schedule, not only when something goes wrong. Use space-available travel where it works, plan around holiday leave periods, and coordinate early with your chief so the timing is not a fight. Call on a schedule, not when you have time.
items.hack: Nobody regrets the leave they took to go home; plenty of people spend the rest of their lives regretting the funeral they made it to instead of the visit they kept postponing. You are going to lose people while you are stationed a thousand miles away, and emergency leave is a terrible way to see your family. Put two trips home on the calendar every year and defend them the way you would defend a duty day.
items.deadline: Ongoing; plan leave a quarter ahead

items.title: The community is small and your reputation arrives before you do
items.who: Everyone
items.value: Rating communities are small enough that the chief at your next command will know someone at your current one. Selection boards, quota decisions and detailing conversations are influenced by phone calls that you will never hear.
items.how: Assume every chief you work for will be asked about you by a future chief. Leave every command with your programs in order, your relief trained, and no unfinished obligations. Keep contact with the good leaders you have worked for; they become your references and your champions.
items.hack: Somebody at your next command is going to call somebody at this one, and the question will not be about your technical skill. It will be some version of would you take him back. Manage your last ninety days at every command like they are your first ninety, because the version of you that people remember is the version that walked out the door, and that is the version that gets described on the phone.
items.deadline: Ongoing; especially the final 90 days at each command

items.title: Volunteer for the hard billet while it is still cheap to do
items.who: First-term and mid-career enlisted
items.value: Deploying units, arduous sea duty, recruiting and instructor duty, independent duty, and high-visibility staff billets produce the awards, evaluations, breadth and stories that selection boards reward. They are far easier to absorb at 22 with no children than at 34 with three.
items.how: Look at what the top of your community's chief and senior chief selectees have in common; it is almost always a deploying tour, a demanding shore tour with visibility, and a leadership billet with people under them. Sequence the hard tours early, then use the easier ones when family needs them.
items.hack: Do the arduous tours in your first eight years, because at that point the only person it costs is you. If you spend your first two tours chasing the comfortable duty station, you will hit the chief board with a record that looks like somebody who avoided things, and by then the hard tour costs your kids a school and your spouse a job. Front-load the pain.
items.deadline: Sequence within the first 8-10 years

items.title: Sailor of the Quarter and Blue Jacket boards: what they really are
items.org: Command; Navy Blue Jacket, Junior Sailor and Sailor of the Quarter/Year programs
items.who: E-1 through E-6, depending on category
items.value: Winning a quarterly board produces a documented achievement, usually a Letter of Commendation or Navy and Marine Corps Achievement Medal, points on later boards, a strong eval bullet, standing for meritorious advancement, and in many commands an automatic look at the annual board. Losing one teaches you exactly what the record is missing.
items.how: Get the command's grading instruction and the actual scoring sheet. Recognize that the hard points are an arithmetic problem you can solve months in advance and the soft points are an interview you can rehearse. Build the record first, then sit the board.
items.hack: The board is not won in the room, it is won six to twelve months earlier when you got the appointment letter, finished the Non-Resident Training Courses, passed the physical readiness test at Excellent or Outstanding, logged the community service hours and completed the professional military education. Ask your chief for the grading sheet today even if you have no intention of sitting a board this quarter, because that sheet is a to-do list with point values on it, and most people never see it until the week they are nominated.
items.deadline: Start building 6-12 months before the quarter you want to win

items.title: Engineer the hard points before you are ever nominated
items.who: Anyone targeting a quarterly or annual board
items.value: Hard points are objective and verifiable: collateral duties formally assigned in the command organization and regulations manual, previous recognition and personal awards, warfare device, education and completed professional military education, apprenticeship completion, correspondence and non-resident courses, physical readiness score, and documented community involvement. They are the only part of the board nobody can argue about.
items.how: Take the scoring sheet and build a gap list. Then close the gaps in the order of points-per-hour: Non-Resident Training Courses and professional military education are free and fast, community service hours are easy to accumulate and must be documented, a physical readiness score improvement takes one cycle, a formal appointment letter takes one conversation, and a degree or apprenticeship takes longer but scores highest.
items.hack: Count your own points before the board does and you will find two or three cheap gaps every time: a completed course with no certificate in your record, volunteer hours you never logged, a collateral duty you have been doing for a year with no appointment letter. Fix those three things in a week and you will beat somebody with a better record and worse paperwork. Boards score documentation, not activity.
items.deadline: Quarterly, before nomination packages are due

items.title: Soft points: how a board of chiefs actually scores you
items.who: Anyone sitting a board
items.value: Soft points cover primary responsibilities, job performance, command climate contribution, collateral duty performance, personal appearance and military bearing, and boardmanship. This is where a board separates two candidates whose hard points are within a few points of each other, and it is entirely within your control.
items.how: Be able to describe your primary job in two crisp sentences and your measurable impact in three. Have a specific example ready for command climate, equal opportunity and taking care of shipmates that is a real thing you did, not a slogan. Have your uniform professionally tailored, ribbons and devices correct and in order of precedence, shoes and brass right, grooming standards exact. Practice with a mock board run by chiefs who are not on the real one.
items.hack: The chiefs decided how you dress and carry yourself before you finished answering the first question. Get your uniform tailored and inspected by a chief a week out, because a crooked ribbon rack tells a board that the person who owns the collateral duty for records also cannot check his own. Then sit a mock board with two chiefs who will actually be hard on you; it will be the most uncomfortable twenty minutes of your quarter, and it is why you will be the calm one in the real room.
items.deadline: Two weeks before the board

items.title: Boardmanship: creed, eye contact, and answering the question you were asked
items.who: Anyone sitting a board
items.value: Boardmanship is explicitly scored. It covers reciting the Sailor's Creed, how you enter, report and take your seat, eye contact and posture, and how you handle questions you do not know.
items.how: Memorize the Sailor's Creed, or the equivalent creed for your branch, until you can deliver it under stress without a hitch. Learn your chain of command up to the Secretary of Defense and the President, your command's mission, your command's motto and history, current events affecting the Navy, and the core values. Practice entering, reporting, and sitting. Answer the question asked, in a sentence, then support it.
items.hack: When you do not know, say I do not know that answer, I will find it and get back to you, then actually do it and send the answer to the board president the next day. Boards forgive a gap and remember the follow-up; what kills people is guessing, rambling, or dropping eye contact and talking to the table. And practice the creed out loud standing up at attention, not in your head lying in a rack, because the two are not the same skill.
items.deadline: Rehearse daily for two weeks before the board

items.title: Farm letters of appreciation, flag letters and safety recognition deliberately
items.org: Command; type commander and flag staffs; safety programs
items.who: Anyone building a board or advancement record
items.value: Letters of appreciation and commendation, flag letters of commendation, safety pins and awards, and the Military Outstanding Volunteer Service Medal are individually small and collectively decisive on hard-point sheets. They also fill the gap for junior people who do not yet rate a personal decoration.
items.how: When you support an outside command, an inspection team, a visiting staff, a community event or a joint evolution, ask the officer or senior enlisted in charge for a letter of appreciation on their letterhead, and offer them a draft. Submit safety suggestions and hazard reports through the command safety program. Track and certify volunteer hours toward the volunteer service medal threshold.
items.hack: Ask for the letter, and hand them a draft. People who ran an event are grateful and busy; a request with a finished draft attached gets signed the same day, and a request without one gets forgotten.
