Do that four times a year for three years and you will walk into a board with a tab of signed letters that most candidates simply do not have, all from work you already did for free.
items.deadline: At the close of every event or support period

items.title: Treat the physical readiness test as scored career currency
items.org: Navy Physical Readiness Program; Army ACFT; Air Force PT test; Marine Corps PFT/CFT; Coast Guard
items.who: Everyone
items.value: Physical readiness scores are hard points on boards, are visible on evaluations, gate school quotas and commissioning program eligibility, and a failure can make you administratively ineligible for advancement and eventually for retention.
items.how: Know the exact score thresholds for your age group and train to the category above the one you are in. Do not test cold; train the specific events. Handle any medical waiver or profile through proper channels and get it documented.
items.hack: The difference between Good and Outstanding is usually a handful of push-ups and thirty seconds on the run, and it is worth real points on a board sheet and a line on your eval. Nobody trains for it, they just take it. Train the events for six weeks twice a year and you will pick up free points that people with better technical records will not have. And never, ever let a failure into your record; it follows you into every eligibility screen there is.
items.deadline: Each physical readiness cycle

items.title: Community involvement only counts if it is documented and certified
items.org: Command community relations program; Military Outstanding Volunteer Service Medal program
items.who: Anyone building a board record
items.value: Community involvement is a scored hard-point category on quarterly and annual boards, supports the volunteer service medal, and produces eval bullets and letters of appreciation. Undocumented hours score zero.
items.how: Pick one or two sustained efforts rather than scattered one-day events, because sustained involvement produces a leadership role, a point of contact who will write a letter, and a number of hours you can certify. Log dates, hours, organization and point of contact as you go, and get the organization to certify totals in writing periodically.
items.hack: Lead one thing instead of attending ten. Organizer of a recurring event beats participant every time, because it produces a signed letter, a quantifiable result and a bullet with a number in it. And log your hours the night of the event, because reconstructing three years of volunteer hours from memory is the same losing game as reconstructing an eval.
items.deadline: Log continuously; certify before each board cycle

items.title: Other branches run equivalent recognition boards
items.who: Non-Navy junior enlisted
items.value: Every branch has a quarterly and annual recognition program with a scored board, and the same strategy applies: objective criteria you can engineer in advance, plus a subjective interview you can rehearse.
items.how: Army: Soldier of the Month, Quarter and Year boards, plus the Sergeant Audie Murphy Club and Sergeant Morales Club for NCOs. Marine Corps: Marine of the Quarter and Year. Air Force and Space Force: Airman, NCO and Senior NCO of the Quarter and Year, with the Twelve Outstanding Airmen of the Year at the top. Coast Guard: Enlisted Person of the Quarter and Year. Get the local scoring criteria, the study guide, and the board composition.
items.hack: Whatever your branch, ask for the scoring sheet or the board study guide and the last two winners' packages. Every one of these programs is a documented rubric that the average competitor never reads. Winning is mostly a matter of being the one person in the room who studied the actual rubric instead of preparing generically.
items.deadline: Per local board cycle

items.title: Advancement exam strategy: study the bibliography, not the rate
items.org: Navy Advancement Center / NETPDC; MyNavy HR
items.who: E-4 through E-6 candidates, and equivalents
items.value: The Navy-wide advancement exam is a large share of the Final Multiple Score for most rates. The exam is written from a published bibliography of specific publications and chapters, which means the material is finite and knowable.
items.how: Pull the current bibliography for your rate and paygrade from the advancement resources on MyNavy HR. Get the actual publications listed, not third-party study guides, and work them chapter by chapter over months. Use your exam profile sheet from prior attempts to target the weakest sections. Study occupational and professional military knowledge material separately.
items.hack: Almost nobody reads the bibliography. They buy a study guide, cram for three weeks, take the exam and then complain about the results. Download the bibliography the week after you take an exam, not the month before the next one, and work one publication a month on the mid-watch with text-to-speech. You will pass in the top band while people with more sea stories keep taking the same test.
items.deadline: Exam cycles typically run in the spring and fall for active duty; confirm current cycle dates

items.title: Read your profile sheet and understand the Final Multiple Score
items.who: All enlisted competing for advancement
items.value: The Final Multiple Score combines exam standard score, performance marks from evaluations, service in paygrade, time in service, awards and in some cycles passed-not-advanced credit. Knowing which component you are weak in tells you where to spend the next year, and it is the only diagnostic you get.
items.how: Get your profile sheet after every exam. It shows how you performed by subject area against the rest of the candidates. Compare your Final Multiple Score to the published cutoff for your rate and paygrade for that cycle, and calculate which component would have closed the gap fastest.
items.hack: Do the arithmetic yourself. Most people who miss a cutoff by two points assume they need to study harder, when the actual gap was performance marks, meaning the fix was a conversation with their chief about eval input eleven months earlier, not another study guide. The profile sheet tells you which lever to pull, and it is free, and most people never open it.
items.deadline: After every exam cycle

items.title: How evaluations are actually written and ranked
items.org: Navy performance evaluation system; MyNavy HR
items.who: All enlisted; officers via FITREP
items.value: Evaluations drive the performance component of advancement, selection board results, and every eligibility screen there is. They are written by a supervisor under deadline pressure, then ranked in a summary group against peers by a command ranking board. Understanding both steps is how you stop being surprised.
items.how: Learn the current trait or competency areas, the promotion recommendation levels, and how your command runs its ranking board. Submit written input in the exact format your chief needs, early, with quantified bullets. Read your eval before signing, and know your options if it is inaccurate.
items.hack: Two things decide your eval: the input you hand in and where you sit in the summary group. You control the first completely and influence the second only by what you did months ago. The single highest-return action available to a junior person is handing in eval input that is so clean and quantified that the chief copies it in verbatim, because the alternative is a tired chief writing eleven evals from memory on a Sunday. Ask which week input is due and hand yours in the week before that.
items.deadline: Per the annual eval schedule for your paygrade; input typically due weeks before

items.title: The Navy performance evaluation system is being modernized; know the current version
items.who: All Navy personnel; especially anyone writing or receiving evaluations
items.value: The Navy has been rolling out a redesigned performance evaluation system, changing trait structures, competency areas, rating scales and the mechanics of how enlisted evaluations and officer fitness reports are produced. Preparing for the old form wastes your input and can cost you marks.
items.how: Pull the governing NAVADMIN for the current evaluation system before each cycle and confirm the form, the competencies, the rating scale, the promotion recommendation definitions and the submission mechanics. Have your command's performance evaluation point of contact confirm which version applies to your paygrade and cycle, because implementation is typically phased.
items.hack: Every time the Navy changes the eval form, the first cycle produces a wave of people whose input was written to the old rubric and whose marks reflect it. Read the current NAVADMIN yourself, map your bullets to the new competency names word for word, and you will be in the small group whose input fits the form. That is free separation from your peers, and it lasts exactly one cycle, so use it.
items.deadline: Verify before each evaluation cycle

items.title: Sustained superior performance is a documented pattern, not a good year
items.who: Anyone competing for chief, senior chief, master chief, or a competitive program
items.value: Selection boards look for a trend line across years and across different commands and job types. One outstanding year surrounded by average ones reads as situational. Consistent top ranking across varied hard jobs reads as a leader.
items.how: Build a record where each tour shows increased scope and a top-tier ranking: more people, more responsibility, harder billet, measurable results. Do not let a single mediocre eval go unaddressed; understand why, fix the cause, and demonstrate the fix in the next cycle. Sequence tours so the record shows variety, not repetition.
items.hack: Boards can tell the difference between five years of experience and one year of experience five times. If your last three evals describe the same job with the same bullets, you have a repetition problem, not a performance problem, and no amount of polish fixes it. Change the scope of what you own every single tour, and make sure the bullets say so.
items.deadline: Multi-year; visible by the E-6 to E-7 transition

items.title: Build toward the Chief's precepts years before the board sees you
items.org: Navy Chief Petty Officer selection board; CPO 365 / Chief Petty Officer development
items.who: E-5 and E-6 aiming for chief
items.value: The chief selection board convenes under a precept from Navy leadership that states what the board is looking for that year. It is published guidance describing the attributes and record characteristics that get selected, and it is the closest thing to an answer key that exists.
items.how: Read the current precept and the convening guidance for your board. Map your record honestly against it: deckplate leadership, technical expertise, breadth of assignments, professional military education, physical readiness, education, community and command involvement, and the absence of derogatory material. Participate in your command's chief petty officer development season and seek out chiefs who have sat on boards.
items.hack: Read the precept and then have a chief who has actually sat on a board read your record and tell you what it looks like without you in the room, because the record is the only thing the board gets. Do this at least two cycles before you are competitive, because almost every gap the precept exposes takes a year or more to fix, and the cycle you are eligible is far too late to start.
items.deadline: Two or more cycles before you are board-eligible

items.title: PACT and undesignated sailors: convert to a rate deliberately and fast
items.who: Undesignated seamen, firemen, airmen and constructionmen
items.value: Undesignated time does not build a career or a civilian resume. Conversion into a rate starts the clock on advancement, technical training, an NEC, credentialing and everything downstream. Every month spent undesignated is a month not spent advancing in a community.
items.how: Work with the command career counselor on the designation process for your intended rate, which generally involves demonstrated performance, command endorsement, meeting the rate's ASVAB and screening requirements, and either an A-School quota or striker designation on the job. Retest the ASVAB if your line scores are the barrier, and get your quals and eval marks strong because those drive the endorsement.
items.hack: Pick the rate in your first six months and make the entire command know which one you want, because designation comes from a chief advocating for you to a career counselor with a quota. The sailors who stay undesignated for three years are almost never the ones who could not qualify; they are the ones who never told anybody what they wanted and got used wherever a body was needed.
items.deadline: As early as possible in the first enlistment

items.title: Selective Reenlistment Bonus: know the multiple before you sign
items.org: Navy SRB program (NAVADMIN-driven); Army SRB; Air Force SRB; Marine Corps SRB
items.who: Anyone in a reenlistment window in a bonus-eligible skill
items.value: Reenlistment bonuses in shortage skills can be substantial and are paid based on skill, paygrade, zone and the number of additional obligated months. The award list changes by message, so the amount available to you is a moving target tied to a date.
items.how: Find the current bonus message for your rate, NEC, paygrade and zone before you commit to a reenlistment date. Understand the obligated service required, how the payment is structured in installments, the tax treatment, and the recoupment rules if you do not complete the obligation. Coordinate timing with your career counselor.
items.hack: Bonus lists get cut and expanded by message with little warning, so the date you sign can be worth thousands of dollars. Ask your career counselor to show you the actual current message, not a summary, and if you are near a window, ask whether reenlisting in an overseas or combat zone tax-exclusion location changes the tax treatment of the payment. Also never let a bonus be the only reason you sign for six more years; the money is real, but it is a fraction of what the wrong six years costs.
items.deadline: Within your reenlistment window; bonus messages change frequently

items.title: C-WAY: the quota system that decides whether you get to stay
items.who: Enlisted approaching reenlistment, conversion, or transition to the Reserve
items.value: Career Waypoints is the Navy's process for reenlistment approval, in-rate and out-of-rate conversion, and transition from active duty to the Reserve component. Quotas are community-by-community, so a strong sailor in an overmanned rate can be denied while a weaker sailor in an undermanned rate is approved.
items.how: Work with your command career counselor to know your application windows, how many looks you get, and the manning picture for your rate. If your rate is overmanned, start the conversion conversation early and identify the undermanned rates you qualify for. If you intend to leave active duty but keep serving, use the Reserve transition option deliberately rather than as a fallback.
items.hack: Your rate's manning is not your fault and it is not going to care about your evals. If you are in an overmanned community, start looking at conversion two years before your window, not two months, because the good conversions require a quota, an ASVAB line score you may need to retest for, and a school seat. The sailors who get non-selected and act surprised are almost always the ones who never asked their career counselor what the manning looked like.
items.deadline: Application windows are tied to your end of active obligated service; typically opening 13-15 months out

items.title: High Year Tenure: the clock that ends careers quietly
items.org: MyNavy HR; equivalents in all branches
items.who: Anyone who has not advanced on schedule
items.value: High Year Tenure caps the years of service you may have at each paygrade. If you reach the cap without advancing, you are separated or retired regardless of performance. The limits are adjusted by policy message as manning needs change, in both directions.
items.how: Look up the current High Year Tenure limit for your paygrade and calculate your date. Work backward from it to determine how many advancement cycles you actually have left and what your Final Multiple Score needs to be. Know the waiver process and who can approve one. Verify the number against current policy rather than what someone told you years ago.
items.hack: Write your High Year Tenure date on your career plan in ink, because it is the one date the Navy will enforce whether or not you were paying attention. If you are inside three cycles of it and have not advanced, stop optimizing and pick a lane: attack the exam and eval components hard, pursue conversion into an undermanned rate, go for a commissioning program, or plan your transition on your terms with the benefits you have earned. Drifting into your gate and getting separated with no plan is the worst version of all four.
items.deadline: Your individual HYT date; policy limits change by message

items.title: Navy COOL and the other branches' COOL portals
items.org: DoD COOL portal (Navy, Army, Air Force, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, Space Force)
items.who: Every enlisted service member, from A-School onward
items.value: Credentialing Opportunities On-Line maps your rate, MOS or AFSC to the civilian licenses and certifications it corresponds to, and in many cases funds the exam, the study materials and the renewal. A funded, nationally recognized credential is the single fastest way to convert military experience into civilian hiring power.
items.how: Look up your rate or specialty on the COOL portal for your branch, read the Learning and Development Roadmap for your paygrade, and identify the credentials with funding available. Apply for funding through the portal process before you pay for anything yourself. Stack credentials over a career rather than cramming them into your last year.
items.hack: Start pulling credentials in your first enlistment, not your last year, because the funding is there the whole time and almost nobody uses it until they are getting out and panicking. Also read the Learning and Development Roadmap for the paygrade above you, because it tells you what your community expects at the next level, which is effectively free intelligence on what advancement boards value. The Navy portal now lives on the joint DoD COOL site rather than the old standalone navycool address.
items.deadline: Anytime while serving; funding subject to annual availability

items.title: Get your credential exams and renewals paid for
items.who: Enlisted pursuing civilian certifications
items.value: Exam fees, study materials, and in many cases recertification and license renewal are fundable while you serve. Paying out of pocket for a certification your branch would have funded is a common and avoidable loss.
items.how: Use the COOL portal's funding request process and your command's credentialing point of contact. Confirm what is covered: exam fee, prep materials, first attempt versus retake, and maintenance or renewal. Bundle related credentials in a sequence so each one builds toward a higher-value one.
items.hack: Apply for the funding before you register for the exam, because reimbursement after the fact is the version that gets denied. And ask specifically about renewal funding while you are still in, then time your last renewal as late in your service as possible so the credential stays current for the longest stretch of your job search.
items.deadline: Before registering and paying for any exam

items.title: Tuition Assistance: the degree you should not be paying for
items.org: Service Tuition Assistance programs; DANTES; MyNavy Education
items.who: Active duty and eligible Reserve members
items.value: Tuition Assistance pays tuition for college coursework up to a per-semester-hour cap and an annual ceiling, with the exact figures and service obligation rules set by service policy. Used steadily, it produces an associate or bachelor's degree during service without touching GI Bill entitlement, leaving the GI Bill for a graduate degree or for a dependent through transferability.
items.how: Go through your branch's education office or education portal, get a degree plan at an accredited school that accepts military credit, and apply for Tuition Assistance before each term starts. Understand the grade requirements and the recoupment rules for failed or dropped courses, and the service obligation that Tuition Assistance incurs.
items.hack: Use Tuition Assistance while you are in and save the GI Bill, because the GI Bill also pays a housing allowance you cannot collect while on active duty and it can be transferred to a spouse or child. Burning GI Bill months on classes Tuition Assistance would have paid for is one of the most expensive mistakes in the enlisted force. Two classes a term, every term, funded, and you walk out with a degree and a full GI Bill.
items.deadline: Apply before each term start; annual fiscal year ceiling

items.title: TA Top-Up for when tuition exceeds the Tuition Assistance cap
items.who: Service members eligible for GI Bill benefits taking courses that cost more than Tuition Assistance covers
items.value: Top-Up lets the VA pay the difference between what Tuition Assistance covers and the actual cost of a course, drawing against your GI Bill entitlement. It makes an expensive program reachable without paying out of pocket.
items.how: Confirm eligibility under the GI Bill chapter that applies to you, get Tuition Assistance approved for the course first, then apply for Top-Up through the VA. Understand that Top-Up consumes GI Bill entitlement, and how much, before you use it.
items.hack: Top-Up spends GI Bill months on a course while you are on active duty and drawing no housing allowance, which is the worst dollar-per-month use of the benefit there is. Use it when the program is genuinely worth it and unavailable cheaper, and not as a habit. For most people the better answer is to find an accredited school whose per-credit cost fits inside the Tuition Assistance cap, and there are many.
items.deadline: Apply after TA approval and before course completion

items.title: USMAP: a Department of Labor journeyman card for work you already do
items.org: United Services Military Apprenticeship Program; Department of Labor
items.who: Enlisted in a rate with a matching trade; Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard participate
items.value: USMAP converts documented on-the-job hours in your rate into a nationally recognized Department of Labor Certificate of Completion of Apprenticeship. It costs nothing, requires no classroom time, and produces a credential that civilian trades, unions and licensing boards recognize immediately. It also scores as an educational hard point on boards.
items.how: Enroll through the USMAP process on the Navy COOL apprenticeship pages, pick the trade or trades that match your rate, and log your on-the-job hours with supervisor verification. Most trades require several thousand documented hours, which a normal sea tour produces. You can pursue more than one trade over a career.
items.hack: You are already doing the hours. The only reason most people finish a twenty-year career without a journeyman card is that nobody enrolled them and they never logged anything. Enroll in your first year, log hours monthly the same night you update your brag sheet, and you will separate with a Department of Labor credential that means something to a union hall, a licensing board and a hiring manager who has never heard of your rate.
items.deadline: Enroll early; completion requires accumulating documented hours over years

items.title: The Navy College Program and your branch's education office
items.org: Navy College Program / MyNavy Education; DANTES; branch education offices
items.who: All enlisted pursuing a degree
items.value: The education office provides free academic counseling, a documented degree plan, credit evaluation, testing services, and the Tuition Assistance process. A counseled degree plan prevents the most common failure mode, which is accumulating credits at four schools that do not combine into a degree.
items.how: Meet with an education counselor and get a written degree plan at a school that maximizes your military credit and accepts credit from the other schools you have attended. Have your Joint Services Transcript evaluated against that plan. Then take courses in the order the plan says.
items.hack: Get the degree plan in writing before you take another class. Enormous numbers of sailors hit twelve years with eighty scattered credits and no degree, because they took whatever was convenient at whatever school was on base at the time. One counseling appointment and one plan turns those same eighty credits into a finished degree, often with a semester or less of work remaining.
items.deadline: Before enrolling in coursework

items.title: United States Naval Community College: tuition-free associate degrees
items.who: Enlisted Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard members
items.value: The Naval Community College offers tuition-free, naval-relevant associate degrees and certificates through partner institutions, in fields tied to naval missions. It does not consume Tuition Assistance or GI Bill entitlement, which makes it the cheapest path to a first degree that exists.
items.how: Apply through the Naval Community College, choose a program in your area of interest, and complete coursework online around your operational schedule. Confirm how its credits transfer into the bachelor's program you eventually want, and coordinate with your education counselor so it fits a longer degree plan.
items.hack: Free is better than funded, because it leaves your Tuition Assistance and your entire GI Bill untouched. Do the associate through the Naval Community College, use Tuition Assistance for the bachelor's, and keep the GI Bill for a master's or for your kid. That sequencing is worth well over a hundred thousand dollars over a family's lifetime, and it requires nothing but doing them in the right order.
items.deadline: Per enrollment cycle

items.title: NCPACE / PACE: college courses while deployed
items.org: Navy College Program for Afloat College Education
items.who: Sailors and Marines attached to deploying units and eligible afloat commands
items.value: NCPACE delivers college coursework aboard ship, in instructor-led and distance-learning formats, at no tuition cost to the member and generally without consuming Tuition Assistance. A deployment becomes a semester.
items.how: Work through your command's educational services officer or command career counselor to see which courses are being offered on your platform for the upcoming deployment and to enroll before you get underway. Make sure the courses map to your written degree plan rather than being taken because they were offered.
items.hack: Enroll before the ship leaves, because the sign-up happens in port and then the opportunity is gone for seven months. A deployment is the single best study environment you will ever have: no commute, no errands, no social life, and a lot of hours. The people who come back from a deployment with nine credits and a completed qualification did not have more time than you did; they signed up in port.
items.deadline: Enroll before deployment; offerings vary by platform

items.title: CLEP and DSST exams: college credit by examination, free
items.who: All service members and, in many cases, spouses
items.value: DANTES funds credit-by-examination tests that can each award three to twelve semester hours. A motivated person can test out of a full year of general education requirements in a few months, for free, without a single class.
items.how: Confirm which exams your target school accepts and for which requirements before you test, then schedule through a DANTES-funded test center or the approved remote proctoring option. Study from free or cheap study guides. Confirm current funding rules for first attempts and retakes.
items.hack: Get the list of CLEP and DSST exams your school accepts, cross off the subjects you already know from your rate training, and test out of them in a single quarter. People spend four semesters and eight hundred hours in seat time on general education requirements they could have tested out of in six weeks. The credit on the transcript looks identical.
items.deadline: Anytime; confirm school acceptance before testing

items.title: Joint Services Transcript: turn your training into college credit
items.org: DoD; Joint Services Transcript (Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Coast Guard); Air Force and Space Force use the Community College of the Air Force
items.who: All enlisted; check yours annually
items.value: The Joint Services Transcript documents your military training, occupational experience and courses with American Council on Education credit recommendations that accredited colleges accept. A typical mid-career technical rate can carry a substantial number of recommended credits, sometimes most of an associate degree.
items.how: Pull your own transcript, verify that every school, course and qualification you completed actually appears on it, and send it to your target school for evaluation. If schools or NECs are missing, work with your command training office and personnel office to get the record corrected, because the transcript only reports what your record contains.
items.hack: Pull your Joint Services Transcript today and read it, because it is almost certainly missing something, and every missing school is credits you paid for with your time and will not get. Fix it while the command that sent you to that school still exists and the training officer can still find the completion record. Waiting until you are applying to college to look at it is how people lose a semester of credit permanently. Air Force and Space Force members should check their Community College of the Air Force record the same way.
items.deadline: Review annually and before any school application

items.title: Non-resident courses and professional military education, done early
items.org: Navy Non-Resident Training Courses / NAVEDTRA; Navy Leadership Development; branch PME systems
items.who: All enlisted
items.value: Completed non-resident training courses and enlisted professional military education are hard points on boards, contribute to advancement eligibility, and in several branches are prerequisites for promotion. They are free and can be done on your own schedule.
items.how: Identify the required and elective courses for your rate and paygrade, and the enlisted professional military education requirement for the paygrade above you. Complete them and confirm each completion is recorded in your official record, not just in an email. Print and file the certificates.
items.hack: Complete the professional military education for the paygrade above you before you are eligible for it, because it is a hard-point line on every board sheet and it costs you evenings rather than money. And verify each completion landed in your official record, because a course you finished that the system did not record scores exactly zero, and the fix takes ten minutes now and three months in two years.
items.deadline: Before board cycles and advancement eligibility windows

items.title: Orders are a career decision, and the detailer is a negotiation
items.org: MyNavy Assignment / Navy Personnel Command detailers; branch assignment systems
items.who: Anyone within a year of their projected rotation date
items.value: Where you go next determines your next three years of professional development, your family's stability, your sea and shore rotation clock, and whether your record shows the breadth that boards reward. Detailers fill billets; they do not optimize your career unless you give them a reason to.
items.how: Know your projected rotation date and when your negotiation window opens. Research the specific billets available for your rate and paygrade, and identify which ones carry the NECs, leadership scope or joint exposure you need. Contact your detailer early, professionally, with two or three prioritized options and a reason for each. Keep everything in writing.
items.hack: Call your detailer before your window opens and ask a single question: which billets in my rate are hardest for you to fill in the next cycle, and what would I need to be competitive for them. Detailers have problems, and the sailor who volunteers to solve one gets treated very differently than the sailor who sends a list of places they would like to live. That one phone call has been worth a shore tour of choice to more people than any other play on this list.
items.deadline: Negotiation window typically opens roughly 9-12 months before rotation

items.title: Pick duty stations for what they build, not only for where they are
items.who: Anyone negotiating orders
items.value: Some duty stations produce records that get selected: deploying operational units, flagship or high-visibility commands, instructor and recruiting duty with documented metrics, joint and combatant command staffs, independent duty, and overseas tours. Others are comfortable and produce nothing a board can read.
items.how: For each option, ask what the billet will let you own, how many people you will lead, whether it produces a qualification or specialty code, whether it deploys, and what the last three people in that billet did next. Also weigh the practical: cost of living, spouse employment market, schools, proximity to family, and whether you can finish a degree there.
items.hack: Ask what the last three people in that billet did next. If two of them made chief and one went to a commissioning program, take it. If nobody can tell you, the billet is invisible, and invisible billets produce invisible records. Also sequence geography honestly: take the career-building tour when your family can absorb it and take the stability tour when they need it, but do not pretend you can take the comfortable option every time and still be competitive.
items.deadline: At each negotiation window

items.title: Follow the leaders who rotate, and let them pull you along
items.who: Anyone who has worked for a leader who valued them
items.value: Effective leaders take known performers with them, or reach back for them, when they move to a new command or staff. A leader who already trusts you is the fastest route to a high-visibility billet and a strong evaluation, because you start at full trust instead of earning it from zero.
items.how: Keep in real contact with the officers and senior enlisted you performed well for, on a professional basis, after you both move. When you know your rotation date, tell them you are negotiating and ask whether they know of billets. Be genuinely useful to them, not just available.
items.hack: When a leader who valued you gets orders to a staff or a command, email them within a month and ask what they are building and whether there is a billet in it. This is how a startling number of career-making assignments actually get filled, and it is entirely legitimate; you are still going through the detailer, you have just given them a command that wants you by name. But keep the relationship real, because the people who only reach out when they need orders are transparent and stop getting answers.
items.deadline: Maintain continuously; act at each rotation window

items.title: Sea and shore rotation: know your community's flow and plan around it
items.org: MyNavy HR; community sea/shore flow policy
items.who: All Navy enlisted; other branches have analogous deployment and station rotation patterns
items.value: Sea and shore flow sets the expected tour lengths in your rate at each paygrade. It governs when you are available for orders, when you can realistically pursue a degree or a commissioning program, and when your family gets stability. It also changes by policy message as manning requires.
items.how: Look up the current sea and shore flow for your rate and paygrade and lay it against your career plan and your family's plans. Identify the shore tour that is your window for finishing a degree, a commissioning application, or an instructor qualification, and protect it.
items.hack: Your shore tour is not a rest period, it is the only block of predictable hours you will get for three to four years, and it is where degrees, commissioning applications and credentials actually get finished. Sailors who treat shore duty as a break show up at the next sea tour with the same record they left with. Decide before you report what you are going to finish there, and tell your chief on day one.
items.deadline: Plan at each rotation; verify current policy

items.title: STA-21: Seaman to Admiral-21, the full-pay commissioning path
items.who: Active duty enlisted sailors meeting age, service, academic and physical requirements
items.value: STA-21 selects enlisted sailors to attend a participating university full time while remaining on active duty at their current paygrade with full pay and allowances, plus a tuition allowance, leading to a commission. It is the most financially favorable enlisted-to-officer path in the Navy because you keep drawing pay and accruing service while in school.
items.how: Review the current instruction for eligibility: paygrade and service windows, age limits, SAT or ACT or ASVAB score requirements, physical readiness, security eligibility, and command endorsement. Assemble the package: transcripts, test scores, evaluations, command interview and endorsement, and a personal statement. Options include general unrestricted line, nuclear, special warfare, information warfare, civil engineer corps, nurse corps and others, each with distinct requirements.
items.hack: The test score and the transcript are the two things you cannot fix in the last month, so take the SAT or ACT two years early and retake it, and knock out college math and English at a community college before you apply. Almost every rejected package fails on academics, not on performance. And get the commanding officer's interview early, because a lukewarm endorsement is a dead package no matter how good your evals are, and you want to know where you stand while there is still time to change it.
items.deadline: Annual application cycle; deadlines set by NAVADMIN each year

items.title: MECP: Medical Enlisted Commissioning Program (nursing)
items.org: Navy Medicine; Medical Enlisted Commissioning Program
items.who: Active duty enlisted sailors pursuing a Bachelor of Science in Nursing
items.value: MECP sends enlisted sailors to a nursing program full time, at current paygrade with full pay and allowances, to commission as a Navy Nurse Corps officer. Nursing is also among the most portable civilian careers in existence, so the credential holds value regardless of how long you stay.
items.how: Confirm current eligibility: prerequisite college coursework in sciences, grade point average minimum, acceptance or eligibility for admission to an accredited BSN program, service and age requirements, physical readiness and command endorsement. Complete the science prerequisites before applying, because they are the standard disqualifier.
items.hack: Start the anatomy, physiology, chemistry and statistics prerequisites two years before you apply, at a community college, paid by Tuition Assistance, and get A grades in them. That is the entire competition. Every corpsman who says they wanted MECP and did not get it usually means they never finished the prerequisites, and a B minus in chemistry is the actual reason a package loses.
items.deadline: Annual cycle; deadlines announced by message

items.title: Medical and health professions commissioning paths
items.org: Navy Medicine; Medical Service Corps In-Service Procurement Program; Health Services Collegiate Program; Uniformed Services University
items.who: Enlisted pursuing medical, dental, allied health, physician assistant or health administration commissions
items.value: Multiple distinct paths exist for enlisted members to commission into medical fields, including in-service procurement for Medical Service Corps specialties, collegiate programs that pay you while you complete a health professions degree, physician assistant programs, and the military medical school.
items.how: Identify the specific corps and specialty you want, then work backward to its educational prerequisites, which differ substantially. Talk to a Navy Medicine officer recruiter or program manager, not only your command career counselor, because these programs are managed outside the standard commissioning pipeline. Confirm current program names and availability, as this portfolio is restructured often.
items.hack: Go find an officer who is currently in the specialty you want and ask which program they came through and what they would do differently. The published requirements tell you the minimum; the person who just did it tells you what the board actually selected on. In the medical community that difference is usually clinical hours, specific prerequisite grades and a letter from a named physician, none of which appear in the instruction.
items.deadline: Varies by program; most run annual boards

items.title: LDO and Chief Warrant Officer: commission on your technical expertise
items.org: Navy Limited Duty Officer and Chief Warrant Officer programs; Army, Marine Corps, Coast Guard and Air Force warrant or technical officer paths
items.who: Senior enlisted, typically E-6 and above, with deep technical expertise in a designated field
items.value: The LDO and CWO paths commission experienced enlisted technical experts without requiring a bachelor's degree for many designators, keeping you in your technical community as an officer. For a strong senior petty officer who does not want to start over academically, it is the most direct commissioning route there is.
items.how: Check the current annual message for eligible designators, paygrade and service windows, education requirements, physical readiness, and package contents. Build a package with a strong commanding officer endorsement, letters of recommendation from officers in the designator you want, and evaluations showing technical mastery and leadership. Identify the designator early because requirements differ sharply.
items.hack: The package is won on the endorsements and the interview, not the paperwork, so go find two officers already in the designator you want and ask them to review your package and write for you. A generic endorsement from your chain reads as compliance; a specific letter from a mustang in your target designator saying this person can do my job reads as evidence. And apply every year you are eligible, because repeat applicants with improved packages get selected constantly.
items.deadline: Annual application cycle announced by message

items.title: Officer Candidate School from the enlisted ranks
items.org: Officer Training Command Newport; equivalents: Army OCS and Green to Gold, Air Force OTS, Marine Corps ECP/MECEP/PLC, Coast Guard OCS
items.who: Enlisted members who already hold a bachelor's degree
items.value: If you already have a degree, Officer Candidate School is the shortest route to a commission. Enlisted applicants compete with civilian applicants but bring evaluations, leadership experience and a command endorsement that civilians cannot produce.
items.how: Confirm degree requirements, age limits, physical standards, and testing requirements for your intended designator, including the ASTB for aviation and the Officer Aptitude Rating for many others. Apply through an officer recruiter, with your command's knowledge and endorsement. Other branches have their own named versions, including the Army's Green to Gold for the ROTC route and the Marine Corps Enlisted Commissioning Program and MECEP.
items.hack: Your enlisted record is your advantage over civilian applicants, so make the package show it: a commanding officer endorsement, leadership scope with numbers in it, and a personal statement that tells a coherent story about why this designator. And take the aptitude test early and retake it, because it is the only part of the package that is a pure score, and a lot of good enlisted packages die on a test score somebody took cold on a Tuesday.
items.deadline: Boards convene multiple times per year depending on designator

items.title: Chaplain and religious program commissioning paths
items.org: Navy Chaplain Corps; Chaplain Candidate Program
items.who: Service members with or pursuing a graduate theological degree and an ecclesiastical endorsement
items.value: The chaplaincy requires a graduate theological degree and an endorsement from a recognized religious organization. Candidate programs allow you to affiliate and serve while completing the degree, and the Navy Chaplain Corps serves the Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.
items.how: Secure the ecclesiastical endorsement from your faith group's endorsing agent, because without it no other qualification matters. Complete the graduate theological degree requirement. Work with a chaplain officer recruiter on the candidate program while you are still in school.
items.hack: The ecclesiastical endorsement is the gate, and it is controlled entirely outside the military, so start that conversation with your endorsing agent years before you finish the degree. People assume the degree is the hard part. The endorsement is the hard part, and it is the one the Navy cannot help you with.
items.deadline: Boards convene per Chaplain Corps accession cycles

items.title: Naval Academy and the prep school route, including from the fleet
items.org: United States Naval Academy; Naval Academy Preparatory School; Naval Academy Foundation
items.who: Enlisted under the age limits; high school candidates
items.value: The Naval Academy reserves a portion of each class for enlisted members of the Navy and Marine Corps, and the Naval Academy Preparatory School exists in part to prepare fleet sailors and Marines academically for that appointment. West Point, the Air Force Academy and the Coast Guard Academy have comparable prep schools and enlisted paths.
items.how: Confirm the current age limit and application timeline, which runs well over a year ahead of the class you would enter. Assemble the package: command endorsement, academic record, standardized test scores, physical fitness assessment and medical qualification. Understand that a prep school year comes before the four academy years, so the total commitment is long.
items.hack: The age limit is the real constraint and it does not move, so if you are within a couple of years of it, apply now and apply every cycle you are eligible. And take the standardized test seriously; a fleet sailor with strong evals and a mediocre test score gets routed to the prep school, which is not a rejection, it is a funded year to fix exactly the thing that was weak. Say yes to it.
items.deadline: Applications typically open more than a year before class entry; age limits are firm

items.title: NROTC and the officer accession pipelines from college
items.org: Naval Service Training Command / NROTC; Army ROTC; Air Force ROTC
items.who: High school and college students; enlisted members eligible for scholarship programs
items.value: ROTC scholarships pay tuition and fees plus a stipend in exchange for a service obligation, and produce a commission alongside a degree. NROTC includes nurse and Marine Corps options, and enlisted members can access ROTC-based commissioning through service-specific scholarship programs.
items.how: Apply in the fall of your senior year of high school for a four-year scholarship, or compete for two- and three-year scholarships once enrolled. Enlisted members should look at the ROTC-based commissioning options in their branch, which for the Army is Green to Gold and for the Navy includes the university-based options under the Seaman to Admiral-21 umbrella.
items.hack: Apply for the scholarship even if you think you will not get it, and apply again as a college freshman and sophomore, because two- and three-year scholarships go unclaimed every year for lack of applicants. And if you are already enlisted, understand the trade honestly: an ROTC route generally means giving up pay and years of service credit, while STA-21 or a full-pay program does not. Do that arithmetic before you fall in love with a school.
items.deadline: High school applications open the summer before senior year; in-college boards run annually

items.title: ASTB-E and the aviation pipeline
items.who: Anyone pursuing Navy, Marine Corps or Coast Guard aviation as an officer
items.value: The Aviation Selection Test Battery gates every naval aviation officer path: pilot, naval flight officer and flight surgeon. It produces multiple scores, including the Officer Aptitude Rating used for many non-aviation designators, so a strong result serves more than one application.
items.how: Study math, mechanical comprehension, aviation and nautical information, reading comprehension and the performance-based measures. Learn the retest rules and waiting periods before your first attempt, because attempts are limited. Combine with a flight physical and the specific designator requirements.
items.hack: Attempts are limited and the waiting periods are long, so do not walk in cold to see how you do. Study for two months, take a full practice battery, and only then schedule. People burn an attempt casually at twenty-two and then spend three years living with the score. Study the aviation and nautical information section specifically, because it is pure memorization and it is the cheapest points on the test.
items.deadline: Before applying to any aviation designator; retest waiting periods apply

items.title: How to build any commissioning package so it survives a board
items.who: Anyone applying to any officer program
items.value: Every commissioning board looks at the same things: academic evidence, performance evidence, physical readiness, endorsements, and a personal statement that explains the choice. The programs differ; the package discipline does not.
items.how: Start twenty-four months out. Fix academics first because they take longest. Get your evals ranked at the top of your summary group in the two cycles before you apply. Max your physical readiness score. Line up three endorsers who know your work and give them your brag sheet and a draft. Write a personal statement about the designator, not about yourself. Have an officer in that designator and a chief who has sat on boards both red-line it.
items.hack: Apply even when your package is imperfect, and apply every cycle. Boards remember improved repeat applicants, and a not-selected with a specific weakness identified is a roadmap, not a rejection. The people who never commission are overwhelmingly the ones who waited for the perfect year, then aged out or hit a service gate. Submit, ask for the feedback, fix one thing, submit again.
items.deadline: Begin 24 months before your target board

items.title: Reserve component service as a deliberate career choice
items.org: Navy Reserve; Army Reserve and Army National Guard; Air Force Reserve and Air National Guard; Marine Forces Reserve; Coast Guard Reserve
items.who: Anyone leaving active duty; anyone choosing an initial path
items.value: Drilling reserve service continues retirement point accrual toward a reserve retirement, keeps you in the promotion system, maintains a clearance and currency in your specialty, and provides access to certain benefits including health care options and continued education support, while you build a civilian career in parallel.
items.how: Affiliate before you separate rather than after, because a break in service complicates rate, paygrade and bonus eligibility. Understand the difference between the Selected Reserve with regular drill and annual training, the Individual Ready Reserve with no drill and no points, and full-time support and active guard and reserve positions. Ask about affiliation bonuses and prior-service programs.
items.hack: Affiliate before your separation date, not six months after, because the paperwork that is routine while you are still in becomes a prior-service enlistment with waivers, quotas and possible paygrade loss once you are out. And do not accept the Individual Ready Reserve as a plan; it earns no points, no pay and no promotion, and a lot of people who intended to drill somewhere sat in it for four years and lost a reserve retirement they were most of the way to.
items.deadline: Before your separation date; affiliation windows and bonuses change by policy

items.title: Reservists: mind your medical records when you are not on orders
items.who: Drilling reservists and National Guard members
items.value: Reserve component service creates a fragmented medical record: some care happens at a military treatment facility, some on civilian insurance, some during drill and some during active-duty periods. For a VA claim, what matters is whether an injury or condition is documented as having occurred or been aggravated during a period of qualifying service, so the continuity of that record is the whole case.
items.how: Complete the annual Periodic Health Assessment honestly and completely every year, and report conditions rather than minimizing them to stay deployable on paper. For any injury during drill, annual training or active duty, insist on a line-of-duty determination in writing before you go home. Keep your own copies of every civilian record that relates to a condition that started in service, and provide them to your unit medical department so the military record reflects them.
items.hack: Get the line-of-duty determination written before you leave the drill weekend, not on Monday when you are back at your civilian job. An injury that happens on a Saturday drill and gets treated at a civilian urgent care on Sunday with no line-of-duty paperwork is, for VA purposes, an injury that happened on your own time. That single sheet of paper is the difference between a service-connected condition and a decade of arguing.
items.deadline: Annual Periodic Health Assessment; line-of-duty documentation immediately after any injury

items.title: Reservists: know which benefits you actually hold right now
items.who: Drilling reservists and Guard members
items.value: Reserve benefits switch on and off depending on your status, your cumulative qualifying active service, and whether your orders are Title 10 or Title 32. Education benefits, health care eligibility, VA home loan eligibility, life insurance, and space-available travel all have different triggers, and guessing wrong is expensive.
items.how: Build a written inventory of your own status: total qualifying active-duty days and under what authority, your accumulated retirement points by year, which GI Bill chapter you have earned and at what percentage tier, your health care eligibility and premiums, your life insurance coverage and beneficiaries, and whether you have met the service requirement for a VA-guaranteed home loan. Update it annually and after every set of orders.
items.hack: Keep every single set of orders and every DD Form 214 or equivalent for every period of active duty, because reserve benefit eligibility is built by adding up days of qualifying service under specific authorities, and the burden of proving those days is on you. Reservists lose education tiers, loan eligibility and retirement points over missing paperwork from a mobilization eleven years ago. Scan every order the week you get it.
items.deadline: Review annually and after every activation

items.title: Reserve retirement points and the gray area years
items.who: All reserve component members
items.value: A reserve retirement generally requires twenty qualifying years, with retired pay computed from accumulated retirement points and normally beginning at age sixty, with reductions in that age available for certain qualifying active service. The period between retirement eligibility and the start of pay is the gray area, and it has its own benefit rules.
items.how: Pull your annual retirement point statement every year, verify that drills, annual training, active-duty periods, and correspondence or membership points are all credited, and correct errors immediately. Track your qualifying years, not just your total years. Understand what your family's health care and identification card status is during the gray area.
items.hack: Audit your point statement every single year, because an uncredited drill weekend or a missing mobilization is nearly impossible to reconstruct a decade later, and a non-qualifying year sitting in the middle of your record can cost you an entire reserve retirement. This is a fifteen-minute annual task that protects a six-figure asset, and the number of reservists who have never once opened their point statement is astonishing.
items.deadline: Review the annual retirement point statement every year

items.title: Reservists: use your branch's transition program, you are eligible
items.org: DoD Transition Assistance Program; branch transition offices; Navy Reserve transition support
items.who: Reservists demobilizing, separating, or reaching retirement eligibility
items.value: Transition assistance, including the Transition Assistance Program curriculum, career counseling, resume and interview support, credential assistance and the SkillBridge-style opportunities, is available to reserve component members, not only to active duty. Many reservists never use it because nobody tells them they qualify.
items.how: Contact your branch transition office and your unit's career counselor as you approach separation, retirement eligibility, or demobilization. Complete the transition curriculum and the individualized planning. Ask specifically about employment rights protections, credentialing funds, and what carries over from your reserve status.
items.hack: Ask for the transition program by name and do not accept the answer that it is for active duty, because that answer is wrong and it is given constantly. Reservists demobilizing off a long mobilization are entitled to transition support and frequently walk away without it, then discover two years later they missed a health care window, an education deadline or a credentialing fund. Make the call before your end date, not after.
items.deadline: Begin as early as your separation or demobilization timeline allows

items.title: Reservists: plan for what comes after, from the first drill
items.org: Self; branch transition and retirement services
items.who: All reserve component members
items.value: A reserve career runs in parallel with a civilian one, which means the after is not a single event. It is a sequence: the end of drilling, the gray area, the start of retired pay, and the point at which your VA claims and health care matter most. Each stage has paperwork with deadlines.
items.how: Build a timeline with your own dates on it: twenty qualifying years, your anticipated transfer to the retired reserve, your gray area span, your retired pay application at the appropriate age, and the windows for VA claims, survivor benefit elections and health care transitions. Keep your record, point statements, medical documentation and orders consolidated so the person doing the paperwork later, which may be your spouse, can find them.
items.hack: Applying for reserve retired pay is not automatic; nobody mails it to you when you turn sixty. People miss it by years. Put the application date in a calendar that will still exist decades from now, tell your spouse where the file is, and keep the point statements and every DD Form 214 in that same file. The reserve career you built over twenty-two years is documented in a folder that only you know the location of, and that is a risk worth ten minutes to fix.
items.deadline: Retired pay must be applied for; typically at age 60 unless reduced by qualifying service

items.title: Medical boards: MEB, PEB, and the Integrated Disability Evaluation System
items.org: DoD and VA; Integrated Disability Evaluation System; Physical Evaluation Board
items.who: Anyone with a condition that may not meet medical retention standards
items.value: When a condition may prevent you from continuing to serve, a Medical Evaluation Board determines whether you meet retention standards, and if not, a Physical Evaluation Board determines fitness for duty and, if unfit, assigns a disability rating that drives whether you are medically separated with severance or medically retired with retired pay and health care for life. The difference between a 20 percent and a 30 percent finding can be a lifetime of retired pay and TRICARE.
items.how: Under the integrated system, the VA typically performs the examinations used by both departments. Read every narrative summary and examination before it is finalized and correct errors in writing immediately. List every condition, not just the one that triggered the board. Use the assigned legal counsel and the recovery care or wounded warrior advocates. Know your rights to rebut findings and to request an impartial review.
items.hack: Read the narrative summary yourself, line by line, and rebut every error in writing before the board sees it, because once a mistaken sentence is in the record it drives the finding and you will be appealing it for years. Take the assigned counsel and take the advocate; people who go through this alone because they want it over with routinely accept separation with severance when the record supported medical retirement. And list every condition, because the board rates what is in front of it and it will never ask you what else hurts.
items.deadline: Timelines are set once a board is initiated; rebuttal windows are short

items.title: Fleet Reserve, retired list, or separation: know which one you are choosing
items.who: Anyone approaching 20 years, and anyone weighing an earlier exit
items.value: Navy and Marine Corps enlisted members who complete twenty years of active service generally transfer to the Fleet Reserve and receive retainer pay, then transfer to the Retired List once total service including Fleet Reserve time reaches thirty years, at which point retainer pay becomes retired pay. Fleet Reserve members remain subject to recall. Separating before twenty years forfeits retired pay entirely, though earned VA and education benefits remain.
items.how: Understand the arithmetic of your own retirement system, whether legacy High-3 or the Blended Retirement System, including the multiplier, the continuation pay decision point, the Thrift Savings Plan match, and the Survivor Benefit Plan election at retirement. Attend the retirement planning seminar well before your date. Know that Fleet Reserve status carries recall liability and specific rules about employment and reporting.
items.hack: Do not let anyone tell you retirement is automatic at twenty, because the paperwork, the Survivor Benefit Plan election, the terminal leave calculation and the VA claim all have to be done by you, on deadlines, in the year before you go. Start eighteen months out. And run the numbers on the last few years honestly: the difference between separating at year seventeen and transferring to the Fleet Reserve at year twenty is a lifetime pension, health care and a multiplier, and people walk away from it over a bad chief and a bad year.
items.deadline: Begin the retirement process 12-18 months out; Survivor Benefit Plan election is made at retirement and is largely irrevocable

items.title: The Blended Retirement System decisions you only get to make once
items.who: Anyone under the Blended Retirement System; anyone who had a legacy election
items.value: Under the Blended Retirement System the government matches Thrift Savings Plan contributions up to a percentage of basic pay, and there is a mid-career continuation pay election in exchange for additional obligated service. Failing to contribute enough to capture the full match is leaving guaranteed compensation on the table every single pay period.
items.how: Confirm which retirement system you are under. Contribute at least enough to receive the maximum government match, and increase it with every advancement. Understand the continuation pay window, the multiplier it uses, and the obligated service it costs, then decide deliberately rather than by default. Review your fund allocation rather than leaving it where it defaulted.
items.hack: If you are not contributing enough to get the full match, you are declining part of your paycheck, and the number of junior enlisted doing exactly that is enormous. Set it the day you check in, raise it one percent with every advancement and every pay raise, and never look at the balance again for ten years. That single automated habit outperforms almost every financial decision you will make in uniform.
items.deadline: Set contributions now; continuation pay election occurs in a specific mid-career window

items.title: Deciding to stay or go, with numbers instead of feelings
items.who: Anyone in a reenlistment window, especially at 6, 10 and 14 years
items.value: The stay-or-go decision is usually made emotionally during a bad tour and then justified afterward. Run as a calculation it looks different: total compensation including the untaxed allowances, the value of a pension at twenty, health care, education benefits, and the real market rate for your skill set with your credentials and clearance.
items.how: Build the comparison honestly. On the military side: base pay, housing and subsistence allowances, special and incentive pays, tax advantages, health care cost, the present value of a pension if you reach it, and education benefits. On the civilian side: actual offers or verified salary data for your credential and clearance in the city you would live in, plus benefits and retirement matching. Then weigh the non-financial: family stability, control over geography, and whether you like the work.
items.hack: Do not make this decision in the last six months of a hard sea tour, which is when almost everybody makes it. Make it on a shore tour, in writing, with real numbers, with your spouse in the room. And get an actual civilian offer if you can, because a hypothetical salary is always bigger than a real one, and a real one is the only thing that makes this comparison honest.
items.deadline: Decide before your reenlistment window closes, not during it

items.title: Build a LinkedIn presence years before you need a job
items.who: Everyone, starting at least three years before separation
items.value: Recruiters source candidates from LinkedIn, and cleared and credentialed veterans are actively hunted. A profile built over years, with a real network, accumulated recommendations and visible expertise, produces inbound opportunity. A profile created six weeks before separation produces nothing.
items.how: Write your headline and summary in civilian language, naming the function and the credentials, not the rate. Translate each tour into scope: budget managed, people led, systems maintained, uptime or readiness achieved, programs owned. List certifications, apprenticeship completion, degrees and clearance level. Connect with every leader you have worked for, every veteran in the companies you would target, and the veteran hiring teams at those companies. Ask for written recommendations from officers and chiefs while they still remember the details.
items.hack: Get your recommendations written while your chief and your division officer still remember what you did, which is now, not in four years when they have had eighty more sailors. Two paragraphs from a lieutenant commander who supervised you is worth more than anything you can write about yourself, and it takes you one message and them ten minutes. Also name the credential in your headline, because recruiters search on the certification, not on your rate abbreviation, which means to a keyword search a rate title is functionally invisible.
items.deadline: Start 3+ years before separation; recommendations are easiest to get while still at the command

items.title: Build the civilian resume years early and translate the jargon out
items.org: Self; transition offices; veteran employment programs
items.who: Everyone, from mid-career onward
items.value: A resume written in military language gets filtered out by applicant tracking systems and by hiring managers who have never served. The same experience, translated into the function, scope and credential language a civilian industry uses, competes at the top of the pile.
items.how: Maintain a running master resume from your brag sheet. For each tour, state the function in civilian terms, the scope in numbers, and the result. Strip rates, hull numbers, acronyms and program names nobody outside the service knows. Mirror the vocabulary of the job postings you are targeting, including the certification names, because those are what get keyword-matched. Have both a veteran and a civilian in your target industry review it.
items.hack: Hand your draft to somebody who has never served and ask them to tell you what you did for a living. If they cannot, the resume is not finished, no matter how impressive it reads to you. Leading Petty Officer of a 24-person work center maintaining $40 million of equipment at 98 percent availability is a resume line. Leading Petty Officer, AIMD IM-3, is not. Build this from your brag sheet years early, because reconstructing it in your last month produces exactly the vague document that gets filtered.
items.deadline: Maintain continuously; polish 12-18 months before separation

items.title: DoD SkillBridge: work a civilian job during your last months in uniform
items.who: Service members within their final 180 days, with command approval
items.value: SkillBridge places you in a civilian industry internship or apprenticeship during your final months of service while you continue to draw military pay and benefits. Many participants are hired directly by the host organization, which means walking out of the service into a job rather than into a search.
items.how: Identify participating organizations in your target industry and location well in advance. Get command approval early, because it is discretionary and commands vary widely in how willing they are to release someone. Confirm the eligibility window, the maximum duration, and that the opportunity is actually structured rather than unpaid labor.
items.hack: Ask your commanding officer for SkillBridge approval twelve months out, not at the 180-day mark, because approval is discretionary and a command that is short-handed will say no to a request that arrives late. Get the yes in writing early, then pick the opportunity. The people who get denied are usually the ones who found the perfect program and then asked.
items.deadline: Final 180 days of service; seek command approval far earlier

items.title: The Transition Assistance Program, started early and taken seriously
items.org: DoD Transition Assistance Program; branch transition offices; VA
items.who: Everyone separating or retiring, active or reserve
items.value: The Transition Assistance Program is mandatory pre-separation counseling plus curriculum covering VA benefits, employment, education and entrepreneurship tracks, financial planning and an individualized transition plan. Started early it is genuinely useful; treated as a checkbox in the last month it is a wasted week.
items.how: Begin as early as your timeline allows, ideally more than a year out rather than at the minimum. Complete the individualized transition plan honestly. Use the VA benefits briefings to start your claim preparation, not just to hear about it. Bring your medical records and your brag sheet.
items.hack: Go to the transition program a year out and then go again near the end, because the first pass tells you what you should have been doing and the second pass is when you actually have documents in hand. Everybody who does it once, in their last month, walks out realizing they missed deadlines that were open for years. Going twice is free.
items.deadline: Begin at least 12 months before separation; mandatory elements have their own timelines

items.title: Cash in every funded credential and course before your end date
items.who: Anyone within two years of separation or retirement
items.value: Credential funding, Tuition Assistance, USMAP completion, apprenticeship certificates and free testing all end when your service does. The last two years are the highest-value window for converting entitlements into permanent assets.
items.how: Two years out, inventory everything unfinished: incomplete apprenticeship hours, credentials with funding available, courses that finish your degree, CLEP and DSST exams that close remaining requirements, and any certification renewals you can push out. Then sequence them so the ones with expiration or renewal cycles land as late as possible.
items.hack: Time your last certification renewal as close to your separation date as you can, so the credential stays current through your entire job search instead of expiring three months in. And finish the apprenticeship hours; people leave with 90 percent of a Department of Labor journeyman card because nobody told them the hours stop counting the day they separate. Check that one specifically.
items.deadline: Complete before your separation or retirement date

items.title: The separation physical and filing before you leave
items.org: VA; DoD; Benefits Delivery at Discharge
items.who: Everyone separating or retiring
items.value: The separation examination is your last chance to get conditions documented in your service record. Pre-discharge claim programs let you file before separation so a decision can be in place at or near your discharge date, rather than waiting many months afterward with no compensation.
items.how: List every condition at the separation physical, including the minor and intermittent ones, and make sure each one is entered. Gather your complete medical record, your own binder documentation, and statements from people who witnessed your injuries or symptoms. File under the pre-discharge program within its window before separation. Get a veterans service organization representative or an accredited representative to review the claim before you submit it.
items.hack: Do not walk out of the separation physical having said you are fine. That appointment is the single most financially consequential hour of your career, and the instinct to look squared away costs people tens of thousands of dollars a year for the rest of their lives. List everything, get copies, and file before you separate so the decision is landing while you still have a paycheck. This is the payoff on the documentation habit you started in year one.
items.deadline: Pre-discharge claims are filed within a defined window before separation; confirm current window

items.title: Audit your DD 214 before you sign it
items.who: Everyone separating or retiring
items.value: The DD Form 214 is the document that proves your service, your character of service, your decorations, your training and your eligibility for nearly every veterans benefit that exists. Errors and omissions on it create years of correction requests, and some benefits are denied outright because an award or a school is missing.
items.how: Review the draft before signing. Verify dates, character of service, narrative reason for separation, reenlistment code, every decoration and award, every school and training entry, and foreign or sea service. Compare it against your binder. Get corrections made before you sign, because afterward it requires a formal records correction process.
items.hack: Compare the draft DD Form 214 against your own binder line by line, not against your memory, because the clerk built it from a record you already know is incomplete. Missing awards and missing schools on a DD Form 214 are the most common reason veterans get denied a benefit they earned, and fixing it afterward means a correction board and eighteen months. You have one afternoon to prevent that.
items.deadline: Before signing at out-processing

items.title: As a senior leader, run the 33% rule downward on purpose
items.who: E-6 and above; officers
items.value: At the senior level your record is built on what your people accomplished, which means developing them is not altruism, it is your performance. Boards read scope and outcomes for your division, not your personal technical work.
items.how: Run career development boards that actually produce a plan, not a signature. Teach your juniors the plays in this section explicitly: the brag sheet, the medical documentation habit, the board scoring sheet, the credential funding, the award they should write themselves. Put your people in for awards without being asked. Push them toward commissioning programs even when it costs you your best performer.
items.hack: Push your best sailor toward the commissioning program or the special program even though losing them will hurt your division, because in five years your reputation will be built entirely on who you produced. Every genuinely respected senior enlisted leader has a list of people they sent somewhere better. The leaders who hoarded talent to protect their own metrics are remembered as exactly that, and the community talks.
items.deadline: Ongoing

items.title: Learn to write and brief, because it is the senior enlisted skill nobody trains
items.who: E-5 and above; anyone aiming at chief or a commission
items.value: Above a certain point the job is writing evaluations, awards, correspondence, instructions and point papers, and briefing officers. The people who can do it clearly get pulled into the jobs with visibility. The people who cannot get filtered out of them quietly.
items.how: Learn your service's correspondence standards and formats. Practice writing evaluation bullets and award citations to standard. Volunteer to write the command's instruction, the point paper, or the brief. Ask a good writer to edit your work and tell you why. Brief standing up, with a time limit, on purpose.
items.hack: Volunteer to write the thing nobody wants to write, then have the best writer in the command tear it apart, and do that four times. Two years of that will put you in front of officers regularly, and being the enlisted person the commanding officer asks to write something is worth more than any collateral duty on the list. It also means when your own award or eval needs writing, you are the one who can do it.
items.deadline: Ongoing

items.title: Protect your record: NJP, page 13s, and the things that end careers
items.who: Everyone
items.value: A single adverse entry, non-judicial punishment, failed drug test, alcohol-related incident, physical readiness failure trend or financial or domestic incident can make you administratively ineligible for advancement, commissioning programs, special programs, clearance retention and retention itself. Recovery is possible but the cost is measured in years.
items.how: Know what goes in your record and check it periodically for entries you did not know about. Read and understand any counseling or administrative remarks entry before signing, and know that signing acknowledges receipt, not agreement, and that you can attach a statement.
