items.deadline: Generally the tax filing deadline for the prior year; combat zone service can extend it

items.title: Backdoor Roth IRA for higher-income years
items.who: Taxpayers whose income exceeds the Roth IRA contribution phase-out - often senior officers and second-career veterans
items.value: A legal, widely used path to Roth contributions after direct contributions phase out.
items.how: Contribute to a traditional IRA (non-deductible if your income is above the deduction threshold), then convert it to a Roth IRA. The conversion is reported on Form 8606. The critical complication is the pro-rata rule: if you hold other pre-tax traditional, SEP, or SIMPLE IRA balances, the conversion is taxed proportionally across all of them, not just the new after-tax dollars. The TSP is not an IRA and does not count in that calculation, which is an advantage military families have. This is well-established and routine, but the mechanics are easy to get wrong. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Because TSP balances are excluded from the pro-rata calculation, a service member who has kept retirement money in the TSP rather than rolling it to an IRA has a cleaner backdoor Roth than most civilians. Think twice before rolling a TSP into an IRA.
items.deadline: Contribution by the tax filing deadline; conversion timing is flexible but affects the tax year

items.title: HSA - the only triple-tax-advantaged account
items.who: Anyone enrolled in a qualifying high-deductible health plan - typically relevant after separation, since TRICARE is not HDHP-qualifying
items.value: Contributions are deductible, growth is untaxed, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are untaxed. No other account does all three.
items.how: You must be covered by an HSA-qualified high-deductible health plan and not be covered by disqualifying other coverage. Contribute, invest the balance rather than leaving it in cash, and pay current medical costs out of pocket if you can afford to - letting the HSA compound. Keep receipts: there is no deadline for reimbursing yourself for a qualified expense, so a receipt from today can fund a tax-free withdrawal decades from now. After a certain age, non-medical withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income without penalty, making it function like a traditional IRA in the worst case. Annual contribution limits and the HDHP deductible thresholds change yearly - see irs.gov. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Active duty members on TRICARE are generally not HSA-eligible. This is a benefit to set up in your civilian second career, not during service - but know it exists before you pick a civilian health plan.
items.deadline: Contributions generally allowed until the tax filing deadline for that year

items.title: Section 121 home-sale exclusion with the military 10-year suspension
items.who: Service members on qualified official extended duty who sell a former primary residence
items.value: Up to $250,000 of gain excluded from tax ($500,000 married filing jointly), with the ownership-and-use clock suspended for up to 10 additional years while you are on qualifying orders.
items.how: The general rule is that you must have owned and lived in the home as your main residence for at least 2 of the 5 years before the sale. Service members can elect to suspend that 5-year period during any time on qualified official extended duty - service at a duty station at least 50 miles from the residence, or living in government quarters under orders, for more than 90 days or an indefinite period. The suspension can run up to 10 years, meaning the effective look-back window can stretch to 15 years. This lets you buy at one duty station, PCS away, rent it out for years, and still sell it under the exclusion. The election generally applies to one property at a time. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Depreciation you claimed while it was a rental is still recaptured and taxed even when the gain itself is excluded. Track your depreciation from the first month you rent it out - your CPA will need that number at sale.
items.deadline: Election is made on the return for the year of sale; the suspension window is limited to 10 years

items.title: Mortgage interest and property tax deductions, even on a home paid for with BAH
items.who: Homeowners who itemize deductions
items.value: You get the BAH exclusion on the way in and, if you itemize, a deduction for mortgage interest and property taxes on the way out.
items.how: Mortgage interest on acquisition debt for a qualified residence is deductible subject to a principal cap, and state and local taxes including property tax are deductible subject to the SALT cap. Both are itemized deductions, so they only help if your total itemized deductions exceed the standard deduction - which, for many military families with modest mortgages, they do not. IRS Publication 3 confirms that using tax-free BAH to pay the mortgage does not disqualify the deduction. The caps and the standard deduction amount change - check irs.gov for current figures before assuming you will itemize. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Run the itemize-versus-standard comparison before you buy a house partly 'for the tax deduction.' For a large share of enlisted families the standard deduction wins and the tax benefit is zero.
items.deadline: Claimed on your annual return

items.title: PCS moving expense deduction - still available to the military
items.who: Active duty members moving under a permanent change of station order
items.value: The moving expense deduction was suspended for nearly everyone else, but active duty members moving on PCS orders kept it.
items.how: If you are on active duty and move pursuant to a military order and incident to a permanent change of station, you can deduct unreimbursed moving expenses on Form 3903 as an above-the-line deduction - meaning you get it whether or not you itemize. Reimbursements and in-kind moves provided by the government are not deducted. Keep receipts for the portion you paid out of pocket. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: A personally procured move (PPM/DITY) has its own tax mechanics - the incentive payment may be taxable income while your actual costs offset it. Keep every weight ticket and receipt.
items.deadline: Claimed on the return for the year of the move

items.title: Reservist travel expense deduction for drills over 100 miles from home
items.who: Guard and Reserve members traveling more than 100 miles from home for drill
items.value: An above-the-line deduction for unreimbursed travel, lodging and meals - available whether or not you itemize.
items.how: If you are a member of a reserve component and travel more than 100 miles away from home and stay overnight in connection with your service, you can deduct unreimbursed travel expenses on Form 2106, carried to Schedule 1 as an adjustment to income. The deduction is capped at the federal per diem rate for the locality. Keep a mileage log and lodging receipts. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Most drilling reservists never claim this. If you have been driving 150 miles each way for years, ask your CPA whether amended returns are worth filing for open years.
items.deadline: Claimed on the annual return; amended returns within the IRS statutory window

items.title: MilTax - free tax prep and filing software with military expertise
items.who: Active duty, Guard, Reserve, and recently separated veterans and their families
items.value: Free federal and multiple state returns, with software that actually understands combat pay, PCS moves, and multi-state residency.
items.how: Access MilTax through Military OneSource. It includes free tax preparation software and free consultation with tax consultants trained on military-specific issues. Many installations also run free VITA sites with IRS-certified volunteers. There is no reason to pay a storefront preparer a percentage of your refund.
items.hack: Never take a refund anticipation loan. The effective annualized cost is enormous and the refund arrives in a couple of weeks anyway with direct deposit.
items.deadline: Generally available January through the filing deadline; combat zone extensions apply

items.title: Electing to include combat pay for the Earned Income Tax Credit
items.who: Lower-income service members who received nontaxable combat pay and may qualify for the EITC
items.value: Because combat pay is excluded from income, a deployment can accidentally lower your earned income enough to shrink or eliminate your EITC. You may elect to count it.
items.how: The EITC is calculated on earned income. Nontaxable combat pay is not automatically included - but you may elect to include all of it (it is all-or-nothing) in the EITC calculation. Depending on where you land on the credit curve, including it may increase or decrease your credit, so it has to be calculated both ways. Good tax software, or a MilTax consultant, will run it both ways for you. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Run it both ways every single year you had combat pay. The right answer flips depending on your income and number of qualifying children, so last year's answer does not carry over.
items.deadline: Election made on the return for that tax year

items.title: Long-term vs short-term capital gains - the one-year line
items.who: Anyone who sells an appreciated asset
items.value: Holding an asset more than one year before selling moves the gain from your ordinary income rate to the preferential long-term rate.
items.how: Hold longer than one year and the gain is long-term, taxed at preferential rates. Sell at one year or less and it is short-term, taxed at your full ordinary income rate - the same rate as your paycheck. Higher-income taxpayers may also owe an additional net investment income tax. Nothing is taxed until you actually sell, which is why simply holding is the cheapest tax strategy available. Current rate brackets and thresholds are published annually at irs.gov. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Check the purchase date before you sell anything. Waiting a few extra weeks to cross the one-year line can be worth more than the price movement you are trying to catch.
items.deadline: Determined by trade date at sale

items.title: Tax-loss harvesting in a taxable brokerage account
items.who: Investors with taxable (non-retirement) accounts holding positions at a loss
items.value: Realized losses offset realized gains, and a limited amount of excess loss can offset ordinary income each year, with the remainder carried forward indefinitely.
items.how: Sell a position that is down, realize the loss, and use it to offset capital gains. Excess losses offset ordinary income up to an annual cap set by the IRS, and anything beyond that carries forward to future years without expiration. The wash sale rule disallows the loss if you buy the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the sale - so you either sit out 31 days or buy a genuinely different fund. This does nothing inside a TSP or IRA, where gains and losses are not taxed. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Carryforward losses never expire. A loss harvested in a bad market year can shelter a gain from selling a rental property a decade later.
items.deadline: Trades must settle within the tax year; December is when most harvesting happens

items.title: Depreciation - the paper deduction that makes rentals work
items.who: Owners of rental property
items.value: A deduction you take every year without spending a dollar, which can make a cash-flow-positive rental show a tax loss.
items.how: The IRS lets you deduct the cost of a residential rental building over 27.5 years (39 for commercial), starting when the property is placed in service as a rental. Land is never depreciable, so you must allocate the purchase price between land and building - your property tax assessment is a common starting point. Because you write off the building while it may actually be appreciating, depreciation shelters rental income from tax. Two catches: rental losses are generally passive and limited in how much other income they can offset (with exceptions for active participation and for real estate professional status), and depreciation is recaptured and taxed when you sell. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Depreciation is not optional in practice - the IRS recaptures depreciation 'allowed or allowable' at sale whether or not you claimed it. Not claiming it does not save you at sale; it just wastes the deduction.
items.deadline: Begins the month the property is available for rent; claimed annually on Schedule E

items.title: 1031 like-kind exchange - deferring gain on investment real estate
items.who: Owners selling investment or business real property who are reinvesting in other real property
items.value: Defers capital gains tax and depreciation recapture when you roll the proceeds into another investment property.
items.how: Since 2018, section 1031 applies only to real property held for investment or productive use in a trade or business - not personal residences, not vehicles, not equipment. The mechanics are strict: you must use a qualified intermediary and never take possession of the proceeds; you must identify replacement property in writing within 45 days of the sale; and you must close on the replacement within 180 days. You must generally trade equal or up in value and debt, or you recognize gain on the difference ('boot'). This is deferral, not elimination - the deferred gain rides along in your basis in the new property. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Line up the qualified intermediary BEFORE you close on the sale. If the proceeds touch your bank account, the exchange is dead and there is no fix.
items.deadline: 45 days to identify, 180 days to close - both run from the sale closing date and are not extendable

items.title: Qualified business income deduction (section 199A)
items.who: Owners of pass-through businesses - sole proprietorships, partnerships, S corporations, and many rental activities
items.value: A deduction of up to 20% of qualified business income, taken on your personal return without reducing your business's own books.
items.how: Eligible taxpayers may deduct up to 20% of qualified business income from a domestic pass-through business. Above certain taxable income thresholds the deduction becomes limited by W-2 wages paid and the unadjusted basis of qualified property, and specified service trades or businesses (health, law, accounting, consulting, financial services, and others) phase out entirely above the thresholds. Rental activity may qualify if it rises to the level of a trade or business; the IRS published a safe harbor with specific recordkeeping requirements. The income thresholds are indexed and change annually - look them up at irs.gov. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: The safe harbor for rental real estate requires contemporaneous time logs. Start the log the day you place the property in service; reconstructing it at audit does not work.
items.deadline: Claimed on the annual return

items.title: S corporation election and the reasonable compensation requirement
items.who: Owner-operators of profitable small businesses, generally once net profit is substantial
items.value: An S election can reduce self-employment tax on the portion of profit taken as a distribution rather than salary - but only within limits the IRS enforces.
items.how: An LLC or corporation that elects S status pays the owner-employee a W-2 salary subject to payroll tax, and remaining profit passes through as a distribution not subject to self-employment tax. The catch is the reasonable compensation requirement: the salary must reflect the market value of the work you actually perform. The leading case, Watson v. United States, upheld the IRS recharacterizing distributions as wages where the owner's salary was far below market for his role, resulting in back payroll tax plus interest and penalties. Document how you set the salary using industry compensation data. The election also adds payroll processing and a separate business return, which costs money - it generally does not pay below a meaningful profit level. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Ask your CPA to run the break-even: at what net profit does the payroll and compliance cost of an S election get exceeded by the payroll tax savings? Below that number, it is a net loss.
items.deadline: Form 2553 generally due within 2 months and 15 days of the start of the tax year the election takes effect

items.title: What an LLC actually protects you from - and what it does not
items.who: Anyone considering an LLC for a business or rental property
items.value: Real liability separation between business creditors and your personal assets - within clear limits that are widely oversold.
items.how: A properly formed and maintained LLC generally shields the owner's personal assets from claims against the business. What it does NOT do: it does not protect you from your own negligence or personal acts; it does not defeat a personal guarantee, which lenders almost always require from small business and small landlord borrowers; it does not by itself reduce your taxes, since a single-member LLC is disregarded for federal tax purposes by default; and it does not survive if you ignore the formalities. The fastest way to lose the protection is commingling - running business money through a personal account. Maintain a separate bank account, a written operating agreement, and documentation of significant decisions. Note also that most U.S. entities face federal beneficial ownership reporting requirements whose status has shifted with litigation - verify the current rule with counsel. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: If you personally guaranteed the loan on your rental, the LLC does not protect you from that lender. Ask what your actual exposure is before paying for a multi-entity structure someone drew on a whiteboard.
items.deadline: Form before you take on the activity, not after a claim arises

items.title: Umbrella liability insurance - the cheapest asset protection there is
items.who: Anyone with meaningful assets, especially landlords and anyone with teen drivers
items.value: Typically one to five million dollars of additional liability coverage above your auto and homeowner policies, for a few hundred dollars a year.
items.how: An umbrella policy sits on top of the liability limits of your auto, home and rental dwelling policies and pays after those limits are exhausted. It also usually covers defense costs, which can exceed the judgment itself. Insurers require you to carry minimum underlying limits first. For most families this is a far better use of money than an elaborate entity structure, because it pays claims rather than merely making you harder to collect from.
items.hack: Before you pay an attorney for a multi-LLC asset protection plan, price an umbrella policy. For the overwhelming majority of veterans and small landlords, insurance solves the actual problem at a tenth of the cost.
items.deadline: Buy before the accident; coverage is not retroactive

items.title: Homestead exemptions and disabled veteran property tax relief
items.who: Homeowners, with expanded benefits for rated disabled veterans in most states
items.value: Reduces or in some states eliminates property tax on a primary residence for qualifying disabled veterans, and in some states protects home equity from creditors.
items.how: Two separate things share the word 'homestead.' The tax version is a state or county exemption that reduces your assessed value; many states offer a much larger exemption, or a complete exemption, for veterans with a qualifying service-connected rating, and some extend it to surviving spouses. The creditor version is a state law protecting some or all of your home equity from judgment creditors - unlimited in a few states, capped or nonexistent in others. Both are governed entirely by state law and both generally require you to apply; they are not automatic. Check your county assessor's office and your state department of veterans affairs. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: File the application the year you close and the year your rating changes. Many counties will not backdate more than a year, so a missed filing is money gone.
items.deadline: County filing deadlines are typically early in the year - check yours

items.title: VA home loan - no down payment, no PMI
items.who: Eligible service members, veterans, and some surviving spouses
items.value: The strongest mortgage product available to any borrower in the country: zero down payment, no private mortgage insurance, and competitive rates.
items.how: The VA guarantees a portion of the loan to the lender, which is why lenders accept no down payment. With full entitlement there is no VA-imposed loan limit - your ceiling is what a lender says you can afford. There is no PMI, which on a conventional low-down-payment loan can cost hundreds of dollars a month. Most borrowers pay a one-time VA funding fee, which can be financed into the loan. Get your Certificate of Eligibility through VA.gov or have your lender pull it. Shop at least three lenders: the VA program is standard but lender rates, fees and underwriting overlays are not.
items.hack: No down payment means you start with no equity. Budget for the fact that you cannot sell in year two without bringing money to closing, because the sale costs alone will exceed your equity.
items.deadline: Entitlement does not expire; get your COE before you shop

items.title: VA funding fee exemption for rated disabled veterans
items.who: Veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability rated 10% or higher, and certain others
items.value: Eliminates the one-time VA funding fee entirely - on a large loan this is thousands of dollars.
items.how: Veterans receiving or entitled to receive VA disability compensation for a service-connected condition are exempt from the funding fee. Certain surviving spouses and some Purple Heart recipients on active duty also qualify. Your Certificate of Eligibility indicates exemption status. If your rating is granted after you closed and the effective date of the rating precedes your loan closing, you may be entitled to a refund of the fee you paid.
items.hack: If your rating came through retroactively after you already bought, contact your lender and the VA regional loan center about a funding fee refund. Many veterans are owed this and never ask.
items.deadline: Exemption applies at closing; refunds are pursued after a retroactive rating decision

items.title: Reusing and restoring VA loan entitlement across duty stations
items.who: Veterans and service members who already used a VA loan
items.value: VA entitlement is not one-and-done. You can restore it after selling and paying off the loan, and in many cases you can have more than one VA loan at a time using remaining entitlement.
items.how: When you sell a VA-financed home and pay off the loan, you can apply to have entitlement restored for full reuse. A one-time restoration is also available in some circumstances without selling. Separately, if you have remaining entitlement you may be able to buy a new primary residence at a new duty station while keeping the first home as a rental - the second loan may require a down payment depending on how much entitlement remains and the county loan limit. Work this out with a VA-experienced lender before you PCS, not after you get orders.
items.hack: Start the entitlement conversation with a lender 6-9 months before your projected PCS. Restoration paperwork and rental history documentation both take time you will not have during a move.
items.deadline: Begin well before your PCS; entitlement restoration is a paperwork process

items.title: Buying at each duty station - the strategy and its honest risks
items.who: Service members with stable orders and adequate reserves
items.value: Over a 20-year career with 5-7 duty stations, buying and holding as rentals can build a meaningful portfolio that a single-location civilian cannot easily replicate.
items.how: Use the VA loan for a primary residence at a duty station, live in it as required by the loan's occupancy terms, and convert it to a rental when you PCS. Repeat with restored or remaining entitlement. The honest risks: you may get orders in 18 months to a market that has not appreciated; every property needs its own reserve fund; managing from overseas is hard; and a vacancy on a zero-down loan hits fast because there is no equity cushion. The strategy works for people who buy conservatively in rentable markets near base, not for people who buy the maximum they are approved for.
items.hack: Buy something that rents well, not something that shows well. Proximity to the gate, three bedrooms, and a floor plan military families want beats granite countertops every time.
items.deadline: Evaluate each PCS independently - this is not a strategy you commit to once

items.title: Occupancy requirements: tell your lender the truth
items.who: Anyone using a VA loan or any owner-occupant financing
items.value: Protects you from mortgage fraud exposure, loan acceleration, and loss of VA benefits.
items.how: VA loans are for a home you intend to occupy as your primary residence, generally within a reasonable time after closing, with specific accommodations for deployment, PCS, and occupancy by a spouse or dependent child in defined circumstances. Owner-occupant financing carries better terms than investor financing precisely because of that requirement. If your plan is to rent the property out immediately, say so and get investor financing. Signing an occupancy certification you do not intend to honor is a false statement on a federally related loan.
items.hack: If circumstances change after you honestly occupied - orders, a deployment, a family situation - document the change and notify the servicer. Changed circumstances are normal and fine. Misrepresenting intent at signing is not.
items.deadline: At application and closing

items.title: VA Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan (IRRRL)
items.who: Veterans with an existing VA loan
items.value: A streamlined refinance to a lower rate with reduced documentation - often no new appraisal and no new income verification.
items.how: The IRRRL, sometimes called a VA streamline, refinances an existing VA loan into a new VA loan at a lower rate or from an adjustable to a fixed rate. It generally requires no appraisal and no credit underwriting package, and costs can be rolled into the loan. It is not a cash-out loan - VA has a separate cash-out refinance product with full underwriting. Compare the total cost including the funding fee (reduced for IRRRLs, and waived for exempt veterans) against your break-even period.
items.hack: Beware of aggressive IRRRL solicitation mail that looks official. VA and your servicer do not cold-mail you urgent refinance demands. Check the lender independently and calculate the break-even in months before signing.
items.deadline: Anytime rates make the break-even math work

items.title: Rent it or sell it? The PCS decision framework
items.who: Homeowners receiving PCS orders
items.value: The single biggest real estate decision most military families make, and it is usually made under time pressure with bad information.
items.how: Run three numbers. First, the sell number: what you net after agent commission, closing costs and repairs - and whether that covers your loan balance. Second, the rent number: realistic market rent minus mortgage, taxes, insurance, HOA, a management fee, a vacancy allowance, and a maintenance reserve. If that is negative, you are paying every month to be a landlord. Third, the tax number: the section 121 exclusion with the military suspension may let you sell tax-free years later, but depreciation recapture accrues while it is rented. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Get a property manager's honest rent estimate, not a Zillow estimate, and subtract 10% for vacancy plus 1% of the home's value annually for maintenance before you call it cash-flow positive.
items.deadline: Start the analysis the day orders drop, not 30 days out

items.title: Property management when you are deployed or stationed far away
items.who: Long-distance and deployed landlords
items.value: A manager is the difference between a rental being an asset and a rental being a second job you cannot perform from a forward location.
items.how: A residential manager typically charges a percentage of collected rent plus a leasing fee for placing a tenant. What you are buying: tenant screening, rent collection, maintenance dispatch, legal compliance with your state's landlord-tenant law, and someone with a key who is in the same time zone as the property. Interview at least three. Ask for their tenant screening criteria in writing, their average days-to-lease, how maintenance approval thresholds work, and whether they hold a separate trust account for owner funds. Check their state real estate license status. Separately, budget a vacancy allowance (commonly 5-10% of annual rent, higher in single-base towns), ongoing maintenance (roughly 1% of property value per year, or about 10% of rent), and a capital reserve for the roof, HVAC and water heater that will eventually fail. Hold several months of the full payment in reserve per property. A rental that is cash-flow positive only if nothing breaks and it is never vacant is not cash-flow positive.
items.hack: Read the management agreement's termination clause before you sign. Some lock you in for a year and charge a fee to leave, which is how bad managers keep clients.
items.deadline: Have the manager lined up before your PCS date, not after the house sits empty

items.title: Legacy High-3 retirement - how the pension is calculated
items.who: Members who entered service before 1 Jan 2018 and did not opt into BRS
items.value: An immediate, COLA-adjusted pension for life starting the day you retire at 20 years, with no bridge period.
items.how: The multiplier is 2.5% per year of creditable service, applied to the average of your highest 36 months of basic pay ('high-3'). At 20 years that is 50% of high-3; at 30 years it is 75%. It starts immediately upon retirement from active duty and is adjusted annually for cost of living. Under High-3 there is no government TSP match - you may contribute to the TSP but the agency match is a BRS feature. A separate CSB/REDUX variant, which involved a career status bonus and a reduced multiplier, applied to a defined earlier cohort. Military retired pay is taxable at the federal level; state treatment varies widely.
items.hack: Because there is no TSP match under High-3, your TSP contribution rate has to do more work. Do not assume the pension alone replaces a retirement portfolio - it replaces roughly half of one income, before taxes.
items.deadline: Vesting at 20 years of creditable active service; retirement application through your service

items.title: Blended Retirement System - smaller pension, portable TSP match
items.who: Generally members who entered service on or after 1 Jan 2018, plus those who opted in during the election window
items.value: A 2.0% per year multiplier instead of 2.5%, offset by automatic and matching TSP contributions that you keep even if you serve fewer than 20 years.
items.how: The pension multiplier is 2.0% per year of service on high-3 average basic pay: 40% at 20 years, 60% at 30 years. In exchange, the government automatically contributes 1% of basic pay to your TSP and matches up to an additional 4% when you contribute 5%. BRS also includes continuation pay - a mid-career cash bonus paid in exchange for an additional service obligation, with the multiplier set by each service. The core design tradeoff: roughly 80% of the legacy pension, but the roughly 80% of service members who separate before 20 years now leave with something instead of nothing.
items.hack: BRS is only 'worse' than High-3 if you actually make it to 20 years AND you do not invest the match. A BRS member who contributes at least 5% from day one and stays in equity funds can close much of the gap over a full career.
items.deadline: Contribute at least 5% every pay period; continuation pay election windows are service-specific and time-limited

items.title: The BRS lump-sum option - understand the discount before you take it
items.who: BRS retirees at the point of retirement
items.value: An option to take 25% or 50% of the present value of your retired pay as a lump sum, in exchange for reduced monthly payments until you reach full Social Security retirement age.
items.how: At retirement a BRS member may elect a lump sum equal to 25% or 50% of the discounted present value of their retired pay through full Social Security retirement age. In exchange, monthly retired pay is reduced by that same percentage until full retirement age, at which point it reverts to the full amount. The critical variable is the discount rate DoD uses to compute the present value - it has historically been well above the return most people would earn on the money, which means the lump sum is worth considerably less than the stream of payments it replaces. The election is irrevocable. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Ask for the actual discount rate applied to your calculation in writing and compare it to what you realistically expect to earn. If the discount rate is higher than your expected return, you are selling your pension at a loss. Most financial analyses conclude the lump sum is unfavorable for most retirees.
items.deadline: Elected at retirement; the decision is irrevocable

items.title: Reserve and Guard retirement - the points system and age 60
items.who: Guard and Reserve members with 20 qualifying years
items.value: A pension based on accumulated retirement points rather than years of active service, generally payable starting at age 60.
items.how: You earn retirement points for drills, annual training, active duty days, and membership. A year counts as 'qualifying' toward the 20-year requirement when you earn the minimum required points in that retirement year. The pension is computed by dividing your total career points by 360 to get equivalent years, then applying the multiplier (2.5% under legacy, 2.0% under BRS) to your high-3 average basic pay. Payment normally begins at age 60, but qualifying active duty service performed after a statutory date can reduce the start age in 90-day increments, subject to a floor. Request your points statement annually and correct errors while the records still exist.
items.hack: Audit your points statement every single year. Reconstructing a missing period of credit five years later, after a unit has been reorganized and the personnel clerk has moved on, is extremely difficult.
items.deadline: Check points annually; apply for retired pay in advance of your eligibility age

items.title: How to think about 20 years versus 30 years
items.who: Mid-career members deciding whether to continue past 20
items.value: The right answer depends on your specific multiplier, your second-career earning potential, and your health - not on a general rule.
items.how: Structurally, serving to 30 raises your multiplier from 50% to 75% of high-3 under legacy, or 40% to 60% under BRS, and raises the high-3 base itself through promotion and longevity. Against that, retiring at 20 starts a civilian career ten years earlier, which means ten more years of civilian earnings, ten more years of civilian retirement contributions and employer match, and ten more years for a second-career pension or equity to vest. The published comparisons that exist generally find that retiring at 20 wins when the civilian job is strong and the member is enlisted or mid-grade, while staying to 30 wins when the promotion trajectory is steep (senior officer) or the civilian earning potential is modest. Build your own model with your actual numbers rather than trusting anyone's table, including one built on a prior year's pay charts. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: The variable that swings the answer most is not the pension - it is the civilian salary you can realistically command at 40 versus 50. Get honest about that number before you model anything else.
items.deadline: Decide with enough lead time to plan the transition, typically 24 months out

items.title: Survivor Benefit Plan - the election you make once, at retirement
items.who: Retiring members with a spouse or dependents
items.value: Continues a percentage of your retired pay to a surviving beneficiary for life. Without it, retired pay stops the day you die.
items.how: SBP pays a designated annuity to your surviving spouse or eligible beneficiary, funded by a premium deducted from your retired pay. The default at retirement is full spouse coverage; declining or reducing it requires your spouse's notarized concurrence. Premiums are paid with pre-tax dollars and the annuity is taxable to the survivor. The election is generally irrevocable with a narrow withdrawal window years after retirement. Compare it against the cost of equivalent term life insurance - but understand that SBP is a government-backed, COLA-adjusted lifetime annuity, which private term insurance is not.
items.hack: Do not decide this in the last week before retirement. Model it: what does your spouse actually live on if you die at 55, and does your portfolio plus life insurance cover it without SBP?
items.deadline: Elected at retirement, before your retirement date; spousal concurrence required to decline

items.title: Estate basics: will, beneficiary designations, power of attorney, advance directive
items.who: Everyone, and urgently anyone deploying
items.value: Free at your legal assistance office, and it determines what happens to everything you own if you do not come home.
items.how: Four documents. A will directs assets that pass through probate and names a guardian for minor children. Beneficiary designations on your TSP, SGLI, IRAs and bank accounts pass OUTSIDE the will and override it - which is why an outdated designation naming an ex-spouse is the single most common estate failure. A durable power of attorney lets someone handle your financial affairs while you are deployed; a special power of attorney limits that authority to defined acts. An advance medical directive and healthcare power of attorney state your medical wishes. Installation legal assistance prepares all of these at no cost.
items.hack: Review every beneficiary designation after every marriage, divorce, birth and death in the family. The form controls, not your intentions and not your will.
items.deadline: Before every deployment, and after every major life event

items.title: Revocable living trusts - what they actually do
items.who: Families with real property in multiple states, minor children, or privacy concerns
items.value: Avoids probate, keeps the estate private, and provides for management of assets if you become incapacitated.
items.how: A revocable living trust holds title to assets you transfer into it during your life. Because the trust, not you personally, owns those assets at death, they pass by the trust's terms without going through probate court. You keep full control and can amend or revoke it while competent. What it does NOT do: a revocable trust provides no asset protection from your own creditors and no income tax benefit - it is a probate and incapacity tool, not a tax shelter. The trust only works for assets actually retitled into it; an unfunded trust is an expensive piece of paper. Irrevocable trusts are a genuinely different instrument with different tradeoffs, and require counsel. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: The most common failure is a trust that was drafted and never funded. After signing, actually retitle the deeds and accounts. Ask your attorney for a funding checklist and work it to completion.
items.deadline: Draft when circumstances warrant; fund it immediately after signing

items.title: Alternative investments - what they are and the questions to ask first
items.who: Investors who already max tax-advantaged accounts and hold a diversified core portfolio
items.value: Real estate syndications, private credit, REITs, commodities, farmland platforms, private equity funds and crypto can add diversification - and add illiquidity, opacity and fee layers.
items.how: Before committing a dollar, get answers in writing to five questions: What exactly do I own, legally? What are ALL the fees, including acquisition, management, and carried interest? When can I get my money out, and under what conditions can the sponsor refuse? What is the sponsor's track record through a full down cycle, verified independently? And what regulatory regime applies - is this a registered offering, a Regulation D private placement, or unregistered? Many private offerings require accredited investor status. Check every person selling you something on FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure before you wire anything.
items.hack: The correct size for a first alternative investment is an amount you can lose entirely without changing your life. If a sponsor pressures you to move faster than your ability to do diligence, that pressure IS the diligence result.
items.deadline: Diligence before funding; most private offerings have no secondary market and no exit

items.title: The boring core: low-cost, broadly diversified index funds
items.who: Every investor, at every income level
items.value: The TSP's expense ratios are among the lowest available anywhere. Costs are the one part of investment returns you can control with certainty.
items.how: Inside the TSP: the C Fund tracks large U.S. companies, the S Fund covers the rest of the U.S. market, the I Fund covers international developed and emerging markets, the F Fund is a broad bond index, and the G Fund is government securities that cannot lose nominal value. The L (Lifecycle) Funds are pre-mixed portfolios that shift more conservative as the target date approaches, and are a reasonable default for anyone who does not want to manage an allocation. The dominant failure mode among service members is the opposite of recklessness: over-allocating to the G Fund for decades, where inflation quietly erodes purchasing power. Pick an allocation you can hold through a 40% drawdown without selling, and then leave it alone. One free refinement: hold tax-inefficient things (bonds, REITs, high-turnover funds) inside the TSP or an IRA where the tax does not apply, and hold broad low-turnover stock index funds in a taxable account where their qualified dividends and deferred gains get preferential rates. That is called asset location, and it changes your tax bill without changing what you own. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Rebalance on a schedule - once or twice a year - not on the news. The behavior gap between what funds return and what investors in those funds actually earn is caused almost entirely by trading at the wrong moments.
items.deadline: Set allocation now; review annually

items.title: SBA veteran business programs and SDVOSB certification
items.who: Veterans and service-disabled veterans starting or running a business
items.value: Free training, counseling, and access to federal contracting set-asides reserved for service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses.
items.how: Boots to Business is a free entrepreneurship course available through the TAP curriculum while you are still in uniform, with follow-on courses for veterans and spouses. Veterans Business Outreach Centers provide free counseling nationwide. SDVOSB and VOSB certification, now administered through SBA's Veteran Small Business Certification program, makes you eligible for federal contracting set-asides where agencies can award directly to certified firms. Certification requires documented ownership and control by the qualifying veteran - it is verified, not self-declared.
items.hack: Start the certification paperwork before you need a contract. Processing takes months and no contracting officer will wait for you.
items.deadline: Boots to Business while on active duty; certification whenever you form the business

items.title: Recordkeeping and estimated taxes for a side business
items.who: Anyone with self-employment or rental income not subject to withholding
items.value: Keeps deductions defensible and prevents an underpayment penalty at filing.
items.how: Separate business bank account and card from day one. Keep contemporaneous records: a mileage log with dates and business purpose, receipts, and a written explanation for anything unusual. The IRS standard for a deductible business expense is ordinary and necessary for the business - not merely 'I spent money and I have a business.' Income without withholding generally requires quarterly estimated tax payments; safe harbor rules based on your prior year's tax can protect you from penalties. The hobby loss rules limit deductions for activities not conducted with a genuine profit motive. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Adjust your W-4 withholding on your military or civilian W-2 job instead of making quarterly payments. Withholding is treated as paid evenly across the year, which can cure an underpayment that quarterly payments would not.
items.deadline: Estimated payments are generally quarterly; recordkeeping is continuous

items.title: Why build wealth: defining the actual objective
items.who: Everyone
items.value: Strategy without a stated objective turns into accumulation for its own sake, which is how people end up asset-rich and life-poor.
items.how: Write down, in your own words, what the money is for. Common answers from the military community: the freedom to walk away from a job you hate; being your own boss; time with family instead of time in someone else's building; travel and seeing the cultures you were deployed near but never saw; philanthropy and helping people who are still struggling; owning real estate at every place you were stationed; and generational wealth so your kids start where you finished. Then work backward: each objective implies a different number, a different time horizon, and a different level of risk. 'Financial independence at 50' and 'leave a business to my children' are not the same plan.
items.hack: Put the number and the date on one page and keep it where you see it. Every financial decision after that becomes a simple test: does this move me toward that number by that date, or not?
items.deadline: Now, and revisited annually

items.title: Choosing a CPA, tax attorney, or financial advisor
items.who: Anyone whose situation has grown beyond free counseling
items.value: The difference between an advisor who is legally obligated to act in your interest and one who is paid to sell you a product.
items.how: Know the three roles. A CPA or Enrolled Agent handles tax preparation and planning and can represent you before the IRS; an EA's credential is federal and tax-specific, a CPA's is state-licensed and broader. A tax attorney is for structure, disputes, and anything with legal risk, and provides attorney-client privilege that an accountant generally does not. A financial advisor manages investments and planning - ask directly, in writing, whether they are a fiduciary at all times, how they are compensated, and whether they receive commissions on anything they recommend. Verify credentials: CPA with the state board, EA with the IRS directory, and any securities or advisory person through FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's adviser database.
items.hack: Ask one question: 'Are you a fiduciary to me at all times, and will you put that in writing?' The answer, and how quickly it comes, tells you almost everything.
items.deadline: Before you act on any strategy with real money at stake

items.title: The line between tax avoidance and tax evasion
items.who: Everyone reading anything about tax strategy
items.value: Knowing where the line sits is what lets you use legitimate planning confidently and recognize a promoter's pitch immediately.
items.how: Arranging your affairs to minimize tax using provisions Congress wrote is lawful and is what every item in this section describes - contributing to a Roth TSP, claiming depreciation, using the section 121 exclusion. Concealing income, falsifying records, claiming deductions for things that did not happen, or misrepresenting facts to the IRS, a lender, or the VA is a federal crime. Between them sits a gray zone the IRS polices with the economic substance and business purpose doctrines: a transaction must have a real non-tax purpose and change your economic position, not merely generate a deduction. The IRS publishes listed and reportable transactions that require disclosure, and maintains an annual 'Dirty Dozen' list of schemes. If a strategy requires you to say something to anyone that is not true, it is not a strategy. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Three warning signs of a promoted scheme: it is sold by the person who profits from your entering it, the fee is a percentage of your claimed tax savings, and you are told not to discuss the details with your regular CPA.
items.deadline: Apply the test before every transaction

items.title: Every dollar figure in tax law moves - here is where to look it up
items.who: Everyone using this section
items.value: Prevents the most common financial planning error: acting on a contribution limit, bracket, or benefit rate that was accurate two years ago.
items.how: Contribution limits (TSP elective deferral, catch-up, annual additions, IRA, HSA), tax brackets, standard deduction, capital gains thresholds, phase-out ranges for the Saver's Credit and Roth eligibility, VA compensation rates, and BAH and basic pay tables all change annually - most with inflation indexing, some by legislation. Bookmark four places and check them each January: irs.gov for limits, brackets and credits; tsp.gov for contribution limits and fund information; va.gov for compensation rates and loan program terms; and militarypay.defense.gov for pay and allowance tables. Tax treatment depends on your individual facts - confirm with a CPA or tax attorney before acting.
items.hack: Any financial article, course, or reference that states a specific dollar limit without a year attached is either out of date or about to be. Always check the primary source before you act.
items.deadline: Every January, and before any major transaction

items.title: PCAFC has two separate eligibility doors — almost everyone only knows the first
items.who: Veterans with a 70%+ service-connected rating who need personal care services for at least six continuous months
items.value: Entry to the only VA program that pays a family member a monthly stipend
items.how: 38 CFR 71.20(a)(3) states the six-month need must arise from EITHER (i) an inability to perform an activity of daily living, OR (ii) a need for supervision, protection, or instruction. These are alternatives, not a combined test. A veteran who can dress, bathe and walk unaided but cannot be left alone safely because of TBI, PTSD, seizures, dementia or psychosis qualifies through door two. Families with a psychiatric or cognitive injury routinely self-reject because they read only the ADL list and conclude they do not qualify.
items.hack: If the injury is cognitive, psychiatric or neurological, build the entire application around door two — supervision, protection, instruction — and do not waste the narrative arguing about bathing and dressing. Name the specific daily safety failures: wandering, leaving the stove on, mismanaging medication, losing orientation, driving when impaired, suicidal ideation requiring presence.
items.deadline: No application deadline; the six-month need must be prospective or established

items.title: The 70% gate is individual OR combined — and it is a rating gate, not a diagnosis gate
items.who: Veterans and servicemembers with a medical discharge date
items.value: The threshold that decides whether PCAFC is even available
items.how: 38 CFR 71.15 defines 'serious injury' for PCAFC as any service-connected disability rated 70% or more individually, or a combined service-connected rating of 70% or more. One 70% rating works. Several smaller ratings that combine to 70% work. The injury does not have to be the thing that causes the care need — the rating is a gate, and the care need is assessed separately.
items.hack: If the veteran is at 60% combined, the real PCAFC task is a rating increase or a secondary-condition claim first. Nothing in PCAFC can be argued around the 70% wall. Servicemembers still on active duty with a medical discharge date can apply before separation, so the stipend starts the day care begins rather than months later.

items.title: The exact seven activities of daily living VA scores — door one, verbatim
items.who: PCAFC applicants arguing physical care need
items.value: The list the clinician is actually filling in
items.how: Under 38 CFR 71.15, 'inability to perform an activity of daily living' means the veteran requires personal care services each time they complete one or more of: dressing or undressing; bathing or grooming to avoid hazard to health; adjusting a prosthetic or orthopedic appliance that the veteran cannot do without aid; toileting (including bowel and bladder control, and attending to the needs of nature); feeding, where the veteran cannot feed themselves through loss of coordination of the upper extremities, extreme weakness, inability to swallow, or the need for nutrition by non-oral means; and mobility, including walking, climbing stairs, and transferring in and out of bed or a chair.
items.hack: The phrase 'each time they complete' is the whole fight. Occasional help does not count; help every single time does. Document frequency, not difficulty — 'requires physical assistance for every transfer, approximately 9 times daily' beats 'struggles with mobility.' Keep a two-week log before the home visit and hand it to the assessor.

items.title: Door two defined: 'need for supervision, protection, or instruction' is a personal-safety standard
items.who: Caregivers of veterans with TBI, PTSD, psychosis, dementia, seizure disorders or severe depression
items.value: The route to a full stipend with zero ADL impairment
items.how: 38 CFR 71.15 defines it as 'a functional impairment that directly impacts the individual's ability to maintain his or her personal safety on a daily basis.' Two words carry the weight: 'daily' and 'safety.' Not occasional. Not inconvenience. Not emotional support. The impairment must threaten the veteran's own safety, every day, and the caregiver's presence must be what prevents harm.
items.hack: Write the application in incident form, not adjective form. 'Veteran left the gas range lit twice in March; wandered from the home at night on 14 Feb requiring police assistance; requires medication handed over dose by dose after a double-dose event in January' is a winning record. 'Veteran has bad PTSD and needs me around' is a denial.

items.title: 'In need of personal care services' is a counterfactual test — what happens if you walk away
items.who: All PCAFC applicants
items.value: The framing that decides borderline cases
items.how: 38 CFR 71.15 defines the term as requiring in-person personal care services from another person, where 'without such personal care services, alternative in-person caregiving arrangements (including respite care or assistance of an alternative caregiver) would be required.' The assessor is deciding whether, if the family caregiver stopped tomorrow, VA would have to buy someone else to do it.
items.hack: Answer that question explicitly in the application: 'If I stopped, he would require a paid aide a minimum of X hours daily, or placement.' That is the sentence the regulation is written around. A caregiver who downplays their role out of pride is writing their own denial.

items.title: The four hidden PCAFC conditions nobody reads in 38 CFR 71.20(a)
items.who: All PCAFC applicants
items.value: Four quiet ways to be denied or revoked
items.how: Beyond the rating, the six months and the care need, 71.20(a) also requires that: participation is in the best interest of the veteran; personal care services are not simultaneously and regularly provided by or through another individual or entity (a paid agency doing the same hours is a conflict); the veteran receives care at home or will upon designation of a Family Caregiver; and the veteran receives ongoing care from a VA primary care team or will upon designation. Failing items 5, 6 or 7 later is a ground for revocation under 71.45(a)(1)(ii).
items.hack: If the veteran currently has agency home health covering the same tasks, expect a conflict finding. Sort out which hours are VA-purchased aide hours and which are family hours before you file, and get the veteran established with a VA primary care team first — community-care-only veterans get tripped by condition 7.

items.title: 'Unable to self-sustain in the community' — the four words that nearly double the stipend
items.who: PCAFC Primary Family Caregivers seeking the higher stipend tier
items.value: The difference between the 62.5% tier and the 100% tier
items.how: 38 CFR 71.15 defines it as a veteran who (a) requires personal care services each time they complete three or more activities of daily living and is fully dependent on a caregiver to complete them, OR (b) has a need for supervision, protection, or instruction on a continuous basis. 'Three or more ADLs with full dependency' and 'continuous' supervision are the two tests. Meet either and the stipend multiplier goes from 0.625 to 1.00.
items.hack: Count the ADLs out loud against the regulation's own seven-item list before the assessment and be ready to name three with full dependency. On the supervision side, 'continuous' means it cannot be scheduled or intermittent — document that the veteran cannot be left alone for any meaningful period, with the incidents that prove it.
items.deadline: Tier is set at approval and re-examined at each reassessment

items.title: PCAFC's era phase-in is complete — every service era is now eligible
items.who: Veterans of all eras, including Vietnam, Korea, WWII and the 1975-2001 gap
items.value: Eligibility for veterans repeatedly told the program was for post-9/11 only
items.how: Under 38 CFR 71.20(a)(2) the serious injury must have been incurred or aggravated in the line of duty on or after 11 September 2001; or on or before 7 May 1975 (opened 1 October 2020); or after 7 May 1975 and before 11 September 2001 (opened 1 October 2022). All three windows are now open, so the era restriction is effectively gone.
items.hack: Older veterans and their spouses were turned away for a decade and never came back. If a family was told no before October 2022, that answer is stale — reapply. Nothing carries over from an old denial, so a fresh VA Form 10-10CG is the move.
items.deadline: Phase three opened 1 October 2022; no closing date

items.title: The caregiver does not have to be family — a friend, neighbour or partner who lives in qualifies
items.who: Any adult 18 or older providing the care
items.value: Opens the stipend to veterans with no family able to serve
items.how: 38 CFR 71.25(b) requires the applicant to be at least 18 and to be the veteran's spouse, son or daughter, parent, step-family member, or extended family member — OR someone who lives with the veteran full time, or will do so if designated. That last clause has no relationship requirement at all. A friend, a church member, an unmarried partner, a former battle buddy: if they live with the veteran or will move in, they can be the Primary Family Caregiver. The applicant must also have no VA determination of abuse or neglect of the veteran, and must pass the assessment and training requirements.
items.hack: This is the single most-missed provision in the program. A single, estranged or childless veteran is not shut out. Note that a relative does NOT have to live in — only the non-relative route carries the live-in condition.

items.title: One Primary and up to two Secondary caregivers — and exactly what Secondary does not get
items.who: Families splitting the care load between two or three people
items.value: Training, counselling, travel and respite for backups; no stipend and no CHAMPVA
items.how: 38 CFR 71.25 caps approval at three Family Caregivers per veteran: one Primary and no more than two Secondary. Under 71.40(b), a Secondary Family Caregiver gets caregiver training, ongoing technical support, counselling (individual and group therapy and peer support, but not medication or inpatient psychiatric care), respite care, wellness contacts at least every 120 days with at least one annual home visit, and beneficiary travel under 38 CFR Part 70 when travelling with the veteran. A Secondary gets NO monthly stipend and NO CHAMPVA — those are 71.40(c) Primary-only benefits, along with the 30-day respite minimum, financial planning and legal services.
items.hack: Name both Secondary slots even if one person is doing most of the work. Secondary status is free, it puts a trained backup on the record, and it is the fastest path to a replacement Primary if the Primary dies, is hospitalised or steps down — 71.45 lets a new Primary's benefits start the day after the prior caregiver's revocation or discharge.

items.title: The PCAFC stipend formula — compute your own number, never trust a quoted figure
items.who: Approved PCAFC Primary Family Caregivers
items.value: A monthly, non-wage payment equal to 62.5% or 100% of one-twelfth of a GS-4 step 1 annual salary for the veteran's locality
items.how: 38 CFR 71.40(c)(4) sets the stipend as the Office of Personnel Management General Schedule Grade 4, Step 1 ANNUAL rate for the locality pay area in which the veteran resides, divided by 12, multiplied by the tier factor: 0.625 for a veteran who meets 71.20(a), and 1.00 for a veteran who additionally is unable to self-sustain in the community. There is no national stipend amount. Washington DC, San Francisco, Houston and Rest of United States all produce different numbers, and every figure changes when OPM updates the General Schedule each January.
items.hack: Do the arithmetic yourself, in four steps, so you can check VA's math: (1) open the OPM General Schedule page for the current year; (2) find the locality pay table covering the veteran's residence — if no metro table covers it, use 'Rest of United States'; (3) read the annual rate at the intersection of GS-4 and Step 1; (4) divide by 12 and multiply by 0.625 or 1.00. Anyone quoting a single nationwide dollar figure is quoting Rest of United States at an older year's rate.
items.deadline: Rates change when OPM updates the General Schedule, normally the first pay period of January

items.title: Why two identical veterans get different stipends — locality pay, and the 30-day address rule
items.who: PCAFC Primary Family Caregivers, especially anyone relocating
items.value: Protects the stipend amount and prevents a recoverable overpayment
items.how: Because the stipend is keyed to the OPM locality pay area where the veteran lives, two veterans with identical injuries and identical tiers receive materially different monthly amounts if they live in different metros. 38 CFR 71.40(c)(4) requires notice of a change of address and makes a relocation-driven adjustment effective the first of the month following notification; failure to notify within 30 days of relocating lets VA seek recovery of the resulting overpayment under 71.47 and the Federal Claims Collection Standards.
items.hack: Before moving, compute the new locality's GS-4 step 1 rate and know whether the stipend goes up or down. Moving from a high-locality metro to Rest of United States is a real pay cut that families discover after the fact. Notify CSP in writing within 30 days either way, and keep the confirmation — this is one of the commonest overpayment letters in the program. One exception: a legacy participant's floor under 71.20(b) only holds while the veteran stays at the same address.
items.deadline: Notify VA within 30 days of relocating

items.title: Legacy participants are paid on a different, three-tier formula — and protected until 30 September 2028
items.who: Veterans with a designated Family Caregiver before 1 October 2020, and legacy applicants who filed before that date
items.value: Protection from a stipend cut or a discharge based on the post-2020 eligibility and stipend criteria
items.how: 38 CFR 71.40(c)(4) pays legacy participants and legacy applicants on the sum of the clinical ratings under the pre-2020 regulations: a total of 21 or more gives a 1.00 multiplier, 13 to 20 gives 0.625, and 1 to 12 gives 0.25 — a quarter-tier that does not exist for anyone else. 71.20(b) adds a floor: the stipend will not be less than what was received before 1 October 2020 while the veteran remains at the same address. Decreases for legacy participants and applicants cannot take effect before 1 October 2028, with advance notice issued on that date and the decrease effective no earlier than 60 days after.
items.hack: If a legacy family also meets the current 71.20(a) criteria, VA pays whichever calculation is higher, and a reassessment that establishes current eligibility can carry a retroactive payment of the difference back to 1 October 2020. Ask CSP in writing to run both calculations and to state which one you are being paid on — many legacy families are quietly on the lower one.
items.deadline: Legacy protection runs through 30 September 2028; decreases permitted from 1 October 2028

items.title: VA Form 10-10CG is a JOINT application — the veteran and the caregiver both sign or it goes nowhere
items.who: Every PCAFC applicant pair
items.value: The only way into the program
items.how: 38 CFR 71.25(a) requires the veteran and each prospective Family Caregiver to submit a joint application. VA Form 10-10CG (available in English, Spanish and Tagalog) can be filed online at va.gov, mailed to the 10-10CG Evidence Intake Center, PO Box 5154, Janesville, WI 53547-5154, or handed to the Caregiver Support Program team at any VA medical centre. VA's own instruction is not to send medical records with the form. If the veteran lacks capacity, a legal guardian or surrogate signs.
items.hack: Two practical traps. First, an unsigned caregiver block or a missing Secondary signature is the most common reason a 10-10CG is returned rather than decided — check every signature line before filing. Second, the benefit start date under 71.40(d) is tied to the date VA receives the application, so file the form the day you decide, even if the supporting narrative is not polished; supplement afterwards.
items.deadline: Benefits date from application receipt — file first, supplement later

items.title: VA has 90 days to decide, and blowing the clock means a denial you have to refile around
items.who: PCAFC applicants waiting on a decision
items.value: A regulatory deadline you can hold VA to
items.how: 38 CFR 71.25(a)(3) gives VA 90 days from receipt of the joint application to complete the eligibility evaluations, the caregiver education and training, and the initial home-care assessment. If VA cannot complete them in 90 days the application is denied and a new application is required — but the regulation lets VA extend the period where the delay was VA's own inability to perform, in which case the original application stays alive.
items.hack: Diary day 60. If training has not been scheduled by then, call the Caregiver Support Line on 1-855-260-3274 and ask CSP in writing to document the delay as VA-caused so the 90-day clock is extended rather than letting the application die. Keep that email — it is also the evidence that protects your benefit start date.
items.deadline: 90 days from VA's receipt of VA Form 10-10CG

items.title: Every VA medical centre has a Caregiver Support Program team — find yours before you file anything
items.who: Any caregiver of a veteran enrolled in VA health care
items.value: A named social worker or nurse who owns your case inside the system
items.how: VA maintains a Caregiver Support Program team at every VA medical centre, listed state by state at va.gov/resources/caregiver-support-teams. The team handles PCAFC intake, PGCSS enrolment, training, respite authorisation and the wellness contacts. The national Caregiver Support Line is 1-855-260-3274, Monday to Friday, 8am to 8pm ET.
items.hack: Go to the team before you submit the 10-10CG. They will tell you which door you are applying through, what the local assessor looks for, and whether anything is missing — and a coordinator who knows your name is worth more at reassessment than any document. Ask for their direct line and email, not the main switchboard.

items.title: The ten competency domains you will be trained and assessed on
items.who: PCAFC applicants completing required training
items.value: Knowing the syllabus before you sit the assessment
items.how: 38 CFR 71.25(c) and (d) require the applicant to be assessed as able to complete caregiver education and training, to demonstrate understanding of the veteran's specific personal care needs, and to complete core competency training covering: medication management; vital signs and pain control; infection control; nutrition; functional activities; activities of daily living; communication and cognition skills; behaviour management; skin care; and caregiver self-care. VA then conducts an initial home-care assessment in the veteran's home to assess the veteran's well-being and the caregiver's competence.
items.hack: The home visit is an assessment, not a social call. Do not tidy away the evidence — the shower chair, the pill organiser, the bed rail, the incident log, the stove knob covers. Caregivers routinely stage the house to look capable and then get denied for not demonstrating need. Have the veteran present and let them answer for themselves; their own statements carry weight under 71.25.
items.deadline: Must be completed within the 90-day application window

items.title: Reassessment and wellness contacts — the compliance obligations that quietly end participation
items.who: Approved PCAFC participants
items.value: Keeping the stipend by not missing a phone call
items.how: 38 CFR 71.30 provides for reassessment of the veteran and the Family Caregiver, in collaboration with the primary care team, normally annually, to determine continued eligibility and whether the veteran is unable to self-sustain in the community for tier purposes; it may include a home visit, and may occur more or less often where documented as appropriate. Separately, 71.40(b)(2) requires wellness contacts at least every 120 days with at least one annual home visit. Failure to participate in reassessments or wellness contacts is noncompliance and a ground for revocation under 71.45(a)(1)(ii).
items.hack: Answer the phone. The most avoidable PCAFC loss is revocation for missed wellness contacts, not for a change in the veteran's condition. Give CSP two contact numbers and an email, and if you will be unreachable — hospital stay, deployment of a spouse, a move — tell them in advance in writing. Noncompliance revocation cannot take effect earlier than 60 days after advance notice, so a letter is a 60-day window to fix the problem, not a final answer.
items.deadline: Wellness contacts at least every 120 days; reassessment normally annual

items.title: The 2020-2022 discharge wave, the June 2022 suspension, and what protection actually survives
items.who: Legacy participants and families discharged or downgraded after the 2020 expansion
items.value: Context that changes how you read any reassessment letter
items.how: When the October 2020 rule rewrote the eligibility and stipend criteria, VA began reassessing legacy participants against the new standards and large numbers were discharged or had stipends reduced. After sustained congressional pressure, a VA memorandum dated 9 June 2022 suspended certain discharges, reductions and reassessments, directing that annual reassessments were unnecessary for the legacy and post-expansion cohorts during the review and that legacy cohort members would not be discharged or reduced based on the eligibility and stipend level criteria. The suspension never covered everything: stipend increases could still be granted, and discharges for death, institutionalisation, domestic violence or noncompliance with wellness contacts continued. Regulation now bars legacy decreases before 1 October 2028.
items.hack: If a family was discharged or cut between October 2020 and mid-2022, that decision was made under a standard VA itself then paused. It is worth asking CSP in writing for a review, and worth filing a supplemental claim with current evidence rather than assuming the old decision is final. Any reassessment letter arriving now should be read against the 1 October 2028 legacy floor before you accept a reduction.
items.deadline: Legacy decreases barred until 1 October 2028

items.title: Revocation versus discharge — different grounds, different dates, and different continuation of benefits
items.who: PCAFC participants who receive an adverse letter
items.value: 30 to 90 days of continued benefits, and the right argument to make
items.how: 38 CFR 71.45 splits adverse actions in two. Revocation is fault-based or compliance-based: for cause (fraud, neglect, abuse or exploitation of the veteran, unmitigated personal safety issues, unwillingness to provide care), noncompliance, or VA error. Discharge is circumstantial: the veteran no longer meets 71.20, death or institutionalisation of the veteran or caregiver (expected 90-plus days, or the 90th day actual), or a request by the caregiver or by the veteran or surrogate. The continuation windows differ: 60 days of benefits after a VA-error revocation; 90 days after a discharge due to the veteran or the caregiver; 30 days after a caregiver's or veteran's request, extended to 90 days where the caregiver's discharge is triggered by domestic or intimate partner violence evidenced by a protective order, police report, or disclosure to a treating provider. Where several bases apply, 71.45(f) controls which one is used, and multiple discharge bases resolve to whichever is most favourable to the caregiver.
items.hack: Read the letter for the word used. 'Revoked for cause' follows the caregiver to any future application and is worth contesting hard; 'discharged because the veteran no longer meets the criteria' is a clinical disagreement you fight on the medicine. Also note a veteran or surrogate who asks to discharge a specific caregiver can rescind within 30 days and have them reinstated — after 30 days it takes a whole new joint application.
items.deadline: Noncompliance revocation and most discharges take effect no earlier than 60 days after advance notice

items.title: Four ways to fight a PCAFC denial, downgrade or discharge — and the one-year clock on three of them
items.who: Anyone holding an adverse PCAFC decision
items.value: Preserves the stipend, CHAMPVA and respite
items.how: For PCAFC decisions dated on or after 19 February 2019 there are four routes. (1) Supplemental claim, VA Form 20-0995, when you have new and relevant evidence VA did not consider — no deadline. (2) Higher-Level Review, VA Form 20-0996, within one year, decided by a more senior reviewer on the existing record with no new evidence and no hearing. (3) Board Appeal, VA Form 10182, within one year, before a Veterans Law Judge, in one of three lanes — direct review, evidence submission, or a hearing with or without new evidence. (4) Clinical appeal, through the VA facility's Patient Advocate to the chief of staff, which does accept new medical evidence and can escalate to the VISN patient advocate and chief medical officer. For decisions before 19 February 2019 the options are a Board appeal on VA Form 10-307 to the Evidence Intake Center, PO Box 5154, Janesville, WI 53547, or a clinical appeal. You may only pursue one option at a time per decision.
items.hack: Choose by what is wrong. If the clinician mis-scored the ADLs or missed the supervision need, that is a clinical disagreement — start with the Patient Advocate clinical appeal, which is fast and takes new medical evidence, and VA's own guidance has described it as roughly six weeks. If the law or the tier was applied wrongly on a correct record, go Higher-Level Review. If you need a judge and a hearing, go Board. And file a supplemental claim with a fresh clinician statement in parallel with nothing else pending — it is the cheapest route to a new decision. Note the Board route on a clinical question is slow; most families should exhaust the clinical appeal first.
items.deadline: One year from the decision date for Higher-Level Review and Board Appeal

items.title: VA Form 10-306 — demand the file behind your PCAFC decision
items.who: Caregivers appealing a PCAFC decision
items.value: The assessor's own reasoning, which is what you have to rebut
items.how: VA Form 10-306 requests information about a past PCAFC decision. It produces the record VA actually relied on — the eligibility determination, the clinical scoring, the home-visit findings. Without it you are appealing a one-paragraph letter.
items.hack: File the 10-306 the week the denial arrives, before you pick an appeal lane. Nine times out of ten the file shows a specific factual error — an ADL scored as independent, a supervision need recorded as 'intermittent', a wellness contact logged as refused — and that specific error is a far stronger appeal than a general argument that the veteran is badly injured.
items.deadline: File immediately; appeal clocks run while you wait

items.title: Why PCAFC applications get denied, and what a winning file contains
items.who: First-time applicants and anyone reapplying after denial
items.value: The difference between approval and a year of appeals
