items.how: The recurring denial patterns are: arguing the ADL door when the real case is the supervision door; describing difficulty rather than frequency, so the assessor cannot find that care is needed 'each time'; a caregiver who minimises their own role; no incident record, so the supervision need reads as emotional support; the veteran absent or silent at the home visit; a concurrent paid agency doing the same hours, triggering the 71.20(a)(5) duplicate-care bar; no VA primary care team; and a missing signature on the 10-10CG.
items.hack: A strong file has five parts. One: a dated two-to-four-week care log with times and tasks, written by the caregiver. Two: the veteran's own signed statement in the veteran's words about what they cannot do alone and what has gone wrong. Three: a letter from the VA or community clinician that uses the regulation's own language — 'requires personal care services each time he completes', 'needs supervision, protection or instruction on a continuous basis to maintain personal safety'. Four: specific incidents with dates. Five: a plain sentence on what would have to be bought if the caregiver stopped. Clinicians will usually sign language you draft for them if it is accurate; most will not invent it.

items.title: CHAMPVA for the Primary Family Caregiver — automatic, and conditional on having no other coverage
items.who: PCAFC Primary Family Caregivers without other health coverage
items.value: Health coverage in the caregiver's own right, not as the veteran's dependent
items.how: 38 CFR 71.40(c)(2) makes a Primary Family Caregiver eligible for CHAMPVA unless they are entitled to care or services under a health plan contract. There is no separate CHAMPVA application: VA determines eligibility from the PCAFC designation and enrols the caregiver automatically. CHAMPVA correspondence goes to CHAMPVA, PO Box 500, Spring City, PA 19475. Secondary Family Caregivers get no CHAMPVA.
items.hack: This is the benefit that makes the stipend workable, because it lets a caregiver leave an employer-sponsored plan without going uninsured. Run the comparison before dropping other coverage — CHAMPVA is a cost-share plan with its own deductible and is secondary to Medicare once the caregiver is 65 — and remember that acquiring other coverage can end CHAMPVA eligibility, which you must report.
items.deadline: Effective on the later of application receipt, start of home care, or start of caregiver services

items.title: At least 30 days of respite a year is a Primary Family Caregiver entitlement, not a favour
items.who: PCAFC Primary Family Caregivers
items.value: A minimum of 30 days per year of paid substitute care, and more where clinically appropriate
items.how: 38 CFR 71.40(c)(1) entitles a Primary Family Caregiver to respite care of not less than 30 days annually, which may exceed 30 days where clinically appropriate, and which includes 24-hour per day in-home care. Respite is a distinct authorisation requested through the Caregiver Support Program team or the veteran's social worker; it can be delivered in the home, at an adult day health care centre, or as a short institutional stay.
items.hack: This is the most under-claimed entitlement in the whole program — families bank it out of guilt and then collapse. Book it in advance and in blocks, as you would annual leave, and ask for 24-hour in-home respite rather than an institutional stay if the veteran will not tolerate placement. If 30 days is not enough, the words to use are 'clinically appropriate': ask the clinician to document why more is needed, because the regulation contemplates exceeding the minimum.
items.deadline: Resets annually; unused days do not bank

items.title: Beneficiary travel pays the caregiver's mileage to the veteran's appointments
items.org: VA Office of Community Care / Beneficiary Travel
items.who: PCAFC Primary and Secondary Family Caregivers travelling with the veteran; medically required attendants
items.value: Mileage or actual expense, whichever is less, plus lodging and meals in some cases
items.how: 38 CFR 71.40(b)(6) and (c) give Family Caregivers beneficiary travel under 38 CFR Part 70 where the veteran is eligible. VA's travel pay rules separately cover a medically required attendant travelling with the veteran. File through the Beneficiary Travel Self-Service System (BTSSS) online, or on VA Form 10-3542 at the facility. VA pays the mileage rate or the actual expense, whichever is less. Plan to file within 30 days — later claims are usually denied.
items.hack: Two distinct routes exist and families confuse them. A designated PCAFC caregiver claims as a caregiver; an undesignated family member claims as a medically required attendant, which requires the clinician to document that an attendant is medically necessary. Get that attendant determination in writing once and it covers recurring appointments. File every trip in BTSSS the same week — the 30-day rule is enforced, and for a weekly specialty clinic 300 miles away the annual total is substantial.
items.deadline: File within 30 days of the trip

items.title: Free legal and financial planning services for Primary Family Caregivers
items.who: PCAFC Primary Family Caregivers only
items.value: Advance directives, powers of attorney, simple wills, guardianship help, budgeting and debt counselling
items.how: 38 CFR 71.40(c) entitles Primary Family Caregivers to financial planning services covering household budgets, debt management and retirement and insurance education, and to legal services covering advance directives, powers of attorney, simple wills, guardianship, legal education and referrals. The regulation excludes adversarial actions against the United States and disputes between the veteran and the caregiver.
items.hack: Almost nobody uses this, and it is exactly what these families need: a durable power of attorney and an advance directive before the veteran's capacity is in question, not after. Ask the Caregiver Support Program team to initiate the referral by name — 'the 71.40(c) legal services benefit' — because front-line staff often do not know it exists. Note the carve-out: it will not fund a VA appeal, which is what VSOs and accredited representatives are for, free.

items.title: Counselling and mental health care for the caregiver, in the caregiver's own right
items.who: Primary, Secondary and General Caregivers, and family members more broadly
items.value: Individual and group therapy, marriage and family counselling, peer support — at no cost
items.how: 38 CFR 71.40 gives Primary and Secondary Family Caregivers counselling under 38 CFR 71.50, which covers consultation, professional counselling, marriage and family counselling, training and mental health services where necessary in connection with treatment of a disability for which the veteran is receiving VA treatment. The scope is psychotherapy, counselling, training and education; it excludes prescriptions and inpatient services. VA also runs a Virtual Psychotherapy Program for Caregivers. 71.50 defines 'family member' broadly — relatives by birth or marriage living with the veteran or in regular contact, legal guardians and surrogates, Primary, Secondary and General Caregivers, and anyone in whose household the veteran has certified an intent to live.
items.hack: The limitation is real and worth understanding: 71.50 care is tied to the veteran's treatment plan, so it is not open-ended personal therapy, and VA may refer a caregiver who needs unrelated treatment out to a community provider. If the caregiver's own depression, anxiety or trauma needs ongoing treatment and medication, use CHAMPVA (Primary caregivers) or your own insurance for that, and use 71.50 for the caregiving-specific work. Both are available at once.

items.title: PCAFC Primary caregivers get commissary, exchange and MWR access — bring the right letter
items.who: Individuals approved and designated as Primary Family Caregivers under PCAFC
items.value: Tax-free commissary groceries, exchange shopping and MWR retail access
items.how: The Purple Heart and Disabled Veterans Equal Access Act of 2018, implemented at 10 U.S.C. 1065, extended commissary, exchange and MWR retail privileges from 1 January 2020 to Purple Heart recipients, former prisoners of war, veterans with a VA-documented service-connected disability rating, and individuals assessed, approved and designated as Primary Family Caregivers under a formalised VA caregiver program. The caregiver presents a letter from the VA Office of Community Care confirming they are the approved and designated Primary Family Caregiver of an eligible veteran, paired with an acceptable credential such as a REAL ID-compliant driver's licence or a US passport.
items.hack: Request that designation letter from the Office of Community Care or your Caregiver Support Program team as soon as you are approved, and keep a photo of it on your phone — gate guards and commissary cashiers are frequently unaware of the caregiver category and will turn you away without it. For a family on a single income plus a stipend, commissary pricing is a meaningful monthly saving, and the caregiver can shop without the veteran present.
items.deadline: Access began 1 January 2020

items.title: The stipend is direct deposit only — no paper checks
items.who: Approved PCAFC Primary Family Caregivers
items.value: Prevents a stipend that is approved but never arrives
items.how: VA has stopped issuing PCAFC paper checks. The Primary Family Caregiver must enrol in direct deposit through the VA Customer Engagement Portal at cep.fsc.va.gov. The stipend is paid to the caregiver, not to the veteran.
items.hack: Do the CEP enrolment the day approval lands, not when the first payment fails. Open the account in the caregiver's own name — paying the stipend into the veteran's account muddies the record for Medicaid, pension income counting and tax questions later, and the stipend is legally the caregiver's.
items.deadline: Before the first payment can issue

items.title: PGCSS — the caregiver program with no rating, no service connection and no application
items.who: Anyone providing personal care to a veteran enrolled in VA health care
items.value: Training, coaching, peer mentoring, telephone support and respite — immediately, for free
items.how: The Program of General Caregiver Support Services runs under 38 CFR 71.35. A General Caregiver is someone who provides personal care services to a covered veteran — a veteran enrolled in the VA health care system who is unable to perform an activity of daily living or needs supervision or protection based on a neurological or other impairment. There is no 70% rating requirement, no service-connection requirement, no relationship requirement, no live-in requirement, no clinical evaluation and no formal application: the regulation says veterans and caregivers request benefits as needed from local VA clinicians, and 71.35 expressly states the covered veteran need not meet the 71.20 PCAFC requirements.
items.hack: If PCAFC says no, this is the same day's second phone call, not next year's project. Call the Caregiver Support Line on 1-855-260-3274 or walk into the local Caregiver Support Program team and say 'I want to enrol as a General Caregiver under PGCSS.' The intake is an assessment conversation, the veteran confirms your role, and you are in. It pays no stipend — but it unlocks respite, which is the benefit exhausted families need most, plus every training and coaching program VA runs.
items.deadline: None — enrolment is open and ongoing

items.title: Respite care for General Caregivers — the PGCSS benefit that matters most
items.who: PGCSS-enrolled General Caregivers of VA-enrolled veterans
items.value: Medically and age-appropriate respite, including 24-hour in-home care
items.how: 38 CFR 71.40(a)(4) gives all General Caregivers respite care that is medically and age appropriate, including 24-hour per day care in the veteran's home. Unlike the Primary Family Caregiver benefit, there is no 30-day statutory minimum attached — it is authorised clinically through the Caregiver Support Program team or the veteran's social worker, and for Secondary and General caregivers respite is limited to veterans enrolled in the VA health system.
items.hack: Ask for in-home respite by name and ask what the local facility's authorisation ceiling is, because it varies by medical centre and by whether VA buys the hours from a community agency. If the local answer is thin, ask the same question of the Area Agency on Aging — the Older Americans Act respite stream (see the NFCSP item) is a separate pot of money with separate rules, and families can use both.

items.title: The named PGCSS programs to ask for by name: Caregivers FIRST, REACH VA, Building Better Caregivers, Peer Support Mentoring, Annie
items.who: Any PGCSS-enrolled caregiver
items.value: Structured skills training, one-to-one coaching, a six-week online workshop, a matched peer mentor and automated text support
items.how: VA delivers PGCSS through named curricula: Caregivers FIRST, a group skills class; REACH VA, a one-to-one evidence-based coaching protocol; Building Better Caregivers, a six-week online workshop; the Peer Support Mentoring Program, which matches a caregiver with an experienced caregiver mentor; VA S.A.V.E. suicide prevention training; Caregiver Health and Wellbeing coaching; the Annie text-messaging program for stress management; and VA Caregiver Connect and VA Video Connect for virtual sessions.
items.hack: Front-line staff will often offer only a pamphlet. Ask for each by name — 'can you enrol me in REACH VA' gets a different answer than 'what support is there'. REACH VA is the one with the strongest evidence behind it for caregiver burden and depression, and it is one-to-one rather than a group, which matters if you cannot leave the house.

items.title: The Dole Act gives 30 days of respite to families DENIED or DISCHARGED from PCAFC
items.who: Caregivers whose PCAFC application was denied, or who were discharged from the program
items.value: At least 30 days of respite care a year despite not being in PCAFC
items.how: Section 124 of the Senator Elizabeth Dole 21st Century Veterans Healthcare and Benefits Improvement Act, Public Law 118-210, enacted 2 January 2025, increases respite care access to a minimum of 30 days annually for caregivers denied or discharged from the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers. Section 122 of the same Act expands grants and contracts to provide mental health services to family caregivers, with a focus on underserved communities.
items.hack: This is brand new and almost no front-line staff will volunteer it. If you were denied or discharged, cite section 124 of the Dole Act by name to the Caregiver Support Program team and ask for the 30-day respite authorisation. Implementation varies by facility and by how far VA has got with the rulemaking, so expect to have to ask twice and to put it in writing.
items.deadline: Enacted 2 January 2025; implementation ongoing

items.title: Veteran-Directed Care — VA hands over a budget and the veteran hires their own family
items.org: VA Geriatrics and Extended Care / Aging and Disability Network
items.who: Veterans enrolled in VA health care with a clinical need for home and community based services, where VDC is available
items.value: A flexible monthly budget the veteran controls, which can pay a spouse, adult child, other relative or neighbour as a personal care aide
items.how: VDC gives the veteran and family a flexible budget for home and community based services that they direct themselves. VA's own program material says veterans can 'hire their own personal care aides (which might include their own family member or neighbor).' The budget is administered through a partner in the Aging and Disability Network — typically an Area Agency on Aging or Aging and Disability Resource Center — which provides the counselling and the financial management service that handles payroll, taxes and timesheets, so the family is not running an employer by themselves. Eligibility is open to enrolled veterans with a clinical need where the service is available locally; copays may apply depending on service-connected status.
items.hack: This is the route that pays a family member when PCAFC is unavailable — no 70% rating, no era test, no serious-injury finding. Two things to know. First, availability has historically been patchy: ask the VA social worker whether your medical centre offers VDC, and if the answer is no, ask when it will under the Dole Act mandate. Second, whether a legally responsible relative such as a spouse can be the paid aide is set by the administering entity's rules and the state context, so get that answer in writing before anyone quits a job. Ask the VA social worker to make the referral; the words are 'I want a Veteran-Directed Care consult.'

items.title: The Dole Act orders Veteran-Directed Care into EVERY VA medical centre by January 2027
items.who: Veterans at medical centres that do not yet offer VDC, including territories and American Indian and Alaska Native veterans
items.value: Turns 'not available here' into a deadline you can hold VA to
items.how: Section 123 of the Senator Elizabeth Dole 21st Century Veterans Healthcare and Benefits Improvement Act, Public Law 118-210, enacted 2 January 2025, requires VA to expand the Veteran-Directed Care program to all VA medical centres, and to ensure accessibility for underserved populations including veterans in the US territories and American Indian and Alaska Native veterans. The statutory implementation deadline is within two years of enactment, that is by 2 January 2027.
items.hack: If your facility says VDC is not offered, the correct reply is to ask for the facility's implementation plan and date under section 123 of the Dole Act, and to copy the patient advocate and your congressional caseworker. A congressional inquiry on a statutory deadline moves faster than any clinical appeal. In the meantime ask whether the facility can purchase Homemaker and Home Health Aide hours instead.
items.deadline: 2 January 2027 statutory deadline for VDC at every VA medical centre

items.title: The Dole Act raised the home-care spending cap from 65% to 100% of nursing home cost
items.who: Veterans whose home care was capped and pushed toward institutional placement
items.value: Up to roughly 35% more purchasable home care, and above 100% for some conditions
items.how: Section 120 of Public Law 118-210 expanded VA's authority for noninstitutional care from 65% to at least 100% of the geographically-adjusted equivalent cost of nursing home care for eligible veterans, and permits exceeding 100% for veterans with conditions such as ALS or spinal cord injury. The old 65% cap was the mechanism by which VA told families that keeping the veteran at home had become 'too expensive' relative to a nursing home.
items.hack: If a VA social worker has ever told you the home care package is at its ceiling, that ceiling moved. Ask for a re-run of the noninstitutional cost calculation under section 120 of the Dole Act, and if the veteran has ALS or a spinal cord injury, ask explicitly about exceeding 100%. This single provision is the difference between home and placement for a lot of families.
items.deadline: Enacted 2 January 2025

items.title: Aid and Attendance pays a family caregiver indirectly — through the care-expense deduction
items.who: Wartime veterans and surviving spouses eligible for VA pension who need aid and attendance
items.value: Raises the pension by lowering countable income, effectively reimbursing paid care
items.how: Aid and Attendance is an increased VA pension, not a care payment. The mechanism that gets money to a caregiver is indirect: VA pension is the difference between the maximum annual pension rate and the claimant's countable income, and unreimbursed medical expenses — including payments for in-home care — are deducted from countable income. Lower countable income means a larger pension cheque. Apply using VA Form 21-2680 (examination for housebound status or permanent need for regular aid and attendance), plus VA Form 21-0779 if in a nursing home; file with the pension claim or on its own to the Pension Intake Center in Janesville, Wisconsin.
items.hack: Understand what you are buying. A&A does not pay a caregiver; it reimburses, through a bigger pension, money the household actually pays out for care. So the family member must genuinely be paid, under a written agreement, with records — paying nothing produces no deduction and no increase. And note A&A is a needs-based pension benefit with income and net worth limits, which is a completely different animal from the SMC-L through SMC-T aid-and-attendance ladder in the compensation system.
items.deadline: No deadline; effective dates run from the date of claim, so file an intent to file early

items.title: 38 CFR 3.278 — the regulation that lets a family member's pay count as a medical expense
items.who: Pension and Aid and Attendance claimants paying a relative for care
items.value: Turns family wages into a deductible medical expense, raising the pension
items.how: 38 CFR 3.278 provides that payments for assistance with activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living by an in-home attendant are medical expenses as long as the attendant provides health care or custodial care. The provider must ordinarily be a health care provider, with two exceptions that cover most families: the disabled individual is rated as needing aid and attendance or is housebound, OR a physician, physician assistant, certified nurse practitioner or clinical nurse specialist provides written confirmation that the individual needs the care because of a physical, mental, developmental or cognitive condition. The regulation expressly contemplates care provided by family or friends. Payments must be commensurate with the number of hours the provider attends to the disabled person.
items.hack: Two documents make or break this. One: the written clinician statement, unless A&A or housebound is already established — get it on letterhead, naming the condition and the need for assistance with ADLs. Two: an hours-based record. 'Commensurate with the number of hours' means VA will compare what you paid to the hours worked; a flat $3,000 a month with no timesheets invites a reduction. Keep a timesheet and pay by traceable transfer, never cash.

items.title: The caregiver agreement — what it must say before VA or Medicaid will respect it
items.org: Private — drafted by the family, often with an elder law or VA-accredited attorney
items.who: Any family paying a relative for care and claiming it for VA pension or Medicaid purposes
items.value: The difference between a deductible medical expense and an unexplained gift that triggers a penalty
items.how: A caregiver agreement (also called a personal care agreement or personal services contract) should be in writing, signed and dated before the care begins, and should state: the parties; the specific services, matched to the ADL and IADL language the agency uses; the schedule and hours; the hourly or daily rate, benchmarked to the local market rate for comparable agency care; the payment method and frequency; a term and termination clause; and a statement that payment is for services rendered and not a gift or an advance on an inheritance. Payments should be made by traceable transfer with contemporaneous timesheets, and the caregiver should report the income.
items.hack: The three mistakes that destroy these agreements: dating it after the money moved, paying a lump sum in advance for future care, and paying far above the local market rate. All three look to a VA or Medicaid reviewer like an asset transfer dressed up as a wage. Get the local agency rate in writing as your benchmark and keep it in the file. Also note the honest tension: respecting the agreement means the caregiver has taxable self-employment or wage income and the family may owe employment taxes — do not treat this as free money.
items.deadline: Must pre-date the care and the payments

items.title: The VA pension look-back: 36 months, and a penalty period up to five years
items.who: Families who moved money, gifted assets or funded a trust before filing for pension or Aid and Attendance
items.value: Avoiding months or years of total ineligibility
items.how: 38 CFR 3.276 defines the look-back period as the 36 months immediately preceding the date VA receives an original pension claim, or a new claim after a period of non-entitlement, excluding dates before 18 October 2018. A 'covered asset' is one that was part of the claimant's net worth, was transferred for less than fair market value, and would have caused net worth to exceed the statutory limit had it not been transferred. VA divides the total covered asset amount by a monthly penalty rate — the maximum annual pension rate for a veteran in need of aid and attendance with one dependent, divided by 12 and rounded down — and rounds down to whole months. The penalty period begins the first day of the month after the transfer, or the last transfer where there were several, and may not exceed five years.
items.hack: This is where well-meaning families destroy their own claim. Paying a daughter $60,000 'for all her care over the years', retitling the house to a son, or funding an irrevocable trust inside 36 months of filing can all read as covered asset transfers. Prospective, documented, market-rate payment under a pre-existing caregiver agreement is the defensible structure; a retroactive lump sum is not. If assets have already moved, get VA-accredited or elder law advice before filing — the claim date starts the look-back, so filing is the irreversible step.
items.deadline: 36-month look-back from the date VA receives the claim; penalty up to 5 years

items.title: Medicaid self-direction — employer authority and budget authority, and why the distinction decides whether you get paid
items.who: Veterans and other Medicaid-eligible people needing long-term services and supports
items.value: In most states, a route to being hired and paid as the personal care attendant for your own family member
items.how: Medicaid self-directed services give the participant decision-making authority of two kinds. Employer authority means the participant can recruit, hire, train and supervise the people who furnish their services — this is the authority that lets a family member be the paid worker. Budget authority means the participant has decision-making authority over how the Medicaid funds in an individual budget are spent. A financial management service handles payroll, employer duties, purchases and budget tracking. Self-direction is available under section 1905(a)(24) state plan personal care, section 1915(c) home and community based services waivers, section 1915(i), section 1915(j), section 1915(k) Community First Choice, and section 1115 demonstrations.
items.hack: Ask your state Medicaid agency or Area Agency on Aging one precise question: 'Which of our programs has employer authority, and may a legally responsible relative be the paid provider?' Those are the two variables. Whether a spouse or the parent of a minor can be paid is set state by state and sometimes program by program — many states pay an adult child freely but restrict spouses. Do not accept a general 'family can't be paid' from a front-line worker; ask them to point you at the program rule.

items.title: California IHSS — the largest consumer-directed program in the country, and the veteran's family can be the provider
items.org: California Department of Social Services / county IHSS offices
items.who: Aged, blind and disabled Medi-Cal recipients in California, including veterans
items.value: An hourly wage paid by the state to a provider the recipient chooses, who can be a relative
items.how: In-Home Supportive Services provides in-home assistance to eligible aged, blind and disabled individuals as an alternative to institutional care. A county social worker assesses need in the home and authorises hours; the recipient hires their own individual provider and is treated as that provider's employer, while the state issues the payments. Apply on form SOC 295 to the county IHSS office; county offices are listed at cdss.ca.gov/inforesources/county-ihss-offices. The application is available in Armenian, Cambodian, Chinese, Farsi/Dari, Korean, Russian, Spanish, Tagalog and Vietnamese.
items.hack: IHSS is the model to understand because so many other states' programs are variations on it, and because it stacks: a veteran can receive IHSS hours and VA services, though VA will coordinate so the same hours are not paid twice — which also matters for the PCAFC duplicate-care bar in 38 CFR 71.20(a)(5). Whether a spouse or parent can be the paid provider, and at what hour limits, is governed by specific IHSS rules; ask the county worker for the rule in writing. IHSS hours are assessed task by task, so the assessment is the whole game — have a care log ready.

items.title: Structured Family Caregiving — a daily stipend to a relative who lives with the veteran, in the states that have it
items.org: State Medicaid agencies, delivered through contracted agencies
items.who: Medicaid HCBS-eligible people who live with the family member who cares for them
items.value: A daily per-diem to the live-in family caregiver, plus agency coaching and oversight
items.how: Structured Family Caregiving, sometimes called adult foster care or caregiver homes, pays a daily rate rather than an hourly wage to a family caregiver who shares a home with the Medicaid member. A contracted agency provides a care coach, oversight and documentation, and passes a mandated minimum share of the per-diem through to the caregiver. As of a 2022 national review, the states operating Medicaid SFC included Connecticut, Georgia, Indiana, Louisiana, Missouri, North Carolina and South Dakota. The programs run under section 1915(c) waiver authority, either embedded in an existing waiver (Georgia's Elderly and Disabled Waiver, South Dakota's HOPE waiver) or stand-alone (Missouri's Structured Family Caregiving Waiver). In the states reviewed, spouses and other legally responsible relatives could be paid, a shared residence was required, and Missouri additionally limited eligibility to Alzheimer's disease and related diagnoses.
items.hack: The structural advantage over hourly personal care is that the per-diem is paid for presence rather than for timed tasks, which fits dementia and supervision cases far better. Two cautions. First, the state list and the rates change — the daily rates published in 2022 are certainly stale, and the pass-through percentage varies by state, so ask the agency what share of the per-diem reaches you. Second, a per-diem is usually well below an hourly wage for the same hours; run the numbers against self-directed personal care in your state before choosing.

items.title: How to find your own state's paid-family-caregiver program in two phone calls
items.org: Eldercare Locator / Area Agency on Aging / state Medicaid agency
items.who: Any family that needs the answer for their specific state
items.value: The only reliable method, because the rules are genuinely different in all 50 states
items.how: Call the Eldercare Locator, a public service of the Administration for Community Living, on 1-800-677-1116, Monday to Friday 8am to 9pm ET, and ask for your Area Agency on Aging and your Aging and Disability Resource Center. Then ask those two bodies three questions: which Medicaid long-term services programs in this state have employer authority or self-direction; may a legally responsible relative such as a spouse be the paid provider in each; and is there a Structured Family Caregiving, adult foster care or caregiver-homes option. Then call the state Medicaid agency's long-term care unit to confirm, and ask for the waiting list position if there is one.
items.hack: Insist on program names, not categories. 'Yes, we have self-direction' is useless; 'the Elderly and Disabled Waiver has employer authority and your daughter can be hired but your wife cannot' is actionable. Ask about waiting lists in the same call — 1915(c) waivers are capped and some states have multi-year queues, so the right move may be to get on the list today and pursue VA routes in the meantime.
items.deadline: Get on waiver waiting lists as early as possible

items.title: Medical Foster Home — the veteran moves into a caregiver's house, and the veteran pays the caregiver
items.who: Veterans who need 24/7 care, cannot live alone, and want an alternative to a nursing home; and people who want to be paid to care for veterans in their own home
items.value: 24-hour care in a private home, historically quoted at roughly $1,500 to $3,000 a month paid by the veteran
items.how: A Medical Foster Home is a private home where a trained caregiver who lives in the home provides care and supervision 24 hours a day, 7 days a week to a small number of residents — help with daily activities, medication management, nursing support, meals and social activities. VA inspects, trains and oversees the caregiver and the home under VHA Directive 1141.02, but VA does not pay for or fund the placement: the veteran pays the caregiver directly, at a rate negotiated in advance, historically described by VA as roughly $1,500 to $3,000 a month depending on income and level of care. Enrolment in Home Based Primary Care is an eligibility requirement, and availability depends on an approved home existing in your area. Ask a VA social worker or case manager.
items.hack: Two angles. For a family that cannot continue caring at home, this is a far smaller and more human setting than a nursing home at a fraction of the price, and Aid and Attendance or SMC can help fund the monthly fee — the cost is a care expense. For a family member who wants to be paid, becoming an approved Medical Foster Home caregiver is a legitimate occupation: VA trains and oversees you, and residents pay you. Note that a relative who becomes the veteran's MFH caregiver and is paid for it is doing something quite different from PCAFC, and the 38 CFR 71.20(a)(5) duplicate-care bar is a live issue — sort out which program is paying before you start.

items.title: Homemaker and Home Health Aide — VA buys the hours, which is not the same as paying your family
items.who: Enrolled veterans whom VA determines need the service, where it is available
items.value: A trained aide supervised by a registered nurse, in the veteran's home, purchased by VA
items.how: Homemaker and Home Health Aide (H/HHA) is a VA-purchased service in which a trained caregiver supervised by a registered nurse comes into the home. Eligibility requires VA health care enrolment, a VA determination of need for the specific service, and local availability. The aide works for a community agency under VA contract, not for the family, so this route does not pay a relative — it substitutes for the relative's hours.
items.hack: This is the right ask when the family needs relief rather than income, and it is also the fallback where Veteran-Directed Care is not yet offered at your facility. Be aware of the interaction with PCAFC: if an agency aide is performing the same personal care services the family caregiver is being paid a stipend for, that can implicate the 38 CFR 71.20(a)(5) bar on care being simultaneously and regularly provided by another entity. Ask the social worker to document which tasks and hours are agency and which are family.

items.title: Adult Day Health Care — daytime care that keeps the caregiver employed
items.who: Enrolled veterans needing supervision and socialisation during the day
items.value: A supervised daytime program with social activities, companionship and recreation, so the caregiver can work
items.how: Adult Day Health Care is a VA-covered program providing social activities, companionship and recreation in a supervised setting during the day. Eligibility requires VA enrolment, a VA determination of need and local availability. Under 38 CFR 17.111 it is a noninstitutional extended care service carrying a copay for non-exempt veterans.
items.hack: For a working caregiver this is often more valuable than a stipend, because it preserves the caregiver's own job, income, health insurance and Social Security earnings record — see the Social Security item for why that last one matters. Pair ADHC with a work schedule rather than treating it as a nice-to-have. Confirm your copay exposure first using the 38 CFR 17.111 exemption list.

items.title: Home Based Primary Care — a VA doctor-led team that comes to the house
items.who: Enrolled veterans with complex chronic disease for whom clinic visits are difficult
items.value: Primary care, nursing, therapy, social work, pharmacy and dietetics delivered in the home
items.how: Home Based Primary Care is a VA health care team led by a VA physician that delivers care in the veteran's home. Eligibility requires VA enrolment, a VA determination of need and local availability. HBPC enrolment is also a prerequisite for the Medical Foster Home program.
items.hack: Ask for HBPC early, for three reasons beyond the medical care. It satisfies the 38 CFR 71.20(a)(7) PCAFC requirement that the veteran receive ongoing care from a primary care team. It gives you a clinician who sees the home and can therefore write the ADL and supervision documentation PCAFC, Aid and Attendance under 38 CFR 3.278, and Medicaid assessments all need. And it is the gateway to Medical Foster Home if home care later becomes impossible.

items.title: VA hospice and palliative care — and the copay consequence
items.who: Veterans with a terminal condition and a prognosis under six months (hospice), or needing comfort care at any stage (palliative)
items.value: Skilled end-of-life or comfort care, in the home or inpatient, with bereavement support for the family
items.how: VA covers hospice care for veterans with a terminal condition and less than six months to live, and palliative care providing comfort care to ease pain at any stage of illness. Both require VA enrolment and a VA determination of need. VA hospice can be delivered in the home, in a VA Community Living Center, or purchased in the community, and VA permits hospice concurrently with disease-directed treatment in circumstances where Medicare would not.
items.hack: The copay point matters at exactly the wrong moment. VA's extended care copay rules at 38 CFR 17.111 treat hospice differently from other extended care, and many veterans in hospice are copay-exempt on other grounds, but families get bills they did not expect. Ask the VA social worker in writing, before admission, what the copay exposure is for this specific hospice arrangement. Also ask about bereavement counselling for the caregiver — 38 CFR 71.45 provides transition assistance and bereavement counselling after a discharge caused by the veteran's death, and Vet Centers provide bereavement counselling separately.

items.title: Extended care copays — 38 CFR 17.111, the first 21 free days, and who is exempt
items.who: Veterans receiving adult day health care, respite, geriatric evaluation or institutional extended care
items.value: Often zero — but only if you know you are exempt
items.how: 38 CFR 17.111 sets copays for extended care services, dividing them into institutional (a hospital, domiciliary or nursing home stay of one or more overnight days) and noninstitutional (no overnight stay). Per-day noninstitutional copays are set for adult day health care, noninstitutional geriatric evaluation and noninstitutional respite care. No veteran owes a copay for the first 21 days of extended care services in any 12-month period; copays apply beyond that and are based on available financial resources. Exemptions include veterans with a compensable service-connected disability, veterans with income below the 38 U.S.C. 1521(b) threshold, Medal of Honor recipients, catastrophically disabled veterans (for adult day health care, noninstitutional respite and noninstitutional geriatric evaluation), care for certain conditions including military sexual trauma and specified exposures, and American Indian and Alaska Native veterans for noninstitutional services.
items.hack: Three practical moves. Check the exemption list before you accept any copay — a compensable service-connected rating is itself an exemption. If the veteran may be catastrophically disabled, ask for a catastrophic disability evaluation, because that status exempts exactly the respite and day care services caregivers use most. And front-load respite into the 21 free days if cost is the blocker. The specific dollar amounts in 17.111 change; read the current regulation rather than any secondary quote.
items.deadline: The 21 free days reset each 12-month period

items.title: FMLA military caregiver leave is 26 weeks, not 12 — and it is a separate 12-month period
items.org: US Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
items.who: Eligible employees who are the spouse, parent, son or daughter, or next of kin of a covered servicemember or covered veteran
items.value: Up to 26 workweeks of job-protected unpaid leave in a single 12-month period
items.how: Military caregiver leave gives an eligible employee up to 26 workweeks of unpaid FMLA leave in a 'single 12-month period' to care for a covered servicemember or covered veteran with a serious injury or illness. That 12-month period begins on the first day the employee uses the leave and ends 12 months later, independent of the employer's FMLA year for other reasons. Within that period the employee has a COMBINED total of 26 workweeks for all FMLA reasons, of which no more than 12 may be used for ordinary FMLA reasons. 'Next of kin' means the nearest blood relative in a priority order: someone with legal custody, then siblings, grandparents, aunts and uncles, then first cousins.
items.hack: Two things employers get wrong. One: HR frequently processes a military caregiver request as ordinary 12-week FMLA. Say the words 'military caregiver leave under FMLA for a covered veteran' in writing and cite DOL Fact Sheet 28M(b). Two: the 26 weeks are per servicemember per serious injury, in a single 12-month period that you effectively choose by when you first use the leave — so the timing of the first day of leave is a decision, not an accident. Note this is unpaid; pair it with a state paid leave program where one exists.
items.deadline: The single 12-month period starts the first day you use the leave

items.title: The five-year rule and the four ways a veteran's injury qualifies for FMLA caregiver leave — PCAFC enrolment is one of them
items.org: US Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
items.who: Employees caring for a recently separated veteran
items.value: Certification that is easy to satisfy if the veteran is in PCAFC or rated 50% or more
items.how: A 'covered veteran' for FMLA military caregiver leave is someone who was a member of the Armed Forces including the National Guard or Reserves, was discharged or released under conditions other than dishonorable, and was discharged within the FIVE-YEAR period before the employee first takes the leave. The serious injury or illness must have been incurred in or aggravated by active duty and must meet one of four alternative definitions: a continuation of a service-related injury that rendered the servicemember unable to perform their duties; a physical or mental condition with a VA Service-Related Disability Rating of 50 percent or greater; a physical or mental condition that substantially impairs the veteran's ability to work because of a service-connected disability; or an injury that qualifies the veteran for the VA's Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers. The optional certification form is WH-385-V; alternatively, documentation of the VA disability rating or the VA caregiver program enrolment papers are sufficient certification.
items.hack: If the veteran is in PCAFC or rated 50% or higher, you do not need a doctor's certification at all — the VA paperwork is the certification. Photocopy the PCAFC designation letter or the rating decision and hand it to HR with the leave request. And watch the five-year clock: a veteran discharged more than five years before you first take the leave is not a 'covered veteran' for the 26-week entitlement, though ordinary 12-week FMLA for a serious health condition may still apply.
items.deadline: Discharge must be within 5 years before the employee first takes military caregiver leave

items.title: State paid family leave — 13 states and DC will actually pay you while you care
items.org: State paid family and medical leave insurance programs
items.who: Workers in states with mandatory PFML, caring for a seriously ill family member
items.value: Partial wage replacement during caregiving leave, which FMLA does not provide
items.how: FMLA is unpaid. Separately, mandatory state paid family and medical leave insurance programs exist in California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island and Washington, plus the District of Columbia. All of them include leave to care for a family member with a serious health condition. Around ten further states offer voluntary paid leave through private insurers. Benefit duration, wage replacement percentage, the definition of family member and the effective dates differ in every state, and several programs have phased in benefits recently.
items.hack: Run state PFML and FMLA together: FMLA protects the job, state PFML replaces part of the wage, and in most states you take them concurrently. Apply to the state program yourself — it is an insurance claim to a state agency, not something the employer files for you, and employers routinely fail to mention it. Check your own state's definition of family member before assuming a parent, in-law or chosen family member is covered; the definitions have been broadening.
items.deadline: State-specific claim deadlines; file as soon as leave begins

items.title: IRS Notice 2014-7 — Medicaid waiver payments to a live-in family caregiver can be excluded from income
items.who: Family caregivers paid under a Medicaid home and community based services waiver who live in the same home as the person they care for
items.value: The payments may be excludable from gross income entirely
items.how: Notice 2014-7 treats qualifying payments to individual care providers under state Medicaid home and community based services waiver programs described in section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act as difficulty-of-care payments excludable from gross income under Internal Revenue Code section 131. The critical condition is residence: the care must be provided 'in the individual care provider's home where the care recipient lives under the recipient's plan of care', and the provider's home means where the provider resides and regularly performs the routines of their private life. A provider who keeps a separate residence cannot claim the exclusion even if they temporarily stay at the recipient's home. The IRS states the exclusion applies to family caregivers — a parent paid to care for a disabled child in the shared family home, or a child who moves into an elderly parent's home — and that more than one provider living in the home may exclude their payments.
items.hack: This is the single largest tax item in the whole caregiver picture and it turns on one fact: whether you genuinely live there. If a family member is going to be the paid Medicaid provider and could live in either home, the shared-residence arrangement may be worth thousands a year. Tell the financial management service or payroll agent that you are claiming the Notice 2014-7 exclusion so the reporting matches. Do not extend this to the PCAFC stipend, which is a different payment under different authority. This is tax advice territory — take it to a preparer who has handled 2014-7 before, and point them at the IRS page rather than describing it.
items.deadline: Applies to the tax year the payments are received

items.title: Is the PCAFC stipend taxable? Treat this as an open question and get it in writing
items.who: PCAFC Primary Family Caregivers
items.value: Avoiding both an unexpected tax bill and an unnecessary one
items.how: The PCAFC stipend is paid under 38 U.S.C. 1720G and 38 CFR 71.40(c)(4) and is described by VA as a stipend rather than wages — it is not employment, VA is not the caregiver's employer, and the payment is not compensation for services in the ordinary sense. VA has historically not treated it as reportable income to the caregiver. There is no IRS ruling squarely addressed to the PCAFC stipend of the kind Notice 2014-7 provides for Medicaid waiver payments, and the analysis is not the same.
items.hack: Do three things rather than relying on any website, this one included. One: keep every VA letter and payment record; if VA issues no Form 1099 for the stipend, that document trail is your position. Two: ask the Caregiver Support Program team in writing whether VA reports the stipend to the IRS, and keep the answer. Three: take both to a tax professional, and have them look at the actual authority rather than a forum post. Anyone who tells you confidently in one sentence that it is or is not taxable, without reference to your facts, is guessing. Start from the IRS, not from a benefits blog.
items.deadline: Settle the question before you file, not after

items.title: The Child and Dependent Care Credit covers a disabled adult — but you cannot pay your own spouse
items.who: Working caregivers who pay someone else to care for a disabled spouse or dependent
items.value: A credit of 20% to 35% on up to $3,000 of expenses for one person, or $6,000 for two or more
items.how: Under IRS Publication 503, a qualifying person includes your spouse who was not physically or mentally able to care for themselves and lived with you for more than half the year, and any person unable to care for themselves who lived with you more than half the year and was your dependent or would have been but for income or filing-status rules. Inability to self-care means persons who cannot dress, clean or feed themselves because of physical or mental disability, plus those who need constant attention to prevent injury to themselves or others. You must have earned income, though a disabled spouse is treated as having a deemed minimum monthly earned income. The expense limit is $3,000 for one qualifying person or $6,000 for two or more, and the credit percentage runs from 20% to 35% depending on adjusted gross income. Critically, you CANNOT claim amounts paid to your spouse, to your own child under age 19, or to the parent of your qualifying child under 13.
items.hack: This credit does not pay a family caregiver — it is the opposite, a credit for buying care so the caregiver can work. The prohibition on paying your spouse is the trap: a husband caring for his disabled wife cannot pay himself and claim it, and a family that routes payment through a spouse to capture the credit has created a problem rather than a benefit. The real use is paying an adult day program, an aide or an adult child over 19 so the primary caregiver can hold a job. Verify the dollar limits and percentages for the current year — these figures are from the publication as reviewed and change.
items.deadline: Claimed on the annual return

items.title: Claiming the disabled veteran as your dependent — VA compensation does not count against the income test
items.who: Caregivers providing more than half the support of a disabled adult veteran relative
items.value: A dependent on your return, with the knock-on credits and filing status that follow
items.how: IRS Publication 501 sets the qualifying relative tests, including a gross income limit for the dependent — reviewed at $5,200 for 2025 and adjusted annually — and a support test requiring you to provide more than half of the person's total support for the year. Gross income for this test includes taxable interest, ordinary dividends, capital gain distributions, unemployment compensation, taxable Social Security benefits, pensions and annuities. Nontaxable income is excluded. VA disability compensation is not taxable, so it does not count toward the gross income test — though it does count as support the veteran provides for themselves, which bears on the support test. Where several people together provide more than half the support but none provides more than half alone, Form 2120 multiple support declaration lets one of them claim. A person who is permanently and totally disabled can be a qualifying child regardless of age.
items.hack: Two distinct levers, and families confuse them. The gross income test ignores VA compensation — that is what makes claiming a severely disabled veteran possible at all. The support test does not: large VA compensation and SMC payments are support the veteran supplies to themselves, and that is usually what defeats the claim. Do the support arithmetic honestly, counting the fair rental value of housing you provide. If two siblings are sharing support, Form 2120 is the mechanism. Verify the current year's gross income figure before relying on it.
items.deadline: Claimed on the annual return

items.title: Deducting the cost of care as a medical expense — including wages you pay an attendant
items.who: Families itemising deductions who pay out of pocket for care
items.value: A Schedule A deduction for medical expenses above 7.5% of adjusted gross income
items.how: IRS Publication 502 allows wages paid for nursing services as a medical expense, and states the services need not be performed by a nurse as long as they are of a kind generally performed by a nurse — giving medication, changing dressings, bathing and grooming. Where an attendant performs mixed duties, the payments must be divided between time spent on household and personal services and time spent on nursing services, and only the nursing portion is deductible. Employment taxes you pay for an attendant who provides medical care — Social Security, FUTA, Medicare and state employment taxes — are includable, apportioned if the attendant also does household work. Maintenance and personal care services for a chronically ill individual are deductible where part of a prescribed plan of care. Only expenses above 7.5% of adjusted gross income are deductible.
items.hack: The apportionment rule is why timesheets matter: keep a log splitting nursing-type tasks from housekeeping, because without it the whole payment is vulnerable. Note the same records serve three purposes at once — the 38 CFR 3.278 VA pension medical expense deduction, a Medicaid personal care agreement, and this deduction. Build one timesheet that satisfies all three. Remember that paying a family member creates household employment obligations; Publication 926 is the companion reading.
items.deadline: Claimed on the annual return; 7.5% AGI floor applies

items.title: There is no Social Security caregiver credit — and that is the hidden cost of caregiving
items.who: Anyone leaving the workforce to provide care
items.value: Knowing the real long-term price, and what to do about it
items.how: Social Security retirement and disability benefits are computed from a worker's own covered earnings record. Years spent caregiving without covered earnings are zeroes in that computation. No federal caregiver credit exists: a Social Security Caregiver Credit Act has been introduced repeatedly across multiple Congresses — 2019, 2021, and again as H.R. 8490 in the 119th Congress in 2026 — and has not become law. Whether the PCAFC stipend produces covered earnings for Social Security purposes follows from its treatment as a non-wage stipend rather than employment, which is the same open question as its taxability.
items.hack: Plan around it rather than hoping. Three concrete moves. One: if the caregiver is married, understand the spousal and survivor benefits on the veteran's record, which may be the practical floor. Two: where there is any earned income, fund an IRA — a spousal IRA works on the working spouse's earned income. Three: prefer the paid routes that DO generate covered earnings. A Medicaid self-directed personal care job or an IHSS provider position usually produces reportable wages and Social Security credits; the PCAFC stipend's status is unsettled. For a 45-year-old facing twenty years of caregiving, that distinction is worth more than the monthly difference between the programs. Get your earnings record from ssa.gov and look at the zeroes before you decide.

items.title: SSDI and SSI for the veteran are separate from VA — and a 100% P&T rating does not decide them
items.who: Veterans unable to work, and their caregivers managing household income
items.value: A second income stream the household is often missing entirely
items.how: Social Security Disability Insurance and Supplemental Security Income are administered by SSA under its own definition of disability, which is all-or-nothing and work-based, not percentage-based like VA's. A veteran can hold a 100% VA rating and be denied SSDI, or hold a lower VA rating and be approved. VA disability compensation does not reduce SSDI, which is not needs-based. SSI is needs-based and VA compensation does count against it. Veterans rated 100% permanent and total, and veterans with a VA Compensation and Pension record showing certain conditions, can request expedited SSA processing.
items.hack: File both. Families routinely assume the VA rating substitutes for a Social Security claim and leave SSDI on the table for years, and SSDI is also the route to Medicare after the waiting period, which matters because VA health care is not insurance and does not travel with the veteran. Ask SSA for expedited handling on the 100% P&T basis and put the rating decision in the file. If the caregiver is managing both systems, be aware the medical evidence overlaps almost entirely — one set of records serves both claims.
items.deadline: SSDI has a five-month waiting period and SSI is payable only from the application month; file early

items.title: Elizabeth Dole Foundation Hope Fund — emergency cash grants specifically for military and veteran caregivers
items.who: Military and veteran caregivers in financial crisis
items.value: Critical financial assistance grants
items.how: The Hope Fund provides critical financial assistance grants to military and veteran caregivers, covering natural disasters, medical and dental bills, home repairs, emergency transportation, vehicle modifications, home appliances and lost income. Applications go through hiddenheroes.org, the Foundation's caregiver-facing platform.
items.hack: This is one of very few funds in the country written for the caregiver rather than the veteran, and 'lost income' is an eligible category — which almost no emergency fund covers. Register on hiddenheroes.org before you need it, because applications in a crisis go faster when the account and documentation already exist. Apply here in parallel with a VSO emergency grant rather than sequentially; they are different pots.
items.deadline: Rolling; funding is finite

items.title: Hidden Heroes and the Dole Caregiver Fellows — the national caregiver community and its leadership pipeline
items.who: Military and veteran caregivers of any era
items.value: Peer network, resources, mental health referrals, and a multi-year leadership fellowship
items.how: Hidden Heroes is the Elizabeth Dole Foundation's flagship campaign and caregiver-facing platform at hiddenheroes.org, carrying resources, peer support, mental health referrals and the Hope Fund application. The Dole Caregiver Fellows program is a multi-year leadership initiative with fellows across all 50 states, Puerto Rico and DC — 290 to date — providing leadership development, peer connection and advocacy opportunities. The Campaign for Inclusive Care is a joint initiative with VA aimed at getting caregivers formally included in the veteran's care team from the outset.
items.hack: The Campaign for Inclusive Care is the one with direct operational value: it exists because VA clinicians routinely exclude the caregiver from clinical conversations about a veteran they care for 24 hours a day. Its materials give you the language to insist on being treated as part of the care team, which is exactly what you need when a clinician declines to document an ADL or supervision need for your PCAFC file. Apply for a Fellowship if you want to change the system rather than only survive it.
items.deadline: Fellows applications open periodically

items.title: Military and Veteran Caregiver Network — free peer mentoring run through the American Red Cross
items.who: Caregivers of military members and veterans from all eras
items.value: A matched peer mentor, online community, facilitated support groups and the Hero Care Resource Directory
items.how: The Military and Veteran Caregiver Network (MVCN) provides a secure online community, one-to-one and group peer mentoring using evidence-based models delivered by trained caregiver peers, regularly scheduled in-person and online peer support groups, and workshops plus access to the Hero Care Resource Directory for local services. Caregivers join via the form on the Red Cross MVCN page; there is an eligibility quiz and a vetting email. Contact is info.mvcn@redcross.org; no phone line is published on the program page.
items.hack: Peer mentoring is the intervention caregivers consistently rate highest and claim least, because it feels optional. Ask specifically for a one-to-one mentor matched on your situation — TBI, polytrauma, dementia, a young caregiver, a parent caregiver — rather than only joining the online community. Note this is a separate network from VA's own Peer Support Mentoring Program under PGCSS; there is no reason not to be in both.

items.title: The civilian caregiver infrastructure veterans' families forget exists: FCA, Caregiver Action Network, Rosalynn Carter Institute
items.org: Family Caregiver Alliance; Caregiver Action Network; Rosalynn Carter Institute for Caregivers
items.who: Any family caregiver, military or not
items.value: State-by-state service navigation, condition-specific guidance, and structured caregiver coaching
items.how: Family Caregiver Alliance hosts the National Center on Caregiving and a state-by-state services guide at caregiver.org/connecting-caregivers/services-by-state; it can be reached on 800-445-8106 or 415-434-3388. Caregiver Action Network at caregiveraction.org maintains a directory of caregiver support organisations and agencies. The Rosalynn Carter Institute for Caregivers at rosalynncarter.org runs Operation Family Caregiver, a structured coaching program built specifically for the families of returning servicemembers and veterans, and has partnered with Wounded Warrior Project on military and veteran caregiver support. The National Alliance for Caregiving is at caregiving.org.
items.hack: Use FCA's state guide as the cross-check on anything a state agency tells you, because it is organised by state and by benefit rather than by program name. Operation Family Caregiver is the specifically military-facing offering and is coaching rather than information — closer to REACH VA than to a pamphlet. The practical point: a veteran caregiver is also just a caregiver, and the civilian caregiving sector is larger, better funded and more mature than the veteran-specific one. Use both.

items.title: Wounded Warrior Project, Semper Fi & America's Fund and Quality of Life Foundation — caregiver-specific programs at the service-organisation level
items.org: Wounded Warrior Project; Semper Fi & America's Fund; Quality of Life Foundation
items.who: Caregivers of catastrophically wounded, ill or injured post-9/11 veterans, and in some cases earlier eras
items.value: Caregiver retreats, respite funding, case management, direct financial assistance and family support
items.how: Wounded Warrior Project runs caregiver-directed programming alongside its Independence Program for veterans needing long-term support, and has partnered with the Rosalynn Carter Institute on military and veteran caregiver support. Semper Fi & America's Fund provides case management and direct financial assistance to critically wounded, ill and injured servicemembers and veterans and their families, including caregiver support. Quality of Life Foundation provides family support and care coordination to wounded veterans' families with a specific caregiver focus. Each organisation sets its own eligibility by era, injury severity and service branch.
items.hack: Apply to all three rather than picking one — their eligibility windows differ and their money comes from different places, so a denial from one says nothing about the others. The thing to ask each for is case management, not grants: a dedicated case manager who knows the VA system is worth more over five years than any single cheque, and it is the service families forget to request. Verify current program names and eligibility directly, because service-organisation programs are renamed and restructured frequently.
items.deadline: Rolling; eligibility windows vary by organisation

items.title: The National Family Caregiver Support Program — a separate federal respite stream most veteran families never touch
items.org: Administration for Community Living / state units on aging / Area Agencies on Aging
items.who: Family caregivers of adults 60 and older; caregivers of people with Alzheimer's disease at any age; relatives 55 and over caring for children under 18 or for adults 18 to 59 with disabilities
items.value: Information, access assistance, counselling and training, respite care, and limited supplemental services
items.how: The NFCSP, authorised under the Older Americans Act and administered by the Administration for Community Living through state units on aging and Area Agencies on Aging, funds five service categories: information to caregivers about available services; assistance in gaining access to services; individual counselling, support groups and caregiver training; respite care at home or in adult day care; and supplemental services on a limited basis. It does not pay caregivers directly. Find your Area Agency on Aging through the Eldercare Locator on 1-800-677-1116, Monday to Friday 8am to 9pm ET.
items.hack: This is a completely separate pot of respite money from VA's, with its own eligibility, and nothing stops an eligible family from using both. It is the answer when the VA facility's respite authorisation is thin or the waiting list is long. 'Supplemental services on a limited basis' is the discretionary line that in many areas pays for home modifications, incontinence supplies or emergency response systems — ask what your AAA uses it for, because it is rarely advertised.

items.title: Caregiver burnout is a clinical problem with a clinical answer — and the respite nobody uses is the treatment
items.who: Every long-term caregiver
items.value: Keeping the caregiver functional, which is the only thing keeping the veteran at home
items.how: The structure VA has built for this is specific, not vague: respite care of at least 30 days a year for Primary Family Caregivers under 38 CFR 71.40(c)(1); clinically authorised respite including 24-hour in-home care for Secondary and General Caregivers under 71.40(a)(4); counselling, individual and group therapy and peer support under 71.40 and 71.50; the Virtual Psychotherapy Program for Caregivers; REACH VA one-to-one coaching; Caregiver Health and Wellbeing coaching; Building Better Caregivers; and the Annie text-messaging program for stress management.
items.hack: The pattern is always the same: the caregiver banks the respite, declines the counselling, and then breaks — and the veteran gets placed, which is the outcome everyone was trying to avoid. Treat the 30 days as a prescription with a schedule. Book the first block within 60 days of approval, before the guilt sets in. And understand the arithmetic plainly: placement in a nursing home costs VA or Medicaid vastly more than respite, so asking for relief is not taking something from the veteran. It is the cheapest thing in the system.
items.deadline: Respite resets annually and does not bank

items.title: The Caregiver Support Line is a triage desk, not a phone number on a page — 1-855-260-3274
items.who: Any caregiver of a veteran, enrolled in anything or nothing
items.value: Live licensed staff who can enrol you in PGCSS, connect you to your local team, and start a respite request
items.how: The VA Caregiver Support Line is 1-855-260-3274, staffed Monday to Friday, 8am to 8pm ET. It is the national front door to both PCAFC and PGCSS: it can explain eligibility, start a PGCSS enrolment, identify and connect you to the Caregiver Support Program team at your local VA medical centre, and route you to respite, training and counselling.
items.hack: Use it as an escalation path, not just an information line. When a local facility says a benefit does not exist, call the national line and ask them to document the request and contact the facility's CSP team — that creates a national record of the ask, which is what moves facility-level answers. Note VA pages have shown slightly different hours for this line at different times, including extended evening and Saturday hours; if you need it outside Monday-to-Friday business hours, call anyway. For an immediate mental health crisis, the Veterans Crisis Line is 988 then press 1, and it serves family members and caregivers too, not only veterans.

items.title: When it ends: transition support, bereavement counselling and the benefits that continue after discharge
items.who: Caregivers facing the veteran's death, institutionalisation, or their own discharge from the program
items.value: 30 to 90 days of continued benefits, transition assistance and bereavement counselling
items.how: 38 CFR 71.45 requires VA to provide transition assistance and bereavement counselling in connection with discharge, and sets continuation periods for benefits: 90 days after a discharge due to the eligible veteran, including death or institutionalisation; 90 days after a discharge due to the Family Caregiver; 30 days after a discharge at the caregiver's or the veteran's request, extended to 90 days where the caregiver's discharge is triggered by domestic or intimate partner violence evidenced by a protective order, a police report, or a disclosure to a treating provider; and 60 days after a revocation based on VA error, unless the caregiver opts out. Vet Centers separately provide bereavement counselling under their readjustment counselling scope.
items.hack: Three things to do in that window, because it closes fast. One: if CHAMPVA was the caregiver's only coverage, that continuation period is your window to get other insurance — a loss of coverage is normally a qualifying life event for a marketplace or employer special enrolment, so start immediately. Two: ask for the bereavement counselling in writing; it is an entitlement under 71.45, not a courtesy, and Vet Centers offer it separately. Three: if the caregiver is leaving because of domestic or intimate partner violence, the 90-day extension exists and is triggered by a protective order, a police report, or telling a treating provider — a disclosure to a clinician is enough.
items.deadline: 30, 60 or 90 days depending on the basis for discharge or revocation

items.title: VA Dental Class I — compensable service-connected dental disability, any needed dental care for life
items.org: VA Veterans Health Administration (Office of Dentistry)
items.who: Veterans with a dental condition or disability that is service-connected AND compensably rated (a percentage, not 0%). Usually jaw or tooth trauma, osteomyelitis, loss of mandible or maxilla, chronic osteitis.
items.value: Unlimited comprehensive dental care — exams, cleanings, fillings, crowns, bridges, dentures, implants, oral surgery — at no cost, for life, with no copay and no rating-percentage minimum beyond being compensable.
items.how: Enroll in VA health care (VA Form 10-10EZ), then ask the VA dental clinic to run a dental eligibility determination against your rating decision. Bring the rating decision page showing the dental diagnostic code (the DC 9900-9916 series).
items.hack: A compensable dental rating at ANY percentage — even 10% for a tooth lost in a service accident — buys unlimited lifetime dental. A 10% dental rating gets the same dental benefit as a 100% veteran. Check your rating decision for a 99xx diagnostic code before assuming you have no dental.
items.deadline: None — eligibility is permanent once the dental condition is compensably rated.

items.title: VA Dental Class II — the one-time dental benefit that expires 180 days after discharge
items.who: Veterans who served 90 or more days of active duty and whose DD-214 does NOT certify that they received a complete dental examination and all indicated dental treatment before separation.
items.value: One-time course of dental care to correct any dental condition that existed at discharge. One time only — it is not a recurring benefit.
items.how: Apply to VA dental within 180 days of discharge. Bring your DD-214 (check the dental certification block) and ask specifically for 'Class II one-time dental treatment.'
items.hack: This is the most-missed dental benefit in VA and the clock is brutal: 180 days from discharge, no extensions. If your separation dental exam was rushed or incomplete and the DD-214 does not certify complete treatment, a one-time full course of dental work is waiting. Most separating members never hear the words 'Class II' and the window closes silently.
items.deadline: 180 days from date of discharge — hard deadline, no waiver.

items.title: VA Dental Class IIA — the 0% dental rating worth lifetime care
items.who: Veterans with a dental condition adjudicated service-connected but rated 0% (noncompensable) because it resulted from combat wounds or service trauma, including documented in-service dental trauma.
items.value: Ongoing dental care — not one-time — to maintain a functioning dentition in the area affected by the trauma. Repeat treatment of the traumatized area is authorized for life.
items.how: File a dental claim (VA Form 21-526EZ) for the specific tooth or jaw injury even if you expect 0%. A 0% service-connected dental rating under Class IIA unlocks lifetime care for that area. Present the rating decision to VA dental.
items.hack: Veterans skip filing for dental trauma because 0% pays nothing. But a 0% Class IIA dental rating is worth lifetime repeat treatment of that tooth, crown replacements included. File the claim for the zero.
items.deadline: None once established, but file the service connection claim while in-service records are still obtainable.

items.title: VA Dental Class IIB — Homeless Veterans Dental Program, a full one-time course of care
items.org: VA Homeless Programs / VHA Office of Dentistry
items.who: Veterans enrolled in a VA homeless program — HCHV, Grant and Per Diem, HUD-VASH, Domiciliary, Compensated Work Therapy or Transitional Residence — who need dental care to relieve pain, secure employment, or treat gum disease.
items.value: A one-time course of dental care sufficient to relieve pain, assist in obtaining employment, or treat moderate to severe gingival or periodontal disease. In practice this routinely includes extractions, fillings and dentures.
items.how: Get into any VA homeless program first, then ask the case manager to submit the Class IIB dental consult. Homeless program enrollment is the gate, not the dental clinic.
items.hack: The 'assist in obtaining employment' prong is enormously broad and the one case managers underuse — missing front teeth are a documented employment barrier. Ask for dentures explicitly and tie the request to a job search.
items.deadline: Must be enrolled in a qualifying VA homeless program at the time of the dental consult.

items.title: VA Dental Class IIC — former prisoners of war get unlimited dental, no rating required
items.who: Any veteran with former prisoner of war (FPOW) status, regardless of disability rating or length of captivity.
items.value: Any needed dental care, comprehensive and unlimited, for life — identical in scope to Class I and Class IV.
items.how: Establish FPOW status in your VA record (DD-214, service records, or the FPOW block on VA Form 10-10EZ). Once FPOW is flagged, dental is automatic with no separate dental eligibility determination.
items.hack: FPOW status also removes copays entirely and raises your priority group. Many older FPOWs never had the status formally flagged in the VA system, so dental was denied in error. Ask the eligibility clerk to verify the FPOW indicator is actually set in your record.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA Dental Class III — dental care when your teeth are making a service-connected condition worse
items.who: Veterans with a dental condition clinically determined to be aggravating an already service-connected medical condition — classically oral infection worsening diabetes, endocarditis risk, or a cardiac condition.
items.value: Dental care limited to resolving the oral condition that is aggravating the service-connected disability. Not comprehensive, but it covers the infection, the extraction and the follow-up.
items.how: Have your VA primary care provider or specialist write the clinical statement linking the dental condition to the aggravation, then submit a Class III dental consult. The statement from the MEDICAL side, not the dental side, unlocks it.
items.hack: This is the back door into VA dental for veterans with service-connected diabetes. Periodontal disease and glycemic control are bidirectional in the clinical literature, so a note saying periodontal infection is degrading A1c control is a legitimate Class III trigger. Almost nobody asks.
items.deadline: None, but the consult must be supported by a current clinical statement.

items.title: VA Dental Class V — dental care while you are in Chapter 31 Veteran Readiness and Employment
items.org: VA Veteran Readiness and Employment (VR&E) / VHA
items.who: Veterans actively participating in a 38 U.S.C. Chapter 31 VR&E program — training, education, or the independent living track.
items.value: Dental care necessary to make the veteran employable or to achieve the goals of the rehabilitation or independent living program. In practice, substantial restorative work when appearance or oral pain affects employability.
items.how: Ask your Vocational Rehabilitation Counselor to issue the Class V dental authorization and get it written into the Individualized Written Rehabilitation Plan. The counselor, not the dental clinic, drives this.
items.hack: Class V dental ends when your VR&E program ends — so front-load it. Get the comprehensive exam and treatment plan in the first semester, not the last. And if your rehab goal is client-facing work, say so in writing: it strengthens the employability nexus for restorative work.
items.deadline: Only while actively in a Chapter 31 program — the benefit terminates with the program.

items.title: VA Dental Class VI — dental care when bad teeth are blocking your medical treatment
items.who: Veterans receiving VA medical care where a dental condition is complicating or impeding that treatment — pre-transplant, pre-cardiac-surgery, pre-chemotherapy, pre-radiation or pre-joint-replacement clearance.
