items.value: Dental care limited to resolving the condition impeding the medical treatment. Full mouth clearance before transplant or chemotherapy is routinely authorized.
items.how: The treating medical specialist submits the dental consult, flagged as Class VI with the specific medical treatment named. Do not go through the dental clinic yourself; it must come from the medical team.
items.hack: Most systems require dental clearance before organ transplant, heart valve surgery, head and neck radiation and certain chemotherapies. If VA is providing that treatment, VA must provide the dental clearance under Class VI. Veterans routinely pay out of pocket for clearance they were entitled to.
items.deadline: Tied to the episode of medical care.

items.title: The VA dental surprise — being enrolled in VA health care does NOT give you dental
items.who: Every veteran enrolled in VA health care who is not in a dental eligibility class. This includes veterans rated 10% through 90% with no dental rating, and most Priority Group 5, 7 and 8 veterans.
items.value: Nothing. This is the gap item: VA medical enrollment covers routine eye exams for everyone but routine dental for almost nobody.
items.how: Verify your dental class with the VA eligibility clerk in writing before scheduling. If you are not in a class, your options are VADIP, a dental school clinic, an FQHC sliding-fee dental clinic, or Dental Lifeline Network.
items.hack: The most common benefits misunderstanding in VA health care. A 70% rated veteran with full medical enrollment and zero copays walks into a VA dental clinic and is turned away. Plan for dental separately from day one: price VADIP in your first year, not after a molar cracks.
items.deadline: None, but the VADIP decision and the Class II 180-day window both have clocks.

items.title: VADIP enrollment mechanics — Delta Dental vs MetLife, and the 12-month lock
items.who: Any veteran enrolled in VA health care (any priority group, any rating, including Priority Group 8), and any spouse, surviving spouse or dependent child enrolled in CHAMPVA.
items.value: Discounted group-rate private dental insurance with no VA cost share — you pay the full premium, but at a negotiated group rate instead of individual-market pricing. Multiple plan tiers from basic preventive to comprehensive with orthodontia.
items.how: Enroll directly with the carrier, not through VA. Delta Dental: feds.deltadentalins.com/vadip/ or 855-370-3303. MetLife: metlife.com/vadip/ or 888-310-1681. You will attest to VA health care or CHAMPVA enrollment.
items.hack: VADIP is now a permanent program with no end date and no annual open-enrollment window, so you can enroll any month. But initial enrollment commits you for 12 calendar months — compare the two carriers' annual maximums and major-services waiting periods BEFORE you sign, because they differ and that is what matters if you need work in year one.
items.deadline: No enrollment deadline (rolling), but a 12-month minimum commitment once enrolled.

items.title: VADIP for CHAMPVA spouses and children — dental for the family VA health care forgets
items.who: Spouses, surviving spouses and dependent children enrolled in CHAMPVA. The veteran does NOT need to be enrolled in VA health care for the CHAMPVA family member to buy VADIP.
items.value: Group-rate dental insurance for the family member. CHAMPVA itself covers essentially no routine dental, so this is the only structured dental option on the CHAMPVA side of the house.
items.how: The CHAMPVA beneficiary enrolls in their own name with Delta Dental (855-370-3303) or MetLife (888-310-1681), attesting to CHAMPVA enrollment.
items.hack: Families of 100% permanent and total veterans on CHAMPVA almost never learn this exists, because the VADIP page is filed under the veteran's dental benefit. A surviving spouse who keeps CHAMPVA for life keeps VADIP eligibility for life too.
items.deadline: Rolling enrollment; 12-month initial commitment.

items.title: Dental and dental hygiene school clinics — well below private fees, nationwide
items.org: CODA-accredited dental schools and hygiene programs
items.who: Anyone, including veterans with no VA dental eligibility. No income test at most schools. Roughly 70 U.S. dental schools plus several hundred dental hygiene and dental therapy programs.
items.value: Substantially reduced-fee comprehensive dentistry — cleanings, fillings, crowns, dentures, implants, endodontics — performed by students under faculty supervision. Hygiene school cleanings are often nominal or free.
items.how: Find accredited programs through the ADA's dental school directory, then call the school's patient admissions line and ask to be screened. Expect a screening appointment and longer chair times.
items.hack: This is the highest-value non-VA dental option for the 10-to-90-percent veteran with no dental class, and it is almost never mentioned in veteran guides. Two tips: ask for the FACULTY PRACTICE price list too (still below market, much faster), and ask whether the graduate prosthodontics or endodontics RESIDENCY clinic takes complex cases — residents are licensed dentists, so quality concerns largely evaporate.
items.deadline: None; waitlists vary by program and academic term.

items.title: FQHC sliding-fee dental — a federally mandated discount based on your income
items.org: HRSA Health Center Program (Federally Qualified Health Centers)
items.who: Anyone with household income at or below 200 percent of federal poverty guidelines gets a sliding-fee discount; at or below 100 percent, a nominal fee only. Veterans qualify on the same terms as anyone else.
items.value: Dental services at a federally required sliding-fee discount. Most FQHCs provide preventive, restorative and emergency dental; many provide extractions and dentures.
items.how: Find a health center at findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov, ask for the 'sliding fee discount program' application, and bring proof of household income. Dental availability varies by site — call and confirm.
items.hack: VA compensation counts as income for the sliding-fee calculation, but the scale is generous and the nominal-fee tier is often under twenty dollars a visit. Critically, an FQHC cannot refuse you for inability to pay — that is a condition of its federal grant. Pair an FQHC for maintenance with a dental school for major work.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA routine eye exams — covered for every enrolled veteran, and nobody knows it
items.org: VA Veterans Health Administration (Optometry and Ophthalmology)
items.who: Every veteran enrolled in VA health care, any priority group, any rating. No separate eligibility determination required.
items.value: Routine eye examinations and preventive vision testing, including glaucoma screening, diabetic retinal screening and refraction. Specialty-care copays apply per your priority group.
items.how: Request an optometry consult through VA primary care, or in many VISNs schedule optometry directly through secure messaging or the clinic line.
items.hack: The asymmetry is the whole item: VA covers the eye EXAM for everyone but the GLASSES for almost nobody. Use VA for the exam and the prescription — including the dilated diabetic exam that private insurers cost-share — then fill it through an online optical retailer for a fraction of optical-shop pricing. Ask for a printed prescription INCLUDING pupillary distance; without PD you cannot order online.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA eyeglasses eligibility — the doors in, and only one is a disability rating for your eyes
items.org: VA Veterans Health Administration (Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service)
items.who: Veterans meeting at least one of: a compensable service-connected disability (any percentage, any body system); former POW; Purple Heart recipient; receiving 38 U.S.C. 1151 benefits; receiving increased pension for being permanently housebound or in need of aid and attendance; vision loss from an illness VA is treating (stroke, diabetes, MS, vascular disease, geriatric conditions); vision loss from an injury or treatment VA provided (medication reaction, eye, ear or brain surgery, TBI); functional or cognitive impairment affecting activities of daily living; or dual sensory impairment (vision plus hearing loss) interfering with participation in your own health care.
items.value: Eyeglasses — frames and lenses — at no cost, with replacement as the prescription changes.
items.how: Have the VA optometrist document WHICH eligibility category you fall under in the consult note; PSAS then issues the glasses. If denied, ask the optometrist to re-document against the specific category list.
items.hack: A compensable service connection for ANY condition — 10% for tinnitus, 10% for a knee — opens the eyeglasses door. The rating does not have to be for your eyes. Thousands of veterans with 10% tinnitus buy their own glasses every year because nobody told them the 10% itself was the qualifier.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA Blind Rehabilitation Centers — inpatient residential blind rehab, free, including travel
items.who: Veterans with VA health care eligibility (and active duty service members) who have a visual impairment not correctable with conventional eyeglasses AND functional difficulty with one or more daily living tasks. Legal blindness is NOT required.
items.value: Weeks of intensive residential rehabilitation: orientation and mobility (long cane, route planning), living skills, manual skills, visual skills, computer access technology, and the full suite of low-vision and adaptive devices issued to take home.
items.how: Get referred by your VIST Coordinator — BRC admission runs through VIST, not self-referral. Beneficiary travel to and from the center is covered, as are lodging and meals during the stay.
items.hack: The admission criterion is FUNCTIONAL, not acuity-based — you do not need 20/200. A veteran with macular degeneration who can no longer read mail or safely cross a street qualifies. And the devices issued at a BRC (CCTV magnifiers, screen readers, talking devices, GPS units) are issued free and kept, often thousands of dollars of equipment.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VIST Coordinator — the single gatekeeper for every VA blind and low-vision benefit
items.who: Any enrolled veteran with a visual impairment causing functional difficulty. Every VA medical center has a VIST Coordinator or is covered by one.
items.value: Case management for life: enrollment in the VIST registry, annual review, referral to a Blind Rehabilitation Center or outpatient blind rehab, coordination of all low-vision devices, and connection to state blind services and talking-book libraries.
items.how: Call your VA medical center's main line and ask for the VIST Coordinator BY TITLE. You do not need a physician referral — self-referral is accepted. Ask to be placed on the VIST registry even if you decline services today.
items.hack: Getting on the VIST registry is the single highest-leverage action a veteran with deteriorating vision can take, and it costs one phone call. Registry membership triggers proactive annual outreach, so when vision worsens in three years the system comes to you. It also unlocks the talking-book library, free equipment loans, and the in-home BROS visit.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: BROS — a blind rehabilitation specialist who comes to your house and teaches you your own kitchen
items.org: VA Blind Rehabilitation Outpatient Specialist (BROS) program
items.who: Veterans in the VIST registry who cannot or will not go inpatient to a Blind Rehabilitation Center — frail, caregiving, rural, or simply unwilling to leave home for weeks.
items.value: In-home and community-based blind rehabilitation: orientation and mobility training on YOUR routes, living-skills training in YOUR kitchen, device training on YOUR equipment, plus assessment and issuance of adaptive equipment.
items.how: Ask your VIST Coordinator for a BROS referral and state explicitly that inpatient BRC is not feasible. BROS coverage is regional — ask which BROS covers your county.
items.hack: Training in the actual environment beats training in a rehab center for anyone not relocating: you learn your own bus stop, your own stove dials, your own stairs. For older veterans and those with caregiving obligations, BROS is strictly better than a BRC admission, and it is the option VIST mentions second.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA Low Vision Clinics and VISOR — the outpatient tier between a magnifier and a residential center
items.who: Veterans with low vision who do not need full residential rehab. VA runs a tiered continuum: Intermediate Low Vision Clinics, Advanced Low Vision Clinics, and VISOR (Visual Impairment Services Outpatient Rehabilitation) programs.
items.value: Low-vision optometric evaluation, prescription of magnification and electronic aids, lighting and contrast assessment, eccentric viewing training, and issuance of devices — all outpatient.
items.how: VIST Coordinator referral. Ask BY NAME for the 'low vision clinic' or 'VISOR program' rather than generic optometry; the low-vision exam is a different, longer appointment with different equipment.
items.hack: A standard VA optometry appointment will not get you a low-vision device evaluation — the general optometrist refracts and sends you home. The low-vision clinic is where electronic magnifiers, portable CCTVs and wearable display devices get prescribed. Ask for it by name.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA dual sensory impairment services — the deaf-blind program almost nobody is referred to
items.org: VA Blind Rehabilitation Service and Audiology
items.who: Veterans with combined vision and hearing loss — extremely common in older veterans with noise-induced hearing loss plus age-related macular degeneration, and specifically recognized in VA policy.
items.value: Coordinated dual sensory rehabilitation, specialized communication devices, tactile and vibrotactile alerting systems, and eyeglasses eligibility under the dual sensory impairment criterion even without a compensable rating.
items.how: Ask the VIST Coordinator and the audiologist JOINTLY for a dual sensory impairment evaluation, and insist they coordinate; left alone, Blind Rehab and Audiology each solve half the problem.
items.hack: The dual sensory impairment criterion is also a standalone eyeglasses eligibility door — a veteran with no compensable rating but documented vision AND hearing loss interfering with participating in their care qualifies for free glasses on that basis alone. It is the least-used entry on the eligibility list.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA hearing aids — and the rule that repairs and batteries stay free forever
items.org: VA Audiology and Speech Pathology Service / Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service
items.who: Veterans enrolled in VA health care whose audiologist determines a clinical need. Eligibility for the DEVICE follows the same statutory categories as eyeglasses: compensable service connection of any kind, former POW, Purple Heart, 1151 benefits, housebound or aid-and-attendance pension, hearing loss from VA-treated illness or injury, functional or cognitive impairment, or dual sensory impairment.
items.value: Hearing aids at no cost, fitted by a VA audiologist, plus all future repairs, batteries, domes, wax guards and tubing at no cost for as long as you maintain VA eligibility. Premium-tier devices from major manufacturers are standard issue, not an upgrade.
items.how: Register at the VA medical center enrollment section with your DD-214 and ID, get an audiology appointment, and have the audiologist document both the clinical need and the statutory eligibility category.
items.hack: Any compensable service-connected rating qualifies you for the device — and 10% for tinnitus is the most common path in. A veteran rated 10% for tinnitus alone is eligible for free hearing aids. That single sentence is worth several thousand dollars every few years and is almost never said out loud. Also: VA-issued aids are top-tier models, so do not assume the private market offers you something better.
items.deadline: None once eligible; devices are replaced on a clinical cycle, not a fixed term.

items.title: VA Form 2346 and the Denver Acquisition and Logistics Center — supplies and repairs without an appointment
items.org: VA Denver Acquisition and Logistics Center (DALC)
items.who: Any veteran issued VA hearing aids, and veterans issued prosthetic socks.
items.value: Free hearing aid batteries, wax guards, domes, tubing, cleaning supplies and prosthetic socks mailed to your home with no appointment and no copay. Delivery typically 7 to 10 days.
items.how: Three routes: mail VA Form 2346 to Denver Acquisition and Logistics Center, P.O. Box 25166, Denver, CO 80225-0166; call 303-273-6200 (press 1 for automated reordering, 2 for customer service and accessories, 3 for repair issues); or order through your VA.gov account under hearing aid batteries and accessories.
items.hack: Press 3 for REPAIRS: you mail the broken aid to Denver in a prepaid mailer and get it back repaired or replaced, free, without burning an audiology appointment. Veterans wait six weeks for an audiology slot to fix something Denver handles in ten days. Also reorder supplies before you run out — standing orders are allowed.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA cochlear implants — covered when hearing aids are no longer enough
items.org: VA Audiology / VA cochlear implant programs
items.who: Enrolled veterans with severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss who get limited benefit from appropriately fitted hearing aids. VA operates designated cochlear implant programs and refers to community care where it does not.
items.value: The implant surgery, the external processor, programming and mapping, aural rehabilitation, replacement processors on an upgrade cycle, and batteries and accessories for the processor — at no cost to the eligible veteran.
items.how: Ask your VA audiologist for a cochlear implant candidacy evaluation. If your facility has no implant program, ask for referral to the nearest VA cochlear implant center or a community care authorization under the MISSION Act access standards.
items.hack: The processor upgrade cycle is the hidden money. Private insurance often fights processor replacement; VA treats the external processor as a prosthetic device and replaces it on a clinical cycle. A veteran who got an implant years ago through private insurance can transfer ongoing processor and accessory support to VA simply by establishing care with VA audiology.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA Progressive Tinnitus Management — the clinical program behind the most-claimed VA condition
items.org: VA Audiology / National Center for Rehabilitative Auditory Research
items.who: Any enrolled veteran with bothersome tinnitus. Tinnitus is the most commonly service-connected condition in VA, yet the clinical program is far less known than the 10% rating.
items.value: A tiered program: education and self-help, group education, interdisciplinary evaluation, and individualized management combining sound therapy (hearing aids with tinnitus maskers, ear-level sound generators, bedside sound machines) with cognitive behavioral coping skills. Devices are issued at no cost.
items.how: Ask VA audiology for 'Progressive Tinnitus Management' by name, or ask for a tinnitus-specific evaluation rather than a general hearing test. Many facilities run PTM group classes you can self-refer into.
items.hack: Hearing aids with built-in tinnitus sound generators are issued under the hearing aid benefit, so a veteran rated 10% for tinnitus with near-normal hearing thresholds can still receive devices as tinnitus TREATMENT. Ask the audiologist to document the devices as tinnitus management rather than amplification when thresholds alone would not justify aids.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA audiology and optometry direct scheduling — you do not need a primary care referral
items.who: Enrolled veterans at VA facilities participating in direct scheduling for audiology and optometry, which is now the broad norm rather than the exception.
items.value: An audiology or optometry appointment booked without going through primary care first — saving one appointment, one wait cycle, and often several months.
items.how: Call the clinic directly, or use VA.gov online scheduling and select Audiology or Optometry. If told you need a PCP referral, ask whether the facility participates in direct scheduling and escalate to the Patient Advocate if answers are inconsistent.
items.hack: Audiology and optometry are the two specialties where VA pushed direct scheduling hardest, and also the two where front-desk staff most often still insist on a referral out of habit. Knowing the policy term — 'direct scheduling' — ends the argument.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service — the largest prosthetics provider in the world, and the catalog is far wider than limbs
items.org: VA Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service (PSAS)
items.who: Any veteran enrolled in VA health care with a clinical need documented by a VA provider. There is no rating requirement for most PSAS items — the gate is enrollment plus clinical need, not percentage.
items.value: PSAS defines a prosthetic as any device that supports or replaces a body function. That covers artificial limbs; hearing aids and eyeglasses; wheelchairs and scooters; walkers and canes; hospital beds and lifts; home oxygen; CPAP and supplies; orthotics and custom shoes; ostomy and urological supplies; wound care; surgically implanted devices (joints, pacemakers, lenses); vehicle modifications; home ramps and structural alterations; adaptive computer equipment; communication devices; recreational and sports equipment; and service dog veterinary insurance.
items.how: Everything runs through a VA clinician's consult to PSAS. Find your facility's PSAS office through the VA facility locator and ask for the Prosthetics Representative; general questions go through ask.va.gov.
items.hack: Learn the phrase 'please enter a prosthetics consult.' PSAS cannot issue anything without a clinician consult, so a denial is almost always a missing consult rather than ineligibility. PSAS items are issued, not loaned — you keep them. And because the catalog is not published, the winning approach is to describe the FUNCTIONAL limitation to the clinician and let them find the item, rather than asking for a product by brand name.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: PSAS recreational and sports equipment — handcycles, adaptive skis and kayaks, issued by VA
items.org: VA Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service / VA Adaptive Sports
items.who: Veterans with a disability where a VA clinician documents that recreational or sports equipment supports rehabilitation goals, conditioning, or community reintegration.
items.value: Adaptive sports and recreation equipment issued as prosthetic items — handcycles, racing wheelchairs, adaptive ski equipment, adaptive kayaking and fishing gear, running feet and sport-specific prosthetic components.
items.how: Have the physiatrist, prosthetist or RECREATION THERAPIST document the functional and rehabilitative purpose and enter a prosthetics consult. Participation in a VA adaptive sports clinic strengthens the justification substantially.
items.hack: The leverage is the recreation therapist. Veterans ask the prosthetist for a handcycle and are told no; the recreation therapist writes the same request as a conditioning and reintegration intervention and it goes through. Attend a VA adaptive sports event first, then request the equipment — the clinical note writes itself.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA assistive technology and adaptive computer access — evaluated, purchased, installed and trained
items.who: Enrolled veterans with a disability limiting computer access, communication, reading, writing or environmental control. VA operates regional Assistive Technology labs and AT clinical teams.
items.value: Screen readers and magnification software, alternative keyboards and mice, eye-gaze and head-tracking systems, speech recognition setups, switch access, tablet-based communication systems, mounting hardware, and reading and OCR devices — evaluated, issued, installed and trained.
items.how: Request an assistive technology evaluation through VA rehabilitation medicine, occupational therapy, speech pathology, or VIST and Blind Rehab depending on the impairment. Ask whether your VISN has an AT lab or AT Coordinator.
items.hack: Run the AT request in PARALLEL with Chapter 31 VR&E if you are pursuing school or work — VR&E can also purchase assistive technology as part of a rehabilitation plan, and the two programs fund different pieces. Getting the clinical AT evaluation report first gives the VR&E counselor the justification they need.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Speech generating devices through VA — SGDs, mounts, and voice banking before it is too late
items.who: Veterans with a severe expressive communication impairment — ALS, post-stroke aphasia or apraxia, TBI, head and neck cancer with laryngectomy, progressive neuromuscular disease.
items.value: A speech generating device (dedicated AAC device or tablet-based system), mounting hardware for wheelchair or bed, the access method (touch, switch, eye gaze), the software, and the speech-language pathology training to use it. Also electrolarynx devices and tracheoesophageal voice prostheses after laryngectomy.
items.how: Speech-language pathology evaluation first, then a prosthetics consult. The SLP's AAC evaluation report is the controlling document.
items.hack: Message banking and VOICE BANKING before speech is lost is what families wish they had known. If a veteran has a progressive diagnosis, ask the SLP about voice banking at the FIRST appointment, not when speech is already failing — the recordings must be made while the voice still works, and VA SLPs can walk a family through it.
items.deadline: No benefit deadline, but voice banking is time-critical in progressive disease.

items.title: Environmental control units — VA will automate the house around a veteran who cannot reach a switch
items.who: Veterans with severe mobility impairment — high-level spinal cord injury, advanced ALS or MS, severe multi-limb amputation — who cannot operate standard controls.
items.value: An environmental control unit: switch-, voice- or eye-gaze-operated control of lights, door locks, bed position, thermostat, telephone, television and call systems, integrated and installed, plus training and maintenance.
items.how: Occupational therapy or spinal cord injury team evaluation, then a prosthetics consult. For installations requiring structural work, pair with a HISA grant from the same medical center.
items.hack: Stack the funding streams: the ECU equipment comes from PSAS, the structural work to install it (wiring, widened doorways, ramps) comes from HISA through the same VA medical center, and vehicle-side controls come from the automobile adaptive equipment benefit. One well-written occupational therapy evaluation can justify all three if it covers the whole environment.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA home oxygen — equipment, supplies, and why you should ask for a portable concentrator
items.who: Enrolled veterans meeting clinical criteria for long-term oxygen therapy, typically documented hypoxemia at rest or with exertion.
items.value: Home oxygen concentrator, portable system, tubing, cannulas, humidifiers, backup supply, delivery and maintenance, plus respiratory therapy follow-up — at no cost, including the contractor's home service calls.
items.how: Pulmonary or primary care documents the qualifying oxygen saturation data and enters a home oxygen consult. VA contracts delivery to a regional oxygen vendor.
items.hack: Ask specifically for a PORTABLE OXYGEN CONCENTRATOR rather than tanks if you still travel, drive or work — POCs are approved for commercial air travel and compressed tanks are not, and the default issue is often tanks. Document the activity you need it for (work, church, grandchildren, flying to see family); 'community participation' is the phrase that moves a POC request.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA wheelchair and seating clinic — and why the seating evaluation matters more than the chair
items.org: VA PSAS / wheelchair and seating clinics
items.who: Enrolled veterans with a mobility impairment. VA issues manual chairs, ultralight manual chairs, power wheelchairs, power-assist wheels, scooters and custom seating systems.
items.value: A clinically fitted mobility device plus the custom seating and positioning system, cushions (including skin-protection cushions), repairs, replacement parts, batteries, and replacement on a clinical cycle.
items.how: Request a wheelchair and seating clinic evaluation through rehabilitation medicine or physical therapy. A proper evaluation includes measurement, pressure mapping and a trial of the device.
items.hack: Insist on the SEATING CLINIC rather than accepting a catalog chair — the cushion and seating system are what prevent pressure injuries, which are the most dangerous and expensive complication of wheelchair use. Separately, ask about a POWER-ASSIST wheel kit for an existing manual chair: it preserves shoulders, costs far less than a power chair, and is routinely approved once shoulder pain is documented.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA Amputation System of Care — the tiered network behind every prosthetic limb
items.who: Veterans with limb loss or limb deficiency, any era, any cause — combat, accident, or disease-related amputation such as diabetic or vascular amputation. The majority of VA amputation care is for non-combat, disease-related limb loss.
items.value: A tiered national network: Regional Amputation Centers for the most complex care, Polytrauma Amputation Network Sites, Amputation Care Teams at most medical centers, and Amputation Points of Contact everywhere else. Includes limb prescription and fabrication, socket refitting, multiple limbs for different activities, gait training, peer support and lifetime follow-up.
items.how: Ask for an Amputation System of Care referral and request your facility's Amputation Point of Contact by title. For complex or high-level amputation, ask for referral to a Regional Amputation Center.
items.hack: You can be prescribed MORE THAN ONE prosthesis — a daily-use limb plus a shower or water leg plus an activity-specific limb such as a running blade. Veterans assume one leg is the entitlement. Document the distinct functional need for each use case and ask the prosthetist to prescribe accordingly.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: VA Form 10-0103 — the service dog benefit pays for the dog's whole life, not for the dog
items.org: VA Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service
items.who: Veterans with a VA clinical determination that a guide dog, hearing dog or mobility service dog is part of their treatment plan, who obtain the dog from an Assistance Dogs International (ADI) or International Guide Dog Federation (IGDF) accredited organization.
items.value: A comprehensive veterinary health insurance policy paid by VA for the dog's working life, plus prescribed hardware such as a harness or backpack, plus travel to the accredited program for team training.
items.how: Submit VA Form 10-0103, Veterans Application for Assistance in Obtaining a Service Dog, after a VA clinician documents the clinical need and names the ADI- or IGDF-accredited provider.
items.hack: Two traps. First, the accreditation requirement is absolute — a dog from a non-accredited trainer gets zero VA support no matter how well trained, so verify ADI or IGDF accreditation BEFORE joining a waitlist. Second, the veterinary insurance does not cover grooming, boarding, food or non-prescribed equipment, so budget for those; file the 10-0103 before placement so coverage starts the day the dog does.
items.deadline: No fixed deadline, but file before placement so coverage is continuous.

items.title: How to actually get a prosthetic item — and what to do when PSAS says no
items.who: Any enrolled veteran denied a device, equipment item or home modification by VA prosthetics.
items.value: A real appeal path. PSAS denials are clinical decisions, so they are challenged clinically and administratively rather than through the disability appeals system — which is why veterans mistakenly file Supplemental Claims and get nowhere.
items.how: Four escalating steps: (1) ask the ordering clinician to amend the consult with stronger functional justification and resubmit; (2) ask for the denial in writing with the stated reason; (3) contact the facility Patient Advocate and open a formal complaint; (4) pursue the facility's clinical appeal process, requesting expedited review if clinically urgent. Benefit-level decisions such as a VA Form 10-0103 denial carry their own appeal rights.
items.hack: Functional language wins; diagnosis language loses. 'Patient has a below-knee amputation' gets denied. 'Patient cannot shower safely without a water-resistant limb, has fallen twice in the shower, and requires a second prosthesis for wet environments' gets approved. Rewrite the justification around falls, safety, caregiver burden and activities of daily living, then resubmit the same request.
items.deadline: No statutory deadline, but appeal while the clinical record is fresh.

items.title: The VA 3D printing network — custom assistive devices VA designs and prints for you
items.org: VA Innovation Ecosystem / VHA 3D printing network
items.who: Veterans at VA facilities in the 3D printing network who need a custom device, adaptive aid or prosthetic component that does not exist commercially.
items.value: Custom-designed and printed assistive devices: adapted utensil grips, custom orthotic components, button hooks and zipper pulls, tool adapters, custom prosthetic socket components, and anatomic surgical models for pre-operative planning.
items.how: Ask your occupational therapist, prosthetist or rehabilitation engineer whether your VISN participates in the VHA 3D printing network. Bring the specific FUNCTIONAL problem, not a product idea.
items.hack: This is the answer when the commercial market has nothing. Veterans with unusual hand function, atypical residual limbs or rare combinations of impairment are told 'there is no device for that.' There often is now, and VA will design and print it free. Ask the occupational therapist — they are the ones who know whether the local lab exists.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Getting the Beneficiary Travel deductible WAIVED — the discretionary request nobody files
items.who: Veterans traveling to VA or VA-authorized care who meet at least one test: a VA disability rating of 30% or higher; travel for treatment of a service-connected condition; receiving a VA pension; income below the maximum annual VA pension rate; inability to afford the travel; or travel for a C&P exam, a service dog, or transplant care. Family caregivers approved under PCAFC and medically required attendants also qualify.
items.value: VA subtracts a monthly deductible from travel reimbursement, subject to an annual deductible cap, which is why a veteran making short frequent trips can net almost nothing. That deductible can be WAIVED on financial hardship grounds, and the waiver is discretionary rather than automatic. Separately, travel for a C&P exam, for a service dog, and for transplant care is reimbursed regardless of rating or income.
items.how: Submit a written request to your VA medical center's Beneficiary Travel office asking that the deductible be waived on financial hardship grounds, stating your monthly income, your monthly VA trip count and the net effect of the deductible. Ask for the decision in writing. Confirm the current mileage rate, monthly deductible and annual cap at the official page before relying on any figure — all three change.
items.hack: The waiver is granted far more often than it is requested, because almost nobody knows it exists: the deductible is presented as a fixed feature of the program rather than a waivable one. For a veteran with four short VA trips a month, a granted waiver roughly converts travel pay from a rounding error into real money. Attach the same financial documentation you would use for a copay hardship determination and request both in one letter.
items.deadline: Request the waiver before the travel period you want covered; individual travel claims still carry the 30-day filing deadline.

items.title: BTSSS filing mechanics — the 30-day wall and the smartphone check-in shortcut
items.who: Any beneficiary-travel-eligible veteran or caregiver with an appointment at a VA or VA-authorized facility.
items.value: Online self-service travel claim filing with status tracking, direct deposit and claim history. Smartphone check-in at the facility can auto-generate a mileage-only claim from your home address.
items.how: Log into VA.gov, open the travel pay portal and file within 30 days. For mileage-only claims from home, check in with the VA appointments app at the facility and accept the travel claim prompt — that is the entire filing. BTSSS support is available by phone (TTY 711) Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern.
items.hack: The 30-day deadline is the top reason veterans lose travel money, and it runs from the appointment date, not from when you remembered. Set a standing reminder for the day after every VA appointment. Also set up direct deposit in BTSSS once — paper checks add weeks, and a stale address silently kills payments.
items.deadline: 30 days from the date of the appointment.

items.title: Special mode transportation — ambulance and wheelchair van, and the preauthorization that makes it free
items.who: Veterans whose medical condition requires a mode other than a private vehicle — ambulance, ambulette, wheelchair van or air ambulance — as documented by a VA clinician.
items.value: VA pays for the special mode transport itself rather than reimbursing mileage. Non-emergency transport requires preauthorization; for genuine emergencies VA can pay after the fact.
items.how: Have the VA clinician document medical necessity and obtain PREAUTHORIZATION from the Beneficiary Travel office before the trip. For an emergency ambulance to a non-VA facility, file promptly and cite the emergency exception.
items.hack: Preauthorization is the whole ballgame for non-emergency special mode transport — without it the veteran eats a four-figure ambulette bill VA would have paid. For recurring appointments requiring a wheelchair van (dialysis, infusion, radiation), ask for a STANDING preauthorization covering the whole treatment course instead of trip-by-trip approvals.
items.deadline: Preauthorization before travel for non-emergency transport; file emergency claims as soon as possible.

items.title: Beneficiary travel for caregivers and medically required attendants
items.org: VA Beneficiary Travel Program / VA Caregiver Support Program
items.who: Family caregivers approved under the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers (PCAFC), attendants whose presence is medically required for the veteran to travel, and support persons traveling for transplant care.
items.value: Mileage, and with approval meals and lodging, for the caregiver's or attendant's own travel — paid separately from the veteran's claim.
items.how: The caregiver files their own travel claim through BTSSS or VA Form 10-3542. For a non-PCAFC attendant, the VA clinician must document that an attendant is medically required — get that note in the chart before the trip.
items.hack: PCAFC caregivers often do not realize their own travel is reimbursable, and attendants almost never do. For a veteran who cannot travel alone, the words 'medically required attendant' documented once in the chart convert every future trip into two reimbursable claims instead of one.
items.deadline: 30 days from the appointment, same as the veteran's claim.

items.title: DAV Transportation Network — free volunteer rides to VA care at more than 247 VA locations
items.who: Any veteran needing a ride to VA medical care. Not limited to DAV members and not limited to rated veterans. Availability depends on local volunteer drivers.
items.value: Free transportation to VA facilities in DAV-donated vehicles driven by volunteers, serving more than 247 VA locations. DAV has donated over 4,180 vehicles to the program since 1987.
items.how: Contact the Hospital Service Coordinator (HSC) at your VA medical center; DAV publishes a national HSC directory. The HSC, not the DAV chapter, schedules rides. Book several days ahead — volunteer capacity is finite.
items.hack: The DAV network and VA's own Veterans Transportation Service are separate programs with separate dispatchers, so a no from one is not a no from the other. Call both. If your county is thinly covered, ask the HSC which neighboring pickup point is served and whether a county veteran service office van can get you there.
items.deadline: None; schedule in advance.

items.title: VA driver rehabilitation — clinical driving evaluation, adaptive equipment training, and getting back behind the wheel
items.who: Veterans whose medical condition affects driving — amputation, spinal cord injury, stroke, TBI, low vision, MS, or age-related change — including veterans whose driving has been questioned by a clinician or family.
items.value: A clinical driver evaluation by a Certified Driver Rehabilitation Specialist, on-road assessment, prescription of adaptive driving equipment (hand controls, left-foot accelerator, spinner knobs, reduced-effort steering and braking, wheelchair lifts and transfer aids), training in the adapted vehicle, and vehicle selection guidance.
items.how: Ask rehabilitation medicine or occupational therapy for a driver rehabilitation referral, and ask whether your facility runs its own program or refers out. Pair with the automobile adaptive equipment benefit (VA Form 10-1394) for the hardware.
items.hack: Sequence matters and veterans get it backwards: get the DRIVER EVALUATION FIRST, then buy the vehicle. The evaluation tells you which equipment you need, and some equipment only fits certain vehicles — people buy a truck and then learn the lift they need requires a minivan. The evaluation is also the clinical document that justifies the adaptive equipment grant.
items.deadline: None, but complete the evaluation before purchasing a vehicle.

items.title: Disabled parking placards and disabled veteran plates — the one VA letter that gets you both
items.org: State departments of motor vehicles / VA
items.who: Veterans with a qualifying mobility impairment under their state's disabled parking statute. Separately, most states issue a Disabled Veteran license plate based on a VA rating, often with free or discounted registration.
items.value: A disabled parking placard or plate, plus in many states exemption from parking meter fees, free vehicle registration, and in some states toll discounts. Rules are set state by state.
items.how: Two different paths. For a standard disabled placard, your state's DMV form requires a licensed medical provider's certification — a VA clinician can sign it. For a DISABLED VETERAN plate, states generally require a VA letter documenting the rating: download your VA Benefit Summary Letter instantly from VA.gov under 'VA letters and documents.'
items.hack: Pull the Benefit Summary Letter yourself from VA.gov instead of requesting it by mail — it is instant and you can toggle which facts it discloses. One letter typically satisfies the DV plate, the property tax exemption, the state park pass and the hunting and fishing license discount, so make several copies before the DMV trip and collect all of them in one pass.
items.deadline: State-specific renewal cycles.

items.title: Free and discounted public transit for veterans — and the paratransit option that is worth far more
items.who: Veterans in cities and regions offering a veteran or disabled-veteran fare. Dozens of U.S. transit agencies offer free or half fares to veterans, disabled veterans, or holders of a DV plate or VA card. There is no national program and no national list.
items.value: Free or reduced fares on bus, light rail, commuter rail and paratransit, often extended to a personal care attendant traveling with the veteran.
items.how: Search your transit agency's fares page for 'veteran,' 'reduced fare' and 'ADA paratransit.' Bring the Veteran Health Identification Card, the Veteran ID Card, or the VA Benefit Summary Letter. Also call your County Veteran Service Officer, who tracks local fare programs agencies barely advertise.
items.hack: Ask about the reduced-fare program AND the ADA paratransit program separately. Paratransit eligibility rests on functional inability to use fixed-route transit, not on a VA rating, and it provides curb-to-curb service at a low fare. A veteran who qualifies for paratransit has vastly more mobility than one with a half-price bus pass, and the two applications are completely different.
items.deadline: Agency-specific; most require a certification application and periodic recertification.

items.title: County Veteran Service Office transport vans — the local ride network nobody indexes
items.org: County and state veteran service offices
items.who: Veterans in counties that operate veteran transport vans. Many U.S. counties fund a van or contract rides to VA medical centers through the County Veteran Service Officer, a veterans council, or a county aging and disability agency.
items.value: Free or low-cost scheduled transportation to VA medical centers and regional clinics, and sometimes to VA regional offices for claims appointments. Some counties also hold small discretionary funds for gas cards.
items.how: Call your County Veteran Service Officer — find them through the National Association of County Veterans Service Officers or your state department of veterans affairs. Ask specifically about a van program, a mileage stipend and gas-card assistance.
items.hack: County programs often cover the trips VA's own services will not: to a community care appointment, to a VSO appointment, or from a county VA's Highly Rural Transportation Grants do not serve. This is the layer of the transportation system that exists almost entirely offline, which is exactly why it is unclaimed.
items.deadline: None; schedule in advance.

items.title: VA hoptel and Fisher House lodging — where you sleep when the appointment is 300 miles away
items.org: VA Veterans Health Administration / Fisher House Foundation
items.who: Veterans traveling long distances for VA care, and in Fisher Houses, their families during an inpatient stay. Hoptel (hospital hotel) beds are VA-operated lodging at the medical center itself.
items.value: Free or nominal-cost overnight lodging at or adjacent to the VA medical center, so a veteran with an early procedure or multi-day workup does not drive four hours at 4 a.m. or pay for a hotel.
items.how: Ask the scheduling clerk or the Beneficiary Travel office for a HOPTEL reservation when you BOOK a distant appointment — hoptel is a VA term and asking for it by name works where 'is there anywhere to stay' does not. For family lodging during an inpatient stay, ask the social worker about the Fisher House.
items.hack: Hoptel is almost never offered proactively; it is granted on request, and at scheduling rather than on arrival, because beds are limited and allocated in advance. If hoptel is full, ask Beneficiary Travel about preauthorized lodging reimbursement instead — that is a separate pot of money with its own rules.
items.deadline: Request at scheduling; lodging reimbursement requires preauthorization before travel.

items.title: SNAP and VA disability compensation — it counts as income, and the medical deduction is how you win anyway
items.org: USDA Food and Nutrition Service / state SNAP agencies
items.who: Veteran households applying for SNAP. VA disability compensation, VA pension and DIC all count as UNEARNED income for SNAP. Military Basic Allowance for Housing is excluded from SNAP income for a servicemember in deployed status under federal rules.
items.value: Monthly food benefits on an EBT card. Allotments are set annually by USDA and vary by household size and state — verify current amounts and income limits with your state agency rather than relying on any published figure.
items.how: Apply through your state SNAP agency (find it at fns.usda.gov/snap/state-directory) or a county office. Report VA compensation as unearned income; do not omit it.
items.hack: The DEDUCTION side is where veteran households win, and it is almost always under-claimed. If any household member is elderly (60 or over) or disabled — which a VA-rated veteran generally is — the household faces NO gross income test and gets an UNCAPPED excess medical expense deduction. Medicare premiums, prescriptions, medical mileage to VA appointments, dental and vision costs, even service animal food can be deducted above a small threshold, often flipping an ineligible household into eligibility. Bring twelve months of medical receipts and a mileage log to the interview.
items.deadline: Report changes within your state's reporting window; recertification is typically every 6 to 24 months.

items.title: The SNAP work-requirement exemption — and the more durable one to use instead
items.org: USDA Food and Nutrition Service / state SNAP agencies
items.who: Able-bodied adults without dependents (ABAWDs) subject to SNAP time limits. Veteran status was added as a federal ABAWD exemption by the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023, and subsequent federal legislation has changed the exemption landscape — the current status of the veteran-specific exemption must be verified with your state agency.
items.value: Exemption from the ABAWD three-month time limit, so SNAP continues without meeting the work-hours requirement. A separate, permanent exemption exists for anyone medically unfit for employment.
items.how: Tell the SNAP worker you are a veteran and ask IN WRITING which ABAWD exemption is being applied to your case. If the veteran exemption is unavailable in your state, pivot to the MEDICALLY UNFIT FOR EMPLOYMENT exemption, which is a separate and far more stable federal exemption.
items.hack: Do not rely on the veteran exemption alone — it is the most volatile rule in the SNAP book and has changed more than once. The robust move is to document unfitness for employment with a VA clinician's statement or your VA rating decision. A veteran with a significant mental health or musculoskeletal rating usually qualifies as medically unfit, which does not depend on which way Congress moved last.
items.deadline: ABAWD clocks run in three-month increments within a 36-month period — act before the clock expires.

items.title: WIC for military and veteran families — and why a SNAP denial tells you nothing
items.org: USDA Food and Nutrition Service WIC / state and tribal WIC agencies
items.who: Pregnant, postpartum and breastfeeding women, infants, and children under five in households at or below 185 percent of federal poverty guidelines, OR automatically income-eligible through SNAP, Medicaid or TANF participation. Military families are explicitly eligible.
items.value: Monthly benefits for specific nutritious foods, infant formula, breastfeeding support and lactation consultation, nutrition education, and health care referrals. WIC Overseas serves families stationed abroad.
items.how: Apply through your state or Indian Tribal Organization WIC agency; find it at fns.usda.gov/wic/wic-contacts. Military families may apply at an installation clinic or a civilian WIC clinic.
items.hack: WIC's treatment of military allowances is NOT the same as SNAP's, and families wrongly read a SNAP denial as a WIC denial. Apply to WIC separately regardless. Adjunctive eligibility is the fast lane: if anyone in the household is on Medicaid, the income test is deemed met. And WIC Overseas exists — almost nobody stationed abroad knows that.
items.deadline: Certification periods are typically 6 to 12 months; apply during pregnancy, not after.

items.title: Free and reduced-price school meals for military children — the BAH exclusion that changes the math
items.org: USDA Food and Nutrition Service / local school food authorities
items.who: Children in households meeting income guidelines for the National School Lunch and School Breakfast Programs, or attending a school under the Community Eligibility Provision where all students eat free. Military families apply on the same terms as civilians.
items.value: Free or reduced-price breakfast and lunch, and in many districts summer meals and after-school snacks. Free-meal eligibility also frequently triggers school fee waivers, reduced activity and testing fees, and discounted internet programs.
items.how: Submit the school meal application to your child's school food authority at the start of each school year, or whenever income drops. Ask the district whether the school is a Community Eligibility Provision school, in which case no application is needed.
items.hack: For active duty families the housing allowance treatment is the hinge: BAH received for privatized military housing is generally EXCLUDED from household income for school meal eligibility, which drops many enlisted families under the threshold. Districts near installations know this; districts far from one often do not. State it on the application and cite USDA military-family guidance if challenged. Also reapply mid-year after a PCS, a deployment change or a spouse job loss — eligibility is not annual destiny.
items.deadline: Apply at the start of the school year and again whenever income changes.

items.title: Basic Needs Allowance — the DoD monthly payment for low-income active duty families
items.org: Department of Defense / Defense Finance and Accounting Service
items.who: Active duty service members with dependents whose gross household income falls below a statutory percentage of federal poverty guidelines for their location and household size. DoD screens pay records automatically, and members can also self-certify.
items.value: A monthly supplemental payment through military pay intended to close the gap to the statutory threshold. The threshold percentage and the treatment of BAH in the formula have both been changed by Congress — verify current rules before relying on any figure.
items.how: DoD screens annually and notifies apparently eligible members, who then certify household income and size. Members who believe they qualify but were not notified can apply through their service's personnel system. Ask the installation financial readiness office or a Military OneSource financial counselor to run the numbers.
items.hack: The annual screen is unreliable for families whose circumstances changed mid-year — a new baby or a spouse job loss creates eligibility the screen misses. Self-certify rather than waiting to be told. And because BAH treatment in the formula has shifted, a member denied in a prior year should re-check against current rules instead of assuming the old answer still holds.
items.deadline: Annual certification; apply as soon as household circumstances change.

items.title: The commissary as a food budget instrument — and the surcharge nobody accounts for
items.who: All honorably discharged veterans with a service-connected disability rating of any percentage, Purple Heart recipients, former POWs, Medal of Honor recipients, and primary family caregivers enrolled in PCAFC have in-person commissary access. Retirees, Guard and Reserve, and active duty have longstanding access.
items.value: Commissary pricing is set against a regional civilian savings target, with no sales tax, and a surcharge is added at checkout that funds commissary construction and maintenance. Net savings are real but smaller than a shelf-price comparison suggests.
items.how: Enter with a Veteran Health Identification Card for the disability-rated path, or the appropriate DoD or retiree credential. Expect to need a REAL ID-compliant credential for base access if you are not using a DoD ID.
items.hack: Run the commissary as a staples-and-meat store, not a one-stop shop: savings concentrate in meat, dairy, produce and case-lot sales, while the surcharge plus the drive erodes savings on a small basket. Two tactics that matter — watch for CASE LOT SALES, the best pricing event of the year, and stack DeCA digital coupons with manufacturer coupons, which DeCA permits more liberally than most civilian chains. Treat the trip as monthly, not weekly.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Veteran food pantries and the VA food insecurity screen that should find you first
items.org: VA Veterans Health Administration / Feeding America network
items.who: Any veteran experiencing food insecurity. VA screens enrolled veterans for food insecurity in primary care and is required to act on a positive screen.
items.value: On the VA side: a social work consult, SNAP application assistance, connection to local pantries, and at some facilities on-site food pantries or veteran food boxes. On the community side: Feeding America food banks run veteran-specific distributions, and many VFW and American Legion posts and county veteran service offices operate pantries.
items.how: Answer the VA food insecurity screening question honestly — a positive answer triggers the social work consult. Separately, find your regional food bank at feedingamerica.org and ask about veteran distributions and mobile pantries; ask your County Veteran Service Officer for the local list.
items.hack: Veterans routinely answer the screen 'no' out of pride and lose the entire downstream referral chain, which includes SNAP enrollment help, pantry access and in many facilities a direct food box. Say yes. The screen is the cheapest intervention in the system and it is designed to be a door, not a judgment.
items.deadline: None.

items.title: Utility shutoff protection — medical certification, weather moratoria, and life-sustaining equipment
items.org: State public utility commissions / utility companies
items.who: Households facing disconnection of electricity, gas, water or heat. Most states combine cold- and hot-weather moratoria, medical certification holds, and a statutory right to a deferred payment plan.
items.value: Temporary protection from disconnection — commonly 30 to 90 days and often renewable — when a household member has a serious illness or relies on life-sustaining equipment, plus seasonal moratoria during temperature extremes, plus the right to a payment arrangement.
items.how: Ask the utility for its MEDICAL CERTIFICATION form and have a VA clinician or any licensed provider sign it. File it BEFORE disconnection; reconnection after shutoff is harder and often carries fees and deposits. File a complaint with your state public utility commission if the utility refuses a lawful payment plan.
items.hack: Veterans dependent on home oxygen, CPAP, a power wheelchair, an electric hospital bed or refrigerated medication have the strongest possible medical certification case, because life-sustaining equipment is the highest protection tier in most state rules. Have the clinician list the specific EQUIPMENT and its power requirement, not just a diagnosis. And file in the fall, before the heating bills arrive.
items.deadline: File medical certification before disconnection; moratorium dates are set by state rule.

items.title: Lifeline — and the little-known fact that VA Pension qualifies you directly
items.org: FCC Lifeline Program / Universal Service Administrative Company
items.who: Households at or below 135 percent of federal poverty guidelines, OR with any member participating in SNAP, Medicaid, Federal Public Housing Assistance, Supplemental Security Income, certain Tribal programs, or the VETERANS AND SURVIVORS PENSION BENEFIT.
items.value: Up to a $9.25 monthly discount on phone or broadband service, or up to $34.25 monthly on qualifying Tribal lands. One benefit per household. Many participating providers bundle the discount into a free or near-free wireless plan with data.
items.how: Apply through the National Verifier at lifelinesupport.org, or through a participating provider. California, Oregon and Texas administer their own eligibility processes. Lifeline Support Center: 800-234-9473 (disability assistance 800-243-9473).
items.hack: The VA Pension qualifier is the hack. A veteran on VA Pension or a surviving spouse on Survivors Pension qualifies on that basis alone, with no income documentation beyond the award letter — and because Lifeline eligibility also feeds many ISPs' own low-income programs, that one letter can unlock internet discounts too. Note the distinction: VA DISABILITY COMPENSATION is not a qualifying program; VA PENSION is. They are different benefits and that difference is everything here.
items.deadline: Recertify annually or the benefit is de-enrolled.

items.title: Internet and device programs after ACP — ISP low-income tiers, EveryoneOn and refurbished computers
items.org: Internet service providers / EveryoneOn / PCs for People / Human-I-T
items.who: Low-income households, including veteran households, qualifying through SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, free or reduced school lunch, VA Pension, or income below a stated percentage of the poverty guidelines.
items.value: Low-cost home internet across major ISP low-income programs, plus low-cost refurbished desktops, laptops and tablets, plus digital literacy training. Some programs include a mobile hotspot.
items.how: Use EveryoneOn's offer locator at everyoneon.org to find offers by ZIP code and eligibility program. For devices, apply directly to PCs for People or Human-I-T, which ship nationally and accept SNAP, Medicaid or income proof.
items.hack: Veterans skip these because they read as charity rather than benefits. The DEVICE side is the underused half: a veteran doing VA telehealth, filing claims on VA.gov, taking VR&E coursework or job hunting needs a real computer, and a refurbished machine from PCs for People costs a fraction of retail with a warranty. Pair the device program with Lifeline and the monthly cost of being online approaches zero.
items.deadline: Program-specific; most are rolling.

items.title: Military child care fee assistance (MCCYN) — DoD pays part of your civilian daycare bill
items.org: Child Care Aware of America / DoD Office of Military Family Readiness Policy
items.who: Active duty service members (and in some branch programs certain Guard, Reserve, DoD civilian and wounded warrior families) who cannot get a space in an on-installation Child Development Center and use a qualifying community provider instead. Each branch runs its own variant: Army Fee Assistance, Department of the Air Force Fee Assistance, Marine Corps Fee Assistance, Navy, and DoD Fee Assistance.
items.value: DoD pays the difference between what the family would have paid at a military CDC and what the civilian provider charges, up to a program cap, paid directly to the provider. Variants MCCYN, MCCYN-PLUS and MCCYNEx widen the pool of acceptable providers where nationally accredited care is scarce.
items.how: Apply through Child Care Aware of America at childcareaware.org, 1-800-424-2246. The provider must be state-licensed, inspected within the last 12 months, FBI-cleared and — for standard MCCYN — nationally accredited. Fee assistance is paid to the provider monthly after attendance sheets are submitted.
items.hack: Two things families get wrong. First, you generally must be on the MilitaryChildCare.com waitlist for installation care to establish that CDC space is unavailable — do that FIRST, on arrival at the new duty station, not after you find a daycare. Second, when no accredited provider exists nearby, ask specifically about MCCYN-PLUS or MCCYNEx, which accept state quality-rating systems in place of national accreditation; families are told 'no accredited providers here' and give up without ever hearing the alternative.
items.deadline: Apply as early as possible; retroactive payment is limited and the waitlist step takes time.

items.title: Army Respite Child Care and EFMP respite — paid hours of childcare for special-needs families
items.org: Child Care Aware of America / service EFMP offices
items.who: Families enrolled in EFMP meeting the program's respite criteria. The Army program is the best known; other services run respite through their EFMP family support programs with differing hour allowances.
items.value: A monthly allowance of paid respite childcare hours through a licensed community provider or approved caregiver, so the parent of a child with special needs gets scheduled relief.
items.how: Enroll in EFMP first, then apply through Child Care Aware of America (1-800-424-2246) for the respite program, or through your installation EFMP Family Support office for service-specific respite.
items.hack: Respite hours are use-it-or-lose-it monthly and are massively underclaimed, almost always because the family cannot find an approved provider. Ask the EFMP Family Support coordinator to help you get a provider APPROVED — in some programs including a known adult or relative — rather than hunting an agency alone. The approval is the bottleneck, not the eligibility.
items.deadline: Monthly allowances generally do not roll over.

items.title: Exceptional Family Member Program — the three components and the 14-day assignment review clock
items.org: DoD Office of Special Needs / service EFMP offices
items.who: Service members with a family member who has a special medical or educational need — a chronic condition, a disability, an IEP or IFSP, or ongoing specialty care. Enrollment is MANDATORY when a qualifying need exists, not optional.
items.value: Three distinct components: (1) identification and enrollment, which documents the need; (2) ASSIGNMENT COORDINATION, which screens prospective duty stations for availability of the required medical and educational services; and (3) FAMILY SUPPORT, where an EFMP Family Support provider makes at least one personal contact per year and connects the family to installation and community resources.
items.how: Enroll through your installation EFMP office and military treatment facility. Use the EFMP & Me tool at Military OneSource for 24/7 guidance. Military OneSource: 1-800-342-9647, including free confidential special needs consultations.
items.hack: Two operational facts. A service member has up to 14 CALENDAR DAYS from assignment notification to request additional review and submit updated medical or educational information — that short window is how a family stops a PCS to a location that cannot deliver their child's therapy. And the three components are run by different offices that do not talk to each other: enrollment at the clinic, assignment coordination at personnel, family support at the installation. Families who get only enrollment conclude EFMP did nothing. Ask for the Family Support provider by name.
items.deadline: 14 calendar days from assignment notification to request additional review; update enrollment at each PCS and when the condition changes.

items.title: DoD STARBASE — free week-long STEM program for military and local children
items.org: Department of Defense STARBASE (National Guard Bureau)
items.who: Primarily fifth-grade students, including military-connected children and students from local schools, at STARBASE academies hosted on military installations across many states.
items.value: A free multi-day STEM program on a military installation — aerospace, engineering, physics, chemistry, goal setting and teamwork — taught by military instructors using real base facilities. No cost to families or schools.
items.how: Find your nearest academy through the DoD STARBASE site and contact the academy director. Enrollment typically runs through schools, so ask your child's teacher or principal to request a cohort slot, or ask the academy about summer and individual options.
items.hack: STARBASE is the rare military youth program open to the broader community, which makes it a credibility builder for a military family in a new town — and it is almost unknown outside the states that host academies. If your child's school has never participated, the academy director will often take the call directly from a parent and work the school from their end.
items.deadline: Academy cohort calendars fill early; inquire well before the school year.

items.title: Operation Purple Camp — free summer camp built around military childhood
items.who: Children of service members, with priority historically given to children experiencing deployment and to children in wounded, ill or injured and caregiving families. NMFA also runs Operation Purple Healing Adventures and family retreats.
items.value: A week of free overnight summer camp at no cost to the family, designed around the experience of military childhood, plus family retreats that bring the whole family together after injury or deployment.
items.how: Apply through militaryfamily.org during the annual application window, which typically opens in late winter or spring for summer sessions. Selection is by lottery and priority category, not first come first served.
items.hack: The window is short and the program is oversubscribed, so set a calendar reminder for late winter and apply the week it opens. Also apply to the FAMILY RETREAT tracks, not just the kids' camp — Healing Adventures and family retreats are less known, less oversubscribed, and built for exactly the wounded-warrior and caregiver families who assume no program fits them.
items.deadline: Annual application window, typically late winter to spring for summer sessions.

items.title: Tutor.com for U.S. Military Families — unlimited free 24/7 tutoring, DoD-funded
items.who: Eligible military-connected students — generally active duty, Guard and Reserve dependents and in many periods the service members themselves, plus certain Coast Guard and DoD civilian populations. Eligibility scope has shifted over time, so verify current terms.
items.value: Unlimited one-on-one online tutoring sessions, 24 hours a day, in math, science, English, social studies, test prep and writing review, with on-demand tutors and no session cap. Fully funded by DoD; no cost to the family.
items.how: Access through the DoD MWR Libraries portal or the military Tutor.com landing page using a military credential. Ask your installation library or School Liaison Officer for the current access link.
items.hack: This is among the highest-dollar-value DoD family benefits that costs nothing and is used by a fraction of eligible families. The 24/7 part matters more than the tutoring itself: a kid stuck on homework at 10 p.m. the night before a test, in a new school after a PCS, with a deployed parent, gets a live human in minutes. Set the account up BEFORE you need it — the registration step is what stops families in the moment.
items.deadline: Verify current eligibility scope; access is tied to military credential status.

items.title: Interstate Compact on Educational Opportunity for Military Children (MIC3) — enforceable school rights at every PCS
items.who: Children of active duty service members, members medically discharged or retired within one year, and members who died on active duty — moving between member states. All 50 states and the District of Columbia participate.
items.value: Enforceable rules on immediate enrollment with unofficial records; records transfer timelines; course and program PLACEMENT based on the sending school's placement rather than re-testing; continued special education services pending evaluation; immediate eligibility for extracurricular activities regardless of tryout or registration deadlines; excused absences for deployment-related events; and flexibility and waivers on graduation requirements so a senior is not held back a year by a move.
items.how: Contact your installation School Liaison Officer first, then your state's MIC3 Commissioner through the interactive map at mic3.net. MIC3: Military Interstate Children's Compact Commission, 1776 Avenue of the States, Lexington, KY 40511; 859-244-8000; mic3info@csg.org.
items.hack: The graduation-requirement and extracurricular-eligibility provisions have the biggest consequences and the lowest awareness. A junior or senior who moves can otherwise be forced to meet the new state's graduation requirements; the Compact lets the SENDING state issue the diploma or requires the receiving district to waive courses. And an athlete who misses tryouts because of a PCS must be given eligibility. Cite the Compact by name, in writing, to the principal — invoking it formally works where asking nicely does not.
items.deadline: Invoke at enrollment, and before the school year's graduation audit or athletic eligibility deadlines.

items.title: School Liaison Officers — the installation employee whose whole job is your child's school problem
items.who: Military families at or near any installation with a School Liaison Officer or program, including active duty, Guard, Reserve and transitioning families, and usually including families who live well off base.
items.value: Free expert help with school transitions: local school options and quality information, enrollment and records problems, special education and IEP advocacy, homeschool and virtual school information, student deployment support, postsecondary preparation, and escalation to district leadership.
items.how: Find your installation's School Liaison through MilitaryINSTALLATIONS on Military OneSource, or call the installation family readiness or MWR office and ask for the School Liaison Officer.
items.hack: The SLO is the person who can make a district take the Interstate Compact seriously, because they have a standing relationship with the superintendent's office. Call the SLO BEFORE the PCS — they will tell you which neighborhoods feed which schools, which districts handle IEPs well, and which have a military-literate registrar. Families call them after a problem; the value is in calling first.
items.deadline: None; call before the move.

items.title: Military OneSource SPECIALTY CONSULTATIONS — the uncapped expert sessions, not the counseling sessions
items.who: Active duty, Guard and Reserve regardless of activation status, their families, and separated service members and families for 365 days after separation. Survivors have extended access.
items.value: Beyond non-medical counseling, Military OneSource provides free specialty CONSULTATIONS by phone or video: special needs, wounded warrior, elder care, adult disability, education, spouse employment and career, adoption, new parent support, health and wellness coaching, peer support, and financial counseling with accredited counselors.
items.how: Call 1-800-342-9647 (24/7, worldwide) or use secure live chat at militaryonesource.mil, and ask for a specific CONSULTATION by name rather than for counseling.
items.hack: Asking for the right product is everything. 'I need help' routes you to non-medical counseling, which is session-capped and oriented to short-term issues. 'I need a SPECIAL NEEDS CONSULTATION' or 'an ELDER CARE CONSULTATION' routes you to a subject-matter expert with no session cap who will research your situation and come back to you. The 365-day post-separation window applies too, so a newly separated veteran untangling VA, school and a parent in decline can use all of it for a year after the DD-214.
items.deadline: 365 days after separation for most services.

items.title: MilTax after separation — you keep it a full year, and the tax CONSULTANTS are the real benefit
items.who: Active duty, Guard and Reserve regardless of activation, and separated or retired service members and their families for 365 days after separation. Survivors and certain other populations have extended eligibility.
items.value: Free tax preparation and e-filing software with no income limit, covering federal and multiple state returns, plus free consultations with MilTax tax consultants who specialize in military tax issues: combat pay exclusion, multi-state filing, SCRA and MSRRA residency, reserve travel deductions, and the tax treatment of separation pay and VA benefits.
items.how: Access MilTax through militaryonesource.mil. For consultations, call 1-800-342-9647 and ask for a MilTax consultant.
items.hack: The separation-year return is the most complicated one a veteran will ever file — partial-year military pay, terminal leave, leave sellback, a possible separation payment subject to VA recoupment, a state residency change, and possibly retroactive VA compensation. That is precisely the year to use a free military tax CONSULTANT rather than DIY software. And because eligibility runs 365 days past separation, a spring-separating veteran often gets MilTax for that return AND the next one. Use it before the clock runs out.
items.deadline: Eligibility ends 365 days after separation — file or at least consult inside that window.

items.title: VITA on base vs VITA in town — two different programs, and only one knows military tax law
items.org: IRS Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) / Armed Forces Tax Council
items.who: On-base VITA sites: service members and families, with no income limit at many military sites. Community VITA sites: taxpayers generally under an income threshold, plus persons with disabilities and limited-English speakers, which covers most veteran households. Tax Counseling for the Elderly serves taxpayers 60 and over.
items.value: Free tax return preparation and e-filing by IRS-certified volunteers. On-base sites operate under the Armed Forces Tax Council with volunteers trained in military-specific provisions; community sites are generalists but free and widely available.
items.how: For on-base VITA, contact the installation legal assistance office or family readiness center in January. For community VITA, use the IRS VITA/TCE locator at irs.gov or call 800-906-9887. AARP Tax-Aide operates many TCE sites with no income cap.
items.hack: Veterans with military retirement plus VA compensation plus a part-time job plus a state property tax exemption are exactly the profile that community VITA volunteers get wrong, because they rarely see military retirement, CRDP or CRSC. Go to an on-base site if you can get on base, or ask the community site whether any volunteer is military-certified. Failing that, use MilTax's consultant line to sanity-check the return before filing.
items.deadline: VITA sites generally operate late January through the filing deadline, and appointments fill fast.

items.title: IRS Free File and Direct File — and the entry-point trap that costs people money
items.who: IRS Free File: taxpayers under an annually adjusted adjusted-gross-income threshold, through partner commercial software. Free File Fillable Forms: ANY income, but no guidance. IRS Direct File was a government-run program whose future has been subject to change — verify current availability before planning on it.
items.value: Free federal return preparation and e-filing. Some Free File partners include a free state return; many do not.
items.how: Start at irs.gov/freefile and use the IRS lookup tool to find a partner you qualify for. Critically, enter THROUGH THE IRS SITE, not through the software company's own homepage, or you may be routed to a paid product. Confirm the current AGI threshold and the status of Direct File at irs.gov rather than relying on a published figure.
