Occupational therapists write these better than physicians do, because the home assessment is their actual job. Ask your VA OT for a home safety evaluation and attach it.
items.deadline: One year from the decision for most review lanes; check the deadline printed on your decision letter.

items.title: HISA runs through your doctor, not the loan office — and it needs a prescription
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Health Administration
items.who: Veterans enrolled in VA health care who need a home modification for medical reasons. Unlike SAH, HISA does not require that the disability be service-connected for the lower tier of the benefit.
items.value: A medical-benefit home modification grant with separate lifetime caps depending on whether the need is service-connected. It is paid out of VA health care, not Loan Guaranty, so it does not consume SAH entitlement and can be used alongside it. Confirm the current caps with your VA medical center — the figures circulating online are frequently out of date.
items.how: This is a prescription-driven benefit. Your VA provider must write the prescription for the modification; you then submit VA Form 10-0103 with the prescription, a plan or estimate, and proof you own or have permission to modify the home, to the HISA coordinator or Prosthetics service at your VA medical center. The Prosthetics and Sensory Aids Service, not a regional loan center, is the office that decides.
items.hack: Ask for a VA occupational therapy home safety evaluation first and let the OT write the recommendations. The prescription then arrives already matched to what HISA pays for — roll-in showers, grab bars, widened doorways, ramps, raised toilets, lowered counters — instead of asking for a general remodel that gets trimmed. Also ask the coordinator directly whether your need is being coded as service-connected or not, because that single coding choice determines which lifetime cap applies to you.
items.deadline: No deadline; rolling applications through your VA medical center.

items.title: USDA Section 504 home repair GRANT — $10,000, age 62+, and badly underused
items.org: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Rural Development
items.who: Homeowners who occupy the home, cannot get affordable credit elsewhere, live in a USDA-eligible rural area, are age 62 or older, and have household income at or below the very-low-income limit for their county. Veterans are not a special category here — they qualify on the same terms as anyone else, which is exactly why veterans overlook it.
items.value: Up to $10,000 as a grant — lifetime limit — to remove health and safety hazards. The grant can be combined with a Section 504 loan for a combined total of up to $50,000. Critical limit: grant funds are restricted to removing health and safety hazards, not general improvement or modernization.
items.how: Contact your local USDA Rural Development office. Applications are accepted year-round, on a rolling basis through the fiscal year. Check the property against the USDA eligibility map first — 'rural' is a statutory definition and includes far more suburban-edge territory than people assume.
items.hack: Two things people miss. First, the grant must be repaid if you sell the property within three years of receiving it — plan around that, because it turns a grant into a clawback if a move is coming. Second, 'rural' under USDA includes a surprising amount of the exurban fringe; do not self-disqualify on geography without checking the map. For veterans under 62, the loan side — 1% fixed, 20-year term, up to $40,000 — is still open to you and is cheaper than any home equity product you will be offered.
items.deadline: Rolling, 1 October through 30 September each year.

items.title: There is no 'HUD Section 504 home repair grant' — the name collision that wastes months
items.who: Anyone who has read a veteran home-repair listicle naming a 'HUD Section 504' grant.
items.value: Saves you from calling the wrong agency. Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, administered in HUD's context, is a civil-rights nondiscrimination rule about disability access in federally assisted programs. It is not a home repair grant and HUD does not run one under that name. The home repair grant everyone means is USDA Rural Development's Section 504 program. Two different statutes, two different agencies, one number.
items.how: For home repair money: USDA Rural Development (rd.usda.gov). For a disability-access discrimination complaint against a federally assisted housing provider: HUD's Office of Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity. For HUD home-repair money generally: it flows to your city or county as Community Development Block Grant and HOME funds, which your local housing or community development department then runs as its own rehab program — that is where you apply, not HUD.
items.hack: Call your city or county housing and community development department and ask the specific question: 'Do you run an owner-occupied rehabilitation program with CDBG or HOME funds, and are applications open?' These local programs routinely offer $10,000 to $50,000 as deferred-payment or forgivable loans, are advertised almost nowhere, and often have veteran or senior priority built into the scoring. This is the single most underused housing repair money in the country, and it is local, not federal.
items.deadline: Varies entirely by locality.

items.title: Weatherization Assistance Program — free efficiency work, no repayment, and automatic LIHEAP crossover
items.org: U.S. Department of Energy, State Energy Programs / local subgrantees
items.who: Low-income households; income limits are set by state and many states grant automatic (categorical) eligibility to households already receiving LIHEAP, SSI, or TANF. Both owners and, in many states, renters with landlord consent.
items.value: Weatherization improvements at no cost and with no repayment — insulation, air sealing, duct work, and in many states repair or replacement of unsafe heating equipment. DOE reports participating households save roughly $372 or more per year, and the program serves about 32,000 homes annually with federal DOE funds alone, on top of what states layer in. Dollar value per home varies widely by state and by what the audit finds; do not rely on a published average.
items.how: Apply through your state weatherization office or the local community action agency that runs it — start at energy.gov's 'How to Apply for Weatherization Assistance' page, or call 211. An energy auditor inspects the home and the scope of work comes from that audit, not from your request list.
items.hack: Apply for LIHEAP first, then weatherization. In most states LIHEAP receipt makes you categorically eligible for weatherization, skipping a second income verification entirely, and the two programs often share the same intake office. Also: a weatherization audit frequently uncovers a failing furnace or a combustion safety hazard, and the health-and-safety line in the weatherization budget can pay to fix it — which is how households get a heating system replaced for free without ever applying for a 'furnace grant.'
items.deadline: Rolling, subject to annual state allocation; waiting lists are common and often reset at the start of the program year.

items.title: State and local housing trust funds — the rehab money that never reaches a veteran list
items.org: State housing finance agencies, cities and counties
items.who: Low- and moderate-income homeowners and renters, by state and local program rules. Veteran status is frequently a scoring preference rather than an eligibility gate.
items.value: Forgivable loans, deferred-payment loans and outright grants for owner-occupied rehabilitation, accessibility modification, roof replacement, lead and asbestos abatement, and down payment assistance. Amounts range widely by jurisdiction — commonly five figures — and are funded through state housing trust funds, state HFA programs, and federal CDBG and HOME dollars passed through to localities. No national figure exists; you must check your own state and city.
items.how: Three calls, in this order: your state housing finance agency, your county or city housing and community development department, and your local community action agency. Ask each: what owner-occupied rehab, accessibility or home repair programs do you fund, are applications open, and is there a veteran or disability preference.
items.hack: Ask specifically whether the assistance is structured as a forgivable or deferred-payment loan and what triggers repayment. Most of this money is technically a lien that forgives after five to fifteen years of continued occupancy — functionally a grant if you stay, a real debt if you sell early. Knowing the forgiveness schedule before you sign tells you whether the program fits your actual plans, and it is the question that separates people who use these programs well from people who get a surprise at closing years later.
items.deadline: Varies; many local programs open and close with their annual allocation.

items.title: Military Founders Lab and Veteran EDGE — the IVMF rungs above the bootcamp
items.org: D'Aniello Institute for Veterans and Military Families (IVMF), Syracuse University
items.who: Military-connected founders with a business already operating. Military Founders Lab is for startups in motion; Veteran EDGE is for businesses scaling.
items.value: Military Founders Lab is a ten-week virtual program providing structured mentorship and a peer founder cohort. Veteran EDGE is a three-day in-person conference in Dallas built around scaling, with access to corporate and investor attendees. Both are delivered by IVMF at no tuition cost to selected participants; confirm current travel and lodging support when you apply.
items.how: Apply through ivmf.syracuse.edu/programs/entrepreneurship/. Cohorts and event registration open on announced cycles.
items.hack: Veteran EDGE is where the corporate supplier-diversity staff actually show up. If you are certified as an SDVOSB or VOSB and trying to break into corporate supply chains rather than federal contracts, the attendee list is worth more than the sessions — go with a one-page capability statement and a specific ask, not a pitch deck. Corporate supplier diversity is a parallel channel to federal set-asides and almost no veteran-owned firm works both.
items.deadline: Cohort and event cycles; check current dates.

items.title: How to spot a fake veteran business grant — nine concrete red flags
items.who: Every veteran who has searched 'veteran business grant' and found forty pages of results.
items.value: Saves money, time and your personal data. The veteran business grant space is the most heavily spammed corner of the entire benefits landscape, because veteran-owned-business intent is expensive advertising inventory and 'grant' is the keyword that buys it.
items.how: Run every opportunity against these nine checks. One, any application fee, processing fee, review fee, or paid 'grant writer' requirement — real grantmakers never charge applicants. Two, the sponsoring organization's own domain does not load, does not match, or has no content dated in the last six months. Three, no IRS Form 990 findable on ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer or Candid for a US nonprofit claiming to award grants. Four, the page collects your SSN, EIN, bank details or a credit check before any eligibility screen. Five, a 'guaranteed' or 'everyone who applies' award. Six, the deadline is a perpetually rolling countdown timer. Seven, the only URLs about it are aggregator and content-farm domains, never a press release, a news story, or a named recipient. Eight, it is described as a grant but the terms mention repayment, equity, revenue share, or a 'funding partner' — that is a loan, an investment, or a merchant cash advance. Nine, the contact channel is a web form with no phone number, no street address and no named staff.
items.hack: The fastest single test: search the program name plus 'recipient' or 'winner' plus a recent year. Real grant programs publicize their awardees because publicity is the point of giving money away. If you cannot find one named human who received it in the last two cycles, it is not a grant program — it is a landing page. Second-fastest test: check whether the 'grant' appears on a site whose own business model is lending, insurance or lead sales. A page about free money hosted by a company that sells debt is an advertisement.
items.deadline: N/A — apply continuously.

items.title: State veteran business grants — where the real money is, and why the lists are empty
items.org: State departments of veterans affairs and state economic development agencies
items.who: Veteran business owners looking for state-level funding.
items.value: Honest answer first: standing, recurring, veteran-specific state business GRANT programs are rare, and most of what appears on 'state veteran business grant' lists is either a loan program, a certification preference, a defunct pilot, or an invention. What does reliably exist at the state level is more valuable and less advertised: state veteran-owned business certification that unlocks state and municipal procurement preferences, state small business revolving loan funds and loan guarantee programs, workforce training reimbursement that pays you to train employees, and periodic competitive grant rounds funded by state economic development dollars.
items.how: Three calls. One, your state department of veterans affairs — ask whether the state certifies veteran-owned businesses and what procurement preference that certification carries. Two, your state economic development agency — ask about current small business grant rounds, revolving loan funds, and workforce training reimbursement. Three, your regional VBOC — ask what veteran businesses in the state actually received in the last year.
items.hack: The state procurement preference is the sleeper. Many states set aside a percentage of state contracting for certified veteran-owned businesses, and state and municipal procurement is far less competitive than federal because far fewer firms bother to certify at the state level. Ask your state's procurement office for its list of upcoming solicitations and its small-business set-aside policy. Workforce training reimbursement is the second sleeper: several states will reimburse a meaningful share of what you spend training a new hire, which is cash back on money you were spending anyway, and it is administered by the labor department rather than anything labeled 'veteran.'
items.deadline: Varies by state and by round.

items.title: Chamber and economic development micro-grants — small, local, and genuinely winnable
items.org: Local chambers of commerce, economic development corporations, downtown and main street associations, community foundations
items.who: Small businesses in a specific city, county, or commercial district. Veteran status is often a scoring preference.
items.value: Typically $500 to $25,000 for facade improvements, equipment, signage, rent subsidy, marketing, or emergency bridge funding. Individually unglamorous; collectively this is where the highest-probability grant money in the country sits, because the applicant pool is a few dozen businesses rather than a few thousand.
items.how: Call four organizations in your own city: the chamber of commerce, the economic development corporation or authority, the main street or downtown district association, and the local community foundation. Ask each the same question: what grant programs do you run or know of for small businesses, and when is the next round. Then ask to be added to their email list, which is how these rounds are actually announced.
items.hack: The single highest-leverage relationship is the community foundation program officer. Community foundations administer dozens of donor-advised and field-of-interest funds, a surprising number of which have veteran, small-business or neighborhood-specific mandates and struggle to find qualified applicants. Program officers will tell you which funds fit you and when they open — and a program officer who knows your name is worth more than any national database. This is the practical form of the rule that five small local funds beat one famous national one.
items.deadline: Rolling and round-based; varies entirely by organization.

items.title: Federal Pell Grant — $7,395, stacks with the GI Bill, and veterans routinely never file
items.org: U.S. Department of Education, Federal Student Aid
items.who: Undergraduate students with financial need, determined by the FAFSA's Student Aid Index. Veterans often qualify easily because GI Bill benefits are not counted as income on the FAFSA and many separating veterans have a low prior-year income on record.
items.value: For the 2026-27 award year, a maximum of $7,395 and a minimum of $740, per Federal Student Aid's Dear Colleague Letter GEN-26-01, effective 1 July 2026 through 30 June 2027. The maximum has been held flat for several cycles — confirm the figure for your award year before you rely on it. Pell does not have to be repaid and it does not reduce your GI Bill entitlement.
items.how: File the FAFSA at studentaid.gov. There is no separate Pell application — the FAFSA is the application. File even if you believe your GI Bill covers everything.
items.hack: This is the most-missed money in veteran education, and the reason is a misconception: veterans assume that having the Post-9/11 GI Bill disqualifies them or that the GI Bill counts as income. Neither is true. VA education benefits are excluded from FAFSA income, so a veteran whose tuition is already covered can receive Pell on top as cash for living costs, books, a laptop, or childcare. Two further points: Pell is now payable in some short-term workforce programs, so ask your school's financial aid office about that if you are in a certificate program rather than a degree; and if you separated mid-year, your low prior-prior-year income may produce a far better Pell result than you expect — file and find out rather than guessing.
items.deadline: FAFSA opens annually; federal deadline is 30 June of the award year, but state and institutional aid deadlines are far earlier — file in the autumn.

items.title: FSEOG — the campus-controlled grant that runs out before most veterans apply
items.org: U.S. Department of Education, administered by participating schools
items.who: Undergraduates with exceptional financial need; Pell recipients get priority. Only available at schools that participate in the program.
items.value: A need-based grant that does not have to be repaid, awarded in a range set by each school, with the Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grant historically running from a few hundred dollars to several thousand per year. Funding was flat in the most recent federal appropriations cycle. The defining feature is that each school receives a fixed allocation and awards it until it is gone.
items.how: File the FAFSA — that is the only application. Then, separately, contact your school's financial aid office and ask whether you are in line for FSEOG and whether their allocation is still available.
items.hack: Because the money is campus-based and first-come, the filing date matters more than your need level. A student with greater need who files in March can lose to a student who filed in October at a school whose allocation emptied in January. File the FAFSA as early as the cycle allows, every single year, and call the financial aid office in the first week of the cycle to confirm you are in the FSEOG pool. Also ask the same office about the school's own institutional grants and veteran-specific scholarship funds in the same call — most campuses hold restricted endowment funds for veterans that are awarded by a committee from whoever happens to ask.
items.deadline: School-specific and first-come; file FAFSA at the earliest opportunity.

items.title: TEACH Grant — up to $4,000 a year, and the conversion-to-loan trap that catches most recipients
items.org: U.S. Department of Education, Federal Student Aid
items.who: Students enrolled in a TEACH-eligible program at a participating school who agree to teach full-time for four complete academic years, within eight years of finishing the program, in a high-need field at a school or educational service agency serving low-income students.
items.value: Historically up to $4,000 per year, subject to federal sequestration reductions that have trimmed the actual disbursement — confirm the current per-year maximum and the sequester reduction for your award year. The honest headline is the risk: if you do not complete the full four-year service obligation exactly as specified, the entire grant converts to a Direct Unsubsidized Loan with interest charged back to the original disbursement date.
items.how: Through your school's financial aid office. You sign an Agreement to Serve or Repay each year and must complete annual certification of your teaching service afterward.
items.hack: The conversions that destroy people are almost never a refusal to teach — they are paperwork. Recipients teach the four years and then get converted because they missed an annual certification deadline, because their school was not on the Teacher Cancellation Low Income Directory for the year they taught, or because their subject was not classified as high-need in that state that year. Before you accept a TEACH Grant: verify your intended school is on the TCLI Directory, verify your subject is listed as high-need in your state, calendar the annual certification, and keep your own copies of every certification you submit. For veterans with Post-9/11 GI Bill entitlement remaining, think hard about whether you need this at all — an unneeded TEACH Grant is a loan with extra steps.
items.deadline: Annual, through your school; agreement signed each award year.

items.title: Why a veteran with full GI Bill coverage should still file the FAFSA every year
items.who: Every veteran, service member, spouse and dependent enrolled in or applying to any school, at any level.
items.value: The FAFSA is not a form for one grant — it is the single gate to Pell, FSEOG, Federal Work-Study, state grant programs, most institutional need-based aid, and a large share of private scholarship programs that require it as documentation. Skipping it does not just forfeit Pell; it silently disqualifies you from several parallel systems at once.
items.how: studentaid.gov, every year you are enrolled, as early in the cycle as it opens. VA education benefits are not reported as income.
items.hack: Three specific things the FAFSA unlocks that veterans overlook. First, state grant programs: many states run need-based grants whose only application is the FAFSA, with state deadlines months earlier than the federal one. Second, Federal Work-Study, which is often a flexible on-campus job that does not count against need in the way outside income does. Third, professional judgment: if your income dropped because you separated, were medically retired, or lost a spouse's income, you can ask the financial aid office for a professional judgment adjustment to recalculate your Student Aid Index on current circumstances rather than prior-prior-year tax data. That adjustment is discretionary, rarely advertised, and can move a veteran from zero Pell to a full award — but only if a FAFSA exists to adjust.
items.deadline: File at the opening of each annual cycle; state deadlines are much earlier than federal.

items.title: MOAA Ed Assist — interest-free education loans and grants, and the officer-parent rule
items.org: MOAA Scholarship Fund (Military Officers Association of America)
items.who: Children of military officers, and children of active-duty or retired enlisted personnel. Children of FORMER enlisted personnel do not qualify. Students must be 24 or younger, enrolled full-time as undergraduates at an accredited institution, with a minimum 3.0 GPA evaluated case by case. If an officer's child is selected, the officer parent must hold a paid MOAA membership.
items.value: Interest-free education loans plus a range of grants. MOAA does not publish most grant amounts — one named exception is a $500 Donor Designated Scholarship — and Senior Grants, Board of Director's Grants and Special Grants are offered without published figures. Ask for current amounts directly at edassist@moaa.org or 1-800-234-6622. No application or program fee.
items.how: Apply through charities.moaa.org during the annual window, which runs 1 November through 1 March, with finalists notified around 1 May.
items.hack: Note carefully what the eligibility rule actually says, because it is counterintuitive and costs families the award: enlisted service qualifies only if the parent is ACTIVE DUTY or RETIRED. A parent who served four enlisted years and separated does not qualify the child. Conversely, the officer path requires paid MOAA membership only if the child is selected — so the membership cost is not a barrier to applying, and families who assume they must join first often never apply at all. Apply in November, not February; interest-free loan pools are finite.
items.deadline: 1 November to 1 March annually; finalists notified about 1 May.

items.title: State tuition waivers and veteran education grants — the biggest money in this category
items.org: State departments of veterans affairs and state higher education agencies
items.who: Veterans, and in many states their spouses and dependent children, who meet state residency requirements. Several states extend full tuition waivers to children of veterans who died in service or are rated permanently and totally disabled.
items.value: In dollar terms this is the largest and most reliably funded education benefit category outside the GI Bill, and it is almost entirely absent from national scholarship lists because every state does it differently. Programs range from partial tuition grants to complete tuition and fee waivers at public institutions, sometimes for a set number of credit hours and sometimes without limit. Amounts, eligibility and residency rules differ by state and change by legislative session — verify with your own state.
items.how: Contact your state department of veterans affairs and your state higher education agency, and separately ask the veterans certifying official at your target school. The certifying official usually knows the state program better than anyone and processes it.
items.hack: The sequencing hack is worth real money: in states with a tuition waiver, use the WAIVER for public in-state tuition and SAVE your Post-9/11 GI Bill entitlement for a graduate program, a private school, or a certificate later. Veterans routinely burn 36 months of GI Bill on a degree their state would have covered for free, then have nothing left for the master's. Ask the certifying official explicitly: 'If I use the state waiver, does that consume any GI Bill entitlement?' In most states the answer is no, and that answer is worth tens of thousands of dollars.
items.deadline: Varies by state; many require application before each term.

items.title: Your own school's restricted veteran scholarship funds — awarded to whoever asks
items.org: Individual colleges, universities and their foundations
items.who: Enrolled or admitted students at that institution; many funds specify veteran, military-connected, or specific-branch or specific-conflict criteria written by the original donor.
items.value: Highly variable, commonly $500 to $5,000 per year, occasionally much more. The structural fact that makes these valuable: college and university foundations hold restricted endowment funds whose donor terms specify veterans or military families, and those funds must be spent on that purpose. When too few eligible students apply, the award goes to whoever did.
items.how: Make three specific requests at your institution. Ask the financial aid office for the list of all institutional scholarships with military or veteran criteria. Ask the university foundation or advancement office the same question — they hold the fund list and the financial aid office sometimes does not. Ask your Veterans Resource Center director, who usually knows which funds go unclaimed.
items.hack: Ask the question in writing, name the term 'restricted endowment funds with veteran or military criteria,' and ask whether any have gone unawarded in recent years. Unawarded restricted funds are an administrative embarrassment, and staff are generally eager to place them. One email to a foundation office has a materially better expected value than fifty applications to national scholarship databases, because you are the only applicant in the room. Do this every single year — these awards are rarely automatically renewed.
items.deadline: Institution-specific; most run an annual internal scholarship application in late winter or spring.

items.title: State National Guard tuition assistance — separate from federal TA and often stackable
items.org: State National Guard and state education agencies
items.who: Current drilling members of a state's Army or Air National Guard, under that state's own program rules.
items.value: State-funded tuition assistance, waivers, or reimbursement at state institutions, administered separately from federal Tuition Assistance and from the GI Bill. Several states offer effectively full tuition at public institutions for drilling Guard members. Amounts and caps are set by state statute and change with state budgets — verify yours each year.
items.how: Through your state's Guard education services officer and your school's certifying official. The application is usually state-specific and must be filed before each term.
items.hack: The stacking question is the one to ask, and ask it in writing: in many states, the state Guard benefit, federal Tuition Assistance, and the Montgomery GI Bill Selected Reserve (Chapter 1606) kicker can be layered so that tuition is covered by one source while another pays you directly. Get the state education services officer and the school certifying official on the same email thread and ask them to confirm the order of operations in writing before the term starts. Getting that sequence wrong is the difference between free school with money left over and a bill.
items.deadline: Per term, before enrollment; state-specific.

items.title: Nebraska Veterans Aid Fund — a real state grant, and the new state service officer route
items.who: Veterans who served on active duty, excluding training, with an honorable or general discharge, plus their spouses and dependents. Allied military service members honorably discharged are also covered.
items.value: A genuine state grant — not a loan. Aid is restricted by statute to a defined list: food, fuel, shelter, transportation, daycare, wearing apparel, funeral expenses, and medical and surgical items. The Department states that all income from the fund goes to aid rather than to administrative expenses. Dollar limits are not published centrally; ask the service officer handling your case.
items.how: Apply through a County Veterans Service Officer, the post service officer of any recognized veterans service organization, or — as of 3 September 2025 — a State Service Officer. State Service Office: 402-420-4021 or ndva.sso@nebraska.gov.
items.hack: The September 2025 addition of the State Service Officer route is the practical change that matters: if your county has no CVSO, a vacant CVSO position, or a backlog, you are no longer stuck. Call the state office directly. More broadly, note what the eligible-expense list includes that most emergency programs exclude: daycare, transportation, and funeral costs. A veteran family that cannot afford childcare to keep a job, or that needs to bury a parent, fits this fund and fits almost nothing else.
items.deadline: Rolling.

items.title: Texas Fund for Veterans' Assistance — the money goes to organizations, and you go to them
items.who: Two different audiences. Organizations — nonprofits, local governments, and veteran service organizations in Texas — apply for the grants. Individual Texas veterans and their families receive the services those grantees deliver.
items.value: One of the largest state-level veteran assistance grant programs in the country, funded through Texas lottery proceeds and specialty license plate revenue, awarding grants across categories that have historically included emergency financial assistance, housing, mental health, transportation, and legal services. Current round amounts, categories and award totals must be confirmed with the Texas Veterans Commission — the grants page was not retrievable at the time of writing.
items.how: Organizations: tvc.texas.gov grants pages. Individual veterans: do not apply to the state. Find the funded grantee near you and apply to that organization. Your County Veterans Service Officer will know which local nonprofits currently hold FVA grants.
items.hack: This is the model that most state veteran funds follow, and understanding it saves months: the state does not write checks to veterans, it writes checks to organizations that write checks to veterans. So the question to ask is never 'how do I apply to the state fund' but 'which organizations in my county currently hold a state veteran assistance grant.' Ask the CVSO, and ask for the list — grantees with unspent funds near the end of a grant period are actively looking for eligible applicants, which is the single best moment to apply anywhere in this entire directory.
items.deadline: Organization grant cycles are annual; individual assistance through grantees is rolling.

items.title: How to find your own state's veteran emergency fund — the CVSO is the whole answer
items.org: State departments of veterans affairs and County Veterans Service Officers
items.who: Every veteran in every state.
items.value: A large majority of states operate some form of veteran emergency relief, trust fund, or hardship grant, funded by state appropriations, lottery proceeds, license plate revenue, or tax check-offs. Verified examples in this directory include the Nebraska Veterans Aid Fund and the Michigan Veterans Trust Fund; Texas runs a large pass-through grant program. Benefit levels, eligible expenses and administration differ completely by state, and several states run them through county-level committees that are invisible online.
items.how: One call does it: find your County Veterans Service Officer. Use your state department of veterans affairs directory, or VA's state DVA index at va.gov/statedva.htm. Ask three questions: does this state have a veteran emergency or trust fund, do I qualify, and what documents do you need from me.
items.hack: The CVSO is the single highest-leverage free resource in the veterans benefits system and is systematically underused. They are usually county employees or state-accredited officers, their service is free, they are accredited to file VA claims, and critically — they hold the local knowledge no website has: which county committee meets when, which local nonprofit has unspent grant funds, which state program quietly reopened. Do not research your way to an answer that a twenty-minute appointment produces. Go in person, bring your DD-214, and ask what you qualify for rather than asking about one program.
items.deadline: Varies by state; many county committees meet monthly.

items.title: Utility hardship funds, arrearage forgiveness and protected-status rules
items.org: Individual utilities, state public utility commissions, and utility-affiliated charitable funds
items.who: Any household behind on an electric, gas or water bill. Several states add legal shutoff protections for households with a medically vulnerable member, a serious illness certification, infants, or elderly residents.
items.value: Three separate things people conflate. First, utility-affiliated hardship funds — often funded by customer donations and administered through a local agency — that pay a portion of an overdue balance as a grant. Second, arrearage forgiveness or arrearage management programs, where the utility forgives part of the past-due balance as you make on-time payments. Third, percentage-of-income payment plans in some states, which cap your bill at a share of household income. Amounts and availability are utility-specific; no national figure applies.
items.how: Call the utility and ask by name for the hardship fund, the arrearage management program, and any percentage-of-income plan. Separately call 211 and ask which local agency administers that utility's fund. Then call LIHEAP for the crisis benefit — these stack.
items.hack: Ask the utility, in the same call, about medical protected status. If a household member has a serious illness or relies on electrically powered medical equipment, most states require the utility to postpone or prohibit disconnection on receipt of a physician's certification — which buys you weeks to assemble assistance instead of hours. Many veterans with service-connected conditions and home medical equipment qualify and have never been told the protection exists. Get the certification form from the utility, have your VA provider sign it, and file it before you are in crisis, not during.
items.deadline: Rolling; shutoff moratoriums in many states are seasonal.

items.title: Community Action Agencies — the local office that administers nearly all of this
items.org: Community Action Agencies (Community Services Block Grant network)
items.who: Low-income households in essentially every county in the United States. Veteran status is not required, which is precisely why veterans skip them.
items.value: The single office that typically administers LIHEAP intake, the Weatherization Assistance Program, emergency rent and utility assistance, food programs, Head Start, and a rotating set of locally funded emergency funds — all in one place, with one intake, one income verification, and one caseworker.
items.how: Find yours through communityactionpartnership.com, or call 211. Go in person if you can, with identification, proof of income, and the bills you need help with.
items.hack: The reason to start here rather than with any individual program is a single intake. One income verification at a Community Action Agency can qualify you simultaneously for LIHEAP, weatherization, and whatever local emergency funds the agency is currently holding — and the caseworker knows which of those pots has money this week. Veterans spend weeks applying to programs one at a time that a single CAA appointment would have screened them for in an hour. Pair it with the CVSO visit: the CVSO covers everything veteran-specific, the CAA covers everything income-based, and between them there is very little left.
items.deadline: Rolling; individual program funding is seasonal and exhaustible.

items.title: 211, Salvation Army and St. Vincent de Paul — the unglamorous money that actually arrives
items.org: United Way 211; The Salvation Army; Society of St. Vincent de Paul; local faith-based consortiums
items.who: Anyone in financial crisis. No veteran status, no income documentation threshold in some cases, no waiting list in many.
items.value: Partial rent, partial utility, prescription, transportation and food assistance, typically in amounts from $100 to $1,500, decided locally and often within days. These organizations will not solve a large deficit alone, and that is not the point — they are the building blocks that close the gap after the larger programs have paid what they will pay.
items.how: Dial 211, free and available 24/7, and describe the specific bill and the specific deadline. Ask for a list of every agency in your county that assists with that bill type, then call all of them.
items.hack: This is the practical version of 'five small funds beat one famous one.' Local charities routinely cap assistance at a few hundred dollars per household per year, but they do not coordinate with each other, and most will pay a PORTION of a bill if another source covers the rest. So call the landlord or utility first, get the exact minimum payment that stops the action, then assemble it from three or four sources — LIHEAP crisis for part, a church fund for part, Salvation Army for part. Caseworkers at these agencies will often help you assemble the stack if you tell them the total and what you have already secured, because a partial payment that prevents eviction is a win they can report and a partial payment that fails is not.
items.deadline: Rolling; many agencies limit assistance to once per household per year.

items.title: Travis Mills Foundation — all-expenses-paid family retreat, free, Maine
items.who: Post-9/11 veterans severely injured, physically or psychologically, during their service — and their families and caregivers. The explicit inclusion of psychological injury is important: this is not an amputee-only program.
items.value: The Foundation states that all its services and programs are free to veterans, families and caregivers, and describes the retreat as all-inclusive and all-expenses-paid. The retreat is designed around the whole family rather than the veteran alone, which is unusual — most adaptive recreation programs take the veteran and leave the family at home.
items.how: Request an application through travismillsfoundation.org. Phone 207-480-3490; the retreat is at 647 Castle Island Road, Mount Vernon, Maine.
items.hack: The inclusion of psychological injury as a qualifying basis is the detail that matters most and is most often missed. A veteran with severe PTSD, TBI or military sexual trauma and no visible injury frequently self-screens out of every 'severely injured' program in the country. Apply. Second point: bring the caregiver. Caregiver burnout is the quiet reason these family placements fail afterward, and a program that explicitly funds the caregiver's attendance is doing something very few others do — confirm travel coverage details with the Foundation when you apply, since the all-inclusive description does not itemize travel.
items.deadline: Rolling application; retreat sessions run in cohorts through the season.

items.title: The Independence Fund — all-terrain trackchairs, about $25,000 each, 2,600+ delivered
items.who: Catastrophically wounded, ill and injured veterans with substantial mobility impairment. Eligibility criteria are not published on the program page — contact them directly rather than assuming.
items.value: All-terrain trackchairs engineered for snow, mud and dirt, enabling mobility where a standard wheelchair cannot go. The Fund states the cost of a trackchair is approximately $25,000 and reports more than 2,600 recipients. This is equipment VA generally does not provide, because VA's durable medical equipment standard is medical necessity for activities of daily living, not outdoor terrain access — which is exactly the gap this fills.
items.how: Contact 888-851-7996 or info@independencefund.org, and see independencefund.org/pages/mobility-program. Confirm current application status when you call, as the mobility program page does not state whether applications are open.
items.hack: Apply here for what VA denied. The productive sequence is: request the equipment from VA Prosthetics first, get the denial in writing, then bring that written denial to The Independence Fund. A documented VA denial establishes both the need and the absence of another funding source, which is the core of what any equipment charity is assessing. Veterans who skip the VA request look like they are shopping; veterans with a denial letter look like a funding gap. Ask also about the Fund's caregiver programs and Operation Resiliency — different pots, same organization, and the caregiver side is far less subscribed.
items.deadline: Confirm current application status directly.

items.title: Wheelchairs for Warriors — custom-fit mobility, and the name you are probably searching wrong
items.who: Veterans and first responders injured in the line of duty. Third parties may nominate someone who fits those categories.
items.value: Custom-fit mobility solutions — the organization frames the goal as independent mobility and function at the highest level possible, rather than simply issuing a chair. No cost or fee to the recipient is indicated anywhere in the application process.
items.how: Apply at wheelchairsforwarriors.org/apply. Veterans must submit a copy of the DD Form 214. The form also asks how you heard about the organization and whether you are the applicant or nominating someone else.
items.hack: Search the correct name: it is Wheelchairs for Warriors, not 'Wheelchairs 4 Warriors.' The numeral variant circulates widely on benefit lists and leads to dead links and, in some cases, to unrelated sites. Second, the nomination path is underused — if you are a case manager, a CVSO, a VSO service officer, or a family member of someone who will not advocate for themselves, you can submit the nomination. Many of the veterans who most need custom seating are the least likely to fill in a form, and this organization explicitly accepts third-party referrals.
items.deadline: Rolling.

items.title: VA home oxygen and durable medical equipment — provided, not reimbursed
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Health Administration
items.who: Veterans enrolled in VA health care with a clinical indication. Home oxygen requires documented qualifying test results.
items.value: Home oxygen systems including concentrators and portable units, plus durable medical equipment — hospital beds, lifts, CPAP and BiPAP machines and supplies, nebulizers, commodes, walkers and canes — supplied by VA with maintenance and replacement supplies included. Critical structural point: VA supplies the equipment through its contracts; it does not generally reimburse you for equipment you bought yourself. Buying first and asking later usually means paying for it yourself.
items.how: Through a VA clinical consult, exactly as with prosthetics. Home oxygen additionally requires qualifying oximetry or arterial blood gas results documented in your record.
items.hack: Two practical moves. First, if you are enrolled in both VA care and Medicare, ask explicitly which system should supply a given item before anything is ordered — getting the same equipment through both creates a billing mess that takes months to unwind, and VA-supplied equipment typically costs you nothing while Medicare leaves a 20% coinsurance. Second, ask about resupply standing orders for consumables like CPAP masks, tubing and filters. Veterans run deteriorated supplies for years because they do not know a standing order exists and assume each replacement requires a new appointment.
items.deadline: No deadline; consult-driven.

items.title: Adaptive automobile equipment is repeatable — the vehicle allowance is not
items.who: Veterans and service members eligible for the automobile allowance, plus a wider group eligible for adaptive equipment only — including those with ankle immobility of the knees or hips, who qualify for equipment without qualifying for the vehicle allowance.
items.value: The structural asymmetry people miss. VA states the automobile grant may be received only once in a lifetime. Adaptive equipment is different: it may be provided more than once, as equipment wears out, as you change vehicles, or as your condition changes. Over twenty years the repeatable equipment benefit is worth considerably more than the one-time vehicle allowance.
items.how: VA Form 21-4502 for the vehicle allowance plus adaptive equipment; VA Form 10-1394 for adaptive equipment only. Prior VA approval is required before purchase, in both cases.
items.hack: Never use your once-in-a-lifetime vehicle allowance on a vehicle that cannot physically accept the adaptations you will need later. Get the adaptive equipment evaluation and the list of required modifications FIRST, then buy a vehicle the modifications fit — minivan versus sedan, rear-entry versus side-entry conversion, roof height for a lift. Veterans spend the one-time allowance on a vehicle they like, discover it cannot take a lift, and have no allowance left. Separately, if your only qualifying basis is ankle, knee or hip immobility, file the 10-1394 — you are eligible for equipment even though you are not eligible for the car, and almost nobody in that category ever files.
items.deadline: No deadline; prior approval before every purchase.

items.title: SSVF for applicants — the largest veteran homelessness grant, FY2027 NOFO published
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Homeless Programs Office
items.who: Private nonprofit organizations and consumer cooperatives that can provide supportive services to very low-income veteran families who are homeless or at imminent risk of homelessness.
items.value: Grants funding rapid re-housing and homelessness prevention — case management, help obtaining VA and other benefits, and temporary financial assistance paid on behalf of the veteran family for rent, security deposits, utility deposits and arrearages, moving costs, child care and transportation. VA has announced awards in the hundreds of millions to over a billion dollars across homeless program grants in recent cycles. A FY2027 SSVF Notice of Funding Opportunity has been published; confirm current award ceilings and the submission deadline in the live NOFO rather than relying on any secondary figure.
items.how: Through grants.gov, under the VA SSVF opportunity. Requires an active SAM.gov registration and Unique Entity ID. Read the NOFO's scoring criteria before writing anything — SSVF scoring is heavily weighted to demonstrated housing outcomes and coordinated entry participation.
items.hack: For veterans rather than applicant organizations: the way to reach SSVF money is the National Call Center for Homeless Veterans at 877-424-3838, free, confidential, 24/7. Ask for the SSVF provider in your area BY NAME and ask specifically about temporary financial assistance for deposits and arrears — this is the single largest source of rent and deposit money for veterans in the country, it is paid on your behalf rather than loaned to you, and you do not have to already be homeless to qualify, only at imminent risk.
items.deadline: FY2027 NOFO published; confirm the current submission deadline on grants.gov.

items.title: Grant and Per Diem — current rates, locked through September 2027 by the Dole Act
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Homeless Programs Office
items.who: Community-based organizations operating transitional housing and service centers for veterans experiencing homelessness.
items.value: Verified current rates, effective 1 January 2026, offered through 30 September 2027 under the Senator Elizabeth Dole 21st Century Veterans Healthcare and Benefits Improvement Act: Per Diem Only $85.37 per day; Service Center $10.67 per hour; Special Need $128.38 per day; Transition in Place $96.29 per day; Veterans with Minor Dependents at 50% of the authorized PDO or TIP rate. The State Home Domiciliary rate is $64.19. Eligible grantees may request 200% waiver rates — up to $128.38 for PDO and TIP and $16.05 for Service Center — case by case. Program components include Per Diem Only, Service Center, Transition in Place, Special Need, and Case Management.
items.how: Capital and per diem grant opportunities are announced through grants.gov and the Federal Register. Current grantees manage rates through the VA GPD provider portal.
items.hack: The Special Need rate at $128.38 per day and the 200% waiver authority are the under-requested levers. Special Need covers veterans who are frail and elderly, terminally ill, have chronic mental illness, or are women veterans including those with dependents — populations that cost far more to serve than the base per diem supports. Grantees serving these veterans on the standard rate are subsidizing VA out of their own fundraising. For veterans: if a transitional housing program says it cannot accommodate your medical or caregiving needs, ask whether they are a GPD grantee and whether they have requested the Special Need rate, because the funding mechanism for your situation exists.
items.deadline: Rates set through 30 September 2027; grant competitions announced periodically.

items.title: SSG Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program — $100,000 to $750,000 per award
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Office of Suicide Prevention
items.who: Entities meeting the Hannon Act definition — incorporated private institutions or foundations, Indian tribes, community-based organizations, and state and local governments that can network with civic and health organizations to deliver suicide prevention services.
items.value: Awards from a $100,000 minimum to a $750,000 maximum, structured as a one-year award with an option to renew for an additional year subject to funds and grantee performance. VA has announced program rounds at scales up to $112 million. The FY2026 opportunity was archived in August 2025; an FY2027 NOFO has been published on grants.gov. Confirm the current ceiling, floor, total program funding and deadline in the live NOFO — the award range has moved between cycles.
items.how: Apply through grants.gov. SAM.gov registration and a Unique Entity ID are prerequisites. The NOFO specifies required outcome measures and the baseline suicide prevention services an applicant must deliver.
items.hack: For organizations: the recurring annual cadence means that if you missed this cycle you should be building the partnership documentation and outcome-measurement capacity now, because the scoring rewards demonstrated community networking and most first-time applicants lose points there, not on program design. For veterans and families reading this: SSG Fox grantees provide free suicide prevention services including outreach, case management and emergency assistance in their service areas, and VA publishes the grantee list — your local grantee is a free service provider you can approach directly, independent of VA enrollment.
items.deadline: Annual cycle; FY2027 NOFO published — confirm the deadline on grants.gov.

items.title: VA Adaptive Sports Grant Program — up to $16 million a year, posted each spring
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, National Veterans Sports Programs and Special Events
items.who: Eligible applicants span state governments, educational institutions, nonprofits with 501(c)(3) status, and other entity types able to deliver adaptive sports programming to disabled veterans and disabled members of the Armed Forces, under 38 U.S.C. 521A and 38 CFR Part 77.
items.value: Up to $16,000,000 per cycle, subject to availability of federal funds. The FY2026 opportunity, VA-SPORTS-26, posted 27 March 2026 and was archived 12 June 2026 — the cycle has closed, and the program recurs annually. Award minimums and maximums have shifted between cycles; take them from the live NOFO, not from a prior year.
items.how: Through grants.gov. Note that for this program VA has directed applicants to apply at www.grants.gov rather than through Simpler.Grants.gov. SAM.gov registration required.
items.hack: The timing is the hack: this NOFO has posted in late March with a window of roughly ten weeks. If you intend to apply next cycle, have your SAM.gov registration, financial statements, and partnership letters complete by February — organizations miss this one on administrative readiness far more often than on program merit. For veterans: VA publishes the list of funded grantees each year, and that list is the authoritative directory of adaptive sports programs that are actually funded and operating near you, as opposed to the many that have a website and no budget.
items.deadline: Annual; FY2026 cycle closed 12 June 2026. Watch for the next posting in spring.

items.title: Legal Services for Veterans grants — 92 organizations, up to $500,000, FY26 cycle running now
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Homeless Programs Office
items.who: Public or nonprofit private entities with the capacity to administer the grant, including local governments, state governments, and federally recognized Indian tribal governments.
items.value: VA awarded up to $500,000 each to 92 eligible organizations for the FY26 two-year grant cycle that began 1 October 2025 — meaning this money is live and being delivered right now, through FY27. Funded legal services cover housing matters, family law, income support, criminal defense in homelessness-related cases, discharge character upgrade requests, protections related to domestic and intimate partner violence, health care access, and employment law. VA prioritizes applicants offering four or more of these service areas and those directing at least 10% of funds to women veterans.
items.how: Organizations apply through grants.gov when the NOFO posts; watch the Federal Register for the Legal Services for Homeless Veterans funding opportunity notices.
items.hack: For veterans: VA publishes a downloadable list of current awarded grantees with referral information on the program page. Two things make this list unusually valuable. First, discharge upgrade representation is funded — that is specialized, expensive legal work, available free through these grantees, and the single highest-value legal service most bad-paper veterans will ever receive. Second, capability varies sharply by grantee, so if the nearest one does not handle your issue, work down the list rather than stopping. The 10% women-veteran set-aside also means women veterans should state that status at intake, because grantees are measured on it.
items.deadline: FY26 two-year cycle began 1 October 2025 and runs through FY27; watch for the next competition.

items.title: Highly Rural Transportation Grants — for the counties where there is no other way to the VA
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Transportation Program
items.who: Applicant side: state veterans service agencies and veterans service organizations operating in counties VA classifies as highly rural — fewer than seven people per square mile.
items.value: Grants to provide transportation for veterans in highly rural counties to VA or VA-authorized health care, covering vehicles, drivers, and operating costs. Per-grant amounts are set by the NOFO and have historically been capped in the low six figures per county served; confirm current figures in the live notice.
items.how: Organizations apply through grants.gov when the Veterans Transportation Program posts the opportunity. Veterans access the service by contacting the grantee or their VA medical center's Veterans Transportation Service.
items.hack: For veterans in rural areas, there are three distinct transportation channels and most people know only one. First, these Highly Rural Transportation Grant services, run by state agencies and VSOs. Second, VA's own Veterans Transportation Service, operated by medical centers with VA vehicles and drivers. Third, Beneficiary Travel, which reimburses your mileage and, for qualifying veterans, can pay for lodging and meals on a long trip. Ask your VA medical center's travel office about all three by name in one call. Veterans drive four hours unreimbursed because they asked about 'a ride' and were told there was none that day.
items.deadline: Periodic NOFO; services ongoing through grantees.

items.title: State Home Construction Grant — VA pays up to 65% to build or renovate a state veterans home
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Office of Geriatrics and Extended Care
items.who: States, through their state veterans home systems. Not open to private operators, counties or nonprofits.
items.value: A grant-in-aid partnership in which VA provides up to 65 percent of the cost to construct, acquire, renovate or repair state-owned and operated nursing homes, domiciliaries and adult day health care facilities, with the state providing the remaining 35 percent. As of 1 June 2026 there are 177 State Veterans Homes comprising 171 nursing homes, 47 domiciliaries and 3 adult day health care programs. VA separately pays per diem to states for the care of eligible veterans in these homes.
items.how: States apply through VA's Office of Geriatrics and Extended Care. VA maintains a priority list for state home construction grants, published periodically.
items.hack: For families rather than states: the existence of the per diem is why a State Veterans Home is often dramatically cheaper for a veteran than a private nursing home, and why eligibility rules differ from Medicaid. Ask the admissions office two specific questions: what is the VA per diem contribution for my relative's service-connected status, and does a 70%-or-higher service-connected rating or service-connected need for nursing care change the cost. For some veterans VA pays the full cost of nursing home care, and families spend down assets for Medicaid without ever asking.
items.deadline: Priority-list driven; state applications on VA's cycle.

items.title: Veterans Cemetery Grants Program — up to 100% of development cost, and a 1 July deadline
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, National Cemetery Administration
items.who: States, territories, the District of Columbia, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and the 574 federally recognized tribal governments. Cities, counties, private organizations and other political subdivisions cannot apply.
items.value: VA may provide up to 100 percent of the development cost of an approved project, and for new cemeteries that includes operating equipment. VA cannot fund land acquisition — the applicant must supply the land by purchase, transfer or donation. Federal funds are appropriated annually. More than 100 grant-funded veterans cemeteries have been dedicated to date.
items.how: Applications must meet basic requirements by the 1 JULY deadline to be ranked on the priority list for the following fiscal year. VA ranks in four tiers: Priority 1 for preventing a disruption of service, Priority 2 for new cemeteries, Priority 3 for planned phased development, Priority 4 for operations and improvements.
items.hack: The requirement that sinks applications is not money, it is authority: to make the priority list, the applicant must demonstrate clear legal authority AND adequate funding to begin the design process. State and tribal applicants routinely submit with a resolution of intent and no appropriated design funds, and drop off the list. Secure the design money and the enabling authority before 1 July, not after. Note also that because VA cannot buy land, a donated parcel is often the fastest path — which makes a landowner negotiation, not a grant application, the critical path item.
items.deadline: 1 July annually for priority-list consideration for the following fiscal year.

items.title: Where VA actually publishes its grant opportunities — three places, checked in order
items.who: Anyone who runs, works for, or advises a veteran-serving organization.
items.value: A reliable monitoring routine instead of discovering a NOFO after it closed. VA runs grant programs out of several different offices — Homeless Programs, Suicide Prevention, National Veterans Sports Programs, the National Cemetery Administration, Geriatrics and Extended Care, Loan Guaranty — and no single page lists all of them with current status.
items.how: Check three sources. One, department.va.gov/grants, VA's own grants landing page, which indexes the programs by office. Two, grants.gov, which is where applications are actually submitted and where the live opportunity listings with ceilings, floors and deadlines sit. Three, the Federal Register, which is where VA is legally required to publish funding availability notices and amendments — this is the earliest signal and the one almost nobody watches.
items.hack: Set a Federal Register email alert on the agency 'Department of Veterans Affairs' filtered to notices. It is free, it arrives before the grants.gov listing is fully populated, and it catches amendments and deadline extensions that grants.gov sometimes reflects late. Pair it with a saved search on grants.gov. The organizations that consistently win VA grants are not better writers — they start six weeks earlier because they saw the notice first.
items.deadline: N/A — ongoing monitoring.

items.title: How to search grants.gov properly — and what changed with Simpler.Grants.gov
items.who: Anyone looking for federal grant opportunities, for an organization or as an individual.
items.value: The current state of the platform, verified: Simpler Search is now the default search for funding opportunities as of early 2026. A simpler application workflow is in a limited pilot with a small number of partner agencies and opportunities. Legacy grants.gov remains operational and is still where most applications are submitted — and VA has explicitly directed applicants for some programs, including Adaptive Sports, to apply at www.grants.gov rather than through Simpler. The Simpler experience is planned to become the default Grants.gov experience in 2027.
items.how: Search on simpler.grants.gov. Filter by eligibility type FIRST — this single filter removes the majority of irrelevant results, because most federal grants are restricted to governments, institutions of higher education, or nonprofits. Then filter by status: set it to Posted (open) rather than leaving Forecasted and Closed in the results, which is why most people's searches return dead opportunities. Then filter by agency. Save the search and turn on email notifications.
items.hack: Two mechanical points that cost people entire cycles. First, 'Archived' on a grants.gov listing does not mean the program is dead — it means that cycle's window closed. For an annually recurring program, an archived listing is a schedule, telling you roughly when next year's will post. Read the archived NOFO now and build the application before the new one appears. Second, register in SAM.gov and get your Unique Entity ID before you find an opportunity you want. SAM.gov entity validation routinely takes weeks and is the single most common reason an organization watches a deadline pass with a finished application it cannot submit.
items.deadline: N/A; Simpler becomes the default Grants.gov experience in 2027.

items.title: Federal grants are almost never for individuals — the sentence that saves you a month
items.who: Any individual who has searched grants.gov for personal financial help.
items.value: A structural fact that the entire 'free government grant money' industry depends on you not knowing: federal grants overwhelmingly flow to states, local governments, tribes, institutions of higher education, nonprofits and businesses — not to individuals for personal expenses. There is no federal grant for paying your rent, your debts, or your bills directly. The individual-facing exceptions are narrow and specific: Pell and FSEOG for education, the SAH and SHA family of VA housing grants, USDA Section 504 repair grants, the SAHAT program's unusual person-or-entity eligibility, and disaster assistance.
items.how: Reframe the search. Instead of looking for a federal grant to you, look for the ORGANIZATION near you that holds the federal grant and delivers the service. SSVF money reaches veterans through nonprofit grantees. LIHEAP reaches households through state agencies and community action agencies. State veteran assistance funds reach veterans through funded local nonprofits. In every case the federal dollar is real and the individual application goes to a local organization.
items.hack: This single reframe is the difference between a productive month and a wasted one. Ask every program 'who holds the grant in my county,' then apply to them. And apply this test to any website offering to find you 'government grants for personal use' for a fee: the thing they are selling does not exist, which is why they are selling a search service rather than a grant. Benefits.gov, which is free and official, screens you against actual federal programs you might be eligible for — use it instead.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: What a 501(c)(3) actually has to have before it can accept a federal grant
items.who: Veterans who run or are starting a nonprofit and assume the IRS determination letter is the finish line.
items.value: An honest list of what federal grant readiness costs, so you do not win an award you cannot administer. Beyond the IRS 501(c)(3) determination you need: an active SAM.gov registration and Unique Entity ID, renewed annually; a DUNS successor identifier where still required; a documented accounting system that can track costs by award and separate direct from indirect; written financial, procurement and conflict-of-interest policies; a federally negotiated indirect cost rate or election of the de minimis rate; the capacity to meet the Uniform Guidance at 2 CFR Part 200; and if you expend $1,000,000 or more in federal awards in a fiscal year under the current threshold, a Single Audit performed by an independent auditor. Confirm the current Single Audit threshold, which has been revised.
items.how: Build in this order: incorporation, IRS determination, bookkeeping system and chart of accounts that supports fund accounting, written policies, SAM.gov registration, then apply. Your free resources are your state nonprofit association, a local community foundation's capacity-building program, and SCORE.
items.hack: The cash-flow trap nobody warns new grantees about: most federal grants are COST REIMBURSEMENT, not advance payment. You spend the money, then you invoice, then you wait thirty to ninety days. A small nonprofit that wins a $500,000 reimbursement grant and has $8,000 in the bank cannot perform the grant and will fail its first drawdown cycle. Before you apply, know your working capital or arrange a line of credit — and consider applying as a subrecipient of an established organization for your first award instead of as the prime. Subrecipient experience is the credential that makes the next prime application credible.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: How to write a hardship letter that gets funded
items.who: Anyone applying to a relief society, a veteran charity, a church fund, or a utility hardship program.
items.value: Funding decisions at these organizations are made by a caseworker or a small committee with a limited budget, reading many requests. They are answering four questions, and a letter that answers all four in one page is approved at a far higher rate than a longer one that does not.
items.how: Answer the four questions in order. One, what specifically happened and when — a dated event, not a general condition. Two, exactly how much you need and to whom it is payable — the creditor's name, account number, amount, and the date something bad happens if it is unpaid. Three, what you have already done — what you paid, what you sold, who else you asked, what partial help you secured. Four, why this will not recur next month — the new job, the approved claim, the reduced expense, the payment plan now in place. Then attach the documents: the bill, the notice, the estimate, the orders, the DD-214.
items.hack: The fourth question is the one that decides it, and almost nobody answers it. A caseworker with a fixed budget is choosing between a request that stabilizes a household and a request that delays a collapse by thirty days. Give them the specific reason this is a bridge and not a leak — 'my VA claim was granted with an effective date of March and retroactive pay is expected within sixty days,' or 'I start work on the 14th, offer letter attached.' Also name the exact amount that solves the problem rather than asking for 'help.' Call the creditor first and get the minimum payment that stops the action, then ask for that number. Precise, documented, bridge-shaped requests get funded.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: Why five small local funds beat one famous national grant
items.who: Everyone using this directory.
items.value: A strategy, expressed as arithmetic. A nationally famous veteran grant may receive thousands of applications for a handful of awards — a success rate in fractions of a percent, with a decision cycle measured in months. A local church fund, a post relief fund, a community foundation field-of-interest fund, a utility hardship fund and a community action agency emergency fund each receive a few dozen requests, decide in days to weeks, and routinely approve. Five awards of $400 arriving in three weeks solves a $2,000 problem. One $25,000 award you do not win solves nothing.
items.how: Build a list of ten local sources before you apply anywhere: your CVSO, your community action agency, 211's county list, your American Legion and VFW posts, your community foundation, two or three local churches with benevolence funds, your utility's hardship program, the local Salvation Army, and St. Vincent de Paul. Apply to all of them in the same week, and tell each one what the total need is and what you have already secured.
items.hack: Stack deliberately and tell the truth about it. Most small funds will pay a portion if someone else covers the rest, and many prefer it — a $300 contribution that prevents an eviction is a better outcome for them than a $300 contribution that delays it. So lead with 'the total is $1,840, I have $900 committed from two sources, I need $940.' That framing converts you from a bottomless request into a closable gap, which is the thing small funders say yes to. Meanwhile, apply to the big national programs too — just do not wait on them.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: Grant, no-interest loan, forgivable loan, matching program — four different things
items.who: Anyone evaluating an offer of assistance.
items.value: Precision here prevents the two most expensive mistakes in this space: refusing good money because you assumed it was debt, and accepting debt because it was labeled a grant. A GRANT is money you keep, with no repayment — though it may carry conditions, like USDA's Section 504 grant which must be repaid if you sell within three years, or a service obligation like the TEACH Grant, which converts to a loan with back-dated interest if you do not teach the four required years. A NO-INTEREST or INTEREST-FREE LOAN, the backbone of the branch relief societies, is real debt you must repay, but at zero cost of capital and usually with no credit check, which makes it dramatically better than any consumer alternative. A FORGIVABLE or DEFERRED-PAYMENT LOAN, common in local housing rehab programs, is a lien that forgives on a schedule if you keep living there — a grant if you stay, a debt if you sell early. A MATCHING program, like Individual Development Accounts, multiplies money you save, so its value is capped by what you can contribute.
items.how: For every offer, ask four questions in writing: Do I ever repay this, and under what circumstances? Is there a lien on my property, and when does it release? Is there a service or occupancy obligation, and what happens if I cannot complete it? Is it reported to credit bureaus?
items.hack: The practical ranking for a household in trouble, best to worst: a true unconditional grant; a forgivable loan whose forgiveness period is shorter than how long you will stay; an interest-free loan from a relief society; a matching program if you have any capacity to save; a conditional grant with a service obligation you are certain you can complete. Note where that leaves the branch relief societies — an interest-free, no-credit-check loan decided the same day beats a competitive grant you might win in eight weeks, and veterans turn these down because the word 'loan' sounds worse than the word 'grant.' It usually is not.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: The application fee rule — one test that eliminates most of the fraud
items.who: Everyone.
items.value: A single, absolute screen. Legitimate grantmakers — federal, state, tribal, foundation, corporate or charitable — do not charge applicants a fee to apply, to be considered, to be 'matched,' to be 'pre-qualified,' or to receive funds. If money has to move from you toward the funder before money moves from the funder toward you, it is not a grant program. This rule alone disqualifies the large majority of fraudulent and predatory offers in the veterans space.
items.how: Walk away. Then, if it was presented as a government grant, report it: the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov, and for anything invoking VA, the VA Office of Inspector General hotline. If you have already paid, dispute the charge with your card issuer immediately — fee-charging 'grant' operations are routinely chargeback-reversible.
items.hack: Learn the adjacent variants, because sophisticated operations have moved past a flat fee. Watch for: a refundable 'deposit' to release the funds; a required purchase of a course, template, or 'grant writing kit'; a 'processing' or 'wire' fee deducted from the award; a requirement to open an account at a specific institution; a request for your bank login or routing details before any eligibility decision; and the grant-writer-on-contingency pitch, where someone takes a percentage of an award — which is prohibited under federal grant rules as an allowable cost and is a sign they know less about grants than you do. Paid grant-writing help can be legitimate for an organization, billed hourly or by project, never as a cut of the award and never to an individual applying for personal relief.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: The documentation packet you build once and reuse for everything
items.who: Every veteran applying to anything in this directory.
items.value: Assembled once, this packet converts a two-week application into a twenty-minute one and is the difference between catching a short funding window and missing it. Nearly every program here asks for a subset of the same documents.
items.how: Scan to PDF and keep in one encrypted folder, with a printed copy in a binder: DD Form 214, member-4 or service-2 copy showing character of service; VA decision letter and current rating sheet; VA benefit verification letter, downloadable instantly from VA.gov; the last two years of tax returns and the last two months of pay stubs or benefit statements; two months of bank statements; a current photo ID and Social Security card; marriage certificate, divorce decree and children's birth certificates as applicable; your lease or mortgage statement; a current utility bill; the specific bill, notice, estimate or invoice driving the request; and for business applications, the EIN letter, formation documents, and the last two years of business returns.
items.hack: Download your VA benefit verification letter from VA.gov today, before you need it — it is instant, it is the document most programs actually want, and it proves income and disability status in one page without exposing your full rating decision. Then, when you call a program, ask one question at the end of the call: 'what else do you need from me.' A file that is complete at submission is reviewed in the first pass; a file missing one document goes to the bottom of the queue and waits for your reply, which is where most applications quietly die.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: Are these grants taxable? The general shape of the answer, and when to ask a professional
items.who: Anyone who receives a significant grant, a donated home, or a vehicle.
items.value: An honest, hedged answer, because this is genuinely fact-specific and getting it wrong is expensive. VA disability compensation and most VA benefits are not taxable income.
