Need-based charitable assistance from a 501(c)(3) to an individual is generally not taxable income to the recipient. Educational grants used for qualified tuition and related expenses are generally excludable, while amounts used for room and board generally are not. Business grants to a for-profit entity are generally taxable income. A donated home or vehicle raises gift and basis questions — note that at least one program in this directory, Military Warriors Support Foundation, structures its awards explicitly as gift-tax-free, which tells you the issue is real enough that programs engineer around it.
items.how: Ask the granting organization in writing whether they will issue a Form 1099 and on what basis. Keep every award letter. Then take the award letters to a free tax preparer: IRS VITA sites, AARP Tax-Aide, and MilTax from Military OneSource, which is free to veterans within a period after separation and to military families.
items.hack: Ask the 1099 question BEFORE you accept a business grant, because the tax is often a quarter to a third of the award and arriving in April is how a $20,000 grant becomes a $6,000 problem. For housing awards, ask specifically how the transfer is structured and whether the organization has obtained a determination or opinion on the recipient's tax treatment — the organizations that do this well will answer immediately, and an organization that cannot answer is telling you something. None of this is tax advice; it is the list of questions to put to someone who can give it.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: Why every grant amount you read is probably wrong, and the three-source rule
items.who: Everyone reading any grant directory, this one included.
items.value: A method for not being misled, including by this reference. Grant figures move for four distinct reasons and they move on four different clocks: statutory indexing, like the VA SAH family re-indexing every 1 October against the Turner Building Cost Index; annual appropriations, which can hold a figure flat for years as the Pell maximum has been; sequestration, which quietly reduces some awards like the TEACH Grant below their stated maximum; and discretionary program decisions by charities, which change cycle to cycle with fundraising.
items.how: Apply the three-source rule before relying on any number. Source one: the program's own primary page or the Federal Register notice. Source two: a human at the program, by phone or email, with the answer in writing. Source three: the date. If you cannot find a date on the figure, you do not have a figure. Never treat an aggregator, a listicle, a law firm blog, or this directory as a primary source for an amount.
items.hack: Watch for the specific tell that a source is stale: a figure cited without a fiscal year or effective date. VA's own automobile allowance page currently prints a figure labeled 'beginning 10-01-18,' which is honest but means the number has not been updated in the body text in years — and that page is more reliable than most of what you will find. If the official page is years behind, every unofficial page copying it is too. When the primary source is ambiguous, the Regional Loan Center, the VA medical center office, or the program's own staff is the authority, and you should get the answer in writing and keep it.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: A closed grant cycle is a calendar, not a dead end
items.who: Organizations and individuals who found a program after its window closed.
items.value: Most of the programs in this directory recur. The VA Adaptive Sports NOFO posted in late March and archived in June. The SSG Fox program runs annual cycles with a published FY2027 NOFO. SSVF runs annually. The Veterans Cemetery Grants Program has a fixed 1 July priority deadline every year. MOAA's education window is 1 November to 1 March every year. Finding a closed cycle tells you exactly when to be ready next time, which is more useful than finding an open one you have two weeks to answer.
items.how: When you find a closed opportunity, do four things. Download the archived NOFO or application and read the scoring criteria. Note the posting and closing dates and put them in a calendar with a sixty-day lead reminder. Complete the administrative prerequisites now — SAM.gov, UEI, audited financials, letters of support. Email the program officer named in the NOFO and ask to be notified when the next cycle posts.
items.hack: Emailing the program officer is the step that separates repeat winners from first-time losers, and it is almost never done. Program officers answer questions, will often tell you candidly whether your project fits the program, and remember the organizations that asked intelligent questions six months before the deadline. For charitable programs with no NOFO, the equivalent move is to call and ask when they expect to reopen and what they wish applicants knew. The answer is usually specific and it is usually not on the website.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: The order of operations — what to do first when you need money this month
items.who: A veteran in an active financial emergency.
items.value: A sequence, because the single biggest cost in a crisis is doing things in the wrong order. Grants are slow; some things in this list are same-day.
items.how: In this order. One: call the creditor, landlord or utility and get the exact minimum payment and date that stops the action, plus ask for a payment plan and any hardship program — this reframes the entire problem and sometimes solves it. Two: if you are a current or recent service member or retiree, call your branch relief society, which can often decide same-day with an interest-free loan. Three: call 211 and ask for every county agency that assists with this bill type. Four: call your County Veterans Service Officer, for the state veteran fund and for a free claims review. Five: apply to LIHEAP's crisis component if it is a utility, and to the utility's own hardship fund. Six: apply to the national veteran charities — Operation Homefront, USA Cares, VFW, American Legion TFA if you have minor children — knowing these take longer. Seven: if you are wounded, ill or injured, contact Semper Fi & America's Fund for case management rather than a single grant.
items.hack: Step one is the one people skip and it is the highest-value step in the list. A landlord who will accept $600 now and the rest over three months has just reduced a $1,800 emergency to a $600 emergency, which five small local funds can close this week. A utility that will enter you into an arrearage management program has stopped the shutoff clock entirely. You cannot assemble assistance against an unknown target — get the number and the date first, in writing, then go get the money.
items.deadline: N/A — act in this order.

items.title: Free accredited help exists — never pay someone to file a VA claim
items.org: County Veterans Service Officers; VA-accredited VSO representatives; VA-accredited attorneys and agents
items.who: Every veteran and survivor.
items.value: County Veterans Service Officers and accredited representatives of VSOs — the American Legion, VFW, DAV, AMVETS, PVA, MOPH and others — provide free, accredited representation for VA claims and appeals, and free navigation to state and local benefit programs. VA-accredited attorneys and claims agents may charge fees, but only on an appeal after an initial decision and only within VA's fee rules; charging for help with an INITIAL claim is prohibited.
items.how: Find a CVSO through your county government or your state department of veterans affairs; find accredited representatives through VA's accreditation search at va.gov. Bring your DD-214 and your medical records.
items.hack: This is the practical answer to the entire 'claim shark' industry. Unaccredited companies charging veterans a multiple of their first retroactive payment for help with an initial claim are operating outside VA's fee rules, and the same work is available free from an accredited representative. Verify accreditation yourself on VA's own accreditation search before signing anything — not on the company's website. And use the CVSO for more than claims: they hold the local map of state funds, county committees, grantee organizations with unspent money, and property tax exemptions, which is a body of knowledge that does not exist online anywhere.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: How this grants directory was verified, and what that means for you
items.who: Every reader.
items.value: Transparency about the evidence behind these entries, so you know which ones to double-check hardest. Entries marked high confidence were checked against the organization's or agency's own site or an official notice, with evidence that the program was operating in the current cycle. Entries marked medium confidence describe organizations verified to exist and operate, where the current cycle, amount, or eligibility detail could not be confirmed from a primary source. Several widely listed programs were excluded entirely because they are defunct, no longer serve veterans, or could not be verified at all.
items.how: Read the confidence field and the value field together. Where a figure appears without a fiscal year, treat it as historical. Where an entry says to confirm the current cycle, do that before you spend effort — and before you make a financial decision that depends on an amount.
items.hack: The three findings that should calibrate your skepticism about every other veteran grant list you read: the StreetShares Foundation's domain now serves an Indonesian gambling site and its award still appears on 2026 grant lists; the Second Service Foundation has voluntarily shut down and the Military Entrepreneur Challenge is not operating; and Operation First Response no longer provides emergency financial assistance to veterans at all, while remaining on nearly every veteran emergency assistance list in circulation. Each of those took one visit to the organization's own website to establish. If a list you are using includes any of them as current, stop using the list.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: Run the Benefits.gov Benefit Finder — twice, and once per adult
items.org: Benefits.gov (interagency, led by the U.S. Department of Labor)
items.who: Anyone who wants to know which federal programs they might qualify for without applying to find out.
items.value: A free, official eligibility questionnaire covering roughly a thousand federal and state-administered benefit programs across housing, food, health care, education, disaster relief, and veteran benefits. It is the tool that the paid 'we'll find your government grants' industry pretends to be, and ACF itself points people here when a program ends.
items.how: Use the Benefit Finder at benefits.gov. Answer honestly about income, household, disability and veteran status. It returns programs you may qualify for with links to the administering agency. It does not apply for you and it never asks for payment.
items.hack: Run it twice — once with your current situation and once with the situation you expect in three months if nothing changes. Benefit eligibility is a cliff function, and knowing that a drop in income or an approved disability rating will open four new programs lets you have the paperwork assembled in advance. Also run it for each adult in the household separately; a spouse or adult child may qualify for programs you do not, and household-level screening hides that.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: Vet any charity in four minutes with its Form 990
items.org: ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer; Candid; IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search
items.who: Anyone about to give an organization their DD-214, financial records, or hope.
items.value: A free, fast, and nearly unbeatable due diligence method. Every US 501(c)(3) above a minimal size must file an IRS Form 990 annually, and those filings are public. They tell you whether the organization actually exists, how much it took in, how much it spent on program services versus fundraising and executive compensation, whether it filed at all in the most recent year, and whether its exempt status has been automatically revoked.
items.how: Search the organization at projects.propublica.org/nonprofits. Check four things: is there a filing for the most recent two years; what share of total expenses went to program services; is the organization's stated program in the 990 the same program the website advertises; and is there a revocation notice. Cross-check exempt status on the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search.
items.hack: The single most diagnostic figure is the gap between a charity's fundraising spend and its program spend. An organization raising millions and granting a few hundred thousand to veterans is not necessarily fraudulent, but it is not the organization its marketing describes, and your application is competing for a much smaller pot than the public numbers suggest. The second-most diagnostic signal is a missing recent filing — an organization that has not filed in two years is usually not operating, whatever its website says. This test is how you would have caught both the StreetShares Foundation and the Second Service Foundation without reading a word of news.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: Your state's Assistive Technology Act program — free device loans and refurbished equipment
items.org: Administration for Community Living, state Assistive Technology Act programs
items.who: People with disabilities of any age, including veterans, in every state and territory. There is no veteran-specific gate, and usually no income test for the device loan and reuse services.
items.value: Every state and territory has a federally funded AT Act program, and almost no veteran has heard of it. Core services typically include a short-term device loan library — try the equipment before anyone buys it; device reutilization, meaning refurbished equipment redistributed free or at very low cost; device demonstration; and in many states an alternative financing program offering low-interest loans for equipment. For a veteran whose VA equipment request was denied, this is the parallel system.
items.how: Find your state program through the ACL assistive technology pages at acl.gov or the CATADA state directory at catada.info/state.html. Call and ask specifically about the device loan library and the reuse or exchange program.
items.hack: Use the device loan library BEFORE you ask VA, a charity, or your insurer to buy anything. Borrowing the equipment for a few weeks does two things: it tells you whether this particular device actually solves your problem, and it gives your clinician documented functional evidence to write into the justification. A prosthetics or DME request supported by 'patient trialed this device for four weeks with documented improvement in transfers' is approved at a much higher rate than a request based on a catalog page. The reuse program is the other sleeper — refurbished wheelchairs, ramps, lifts and shower chairs are often available free within days, which no grant can match.
items.deadline: Rolling; no application window.

items.title: Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services waivers — the home modification money outside VA
items.org: State Medicaid agencies, under Section 1915(c) and related authorities
items.who: People who meet their state's Medicaid financial and functional eligibility for long-term services and supports. Many veterans are dually eligible for VA care and Medicaid and never apply for the second.
items.value: Many state HCBS waivers cover environmental modifications — ramps, grab bars, bathroom modification, doorway widening, stair lifts — plus personal care attendants, respite for caregivers, and in some states vehicle modification. Covered services and dollar caps are set state by state and change with each waiver renewal, so there is no national figure; your state's waiver document is the authority.
items.how: Contact your state Medicaid agency or your Area Agency on Aging and ask for a long-term services and supports assessment. Ask by name whether the waiver covers environmental modifications and what the per-person cap is.
items.hack: The stacking move: use VA's HISA grant and a Medicaid HCBS waiver on the same house for different work. HISA has a lifetime cap and is prescription-driven through VA health care; the waiver has its own cap and its own assessment. A veteran who exhausts HISA on a bathroom can often get the ramp and the doorway through the waiver, or vice versa. Ask both the VA HISA coordinator and the Medicaid case manager explicitly whether using one affects the other — in most cases it does not, and nobody volunteers that because the two systems do not talk to each other.
items.deadline: Rolling; many waivers maintain waiting lists, so apply before you need it.

items.title: Area Agencies on Aging — Older Americans Act money for home repair and caregiver relief
items.org: Area Agencies on Aging, under the Older Americans Act
items.who: Adults aged 60 and over, and their family caregivers, regardless of veteran status. Some services have no income test at all.
items.value: Older Americans Act funding reaches every county through an Area Agency on Aging and typically supports minor home modification and repair, home-delivered and congregate meals, transportation, in-home personal care, legal assistance, and — under the National Family Caregiver Support Program — respite care and supplemental services for family caregivers. Amounts are small per household and set locally; the value is speed, breadth, and the absence of a competitive application.
items.how: Find your Area Agency on Aging through the Eldercare Locator at eldercare.acl.gov or 1-800-677-1116.
items.hack: The caregiver side is the most underused benefit in this entire directory. If you are caring for an aging veteran — or you are an aging veteran with a spouse caring for you — the National Family Caregiver Support Program can fund respite hours, and respite is what keeps a home placement from collapsing into a nursing home admission. Ask for it by name. Also ask about the minor home modification and repair line, which is usually a few hundred to a few thousand dollars, requires no competitive application, and can install the grab bars and ramp while a VA HISA request is still in process.
items.deadline: Rolling; funding is annual and exhaustible.

items.title: State vocational rehabilitation — a second, non-VA system that buys equipment and training
items.org: State vocational rehabilitation agencies, under the Rehabilitation Act
items.who: People with a disability that is a substantial impediment to employment, who can benefit from services to get or keep a job. This is the STATE VR agency, entirely separate from VA's Veteran Readiness and Employment (Chapter 31) program.
items.value: Depending on the state and your approved Individualized Plan for Employment: vocational assessment, training and tuition, assistive technology and equipment, vehicle modification, job placement, and in some states self-employment and small business start-up support. Veterans frequently assume VR&E is their only option and never open a second file.
items.how: Contact your state vocational rehabilitation agency directly. Eligibility is determined on the disability-and-employment test, not on service connection, so a veteran with a non-service-connected disability qualifies here even where VR&E does not.
items.hack: Run state VR and VA VR&E in parallel rather than choosing. They are separately funded, have separately negotiated plans, and coordinate services rather than offsetting each other — one may fund a degree while the other funds the adaptive equipment or the business plan. Ask each counselor to coordinate with the other in writing and keep both plans on file. Also ask the state agency specifically about its self-employment or supported self-employment track; several states will fund equipment and start-up costs for a disabled person's business under an approved plan, which is closer to a genuine business grant than most things carrying that label.
items.deadline: Rolling; eligibility determination has statutory timelines.

items.title: WIOA and Dislocated Worker funds — free retraining at the American Job Center
items.org: U.S. Department of Labor, through state and local workforce boards and American Job Centers
items.who: Adults, dislocated workers, and — under a statutory priority — veterans and eligible spouses, who receive priority of service in all DOL-funded employment and training programs.
items.value: Individual Training Accounts that pay tuition for approved occupational training at community colleges and private providers, plus supportive services that can include transportation, tools, licensing fees and childcare while training. Amounts are set by local workforce boards. Separately, every American Job Center has a Disabled Veterans' Outreach Program specialist and a Local Veterans' Employment Representative funded specifically to serve veterans.
items.how: Find your American Job Center at careeronestop.org. Ask for the veteran representative by name and ask about an Individual Training Account and the state's Eligible Training Provider List.
items.hack: Priority of service is a statutory right, not a courtesy — veterans and eligible spouses must be served before non-veterans in DOL-funded programs. Say the words 'I am requesting veterans priority of service' at intake and it changes your position in the queue. Second: use a WIOA Individual Training Account for a short occupational credential and SAVE your GI Bill for the degree. Veterans burn GI Bill months on a twelve-week certificate that the workforce board would have funded for free, which is among the most expensive avoidable mistakes in this whole directory.
items.deadline: Rolling; local funds are annual and exhaustible.

items.title: FEMA Individual Assistance — the one federal grant that does go to individuals
items.who: Households in a county covered by a Presidential major disaster declaration that includes Individual Assistance. Citizenship or qualified-noncitizen status required for the applicant household.
items.value: A genuine individual-facing federal grant, which makes it the exception to the rule that federal grants go to organizations. Assistance can include Housing Assistance for repair, replacement, rental assistance and lodging reimbursement, and Other Needs Assistance for personal property, medical and dental costs, childcare, moving and storage, and funeral expenses. Maximum award amounts are set annually and adjusted for inflation — take the current figure from FEMA, not from an article.
items.how: Apply at disasterassistance.gov, through the FEMA app, or at 1-800-621-3362, within the application period for your declaration. Register even if you have insurance — FEMA covers uninsured and underinsured losses, and you cannot be considered for the gap without a file.
items.hack: Three things that decide FEMA outcomes. First, apply before you have your insurance settlement, because the FEMA deadline will not wait for your adjuster and FEMA can reconsider once the settlement arrives. Second, document everything with dated photographs before you clean up, because an undocumented loss is an unfunded loss. Third, a FEMA denial is very often an administrative problem — missing insurance documentation, an unverified occupancy, an unreachable phone number — and the appeal, filed in writing within the stated period, has a meaningful success rate. Most people treat a FEMA denial as final. It is not.
items.deadline: Set by each disaster declaration; typically a limited window from the declaration date.

items.title: Individual Development Accounts — matched savings, often two or more to one
items.org: Community action agencies, community development financial institutions, and nonprofit sponsors
items.who: Low- and moderate-income households, by program rules. Many programs are open to anyone meeting the income test; some are veteran- or disability-specific.
items.value: A matched savings program: you save toward a defined goal — usually a home purchase, post-secondary education, a vehicle for work, or small business capitalization — and the sponsor matches your deposits, commonly at one-to-one up to several-to-one, within a cap. Match rates, caps and allowable uses are entirely program-specific. Financial education is usually required and is the point as much as the match.
items.how: Ask your community action agency, your local CDFI, and your community foundation whether anyone in the area operates an IDA or matched savings program. There is no national application.
items.hack: This is the highest-return program in this directory for anyone with even small savings capacity, and almost nobody uses it, because it requires patience rather than urgency. A two-to-one match turns $1,000 of your own money into $3,000 toward a down payment or business equipment. If you are not currently in crisis, this is where to put attention — and because match funds are allocated per enrollee, programs often have capacity precisely because the application requires a savings commitment rather than a hardship story. Ask whether VA disability compensation counts as qualifying earned income for the program, since rules differ and that single answer determines eligibility for many veterans.
items.deadline: Enrollment windows vary; savings periods typically run one to three years.

items.title: How to read a NOFO — the five sections that decide whether you win
items.who: Anyone writing a federal grant application for an organization.
items.value: A Notice of Funding Opportunity is a scored rubric wearing the costume of a document, and most losing applications lose on readable, mechanical grounds. Reading it correctly is worth more than writing well.
items.how: Read five sections before anything else, in this order. One, Eligibility — is your entity type listed, verbatim; if not, stop. Two, Award Information — the ceiling, floor, expected number of awards, project period, and whether cost sharing is required; a required match you cannot document disqualifies you. Three, Application Review Information — the scoring criteria and the points assigned to each; this is the rubric and your narrative should be organized in its order, using its words. Four, Application and Submission Information — page limits, formatting, required forms, attachment rules, and the exact submission deadline including time zone. Five, Agency Contacts — the program officer you should email with questions.
items.hack: Write your narrative with headings that match the scoring criteria exactly, in the NOFO's order, and name the point values in your outline. Reviewers score against the rubric with the rubric in front of them, and a narrative organized in its sequence lets them find and award every point. A beautifully written narrative organized the way you think about your program forces the reviewer to hunt, and unhunted points are unawarded points. Second rule: formatting non-compliance is a non-responsiveness screen before scoring ever happens. A single page over the limit can end your application without a reviewer reading a word.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: Free grant-writing help exists — four places, none of which take a cut
items.org: Public libraries with Candid access; state nonprofit associations; SCORE; community foundations
items.who: Veteran-serving nonprofits and veteran business owners who need an application written and cannot pay for it.
items.value: Four free or near-free channels. Many public libraries hold a Candid Foundation Directory subscription that is free to use on-site — a searchable database of private foundation grants that otherwise costs hundreds of dollars a year. State nonprofit associations run low-cost capacity-building training and often maintain grant-opportunity bulletins. SCORE provides free mentoring from retired executives, including people who have administered grants. Community foundation program officers will read a draft and tell you candidly whether it fits a fund they manage.
items.how: Call your main public library and ask whether they have Foundation Directory or Candid access for patrons. Find your state nonprofit association. Request a SCORE mentor at score.org. Call the community foundation serving your county and ask for a program officer conversation.
items.hack: Ask the community foundation program officer one specific question: 'Which of the funds you administer would you encourage us to apply to, and which would you discourage?' Program officers cannot promise an award but they will reliably steer you away from a bad fit, and avoiding four wrong applications is worth more than writing one good one. On the paid side, the rule is simple: grant writers may charge hourly or by project; a writer taking a percentage of the award is a red flag, and contingency fees are not an allowable cost under federal grant rules.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: 'Veteran' in a program's name tells you nothing about whether you are eligible
items.who: Everyone searching for veteran-specific help.
items.value: A filter that cuts both ways and costs people real money in both directions. Programs with 'veteran' in the title are frequently restricted in ways the name hides — to post-9/11 service only, to combat-wounded only, to a specific branch, to those with minor children, to active duty rather than separated veterans. The clearest live example in this directory: Operation First Response, whose name and reputation say veterans, no longer provides emergency financial assistance to veterans. Meanwhile some of the largest sources of help have no veteran branding at all: USDA Section 504, LIHEAP, weatherization, state Assistive Technology programs, Medicaid HCBS waivers, Older Americans Act services, WIOA training, Pell and FSEOG.
items.how: For every program, read the eligibility paragraph rather than the title, and look for four hidden gates: service era, discharge characterization, combat or wounded status, and household composition. For every need, search the generic version of your problem as well as the veteran version — 'home repair grant low income county' alongside 'veteran home repair grant.'
items.hack: The practical consequence: the best-value programs for most veterans are income-based and disability-based rather than veteran-based, because the veteran-branded pots are small, heavily advertised and oversubscribed, while the income-based pots are enormous, unadvertised and administered by an office in your own county. Run both searches every time. And when a veteran program turns you down on an era, discharge or injury gate, that is not a statement about your need — it is a statement about that program's funding restrictions, and the generic program next door may have no such gate.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: A charity's 'no' is usually about this month's budget — reapply correctly
items.who: Anyone denied by a veteran charity, relief society or local fund.
items.value: Charitable denials come from four distinct causes, and only one of them is permanent. Permanent: you fall outside a hard eligibility gate — wrong era, wrong discharge, no minor children, no service connection. Not permanent: the fund was exhausted for the period; your file was incomplete; or the need as described did not look like a bridge to stability. Three of four causes are fixable, and most people treat every denial as the first.
items.how: Ask the denying organization one question: 'Was this a question of eligibility, of available funds, or of the application itself?' The answer determines your next move. Eligibility — go elsewhere. Funds exhausted — ask when the next funding period opens and whether you can be put on a list. Application — ask what documentation would have changed the outcome, supply it, and resubmit.
items.hack: Most relief organizations run on a fiscal or program year and many limit assistance to once per household per period. So the second-best question after a denial is 'when does your assistance period reset?' A denial in September from an organization whose year turns over in October is a two-week delay, not a refusal. And if the cause was the application itself, the fix is almost always the fourth element of a good hardship letter: a specific, documented reason the situation stabilizes after this payment. Rewrite for that and resubmit rather than starting over somewhere new.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: SBA put $4.9M into new VBOCs in September 2026 — three states just got coverage
items.org: U.S. Small Business Administration, Office of Veterans Business Development
items.who: Veteran and military-connected entrepreneurs in Alaska, Florida and Louisiana especially, and anyone who was told there was no VBOC near them.
items.value: Verified current funding news rather than a static program description. On 25 September 2026 SBA announced nearly $4.9 million in grant awards over five years to stand up new Veterans Business Outreach Centers, with satellite offices planned: $400,000 to the State of Alaska Office of Veterans Affairs, $400,000 to Veterans Florida, and $175,000 to The Boot in Louisiana. VBOC services are provided at no cost to veterans, active-duty service members, National Guard and Reserve members, military spouses and eligible family members.
items.how: Search your ZIP at SBA's VBOC page. If you previously found no center in range, check again — the network changed in late 2026 and satellite offices are being added under these awards.
items.hack: New centers are the best time to approach one. A VBOC standing up under a fresh five-year cooperative agreement has performance targets to hit, staff with open calendars, and funding certainty for years — which means more counselor time per client than a long-established center operating at capacity. If you are in Alaska, Florida or Louisiana, get in the door in the first year. Note also where two of these awards went: a state veterans affairs office and a state-level veteran organization, which means in those states your VBOC and your state veteran benefits office are now the same conversation.
items.deadline: N/A; ongoing counseling.

items.title: The VetCert self-certification sunset dates — and why old guidance is dangerous
items.who: Any veteran-owned firm that has ever self-certified as an SDVOSB in SAM.gov.
items.value: The specific dates, because guidance written before them is actively misleading. SBA's direct final rule eliminating SDVOSB self-certification took effect 5 August 2024. A firm that had filed an SDVOSB certification application with SBA by 22 December 2024 could continue to self-certify for federal contracts and subcontracts until SBA made a final decision on its application. After that, self-certification is no longer permitted. SBA administers certification under Section 36 of the Small Business Act; there is no fee.
items.how: Check your SAM.gov representations today. If they still assert SDVOSB status without an SBA VetCert approval, correct them and file at veterans.certify.sba.gov. Your free help is a VBOC counselor or a local APEX Accelerator.
items.hack: The risk is not just lost opportunity, it is exposure. Representing SDVOSB status you no longer hold in a SAM.gov profile that an agency relies on for a set-aside award is a false certification problem, not a paperwork problem — and the set-aside protest mechanism means a competitor has both the motive and the means to raise it. Fix the representation first, then file. And when you read any SDVOSB guidance, check its date: anything written before August 2024 describes a world that no longer exists, and a surprising amount of currently published advice does.
items.deadline: Self-certification ended; certification is a prerequisite, not a cycle.

items.title: Corporate supplier diversity — the veteran-business channel that is not a grant and not federal
items.org: Large corporations with supplier diversity programs; NaVOBA
items.who: Veteran-owned and service-disabled veteran-owned businesses with a product or service a large company buys.
items.value: A revenue channel rather than an award. Many large corporations maintain supplier diversity programs with veteran-owned business categories and internal spend targets, and several certify veteran-owned suppliers through third parties such as NaVOBA's Certified Veteran's Business Enterprise program. The money here is contractual and recurring, which makes it structurally better than any one-time grant, and the competition is far thinner than for federal set-asides because most veteran firms never register.
items.how: Identify the ten largest companies that buy what you sell, find each one's supplier diversity or supplier registration portal, and register. Then find the supplier diversity manager by name and send a one-page capability statement with a specific, narrow ask. Consider third-party veteran-business certification if your target customers require it — verify what your actual buyers accept before paying for any certification.
items.hack: Register, then go to the events. Supplier diversity managers attend a small number of conferences a year — including IVMF's Veteran EDGE and NaVOBA events — specifically to meet certified diverse suppliers, because meeting their targets requires finding firms that exist. A fifteen-minute conversation at one of those events accomplishes what a year of portal registrations does not. And be precise about what you want: supplier diversity managers cannot buy anything, they can only introduce you to the category buyer who can. Ask for the introduction, not the contract.
items.deadline: N/A; rolling registration.

items.title: The LIHEAP crisis component and the equipment line — two parts nobody asks for by name
items.org: HHS Administration for Children and Families, through states and tribes
items.who: Low-income households facing a shutoff, out of fuel, or with a broken heating or cooling system. Income limits are set by each state, territory and tribe.
items.value: LIHEAP is not one benefit, it is several, and the fast ones are not the default. Beyond the regular bill-payment benefit, ACF describes LIHEAP as covering the prevention of energy shutoffs, reconnecting service, and repairing or replacing heating equipment. The crisis component carries its own expedited decision clock — many states must act within a short statutory window where there is a life-threatening situation. Benefit amounts vary entirely by state. ACF is explicit that LIHEAP does not charge a fee for receiving a benefit, and that benefits are generally paid to the utility rather than as a direct grant to the household.
items.how: energyhelp.us, or the National Energy Assistance Referral hotline at 1-866-674-6327, weekdays 9am to 7pm Eastern, available in English, Spanish, Traditional Chinese and Simplified Chinese. State the specific situation — shutoff notice, no fuel, broken furnace — rather than asking for help with a bill.
items.hack: Say three words at intake: 'crisis,' 'shutoff notice,' and if applicable 'no heat.' The regular benefit sits in a queue for weeks; the crisis component has a clock. Then ask separately about the heating equipment repair and replacement line — a household can get a failed furnace replaced through LIHEAP in several states, and almost nobody asks because the program is universally described as bill assistance. Finally, ask the intake worker to screen you for weatherization in the same appointment, since LIHEAP receipt usually confers categorical eligibility and the same office often runs both.
items.deadline: Varies by state; many states exhaust funds before the stated program end date.

items.title: VFW financial assistance now reads as a service-member program — check before you count on it
items.who: Read the current page, not the old name. VFW's financial assistance program is presented as serving ACTIVE-DUTY service members, including activated Guard and Reserve members, and their families, facing unexpected financial difficulty from deployment or other military-related activity or injury.
items.value: Up to $2,500, paid directly to the creditor, as a grant with no repayment and no VFW membership requirement. The significant point for anyone using an older list: the broad 'Unmet Needs' framing that many directories still use — describing this as open to veterans generally — does not match how the program is currently presented. If you are a separated veteran, verify your eligibility with VFW before investing the effort.
items.how: Apply through vfw.org/assistance/financial-grants, or contact 1-866-789-6333 or financialassistance@vfw.org. Review the formal eligibility document linked from the program page before applying.
items.hack: Because the grant is paid to the creditor rather than to you, build the disbursement information into the application at submission: the creditor's legal name, the account number, the exact amount, the remittance address or payment portal, and the date adverse action occurs. Applications in creditor-paid programs stall at disbursement more often than at decision. And if you are a separated veteran who finds you are outside this program, redirect to your branch relief society, your state veteran fund through a CVSO, and the national charities that do serve separated veterans — the $2,500 exists elsewhere.
items.deadline: Rolling; accepting applications.

items.title: Air & Space Forces Aid Society — the rebrand, the Guardians, and the $2,500 spouse line
items.org: Air & Space Forces Aid Society (formerly Air Force Aid Society)
items.who: Active-Duty, Active Guard Reserve, Title 10 and Title 32 Guard and Reserve, and RETIRED Airmen and Guardians, plus their families. Space Force Guardians are explicitly covered.
items.value: The name change matters because old bookmarks and old search terms fail. Current programs include no-interest loans and grants for emergencies; the General Henry H. Arnold Education Grant; AFAS Merit and Grit Scholarships; a CSU scholarship; supplemental education loans; a free self-paced GED program for spouses and dependents; the 'Bee' Arnold Spouse Tuition Program; Bundles for Babies; a car seat program providing a $200 monetary gift for E1 through E5; childcare assistance; and spouse job training support of up to $2,500 for certifications or degrees. The Society reported $11.6 million in total support across more than 12,600 individual assists in 2025.
items.how: Apply through portal.afas.org or call 703-972-2650.
items.hack: The two things people leave on the table. First, retirees are eligible — a large share of retired Air Force and Space Force families believe the Society serves only the active force and never apply, for either the emergency or the education side. Second, the $2,500 spouse certification support is the best effort-to-dollar ratio in the catalog: it funds the specific credential that keeps a military spouse employable through a PCS, it is not a competitive essay scholarship, and it is approved far more often than it is requested. Ask for it by name alongside whatever else you are applying for.
items.deadline: Annual cycles for education grants; rolling for emergency, spouse and community programs.

items.title: CGMA covers Coast Guard civilians and Auxiliarists — almost nobody knows it
items.who: An unusually wide eligible population: active duty, Reserve and AUXILIARY members, retirees, CIVILIAN EMPLOYEES, Public Health Service officers and chaplains serving the Coast Guard, and SURVIVING SPOUSES.
items.value: Interest-free loans, grants, financial counseling and referrals, organized in three categories — Emergencies, Day-to-Day, and Education. CGMA reports more than $260 million distributed to the Coast Guard community since its founding. Individual amounts are set case by case and are not published; ask your representative.
items.how: Start with a local CGMA representative — there are more than 600 of them — rather than a central portal. Toll-free 800-881-2462, or 703-875-0404.
items.hack: The eligibility breadth is the whole story and it is close to unique among the relief societies. Coast Guard civilian employees and Auxiliary volunteers have access to a service relief society, and most have no idea. So do surviving spouses, who typically assume eligibility ended with the member. If you are in any of those three groups, make the call. And because the entry point is a human representative rather than a form, the representative can tell you in one conversation which of the three categories fits your situation — which is how people get an answer in days instead of applying to the wrong program and waiting weeks.
items.deadline: Rolling, through local representatives.

items.title: There is no application for VA equipment — there is a consult, and a therapist writes it
items.org: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, Prosthetic and Sensory Aids Service
items.who: Veterans enrolled in VA health care. Items may be provided for service-connected and, in many cases, non-service-connected conditions when clinically indicated.
items.value: The mechanism, which is the part that determines outcomes. VA's prosthetics benefit is far broader than the word suggests — artificial limbs, wheelchairs and power mobility, orthotics and braces, home medical equipment, environmental control units, computer and communication assistive technology, and the hardware side of the service dog benefit. But there is no form to submit and no dollar cap to apply against. There is a clinical consult, and whether you get the item depends almost entirely on who writes it and how.
items.how: Ask your VA provider for a prosthetics consult naming the specific item and the clinical reason. Better: ask for a referral to physical therapy, occupational therapy or audiology first, and let that specialist evaluate you and write the recommendation.
items.hack: A PT or OT functional assessment is the evidence standard the Prosthetics service actually applies; a veteran's verbal request is not. So the sequence that works is: therapy referral, documented functional evaluation, therapist's recommendation, prosthetics consult. If you can borrow the device first from your state Assistive Technology Act program's loan library, the therapist can document a trial with measured improvement, which is close to unrefusable. And if the item is denied anyway, get the denial in writing — it is both the basis for a stronger second consult and the single document every equipment charity in this directory wants to see.
items.deadline: No deadline; consult-driven.

items.title: Short-term Pell for workforce credentials — ask your school whether it applies to you
items.org: U.S. Department of Education, Federal Student Aid
items.who: Students in short-term occupational and certificate programs that have historically been too short to qualify for Pell.
items.value: The long-standing limitation was that Pell required a program of a minimum length and credit structure, which excluded most short occupational credentials — exactly the programs that get people employed fastest. Expansion of Pell to shorter workforce programs has been enacted and is being implemented, with eligibility turning on program length, institutional and state approval, and outcome requirements. Do not assume your specific program qualifies: the implementation details and the list of approved programs are what matter, and they are school- and state-specific.
items.how: File the FAFSA, then ask your school's financial aid office one precise question: is this specific program Pell-eligible for the award year I am enrolling in, and if not, why not. Get the answer in writing before you enroll and pay.
items.hack: If the answer is no, do not pay out of pocket yet — take the same program to your local American Job Center and ask whether it is on the state's Eligible Training Provider List, because a WIOA Individual Training Account can fund a short credential that Pell will not, and veterans have statutory priority of service in that system. Between short-term Pell, WIOA, state VR, and VA VR&E, most occupational credentials can be funded by someone; the error is paying for it yourself or burning GI Bill months on a twelve-week certificate.
items.deadline: FAFSA cycle; program eligibility determined by school and state.

items.title: USDA Farm Service Agency — veterans get a target-funded lane in farm lending
items.org: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Farm Service Agency
items.who: Veterans and beginning farmers and ranchers. USDA designates 'veteran farmers or ranchers' as a category and reserves a portion of certain farm loan funds for beginning farmers, with veteran status carrying advantages in several programs.
items.value: Be precise about the instrument: these are predominantly LOANS — direct and guaranteed farm ownership and operating loans, microloans for small-scale operations, and down payment loan assistance for beginning farmers — not grants. What makes the veteran designation valuable is targeted funding reservations, reduced down payment requirements in the beginning farmer down payment program, and in some programs a higher cost-share rate on conservation practices. Current loan limits, interest rates and cost-share percentages change annually; take them from FSA.
items.how: Contact your local USDA Service Center — FSA and NRCS staff sit in the same office. Ask specifically to be coded as a veteran farmer or rancher in your records, because that designation is what triggers the targeting.
items.hack: The conservation side is where the actual grant-like money is. NRCS cost-share programs such as EQIP pay a percentage of the cost of practices — fencing, water systems, high tunnels, irrigation efficiency — and historically apply an elevated payment rate for beginning, limited-resource, socially disadvantaged and VETERAN producers. That is money you do not repay, for infrastructure you were going to buy anyway. Ask the NRCS conservationist in the same office about EQIP and about the veteran payment rate by name, in the same visit as the FSA loan conversation. Veterans go in asking about a farm loan and never cross the hall.
items.deadline: Loans rolling; conservation program sign-up periods are announced annually by state.

items.title: Elks, Rotary, Masonic and Knights of Columbus — local money, no national application
items.org: Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks; Rotary International clubs; Masonic lodges and Shriners; Knights of Columbus councils; Moose, Eagles and similar
items.who: Varies entirely by local club or lodge. Most have broad discretion and many have explicit veteran service commitments.
items.value: Small discretionary grants — commonly $100 to $2,500 — for a specific, concrete need: a ramp, a wheelchair, eyeglasses, hearing aids, a utility bill, car repair, a child's school expenses, a medical travel cost. Elks lodges in particular run substantial national veterans service programming delivered locally. There is no national application form, no published amount, and no deadline, which is why these organizations appear on no grant list and why their money sits unclaimed.
items.how: Find the clubs and lodges in your town and call the secretary or the veterans service chair. Ask one question: 'Does the lodge have a fund that could help a veteran with a specific need, and how would I make that request?' Be prepared to attend a meeting and ask in person — many clubs decide by vote at a monthly meeting.
items.hack: Bring the quote, not the story. Service clubs vote on concrete, bounded requests: a $600 contractor estimate for a ramp gets funded at a meeting; 'I need help' does not. And ask the local VFW or American Legion post to make the introduction — posts and lodges in the same town know each other, and a request that arrives through a known member is treated differently from a cold call. This is the clearest expression of the rule that five small local funds beat one famous national one: four lodges at $500 each, decided at this month's meetings, beats a national grant you will not hear about until spring.
items.deadline: N/A; most clubs decide at monthly meetings.

items.title: Patient assistance programs — free brand-name medication from the manufacturer
items.org: Pharmaceutical manufacturers; NeedyMeds; RxAssist; the Partnership for Prescription Assistance successors
items.who: Uninsured and underinsured patients, with income limits typically set well above the poverty line — often several times it — which means many working households and many veterans on fixed incomes qualify.
items.value: Manufacturer patient assistance programs provide brand-name medications free or at nominal cost to qualifying patients. Separately, manufacturer copay cards reduce out-of-pocket cost for the commercially insured, and nonprofit copay foundations cover copays for specific diagnoses. These are not grants in the usual sense but they are free money in the form of a drug you otherwise could not afford, and they are substantially underused.
items.how: Search the medication at needymeds.org or rxassist.org to find the manufacturer's program and its application. Most require a prescriber's signature, so bring the form to your appointment. Your hospital or clinic social worker or a pharmacy technician often handles these routinely and will do it for you.
items.hack: For veterans, run this in parallel with VA pharmacy rather than instead of it. VA pharmacy copays are low and often zero for service-connected conditions, which usually makes VA the better channel — but VA formulary restrictions mean the specific brand your specialist wants may require a non-formulary request that gets denied. That is the moment to use a manufacturer program: you get the exact drug, free, while the formulary question is unresolved. Ask the VA pharmacist directly whether a non-formulary request is worth filing and what the manufacturer program for that drug is; pharmacists know both answers and are rarely asked.
items.deadline: Rolling; most programs require annual re-enrollment.

items.title: Child care subsidy — the benefit that makes every other plan possible
items.org: State child care assistance programs under the Child Care and Development Fund; Child Care Aware of America for military families
items.who: Working, job-searching or in-training families under state income limits. Several states give priority to families in approved training programs, to families with a child with a disability, and in some cases to military families.
items.value: Payment of a substantial share of child care cost directly to a licensed provider, which converts an unaffordable job or training program into a viable one. Amounts, copays and income limits are set state by state. Separately, Child Care Aware of America administers military fee assistance programs for eligible service members and, for some programs, recently separated or wounded veterans — verify current eligibility, because the military programs have specific and changing criteria.
items.how: Apply through your state child care assistance agency; find it through childcare.gov. Military and veteran families should also check childcareaware.org for fee assistance program eligibility.
items.hack: The sequencing point that people miss: apply for child care subsidy BEFORE you enroll in training or accept the job, not after. Waiting lists are common, approval takes weeks, and a training program that starts before your subsidy is approved is a program you drop out of. Also note that several eligible-expense lists in this directory — the Nebraska Veterans Aid Fund among them — explicitly include DAYCARE, and SSVF temporary financial assistance can cover child care. So if the state subsidy has a waiting list, the veteran-specific funds can bridge it, which is a combination almost nobody assembles.
items.deadline: Rolling with waiting lists; apply before you need care.

items.title: Indirect costs and the de minimis rate — the line small nonprofits leave blank and regret
items.org: Directory guidance, under the Uniform Guidance at 2 CFR Part 200
items.who: Any organization applying for a federal grant, especially a first-time applicant.
items.value: Real money, routinely forfeited. Indirect costs — rent, utilities, accounting, insurance, executive time, IT — are legitimately chargeable to federal awards, either through a federally negotiated indirect cost rate agreement or by electing the de minimis rate available under the Uniform Guidance to organizations without a negotiated rate. The de minimis percentage was revised in the 2024 Uniform Guidance update; confirm the current rate at 2 CFR Part 200 before you build a budget. An organization that budgets only direct costs delivers the program out of its own unrestricted funds, which is how grant-funded nonprofits go broke while winning awards.
items.how: Decide before you write the budget whether you will negotiate a rate with your cognizant federal agency or elect the de minimis rate. Elect it explicitly in the budget narrative, show the base you are applying it to, and keep the documentation. Your free help is your state nonprofit association or a CPA with single-audit experience.
items.hack: Elect the de minimis rate on your first award rather than attempting a negotiated rate. Negotiating a rate requires a cost allocation study, takes months, and is worth it only once your federal portfolio is large. The de minimis election takes one paragraph. Second point: some programs cap or disallow indirect costs by statute — read the NOFO, and if indirect is capped below your real overhead, factor that into whether the grant is worth winning. A $200,000 grant that forbids indirect recovery can cost a small organization money.
items.deadline: N/A; decide before budget submission.

items.title: Crowdfunding versus grants — what each is actually good for
items.who: Anyone deciding whether to launch a fundraiser instead of applying for assistance.
items.value: An honest comparison, because crowdfunding is usually chosen for the wrong reasons. Crowdfunding is fast, has no eligibility criteria, and can raise an unbounded amount — but it depends entirely on the size and wealth of your existing network, platform and payment fees take a cut, funds may be reportable depending on structure and characterization, and a public campaign permanently publishes your financial and often medical circumstances. Grants and charitable assistance are slower and gated, but do not depend on who you know, do not expose you publicly, and come without fees.
items.how: Use crowdfunding for what grants cannot cover: travel to a distant specialist, a deductible, a funeral, a time-critical gap of days. Use grants and charitable assistance for recurring and structural costs: rent, utilities, home modification, equipment, tuition. Run both, with the crowdfunding target set to the gap the grants will not close.
items.hack: If you do crowdfund, have one other person run it. Campaigns run by a friend, a post commander, or a unit buddy raise materially more than campaigns run by the beneficiary, because third-party narration is more credible and shareable than self-advocacy — and because the beneficiary is usually in no condition to post updates, which is what sustains a campaign. Also ask about the tax and benefits treatment before you raise a large sum: a lump of cash in a bank account can affect eligibility for income-tested programs like Medicaid, SSI and some housing assistance, and people have lost more in benefits than they raised. That question goes to a benefits counselor, not to the platform.
items.deadline: N/A.

items.title: Build one page: the annual grant calendar for your own situation
items.who: Anyone who will be dealing with this for more than one year — which is most people.
items.value: The structural fix for the single most common failure in this directory, which is finding the right program two weeks after it closed. Most of these programs are annual and most of their dates are stable, so one page built once converts a scramble into a routine.
items.how: Write down every recurring date that applies to you. Verified examples from this directory: 1 October, VA SAH, SHA and TRA maximums re-index for the new fiscal year. 1 November to 1 March, MOAA Ed Assist application window. 1 July, Veterans Cemetery Grants Program priority-list deadline. Late March to mid-June, the VA Adaptive Sports NOFO window in the FY2026 cycle. 30 September, federal fiscal year end, when agencies spend remaining contract dollars. Autumn, LIHEAP heating applications open in most states and funds are often exhausted well before the stated end date. FAFSA cycle opening, plus your state's earlier deadline. Then add your own: your utility's shutoff moratorium dates, your local community foundation's grant rounds, your post's and lodge's meeting schedule.
items.hack: Put a sixty-day lead reminder on every date, not a reminder on the date itself — every one of these requires preparation you cannot do in the final week, whether that is a SAM.gov registration, a therapist's evaluation, a contractor's estimate, or a transcript. And review the calendar once a year against primary sources, because dates do move: the Adaptive Sports NOFO window and the SSG Fox cycle have both shifted between years. One annual hour of maintenance is the difference between using this directory and reading it.
items.deadline: N/A — build it now.

items.title: Before you accept a large award, check the benefits cliff
items.who: Anyone receiving an income-tested benefit — SSI, Medicaid, SNAP, housing assistance, VA Pension — who is about to receive a lump sum.
items.value: Protection against the most painful outcome in this entire directory: winning money and losing more than you won. Several of the benefits that veterans and low-income households rely on are means-tested on income AND on countable resources. A lump-sum grant, a crowdfunding payout, or a retroactive award sitting in a bank account can push you over a resource limit and suspend SSI, Medicaid, SNAP, or VA Pension — and Medicaid loss in particular can cost far more than any grant is worth. Note the distinction: VA disability COMPENSATION is not means-tested; VA PENSION is.
items.how: Before accepting a large sum, ask a benefits counselor three questions: is this payment counted as income, as a resource, or neither, in each program I receive; is there an exclusion period during which it does not count; and is there a lawful way to hold or spend it that preserves eligibility. Free counsel: your CVSO, a Social Security Work Incentives Planning and Assistance project, a legal aid office, or a benefits counselor at your Area Agency on Aging.
items.hack: Three tools exist for this and almost nobody is told about them. Many programs exclude certain lump sums for a defined period, during which spending the money down on exempt purchases — a vehicle, home repairs, medical costs, a prepaid burial — preserves eligibility. ABLE accounts allow people whose disability began before a statutory age to hold savings that do not count against SSI and Medicaid resource limits, up to annual and total caps. Special needs trusts do the same in other situations. Ask about all three BEFORE the money arrives, because after it lands in a checking account your options narrow sharply. And if the grant is for a specific purpose — a ramp, a vehicle, tuition — ask whether the funder can pay the vendor directly instead of paying you, which in many cases keeps it off your resource statement entirely.
items.deadline: N/A — ask before accepting.

items.title: Disability compensation is tax-free and graduated from 10% to 100% in 10% increments
items.who: Veterans with a disease or injury incurred or aggravated during active military service, including physical and mental health conditions resulting from MST
items.value: Tax-free monthly cash benefit scaled to the degree of disability
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Disability compensation is a tax-free monetary benefit... The benefits amount is graduated according to the degree of the Veteran's disability on a scale from 10% to 100% (in increments of 10%)."
items.hack: The handbook names MST-related physical AND mental health conditions explicitly as compensable — useful language to quote in a claim.
items.deadline: None - no filing deadline

items.title: Dependent allowances begin at a 30% rating - not before
items.who: Veterans rated 30% or higher with a spouse, minor children, school children 18-23, or dependent parents
items.value: Additional monthly amount on top of the basic compensation rate, varying by rating and number of dependents
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Veterans with disability ratings of at least 30% are eligible for additional allowances for dependents."
items.hack: The 30% floor is the reason a 20%-to-30% rating increase is worth far more than one step: it switches on dependent money for the first time.
items.deadline: None - but add dependents promptly; retroactive dependency pay is limited

items.title: Children aged 18 to 23 still count as dependents while they are in school
items.who: Veterans rated 30%+ whose children aged 18-23 are attending school
items.value: Continued dependent allowance past the child's 18th birthday
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: dependents include "spouses, minor children, children between the ages of 18 and 23 who are attending school."
items.hack: Dependency for an 18-23 year old is not automatic - VA needs school certification, so the allowance stops silently if you never file it.
items.deadline: File school certification at each enrollment

items.title: An other-than-dishonorable discharge is the gate for disability compensation
items.who: Any veteran seeking service-connected compensation
items.value: Eligibility for the entire compensation system
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "To be eligible for compensation, a Veteran must have been separated or discharged under conditions other than dishonorable."
items.hack: Note the wording is 'other than dishonorable', not 'honorable' - General, OTH and even some bad-conduct discharges can still clear this bar.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Direct deposit is required to receive VA benefit payments
items.who: All VA benefit recipients
items.value: Payment delivery - no paper check by default
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Direct deposit is required to receive VA benefit payments."
items.hack: A stale bank account is one of the quiet ways a payment stops; update it before you move or close an account.
items.deadline: None - but update before any bank change

items.title: The 2026 handbook publishes NO disability compensation rate table - it points to the rate page instead
items.who: Anyone trying to verify a monthly compensation figure against VA's own handbook
items.value: Knowing where the authoritative rate actually lives
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "For detailed compensation rate information visit www.va.gov/disability/compensation-rates/veteran-rates." No rate table and no effective date appear in the chapter.
items.hack: Do not treat the handbook as a rate source. It deliberately defers to the rate page, so the rate page - not the handbook - is the citation for any dollar figure.
items.deadline: Rates change each December 1 with the COLA

items.title: Special Monthly Compensation is a higher rate for specific losses or for needing another person's help
items.who: Veterans needing regular aid and attendance, or with a specific loss such as loss of use of one hand, leg or reproductive organ
items.value: A higher tax-free rate than the percentage schedule alone would pay
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "For Veterans, SMC is a higher rate of compensation paid, due to special circumstances such as the need for aid and attendance by another person, or due to a specific disability such as the loss of use of one hand, leg or reproductive organ."
items.hack: The handbook names loss of use of a reproductive organ in the same breath as a hand or leg - that is SMC-K, the single most under-claimed award in the system.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Permanently housebound status is its own route to extra payment
items.who: Veterans VA determines need regular aid and attendance of another person, or who are permanently housebound
items.value: Additional monthly payments above the scheduled rate
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "A Veteran who is determined by VA to need the regular aid and attendance of another person or a Veteran who is permanently housebound may be entitled to additional payments."
items.hack: Housebound and aid-and-attendance are alternative routes, not a ladder - you can qualify on the housebound test without needing hands-on care.
items.deadline: None

items.title: The handbook publishes NO SMC levels or amounts
items.who: Anyone verifying an SMC-K through SMC-T figure
items.value: Knowing the handbook is not a source for SMC dollar amounts
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: the SMC section gives no letter levels and no amounts, only "www.va.gov/disability/compensation-rates/special-monthly-compensation-rates."
items.hack: Because VA's own handbook declines to print SMC amounts, the SMC rate page is the only citable VA source - quote it with its effective date.
items.deadline: SMC amounts move with the December 1 COLA

items.title: Automobile allowance: $27,074.99, effective October 1, 2025
items.who: Service members and veterans with certain service-connected disabilities
items.value: $27,074.99 one-time payment toward the purchase of an automobile or other conveyance
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Effective October 1, 2025, service members and Veterans may be eligible for a payment of $27,074.99 toward the purchase of an automobile or other conveyance if they have certain service-connected disabilities."
items.hack: This is the figure VA's own 2026 handbook stands behind. Any higher number circulating for FY2027 needs a Federal Register notice before you rely on it.
items.deadline: None

items.title: A SECOND automobile grant is possible after 30 years
items.who: Veterans or service members who last received VA automobile purchase assistance more than 30 years ago
items.value: An additional automobile or other conveyance - the allowance is not strictly once-per-lifetime
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Effective January 5, 2023, VA may provide or assist in providing an additional automobile or other conveyance if more than 30 years have passed since the Veteran or Service member most recently received VA financial assistance to purchase an automobile or other conveyance."
items.hack: Anyone who took the grant in the early 1990s or before is now in range for a second one. This is a 2023 change that most summaries still get wrong by calling the allowance one-time-only.
items.deadline: None - but the 30-year clock runs from your last grant

items.title: How to claim the automobile allowance - the three phone routes
items.who: Veterans pursuing the automobile or conveyance allowance
items.value: Access to the application process
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "To apply, contact a VA regional office at 800-827-1000, 1-800-MyVA411 (1-800-698-2411), or the nearest VA health care facility."
items.hack: The handbook routes this through a regional office or a health care facility rather than an online form - the clinical side is often faster because the medical finding drives the award.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Clothing allowance: the device must actually damage your clothing
items.who: Veterans with service-connected disabilities requiring a prosthetic or orthopedic appliance
items.value: An annual clothing allowance
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "A Veteran with service-connected disabilities that require prosthetic or orthopedic appliances may receive an annual clothing allowance. The prescribed device must cause wear and tear to the clothing."
items.hack: Wear and tear is the operative test, not the severity of the rating. A rigid brace, a prosthetic limb or a wheelchair that abrades clothing all qualify.
items.deadline: Annual - the handbook does not print a filing deadline

items.title: Clothing allowance also covers skin medication that ruins outer garments
items.who: Veterans whose service-connected skin condition requires prescribed skin medication that irreparably damages outer garments
items.value: The same annual clothing allowance, with no appliance involved
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "This allowance is also available to a Veteran whose service-connected skin condition requires prescribed skin medication that irreparably damages their outer garments."
items.hack: This is the forgotten half of the benefit. A service-connected skin condition on a staining or corrosive topical qualifies with no brace, no prosthesis and no minimum rating.
items.deadline: Annual - the handbook does not print a filing deadline

items.title: Clothing allowance is filed on VA Form 20-8678 to the PROSTHETICS department
items.who: Veterans claiming the annual clothing allowance
items.value: A correctly routed claim
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "To apply, submit VA Form 20-8678, Application for Annual Clothing Allowance, to the prosthetics department."
items.hack: Filing this at a regional office with your other claims is the classic mistake - the handbook sends it to the prosthetics department at your VA medical center, because prosthetics certifies the device.
items.deadline: Annual; deadline NOT stated in the handbook

items.title: Adoption expense reimbursement: up to $2,000 per adopted child
items.who: "Covered Veterans" adopting a child under 18
items.value: Reimbursement of up to $2,000 per adopted child for qualifying adoption expenses
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Covered Veterans may request reimbursement of up to $2,000 per adopted child for qualifying adoption expenses incurred by the Veteran in the adoption of a child under 18 years of age."
items.hack: The handbook prints the per-child figure only. It does NOT state an annual aggregate cap, so do not assume a per-year ceiling without checking the governing regulation.
items.deadline: Child must be under 18 at adoption

items.title: "Covered Veteran" for adoption reimbursement is a narrow infertility definition
items.who: Veterans with a service-connected disability causing inability to procreate without fertility treatment
items.value: Gateway to the $2,000-per-child adoption reimbursement
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "'Covered Veteran' means a Veteran with a service-connected disability that results in the inability of the Veteran to procreate without the use of fertility treatment."
items.hack: This is not a general adoption benefit for veterans. It is tied to service-connected infertility, which is why so few claims are filed - and why anyone with a service-connected reproductive injury should look at it.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Adoption reimbursement only for adoptions finalized after September 29, 2016
items.who: Covered veterans whose adoption became final after September 29, 2016
items.value: Eligibility for reimbursement - adoptions final before that date are excluded
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Reimbursement for qualifying adoption expenses may be requested only for an adoption that became final after September 29, 2016."
items.hack: A hard statutory cutoff that is easy to miss. Finalization date, not filing date, is what governs.
items.deadline: Adoption must have become final after September 29, 2016

items.title: Foreign adoptions: reimbursement waits for U.S. citizenship
items.who: Covered veterans adopting a child from another country
items.value: Reimbursement, but only after the citizenship step
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "In the case of adoption of a foreign child, reimbursement... may be requested only after United States citizenship has been granted."
items.hack: Budget for the gap: intercountry adoption costs land years before citizenship is granted, and the reimbursement clock does not start until it is.
items.deadline: Request only after U.S. citizenship is granted

items.title: Adoption reimbursement covers single parents, infants, intercountry and special-needs adoptions
items.who: Covered veterans, married or single
items.value: Broad coverage of adoption types within the $2,000-per-child limit
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "An adoption for which expenses may be reimbursed includes an adoption by a married or single person, an infant adoption, an intercountry adoption, and an adoption of a child with special needs (as defined in section 473 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 673(c))."
items.hack: Single veterans are explicitly covered - a point often assumed otherwise.
items.deadline: None

items.title: CRDP: both retired pay and VA compensation at 50% or more
items.who: Military retirees with a VA service-connected rating of 50% or greater who are eligible to receive retired pay
items.value: Concurrent receipt of military retired pay and VA disability compensation, ending the offset
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Concurrent Retirement and Disability Pay (CRDP) is a program that allows some individuals to receive both military retired pay and VA disability compensation simultaneously. Normally, such concurrent receipt is prohibited." Requires "a VA service-connected disability rating of 50% or greater."
items.hack: 50% is the switch. Climbing from 40% to 50% can be worth far more than the rate table shows, because it ends the retired-pay offset entirely.
items.deadline: None

items.title: CRDP's three qualifying retirement paths
items.who: Longevity retirees; disability retirees with 20+ years; Guard and Reserve retirees with 20+ qualifying years
items.value: CRDP eligibility
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Must have retired from military service based on longevity... or must have retired due to disability with 20 or more years of service... or must have retired from National Guard or Reserve service with 20 or more qualifying years."
items.hack: A medical retiree with 20+ years qualifies for CRDP; a medical retiree under 20 years does not, which is what pushes that group toward CRSC instead.
items.deadline: None

items.title: CRDP requires no application - payment is coordinated for you
items.who: Retirees who meet the CRDP tests
items.value: Automatic restoration of offset retired pay
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Veterans do not need to apply for this benefit, as payment is coordinated."
items.hack: Nothing to file, but plenty to verify - check your DFAS Retiree Account Statement after any rating change to confirm the offset actually stopped.
items.deadline: None - automatic

items.title: Housing grants can be used up to SIX times
items.who: Service members and veterans with qualifying service-connected disabilities
items.value: Up to six separate uses of the SAH/SHA grant, subject to a lifetime dollar ceiling
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 3: "Eligible Veterans or Service members may now receive up to six uses of the grant, with the total dollar amount of the grants not to exceed the maximum allowable amount."
items.hack: Six uses, one money pot. Spend a use on a small adaptation and you have not reset the dollar cap - plan the sequence around the ceiling, not the use count.
items.deadline: None
