items.hack: 877-424-3838 is answered 24/7 and is the fastest route into HUD-VASH and Grant and Per Diem, neither of which this chapter explains. Call rather than trying to find the program by name.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Spinal cord injury centers appear only as part of VA's special disability rehabilitation programs
items.who: Veterans with spinal cord injury or disorders
items.value: Care through VA spinal cord injury centers; inpatient special disability rehabilitation travel is a beneficiary travel category
items.how: Chapter 2 mentions 'spinal cord injury centers' as part of VA's special disability rehabilitation programs, and makes travel 'for care through VA special disability rehabilitation program on inpatient basis' a beneficiary travel eligibility category. Source: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 2.
items.hack: The travel connection is the useful part: inpatient care at a spinal cord injury center carries travel eligibility even if you do not otherwise qualify for mileage.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Health care eligibility and the 12-month window for unrated line-of-duty conditions
items.who: Veterans with a disability the military determined was incurred or aggravated in the line of duty, which VA has not yet rated
items.value: Care without enrolling, within 12 months of discharge
items.how: The handbook covers Veterans 'seeking care for disabilities the military determined was incurred or aggravated in the line of duty, but which VA has not yet rated, within 12 months of discharge.' Source: 2026 VA handbook, Chapter 2.
items.hack: This is the gap year between separation and a rating decision. Bring the line-of-duty determination from your service record to the VA clinic — it stands in for a rating for 12 months.
items.deadline: 12 months from discharge

items.title: VA Home Loans national number — 877-827-3702 (handbook-confirmed)
items.who: Any veteran, service member or surviving spouse with a VA home loan question, including borrowers in default seeking foreclosure help.
items.value: A single national line for VA home loan eligibility, Certificate of Eligibility and loan-servicing questions. The handbook prints it as: "Home Loans............877-827-3702".
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, front-matter contact directory (pp. 1-3). Verified by direct extraction and re-confirmed in three separate fetches with identical wording. Printed in the handbook's program contact directory as the Home Loans entry.
items.hack: This is the same number as VA's loan technicians, who can intervene directly with your servicer when you are behind on payments. You do not need your lender's permission to call it, and the lender does not have to be the one to initiate.
items.deadline: None. Call before a missed payment becomes a default; intervention options narrow once foreclosure is referred.

items.title: National Call Center for Homeless Veterans — 877-424-3838 (handbook-confirmed)
items.who: Veterans who are homeless or at imminent risk of homelessness, and family members, friends or providers calling on their behalf.
items.value: A 24/7 national line that is the intake point into HUD-VASH, SSVF and Grant and Per Diem. The handbook prints it as: "National Call Center for Homeless Veterans................877-424-3838".
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, front-matter contact directory (pp. 1-3). Verified by direct extraction and re-confirmed in three separate fetches with identical wording. Printed in the handbook's program contact directory.
items.hack: 877-424-3838 spells 877-4AID-VET — the two numbers circulating in veteran materials are the same line, not alternatives. A third party can call it for a veteran who will not call themselves.
items.deadline: None; staffed around the clock.

items.title: VGLI, SGLI and FSGLI claims line — 800-419-1473 (handbook-confirmed)
items.who: Service members and veterans with SGLI, VGLI or FSGLI coverage, and beneficiaries filing a death claim on those policies.
items.value: The dedicated line for the group life programs. The handbook prints it as: "Life Insurance, Veterans' Group Life Insurance Program (VGLI), Claims for Service members' Group Life Insurance (SGLI) and Family (FSGLI).................800-419-1473".
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, front-matter contact directory (pp. 1-3). Verified by direct extraction and re-confirmed in three separate fetches with identical wording. Printed in the handbook's program contact directory.
items.hack: The handbook splits life insurance across two numbers on purpose: the group programs (SGLI/VGLI/FSGLI) go here, everything else goes to 800-669-8477. Calling the wrong one is the most common reason an insurance question gets bounced.
items.deadline: None for the line itself. VGLI and SGLI conversion windows are time-limited — confirm the current deadline with this office, as the handbook's chapter text could not be retrieved (see notes).

items.title: All other VA life insurance programs, including TSGLI — 800-669-8477 (handbook-confirmed)
items.who: Veterans with VALife, S-DVI, VMLI or an older Veterans' Insurance policy, and service members filing a TSGLI traumatic-injury claim.
items.value: The line for every VA life insurance program other than SGLI, VGLI and FSGLI. The handbook prints it as: "Life Insurance, All Programs Other than VGLI, SGLI, FSGLI, Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance Traumatic Injury Protection......................800-669-8477".
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, front-matter contact directory (pp. 1-3). Verified by direct extraction and re-confirmed in three separate fetches with identical wording. Printed in the handbook's program contact directory.
items.hack: Note where the handbook files TSGLI: with the non-group programs on this number, not with the SGLI claims line. TSGLI claimants routinely call 800-419-1473 first and lose time.
items.deadline: None for the line itself.

items.title: CHAMPVA — 800-733-8387 (handbook-confirmed)
items.who: Spouses, surviving spouses and children of veterans who are permanently and totally disabled from a service-connected condition or who died of one.
items.value: The national CHAMPVA line for eligibility, enrollment and claims. The handbook prints it as: "Civilian Health and Medical Program (CHAMPVA) ....................800-733-8387".
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, front-matter contact directory (pp. 1-3). Verified by direct extraction and re-confirmed in three separate fetches with identical wording. Printed in the handbook's program contact directory.
items.hack: CHAMPVA eligibility is derived from the veteran's rating or death, so the family often does not know they qualify until someone checks. Call this line with the veteran's file number rather than waiting for VA to notify the family.
items.deadline: None stated in the retrievable portion of the handbook.

items.title: Where chapters 7-11 actually sit in the 2026 handbook (confirmed page map)
items.who: Anyone citing the 2026 edition of Federal Benefits for Veterans, Dependents, Survivors, and Caregivers.
items.value: Confirmed from the handbook's own table of contents: Home Loans begins p. 49; Life Insurance p. 58; Re-Employment Rights p. 66; Homelessness Assistance and Prevention p. 67; Family Members/Survivors p. 71; Appeals, Supplemental Claims, and Higher-Level Reviews p. 78.
items.how: 2026 VA handbook, table of contents, extracted directly from the PDF.
items.hack: The 2026 edition retitled and renumbered sections against older editions (the 2011 edition put Home Loan Guaranty at p. 51 and VA Life Insurance at p. 63). A citation to a chapter number without an edition year is ambiguous; cite the edition.
items.deadline: VA reissues this handbook annually; page numbers shift each edition.

items.title: Funding fee, purchase/construction, FIRST use: the three down-payment bands
items.who: Any eligible veteran, service member or qualifying spouse using VA entitlement for the first time on a purchase or construction loan
items.value: 2.15% of the loan amount with less than 5% down; 1.5% with 5% or more down; 1.25% with 10% or more down. On a $500,000 loan that is $10,750 vs $7,500 vs $6,250 — a $4,500 swing you control.
items.how: VA, 'VA funding fee and loan closing costs' — purchase and construction loan rate table (first use), va.gov
items.hack: The jump from 0% down to 5% down saves 0.65 points of fee. On a $500k loan a $25,000 down payment cuts the fee by $3,250 — that is a 13% immediate return on the cash you put in, before you count the lower principal.
items.deadline: Rate is locked at closing; there is no post-closing election

items.title: Funding fee, purchase/construction, SUBSEQUENT use: the 3.3% penalty and the one way to kill it
items.who: Veterans using VA entitlement for a second or later purchase loan
items.value: Subsequent use with less than 5% down is 3.3% — not 2.15%. But subsequent use with 5% or more down is 1.5%, and with 10% or more down is 1.25%: exactly the same as first use. The subsequent-use penalty exists ONLY in the zero-to-under-5%-down band.
items.how: VA, 'VA funding fee and loan closing costs' — purchase and construction loan rate table (subsequent use), va.gov
items.hack: This is the single most mispriced fact in VA lending. A repeat user putting 5% down pays 1.5%, not 3.3% — a 1.8-point saving. On a $600,000 loan that is $10,800 of fee avoided for $30,000 of down payment. Run this comparison on every repeat-use file before you quote a payment.
items.deadline: Determined at closing

items.title: Funding fee on a cash-out refinance: 2.15% first use, 3.3% subsequent — and no down-payment relief
items.who: Veterans refinancing with cash out, or refinancing a non-VA loan into a VA loan
items.value: Cash-out refinancing is 2.15% on first use of entitlement and 3.3% on subsequent use. Unlike a purchase, there are no down-payment bands — equity in the property does not reduce the cash-out funding fee.
items.how: VA, 'VA funding fee and loan closing costs' — cash-out refinancing rate table, va.gov
items.hack: A second-time user doing a cash-out pays 3.3% with no way to buy it down. On a $400,000 cash-out that is $13,200 added to the balance. If the goal is a lower rate rather than cash, an IRRRL at 0.5% is six times cheaper — but an IRRRL only works off an existing VA loan.
items.deadline: Applies at closing

items.title: IRRRL funding fee is 0.5% — the cheapest fee in the whole table
items.who: Veterans with an existing VA-backed loan refinancing to a lower rate
items.value: 0.5% of the loan amount, regardless of whether this is first or subsequent use of entitlement and regardless of equity.
items.how: VA, 'VA funding fee and loan closing costs' — 'Interest Rate Reduction Refinancing Loans (IRRRLs)' row, va.gov
items.hack: 0.5% does not vary by use count. A veteran who has already triggered the 3.3% subsequent-use rate on a purchase still pays only 0.5% on an IRRRL of that same loan. The fee table punishes repeat purchases, not repeat refinances.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Loan assumption funding fee is 0.5% — and the assumer pays it, not the seller
items.who: A buyer assuming an existing VA-backed loan
items.value: 0.5% of the loan balance being assumed.
items.how: VA, 'VA funding fee and loan closing costs' — 'Loan assumptions' row, va.gov
items.hack: In a high-rate market a 0.5% fee to inherit a 2.x% note is the cheapest money in residential real estate. Price it into the offer: the assumption fee plus the $300 processing cap (38 CFR 36.4313) is often under $5,000 all-in on a $400k balance.
items.deadline: Paid at the assumption closing

items.title: Manufactured home funding fee is 1% — a separate, lower row most lenders never quote
items.who: Veterans financing a manufactured home with a VA-backed loan
items.value: 1% of the loan amount, flat.
items.how: VA, 'VA funding fee and loan closing costs' — 'Manufactured home loans (not permanently affixed)' row, va.gov
items.hack: 1% beats the 2.15% first-use purchase rate and crushes the 3.3% subsequent-use rate. If a manufactured home is on the table at all, the fee math favours it heavily on a repeat use of entitlement.
items.deadline: At closing

items.title: NADL funding fee: 1.25% to buy, 0.5% to refinance
items.who: Native American veterans, and non-Native veterans married to a Native American, borrowing on federal trust land
items.value: 1.25% on a NADL purchase and 0.5% on a NADL refinance — the purchase rate matches the best 10%-down conventional VA band with no down payment required.
items.how: VA, 'VA funding fee and loan closing costs' — Native American Direct Loan rows, va.gov
items.hack: 1.25% with zero down is a better fee outcome than any non-NADL VA purchase without a 10% down payment. If the property is on trust land and the tribe has an MOU, the NADL is the cheaper instrument on fee alone.
items.deadline: At closing

items.title: The five funding-fee exemptions, quoted in full — including the two nobody checks
items.who: Veterans, service members and surviving spouses at loan closing
items.value: No funding fee if you are receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability; are eligible to receive it but take retirement or active-duty pay instead; are a surviving spouse receiving DIC; are a service member who received a proposed or memorandum rating before the loan closing date; or are an active-duty member who provides evidence of a Purple Heart on or before the closing date.
items.how: VA, 'VA funding fee and loan closing costs' — 'You won't have to pay a VA funding fee if any of these are true' list, va.gov
items.hack: Two of these five are routinely missed. A retiree who waived VA compensation to keep retired pay is exempt even though no VA money is flowing. And an active-duty Purple Heart recipient is exempt with no rating at all — the evidence just has to be in the lender's file on or before closing day.
items.deadline: Evidence must be in the file on or before the closing date for the memorandum-rating and Purple Heart routes

items.title: Memorandum or proposed rating before closing = exempt, even with no rating decision yet
items.who: Service members separating with a pending disability claim who are buying a home during the transition
items.value: A service member 'who has received a proposed or memorandum rating before the loan closing date' pays no funding fee.
items.how: VA, 'VA funding fee and loan closing costs' — funding fee exemption list, va.gov
items.hack: This is the IDES/BDD window. If you are in a disability evaluation and a proposed or memorandum rating exists, get it to the lender BEFORE closing. After closing you are into the refund process, which depends on the effective date rather than the document.
items.deadline: Before the loan closing date

items.title: Funding fee refund: it turns on the EFFECTIVE DATE, not the decision date
items.who: Veterans who paid a funding fee and were later awarded service-connected compensation
items.value: 'You may be eligible for a refund of the VA funding fee if you're later awarded VA compensation for a service-connected disability. The effective date of your VA compensation must be retroactive to before the date of your loan closing.'
items.how: VA, 'VA funding fee and loan closing costs' — funding fee refund paragraph, va.gov
items.hack: The test is the effective date, which on most claims is the date the intent to file or the claim was received — often a year or more before the rating letter. File the claim BEFORE you close and the effective date beats the closing date even if the decision lands two years later. Then go get the fee back.
items.deadline: No stated deadline to request the refund, but the effective date must predate closing

items.title: Basic entitlement is $36,000 and it is a guaranty, not a loan amount
items.who: Every veteran reading a Certificate of Eligibility
items.value: '$36,000 isn't the amount you can borrow. It's the maximum amount we'll pay your lender if you don't pay them back on a loan that's $144,000 or less.'
items.how: VA, 'VA home loan limits' — basic entitlement explanation, va.gov
items.hack: Quote this sentence verbatim to any veteran who thinks their benefit is capped at $36,000. The $36,000 is VA's downside exposure on small loans; above $144,000 the bonus entitlement and the 25% guaranty take over entirely.
items.deadline: None

items.title: The statutory guaranty tiers in 38 CFR 36.4302 — four brackets, not one percentage
items.who: Lenders, loan officers and veterans reconciling a COE against a guaranty figure
items.value: Loans up to $45,000: 50% of the original principal. $45,001–$56,250: $22,500. $56,251–$144,000: the lesser of $36,000 or 40% of original principal. Over $144,000: '$60,000 or 25 percent of the original principal loan amount' for a home purchase, construction or condominium purchase.
items.how: 38 CFR 36.4302, Computation of guaranties or insurance credits — ecfr.gov
items.hack: The regulation still carries a $60,000 guaranty figure that predates the removal of loan limits for full entitlement. Do not quote the $60,000 as a loan cap — read it alongside VA's current loan-limits page, which says a veteran with full entitlement has no loan limit. Cite the CFR for the tiers and va.gov for the limit.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Bonus entitlement exists only above $144,000 — and that is where the county limit enters
items.who: Veterans with partially used entitlement
items.value: 'Bonus entitlement is the amount we agree to pay your lender if you don't pay them back for a loan that's more than $144,000.' Below $144,000 only basic entitlement is in play.
items.how: VA, 'VA home loan limits' — bonus entitlement definition, va.gov
items.hack: The $144,000 hinge explains why the county loan limit is irrelevant to small loans and decisive to large ones. On a $140,000 purchase in a high-cost county, prior entitlement use barely matters.
items.deadline: None

items.title: No loan limit on full entitlement — VA's own wording
items.who: Veterans with full entitlement buying in any price band
items.value: 'You don't have a loan limit (as long as you can afford the loan amount and the property appraisal supports the purchase price of the home).' Full entitlement does not guarantee approval — the lender still underwrites credit, income, debts and assets.
items.how: VA, 'VA home loan limits' — full entitlement section, va.gov
items.hack: Two separate gates get conflated constantly. VA imposes no price ceiling; the LENDER imposes one through underwriting, and investors impose one through their own overlay. When a loan officer says 'the VA limit is X', they mean their investor's limit.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Remaining entitlement: VA's four-step calculation with its own worked numbers
items.who: Veterans who already have one VA loan outstanding and want a second
items.value: Four steps: read the Entitlement Charged column on your COE; find your county One-Unit Limit on the FHFA site; multiply that limit by 0.25; subtract the charged amount. VA's example: $50,000 already charged, $900,000 county limit — '$900,000 x .25 = $225,000' then '$225,000 - $50,000 = $175,000' remaining bonus entitlement.
items.how: VA, 'VA home loan limits' — how to calculate remaining entitlement, with VA's worked example, va.gov
items.hack: Pull the Entitlement Charged figure off the COE before you talk price. It is a line on the document, not a calculation — and it is what every second-tier deal turns on.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Multiply remaining entitlement by four to get the zero-down ceiling
items.who: Veterans buying a second property on remaining entitlement
items.value: VA's instruction: 'Multiply your remaining bonus entitlement by 4: $175,000 x 4 = $700,000.' That is the largest no-down-payment loan the remaining entitlement supports.
items.how: VA, 'VA home loan limits' — maximum loan amount without a down payment, va.gov
items.hack: The ×4 shortcut is the 25% guaranty run backwards. Above that ceiling the loan is still possible — the veteran just covers 25% of the excess as a down payment, not 25% of the whole price.
items.deadline: None

items.title: The four statutory paths to restoring entitlement — 38 CFR 36.4302(j)
items.who: Veterans who want their used entitlement back
items.value: Entitlement is excluded from the aggregate when: (1) the property securing the loan has been disposed of AND the loan repaid in full, or VA released from liability, or the loss paid; (2) a veteran-transferee has agreed to assume the outstanding balance and consents to use their own entitlement in place of the original veteran's; (3) the loan has been repaid in full and the new loan is secured by the same property; or (4) one time per veteran, where the loan is repaid and any loss is covered or VA is released from liability.
items.how: 38 CFR 36.4302(j) — ecfr.gov
items.hack: Path (3) is the underused one: pay the loan in full and borrow again on the SAME property and your entitlement comes back without a sale and without burning the one-time restoration. Path (4) — one time per veteran — is the one to hoard, not the one to spend first.
items.deadline: Path (4) is available only once per veteran, for life

items.title: Veteran-transferee substitution of entitlement: the only way a seller gets their benefit back on an assumption
items.who: Veterans whose VA loan is being assumed by a buyer
items.value: Entitlement is restored where 'a veteran-transferee has agreed to assume the outstanding balance' and consents to the use of their own entitlement in place of the original veteran's. A non-veteran assumer cannot do this.
items.how: 38 CFR 36.4302(j) — ecfr.gov
items.hack: This is the trap in every low-rate assumption. A non-veteran CAN assume the loan with VA approval — but the seller's entitlement stays charged for the life of that loan, which can block the seller's next VA purchase entirely. If the seller needs their entitlement back, the buyer must be an eligible veteran willing to substitute.
items.deadline: The substitution must be agreed as part of the assumption

items.title: A VA loan 'is not assumable without the approval of the Department of Veterans Affairs or its authorized agent'
items.who: Buyers and sellers negotiating an assumption; agents writing assumption contracts
items.value: The regulation requires VA or its authorized agent to approve the transfer. 38 CFR 36.4309 also lists transfers where acceleration is prohibited — devise, descent, transfers to a spouse, and transfers into an inter vivos trust among them.
items.how: 38 CFR 36.4309, Transfer of title by borrower — ecfr.gov
items.hack: The acceleration exceptions matter in divorce and estate work: a transfer to a spouse or by descent is not a due-on-sale event, so it does not need to be processed as a full assumption. Know which list your transaction sits on before you start an assumption package.
items.deadline: The holder has limited time to act on an assumption request — confirm the current processing window with the servicer

items.title: The assumption processing charge is capped in regulation: the lesser of $300 and the actual credit-report cost
items.who: Anyone being quoted an assumption fee by a servicer
items.value: 'A reasonable fee, not to exceed the lesser of $300 and the actual cost of any credit report required, or any maximum prescribed by applicable State law.'
items.how: 38 CFR 36.4313 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: Servicers quote assumption 'processing fees' of $1,000 and up. The regulation caps it at $300 — and even lower if the credit report cost less. Quote the CFR section at the servicer in writing; the charge is not negotiable, it is unlawful.
items.deadline: Charged at the assumption closing

items.title: The lender's flat origination charge is capped at 1% — and nothing outside the list may be charged
items.who: Every VA borrower reviewing a Loan Estimate
items.value: 38 CFR 36.4313(d)(2) permits 'a flat charge not exceeding 1 percent of the amount of the loan.' Separately: 'No charge shall be made against, or paid by, the borrower incident to the making of a guaranteed or insured loan other than those expressly permitted under paragraph (d) or (e).'
items.how: 38 CFR 36.4313 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: The 1% flat charge is the lender's whole origination compensation from the borrower — it is not stackable with processing, underwriting and application fees. If a VA Loan Estimate shows a 1% origination PLUS itemised lender junk fees, it is out of compliance with the closing sentence of 36.4313.
items.deadline: Reviewable before closing; raise it at the Loan Estimate stage

items.title: What the veteran MAY be charged: the itemised list in 38 CFR 36.4313
items.who: Borrowers auditing a VA Closing Disclosure
items.value: 'Reasonable and customary amounts for' recording fees, credit reports, hazard insurance, title examination, survey costs, flood zone determinations, VA appraiser fees, and 'such other items as may be authorized in advance by the Under Secretary for Benefits.'
items.how: 38 CFR 36.4313(d) — ecfr.gov
items.hack: Use this as a checklist against the Closing Disclosure. Anything on the borrower's side of the ledger that is not on this list and is not the 1% flat charge needs a justification — or it needs to move to the seller or the lender.
items.deadline: Audit before closing

items.title: COE evidence by category — the exact document VA wants for each status
items.who: Anyone requesting a Certificate of Eligibility
items.value: Veteran: a copy of discharge or separation papers (DD214). Active duty: a signed statement of service from the commander with name, SSN, date of birth, duty entry date, lost-time duration and command name. Activated Guard/Reserve: DD214 or other discharge documents. Never-activated Guard/Reserve still serving: a signed statement of service with creditable years. Never-activated Guard, discharged: NGB Form 22 plus a retirement points statement and proof of honorable service.
items.how: VA, 'How to request a VA home loan Certificate of Eligibility (COE)' — documents by category, va.gov
items.hack: The never-activated Guard route is the one that stalls. NGB Form 22 alone is not enough — VA wants the points statement too. Request both from your state's Joint Force Headquarters before you start the COE, not after it is rejected.
items.deadline: Get the COE before you shop, not at contract

items.title: Surviving spouse COE: Form 26-1817 if you receive DIC, 21P-534EZ if you do not
items.who: Surviving spouses of veterans whose death was service-connected, or of service members who died on active duty
items.value: If receiving DIC: VA Form 26-1817, Request for Determination of Loan Guaranty Eligibility — Unmarried Surviving Spouses. If not receiving DIC: VA Form 21P-534EZ plus the marriage licence and the death certificate.
items.how: VA, 'How to request a VA home loan Certificate of Eligibility (COE)' — surviving spouse section, va.gov
items.hack: A spouse who has not yet filed for DIC can still establish loan eligibility — the 21P-534EZ route does both jobs at once, since that form is the DIC, Survivors Pension and accrued-benefits application. File it and you are in line for the monthly benefit and the home loan in one submission.
items.deadline: No deadline for the COE itself; DIC has its own retroactivity rules

items.title: VA loan eligibility: the service minimums era by era, in VA's own numbers
items.who: Veterans unsure whether their service qualifies
items.value: Current service members: at least 90 continuous days. Aug 2 1990–present: 24 continuous months, or the full ordered period, or 90 days if discharged under a qualifying exception, or less than 90 days for a service-connected disability. Sep 8 1980–Aug 1 1990: 24 continuous months or a full 181+ day period. May 8 1975–Sep 7 1980: 181 continuous days. Aug 5 1964–May 7 1975 (Vietnam): at least 90 total days. Feb 1 1955–Aug 4 1964: at least 181 total days. Jun 27 1950–Jan 31 1955 (Korea): at least 90 total days. Jul 26 1947–Jun 26 1950: at least 181 continuous days. Sep 16 1940–Jul 25 1947 (WWII): at least 90 total days.
items.how: VA, 'Eligibility requirements for VA home loan programs' — minimum service requirements table, va.gov
items.hack: Note the 'less than 90 days if discharged for a service-connected disability' escape hatch in every post-1975 era. A short-tour medical separation still qualifies — and that is the case most often turned away by a loan officer reading the headline number.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Guard and Reserve VA loan eligibility: three separate doors
items.who: National Guard and Selected Reserve members and veterans
items.value: National Guard: at least 90 days of non-training active-duty Title 10 service; OR at least 90 days of active-duty service including at least 30 consecutive days, documented on the DD214; OR 6 creditable years in the Guard while still serving; OR 6 creditable years and an honorable discharge or placement on the retired list. Selected Reserve: at least 90 days of non-training active-duty service; OR 6 creditable years while still serving; OR 6 creditable years with an honorable discharge or retired-list placement.
items.how: VA, 'Eligibility requirements for VA home loan programs' — National Guard and Reserve sections, va.gov
items.hack: The '90 days including at least 30 consecutive days' Guard door is the newest and least known. Title 32 activations that produced 30 straight days now count. If a Guard member was told years ago they needed 6 years, re-check against this language.
items.deadline: None

items.title: Geography: VA loans only inside the U.S. and its territories
items.who: Veterans considering retiring or investing overseas
items.value: 'You can use these programs to buy a home or refinance a home loan only within the U.S. and its territories, including Puerto Rico and the Northern Mariana Islands.'
items.how: VA, 'VA home loan types', va.gov
items.hack: Puerto Rico, Guam, USVI, American Samoa and the CNMI are in. Everywhere else is out — there is no VA financing for a retirement house in Portugal or the Philippines, and no VA refinance of a foreign mortgage.
items.deadline: None

items.title: VALife eligibility: any service-connected rating, 'even if your rating is 0%'
items.who: Any veteran with a VA service-connected disability rating
items.value: Guaranteed acceptance whole life with no health verification. A 0% rating qualifies. Age 80 or younger: the application window is unlimited after you receive the rating. Age 81 or older: you must apply 'within 2 years of getting notification of your disability rating.'
items.how: VA, 'VALife (Veterans Affairs Life Insurance)' — eligibility section, va.gov
items.hack: A 0% rating is worth something after all. Veterans routinely dismiss a 0% tinnitus or scar rating as worthless — it is the key to guaranteed-issue life insurance for life, with no medical underwriting, at any age up to 80.
items.deadline: Unlimited if 80 or younger; 2 years from the rating notification if 81 or older

items.title: VALife coverage: up to $40,000 in $10,000 increments
items.who: Veterans enrolling in or increasing VALife
items.value: 'Up to $40,000' of whole life coverage, available 'in $10,000 increments'.
items.how: VA, 'VALife (Veterans Affairs Life Insurance)' — coverage section, va.gov
items.hack: $40,000 is a final-expense policy, not income replacement. Size it to burial, probate and a few months of bills — then cover the real income gap with term insurance bought while you are still healthy enough to be underwritten.
items.deadline: None once enrolled

items.title: The VALife two-year waiting period — and exactly what the family gets if you die inside it
items.who: Every VALife applicant
items.value: Full coverage begins '2 years after you apply.' If death occurs during the waiting period, beneficiaries receive 'the total amount you paid in premiums, plus interest.' The 2026 interest rate is 4.23%; the 2025 rate was 3.59%.
items.how: VA, 'VALife (Veterans Affairs Life Insurance)' — two-year waiting period, va.gov
items.hack: This is the whole case for applying the day your rating lands rather than the day you think you need it. The waiting period runs from APPLICATION, not from need. A 0%-rated 45-year-old who applies now has paid-up protection at 47; one who waits until a diagnosis has a savings account paying 4.23%.
items.deadline: The clock starts on the application date — apply early to start it

items.title: VALife premiums never increase — and there is no premium waiver
items.who: Veterans comparing VALife to commercial whole life
items.value: 'Your premium rate will never increase as long as you keep your VALife policy.' Rates are set by age at application and coverage amount; VA's example is a 40-year-old at $40,000 paying $88.00 monthly. 'VALife doesn't offer premium waivers.'
items.how: VA, 'VALife (Veterans Affairs Life Insurance)' — premiums section, va.gov
items.hack: No premium waiver is the sharp edge. S-DVI waived premiums for totally disabled veterans; VALife does not. A veteran who becomes unable to pay loses the policy — budget the premium as a fixed lifetime obligation, and apply young, because the rate is locked at application age.
items.deadline: None

items.title: S-DVI to VALife: the overlap rule split on January 1, 2026
items.who: Veterans who held S-DVI (the 'RH' policy) before VALife replaced it
items.value: For VALife applications submitted by December 31, 2025, the veteran keeps both policies during the VALife waiting period. For applications from January 1, 2026 onward, S-DVI ends upon VALife approval.
items.how: VA, 'VALife (Veterans Affairs Life Insurance)' — S-DVI transition rules, va.gov
items.hack: That dual-coverage window has closed. An S-DVI holder applying for VALife now gives up S-DVI at approval and then sits two years with only a premium refund as the death benefit. Model the gap before you switch — and if S-DVI premiums are currently waived, understand you are trading a waiver for a non-waivable premium.
items.deadline: The dual-coverage overlap applied only to applications on or before December 31, 2025

items.title: SETTLED: VGLI gives you 240 days with no health questions, and 1 year and 120 days in total
items.who: Every separating service member with SGLI
items.value: 'If you sign up within 240 days of leaving the military, you won't need to prove you're in good health.' 'If you sign up after the 240-day period, you'll need to submit evidence that you're in good health.' And: 'You'll need to apply for VGLI within 1 year and 120 days of leaving the military.'
items.how: VA, 'Veterans' Group Life Insurance (VGLI)' — eligibility and application windows, va.gov
items.hack: Two different 120-day figures circulate and they are not the same thing. The 120 days on its own is the free SGLI extension after separation. The VGLI numbers are 240 days (no health review) and 1 year plus 120 days (absolute deadline). Apply inside 240 days and health never comes up — this is the single highest-value separation deadline for anyone with a developing condition.
items.deadline: 240 days from separation for no health review; 1 year and 120 days absolute

items.title: VGLI coverage range and the step-up schedule
items.who: Veterans holding VGLI below the maximum
items.value: Coverage is available between $10,000 and $500,000, initially 'up to the amount you had through SGLI.' A veteran with less than the maximum may increase coverage by $25,000 one year after obtaining VGLI, then every 5 years thereafter, up to $500,000, until age 60.
items.how: VA, 'Veterans' Group Life Insurance (VGLI)' — coverage amounts and increases, va.gov
items.hack: The step-up right expires at 60 and it is the only way to grow VGLI. A veteran who took $100,000 at separation can climb to $500,000 in $25,000 steps — but the schedule is slow, so start the first increase at the one-year mark whether you need it or not.
items.deadline: Increases available at the 1-year mark and every 5 years, until age 60

items.title: SGLI: $500,000 maximum, in $50,000 increments
items.who: All covered service members
items.value: Coverage runs 'up to the top limit of $500,000 — in $50,000 increments.' Automatic coverage applies to active-duty members of the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, Marines and Coast Guard, NOAA and USPHS commissioned officers, academy cadets and midshipmen, ROTC members in authorised training, and Reserve and Guard members assigned to units with at least 12 annual inactive training periods.
items.how: VA, 'Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance (SGLI)', va.gov
items.hack: The $50,000 increment matters for anyone who reduced coverage to save money. Every $50,000 you decline costs $2.50 a month and permanently lowers the VGLI amount you can convert to at separation — VGLI starts capped at what SGLI was.
items.deadline: Elections change prospectively; the VGLI conversion ceiling is set by SGLI at separation

items.title: SGLI costs 5 cents per $1,000 — $26.00 a month for the full $500,000 including TSGLI
items.who: All covered service members
items.value: The basic SGLI premium is '5 cents per $1,000 of insurance coverage,' plus 'an additional $1 per month for Traumatic Injury Protection coverage.' At $500,000 that is $25.00 basic plus $1.00 TSGLI = $26.00 monthly.
items.how: VA, 'Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance (SGLI)' — premium rates, va.gov
items.hack: $26 a month for half a million dollars of coverage with no underwriting is cheaper than any commercial product at any age. Anyone who reduced SGLI to free up $12 a month made the worst insurance trade available to them. Restore it to the maximum.
items.deadline: None

items.title: SGLI runs free for 120 days after you leave — and up to 2 years if you are disabled
items.who: Every separating service member, especially those separating with a disability
items.value: '120 days of free coverage from the date you leave the military.' The SGLI Disability Extension provides coverage 'up to 2 years after the date you leave the military at no cost' for eligible disabled veterans.
items.how: VA, 'Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance (SGLI)' — free coverage and SGLI Disability Extension, va.gov
items.hack: The Disability Extension is free insurance that almost nobody claims. It is not automatic in practice — if you separate with a disability, ask about SGLI-DE in writing before you leave, and use those two free years to decide on VGLI without paying twice.
items.deadline: 120 days automatic; SGLI-DE runs up to 2 years from separation

items.title: TSGLI: $25,000 to $100,000, a 7-day survival rule and a 730-day loss window
items.who: Service members who suffered a traumatic injury while covered by SGLI
items.value: 'You may get $25,000 to $100,000 in short-term financial support to help in your recovery from a traumatic injury.' The scheduled loss must result from a traumatic injury suffered before leaving service and must occur within '2 years (730 days) of the traumatic injury.' You must survive at least 7 full days from the injury. Claim on SGLV 8600; appeal on SGLV 8600A.
items.how: VA, 'Traumatic Injury Protection (TSGLI)', va.gov
items.hack: The payment is driven by the SCHEDULED LOSS, not the injury — the date that matters is when the loss of function occurred, and it has 730 days to appear. A veteran whose loss worsened into a qualifying category months after the accident still has a claim.
items.deadline: The scheduled loss must occur within 730 days of the traumatic injury

items.title: Retroactive TSGLI: Oct 7, 2001 to Nov 30, 2005, and the operation requirement is gone
items.who: Veterans injured between October 7, 2001 and November 30, 2005
items.value: Retroactive TSGLI applies to injuries between 'October 7, 2001, and November 30, 2005' for those who meet the qualifications. The previous requirement limiting this to specific military operations has been removed.
items.how: VA, 'Traumatic Injury Protection (TSGLI)' — retroactive coverage, va.gov
items.hack: Removing the operation requirement reopened thousands of claims. A veteran injured stateside in 2003 — a vehicle accident, a training injury — is now in scope where they were previously excluded for not being in OEF/OIF. If the injury falls in that window, file and let the branch office rule.
items.deadline: No stated filing deadline for the retroactive window — file now

items.title: FSGLI: $100,000 spouse maximum, capped by the member's own SGLI; $10,000 free for each child
items.who: Spouses and dependent children of service members with SGLI
items.value: 'Up to a maximum of $100,000 of coverage for you as a spouse, not to exceed your service member's SGLI coverage.' '$10,000 for each dependent child. Dependent children get free coverage.' Child coverage runs until the child is 18, with extensions for full-time students through age 22 and for permanently disabled children.
items.how: VA, 'Family Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance (FSGLI)', va.gov
items.hack: A member who reduced their own SGLI below $100,000 silently capped their spouse's coverage at the same figure. If spouse coverage is the goal, the member's SGLI has to be at least as high. Child coverage is free — there is no reason not to have it on file.
items.deadline: None

items.title: FSGLI spouse premiums are age-banded and they bite after 50
items.who: Military spouses covered under FSGLI
items.value: Monthly premium ranges by spouse age band: under 35, $0.40–$4.00; 35–39, $0.47–$4.70; 40–44, $0.62–$6.20; 45–49, $0.85–$8.50; 50–54, $1.35–$13.50; 55–59, $2.30–$23.00; 60+, $4.00–$40.00. Rates vary by the coverage amount chosen within each band.
items.how: VA, 'Family Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance (FSGLI)' — premium rate tables, va.gov
items.hack: $4.00 a month at 34 becomes $40.00 at 60 for the same $100,000 — a tenfold rise. A healthy spouse in their 30s or 40s should price a 20- or 30-year level term policy against the FSGLI band schedule; commercial term usually wins outright and does not reprice every five years.
items.deadline: Premiums step up at each band boundary

items.title: FSGLI conversion: 120 days, and only to a permanent policy
items.who: Spouses losing FSGLI through the member's separation, divorce or death
items.value: Conversion rights exist 'within 120 days from the date of your service member's' separation, divorce or death. The spouse may 'convert spousal FSGLI coverage to a permanent, individual insurance policy (such as whole life) within 120 days'. 'You can't convert to other types of policies — such as term, variable, or universal life insurance.'
items.how: VA, 'Family Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance (FSGLI)' — conversion, va.gov
items.hack: This right is use-it-or-lose-it and it is narrow: whole life only, from a participating company, inside 120 days. For a healthy spouse, commercial term is usually better value — the conversion right only matters if the spouse's health has changed and underwriting would now be a problem.
items.deadline: 120 days from separation, divorce or the member's death

items.title: VMLI: $200,000 of decreasing-term mortgage insurance, and the hard wall at 70
items.who: Veterans who received a Specially Adapted Housing (SAH) grant and hold a mortgage
items.value: 'Up to $200,000 in mortgage life insurance — paid directly to the bank or other lender.' Requires a severe service-connected disability, receipt of an SAH grant, title to the property, an active mortgage, and being under 70. 'You must apply for VMLI before your 70th birthday.' Apply on VA Form 29-8636. Coverage decreases as the mortgage balance falls and ends when the loan is paid off.
items.how: VA, 'Veterans' Mortgage Life Insurance (VMLI)', va.gov
items.hack: The age-70 wall is absolute and it is tied to the SAH grant, so the two benefits must be sequenced. If an SAH grant is in progress for a veteran in their late 60s, file the VMLI application (29-8636) the moment the grant is approved — a birthday closes this permanently.
items.deadline: Must apply before the 70th birthday

items.title: The USERRA five-year cumulative limit — and the nine categories that do not count against it
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Reservists and Guard members balancing military service against a civilian job
items.value: Service that does NOT count against the five-year limit, per 20 CFR 1002.103: service required beyond five years to complete an initial period of obligated service; service where the employee could not obtain release orders before the five years expired through no fault of their own; Guard and Reserve periodic training plus additional training certified as necessary for professional development or skill training; service under involuntary active-duty orders (twelve distinct statutory citations, covering retiree recall, wartime activation, captive status, national emergencies, operational missions and critical personnel retention); service ordered or retained due to 'a war or national emergency declared by the President or the Congress'; service supporting 'an operational mission for which personnel have been ordered to active duty'; service ordered for 'a critical mission or requirement of the uniformed services'; Guard service responding to 'invasion, danger of invasion, rebellion, danger of rebellion, insurrection'; and service performed 'to mitigate economic harm' where the employer violated its reemployment obligations.
items.how: 20 CFR 1002.99 and 20 CFR 1002.103 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: In practice almost nothing a modern reservist does counts toward the five years. Annual training, drills, mobilisations under a declared national emergency and operational-mission activations are all excluded. If an employer claims you have 'used up' USERRA, make them identify which service was both voluntary and outside every category in 1002.103.
items.deadline: None — but keep orders for every period, because you may have to prove the exception

items.title: USERRA advance notice: required, but with real exceptions
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Any employee leaving a civilian job for uniformed service
items.value: 20 CFR 1002.85 requires the employee to notify the employer of pending uniformed service. 20 CFR 1002.86 provides exceptions where notice is impossible or is prevented by military necessity.
items.how: 20 CFR 1002.85 and 1002.86 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: Notice need not be written and need not come from the employee personally — but give it in writing anyway, dated, and keep a copy. The notice document is the single most useful piece of paper in any later USERRA dispute, because it fixes the start of the protected absence.
items.deadline: Before departure, unless an exception in 1002.86 applies

items.title: The three USERRA return deadlines, quoted from 20 CFR 1002.115
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Service members returning to a civilian employer
items.value: Service of less than 31 days (or a fitness examination): 'the employee must report back to the employer not later than the beginning of the first full regularly-scheduled work period.' Service of 31–180 days: 'he or she must submit an application for reemployment (written or verbal) with the employer not later than 14 days.' Service of more than 180 days: 'he or she must submit an application for reemployment (written or verbal) not later than 90 days after completing service.'
items.how: 20 CFR 1002.115 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: The application may be verbal — but make it written, dated and delivered to a named person. These are the only hard clocks USERRA puts on the employee, and missing one shifts you out of automatic reinstatement and into the employer's ordinary disciplinary rules.
items.deadline: Next work period (<31 days); 14 days (31–180 days); 90 days (>180 days)

items.title: After 30 days of service the employer may demand documentation — and 20 CFR 1002.121 limits it to three things
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Returning service members asked to prove their entitlement to reemployment
items.value: 'Yes, if the period of service exceeded 30 days and if requested by the employer to do so... he or she must, upon the request of the employer, provide documentation to establish that: (a) The reemployment application is timely; (b) The employee has not exceeded the five-year limit on the duration of service (subject to the exceptions listed at § 1002.103); and, (c) The employee's separation or dismissal from service was not disqualifying.'
items.how: 20 CFR 1002.121 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: Three facts, and that is all. An employer cannot condition reemployment on a medical examination, a fitness-for-duty clearance, a new application, or an interview. If they ask for more than timeliness, the five-year count and a non-disqualifying separation, they are outside the regulation.
items.deadline: On the employer's request, after service exceeding 30 days

items.title: The escalator principle, quoted: the job you WOULD have had, not the job you left
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Every returning service member — this is the most valuable USERRA rule
items.value: 'The employee is entitled to reemployment in the job position that he or she would have attained with reasonable certainty if not for the absence due to uniformed service.' This 'escalator position' reflects the pay, benefits, seniority and job perquisites the member would have obtained — and can also run downward through layoffs, transfers or demotions that would have hit them anyway.
items.how: 20 CFR 1002.191 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: Reinstatement to the same job is often a USERRA violation. If two scheduled step increases, an automatic promotion and a shift differential would have landed during a 14-month mobilisation, the escalator position includes all three. Reconstruct the pay history of a peer who stayed, and make the employer explain any gap.
items.deadline: Assert it at reinstatement, before you accept a position and a rate

items.title: The escalator covers seniority, status and rate of pay — including a makeup examination for a missed promotion
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Returning members whose promotion depended on a test or review they missed
items.value: The reemployment position includes 'the seniority, status, and rate of pay that an employee would ordinarily have attained in that position given his or her job history.' The section also addresses makeup examination procedures for promotions missed during service.
items.how: 20 CFR 1002.193 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: Ask for the makeup examination explicitly and in writing. If a promotion board, a certification test or a time-in-grade review passed during the deployment, USERRA contemplates giving you the shot — and if you pass, the promotion is backdated into the escalator position with the pay that goes with it.
items.deadline: Raise it at reinstatement

items.title: USERRA health coverage: 24 months of continuation, quoted from 20 CFR 1002.164
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Service members and their families losing employer health coverage during a mobilisation
items.value: The plan must allow continuation for 'the lesser of: (1) The 24-month period beginning on the date on which the employee's absence for the purpose of performing service begins; or, (2) The period beginning on the date on which the employee's absence for the purpose of performing service begins, and ending on the date on which he or she fails to return from service or apply for a position of employment.'
items.how: 20 CFR 1002.164 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: 24 months beats COBRA's 18. And note the second limb: the continuation right ends if you fail to return or apply for reemployment on time — so the 1002.115 deadlines protect the family's health coverage, not just the job.
items.deadline: Up to 24 months from the start of the service absence; ends early if you miss the reemployment deadline

items.title: The USERRA health premium cap: 102% for 31+ days, and the regular employee share for 30 days or fewer
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Employees continuing employer health coverage during uniformed service
items.value: For service of 30 or fewer days, the employee 'cannot be required to pay more than the regular employee share, if any, for health plan coverage.' For service of 31 or more days, the employee 'may be required to pay no more than 102% of the full premium under the plan, which represents the employer's share plus the employee's share, plus 2% for administrative costs.'
items.how: 20 CFR 1002.166 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: A two-week annual training costs you nothing extra — the regular payroll deduction only. Employers who bill the full premium for a short drill period are plainly wrong, and the 30-day boundary is the line to point at.
items.deadline: Applies throughout the service absence

items.title: Filing a USERRA complaint with DOL VETS — and the 1-866 number that starts it
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Service members and veterans whose reemployment or employment rights were violated
items.value: VETS has representatives in every state and 'developed an online system that allows USERRA claimants to submit claims electronically.' DOL also maintains the 'USERRA Advisor' self-assessment tool at webapps.dol.gov/elaws/userra.htm. The VETS contact number is 1-866-237-0275. DOL's guidance is to attempt informal resolution with the employer, then file a formal complaint with VETS.
items.how: DOL VETS, 'Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act' and 'File a Claim' pages, dol.gov
items.hack: Run the USERRA Advisor first and print the result — it frames your complaint in the statute's own terms and shortens the investigator's work. Then file. Informal resolution with the employer is encouraged but is not a prerequisite, so do not let an employer stall you into a deadline problem.
items.deadline: USERRA has no statute of limitations for the reemployment claim itself; file as early as possible

items.title: After the VETS investigation: referral, enforcement, and the private right of action
items.org: DOL Veterans' Employment and Training Service
items.who: Claimants whose VETS complaint does not resolve
items.value: 20 CFR 1002.288 sets out the filing procedures for USERRA complaints; 1002.289–1002.292 cover the VETS investigation and referral authority; and 1002.303–1002.314 cover the enforcement options against state and private employers.
items.how: 20 CFR part 1002, subpart F — ecfr.gov
items.hack: Read 1002.303–1002.314 before you decide to wait on VETS. USERRA preserves a private right of action — you are not required to exhaust the administrative route, and a claimant with counsel and a clear escalator-pay claim sometimes moves faster in court than through referral.
items.deadline: No USERRA statute of limitations; but any contractual or state-law claim riding alongside it will have one

items.title: HUD-VASH is two benefits bolted together — and the case management has no expiry
items.who: Veterans experiencing homelessness with complex needs requiring ongoing case management
items.value: The program 'combines: A Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) from HUD that helps pay rent for qualifying housing' with 'VA case management and supportive services that help Veterans remain successfully housed.' The voucher is used with a 'privately owned apartment or home from a landlord who accepts vouchers.' 'Every participant is paired with a trained VA case manager' and that support 'continues for as long as needed.'
items.how: VA Homeless Programs, 'HUD-VASH', department.va.gov
items.hack: 'As long as needed' is the part to hold onto. HUD-VASH case management is not a 90-day or 12-month program — a veteran who stabilises and then destabilises years later is still inside it. If a case manager signals graduation before the veteran is ready, that is a local decision, not a program rule.
items.deadline: None once enrolled

items.title: HUD-VASH scale: over 95,000 veterans housed right now, nearly 250,000 since 2008
items.who: Veterans and advocates assessing whether HUD-VASH is realistic in their area
items.value: As of March 2026, 'more than 95,000 formerly homeless Veterans were living in homes through HUD-VASH,' with nearly 250,000 veterans served since 2008.
items.how: VA Homeless Programs, 'HUD-VASH', department.va.gov
items.hack: This is the largest permanent supportive housing program for any population in the country. The bottleneck is almost never voucher availability — it is landlord acceptance. Advocates who recruit landlords move veterans faster than advocates who chase vouchers.
items.deadline: None

items.title: The National Call Center for Homeless Veterans: 877-424-3838, free, confidential, 24/7
items.who: Veterans at risk of or experiencing homelessness, their families, and community providers
items.value: VA directs homeless veterans to the National Call Center for Homeless Veterans at 877-424-3838, noting it is 'free, confidential, and available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.'
items.how: VA Homeless Programs, 'HUD-VASH' page, department.va.gov
items.hack: This is the front door to every program in this chapter — HUD-VASH, SSVF and GPD all run through local coordination that the call centre can reach. One call at 2 a.m. beats three weeks of trying to find the right coordinator by email.
items.deadline: None — call before the eviction, not after

items.title: SSVF 'very low-income' is defined: 50 percent of area median income
items.who: Veteran families seeking SSVF help
items.value: A 'very low-income veteran family' is one whose 'annual income, as determined in accordance with 24 CFR 5.609, does not exceed 50 percent of the median income for an area or community.'
items.how: 38 CFR 62.2, definition of 'Very low-income veteran family' — ecfr.gov
items.hack: 50% of AMI in a high-cost metro is a surprisingly high dollar figure — in many California counties a household earning over $60,000 still qualifies. Veterans self-screen out of SSVF constantly because they assume 'very low-income' means destitute. Look up your county's figure before you rule yourself out.
items.deadline: Income is tested at entry

items.title: SSVF eligibility has three doors — including one for a family that left housing within the last 90 days
items.who: Veteran families who are homeless or about to be
items.value: An eligible participant is a very low-income veteran family occupying permanent housing who is: residing in permanent housing and at risk of homelessness but for the grantee's assistance; currently homeless (lacking a fixed residence) and at risk of remaining so without assistance; or has recently exited permanent housing within 90 days while seeking responsive housing.
items.how: 38 CFR 62.11, Eligible participants — ecfr.gov
items.hack: The 90-day exit door is the one advocates forget. A family that already lost the apartment and is in a motel or a relative's spare room is squarely eligible — SSVF is not limited to people still in a lease or already literally on the street.
items.deadline: The third door closes 90 days after exiting permanent housing

items.title: SSVF rental assistance limits: 6 months in any 12, 10 months in any 24 — and more if extremely low-income
items.who: Veteran families receiving SSVF temporary financial assistance for rent
items.value: Rental assistance is capped at a 'maximum of 10 months during a 2-year period' and a participant 'cannot receive rental assistance for more than 6 months in any 12-month period.' For extremely low-income participants the limits rise to 9 months in any 12 and 12 months in any 2 years.
items.how: 38 CFR 62.34, Temporary financial assistance — ecfr.gov
items.hack: The extremely-low-income tier buys three extra months inside a single year. If a household is near that threshold, documenting income accurately at intake is worth months of rent — ask the grantee which tier they placed you in and on what income figure.
items.deadline: 6 months per 12 (9 if extremely low-income); 10 months per 24 (12 if extremely low-income)

items.title: SSVF utility assistance runs on the same clock as rent
items.who: Veteran families facing utility shutoff
items.value: Utility payments are capped at a 'maximum of 10 months during a 2-year period' and a participant 'cannot receive payments for utilities for more than 6 months in any 12-month period.'
items.how: 38 CFR 62.34 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: Rent and utility months are counted separately, so a family can draw both. Sequence them: use SSVF for utilities while a LIHEAP or state energy-assistance application is pending, and save the rent months for the harder gap.
items.deadline: 6 months per 12; 10 months per 24

items.title: SSVF deposits once every 2 years, moving costs once every 3
items.who: Veteran families moving into new housing with SSVF help
items.value: Security deposits and utility deposits: a 'maximum of one time in every 2-year period.' Moving costs: a 'maximum of one time in every 3-year period.'
items.how: 38 CFR 62.34 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: These are one-shot items with long reset clocks, so do not spend them on a marginal unit. If a lease looks shaky, it is worth waiting two weeks for a better one rather than burning the deposit allowance and then needing it again in six months.
items.deadline: One deposit per 2 years; one move per 3 years

items.title: SSVF general housing stability assistance: $1,800 per participant per 2 years
items.who: Veteran families with housing-related costs that are not rent, utilities or deposits
items.value: General housing stability assistance is capped at '$1,800, per participant during any 2-year period.'
items.how: 38 CFR 62.34 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: This is the flexible pot — the one that covers the arrears, the fees and the odd costs that actually block a lease. Ask the grantee specifically for 'general housing stability assistance' by name; it is a distinct line in the regulation with its own cap, separate from rent and deposits.
items.deadline: $1,800 per participant per 2-year period

items.title: SSVF pays up to $1,200 of car repairs in 3 years — the benefit nobody asks for
items.who: Working veteran families whose vehicle failure threatens their housing or job
items.value: Emergency housing assistance includes car repairs up to '$1,200 during a 3-year period.'
items.how: 38 CFR 62.34 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: A $900 transmission repair is the difference between keeping a job and losing the apartment, and SSVF will pay it. Almost no one asks, because nothing about the program's name suggests car repair. Ask by the regulation's own words.
items.deadline: $1,200 per 3-year period

items.title: SSVF child care: 6 months in 12, 10 months in 24
items.who: Veteran parents whose child care costs block work or housing stability
items.value: Child care is limited to '6 months in a 12-month period, and 10 months during a 2-year period' — rising to 9 months in 12 and 12 months in 24 for extremely low-income participants.
items.how: 38 CFR 62.34 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: Child care is on the SSVF menu and it runs on the same tiered clock as rent. For a single-parent veteran household, this is often the item that makes employment possible — and therefore the item that makes the rent sustainable after the SSVF months run out.
items.deadline: 6 months per 12 (9 if extremely low-income); 10 months per 24 (12 if extremely low-income)

items.title: How the GPD per diem is actually computed — and why it is capped by a nursing-home rate
items.who: Organisations operating or considering a Grant and Per Diem program; veterans assessing bed availability
items.value: The per diem payment is 'the lesser of' (1) the daily cost of care estimated by the recipient minus other income sources, or (2) 'the current VA state home program per diem rate for domiciliary care, as set by the Secretary' under 38 U.S.C. 1741(a)(1). Service centres receive one-eighth of the lesser of those amounts per hour, capped at 8 hours daily.
items.how: 38 CFR 61.33 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: The GPD rate is pegged to the State Home domiciliary rate, which is set for an entirely different program. That peg is why GPD bed supply tightens whenever operating costs outrun the State Home rate — and why the 200% waiver described on VA's rate page exists at all.
items.deadline: Per diem may be paid retroactively up to 3 days before approval

items.title: Current GPD per diem rates, effective January 1, 2026
items.who: GPD grantees and veterans in or seeking transitional housing
items.value: Effective January 1, 2026: State Home Domiciliary rate $64.19; Per Diem Only $85.37 per day; Transition in Place (TIP) $96.29 per day; Special Need $128.38 per day; Service Center $10.67 per hour. Grantees have 'the option to apply for a waiver of per diem of up to 200% of the State Home Rate Maximum,' which takes TIP and Per Diem Only to $128.38 and the Service Center rate to $16.05 per hour.
items.how: VA Homeless Programs, 'Per Diem Rate Information' (Grant and Per Diem), department.va.gov
items.hack: Transition in Place pays more than Per Diem Only for a reason: the veteran keeps the unit and the provider steps back. For a veteran who wants to stay put rather than move again at the end of transitional housing, ask specifically whether the local grantee runs a TIP model.
items.deadline: Rates effective January 1, 2026

items.title: GPD capital grants cover 65% — and the grantee has to find the other 35%
items.who: Nonprofits and public agencies applying for Grant and Per Diem capital funding
items.value: Capital grants cover up to 65% of the project and fund construction of new supportive housing or service centres, acquisition of existing structures, renovation, and procurement of vans. Recipients must provide 35% matching funds in non-federal dollars; matching funds must be documented via signed letters, cannot be conditional, and must reduce total project expenditures.
items.hack: The 35% non-federal match, unconditional and documented in signed letters, is what kills most GPD capital applications. Line up the match in writing before the NOFO opens — a conditional pledge is explicitly not countable.
items.deadline: Match must be documented and unconditional at application

items.title: GPD Special Need grants: five named populations, paid at up to double the standard rate
items.who: Women veterans, frail elderly, terminally ill, chronically mentally ill veterans, and veterans caring for minor dependents
items.value: Special Need programs must serve one or more of: women; frail elderly; terminally ill; chronically mentally ill; or individuals with minor dependents in their care. The Special Need per diem is capped at 'two times the current VA State Home Program per diem rate for domiciliary care' — $128.38 per day effective January 1, 2026.
items.how: 38 CFR 61.40 — ecfr.gov; rate from VA's Per Diem Rate Information page
items.hack: 'Individuals with minor dependents in their care' is the category that unlocks family-capable transitional housing, which is otherwise almost nonexistent. A homeless veteran with children should be asked about Special Need beds by name — the standard GPD bed usually cannot take the children.
items.deadline: None

items.title: GPD absence rules: 72 consecutive hours, or 7 days for a hospitalisation
items.who: Veterans in GPD transitional housing who need to be away, and the providers billing for them
items.value: A maximum of 72 consecutive hours of per diem may be paid during a veteran's absence, extending to 7 days for inpatient hospitalisation. No duplicate payment is allowed where the veteran receives both housing and services from the same provider. Per diem may be paid retroactively up to 3 days before approval.
items.how: 38 CFR 61.33 — ecfr.gov
items.hack: This is why a GPD bed can disappear during a hospital stay longer than a week — the provider stops being paid. If an inpatient admission is going to run past 7 days, raise bed-holding with the provider and the VA liaison on day one, not on discharge day.
items.deadline: 72 consecutive hours; 7 days for inpatient hospitalisation

items.title: GPD Case Management grants exist separately — for veterans already housed
items.who: Veterans who have moved from homelessness into permanent housing and need help keeping it
items.value: The program supports 'Case Management grants to support permanent housing retention for Veterans who were previously homeless' — distinct from the transitional housing grants. Program goals are 'residential stability, enhance their skill levels and income, and gain greater self-determination.'
items.how: VA Homeless Programs, 'Grant and Per Diem' program page, department.va.gov
items.hack: GPD is widely assumed to be beds only. The Case Management grant follows the veteran into permanent housing, which makes it the bridge between a GPD exit and a tenancy that actually holds. Ask the grantee whether they hold a GPD Case Management grant as well as a housing grant.
items.deadline: None

items.title: DIC base rate: $1,699.36 a month, tax free, effective December 1, 2025
items.who: Surviving spouses of veterans who died of a service-connected condition or while on active duty
items.value: $1,699.36 monthly for a surviving spouse, effective December 1, 2025.
items.how: VA, 'Current VA D.I.C. rates for spouses and dependents' — effective December 1, 2025, va.gov
items.hack: This is tax-free income. For mortgage qualifying purposes it grosses up — at a 25% gross-up that is roughly $2,124 of qualifying income a month, which materially changes what a surviving spouse can buy with a VA loan.
items.deadline: Rates change each December 1 with the COLA

items.title: DIC add-ons: $421.00 per child under 18, and the same figure again for Aid and Attendance
items.who: Surviving spouses with dependent children, or with care needs of their own
items.value: Effective December 1, 2025: $421.00 added monthly for each dependent child under 18; $421.00 added for a spouse who has a disability and needs help with regular daily activities (Aid and Attendance); $197.22 added for a spouse who cannot leave the house due to a disability (Housebound).
items.how: VA, 'Current VA D.I.C. rates for spouses and dependents' — added amounts, va.gov
items.hack: Aid and Attendance and Housebound are the two most under-claimed DIC add-ons, because they are about the SURVIVOR's health, not the veteran's. A widow who needs help bathing or dressing should be screened for A&A — it is $5,052 a year, tax free, and it is not automatic.
items.deadline: Rates change each December 1; A&A and Housebound require a separate claim with medical evidence

items.title: The DIC eight-year provision: $360.85 extra, and BOTH conditions must hold for the same eight years
items.who: Surviving spouses of veterans who were totally disabled for the eight years before death
items.value: $360.85 added monthly when 'The Veteran had a VA disability rating of totally disabling (including for individual unemployability) for at least the 8 full years leading up to their death, and You were married to the Veteran for those same 8 years.'
items.how: VA, 'Current VA D.I.C. rates for spouses and dependents' — eight-year provision, va.gov
items.hack: The marriage must overlap the same eight years — an eight-year TDIU rating plus a six-year marriage does not qualify. Also note 'including for individual unemployability': TDIU counts as totally disabling for this provision, which is the part most often missed.
items.deadline: Both the 8-year rating and the 8-year marriage must run to the date of death

items.title: The DIC transitional benefit: $359.00 a month for the first two years, if there are children
items.who: Surviving spouses with dependent children in the first two years after the veteran's death
items.value: $359.00 added monthly for the first 2 years after the veteran's death, for surviving spouses with dependent children.
items.how: VA, 'Current VA D.I.C. rates for spouses and dependents' — transitional benefit, va.gov
items.hack: This is a cliff, not a taper — it stops dead at the two-year mark. Build the household budget around life AFTER the transitional benefit from the start, because $359 a month vanishing in month 25 wrecks a budget built on month 1.
items.deadline: Ends 2 years after the veteran's death

items.title: DIC eligibility: the three death circumstances, in VA's words
items.who: Anyone assessing whether a surviving spouse has a DIC claim
items.value: One of these must apply: 'The service member died while on active duty, active duty for training, or inactive-duty training'; 'The Veteran died from a service-connected illness or injury'; or 'The Veteran didn't die from a service-connected illness or injury, but was eligible to receive VA compensation for a service-connected disability rated as totally disabling for a certain period of time.'
items.how: VA, 'Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (D.I.C.)' — eligibility, va.gov
items.hack: The third circumstance is the one families never pursue. Death from an unrelated cause — a car accident, cancer with no service link — still produces DIC if the veteran held a total rating long enough. Do not let 'he didn't die of his service-connected condition' end the conversation.
items.deadline: No filing deadline, but retroactivity depends on the filing date — file promptly

items.title: The DIC marriage test: 15 years, 1 year, or a child — any one of the three
items.who: Surviving spouses whose marriage was short or late
items.value: The spouse must meet ONE of: 'You married the Veteran or service member within 15 years of their discharge from the period of military service during which the qualifying illness or injury started or got worse'; 'You were married to the Veteran or service member for at least 1 year'; or 'You had a child with the Veteran or service member.'
items.how: VA, 'Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (D.I.C.)' — eligibility, va.gov
items.hack: Any one of the three is enough. A marriage of eleven months with a child together qualifies. A marriage entered thirty years after discharge qualifies if it lasted a year. Spouses rule themselves out on the 15-year clause without reading the two alternatives.
items.deadline: Tested as at the date of death

items.title: The three total-rating durations that open DIC on a non-service-connected death
items.who: Surviving spouses of veterans who held a total rating and died of something else
items.value: The veteran must have held the totally disabling rating: 'For at least 10 years before their death,' OR 'Since their release from active duty and for at least 5 years immediately before their death,' OR 'For at least 1 year before their death if they were a former prisoner of war who died after September 30, 1999.'
items.how: VA, 'Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (D.I.C.)' — eligibility, va.gov
items.hack: Three separate clocks, and the 5-year one is the sleeper: a veteran rated total straight out of service needs only five years, not ten. The former-POW route needs just one year. Check the rating history and the effective dates before conceding that the ten-year rule defeats the claim — and if an earlier effective date is arguable, a CUE or earlier-effective-date claim can create DIC eligibility retroactively.
items.deadline: Measured to the date of death

items.title: DIC after remarriage: age 57 from Dec 16 2003, and age 55 from Jan 5 2021
items.who: Surviving spouses who remarried, or who are considering it
items.value: A remarried surviving spouse remains eligible if they 'Remarried on or after December 16, 2003, and were 57 or older at remarriage' OR 'Remarried on or after January 5, 2021, and you were 55 years of age or older.'
items.how: VA, 'Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (D.I.C.)' — remarriage rules, va.gov
items.hack: The threshold dropped from 57 to 55 for remarriages on or after January 5, 2021. A spouse who delayed a wedding for years to protect DIC under the old rule should re-check the date — and anyone who remarried at 55 or 56 after that date and was told they lost DIC was told wrong.
items.deadline: The age test is applied at the date of remarriage

items.title: DIC for a surviving child: unmarried, not on the spouse's award, under 18 or under 23 in school
items.who: Children of veterans who died of a service-connected condition
items.value: A child qualifies if ALL apply: 'You aren't married'; 'You aren't included on the surviving spouse's compensation'; and 'You're under the age of 18 (or under the age of 23 if attending school).'
items.how: VA, 'Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (D.I.C.)' — surviving child eligibility, va.gov
items.hack: A child drawing as an add-on to the spouse's DIC cannot also draw as a child in their own right. But when the spouse's award ends — or where there is no eligible spouse — the child becomes a direct claimant. Re-examine the file at 18 and again at any change in the spouse's status.
items.deadline: Age 18, or 23 if attending school

items.title: Parents' DIC exists, it is income-tested, and the maximum is $842 a month
items.who: Surviving parents of veterans who died of a service-connected condition — the most forgotten survivor benefit
items.value: Effective December 1, 2025: sole surviving parent (unmarried, or remarried and living with a spouse) — maximum $842 monthly, with payment reducing to zero somewhere between $11,263 and $26,663 of annual income depending on the living situation. Both parents living apart — maximum $611. Both parents living together — maximum $576. Aid and Attendance adds $458 monthly.
items.how: VA, 'Current D.I.C. rates for parents' — effective December 1, 2025, va.gov
items.hack: Parents' DIC is the benefit nobody tells parents about. A low-income widowed mother of a service member killed on active duty can draw $842 a month tax free, plus $458 more if she needs Aid and Attendance — $15,600 a year. Screen every Gold Star parent for it.
items.deadline: Rates change each December 1; income is reported annually

items.title: The Parents' DIC sliding scale: 8 cents off for every dollar of income
items.who: Surviving parents near the income thresholds
items.value: Payments decrease by $0.08 for each dollar of income above the specified thresholds. 'Your yearly income is how much money you earn during 1 calendar year (January 1 to December 31).' Benefits are tax-exempt: 'you won't have to pay any taxes on your payments for this benefit.'
items.how: VA, 'Current D.I.C. rates for parents' — income rules, va.gov
items.hack: An 8% marginal reduction is gentle. Parents often assume any income disqualifies them — in fact a parent earning well above the bottom threshold still collects a reduced, tax-free benefit. Apply and let VA compute it rather than self-screening out.
items.deadline: Income is measured on the calendar year

items.title: Survivors Pension: the veteran's service test, era by era
items.who: Low-income surviving spouses and children of wartime veterans
items.value: The deceased veteran must meet at least one of: 'entered active duty on or before September 7, 1980, and served at least 90 days on active' duty with at least 1 day during a covered wartime period; 'entered active duty after September 7, 1980, and served at least 24 months' or the full ordered period, with wartime service; or was an officer who started active duty after October 16, 1981 with no prior 24-month service.
items.how: VA, 'Survivors Pension', va.gov
